TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1950 CONGRESS OF THE UNITED STATES, UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS, AND HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS,  

The committees met in joint session, pursuant to notice, at 10:30 a. m., in the caucus room, room 318, Senate Office Building, Senator 

Tom Connally presiding. 

Present: Senators Connally, George, Thomas of Utah, Tydings, 

Green, McMahon, Fulbright, Wiley, Smith of New Jersey, and Lodge; 

Representatives Kee, Richards, Gordon, Carnahan, Zablocki, Ribicoff, Burleson, Eaton, Vorys, Mrs. Bolton, Smith of Wisconsin, Merrow, and Javits. 

Senator CONNALLY. The committees will please come to order.

The Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate, and the Foreign 

Affairs Committee of the House are meeting today for the purpose of hearing opening testimony on the ECA authorization bill. 

As you know, this is probably the most stupendous undertaking of its kind in history, a tremendous responsibility, and carries with it a tremendous burden on the people of the United States. 

Our purpose, of course, is to be of aid in the rebuilding of Europe. 

That must require, not only our funds, but cooperation and willingness, and there ought to be the enthusiastic support and cooperation of the beneficiaries of this plan.

It is altogether likely that the authorization will be cut or reduced from what it has heretofore been. Since it is anticipated that the plan will terminate in 1952, it seems to me that it is entirely appropriate that we begin to cut back, with a view of teaching, or suggesting to the Europeans that they accommodate their economy to what they may expect, rather than to go on in high through the red lights. 

Judge Kee, the chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the House, is here and I will be glad to invite him to make any observation he cares to in initiating these hearings. 

Mr. KEE. The only observation that I will make at this time is to express the hope that by Senator Connally's suggestion that the authorization should be cut in amount, he did not mean to suggest that it should be cut below the amount that the ECA Administrator has determined to be necessary for the purposes of the ECA program. 

That is all; thank you.

Senator CONNALLY. Very well, Judge. 

1

The Senator from Texas didn't mean to observe the exact figure; but the authorization, of course, must be large enough to cover the inevitable expenditures. However, the appropriation itself, which will follow, will actually determine the amount of money, which must be within the authorization and not exceed it. (The bill under consideration, without number as yet, is as follows:) [Committee print, February 21, 1950]

A BILL To amend the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948, as amended Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That section 111 of such Act is hereby amended by adding at the end thereof the following new subsection: "(d) The Administrator is authorized to transfer funds directly to any central institution or other organization formed to further the purposes of this Act by two or more participating countries, or to any participating country or countries in connection with the operations of such institution or organization, to be used on terms and conditions specified by the Administrator, in order to facilitate the development of transferability of European currencies, or to promote the liberalization of trade by participating countries with one another and with other countries."

SEC. 2. (a) Section 114 (c) of such Act is hereby amended in the following 

(1) By striking out the period at the end of the first sentence and inserting in lieu thereof a colon and the following: Provided further, That, in addition to the amount heretofore authorized and appropriated, there are hereby authorized to be appropriated for carrying out the provisions and accomplishing the purposes of this title not to exceed $2,950,000,000 for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1951: Provided further, That, in addition to the foregoing, any balance unobligated as of June 30, 1950, or subsequently released from obligation, of funds appropriated for carrying out and accomplishing the purposes of this title for any period ending on or prior to that date is hereby authorized to be made available for obligation through the fiscal year ending June 30, 1951, and to be transferred to and consolidated with any appropriations for carrying out and accomplishing the purposes of this title for said fiscal year." 

(2) By amending the last sentence of such section 114 (c) to read as follows: 

"The authorizations in this title are limited to the period ending June 30, 1951, in order that the Congress may pass on any subsequent authorizations." (b) Section 114 of such Act is hereby further amended by adding at the end thereof the following new subsection: 

"(h) of the amounts authorized to be appropriated for carrying out the provisions and accomplishing the purposes of this title and allocated for assistance to Germany the President may transfer such amounts as he deems appropriate to any department or agency which may be used without regard to other provisions of this title as the President may specify, for expenses not otherwise provided for, necessary to enable the President to meet the responsibilities and obligations of the United States in connection with the rehabilitation of occupied areas of Germany, including such minimum supplies for the civilian population of such areas as may be essential to prevent starvation, disease, or unrest prejudicial to the objectives sought to be accomplished, and the cost of such supplies, commodities, equipment, and services as may be essential to carry out the purposes of this subsection: Provided, That any such funds which are so transferred may be expended either under the authority contained in this subsection or under any provisions of law applicable to the department or agency to which so transferred and not inconsistent herewith: Provided further, That such part, as may be agreed upon by the Secretary of State and the Administrator for Economic Cooperation, of the local currency deposited or to be deposited by Germany under the bilateral agreement entered into by the Government of the United States and the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany on the 15th day of December 1949, or any supplementary or succeeding agreement which shall not substantially alter the basic obligations of either party in this respect, shall be deposited into the GARIOA Special Account under the terms and conditions contained in article V of the afore-mentioned bilateral agreement, and shall be available without reimbursement from any appropriation to the Department of State in such quantities and under such terms and

conditions as may be determined by the Secretary of State after consultation with the Administrator for Economic Cooperation, for carrying out the responsibilities of the United States in the occupation of Germany, including any contingencies which may arise in connection therewith." 

SEC. 3. Section 115 of such Act is hereby further amended by adding a new subsection as follows: 

"(j) The Administrator shall utilize such amounts of the local currency allocated pursuant to subsection (h) as may be necessary, to give full and continuous publicity through the press, radio, and all other available media, so as to inform the peoples of the participating countries regarding the assistance, including its purpose, source, and character, furnished by the American taxpayer." 

Senator CONNALLY. I might explain that there will be no questions of the witnesses appearing before us at the present time. Each committee, after the initial appearance, will conduct its own hearing, even as to these two that testify this morning, the Secretary of State and 

Mr. Hoffman.

It has been agreed that the first witness should be Mr. Hoffman. 

Mr. Hoffman, we are glad to greet you.

STATEMENT OF PAUL G. HOFFMAN, ECONOMIC COOPERATION ADMINISTRATOR 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Senator Connally, Mr. Kee, and gentlemen.

The Congress, through Public Law 472, assigned to the Economic 

Cooperation Administration two major tasks. 

The first to help the free nations of western Europe achieve a degree of economic recovery by June 1952, which will permit them to function without extraordinary outside aid. 

The second, and I quote from the statute: "To encourage the unification of Europe," as an essential means of strengthening and sustaining that recovery.

European economic recovery and progress toward European unification buttress each other. Though each cannot be achieved with the same rapidity, they are mutually consistent. 

In the field of economic recovery, the conditions which had to be met first were those stemming directly from World War II. Europe's devasted economic machine desperately needed to be restored without delay. I do not hesitate to say that the accomplishments to date in this field go far beyond the most optimistic forecasts of 2 years ago. 

Western European unification is the related and longer-range objective on which the Congress rightly placed so much stress. In this field the ECA is dealing with economic and political conditions and difficulties of long standing for which no real corrective was achieved during all the years between the wars. propose to report to you on the progress-and the problems remaining to be resolved-affecting these central responsibilities which you assigned to us, and to request the necessary legislative authority for the third year of our operation.

The facts on western Europe's economic recovery are these: 

THE RECORD OF INCREASED INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION 

I use the word carefully when I say that what has been accomplished here is "spectacular." The recovery of industrial production, built almost literally from the ashes of World War II, has been a near miracle. The story can be told in just a few figures.

Despite the fact that western Europe has been through the most destructive war in history, industrial production as a whole has been raised a third higher than it was in 1947 when the Marshall plan took form, and is now well above prewar level. 

Remember, that it took western Europe 7 years to regain just the prewar level of industrial production after World War I. Today, after 2 years of ECA program, and less than 5 years after the end of World War II, in which the devastation was far greater than in 1914 to 1919, industrial production has not merely been lifted to the prewar level, but stands 20 percent above it. In these 2 years, hard-coal production has expanded 17 percent, steel 52 percent, electric power 21 percent, cement 58 percent, cotton yarn 31 percent. Thus are the sinews of production being restored and strengthened in western Europe.

THE RECORD OF INCREASED AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION 

When ECA started operation, millions of people in Europe were hungry. Today the menace of hunger in western Europe has passed. 

Agricultural production as a whole has been brought nearly to the level of prewar and, given favorable weather conditions, will reach the prewar level or exceed it during the present crop year. In the past 2 years, after the grave crop failures of 1947, total grain production rose 30 percent, sugar 40 percent, meat 16 percent, milk 19 percent, and fats and oils 19 percent.

But even these gains are not sufficient. The record of progress in raising agricultural production has not been as satisfactory as in raising industrial production. We and the participating nations must place even greater emphasis in this field in the coming year. Western 

Europe must make up for many of the agricultural imports it used to receive from eastern Europe and western Europe now has a 10 percent larger population than it had before the war. And lest anyone get the false idea that Europe's improved diet means anything more than a bare diet as a whole, let me mention another fact. Out of the 1938 gross income, $114,000,000,000 were spent for consumer needs. 

Last year, with 20,000,000 more people to feed and clothe, only $115,- 000,000,000 at comparable prices were spent for consumer needs. That means, of course, that practically all of the added income is going into capital assets. Western Europeans are not living in the lap of luxury at Uncle Sam's expense; far from it. 

PROSPECT OF FUTURE PRODUCTION GAINS 

I would like to make it quite clear that in our judgment the pace of further gains in industrial and agricultural production cannot be expected to match the spectacular results already accomplished. One reason is that many of the principal bottlenecks-in rail transportation, in coal production, in raw materials-have already been eliminated. Further increases in production will have to depend, in larger degree than before, on increased productivity on the farm and in the factory brought about by the introduction of better methods and more efficient practices. This is the reason we are placing such emphasis on the ECA technical assistance program.

THE RECORD OF INTERNAL FINANCIAL STABILITY AND CURRENCY ADJUSTMENT 

In the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948, the Congress recognized that the "creation and maintenance of internal financial stability" was indispensable to European recovery. With courageous efforts, involving self-restraint by the Europeans and especially organized labor, the governments have put their financial houses in much better order and financial stability is, in most of the countries, being well maintained. An end has been put to the rampant inflation of 1947-48. 

Prices are generally being held. The prospect for sustaining this financial stability, despite some new inflationary pressures from the currency devaluations of last fall, is definitely encouraging. 

The currency devaluations themselves were also a major step forward. By bringing European price levels closer into line with world prices they laid a foundation for moving ahead on expanding dollar earnings and necessary dollar savings. They also greatly improved the balance of payments within Europe. 

THE RECORD ON TRADE 

With increasing production and sounder financial conditions, western Europe's performance in trade has also strikingly improved. 

Total exports have risen 50 percent since 1947, and except for the allimportant dollar area, western Europe's payments are now about in balance. Intra-European trade has been restored almost to prewar levels. Dollar earnings are also rising, but there is a long way to go before the European dollar gap is closed.

THE PROBLEM OF CLOSING EUROPE'S DOLLAR GAP 

The evidence is abundant that the progress of western Europe in production and trade, in expanding productive capacity, in restoring internal financial stability, and in raising living standards, has been solid and significant. The foundation of a self-supporting recovery has been laid. But the Marshall plan countries have not reached and will not reach a position of real self-support until their dollar gap is brought into hand without the need for extraordinary outside assistance. 

Such technical phrases as "dollar gap" and "balance of payments deficits" may seem mysterious, but there is no mystery in the facts they describe. The very life of western Europe depends on maintaining a huge flow of food and raw material imports which for the most part are normally paid for by exporting manufactured goods. A very large share of the needed imports can come only from the United States and other areas requiring payment in dollars. 

Following World War II, western Europe was desperately short of the dollars it needed to buy the essential goods and services-food, raw materials, machines-to get her economy back on a functioning and healthy basis. At the same time, nondollar sources of supply in eastern Europe and southeast Asia had largely dried up. With production disrupted, Europe could earn only a mere fraction of its needed dollars and its reserves had been almost totally depleted by war. The United States stepped in and filled that dollar gap with loans and grants.

In the last 2 years, the dollar gap has been cut by almost 45 percentfrom 7.4 billion dollars in 1947 to slightly over $4,000,000,000 in 

1949-50. The urgent task ahead is further to reduce that gap to manageable proportions without reversing the processes of recovery or reviving the threat of social and political crisis so narrowly averted 

2 years ago.

That task is not merely closing Europe's dollar gap at any level of trade. The gap could be closed tomorrow if exports from the dollar area to Europe were reduced to what Europe can now earn. That would call for a reduction in exports of more than $3,000,000,000. The effect of such a drastic reduction would obviously mean catastrophe for Europe and severe dislocation of our own economy. 

I would like to emphasize that point; a stopping of dollar aid at this time would mean that there would be a $3,000,000,000 drop in exports from the dollar area to Europe. I repeat-that would mean catastrophe for Europe and severe dislocations for the United States. 

There are only two sound ways of closing Europe's dollar gap.

They are by reducing requirements for dollar imports through building up economical sources of supply in Europe itself and in other nondollar areas, and by increasing Europe's dollar earnings through direct and triangular trade. This means, of course, that we must sell less to and buy more from Europe. There is little appeal in such a program, but if we do not sell less and buy more, we must either continue our aid or see the European economy placed in grave danger. 

Bearing this in mind, with the ECA's full cooperation and support, aggressive campaigns are now under way in all European countries to develop replacements for imports from the dollar area and to expand exports to the dollar area.

It should be recognized that in certain commodities Europe's postwar dollar imports have been abnormally high. There is no reason, in normal times, for example, for Europe with its vast coal resources to import American coal; yet mining was so dislocated after the war that American exports of coal to the OEEC nations in 1947 had a value of approximately $675,000,000 in landed cost. Europe's postwar imports of grain, machinery, and many other items have also been abnormally high.

While the dollar-saving drive means that the United States will sell less to Europe in 1951 than in preceding years, and considerably less in 1952, the only limit to what America can sell to Europe is the dollars that Europe has available. American farmers and manufacturers will not take payment in pounds, francs, guilders, lire, marks, or drachma. Europe and the rest of the world are hungry for American goods. It is not lack of demand that holds down American exports-it is the problem of payment. 

In the matter of dollar earnings, it must be kept in mind that Europe can earn dollars only by selling goods and services directly to the United States or by selling its goods and services to another country which has already earned those dollars. In the final accounting, the 

United States is the only source of dollars. 

To help the OEEC countries increase their dollar earnings, ECA is setting up a staff of export trade counselors in Paris. ECA has also urged that appropriate incentives be offered to European exporters to encourage them to seek sales in dollar areas. Within the United States

we must more actively assist the European effort to earn dollars. It is our hope as a result of all these activities that sales of goods to the dollar areas may be increased within the next 2 years by several hundred million dollars.

The total increase in direct dollar earnings from the United States which must be achieved by the Europeans to bring the dollar gap to manageable proportions is approximately $1,000,000,000. In addition to increased sales of goods, it is anticipated that there can be substantially increased earnings from tourism and from invisibles. Beyond this billion dollars of earnings, it is the expectation that American investments in Europe may be stepped up considerably. 

ECA has been subjected to some criticism because of its encouragement of increased European exports to the United States, because, it is charged, such increased exports will compete unfairly with domestically produced goods. A percentage of exports to the United States which contributes to Europe's dollar earnings are noncompetitive in character. A most liberal estimate of the volume of competitive goods that Europe could sell in the United States, and I should say that this would be a miracle, even in the year 1953, would be less than a billion and a quarter dollars. This billion and a quarter dollars should be measured against the total production of goods in the United States of America of more than $140,000,000,000. Clearly, the absorption of any such amount of competitive goods could not have any appreciable effect upon our total economy. True, this new competition would create problems in a few localities-competition always does; but if there must be some relief in this situation, I suggest that it be given directly. Europe must have dollars to buy goods from us, and if we don't want to give her those dollars, we should let her earn them. Quite apart from the financial aspects of this problem, the relationship between the United States and Europe will never be on a sound basis until Europe is a cash-on-thebarrel-head customer, paying for what she gets. 

If western Europe continues its resolute pursuit of additional production and productivity, if it concentrates its efforts on additional dollar earning and dollar savings, and if the United States gives it full cooperation and support, the western Europe dollar deficit can be brought to manageable proportions by 1952. For this to happen, the continuance of American aid is absolutely essential on a progressively declining but adequate scale. The appropriation which I am requesting today can be justified on many cogent grounds-on the grounds of national safety, on the grounds of securing the peace, on the grounds of preserving the free world from aggressive communism. 

Even if these compelling grounds were not present, it could be fully justified on the basis that its continuance is imperative in order to complete and secure the recovery to which the United States set its hand in partnership with western Europe 2 years ago.

It all adds up to this. We believe that by June 30, 1952, we can have met the first objective assigned to us by the Congress, which is putting Europe in a position where Europe will no longer, as an entire continent, be in need of extraordinary outside assistance.

THE RECORD AND THE PROSPECTS ON ECONOMIC UNIFICATION 

In the preamble to the original Economic Cooperation Act and more explicitly last year in its amendment to Public Law 472, the Congress stated it to be the policy of the people of the United States "to encourage unification of Europe." As the program has gone forward during its first 2 years, we have come to appreciate more and more the wisdom of the Congress in emphasizing the importance of this goal. 

Of course, complete unification cannot be achieved quickly. Even if it could, it would have little immediate effect in closing the dollar gap and reducing the amount of American aid required by Europe. 

Its importance lies not in an immediate step-up in production and exports, but in its long-range effects in making possible a dynamic, expanding economy comprising a vast market. Integration is a necessary foundation for sustained recovery and a necessary safeguard against a return to the narrow economic isolationism, which is one of the deep roots of Europe's economic weakness. 

It is not enough for western Europe merely to return to the level of production and consumption which prevailed before World War II. 

As long as western Europe remains compartmentalized, with each of its 18 nations striving for self-sufficiency, it cannot realize its great potentialities for both prosperity and security. Europeans today are becoming aware that it is the integration of the American economy as well as its dynamic competitive character and our great natural resources that have made possible our unrivaled productivity. The 

United States, with 150,000,000 people, turned out in 1949 a gross national product of about $260,000,000,000. Western Europe, with 

270,000,000 people, had a gross national product of $160,000,000,000. 

If European per capita output had been on a par with ours, its gross national product would have been $470,000,000,000 instead of $160,- 000,000,000. Of course, Europe hasn't the coal or the iron or the farm land or the raw materials to permit production at any such level, even if the European economy could be put completely on a par with ours from the standpoint of plant and horsepower. 

But Europe doesn't need to achieve a $470,000,000,000 output to get an expanding standard of living which will immunize it completely against the threat of aggressive communism. 

On the basis of my own first-hand knowledge, I can say that the participating governments recognize that Europe has got to attain a broad, freely trading market so that its industry can take advantage of large-scale, low-cost production. They are beginning to realize that there is no compelling incentive to further large increases in production and in productivity unless there is an adequate European market in which to sell the goods, and unless there is plenty of competition within that market. These conditions can only be realized by taking the necessary steps to promote economic integration. 

I should like to add that such integration will provide the means to bring the new German Republic fully into the western European family of nations-an essential condition for a peaceful and prosperous western Europe.

The OEEC, that is, the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, and the ECA realized that a substantial degree of recovery had first to be achieved before fundamental structural changes in Europe's economy could be pushed forward with prospects for success.

The progress of recovery has now been such that recently the ECA has vigorously placed before the OEEC the need and urgency of speeding these structural changes.

These are the steps which have been taken: 

First, concrete meaning and substance had to be given to the word "integration." I presented some specific suggestions designed to accomplish this to the Ministerial Council of the OEEC on October 31. 

In cooperation with the Council, integration was defined in practical terms to mean the creation of a single, large market, to be brought about by (1) the removal of all quantitative restrictions on the movement of goods, (2) the elimination of monetary barriers to intra- European trade, and (3) the progressive reduction of tariffs among the participating countries. 

As a result of these discussions, the OEEC nations drew up their own program in which they resolved: (1) To remove by December 15 quantitative restrictions on at least 50 percent of their imports in private trade; (2) To decide on further steps toward trade liberalization by the end of January; (3) To devise far-reaching new measures to bring about the mutual transferability of their currencies; (4) To report at the earliest possible date on ways and means to eliminate dual pricing.

Finally, informal discussions took place on creating a new post within the OEEC and the appointment of a European of high prestige to that post so that economic proposals could more readily and promptly be translated into the necessary political decisions. 

The OEEC countries have now removed quota restrictions from 50 percent of trade which had previously been restricted. They are now working to decrease these restrictions still further. Some progress is being made toward ending dual pricing. The OEEC countries are now negotiating a new European Payments Union which, with our help, will further remove monetary barriers to intra-European trade and make possible the next steps in eliminating quota restrictions. 

An important indication that this intent will be translated into action lies in the fact that 3 weeks ago the Council acted unanimously to create the new high-level post I have mentioned earlier and appointed to it one of the most highly qualified and respected statesmen in Europe today, Dr. Dirk Stikker, Foreign Minister of the Netherlands. I am gratified that Dr. Stikker is arriving in the next few days for consultations in Washington.

This is the record, to date, in western European integration. In a sense it is not a bad record, but it is not good enough. I have not hesitated to say to the OEEC and I do not hesitate to report to you that, while western European recovery in increasing production, consumption, and trade has exceeded our fondest hopes, western Europe's progress toward economic integration has been disappointing. 

In all fairness it deserves to be stated that the progress which has been made in the past few months toward the better organization of the European economy would, in normal times, be worthy of high praise. It is only because the need is so great and the time so pressing that I am disappointed with the progress made thus far. 

But I do not want to confuse disappointment with discouragement.

I am not discouraged, because I believe that the job can be done and is beginning to be done. True, the OEEC countries will need to accomplish within the next 25 months-between now and the termination of the ECA-what would normally take 25 years. I am convinced that before the Marshall plan is completed 2 years hence, our friends in western Europe, with our help, will take those major steps toward the creation of a single market in Europe which they have accepted as a prime objective and which has the full support of the United 

States Government. 

THE TASKS AHEAD AND THE 1950-51 APPROPRIATION 

It is the intention of the ECA to administer ERP aid in such a fashion as will provide the strongest incentive to participating countries to make maximum progress toward internal unification and external balance in their payments. This encouragement would be applied in a positive fashion-that is, a large portion of the total ECA aid will be extended to countries, collectively or individually, which commit themselves to undertake important steps toward those goals.

After considerable discussion with the OEEC, we have decided to change the basis on which we determine requirements of the various countries. Instead of asking them to compute their requirements for all types of commodities and services, add these up, and present the resulting total to us, we have adopted a different method. We now have enough experience to determine with reasonable accuracy the total each country will need in the coming fiscal year if it makes maximum efforts and takes all steps, however difficult, to minimize its requirements for dollar aid. We have set these levels of aid first, and then required each country to present its plan as to which measures it will adopt to bring its aid figure down to the amount we have set, without halting its progress toward recovery. This new method requires a country to put emphasis on the measures it can take to reduce aid requirements.

In arriving at the greatest possible reduction in proposed ERP aid for 1950-51 we have made the following estimates :

We look for a 10-percent increase over the current year in dollar earnings by the participating countries through exports, tourism, and invisible services.

We look for an 11-percent decrease in dollar requirements of the participating countries through dollar-saving gains in domestic production and additional supplies of needed items from nondollar areas. 

Based upon these calculations, the minimum amount needed to operate the Marshall plan successfully for the next fiscal year, including the requirements for Germany, is $3,100,000,000. 

You will recall that last year, in discussing the size of the appropriation required to carry on the program effectively during the current fiscal year, I pointed out repeatedly that nobody could predict with perfect accuracy, so far in advance of the time when the appropriation was to be used, the exact amount which would ultimately prove to be required. You will recall that I gave my solemn pledge to the Congress that if, as things developed, we found any way of saving money which would not jeopardize the success of the program, we would do so. It gives me great pleasure to report to you that,

according to our present estimates, it will be possible to save $150,- 000,000 out of the appropriation money for the present fiscal year. 

We have tried to overlook no opportunity for saving consistent with continued recovery, and we have had good luck in several directions, notably the excellent European harvests of last year. 

We are asking that this sum of $150,000,000 be carried over into the next fiscal year to help meet the 1950-51 requirements of $3,100,000,000. 

This leaves as our net request for new funds the sum of $2,950,000,000. 

Because of the surpassing importance of getting ahead with the program of integration and because of our conviction that the participating nations which undertake the risks and temporary dislocations inherent in the program will need and deserve special help, it is our plan to withhold at the start from allocations to individual countries not less than $600,000,000 from the total 1950-51 appropriation which will be available to encourage the aggressive pursuit of a program of liberalized trade and payments. A part of this sum will be used to support a proposed European Payments Union and the balance will be made available directly to the qualifying countries. Only as an effective payments union is put into operation will the full amount of the 1950-51 appropriations be made available to the participating countries.

I would like to call attention to the rapidity with which American aid to Europe is declining from year to year. 

You will recall that American aid to western Europe for the fiscal year 1948-49 was about $5,800,000,000, including the special appropriation for Germany.

The appropriation for 1949-50 was about $4,200,000,000 including 

Germany. 

The requested appropriation for 1950-51 is $2,950,000,000, including Germany.

Two aims have constantly guided us in arriving at our appropriation requests: To carry out faithfully and vigorously the principle of declining aid; to ask this year, as before only the very minimum required to attain success.

I wish to repeat again, as applying to the request we are now making, that we are laying before you our best carefully screened estimates as to the requirements for the fiscal year beginning July 1. This is the minimum we think we shall need but, if we can save any of it without wrecking the recovery program, I again pledge you my word we shall do so.

I ask you to weigh two considerations, particularly, in making your decision.

The first is, as I previously said, that it would be a cruel waste for America not to finish the task it has accepted in helping our partners in western Europe to achieve a stable and secure recovery. Not only would continued recovery be blocked, but the great progress achieved to date would be put in jeopardy; the recovering Europe of 1950 would almost certainly again become the vulnerable Europe of 1947. 

The second consideration is the need fully to take into account the titanic struggle which the free nations, under American leadership, are waging against the dangerous forces of Soviet communism. 

We all know that this is a struggle between the free world and the slave world, between the democratic way of life and the police state way of life.

This has been called the cold war. That is not an adequate phrase,. because it gives the impression that this struggle in which we are now engaged is not comparable in importance with a shooting war. But 

I want to say here and now that it is just as vital to win this battle for the minds and loyalties of free men as it was to win World War II. 

And if we want to avert World War III, with the awful threat of the H-bomb, we have simply got to win it. 

I sometimes feel that we as a people-and this applies to Europeans. also do not wholly sense the importance of winning this conflict which has been imposed upon us. 

This is understandable because there are few headlines and little drama in the battle of recovery. 

There are no jet planes, no guided missiles, no big bombers used in carrying on this fight. The weapons of the opposition are political strikes, sabotage, and deceptive propaganda. The weapons of the free nations are the weapons appropriate to democracy. They are the weapons of food for hungry people, tools for the men who want to work, and hope for those who had all but lost their hope. They add up. to the greatest peacetime cooperative enterprise which freemen have. ever fashioned. And in helping to win this cold war America is actually building for the peace. 

The vortex of today's struggle is in western Europe. I know that the Kremlin is losing no chance to try to wreck European recovery and for a very sound reason. The reason is that if Moscow can halt recovery and can win in western Europe, its schemes for world domi-. nation will be given terrible impetus. And Moscow knows that its failure to halt recovery will mean that its ambition to dominate the world will be blocked.

Six months ago, the Communists in western Europe showed themselves discouraged and despairing. The Marshall plan had frustrated them and turned them back. But there are undeniable signs that they are taking heart again. Their hopes have been renewed in part by the unhappy plight of China and by their wishful propaganda that some in the United States are becoming weary in their resolution to carry on firmly in their support of the European recovery program. 

It is against this background that we ask you to consider our request for 1950-51 appropriation of $2,950,000,000. I am fully conscious of the hugeness of this sum. As far as we are concerned, $3,000,-- 

000,000 is three thousand million dollars-and that is a lot of money.. 

I hold it in the greatest respect-every penny of it. 

But you and I also know that a shooting war is definitely more costly. 

Secretary of the Army Gordon Gray recently has stated that World War II will have cost the United States $1,300,000,000,000 before it is. finally paid for, and a trillion is a thousand billion. 

In closing, I wish to repeat the statement I made, when I testified' last February: That the Marshall plan will turn out to be the greatest bargain the American people ever had, and to that I would like to add these words. We are starting upon the second half of the twentieth century. We have been carrying this struggle against Russia with weapons, as I cited, appropriate to democracy, with food for the hungry, and with tools for those who want to work, so that hope and confidence could return to the people of Europe. And the people of 

Europe, with our help, are winning that war with tools of that kind,.

and I think that all of us have a right to take great cheer and great hope that this kind of a cold war can be won with those kinds of tools. 

Thank you very much. 

Mr. KEE. Thank you, Mr. Hoffman.

STATEMENT OF HON. DEAN ACHESON, SECRETARY OF STATE 

Secretary ACHESON. Senator Connally and Judge Kee, and members of the Senate and House committees, I am happy to have this opportunity to appear before you in support of action to continue our full participation in the European recovery program. 

Two antithetical concepts of foreign relations are loose in the world. 

One concept is that no state is friendly which is not subservient. An official report to the Cominform defines an internationalist as one who "unreservedly, without any hesitation, and unconditionally, is ready to defend the U. S. S. R." Anyone who rejects this notion is a warmonger. Even a Communist state cannot live on friendly terms with the Kremlin unless it shows complete subservience and submission, as the Yugoslav experiment has shown. The very prospect of peaceful cooperation among non-Soviet states to defend their own interests and to solve their own problems is anathema to the Kremlin, as is shown by the histories of the European recovery program and the 

North Atlantic Treaty. 

The other concept is that no state is unfriendly which, in return for respect for its rights, respects the rights of other states. This concept is one which permits and encourages variety, which demands only that conflicts of interest be resolved by peaceful means, and which calls, in the modern world, for an international framework to secure the peace. 

The world stands to gain or lose something very precious depending on which of these concepts wins dominion. This is, in modern dress, the ancient conflict of tolerance versus intolerance, of diversity versus uniformity, of freedom under the law versus authority above the law. 

The present world crisis is a product of the conflict between these fundamentally opposed concepts. The Kremlin has had major successes, though they fall short of its ambitions, and it now inescapably confronts the nations of the free world, which cannot accept its definition of internationalism and which are by that fact a threat, in the Kremlin's view, to its security. The Kremlin can and is pursuing its course with efficiency and with signs of increasing boldness, using whatever means seem appropriate to it in a given situation. The question before us is, How can the threat be met, how is the Kremlin's design to be frustrated? The task is a difficult one, because the 63307-50-pt. 1-2

answer is that we must make our system work successfully and prove itself by the practical test of its worth. I do not imply that the only reason for continuing the European recovery program is the threat of further expansion by the Soviet Union. On the contrary, the free world, even if no threat of this kind existed, would face the same hard task of building a successfully functioning system. I do mean, however, that in the context of the present world crisis the task is doubly acute and doubly urgent.

The free world also has important successes to record. The Soviet world has nothing to match ERP and the Point IV concept in the economic field; it has nothing to match the coming to independence of India, Pakistan, Indonesia, the Philippines and other nations in the political field-on the contrary it has built a system of satellite states, the very term being descriptive of the negation of freedom and the frustration of nationalism. It has nothing to match the North 

Atlantic Treaty concept in the field of defense. Our job is to do our full part in carrying out these programs and concepts to a successful conclusion. Nor is conclusion the right word, for although the need for extraordinary assistance will come to an end, the need for our affirmative cooperation and participation will be continuously required if the free world is to be a going concern. 

The free world must meet the threat to its existence both defensively and constructively. The first test of any society is its ability to defend itself, in order to deter an attack upon it by making it a hazardous gamble and, in the event of attack, to defeat it. As Madison wrote, every society must have means of security "which can only be regulated by the means and danger of attack." This is the defensive task-to create the will and the means to defend the free world-but success in this task depends mainly on the use the free world makes of its constructive opportunities. 

The fundamental answer is, therefore, to build a successfully functioning political and economic society of free nations. This is the positive task in the doing of which we create the spiritual and material base essential of our defense and to the preservation of the integrity of our way of life. 

It is a very difficult job to build a successfully functioning system. 

It requires adjustments to the changed and changing facts of international life. And it is hard to make adjustments-people tend to resist change and to stick to old ways of doing things. A conscious effort of will is necessary to overcome our native inertia. 

And now, turning to Europe, I think we must decide what we need to do and are prepared to do to help carry forward the recovery gains which have been achieved and to help create a secure and firm foundation for the future.

Mr. Hoffman has recited to you the magnificent record of European production over the past 2 years. He has also stressed the need for bringing about conditions under which Europe can sell enough products and services to us and the rest of the world so that she can stand on her own feet. To solve this problem requires further strenuous action both on our part and on the part of the countries participating in the program.

The Europeans must not only expand their productive capacities but must, through greater efficiency, through lower costs and im-

proved marketing methods, improve the competitive position of their products in the markets of the United States and the rest of the world.

This is the reason why we favor the closer association of the free countries of Europe in the economic field, as we do in the political and military fields. Such association is necessary if they are to put their economies on a sound, competitive, self-supporting basis. If 

Germany, instead of being a threat to world peace, is to be a constructive partner in Europe, it is necessary to build a European framework within which her skills and energies can be used for the benefit of all. 

We hope this drawing together of the European countries will take place within a framework of closer association of all the free countries of the world, including our own. Unity in Europe requires the continuing association and support of the United States. Without it free Europe would split apart.

The Brussels Pact, the OEEC, and the Council of Europe, which have been established to deal with common European problems, are associations of sovereign states. While there is growing popular debate in Europe on the problem of federation, neither the people, nor their governments, appear ready for this step. We recognize their right to decide democratically as our founding fathers did, when, how, and whether they will federate. We reserve the same right for ourselves, as we approach, on a step-by-step basis, a closer association with other nations, through the UN, the North Atlantic Treaty, and other arrangements.

Progress toward the economic integration of Europe requires action on many fronts, including the liberalization of trade, currency arrangements, and programs for the movement of manpower. But I want to emphasize one step which is particularly important at the present time. That is the establishment of a European payments union to permit the free exchange of European currencies. I hope that in the near future the European countries will take this essential step. They have our support and encouragement in this difficult task. 

The peoples of Europe can be expected to make these necessary drastic adjustments with confidence in the success of their efforts only if they can have confidence that we are prepared to cooperate with them. They must be convinced that we will not falter or lose interest. 

What can we do?

First,we must continue our assistance under ERP at a level which will permit the European countries to make necessary purchases in the dollar area. Without this assistance, each country will be compelled to engage in a futile attempt to earn gold and dollars from the others and the cooperative effort to coordinate national economic policies and to develop institutions for this purpose will be struck a deathblow. 

There must be no wavering in support of this program now, for the years ahead are in every way as important as the years behind. The important decisions about Europe's future are still to be made. 

But this appropriation of the funds which Mr. Hoffman asks for is not enough. Readjustments of United States economic policies will be necessary. The problem which confronts us can be stated very simply: To maintain the volume of American exports which the free world needs and which it is in our national interest to supply as a necessary part of building a successfully functioning political and eco-

nomic system, the free world must obtain the dollars to pay for these exports. They can be obtained in only three ways: By our imports of goods and services from them; by our public and private loans and investments abroad; and by continued gifts. In the long run, the only reliable and desirable way is to increase our imports, but that is a big job and until it has been done we have to continue assistance to countries which need it and which it is in our national interest to help. 

Whatever we can do to build up our imports from abroad and to make our exports available at reasonable prices contributes to the success. of ERP and more broadly to the building of a successful free world system.

This is a positive and an ambitious program for the United States. 

No one can predict with confidence how long it will take nor what demands it will place upon us. Support of ERP is only one part of it, although it is a vital part. Let us be clear in our own minds, and make clear to our European friends, that economic collaboration is a continuing part of our broader relationship. Whatever form it may take that collaboration must continue to be a basic element of our national policy.

It is in the carrying out of such a policy, in our determination and our will to do it however long it takes and whatever it requires of us, that the frustration of the Kremlin's design for world dominion lies. 

We are in the midst of a struggle in which we must prove the superiority of our way of life and of our concept of foreign relations by building a free and just and advancing society of nations based on the principles of tolerance and restraint. What is at stake is our concept of internationalism as opposed to the Kremlin definition of internationalism as the unreserved and unhesitating and unconditional readiness of every state to take the part assigned to it by the Kremlin. That is a role which we and the free world cannot and will not accept. In the legislation before you, the Congress, which is the traditional guardian of our liberties, can reaffirm that determination. 

Senator CONNALLY. Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary.

The committee will probably recall you at a later time to crossexamine you not to cross-examine but to propound certain questions to you regarding your testimony and the general situation.

Mr. KEE. Í have nothing to add.

DESIRABILITY OF ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO CHINESE STUDENTS IN THE UNITED STATES 

The Department believes it is desirable and highly important to make available additional funds for emergency assistance to needy Chinese students in the 

United States. 

The present program of emergency aid is not sufficient to meet the educational needs of all qualified Chinese students in the United States. Many of these who have completed a course of study now find it impossible to return to China because of transportation difficulties. Many others are not eligible for assistance under the present program with its limited fund. 

The Department is of the opinion, that, for the large majority of Chinese students in the United States, all other financial resources have been virtually exhausted. The Department believes that an expanded program of emergency assistance is desirable to enable these Chinese students to continue their train-

ing in a friendly atmosphere and a democratic environment, until such time as present transportation difficulties are overcome and they can return to China. 

The United States Government must not neglect this opportunity to demonstrate our continuing interest in the welfare of the Chinese people by assisting this representative group of China's postwar generation who are in our midst. 

Chairman KEE. Mrs. Bolton, will you yield? 

Mrs. BOLTON. Yes.

Chairman KEE. Your unexpended fund is part of the unexpended balance of the appropriation made for aid to China? 

Mrs. BOLTON. Yes; it would be with the ECA, or aid to China.

How important does the State Department feel this to be, and what is their suggestion for helping these students? 

Chairman KEE. Is it not your idea to take that amount you want allocated for the aid of these students out of the appropriations made by this bill or authorized by this bill to the ECA, or is it to take it from the appropriation already made? 

Mrs. BOLTON. The appropriation already made, if possible, yes. 

Then I would also like to ask you something about the European countries and their attitude toward Mr. Hoffman's insistence on integration in the economic areas. 

As I understood, from an article which I confess I read rather hastily in the paper, Great Britain and Switzerland and one other country were rather standing out against integration of that kind. 

Do you have any information in the Department on that?

Secretary ACHESON. I think we are familiar with the difficulties which have arisen. You will remember Mr. Hoffman talked about that this morning. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Yes; he did. 

Secretary ACHESON. If you will remember, he said that the OEEC nations drew up their program last October 31 and they laid down four steps which they were going to undertake: (1) To remove by

December 15 quantitative restrictions on at least 50 percent of their imports in private trade; (2) to decide steps for trade liberalization by the end of January; (3) to bring about the mutual transferability of their currencies; and (4) to report at the earliest possible date on ways and means to eliminate dual pricing.

He pointed out that they had done No. 1. They were making some considerable progress on No. 2. The measures to bring about transferability have to do with this European Payments Union, and that is a matter upon which we are now much more encouraged than we were some weeks ago. We believe that that matter can be worked out. There are some difficulties to surmount yet, but we think the prospect is much brighter than the situation has been before. 

So far as the dual pricing is concerned, which is very important, some progress has been made but not enough and we are going back at that and we hope to get that one worked out. 

There have been troubles from various countries. I do not think at this point it does much good to put the finger on anybody. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I am willing to accept that as an answer, but not the rest of it. I am perfectly willing to accept that as your answer, Mr. 

Secretary. Thank you. 

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Mr. Secretary, I am sorry we have a roll call going on down there, but members will be coming in and going out until that roll call is answered. That explains the absence of some of the members.

Mr. Merrow 

Mr. MERROW. Mr. Secretary, in reference to this whole matter of 

European integration, I am glad we are making some progress and that there has been an attempt to bring about closer cooperation of the various countries so that they would have a single market and so on. 

It was indicated this morning that not as much progress has been made as we would like to see. Now, in continuing aid for the next fiscal year and the final fiscal year in this program, is it not possible to increase pressure so that we can bring about this integration at a more rapid rate and achieve the goal sooner?

Secretary ACHESON. I think that is true, Mr. Merrow, and I think 

I should be in favor of leaving that to Mr. Hoffman. It is an extremely delicate thing to do. You can get much further by encouraging people to do things in a voluntary way than you can by trying to drive them. We got all sorts of integration under Hitler in Europe and the whole thing goes to pieces when that coercive pressure goes off. I think you will make more lasting progress if we try to do it in a slightly slower way. 

Mr. MERROW. I can see that but I have always felt that what we should have done and I do not mean to go back over the history of the program because hindsight is always better than foresight-was to establish certain conditions precedent to the giving. We came to the summer of 1949 and the administrator, began to put on the pressure for integration and certain progress has been made but not as much progress as we would like to see. Now, are we going to appropriate a great deal of money to continue this program and while we have this as a leverage it seems to me that perhaps the pressure should be stepped up if there is any possible way of doing it. 

Mr. ACHESON. I agree if there is any effective and possible way of doing it, it should be done. 

Mr. MERROW. You think it will be done in the next 2 years?

Mr. ACHESON. I think Mr. Hoffman will do as he said this morning, everything that conceivably can be done to accomplish the purposes of the ECA Act. Now you must realize it is not a place where you could say we will not do anything until certain steps precedent are taken. It is not a case where we can sit around and talk about what can be done. We are talking to the entire world when I answer this question for you. As Mr. Churchill once said in a speech to the 

French people, hostile ears are listening. We will work with our friends in Europe just as earnestly as we possibly can to bring about what they agreed to bring about when we went into this cooperative effort, which is the mutuality of aid. This means a closer relationship, economically and politically and under the North Atlantic Treaty, militarily, in Europe. 

Mr. MERROW. I think it is gratifying so much progress has been made, but it seems to me that integration is extremely urgent because the future of Europe, in my opinion, depends upon the degree of unity they can obtain and the soundness of the continent depends upon the unity that can be obtained. 

Mr. ACHESON. You could not be more right.

Mr. MERROW. There is one other question, Mr. Chairman: The point was made this morning that in order to close the dollar gap it is necessary for us to take more imports. Now, as a practical matter,

it would seem to me that this is going to be exceedingly difficult. I wonder if you would comment on the question of bringing more imports into the United States. 

Mr. ACHESON. I think it will be extremely difficult. The steps we will have to take will be very substantial steps. As we take those, they will cause difficulty and hardships of one sort or another to some groups in the United States. That would seem to me as this matter is studied, to be a problem of concern to the Government. I do not think we should say, "Well, we must do it and the chips will have to fall where they fall, and whoever suffers will have to suffer." 

I should think it would be a matter of governmental concern to see that there is help in the adjustments to these new situations. But if we are really going to help knit what we call the free world together, at such an economic level that it can survive, then we are really faced with this problem, and we have to take the steps necessary to achieve it. 

Mr. MERROW. Do I understand from that, Mr. Secretary, that you mean if we take more imports in the United States, and that certain industries are injured because those imports are brought in, that the 

Government must assist those industries?

Mr. ACHESON. I am not giving you a program, Mr. Merrow, and 

I really can do no more than I have already done, which is to say that this is a responsibility of all of us represented in the Government. It is not enough to say, if there is a difficulty in some industry which becomes marginal, then the fate of the management and the investors and the workers is of no concern to all of us. It is of concern to all of us. Now, what we should do about it, I do not know, but I think we should be able to come to conclusions on that very rapidly.

Mr. MERROW. It is easy to state that we can close this dollar gap if we increase our imports, but it would seem to me that the difficulties of doing this are so great that it may be almost impractical. 

Secretary ACHESON. If we take that attitude, and push exports down to the present level of imports, I think we have to reach the conclusion that certain other things may be impractical which we would not really like to contemplate. This is a very, very serious question. There is no question more serious than this before us at the present time.

Mr. MERROW. The import question is the most serious? 

Secretary ACHESON. It is. 

Mr. MERROW. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Judd 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, may I yield to Mr. Vorys, who was out of the room when his turn came up? 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Vorys- 

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Secretary, you covered the world in your statement this morning and your Department covers the world. You must function through subordinates. Have you anything further to say now as to your attitude on loyalty and security in your Department? 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes; I should be very glad to talk about that.

We have a program and system in regard to the loyalty of our employees in the Department of State, which was inaugurated by Gen-

eral Marshall. In inaugurating it he put Mr. Peurifoy in charge of it. He has continued in charge of it throughout General Marshall's administration and under mine. I have followed the matter as closely as I possibly can, with the other things I have to do. I am thoroughly convinced that Mr. Peurifoy has done it in an efficient, vigorous, and fair way. I have complete confidence in him and in the way in which he is working. We will continue to administer it as we have. I can assure you that I have no question whatever about the loyalty or devotion of the employees of the Department of State. 

I also would like to point out to you that we must expect from time to time to find some people in any department who would be better not there. That does not seem to me to indicate a defect in the system but to indicate that the system is working properly. If you attempt to get 100 percent security so that you never get in the Department anyone whom you might want to eliminate you will probably defeat your own end. What we must do is to be alert to discover anyone of that sort and promptly remove that sort of a person. But you must give the people who work in the Department the feeling that we do have confidence in them, that they are not all suspects or all watched by detectives every minute. These people are loyal, devoted people who have given their lives to the service of the United States and they are entitled to be regarded in that way, and I do regard them in that way.

Our system is to discover if, as, and when anyone is in our midst who is not worthy of that confidence, and eliminate him.

Mr. VORYS. What sort of proof of disloyalty do you require before you act? 

Secretary ACHESON. I cannot answer that question because that matter is entirely in the hands of Mr. Peurifoy. When he has a situation which he thinks I should know about he brings it to me and I act on it.

Mr. VORYS. I have no further questions.

Mr. MORGAN. No questions at this time, Mr. Chairman.

Chairman KEE. Dr. Judd—— 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Secretary, this morning Mr. Hoffman laid down certain conditions that he considered requisite for the success of this program, conditions we have discussed many times, of course, in these last 2 years, such as increase in their exports, integration of their economies to which Mr. Merrow was referring, our willingness to take more imports, and so forth.

How important do you consider it as a condition to the success of this program in Europe, that southeast Asia be kept free and therefore its economy available to the countries of Europe? 

Secretary ACHESON. I consider it very important, Dr. Judd.

Mr. JUDD. If you believed that the loss of southeast Asia to Communist control would make it almost certainly impossible for the European recovery program to succeed in the sense that the countries there become self-supporting and secure, would you then feel justified in voting to continue the program in Europe, if you saw southeast 

Asia going down?

Secretary ACHESON. I do not agree with the implication which there was in your question that it would be impossible. You asked me

if I regard it as important. I do regard it as important. We must continue this program in any event. We must do everything we possibly can effectively do to strengthen the free world wherever we think we can strengthen it. But I think we must not get into a position in which we say, because it is difficult to do one thing therefore we do not even try to do something else. 

Mr. JUDD. I do not think that is quite what my question contained. 

Secretary ACHESON. I did not think it was.

Mr. JUDD. May I come at it this way. There has just been a conference held out in Bangkok. I presume one of its major concerns was what the United States can properly and effectively do to keep those countries in the free column; is that right? 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes, I think it was to review the whole situation on the spot, see what the dangers were and what was the best way of meeting them. It was to see not merely what the United States could do, but what we thought the whole situation called for. 

Mr. JUDD. Can you give us any of the conclusions that may have been reached at that conference with reference to this matter, beyond those that were published in the papers which were, I thought, largely negative rather than suggestive of remedial measures?

Secretary ACHESON. No, I should prefer not to do that at the present time. When I get a full report on the conference I shall be very glad to meet in executive session with this committee and go over the conclusions reached. 

Mr. JUDD. I think that should be of great value, sir, and I hope you will do so. I have believed, as you know, since 1947 when the first interim aid program was proposed, that unless we succeed in keeping Asia free we would almost certainly lose in Europe, too. I had a struggle with my conscience as to whether it was justifiable to vote for the program in Europe unless there was assurance that the same sort of principle and program would be applied in Asia also. 

I did vote for it, largely in hope. Four times I have done so; once on the Interim Aid Act of 1947; second, establishment of ERP in 

1948; third, on the 1949 extension of ERP, and fourth, the aid to

Korea bill just a few weeks ago. Can I rightly do it again? If one is genuinely convinced that a program cannot succeed unless certain conditions are met and those conditions are not being met, then I do not quite see, with our budget already in the red, how I can justify putting it $3,000,000,000 further in the red for that program. I fear much as I regret it, that it cannot succeed, unless our policies in Asia are changed. I would like to get a slant on how you would feel if you were on my side of the table. 

Secretary ACHESON. I think if I believed your premise I should come very close to reaching your conclusion. I do not think the difficulty is in the logic; I think the difficulty is in the premise, plus one further fact, that if I thought every possibility was against this, I would still vote for it. It seems to me that we are in a situation where we cannot afford to leave to imperfect premises-because all premises must be imperfect when they are forecasts of the futurewe cannot leave to them, to our belief in the correctness of these premises, the extent of the vigor with which we go ahead pressing this struggle. This is a matter which involves the very fundamentals of our country and all the principles to which we are devoted.

I am far from being pessimistic about the situation or discouraged about it in any way, but even if I were I think I should go forward the way we are now going forward. 

It seems to me that if one had argued with Mr. Churchill in the latter part of 1940 one could have shown him that almost everything he was doing did not have any possibility of success. How could anyone have argued one's self into the belief that Great Britain was really going to come out victorious in the war in the latter half of 1940?

But one of the things that counts in the struggle is the degree of determination that people have. That is a factor of incalculable importance, and therefore I just go right ahead with it, whatever I guess will be the success or failure of the effort. 

Mr. JUDD. Then I cannot understand, Mr. Secretary, why you have adopted an exactly opposite attitude in dealing with the situation in China. I have recognized all the difficulties there just as keenly as you have. Yet you would not follow the course we urged of making the utmost effort there as well as in Europe no matter how discouraging or how improbable that we would succeed. Your premises of failure there were also imperfect, and I believed we should still make the effort, because it was so important to the success of the European recovery program and our own security.

Secretary ACHESON. It depends what the effort is. You can go ahead doing the same thing, you can beat your head against the same wall, or you can find another way of accomplishing the same thing. 

I have no question about what the objective is, and the objective is not to have this thing that we feel is so dangerous to all freedom in the world, spreading. The question is what is the best way to accomplish that objective.

You believe that the best way to accomplish that is to do one thing. 

I may think that the best way to do it is another thing. But both you and I are determined that we ought to go ahead and try to do it. We may differ on the means. I think in the case of China we are differing on the means and not as to the objective. 

Mr. JUDD. There is no question about the difference or the means. 

The point is I believe we have to consider two risks. One is the risk that we take in Europe if we do not continue the effort there. 

If we do not, there is no hope. If we do, there is some hope. That is the way I feel about that, as I have felt the same about Asia. On the other hand, there is a risk if we do continue the effort. If you became convinced that the loss of China and threatened loss of Asia is reducing hope of recovery in Europe almost to the vanishing point, would you dare run the risk of endangering further the solvency of the United States? In other words, we are justified in increasing the burden and drain on our country only if there is a reasonable probability that out of it will come increase in Europe's strength that will more than compensate for the temporary drain on ourselves. 

Secretary ACHESON. That might, of course, be true. 

Mr. JUDD. That is the calculated risk, is it not? 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes; I should think the future would be pretty black if you came to the conclusion that you do.

Mr. JUDD. Certainly; it is black. There are people, with whom 

I do not agree, who argue more cogently today than ever before that

we cannot longer carry this load. It is not going to be ended in 1952. 

You will recall that former Ambassador Joseph Kennedy took that stand when ERP was first proposed. He feared it would wreck us without saving them. Therefore, he argued, let the Communists take 

Europe and Asia, and let them wear themselves out trying to hold them. In the meantime, at least preserve America. 

That argument which I did not pay much attention to then, because it seemed too heartless, concerns me today more than it has previously, because of the deficit in our economy, the failure to try to save Asia, and so forth.

I suppose in the end I will probably do what you are going to do; keep on going at it, no matter what the odds. 

Secretary ACHESON. I feel sure you will.

Mr. JUDD. But there was no need for the odds to be so strongly against us. The reason I am more concerned now than I have been at any time previously is partly because we have not made the same kind of effort in China, and we are not making in southeast Asia now the kind of vigorous effort we have made and you are advocating with respect to Europe. That is what disturbs me-that we are going all out in the one place and not really trying in the other. I am afraid that the half-heartedness of the effort in Asia will ruin the all-out effort in Europe. I want you to have the same kind of determination with regard to southeast Asia that you have with regard to Europe. 

Secretary ACHESON. You keep working on me.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield- 

Mr. MANSFIELD. As always, Mr. Secretary, it is a real pleasure to have you before this committee. I am sorry I missed part of the questioning, but taking up where Mr. Judd left off, I recall that 2 years ago in this committee there were some of us who were very interested in extending aid to China, not on a free-loading basis but rather under the same conditions that we were then contemplating extending aid to the countries of western Europe. We felt that if some supervision could be brought into the picture, if something along the same conditions laid down for Europe were laid down for China, that we would stand a greater chance of success there. 

Unfortunately, we did not take that into consideration when we passed the China aid bill. It was something in excess of $500,000,000, as I recall it, and the result has been that we have failed China, not because of our contributions and efforts, which have been very great since the end of the war. We failed because we just did not have the right kind of cooperation. I take that back: We did not fail, but there was a failure in China because we did not have the right kind of cooperation-not because we did not try hard enough, not because we did not appropriate money enough, but probably because we did not have enough to say in the way of supervision.

One thing that has always bothered me is that in effect our aid to China, at least in a military sense, the materials of war, rifles and what not, have eventually found their way into the hands of the Communists to be used against our friends. 

Now, Mr. Secretary, is it your belief that the ECA program as such should end in 1952? 

Secretary ACHESON. This ECA program as such?

Mr. MANSFIELD. Yes 

Secretary ACHESON. When you were out, Mr. Mansfield, I said that it was the view of the administration, expressed by Mr. Hoffman and the 

President, that the ECA program was a program represented to Congress to take 4 years and that it would take those 4 years and at the end of those 4 years it would come to an end. 

I said I did not believe that in 1952 all foreign aid would come to an end. I thought it probably would be necessary in regard to some countries, to continue some form of assistance. The amount of assistance would depend upon the particular condition of the particular country and also on the general success that we had in meeting the dollargap problem.

Mr. MANSFIELD. Is it your contention that the ECA has been the weapon most responsible for helping to bring about the rehabilitation of western Europe to the condition which exists at the present time? 

Secretary ACHESON. I think that the European recovery program and the North Atlantic Treaty have been the two greatest instruments of policy which have so radically changed the situation in Europe from what it was in 1947.

Mr. MANSFIELD. Is it the contention of the State Department that by 1952 western Europe, with certain excepted countries, all of which I think are known to the members of this committee, would be in a position to stand on its own feet and carry on normal economic relations with the rest of the world? 

Secretary ACHESON. No; I do not think I would say that it is the contention that that would be so. As I said, it all depends upon the success which we will have in dealing with the dollar-gap problem. 

There is somewhere, unknown to me, a level at which payments if balanced would continue Europe and all those parts of the world which depend upon their trade with Europe, in a strong and healthy situation. It will be a difficult struggle to balance payments at that point. I would not like to say that I hold a brief for the fact that that is going to be done. I think it is the objective. 

I think we have to bend every possible effort to it, and I understand it to be the intention of the administration that this ECA proposal will, as represented to Congress, come to and end in 1952. We may be confronted with other problems. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. Undoubtedly we will become confronted with other problems, and I do not see at the present time any escape from such. 

Do you think the countries of western Europe by and large have recognized the benefits of the ECA program, the sacrifices made by the American people, and in turn are doing their utmost to do what they can to achieve the kind of an economic union, at least, that we would like to see them have?

Secretary ACHESON. Again, I think I do not want to overstate the position with regard to your question in any way. I think one must be perfectly candid and perfectly frank about it. As was said this morning by Mr. Hoffman, the strides which have been made in the field of production have been-and I think he used the word carefully-spectacular.

In the field of achieving financial stability the results have been good. They have been fair in removing trade barriers. They have not been impressive at all in getting the convertibility of currencies upon which further progress depends.

Mr. Hoffman said that the latter half of the program will have to give special attention to the essential building up of integration. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. If Mr. Churchill's party wins the election in England this week and if they carry on the so-called socialistic policies of the present labor government they will, I presume, still be eligible for American assistance under the European recovery program. 

Secretary ACHESON. If you would indulge me today, only two days before the British election, I would like to make no indications in the direction of a forecast. I would like to say nothing whatever about the possibility of the English elections. They can only resent my interference.

Mr. MANSFIELD. We hear about socialistic England and what we are doing to build it up and I am just wondering what those people who will use that argument are going to say if Mr. Churchill comes in, and if these socialistic reforms are continued by the conservative government. 

That is all, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. FULTON. But there is that class. If there is this group upon whom there can be no absolute proof of their loyalty, I would like to ask you if your Department is hampered by the civil-service laws and regulations now in effect on reaching that class of people who had "better not be there"?
