Then on the amount of this bill, $2,950,000,000 for the fiscal year ending January 30, 1951: In making up that figure, was the figure made with the idea of a balanced United States budget in mind, and also no tax increase? My direct question is, Can we spend $2,950,000,000 on the ECA program in this coming fiscal year without unbalancing the budget and without a tax increase?

Secretary ACHESON. That is a question which really depends upon the over-all administration point of view. The President has presented his budget and has made his tax recommendations. Mr. FULTON. May I quickly refer to a specific provision, Mr. Chairman. If you will look on the first page of this committee print of the ECA Act of 1948, on the proposed amendment, on line 5: "The 

Administrator is authorized to transfer funds directly to any central institution." It does not say how much can be transferred and it does not say the type of central institution. 

Then on line 6 it says, "Other organization." That is as broad a transfer as Congress ever made, because it does not say whether it is man, bird, or beast. When it says "formed," it does not say whether it is formed at present or to be formed in the future. It also says "two or more participating countries," when you can then on line 8 give it to any participating country, regardless of whether it is one or two.

Then I look down on line 10 and see that the "terms and conditions" are specificed only as those "to be used on terms and conditions specified by the Administrator." 

May I point out that provision is not Congress saying how the money shall be spent or the terms and conditions, but the Administrator has a complete delegation of congressional powers. 

In addition, the recipient is in nowise designated. 

Go over to page 2 and you will find on lines 1 and 2, even the purposes for the transfer are so indefinite in the wording, "to promote the liberalization of trade by participating countries with one another and with other countries."

Now, I brought up the fact that there are other countries such as Egypt who might like to be coming into this program and cooperating-not within the terms of it but at least cooperating and you have said it is not possible, in your answer, but on page 2 there the act itself says we are looking to expanding it somewhat to other countries outside of the ECA program. I just want to raise those questions. 

Secretary ACHESON. Mr. Hoffman discussed this provision this morning and this is the provision under which they hope to aid in setting up the European Payments Union. He said it was his hope and expectation to use at least $600,000,000 for the purpose of the workings of this union and other efforts at economic integration and it would be for the purposes which he described. Now, whether this language is proper language to accomplish that, I am not really competent to tell. 

Mr. FULTON. Do you not at this point think the language is too broad for Congress to delegate such a power without the rules, regulations, and general policies laid out that the fund will be managed on? 

Secretary ACHESON. I should think the whole matter could be dealt with in the committee report. It is very difficult for the Congress of the United States to lay down how a European Payments Union would work when the whole thing has to be negotiated and we are not quite sure whether all the countries would come in or whether all would come in on the same basis or what the details of it would be. I think you could be sure in dealing with Mr. Hoffman in the ECA that he will make the whole thing entirely clear to you, and he will operate it in accordance with what he says. There is no hidden purpose in this.

Mr. FULTON. These countries can do this without violating any of their obligations under the Monetary Fund or the Bretton Woods agreement?

Secretary ACHESON. Yes.

Secretary ACHESON. Yes. We are negotiating now. three-cornered negotiations going on between the United States Government, the British Government, and the oil companies involved.

The National Advisory Council considers that the following principles should apply to the establishment of a European Clearing Union:

The Congress hereby expresses itself as favoring the creation by the free countries and free peoples of the Far East, of a joint organization consistent with the Charter of the United Nations to establish a program of self-help and mutual cooperation designed to develop their economic and social well-being, to safeguard the basic rights and liberties, and to protect their security and independence.

Secretary ACHESON. I had not thought the situation was as you described it. I had not thought they were forming a closer economic or political association which we halted in any way. I believe in fact the tendency in the face or dollar shortages has always been the other way, Mr. Judd. If they are faced with a desperate dollar shortage, what they tend to do is not cooperate with other countries, but to do everything they can to hang on to all the dollars that they can get hold of and part with as few as possible. You begin to get increasing barriers and increasing isolationism instead of increasing cooperation.

Mr. JAVITS. Suppose we quit the Marshall plan, now. 

Would your answer change? 

Secretary ACHESON. It would very drastically.

Mr. JAVÍTS. Can you tell us how? I think that is an important question on the floor?

Secretary ACHESON. I think you would immediately get a slackening off of productivity and production in Europe and with that you will have discontent and unemployment. Then you would have inflation, again, too. Those are the conditions necessary to produce the greatest possible Communist agitation. If you have unemployment, inflation, and insufficient imports of food and clothes, and a high price of housing, then you will have Communist difficulties. 

Mr. JAVITS. When we talk about the possibility of closing the dollar gap as Mr. Hoffman did, we are talking about the end of the Marshall plan period in 1952. If you left them denuded of this money right now, would they be back where we began with them in 1947? That is what I am trying to get at.

Mrs. BOLTON. Mr. Secretary, at page 3 of your prepared paper you say: "While there is growing debate in Europe on the problem of federation, neither the people nor their governments appear ready for this step.'

OEEC and the Counsel of Europe have been established to deal with European problems and the association of sovereign states. They wanted the whole effort pointed toward this particular phase. I am just wondering what is the basis of your sentence, here, or your paragraph. 

Secretary ACHESON. I think there is great interest. I would not be able to say whether it is a majority interest or not. There is a lot of interest and useful, desirable discussion on this subject of federation.

I think if you started to lay down some kind of agreement, you would find very great difficulty in getting people together, at this time. This is something which I hope will grow out of this discussion. 

Mrs. BOLTON. You say the people and the governments do not appear ready. First there has to be the desire. That certainly is very alive in Europe. They recognize the fact that they are going to hang separately if they do not get together. Our Constitution wasn't written overnight, and we had a common language and common needs. They do not have the language and have centuries of wars and rumors of wars behind them. Yet they are pursuing this thing, some of them almost with fanatic fervor.

Secretary ACHESON. I think that is right and I think it is highly desirable that they should. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Your statement that "neither the governments nor the people appear ready for this step" troubles me, because it is official. 

To say that "the people are not ready for it" when they are really struggling extremely hard to bring something about against the heaviest of odds, seems hardly a fair statement. The Strasbourg meeting was held and work is going forward under its recommendations.

It would seem that these efforts should have all possible encouragement, rather than discouragement. I wondered what was the basis for your words. You say there is no basis for feeling there is a majority who desire to come together. What is your basis for saying this?

Secretary ACHESON. What I was trying to point out in this paragraph is that certain concrete things have been done and we hope that certain other concrete steps will have been taken. Now those things must come first. If you started to say "Let's get forward right away with this question of federation," I think you would find a good deal of time would have to elapse. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Mr. Hoffman says they must get together economically. We have those two statements.

Secretary ACHESON. What I was trying to do is say there are certain concrete steps which we are now working for and we believe that the way to get on toward the goal is to press forward with those concrete steps, and that the rather difficult and tricky business of a political federation in Europe is not one which is around the corner, now. It is around several corners. Perhaps it was not well expressed. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Certainly it is to be regretted that our Government should say that the people are not ready, for the Strasbourg meeting was a peoples' movement in all countries. It is an exceedingly concrete, practical step toward an integrated Europe. 

Secretary ACHESON. Perhaps it is not well worded.

Mrs. BOLTON. I regret the pressure of work upon the secretary, but are happy to have this suggestion that he might be happy to give recognition and encouragement to this practical demonstration of the thinking of the people of Europe.

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948, AS AMENDED WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

The committee met, pursuant to call at 10:45 a. m., in the Foreign

(chairman) presiding.

Chairman KEE. The committee will be in order. We have with us Ambassador Harriman who will testify this morning on the ECA legislation in connection with the appropriation proposed to continue that program of European assistance. 

Mr. Ambassador, we are very glad indeed to have you here today. 

If you have a statement to make, we will be very happy to have you present it.

STATEMENT OF AMBASSADOR W. AVERELL HARRIMAN, UNITED STATES SPECIAL REPRESENTATIVE IN EUROPE FOR ECH Ambassador HARRIMAN. I have a statement here, Mr. Chairman, which will cover certain aspects of the situation in Europe as I have observed them. I have not attempted to cover the ground that 

Mr. Hoffman did yesterday, which was a broad outline of the progress of recovery, and of the prospects of its continued success. 

I would like to recall that when I appeared before your committee last year, sir, I expressed my conviction that we were winning the struggle for reconstruction and freedom in Europe. During the past year, political stability and democracy have been strengthened throughout. This has been demonstrated in one national election after another. For example, in the Norwegian elections of last 

October, the Communist representation in the national assembly was wiped out completely. They lost all of the 11 seats they had previously held.

In August, the people of western Germany had their first opportunity to register a free choice as to the kind of Federal Government they wanted. Out of 402 seats, only 15 went to the Communists. 

When the Belgian people went to the polls last June, the Communists were left with only 12 seats out of 213 in the assembly as compared with 23 out of the 197 in the previous election. In the senate, the Communists lost even more, reducing their number from 17 to 7. 

The people of Austria, even with part of their country under Soviet occupation, have been firm in their rejection of communism, 63307-50-pt. 145

with only 5 percent voting the Communist ticket and the number of seats in the Parliament held down to 5 out of 165. 

Communism has experienced its most notable set-back in the European trade-union movement which it sought to penetrate and control at all costs. Intent on using the labor movement as the spearhead of their drive, the Communists had captured the major trade-union federations in Italy and France before the Marshall plan took shape. 

The labor movements in these two countries were virtually under control of the Communists. Now that control is losing its grip and the_non-Communist labor movements are rapidly gaining strength. 

In France, the Force Ouvriere, together with other non-Communist trade-unions, is challenging the Communist control of the French labor movement.

In Italy two major non-Communist labor federations have broken away from the Communist confederation, and are now combining their forces of considerably more than 1,500,000 free Italian workers. 

At a convention held last October in western Germany at which the trade-unions formed a single federation, the Communists could muster only a handful of delegates.

In other countries like Austria, Belgium, and Norway, where Communists had once been strong, their influence in organized labor has diminished to insignificance. Of course, there are other countries where they never played an important part at all. 

In many of the countries, Communists are still in control of some labor unions and are still in a position to cause economic dislocations, and otherwise capitalize on social unrest, but their power is steadily declining.

The rising determination of workers to drive out Communist agents from positions of control and influence in the labor movement has had world-wide repercussions. The walk-out of free labor organizations from the once powerful World Federation of Trade Unions, which has been an instrument of Communist intrigue, was a significant advance in the march of labor toward freedom and democracy. Meeting in London early last December, representatives of free tradeunions from 53 countries, including 15 ERP countries and the United 

States, formed the new International Confederation of Free Trade

Unions with a total membership of over 48,000,000. This great new labor organization issued a forceful declaration in support of the Marshall plan. We in America can be justly proud of the leadership of the great labor organizations of the United States, who, working closely with labor organizations in other lands, have helped establish the new confederation as a world organization devoted to the advancement of workers' welfare and the defeat of communistic infiltration. 

These are notable gains scored in the struggle of freedom against communism. But the insidious campaign to capture and control 

Europe is still being relentlessly waged in many forms and in many guises.

The gains made by the voters and workers of Europe toward the free way of life would have been impossible if economic recovery with American aid had not given them new confidence and new hope. 

The people of Europe are increasingly aware of the part which our country and our people have played in the joint-recovery effort.

At the express direction of the Congress, in the 1949-50 appropriation act, the ECA is carrying forward a vigorous information program to make certain that the full story of American aid and its purposes gets to the people of western Europe. The participating governments, despite a slow start by some, are showing increasing initiative in doing their part to get the facts of the recovery effort and the role of American assistance faithfully to the public. 

There is reassuring evidence that the Marshall-plan story is getting over to western Europe and is creating the understanding vital to its success.

Western Europe's 2,000 daily and weekly papers, with a combined circulation of 110,000,000, are now publishing some 4,000 Marshall-plan articles per week-double the number of a year ago. 

In cooperation with the governments, Marshall-plan news, explanatory interviews and programs dramatizing the ERP are broadcast on the nation-wide radio networks of all the Marshall-plan countries. . The European radio listener in each country now has available in his own language an average of two special ERP broadcasts weekly. Our studies show that they are being heard by some 40,000,000 listeners. 

In addition to all this, there is constant covereage by the Voice of 

America. 

Already 59 ECA documentary films have been made, each adapted to particular countries and reproduced in various languages. Individual news-reel shots on Marshall-plan subjects are being shown in commercial theaters with an average weekly audience of 30,000,000 Europeans. This distribution is being steadily increased. 

Last summer, some 5,000,000 European fair-goers saw ERP exhibitions which were prepared and shown in collaboration with the participating governments, and this year, the ERP will be graphically portrayed at an even larger number of fairs. 

The story is told in many other ways. In some places, the European postman has spread the word of American aid with every letter in his sack through special ERP stamps. A million ERP schoolbooks are in use in the German schools. This year, four ERP showboats will ply the inland waterways of the Continent. 

In connection with the ECA information program in Europe, there are two points I should like to mention:

One is that the principal cost of this activity-more than four-fifths of all expenditures-is paid out of the local currency counterpart funds.

The second is that the Marshall plan must meet imaginatively and without timidity the unceasing attacks and propaganda directed against American aid and American motives by the obedient Communists in every country. 

Despite all this, a big job remains to be done both by the participating governments and by the ECA itself. Propaganda is the principle weapon of the Communists and the more the ERP succeeds the more they try to misrepresent it. While most, and almost all, I would think, Europeans are now aware of the Marshall plan, there are still too many who do not know enough about it or adequately understand it. 

You have before you today the Second Report of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation. This is more than a staff study

by a group of experts. It represents the unanimous judgment of the participating governments, appraising the progress that has been made and the problems confronting them and the United States in our joint effort to achieve sound and lasting recovery in Europe. 

It defines economic objectives and the policies necessary to achieve them. It contains commitments to positive action, individual and collective, by the 18 responsible member governments. 

Among these 18 is the new German Federal Republic. It is significant that the OEEC is the first international organization into which the new German Government has been admitted as a full partner. This is an earnest of our hopes for the peaceful and constructive association of Germany in the western European community.

The OEEC proceeds, in its day-to-day work, from appraisal of specific problems to negotiation of the necessary commitments by the governments and a follow-through on the action required. These are no easy tasks. I and the members of my staff have participated. as observers in countless meetings of OEEC committees. We have been deeply impressed with the earnest concentration and determination to solve a wide range of common problems which is shown by the national delegates and the able international staff brought together in Paris.

There are many ways in which the Organization is contributing day by day to steady progress in the building of a healthy European economy.

During the past year, for example, its Food and Agriculture Committee has initiated far-reaching activities for the expansion of farm output in Europe. They are using their own information to disseminate as well as information coming from America. It is a cooperative undertaking of the farm experts and the farm groups and the governments throughout Europe. The Electric Power Committee has developed plans for speeding the expansion of power supply, including internationally interconnected systems which will go far to remove the one remaining major physical bottleneck in European production.

Through the work of the OEEC Manpower Committee, solid progress has been made in facilitating the resettlement of workers within Europe, in encouraging overseas emigration from surplus population countries, and in providing assistance for industrial training and improved employment services. Freedom of movement of workers. across national boundaries has been increased and higher employment in Europe has been promoted by this pioneer effort of concerted international action.

In the field of trade liberalization, a special committee has scrutinized each member nation's proposals, defining rigorous common standards of performance to test compliance with the agreed course. of action. Another committee has made a searching and critical review of the internal financial position and policies of each participating country. A second review is now under way. Such action in an international organization is without precedent. 

A new study is being undertaken of ways and means to encourage private international investment-especially American investment in the member countries and their overseas territories.

Mr. Hoffman has described to you the work of the OEEC and the formidable problems which it faces in connection with economic integration of Europe. These problems are occupying an increasing share of the Organization's attention and we must look for more vigorous and effective progress in their solution. 

This constant process of collaboration on every aspect of economic policy has helped to build in western Europe a growing sense of com mon purpose and community of interest. Even the disputes that have taken place in the Organization and attracted a good deal of public attention demonstrate the vital character of the issues it deals with and the decisions it makes. It is fair to say that no important economic policy is now adopted by any one of the participating countries without serious consideration of its repercussions on that country's OEEC partners and on the progress of the European recovery program.

I should like to stress one feature of Europe's economic effort which seems to me particularly significant. That is the very large share of 

Europe's total economic resources which is going into investment rather than current consumption. Although European living standards are far below our own and in most countries still below prewar, the rate of investment is much higher than prewar. European investment averages about 20 percent of gross national product compared with 15 percent in the United States.

These investments are mainly for the direct expansion of production; they are in power projects, transportation systems, production of basic materials, and in export industries. They are the means by which Europe can use this period of American aid to build up its production and export potential to the point where aid can safely be terminated without leaving impoverishment and unemployment in Europe. These high levels of investment mean that consumption is being held down. The respite afforded by our aid is not a period of mere living on charity. The ERP is no international dole; it is a program for genuine recovery.

This vital progress toward a healthy European economy, with which our own long-run prosperity is bound up, is made possible only by ERP aid. Almost half of western Europe's needed imports of goods and services must at the present time be paid for in dollars. Threefifths of these dollars are being supplied by American aid.

It is all too easy to see what would happen if aid were cut off in the middle of the program. The European countries would simply have to slash drastically their imports from us. 

They would have to eliminate imports of capital equipment, without which they cannot achieve self-support. They would have to cut down imports of industrial raw materials, throwing millions out of work. Cuts in food and feed imports would at once reduce living standards and farm output. With production down, exports would dwindle and imports would have to be still further cut. The fateful downward spiral would be started. Europe would again be faced with the hunger, chaos, and despair in which communism breeds. 

On the other hand, if our assistance were continued, but cut to a level below the minimum needed-and I may say that in my judgment it is the minimum that is asked for-there would be no margin left for the expansion of production and earning power. Self-support

could not be achieved. The program would shift from recovery tomere relief.

I think it is important that we remember the present and potential significance of the European economy. We are concerned with thefuture of 275,000,000 people. We are concerned with an area whose industrial output is second only to ours and far exceeds that of the Soviet Union and all its satellities. The combined resources of the western European countries must remain on the side of freedom. 

Any other outcome would spell disaster not only for them, but for us and for free men everywhere.

In closing, I should like to express a conviction which I hold deeply. 

It is simply this: That the American people, and the Congress which has acted in their name in launching the greatest cooperative venture ever known in peacetime, have a right to be proud of the role which the United States is playing in Europe today. I have found among the nations participating in this effort the will to do their sharethe determination to stand and work with us to preserve the liberties which we and they cherish in common. If this Nation remains steadfast in its purpose to complete the great work it has undertaken, we will find our partners firm at our side. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Ambassador, we thank you very much for that statement. You covered, I think, a number of points and a wide range of information with astonishing brevity and clearness.

Upon at least two of the questions we have heretofore been seeking information and will continue to seek information, you have given valuable information concerning them. One of them is the very im-portant question of just how far this program has succeeded in its great purpose of stopping in their tracks the march of the communistic armies. We are very grateful for your information in that respect. It is very encouraging indeed to know that we have succeded to the extent indicated by your statement. 

The other question of grave importance is the question of the dissemination in European countries of information with regard to theprogram and America's part in it. For a number of years we have had the unhappy experience of being advised that few people in Europe knew just where all this help was coming from, or knew that it was coming from America and were aware of the motives of the people of the United States in supplying it. 

Your information will be very valuable to the members of the committee in making up their minds upon this measure. I was very glad to get the information with reference to the broad scope and the extent of your information facilities, and the manner in which you cover the whole European field with information respecting the program. 

Dr. Eaton, have you any questions? 

Mr. EATON. I would like first of all to thank the Ambassador for his very comprehensive and lucid statement. In my judgment he is dealing with one of the greatest movements in human history. I may be wrong about that but I have felt all along that it is the very keystone in the arch of modern civilization. 

I would like to raise one question: In this country there is a continuous resentment and agitation against the fact that England has become socialistic and we are helping a socialistic government. Could

you set out any difference of these funds in socialistic England and how you handle them in France and Italy and Belgium?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I will answer your question, if in answering it, it will not give the committee the impression that I believe in the nationalization of industries or some of the internal policies of the governments.

Actually there is a very fair distribution of food and of consumer goods which are in short supply in Britain. The lower-income groups are eating as well as they did before the war but the middle-income groups and the higher-income groups of course do not have the variety that they once had before the war. It has been an achievement which comes from the great work that was done during the war in their rationing system. The British are one of the most disciplined people in the world and have respect for the objectives that are set down by their Government. Their rationing during the war was better than in any other country, even Germany. It has been continued and that principle does lead to a very fair distribution of those goods which are in short supply.

On the Continent where there is a freer distribution of goods under a price system rather than rationing, and where there has not been the same type of rationing that was worked out during the war, during the occupation and otherwise, there is no question about the fact that the lower-income groups are not faring as well and the people with money are living just about as well as they did before the war. 

I am sure those who have gone to Paris have seen that. That is in answer specifically to the one question that you asked.

On the question of their use of our aid, they are using it of course for food for the people, which is raw material for the working man to do his work. They are importing raw materials necessary to expand their industry and they are one of the countries that has expanded its industrial production the most. 

Mr. EATON. That is England.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes, England. They have concentrated on exports through their Government control so that they have a remarkable showing in export trade, also. It is better than in places where there is freedom from controls. In other words they have directed their industries toward export by specifically restricting internal consumption.

Mr. EATON. The objective of the ECA as I understand it is to develop the production powers of these countries, in food and in consumer goods and capital goods. That is our objective so they can become self-supporting.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is right. 

Mr. EATON. When you go to work on that do you deal entirely through the Government or do you take individual enterprises, for instance?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. We deal through the governments in the establishment of the program, but private industry is involved in that program and obtains import licenses from their government in order to buy the raw materials and machinery they need to carry on and expand their production. 

Mr. EATON. You have a nationalized industry in England, for example, which needs assistance. You give that to the Government and they distribute it?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Their Control Board is similar to our TVA 

operation. There is an independent board who operates it. We screen those programs if they use dollar, ECA assistance, and they get import licenses as does private industry. 

Mr. EATON. The essence of our effort abroad is the infusion of blood into a system out of which the economic blood has been drained? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is as good a definition as one can make. It is a system which was bled pretty dry during the war and "transfusion" is as good a way to put it as is possible. 

Mr. EATON. There is a considerable amount of blood being circulated now?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Very much so. It is a healthy situation in 

Europe as it stands today.

Mr. EATON. Thank you Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Has the austerity of the British life been relieved to a certain extent? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes; I would think so. I think you will probably want to ask Mr. Kenney that question to secure more detail than I can give. I am over there constantly and I do note a definite improvement in the austerity, but the austerity, as I have said, particularly falls on the middle-income groups and the higher-income groups. of Chairman KEE. They have certainly had to live for a great number years with very tight belts over there.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes; they have. As far as labor is concerned, the unions have been very restrained in asking for increased wages and the number of strikes has been very small. Perhaps Mr. 

Kenney can give you the details.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Gordon- 

Mr. GORDON. I am very glad to see you again Mr. Ambassador. I am convinced you are doing a very fine job. While on a recent trip to the Marshall-plan-recipient European countries, I noted much improvement. Do you believe you will have to go way beyond the 1952 program that has been laid out? Do you think the people will have a sufficient foundation to continue, themselves?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. We are working with a single objective and so are the participating countries and the OEEC, to carry out the objectives of the act by 1952. It is Mr. Hoffman's determination and mine to see that ECA terminates at the set date in 1952. 

Now, if you ask me to predict what conditions will be in 1952, I would have to ask you some questions, first. First, I would ask, What will be the state of business activity in the United States? That will have a very important bearing on the position of Europe because we have about half the industrial production of the world. 

That means we use and chew up a lot of raw materials that come from the sterling area and the overseas dependent territories of the European countries, and also some from Europe. A drop in industrial production here means a loss of direct and indirect dollar earnings. I am going into that in perhaps too much detail. Then there is the question as to whether they are able to carry out what they have set out to do, which is to create a climate to attract private capital, and whether we do the same thing here. There may be certain situations in particular countries where, from a political standpoint,

or because of special conditions, there may be some questions, but I personally believe they should be dealt with in a different way if we decide we wish to deal with them. In addition to that, a great deal depends upon how aggressively we pursue Point IV. If there is a healthy investment by the United States in the underdeveloped countries and in Europe, it will start cycles of trade. Also, I would say that important in Europe is the character of the development of our own trade policies in being prepared to accept imports if we wish to export. I do believe if we have a reasonable break we will find Europe generally in a condition to be self-sustaining without need for extraordinary help. I say "generally." There may be special situations.

It is sometimes said that those in Europe desire to stay on the dole. 

I want to assure you they do not feel that way. They are the same type of people as we are, and the British Government and the British people and the others do not want to depend on us. They do not like it. 

Mr. GORDON. They just want a start, in other words?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. 

Mr. GORDON. That is all the questions I have this morning, Mr.

Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mrs. Bolton- 

Mrs. BOLTON. Mr. Ambassador, it is very nice to see you here.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Thank you, Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I appreciated very much your courtesy in Paris, seeing the things you have accomplished there, and discussing many matters with your staff and the people in the offices there. I am interested in the fact that in your statement you emphasize rather largely the Communist side of the program. Was that your intent? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I made the statement last year that we were winning the struggle, and I thought I would report on the events that had come about to show the progress that had been made. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Without in any way discounting the importance of all the rest of it. I mean you are not saying that is the only reason we are over there?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Not at all. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I wanted that in the record because we had a little discussion of that.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. As you know, it is my firm belief that the free countries must stand together and if we do we can win the struggle against the aggression that is unfortunately before us. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I would like to get your sense of this, although we will perhaps get more from the information people: In the carrying out of an information program, are you contemplating any program which would come back to the United States so that the people of the United States would be more aware of the actual work of ECA, of the accomplishment of their dollars?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Of course we are not engaged in that activity except to make available to the people who ask us for the information, and for Washington, here, such material. Perhaps Mr. 

Hoffman could best discuss the informational needs here at home. Of course, there are very definite limitations on what a Government agency can do, but the trade-unions, for example, in the United States want

information, and we see they are supplied with the information which they want. We are involved only in giving the information to ECA, Washington, and to the organizations which ask for the information that they particularly require. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I was particularly glad to have you emphasize the very fine work that our trade-union people have done over there. I suppose it cannot really be emphasized enough. They have such direct access to the people who are involved in all of the Communist propaganda, that they can be peculiarly effective. 

On page 5 you speak of the constant process of collaboration on every aspect of economic policy which has helped to build in western Europe à growing sense of common purpose and community of interest. Does the work of the ECA dovetail with some of the work contemplated by the Strasbourg group?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. OEEC is an active organization and de velops programs which are carried out by the different governments. 

So far the Strasbourg group has been discussing policies and making recommendations. 

Mrs. BOLTON. They do not clash?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. They do not. It was arranged that there would be cooperation between the OEEC staff and the Strasbourg staff, in terms of supplying information and otherwise being helpful. 

Mrs. BOLTON. So the two would be very closely allied?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. We must remember the membership of the OEEC is different from the membership of the Council. In my judgment there is a great field for cooperation. 

Mrs. BOLTON. One of our problems in the continuing of the ECA bill is the feeling that is becoming constantly stronger in this country relative to insecurity of our own financial situation and the possibilities of our not being able to do everything we would like to do. Some of the Members of the House feel that unless there is a very definite security reason for such a continuance that they would perhaps have great difficulty in getting their people to understand that it is not only an advisable but a necessary thing to do. 

Can you tie it in with security in a few words? I know how you feel about it. Can you tell us why it is so important that we should continue this on the minimum basis that has been suggested? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I have felt as I have testified before, before this committee, during the hearings on the Atlantic Pact and the military-assistance program, that military assistance and ECA are part of our over-all foreign policy. I do believe that the recovery program which, as Dr. Eaton has said, was really the greatest undertaking that has ever even been contemplated in peacetime and is the basis of our security, is quite remarkable. In the first place unless we have a healthy social condition there cannot be a stable political situation in western Europe. You must have stable social and political situation before you have associates and partners who are able to carry on with us.

As I have pointed out in my presentation there is a very great present-day production in Europe, second only to us. I think it is roughly two-thirds of ours and is very considerably greater than the Soviet Union and her satellites. I believe and feel very strongly that if we can develop a sound social, economic, political situation through the

Marshall plan, we will have associates who will be strong in the concept of the North Atlantic community and will add materially to our security. We need partners in the world and I think we will have strong, healthy, and vigorous partners if we carry this program out.

Mrs. BOLTON. You feel it is quite imperative that we have those partners.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I think it is essential. We would have an unmanageable situation in the world if the Communists' design to seize Europe is carried out or was carried out. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you very much. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield, have you any questions?

Mr. MANSFIELD. Mr. Ambassador, it is nice to have you before the committee again to bring us up to date on the progress of the European recovery program.

Is it true that you and Mr. Hoffman have been very consistent over the past year at least, in notifying the various governments and through them the peoples of Europe that as far as the ECA program is concerned, it will end in 1952. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I think I said it in the first statement I made publicly when I arrived in Paris in May of 1948. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. Do you think that feeling is known to the peoples in western Europe or is it your impression that the people think, regardless of what happens, that we will always come to their assistance and give them the aid necessary to survive and get along? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Those people-and they are growing in numbers who understand the situation, thoroughly appreciate that. 

Those we have not yet reached do not have full knowledge of the Marshall plan and do not realize its importance. The answer to your question is definitely "Yes."

Mr. MANSFIELD. What do you contemplate will be the full cost of the Marshall plan in 1952?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. The rough figure which has been discussed is something in the nature of $3,000,000,000 this year and $2,000,000,000 in the following year which would make a total of around $15,000,- 000,000 for the entire program. I would like to recall to you that in our original presentation of the plan it was estimated that the entire program would cost $17,000,000,000. If the Congress carries through the program recommended this year, and if it is decided next year $2,000,000,000 is the correct sum, there will be a saving of $2,000,- 000,000 from the original presentation which was made to this committee.

Mr. GORDON. Of the 4-year plan. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. I believe you said, Mr. Ambassador, that the sum requested this year is the lowest possible sum to keep this program on a rehabilitation basis and to cut it would in effect turn the program back into a relief measure, something which we have not envisaged in all our discussions of this proposal. Therefore, the 2.9 billion dollars is the absolute minimum required to carry on the program effectively on a rehabilitation basis? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is my opinion and the opinion of my associates in Paris, as well as Mr. Hoffman and his staff, here.

Mr. MANSFIELD. I was very interested and pleased in the emphasis you placed on the information program. I know you have many worth-while individuals doing that kind of work in Europe, but I want to call your attention, specifically, to the work of two individuals I had the opportunity to look into. They are Tom Hodges in 

Paris and Andrew Berding in Rome. I think Mr. Berding has done an outstanding job in conveying to the Italian people through all media of information, just what the ECA program is and what it is accomplishing. I was very pleased with the work of those two gentlemen and especially the latter because of the great impact it had had upon the thinking of the Italian people as a whole. 

That is all, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Merrow, have you any questions?

Mr. MERROW. Mr. Ambassador, in connection with the replies you just gave to Mr. Mansfield, does it mean that 2.95 billion dollars was in your opinion the absolute minimum. Is it true that 150 million dollars is to be carried over from the present year? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is the estimate Mr. Hoffman gave yesterday.

Mr. MERROW. That is the estimate which is to be carried over for the next fiscal year.

Now is it entirely possible that there may be some left out of the 

2.95 billion dollars to be carried over into the following year?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Mr. Hoffman has testified, and I fully endorse it, that in the administration of the ECA, we will save every conceivable dollar that can be saved, if it is found it can be saved, but it is our present judgment that this is the minimum which should be appropriated for this purpose and it would be dangerous to appropriate a lower sum. I think the very fact that Mr. Hoffman has been able to testify in such manner, I hope, will give the committee assurance that the use of the money is very carefully scrutinized. It is fair to say it would have been very easy to have spent not only the $150,- 000,000, but substantially more than that if that care had not been exercised.

Mr. MERROW. I think the money has been carefully scrutinized, but 

I have the feeling that since we have some money that may be carried over from this year it may be possible to appropriate a lesser amount for the coming year. However, I do appreciate your feeling on the matter.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I would think that if Mr. Hoffman has served you faithfully, it would give you confidence instead of the feeling that because he has brought back $150,000,000, he should be penalized for having been a faithful servant of the Congress. You see there was some good luck that occurred. There were far better crops than we expected. Also, there were some things that did not go quite so fast. There were some investment programs which were not carried through as fast, and that was disappointing. We cannot foresee all of the conditions which will arise and therefore I want to reiterate that I do believe this sum is the minimum that is safe to appropriate for this program.

Mr. MERROW. It is very gratifying to note this sum is lower than the sum of last year, because as you know, there is a feeling that it should be kept as low as possible for the coming fiscal year.

Mr. Ambassador, if you have not already done so, would you be willing to comment on what you anticipate to be the progress toward European integration during the remainder of this program? I realize considerable progress has been made, but do you expect that to be accelerated?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I do expect it to be accelerated. As Mr. 

Hoffman testified, the objectives were defined last autumn, and the Council of Ministers passed certain resolutions on November 2 which included the acceptance of a program of further integration. I believe that program will be carried out next year, and I am hopeful it will be expanded the following year.

Mr. MERROW. You anticipate progress toward the solution of the current difficulties during the next 2 years?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. We are hopeful that we will attain transferability of currencies for current transactions at least during that period so that the bilateralism that sprang up after the war will be broken and a multilateral trading system will develop in Europe which will last after the termination of ECA.

Mr. MERROW. Does there seem to be a willingness and desire on the part of participating governments to get at the solution of these problems as rapidly as possible?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. There has been a committee of the Council working since November 2 on the development of the Payments Union. 

The group is still at work and I am optimistic they will reach agreement on a satisfactory Payments Union by June. 

Mr. EATON. Is that a union politically or economically or both?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. This is a payments union. It is a clearing union.

Mr. MANSFIELD. Would the gentleman yield to clarify a point in my own thinking?

Mr. MERROW. I yield. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. In relation to this 150 million dollars which Mr. 

Hoffman has told the joint committees has been saved, am I correct when I state that when the original budget request was sent down it was for 3.1 billion dollars, and on the basis of the bill introduced for 

2.9 billion dollars, that would indicate good faith on the part of Mr. 

Hoffman in thereby asking for a lower amount. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Ribicoff, have you any questions?

Mr. RIBICOFF. Yes, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Harriman, through you I would like to express my high regard for the enire ECA staff in Europe in every category. I found some hard, realistic thinking and great conception of the problems we are facing in the world today. As the ECA men took me around to different Europeans, there was no question as to the high regard and confidence the various Europeans have in the point of view and intelligence of the Americans representing ECA abroad. That is very, very important. I often think that I would like to see some of the wraps taken from the thinking of ECA, publicly, and some of the men in the higher categories telling the public what they actually think, even though some of the facts may not be palatable. The American people can take hard thinking even better than some of the men in Government and some of us in Congress, too.

Out of this $150,000,000, how much of that is saved by the nonuse of the guaranty fund of ECA last year?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. None. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you have any confidence in a greater use of private capital during the guaranty program? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I haven't studied the details of it but I understand there is under consideration a general insurance operation under the Export-Import Bank. I think that will be helpful. I think if there is a certain encouragement on this side, there will be a movement of private capital. I understand that exists. On the other hand, the countries have undertaken to make a study of the conditions that are necessary to attract private capital in the European countries and their overseas territories. If that work is fruitfully done and the countries, which they are now disposed to do, adopt those policies, I think you will see an increasing flow of private capital. There is a recognition in Europe of the need of private capital in all of the countries, both in the metropolitan areas and in the overseas territories, and there are certain things, certain practices and laws, which have to be changed in order to give the encouragement that is necessary. 

Thus far, as you know, there has been relatively little private capital flowing.

Mr. RIBICOFF. I would say to a great extent that due to the type of law we have on the books, it is difficult to see why any man would risk his own money or his company's money so long as there is no guaranty against extraordinary political risks. Of course, the House passed such a law. My feeling is that if we are going to get private capital flowing into Europe, we will have to give them guaranties against these extraordinary risks which are not in the normal course of business.

In talking to many of your chiefs over in Europe, I got the feeling that they thought the time was now ripe to extend these guaranties and encourage Americans to invest capital in Europe. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. My suggestion would be that such a program should set up separate legislation under the Export-Import Bank rather than for ECA to handle it. I think it would be better to do it on a world-wide basis. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You have one problem where you are giving it to undeveloped areas. That is a problem of its own. Here you have 

European recovery. I know of no better agency than the present 

ECA set-up because they know what would help European recovery. 

I am not talking about unrestricted investments; I am speaking of the type of investment that would help and forward European recovery and to that extent take some of the burden off the taxpayers' backs.

Now, in this first amendment that has been proposed, this fund will facilitate the development of transferability of European currencies, I assume, you are aiming toward multilateral trade. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is correct. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You should be highly commended for suggesting it. 

I think that is one of the major factors right now in Europe. 

What would you say the prognosis would be of this particular section? You are going to get a fund and you are going to set up a socalled over-all agency in OEEC to manage it; is that it?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is right. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You are going to use this fund to clear the balances from one country to the other. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. A certain part would be used for that. 

There will be credits given within the system by the countries themselves, and in certain cases, they would use their own dollars. Of course, any dollars that are used, which are ECA dollars, would be only used by the Payments Union with our approval. It would not be giving the Payments Union a free hand in the use of it. We would sit in on such use of the ECA dollars.

Mr. RIBICOFF. If this fund is going to work, you are first going to have to break down many of these present trade restrictions. It will then be easier to have a free flow of trade from one country to another without regard to whether or not they have the money to pay for that particular transaction. That, basically, will help everybody in the world.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. It relates to intra-European trade only. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. But, eventually, it would help all around. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. If this works, it is designed to be a step in world convertibility of currencies. However, this is the first step to get convertibility for certain types of transactions within Europe itself. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You are hopeful that this will come.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. Its objective is to be a step in world multilateral trade and world convertibility of currencies. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Burleson.

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Harriman, yesterday the Secretary of State said the Kremlin was showing signs of increasing boldness in its activities against the Marshall plan. What is your explanation of that increasing boldness on their part?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Well, they had a pretty strong set-back. 

It is a reformation of their program and they are going to work again on the objective which they had from the beginning, to handicap the recovery program.

Mr. JUDD. You think that it is just a reformation of their lines; that it isn't because of their victory in the Far East which gives them satellites and security there, allowing them to concentrate more of their efforts on Europe?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I do not know what the motivation of the mentality in the Kremlin is. 

Mr. JUDD. What form does this increasing boldness take?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Increased propaganda, liquidating Tito ism from the ranks of the Communist parties in the different countries; getting out some of the unions with the expectation of creating trouble in the shipment of arms; holding up on the Austrian Peace Treaty; and so forth.

Mr. JUDD. How much of a drain on France do her military efforts in Indochina constitute?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. She has a number of her effective troops in Indochina and it does affect her ability to play a larger part in 

North Atlantic security.

Mr. JUDD. Is it not also a drain on her economy, apart from the military effort?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. She has a military budget of something over 400,000,000,000 francs and it affects her ability to carry out certain other things.

Mr. JUDD. Do you know what it might cost her to hold Indochina? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I do not know. 

Mr. JUDD. Would it be embarrassing for you to get those figures?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I do not know if they have them and if they have them whether they are in a shape that can be exposed. 

Mr. JUDD. The question has been raised, would it be better for France to let Indochina go and concentrate on recovery in Europe, or is it better to continue to try to hold Indochina, even though that jeopardizes her recovery in Europe, or forces us to put in a good deal more money?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I am told Mr. Bingham has certain figures which he is prepared to give this committee in executive session. 

On the other question, my view is that Indochina is an area which I hope can be saved. I do not know the conditions there, however. 

Mr. JUDD. Nearly everybody hopes it can be saved, but do you think that is sufficiently important to justify jeopardizing her own recovery?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I am not in a position to discuss the Far 

East so I cannot go further than that. Indochina was an important trading country with the Western World and it is my hope she will again become one.

Mr. JUDD. If she is free, she is an asset, but the present struggle is a liability and a drain.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, I hope somewhere in our hearings we can get some testimony on this because it is one of the vital links in the whole program.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. That is a question which I think should have been addressed to the Secretary of State.

is partly due to the fact that the East does not have the products which the West wants.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Turkey's has quite substantially. Greece, of course, because of civil war, has been rather behind in the development of its products and trade since so much of its national effort has gone to the war up to now.

On these countries that are the fringe countries surrounding the ECA participating countries, is there anything being done to stimulate the trade to those countries, with ECA countries, and also are ECA countries being asked to stimulate trade with those countries; for instance, Egypt and the United States?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. In that part of the Mediterranean, we deal only with Turkey and with Greece. Of course, the fact that 

Britain is the banker for the sterling area does encourage trade, generally, with those nations which use sterling as their international currency, so it has stimulated some trade with all of the sterling area nations.

Mr. FULTON. The countries that are near the participating countries are what I have called the fringe countries. Now, then, when we are stimulating the development of certain participating countries, are we also trying to help these fringe countries, too? Is the ECA program being integrated so it has effect beyond the limits of the act? Are we trying to develop any recovery just outside of the confines of the ECA countries?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Not directly, but indirectly it does have an effect upon the expansion of their trade. In Egypt, their longstaple cotton, of course, is moving because of the development of industry in Europe and that gives Egypt an opportunity to buy from these other countries, but it is the indirect effect of a healthy economy in Europe rather than any direct action that we are taking. 

Mr. FULTON. Mr. Black of the World Bank said the other day at lunch that he felt the World Bank could handle any loan requirements of any countries, for reconstruction or development, from here on.

Is there an overlapping between the world bank's sphere, then, and what you are doing at this point?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. We haven't felt so up to the present time. 

You will remember, when the original presentation was made to Congress, it was expected there would be substantial World Bank loans to the participating countries. There have only been a few in rather limited sums and substantially less than was originally contemplated, but we are certainly hopeful that if conditions are sound at the end of this period as we expect they will be, the World Bank will be able to take care of the expanded capital requirements of the participating countries and their overseas territories, which will help carry on, after ECA is over, the expansion of the European economy and the economy of the overseas territories. 

Mr. FULTON. The Secretary, yesterday, spoke of assistance after 

1952. There will be need of assistance after ECA terminates. Can you give us, in your estimation, what the standards for aid should be when and as that time comes? Just as a general statement on the standard. Do you mean the 1938 level?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. I made a general statement on this subject in answer to a previous question. I said that ECA, in my judgment, should end as was contemplated, and the situation dealt with, if there were any special situations, or policies, in terms of encouraging private capital or World Bank loans. That should be considered on the basis of conditions that exist at that time. 

Mr. FULTON. What would your standard be? What would you measure the conditions existing at that time against? My question goes a little beyond the other item. Should we look and say, "What were you in 1938?" Or should we ask if participating countries are up to the average of other countries in our civilization, or should we determine what people in that economy need to live, a norm or standard, generally? How should we in Congress proceed to determine what the need is and what standards should be laid out? 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. There is an imbalance in our trade with the world which has gradually come down. It was in the nature of 

11.25 billion dollars in 1947 and is down now to around 5 billion dollars. I think we should recognize that condition as an unhealthy one and we should concentrate on national policies in encouraging two-way trade, and encouraging sound loans through the International Bank, through private capital and investment. If we do balance our payments throughout the world, it will benefit everybody if we can get back to a multilateral-trading system, and then we should consider each project. The private individuals will consider it from the standpoint of whether they have an opportunity for the lending or investing of money, and the quasi-public institutions such as the International Bank would be considering it, based on the value of each project, based on the standards which have been set by their institution.

Mr. FULTON. So, it is partly a balance of payments question. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes. 

Mr. FULTON. In addition, it is a budgetary question within the country and, thirdly, it is an economic question of the level of living within the country as to whether it is a healthy economy. 

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Each country has different views about. that. In my testimony, I pointed out the very high investment rate

in Europe which is an indication that these countries are, through their policies, encouraging a limitation of consumption and a maximizing of the expenditures for capital investment. That varies to some degree, country by country, but those are matters which by and large each country will have to decide itself. Then the particular institution dealing with the problem can judge whether those policies are sound, and make loans or investments as they may judge the soundness of the policies, or the conditions in those countries. 

Mr. FULTON. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, may I ask a few additional questions?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. Yes.

Now, on the last page of your testimony, you speak eloquently and accurately, I think, of the importance to us of the future of the

Europe does not have?

Ambassador HARRIMAN. If she is able to buy the raw materials, it is of great importance.

Ambassador HARRIMAN. One of the wise aspects of the Point IV 

program is that if all of the people of those underdeveloped countries see some hope, I am confident they will not be subjected to the type of Communist infiltration that you have seen in other places.

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS,  

The committee met, pursuant to call at 10: 50 a. m., in the Foreign

(chairman), presiding.

We have this morning a continuation of our hearings on H. R. 7378, the bill to amend the ECA Act. We have with us Mr. Hoffman, the 

Administrator of the Economic Cooperation Administration. 

Mr. Hoffman, we are very happy indeed to have you with us this morning. I believe the understanding was that this was to be a questioning period based upon the testimony you have previously given before the committee. 

Mr. Richards, have you any questions?

STATEMENT OF HON. PAUL G. HOFFMAN, ADMINISTRATOR, ECONOMIC COOPERATION ADMINISTRATION 

Mr. RICHARDS. Will you tell us something of your efforts to get these people to unify their currencies and cut out trade quotas? They are always going to do these things but they do not seem to get to it. 

I do not believe they are going to do it until something is written in this bill for you to use as a lever. What do you think of writing something in this bill of that nature?

Mr. HOFFMAN. As you know, we are not proposing there be such a change in the law. That may or may not be necessary. But nevertheless we want the Congress to understand what we propose doing. 

The amendment proposed in the bill, instead of advancing funds in all cases directly to the participating nations, would give us the right, after setting aside a certain amount of the funds, to advance those funds to a central institution. The funds so advanced would in turn reach the individual nations but in such a way that we think the effect of recovery would be multiplied. 

Mr. RICHARDS. That is the $600,000,000.

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes. We are not set on the amount but we said not less than that figure. We want to set aside whatever we have to set aside in order to encourage the kind of action that you are suggesting. 

I would like to repeat one line of my testimony, only, and that is that we really are expecting the Europeans to accomplish as much in 69

the way of integration of their economies in 25 months as what might reasonably be expected in 25 normal years. If you will just reverse this picture and see what our reaction would be in this country, I think you can understand why we have had some difficulties abroad that have in no way discouraged us. In other words, it is interesting, I think, to note that 40 years ago you had relatively few barriers to trade and commerce in Europe. "Relatively," I say. We had none among our 48 States. Actually, due to improvement in communication and transporation in that 40 years, ours became the most closely integrated economy in the world. 

Now, suppose that had been reversed. Suppose 40 years ago each one of our 48 States had started to erect trade barriers and behind those barriers had built up protected industries, and in those industries you would have a labor interest also. And then suppose, as a result of our having taken that route, we found, as the Europeans now have found, that the economy is not as efficient as it should be. 

Suppose the situation developed where we were once more getting our capital from Europe as we once did, you see, and one of the strings attached to that was that these barriers had to come down. Well, it does not take much imagination to picture the kind of protests you would get from every protected industry in every State. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Right there, Mr. Hoffman, I do not remember that the European nations ever handed out to us $8,000,000,000. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. This act of ours in contributing funds for the rebuilding of Europe is an act without precedent in the history of generosity. There is nothing like it I know of that has ever been done before. I hope it pays off sufficiently well so that perhaps it will not be the last act of its kind, but it is almost the first. You can put it that way. I am just trying to picture a situation. In other words, if somebody came over here from Europe and said, "Obviously, gentlemen, these trade barriers must come down in the United States," I can just see the broom manufacturers in Tennessee saying, "This is terrible. We cannot compete with those awful broom manufacturers up in Michigan. They employ slave labor. It is a terrible industry they have up there making brooms."

Soon you would have that multiplied 10,000 times, and that is what has been going on in Europe. It is natural, it is normal, and no one should be distressed by it. You expect it. However, you have to get some pressure in there to offset the pressure of those who want to see the protections continued.

Those who have no special interest in a given industrial or labor situation are almost all of one mind, and that is that Europe must bring these barriers down and must create this free market or it can never realize its potentials for both prosperity and security. It cannot be done.

Mr. RICHARDS. I believe you have said there is going to be no permanent road to prosperity for Europe after 1952 unless they do these things.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I feel that a great deal of progress has been made, Mr. Richards, in getting acceptance of the idea that this must move forward, and it must move forward not in order to comply with any directive from us. In other words, to be successful you have got to bring these people along to where they finally make up their minds that this is hard to do but they are going to do it. 

There is one situation which has developed which gives us our real hope that this can be brought off and brought off in such a manner that there can be no criticism from anybody anywhere about it. In the first instance we told the members of the Council of the 

OEEC what we felt should constitute a first step toward integration: 

We did not say, "This is what you must do," but we said, "these are our ideas as to what would be an adequate first step." Then the members of the Council, after considering it, came to a unanimous decision as to what they would do. This was their decision. In other words, we did not say, "This is our program which we think will do this for you," but we said, "Here are certain goals we are mutually agreed upon. Here are certain avenues that should be explored as avenues that would take us toward that goal, but you figure it out for yourselves." So they developed their own program on November 2 and that program was a program which was not entirely satisfactory from our standpoint, but one that we were glad to accept because it constituted in our opinion a thoroughly satisfactory first step. 

Now, this is their program and all we have kept insisting is that they carry out their own program. 

Of course, as I say, they perhaps adopted this program, I think, in entire good faith and afterward began to realize there were some pretty tough obstacles that had to be overcome to get that program into effect. Then the natural reaction was to postpone until tomorrow what is unpleasant to do today. As I say, they began to get all the protests from all the people whose interests would be adversely affected.

I have never thought it wise to use any coercion. It may sound strange. We have a perfect right to use it. I think we have a right to lay down the law just as hard as we want to do it, but I doubt the wisdom of doing so. At least in my business experience I have

never gotten the same results from people who were coerced as I have from people who were persuaded. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Let us say you have a board of directors of this corporation over there, say. Every man sitting there says, "This should be done." Mr. HOFFMAN. I do not think our views are apart at all, because we are asking for this change in the law so that we can hold this money out in the first instance and not allocate it. In other words, we are advocating we hold out not less than $600,000,000. 

Mr. RICHARDS. But it puts the pressure on you. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. We do not mind pressure, and as far as we are concerned we will hold out wherever we have to hold out to see that there is an effective union, and at least $600,000,000 will not be distributed unless an aggressive program of trade liberalization is undertaken through an effective payments union. 

I do not know exactly how that will come out, but it is our hope, because it is the only sound result, that all the nations will join in that payments union. If in the first instance some nations say they cannot join for some particular reason, it simply means they do not get their proportionate share of the $600,000,000, or whatever is held out, for their particular countries.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I have felt, or at least in making our presentation we felt that the case for further appropriations had to rest squarely on the first goal; namely, that of putting the European countries in a position where they could go on without extraordinary outside assistance. In other words, you have this problem of the dollar gap, with which you are familiar. If you do not go ahead with this program or if we do not go ahead with this program, and if we terminated this program today, literally there are not the dollars in Europe to buy from America what they need to keep their economies functioning and to keep their economies recovering. There is, as nearly as we can figure it, for the next year a requirement for $3,000,000,000 in addition to what they earn just to buy what they have to buy to keep going. You cannot make cotton cloth without cotton and if we do not give them the money to buy the cotton their mills go down and then their economies are no longer balanced. It is not because they are not producing, but it is because they need what they can get from the United States. Some countries need food. They need wheat because they cannot grow enough in Europe, and as a matter of fact should not grow enough because I do not believe that Europe ever will be self-sufficient when it comes to food. They have to get more tools, and they have to get some equipment from us which will help them build up their power supply. The fundamental lack in Europe is nonhuman energy, to supplement human energy and multiply its value.

1 If you pull $3,000,000,000 out, or if you give an inadequate appropriation, you would put Europe back to where she was in 1947. This would not happen quickly, but she would go back because the effect would spiral. As I say, these are not dollars that they are going to throw around; these are dollars they are going to spend in the dollar area for goods they can get only in the dollar area. Whether that money goes in the first instance directly to the countries, or channels out through the payments union, essentially it comes back to America and is spent for goods either here or elsewhere in the dollar area.
