Mr. EATON. I want to say first it is one of the strange events if not accidents of history that we should have been able to obtain the leadership of our friend Mr. Hoffman in this great enterprise. I feel more grateful for that every day and if the enterprise succeeds, the key to the situation will be Mr. Hoffman's leadership.

Now having received the endorsement of the Republicans on that issue and of the Democrats as well, I raise this question which comes to us today through the newspaper reports: There is a tremendous

growth of questioning and antagonism in this country with reference to the socialistic government of England being supported by this enterprise, and judging from.the early election reports they have been returned to power. Now are we going to continue to build up the socialistic government of England in preparation for our own launching into that abyss?

Mr. HOFFMAN. That is a very fair question. I think I would like to answer in this way: We have had to work through governments, obviously, in trying to reach our goals, but we never have forgotten what to my mind was the basic concept of the Marshall plan, and that was an effort to bring about a situation in which free men could live in decency and dignity. If they did live in decency and dignity, it was assumed that we would see free institutions maintained. That is the basic concept and I still hold it is a sound and a good concept. 

Working through governments, we have worked through all kinds of governments. If you want me to make a case against almost any government we are working through, I can do it. 

Mr. EATON. Including the American Government?

Mr. HOFFMAN. I might even make a case sometimes against a government which is fairly close, but we have worked with governments, as I say, that vary substantially from one benevolent dictatorship to free economies, and from economies that are still in my opinion not sufficiently advanced to those that are experimenting in ways that are interesting.

You have going on in Great Britain this experiment with a socialistic economy. In the first place I think we would be very wise in trying to see what is going on, and in getting away from the word "socialism," because "socialism" in Europe has so many varied meanings. I should say that a great many of the so-called Socialists in Europe are thinking in terms of bringing about a situation where there is social justice, where there is no longer an exploitation of the workers. Let us not forget there has been an exploitation of the workers in different economies of Europe in the past, and I think that drove a good many people into a socialism that was primarily a protest against conditions and primarily a desire to see social justice rendered. I do not want to name names, but two or three of the men who are most prominently tagged as Socialists, in my opinion, are Socialists only in that respect.

Then you have another economic concept that carries a tag of socialism. You have Hitler's national socialism. I think the central point of difference is this: You have economies such as ours. I think we are the great example in the world and I think at some time the world will realize what has been accomplished here. We have an economy in which there is a wide diffusion of decision-making. In other words, 150,000,000 people decide what they want to buy for themselves, and 3,000,000 heads of separate businesses decide how they will conduct their separate business. As long as they have stayed within the law, they have little intervention from the law in the operation of their business, and individual decision-making is our cwn.

Against that you have what is not a new concept, at all. It is a very ancient concept, and that is that a few people can better make the

decisions for the many than can the many for themselves. And that, I think, is the basic difference. in concept between these economies. 

Now, the British economy is a planned economy. The Australian economy was a planned economy. The New Zealand economy was a planned economy. I think as long as the people have a free ballot they have a perfect right to decide how much decision-making they want to give up. The giving up of decision-making becomes very dangerous when it gets to the point where a few decide that in order to enforce their decisions they are going to use bayonets or bullets. 

I do not think there is the slightest danger of the English people ever letting their decision-makers use bayonets or bullets in order to enforce decisions. I think, as a matter of fact, in certain areas they have already found that decision-making is very difficult to have carried out, for example, in the movement of people from one town to another.

Here is what I said a year ago, and I repeat it, and if history does not bear me out on this, then I am sure I will have been proved a very false prophet indeed. As long as the people have a free ballot, give them time and they will get pretty sick of having other people make their decisions for them. Now, it does take time because there are alternatives. Where a system has not done well by its people as a free system, alternatives may be chosen which we do not quite understand, but as I say, human nature being what it is, as long as a country is reasonably prosperous you will find, in my opinion, more and more resentment against centralized decision-making. I am not saying what will happen. I do not know. I just say that I for one am very glad that the British people have decided to try this experiment. 

As long as the American people do not decide to try it, it is all right with me.

Mr. EATON. They do not want us to pay the bill for it, do they? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. There is nothing to that story. Indirectly and over the long pull, I do not say whether it will or will not come out. I do not get into that argument. We would not be interested in advice from any other people as to how we would benefit by a greater concentration of decision-making in the few, as against our present disorderly diffusion, which I love, sir.

Mr. EATON. Your view is that we are over there to develop as far as possible economic safety and prosperity for the masses of the people of these countries, and so far as possible to help organize a political unity among them and in order to accomplish that you have to use the government that is in power where it is necessary, without any enforcement on your part as to their fundamental principles. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Our job really has been a job of seeing that people had food where they are hungry, seeing that they had tools to work with. The kind of governments we have had to work with have in some cases complicated that problem, in some cases made it relatively easy, but in no case that I can recall have we been unable to work with these governments, even though they vary very widely in their ideologies.

Mr. HOFFMAN. Mr. Vorys, I think that we would be in favor of putting as much of that into loans as could possibly be repaid, but here the general figures on debt are not important. The only figure that is important is the capacity to earn dollars. In other words, that is the thing that is really at the present moment causing us our greatest concern, and that concern would be added to if they had to pay us back dollars when they cannot even now make enough dollars to buy what they need to buy from us in order to just survive. I think, in the effort to get back a few dollars, we would only embarrass our relationships, because the one thing we do not want in my opinion is the creation of more bad debts, debts that cannot be paid. They

will pay us. I mean if we would take their goods, the things they want us to take, we could probably get it back, but we do not want their goods because their goods have been too high-priced and for other reasons. Sometimes we have had tariffs against them and would not take the goods. We have barred them. But they cannot service the debt except with dollars they earn. As I say I think we have had something in the way of a near miracle in the way of production in Europe, but it will take another miracle to get them to the point where, from the standpoint of the dollars they need, they will have enough dollars when we pull out. We are right in the middle of, I think, organizing as energetic a drive to try to expand dollar earnings as some very competent Americans can conceive. But

I would be exaggerating wildly if I told you there is any hope that that drive can do more than add three or four hundred million dollars to the dollar income.

They have to get three or four hundred million dollars from increased exports, and they have to bring up their earnings from invisibles like tourism and invisible services, and we have to hope that Americans will make some investments in Europe, in order to let them get their noses above water in 1953. I do not see getting any substantial improvement in that for another decade. In the face of that, to ask them to take loans instead of grants is to ask them to commit what I think is an immoral act, because I do not believe people should sign notes they cannot pay and I will tell you they cannot pay them. 

As you know, we have not given for the past year any but conditional aid to Belgium or Sweden. On this point of ability to repay dollar loans, it is not the internal fiscal situation of the country that is important; Ireland shows a wonderful statement as far as a little country is concerned, but how can you get dollars out of Ireland. They do not earn any.

Mr. HOFFMAN. We cannot get them on a 35-year basis, Mr. Vorys. 

Mr. VORYS. The British did rather well for a couple hundred years making loans that were not paid back in 2 years but over long periods.

Mr. HOFFMAN. We do not want to make bad loans and I do not know where they will get these dollar earnings for a long time ahead.

Mr. VORYS. If Europe is in that bad shape I am wondering whether this is a recovery or a relief program we are dealing with. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I have not made myself clear: It is not that Europe cannot do well by herself. Most of these countries, I think, can be gotten into a state of internal balance. That can be done. But the tough question is how they can earn dollars, because this is the world's toughest market. This economy of ours is so efficient, today. Tomorrow, if there was any way in the world of having people earn dollars, we could sell goods abroad to the tune of $12,000,000,000 or $15,000,- 000,000 a year without a bit of effort, and maybe $25,000,000,000 a year. 

The problem is getting paid for it. They have to get those dollars. 

They have to earn them. And they have to get them by selling us goods and services, or selling goods and services to somebody else that has sold to us, and I do not mind telling you that their economy today, their industrial economy, from the standpoint of output per manhour, is not 50 percent as efficient as ours. That means that all they can sell us are those goods which have high labor content, handicraft goods which we are no longer in the market for, and some raw materials through triangular trade, such as tin and the like. But the pattern of triangular trade is all changed because these European nations which were able to earn dollars by this means up until the war now find that in the case of those dollars they earned through triangular trade the people who earn them want to keep them to use themselves for buying in the United States. In other words, the Indonesians no longer want to pay their dollars to Holland for imports from Holland so the Dutch can buy from us. They want to buy from us direct. 

The Malayans want to buy from us direct. The Indians are independent now, and they do not want to siphon all their trade through Great Britain. They do not want the British to get the dollars they earn selling jute to us by selling cloth to them. They want to buy cloth from us because it is cheaper, and better for the most part. 

That is the kind of a world we are in. We do not recognize yet, I do not believe, the completely dominant position we have in the world from the standpoint of production. There has been built up in 

America in the last 50 years an efficiency in production that has put us so far ahead of the rest of the world that the rest of the world is having, and is going to have in the foreseeable future, an extremely difficult time earning dollars. Now the only thing I say is, I know as a good businessman you do not want us to make bad loans, and if you can show us any place we can make a good loan, we will make it, but we do not want to be accused here, and you do not want to be accused, of having deceived the American public by making them think this program is going to cost them less than it really is. Bad paper is not an asset; it is a liability. All that does is create friction between the person who holds it and the person who owes the money. That is all we would get out of loans in my opinion at the present, and all we

would get over the next 35 or 40 years would be headaches. We would not get dollars.

I am talking about the long pull. I think over the long pull we would never want ourselves in a position where we are relying on any kind of a give-away program to help this economy because I happen to believe that that is approaching it in a way I consider to be unsound. Chairman KEE. Mr. Carnahan, have you any questions? 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Mr. Chairman and Mr. Hoffman, the big problem confronting us seems to be the closing of the dollar gap or the ability of foreign countries to earn dollars. Now, just to close the dollar gap, there are but two ways to do it. That is by grants or imports. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I would say there are other ways it can be closed. 

You have touched on the basic ways. In other words, putting it in the most simple terms, they can close it by buying less from us, by selling more to us, or by getting us to invest dollars, which gives them dollars, although not on a very sound basis because it is only by getting balance on an earning rather than a capital investment basis that you can be sure of your ground; but that is, nevertheless, a factor in the situation. In other words, if the world situation were such that we were exporting capital every year to the tune of $1,000,- 000,000 a year, that billion dollars would be a very important factor in closing the dollar gap.

Mr. CARNAHAN. These loans would have to be classed against the import source. If we make a loan to Britain, for instance, we are just postponing the headache.

Mr. HOFFMAN. We will have to take that in imports someday. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. We will have to take the imports 25 years from now. 

It is just a question of whether we want to adjust the problem now or whether we want to dodge the problem and say, "Well, 25 years from now, we will worry about it then" if we make a loan. 

In your opinion, would it be a healthy situation for us, if we have countries all over the world owing us sizable sums? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I think it would depend entirely upon the ability of those countries to repay those loans. If a country can usefully use the money to build its economy and can see a way to pay it back, then I think that is a good, sound loan. I think about the same conditions govern there that govern in any other business loan. It is not good business to loan money to someone who cannot pay it back. You have to find out how they are going to pay it back. On the other

hand, if they can use that money and create new dollar earning power with it, then it is a good loan. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. I was thinking what the effect might be on our own economy. Should large loans be made? The countries are going to have to earn the dollars and, as you said, there are only two sources of dollars. There is really only one source of dollars and that is selling either goods or service produced by the other country with their labor and their national resources to us for dollars. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I do not think I answered that too well. Let me illustrate particularly what I meant. I think, if we started making loans, and if, just on a straight banking basis, we could not see how those loans would be repaid, then I say making that type of a loan is simply storing up trouble for ourselves. But, let us take a different kind of a situation. Let us say this country is running short of iron ore. Let us say there are great iron-ore deposits in South America that might be developed, and we need the ore. Investments in that type of development would be thoroughly sound and would improve relations with the country because we need the iron ore; we would pay for it in dollars and the loan could be serviced and amortized. I think there has been too little thought of the dollar aspect of the loans. 

Any more loans to Great Britain, for example, would have no meaning, because as it is, Great Britain is going to have a very rough time earning the dollars to buy what she needs to buy with dollars and to service her present debt. I don't see how she can get out from under that. I do not think you can generalize. I think you have to take the situation and analyze it and say, "Can this country pay it back?"

We have made a loan, which we hope is good, to Iceland. They are using it up there for expanding their only industry, which is fishing. 

They are getting so many new types of refrigerating ships. There is a gambling chance that they can earn enough money to make that a good loan. That is all right. It helps Iceland and helps us, and we all gain by it. Too often, we have loaned money on the general credit of the country without ever getting into this question of whether they can earn the dollars to service the loan. You can have a situation in which a country might be running a very substantial surplus internally and not be able to service a very small dollar loan because they can't get the dollars.

Mr. CARNAHAN. I do not want to be misunderstood, that I would oppose any loan. I am sure there are loans that are perfectly worthy. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I think the point you make is a real one. In other words, our loan policy should have much more realism and much more good, sound banking sense in it than it has had up to now. We have loaned on what we consider the assets of a country. The assets mean nothing. The question is can they earn enough dollars to service the loan, and there are not many places that can.

Mr. Hoffman, I have been one of those fighting for economic integration and political federation in Europe.

Now, may I turn to Asia, which has been my second greatest concern in working for European recovery, second only to the necessity for the countries in Europe to make a most vigorous integrated attack upon their problems as well as a vigorous individual attack. 

The latter, they have done well; the former they haven't done very well.

It is my firm conviction that they cannot become self-supporting in Europe if they lose access to the markets and materials of the Far East. How much has it taken out of the French economy to carry on its defense of Indochina?

I asked this of Mr. Harriman and the Secretary of State the other day and neither one of them had the figures.

Mr. BISSELL. Mr. Judd, I can supply you with fairly accurate figures, I think; perhaps by this afternoon. I think that has been running in the order of over $500,000,000 worth of costs per year, although a very small part of that cost is a cost that has to be paid in dollars, but it has represented a large drain on French economic resources. 

(The statement referred to is as follows:) 

French Indochina has traditionally been one of the most valuable parts of the French Union. The three areas of Indochina-Laos, Cambodia, and the new state of Viet Nam-contain abundant agricultural and industrial resources, such

as rice, rubber, corn, cotton, coal, tin, zinc, manganese, iron ore, phosphates, timber, jute, and pepper. Before the war, Indochina had a favorable balance in its trade with the rest of the world and thus was an important source of foreign exchange for metropolitan France and the French Union as a whole. Indochina was one of the few countries of the world which had a trade surplus with the United States, as a result of its sizable exports of rubber. 

The unsettled political conditions which followed the liberation of Indochina after the Second World War prevented the area from regaining its prewar position in foreign trade. In the past few years, moreover, France has been engaged in an active military struggle against Ho Chi-Minh and his Communist and pro-Communist forces. Exports of rice and rubber, the two principal export commodities, have been greatly reduced because of unsettled labor conditions, blockades and counterblockades, and guerilla or open warfare. As a result, French Indochina now has the most unfavorable balance of payments in the world, including a substantial deficit with the United States. Since Indochina remains part of the French Union, this deficit is in the last analysis borne principally by metropolitan France, and most of the deficit arises in fact from the extensive shipments of supplies and military equipment from the Metropole. 

In addition to these trade considerations, the war in Indochina is imposing a crushing burden on the internal financial structure of the French economy. 

It is estimated that in 1949 the expenditures paid out of the French budget, connected directly or indirectly with the war in Indochina, amounted to 167 billion francs, the equivalent of $475,000,000. Most of these were military expenditures, but the French treasury has also been obliged in effect to siphon off the excess purchasing power of the area in order to prevent the inflationary situation from getting completely out of hand. Indochinese expenditures were about 8 percent of the total expenditures of the French Treasury in 1949. They were thus an important obstacle to the achievement of budgetary equilibrium and, consequently, a continuing element in the inflationary pressures which still exist in France. From this it is clear that the Indochinese War represents a very large drain on French economic resources. 

Mr. JUDD. Upon its own internal economy but it has not been too much of a drain upon its dollars? 

Mr. BISSELL. That is correct.

Mr. HOFFMAN. This program which was presented to the Council of OEEC in the latter part of October had been thoroughly discussed with the Government here. We have had the soundest kind of support from the Department of State here. I must make that statement that there has been no lack of complete coordination and complete support of this program as far as the State Department is concerned.

Areas of southeast Asia were the source of considerable dollar earnings for the Netherlands and the United Kingdom during the prewar period. 

Direct Indonesian trade with the United States resulted in a net surplus of Indonesian merchandise exports over imports of approximately $90,000,000 in 1937 and $40,000,000, in 1938; total remittances of dollars to the Netherlands may have been considerably larger since not all the activity was on direct account. 

British Malaya and India (which then included Pakistan) averaged about $185,000,000 in combined dollar earnings on merchandise account prewar, but had to pay net dollars on services and other transactions. Malaya nevertheless earned approximately $75,000,000 net annually. 

The role of these areas in Europe's economic patterns should not however be defined solely in terms of their net dollar earnings. Essential materials, such as tin, rubber, and jute, of which these areas are principal producers, are thus available to Europe. Southeast Asia is a valuable and extensive market both presently and in terms of potential future sales of western European exports.

Mr. JUDD. In your statement, Mr. Hoffman, you said the nations drew up a four-point program. One thing was they were going to remove quantitative restrictions on at least 50 percent of their imports. They have done that. Second, they were going to eliminate dual pricing. Third, they were going to bring about the mutual transferability of their currencies. That is the thing which you say will move rapidly in the next 90 days. The fourth point was to decide on further steps toward trade liberalization by the end of January. This is the end of February. Have they decided on those steps?

Mr. HOFFMAN. They would take a further 10 percent of the quantitative restrictions off trade almost immediately upon completion of the Payments Union, which would mean in July of this year, and would attempt to get another 15 percent off before the end of the year. 

Mr. JUDD. In addition to the 50 percent?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes. In other words, what they are committed to, I think, is a reduction of a further 25 percent in the quantitative restrictions if the Payments Union is developed. 

Mr. JUDD. What is your over-all estimate of the benefit or harm of the currency devaluations carried out last fall? We have now had 

5 months' experience. Have they produced as good results in the overall picture as some of the advocates of devaluation prophesied would follow?

Mr. HOFFMAN. I think Mr. Bissell's views on that, which I happen to go along with completely, are based on a great deal of technical knowledge of the situation and might be worth hearing. 

Mr. BISSELL. I think, Mr. Judd, it has been a very great success. I think it is almost impossible as yet, and will be for a number of months, to measure statistically the effect of those devaluations in closing the dollar gap of the whole group of European countries. I do not know whether an estimate has any meaning, but I believe even by now the European position is better off to the tune of perhaps $200,000,000 a year by reason of the devaluations that took place. If they can continue to hold down their domestic costs and prices so that the devaluation is not offset by raising costs and prices, I would expect that that benefit would be considerably greater in a few more months. 

There is no doubt that the devaluation has had another effect which is measurable. It reversed what was essentially a speculative outflow of funds, especially from Britain, just before the devaluation, an outflow that was prompted by the lack of confidence in European currencies, and this reversal has made possible, as has been publicly stated, a considerable rebuilding of Britain's monetary reserves. That effect is very tangible and has greatly strengthened the financial position of those countries.

One final effect that is also measurable is the effect on trade among the European countries themselves. Prior to the devaluation, the trade deficits of those European countries that were debtors in their trade within Europe amounted to at least six or seven hundred million dollars a year, and those have now been cut to probably about a third of that amount. France, which was a heavy debtor country, is now a surplus country; Belgium, which had a very large surplus in its trade within Europe-that is, they sold a great deal more than they bought from their neighbors-is now much more nearly in balance. In every way, the present state of trade and of other international payments within Europe and among the European countries is much healthier

than it was before. I believe that the devaluation did, on the whole,. fulfill what it was expected to do. 

Mr. JUDD. What is the black-market rate on the pound today? I have read stories that it has gone below par of $2.80. 

Mr. BISSELL. It has gone below that. My impression is $2.40. 

Mr. JUDD. If it is selling below the fixed rate on the black market,. how do you figure it commands confidence?

Mr. BISSELL. As long as tight exchange controls are preserved by any one of these countries, there is almost sure to be a black-market rate that is below the legal rate, whatever the real rate is, because ex-change control simply means that many holders of the currencyin that case, sterling-throughout the world are prohibited from using their sterling for certain purposes. Many of those holders have sterling and, therefore, feel they will seek to realize on it, illegally, in ways that they cannot legally, and that creates a black market. Theblack market can be a very small market in volume, a very thin market, but it is still quite possible to have a rate there established that is well below official rates, and I think that the black-market rate, when the black market is a thin market, is not a proper indication at all of the true value of the currency. 

Mr. JUDD. It is not because they lack confidence in the pound but because they need something so urgently that they are willing to sell their pounds at whatever rate they can get in order to get the desired: products.

Mr. BISSELL. Yes.

That is used for another purpose entirely. As I say, indirectly, it helps balance the budget. In France, a great deal of our counterpart has been used to rebuild railroads, and rebuild roads. In almost all cases, that was war damage. In some cases, it was not. In some cases, it was expansion. You can quite reasonably argue that if they had not had counterpart, they would have had to use their own funds; but, except in that indirect way, counterpart has not been used to balance budget. Mr. BISSELL. Substantially so.

Mr. HOFFMAN. The quisling currency which was creating inflationary pressure.

Mr. HOFFMAN. Very well. 

(The information requested is as follows:)

The answer to the question of whether the United States should divert aid from the United Kingdom directly to India and Pakistan seems to me to depend upon four considerations: (1) Would ECA aid directly to India and Pakistan break up or weaken the sterling area and would this be desirable?

(2) Would ECA aid directly to India and Pakistan reduce the total dollar drain on the United Kingdom by a like amount? (3) Would aid be used more effectively if extended directly to India and 

Pakistan than indirectly via the United Kingdom? (4) What political gains would be achieved by direct ECA aid to India and Pakistan? 

1. If ECA aid extended directly to India and Pakistan would in fact entail the dissolution of the sterling area or would seriously impair its operation, the benefits achieved would not be worth the losses involved. The sterling area, including the United Kingdom, is still the largest multilateral trading area in the world and carries on almost one-third of the world's trade. Although the sterlingarea countries including the crown colonies but excluding the United Kingdom had, as a group, a net deficit with the dollar area in 1948-49, it is anticipated that by 1952-53 they may be net dollar earners and therefore may be able to make a substantial contribution toward the solution of the United Kingdom's own dollar problem. Also, since the beginning of the ERP, the sterling area as a whole including the United Kingdom has made a substantial contribution toward the recovery of the other countries participating in the ERP by supplying them with more goods and services than they received in return. Therefore, no useful purpose is likely to be served by any action which at this time purposely or inadvertently threatened the continuation of the sterling area. 

2. If ECA aid were given directly to India and Pakistan, it is highly probable that the net effect would be to enable India and Pakistan to increase their total dollar imports. There might be no dollar saving at all to the United Kingdom, or the saving would be less than the ECA aid diverted away from the United Kingdom and given directly to India and Pakistan. The political and commercial disputes between India and Pakistan and the social and economic tensions within each of those countries are now so acute that their dollar imports cannot be predicted with any certainty nor very effectively controlled. The trade data demonstrate how erratic the dollar imports of these countries have been over the past 2 years. There is no assurance that direct aid to India and 

Pakistan would reduce their claims upon the United Kingdom's gold and dollar reserves. Nothing would be gained, therfore, in diverting ECA aid directly to India and Pakistan unless there were explicit assurance that an equivalent amount of dollars would be saved by the United Kingdom. 

3. Nor it is clear that a given amount of aid would be used more effectively if extended directly to India and Pakistan, rather than through the United Kingdom. As seen in the answer to question 2 above, the political and economic situations of India and Pakistan are now so difficult that their dollar requirements are not easily controlled. It may well be that the British, with the wellestablished machinery of the British Commonwealth available to them, could eventually be more successful in inducing India and Pakistan to hold their dollar requirements to a minimum. 

4. It is also questionable whether the political gains to the United States in 

India and Pakistan would compensate for the political losses which would result from a further weakening of the sterling area in general and of the United Kingdom in particular. The effective use of any United States aid to India and Pakistan would in any event require the closest coordination with the 

United Kingdom.

Unless all four questions could be answered beyond reasonable doubt in the affirmative, it would clearly not be wise to divert ECA aid from the United Kingdom and extend it directly to India and Pakistan. In general, for United 

States aid extended directly to these two countries to be effective, it would have to be done in such a manner as would not prejudice the operation of the sterling area and would reduce the over-all drain on the United Kingdom by at least an equivalent amount. In any event, it is unlikely that the provision of direct United States assistance to India and Pakistan would be effective unless it were undertaken in accordance with an agreement not only with those two countries but with the United Kingdom as well.

In some cases that calls for industrialization and in some cases it does not. One thing we have been attempting to fight is this idea that every little precinct has to have a steel mill and a cement mill and every kind of a mill, and an oil refinery. What we are trying to do is to get consideration on an entirely different basis. Now in Ubangi, Africa, what should they raise? You don't want a steel mill down there, but in most of these underdeveloped areas there are undeveloped resources and the thing to do is to plan a program that will bring out the resources of that country to the benefit of the people there, and generally when you do that you will find it also benefits us.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I am very glad to have that question asked. I have a statement on this payments union. 

(The statement referred to is as follows:) THE PROPOSED EUROPEAN PAYMENTS UNION 

1. THE USE OF EUROPEAN RESOURCES AND INTRAEUROPEAN TRADE 

One of the urgent problems that confronted the ECA at the very beginning of the Marshall plan in the summer of 1948 was that of freeing trade among the participating countries from the many restrictions, especially exchange controls of various forms, that were strangling it. Only through an expanded trade could the Europeans make the fullest possible use of their resources by supplying one another with the goods and services they could produce. Clearly, the more use the Europeans could make of their own resources the more rapid could be the pace of recovery and the lighter would be the burden on the United States. 

The most severe restrictions on trade among the western European countries grew out of the dollar shortage. Any European country which buys more from one of its neighbors than it is able to sell to that neighbor has to find some way of paying for the difference. Prior to the European recovery program this usually meant a payment in gold or dollars. Practically every country was reluctant to pay out dollars in order to make purchases in Europe and other soft-currency areas. The result was a general tendency to restrict imports by imposing exchange controls and quantitative restrictions on trade. 

For instance, Belgium has traditionally been an exporter of steel; Greece and 

Norway have to import it. Yet, Greece cannot sell enough olive oil, tobacco, and fruit to Belgium, and Norway cannot sell enough fish, lumber, and paper pulp to pay for the steel and all the other goods they wish to buy in Belgium. Therefore, under the conditions prevailing at the beginning of the Marshall plan these two countries might have had to use their ECA aid to buy steel in the United States at a time when the steel could have been produced in Europe. Obviously, this would have increased the cost of the recovery program. The only other course that the Greeks and Norwegians might have followed was that of restricting the importation of most goods from Belgium so as to save their earnings of Belgian currency for such highly essential items as steel. Either way, European trade was stifled, European resources were not put to their best uses, and recovery was impeded.

Given the nature of this situation, the quickest way to stimulate an expansion of European trade and, thus, a fuller use of European resources was to provide the means whereby any participating country could pay for the excess of its purchases from its neighbors over its sales to the same neighbors. 

2. OFFSHORE PURCHASES 

The first device that was employed to accomplish this purpose was to allow each participating country to use its ECA dollars to buy goods in other participating countries. To use the previous example, Greece and Norway would pay for as large a part as possible of their purchases in Belgium with their own earnings of Belgian francs. The balance of their purchases they would pay for with ECA dollars. The dollars that the Belgians earned from their neighbors in this fashion could then be used to finance imports into Belgium from the dollar area. In this way, these dollars were used twice: once to finance purchases in

Belgium by other European countries and a second time to help cover Belgium's dollar deficit. Since the dollars would otherwise have gone directly to Belgium for the latter purposes, there was, of course, no increase in the amount of aid required.

Offshore purchases with ECA dollars were an effective emergency method of preventing the further shrinkage of European trade. But this method had disadvantages. The fact that ECA dollars could be used in this fashion led more and more sellers, often with the support of their governments, to insist on payment in dollars. In this way, the countries tried to earn dollars from one another. Often prices quoted in dollar transactions were lower than the prices asked for the same goods by the same seller when they were sold for European currencies. If long continued, therefore, this practice would have disrupted trade in Europe, even though, initially, it acted as a stimulant. 

3. THE INTRA-EUROPEAN PAYMENTS PLAN 

In September 1948, therefore, a second and more effective arrangement was devised which was called the intra-European payments plan. Its basic principle is simple. A part of the ECA dollar aid to each creditor country, which it needs to pay for its necessary imports from the dollar area, is given only on condition that the recipient country extend grants-in-aid of the same amount in its own currency to the other participating countries with which it has a trade surplus. (This part of the aid is called conditional aid.) In this way, the debtor country receives a grant, which is called a drawing right, in the currency of each country with which it has a trade deficit. Stated in terms of the earlier example, Belgium receives ECA dollar financing (as conditional aid) to pay for goods and services from the United States and elsewhere in the dollar area on condition that it make a grant of Belgium francs to Greece with which Greece can buy steel in Belgium.

The intra-European payments plan has made a major contribution toward the freeing of European trade and, consequently, the better use of European resources. By financing trade deficits, it has removed, or weakened, the incentive of each country to husband its dollars, or to earn dollars from its neighbors, by restricting its imports from them. But it is based on a series of bilateral arrangements between pairs of countries. The drawing rights that Belgium gives Greece can (except for a small portion) be used only in Belgium. Greece cannot shop around and buy its steel in the cheapest market in Europe. More over, the present payments plan does not furnish enough stimulus to the individual countries to bring their trade into balance. Accordingly, it is time to take a further step through the creation of a European payments union which will make European currencies freely convertible into one another (for current as distinguished from capital transactions) and thus facilitate a further dismantling of restrictions on trade among the participating countries. 

4. EUROPEAN PAYMENTS UNION 

The fundamentals of the proposed payments union are similar to those of the present payments plan but the mechanics of the operation will be quite different. 

The payments union will not be a device for underwriting European currencies or protecting overvalued currencies. Its basic function, like that of the present payments plan and the earlier offshore purchases, will be to provide the means whereby a debtor country can cover the deficit in its trade with its neighbors without having to make full payment in gold or dollars. Europe's internal trade is not yet in balance. Some countries still have to buy more from their neighbors than they sell to them. These countries must still have help in financing their trade deficits if they are to feel free to eliminate trade restrictions. 

The operation of the payments union will not change either the amount of aid needed, or the purposes for which ECA dollars are ultimately used by the Europeans. The ECA dollars which are used to support its operations (and which correspond to the conditional aid of the intra-European payments plan) will find their way to the countries that turn out to be creditors in their trade with the rest of western Europe to be used by those countries to buy the goods and services they must have from the dollar area. The only difference is that, under the proposed amendment, assistance may be furnished to the participating countries indirectly through the payments union and may be in the form of dollars not earmarked for the purchase by the recipient country of particular goods and services.

This new payments union will be an improvement over the old intra-European payments plan in two important respects. 

The first is that it will permit trade to be conducted within Europe on a truly multilateral basis. The payments union will be, in effect, a clearinghouse of which all the central banks of the participating countries will be members and through which they will be able to settle their accounts with one another. Even at the present time, individual private transactions between the citizens of any two countries are offset against one another by their two central banks so that only a single payment from one to the other is necessary. In the payment union this clearinghouse operation will be carried a step further. Each country's deficits with some of its neighbors will be offset against its surpluses with others so that only a single net settlement between its central bank and the clearinghouse will be necessary. In this way an enormous volume of transactions can be handled with minimum payments between countries. 

The financing of trade deficits through the payments union will also be done entirely on a multilateral basis. A country that is a debtor in its trade with other European countries, instead of receiving drawing rights consisting of fixed amounts of the currencies of each of its prospective creditors (as in the present plan), will have the right to draw upon the central clearinghouse for any European currency it needs to make purchases from its neighbors. There will, of course, be a limit to the total amount a country may borrow in all currencies. 

A creditor country, instead of supplying drawing rights consisting of fixed amounts of its own currency directly to various prospective debtor countries, will provide its own currency to the clearinghouse as needed, up to a stated limit. To refer once more to the earlier example, Greece will be able to choose freely whether it will draw on the clearinghouse from Belgian francs to buy its steel in Belgium, or in German marks to buy its steel in Germany, or in pounds sterling to buy its steel in Britain.

In such a completely flexible system, it will be impossible to predict in advance the exact amount that any particular debtor country will need to obtain from the payments union or that any particular creditor will need to furnish to it. 

Therefore, it will not be possible to allocate in advance a definite sum of ECA conditional aid to each country that will be a creditor. Instead, dollars can be paid to the creditor country only when it actually has to supply its own currency to the clearinghouse. Thus neither the countries that will ultimately receive these dollars, nor the amounts they will receive, nor the time during the year when the payments will be made, can be accurately foreseen. It is proposed, therefore, that a considerable part of the ECA funds required for the financing of European trade deficits be granted as aid to the payments union and, in effect, earned from the clearinghouse by the creditor countries. It is for this reason that the ECA seeks the authority to furnish a part of the aid to Europe next year by means of the transfer of dollars through a central institution of this character. 

The second major change and improvement in the new payments union (as compared with the present payments plan) is that the trade deficits that develop among the European countries will be paid for only partly with ECA aid in the manner just described. The balance will be paid for partly out of the dollar resources of the countries themselves and partly out of funds loaned to the payments union by the creditors, without any relation to ECA aid. 

Whenever a country turns out to be a debtor-that is, whenever it buys more from its neighbors than it sells to them-it will have to meet part of the deficit thus incurred by the payment of its own gold or dollars to the payments union (unless its deficit is held within fixed limits or is of a purely seasonal character). Whenever a country turns out to be a creditor-that is, when it sells more to its neighbors than it buys from them it will receive payment to cover this trading surplus only partly in gold or dollars. The balance due will remain simply as a debt in European currencies owed to the creditor country by the clearinghouse.

The advantage of requiring debtors to make part payment in gold or dollars and creditors to finance a part of their exports with loans is that the European countries are in this way given a strong incentive to bring their trade into a reasonable balance. The debtor's obligation to cover a part of its trade deficit in hard money gives it an incentive to reduce the size of its trade deficit. 

Likewise the creditor, having to finance a part of its export surplus by extending credits will be more willing to import from its neighbors and thus bring its trade more nearly into balance. It is in this way that the operation of the payments union will help to cure the disease and not merely to alleviate its symptoms. 

Moreover, a payments union that operates in this manner can prepare the way for the end of ECA aid. By 1952 the trade surpluses and deficits among the

European countries will have to be small enough to be financed entirely by a combination of credits and gold and dollar payments through a central institution without the help of any ECA funds. The establishment of the payments union is a significant step in this direction. After its first year of operation, it can be modified in such a way as to reduce its dependence on ECA funds. We hope that, by the end of the ERP, it can operate as an independent institution financed entirely out of European resources. 

That concludes my prepared answer to the chairman's question. 

This matter of setting up a payments union does call for the use of sound techniques and those techniques do have to be explained in technical language. You cannot reduce them to lay language too easily. I think these things should be understood: No. 1, the amount of funds requested covers the needs of these countries for goods. We are not requesting any additional appropriation for this payments union because as the payments union operates the dollars involved are used in the final analysis to pay for goods from the United States. 

They may not go in the exact amounts to the countries to which they would go under an allocation system, but they still go to the countries, so it is goods we are talking about. And the purpose of the payments union is to help us make better use of Europe's resources. 

The better and more fully we can use Europe's resources the less the bill will be to us.

I want to go back and point out the condition we found in July of 1948 where, as a result of not only tariffs but the QR's as they call them, and exchange controls, trade in Europe had been reduced to a trickle. We were faced with a shut-down of Belgium production of steel in the face of terrific needs for steel in Europe because Belgium could not take Greek drachma for her steel. We were at that time short of steel in the United States, too. We could have shipped the steel to Greece and drawn on our own resources or we could have provided Greece with a way to get steel from Belgium. The simple way was what we call an offshore purchase. That is what we did. 

In order to quickly break this thing we gave Greece some dollars and said, "Go ahead and buy some steel from Belgium," and Greece bought the steel. The following year we developed what we call a payments plan which was an improvement on the simple offshore purchase, in that we gave a credit to the producing country on the condition that that country make available to certain other countries an equivalent amount of production in the form of drawing rights, so that those countries could draw on the country that had the surplus production. 

It made a more operable method of effecting offshore purchases. We did one thing there which was an improvement of last year's model. 

We found out as long as a creditor country had complete control of the credit, and other countries could draw upon it in the amounts and only upon it in the amounts requested, there was no competition. 

Thus they would offer their goods at any price they thought reasonable and at times the price might or might not be reasonable. We suggested, and the suggestion was accepted, that 25 percent of these drawing rights given to these countries be transferable, that is, spendable in any of the participating countries and not only in the country granting the drawing rights, so they could do a little shopping around and get a lower price.

The difficulty with that whole program is it would leave Europe dependent when we pull out upon this stimulation we provided by way of directly or indirectly making offshore purchases with dollars.

What we want to get back into operation is the normal European system where they will swap drachma for francs and Belgian francs for kroner. Then they could get goods where they are available on the best terms and get rid of exchange controls. There is nothing blocking trade more than exchange controls. An individual seller has to go to his bank and he has to make application, after he gets his export license, to exchange the currency of the country to which he sells his goods into the currency of his own country. He has to make application for exchange or get an exchange of the currency of the country to which he is sending the goods to his own currency. Under the well-known bureaucratic methods that usually takes longer than one can afford to wait for the goods, so you have an additional way to slow down trade. Sometimes they do not make the exchange available even though the seller may have the export license. 

We have had the European technicians working with us in an attempt to develop a payments union to overcome these obstacles. 

The payments union is not a method for underwriting the credit of these countries. It has nothing to do with the question of attempting to guarantee a certain value of currencies. That is not the point at all. Currencies have value only as a result of internal policies within the country.

Chairman KEE. It was that idea that prompted the question. I am glad to learn that no attempt is to be made to guarantee the value of the various currencies.

Mr. HOFFMAN. We have to come in here for the reason that trade is drawing into balance in Europe, but is not in balance at this time. 

So as these people approach the idea of letting down the bars by reducing quantitative restrictions on trade, they get terribly concerned that a flood of goods might strike them and put a great strain on their reserves. It is a very reasonable fear on their part. You have to give them some protection from these dangers before they will remove further quantitative restrictions and before they will remove exchange controls, so what we are saying to them is this: If this payments union is organized, there will be established for each country a certain credit that they have there upon which to draw for any currency. 

Mr. JUDD. Except dollars?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Except dollars. The central banks of the countries, which would of course be the members of this payments union, are there. In the case of Greece, if they have a credit in the payments union they can get for their drachma French francs or English pounds or whatever is needed up to the limit of their credit. If they go beyond that the plan is of course that they will have to start paying for part of the goods in gold. So it has a deterrent effect on the country's asking for any additional credits. So there is a pressure to get trade back into balance; to export more or import less. That is one of the features of the plan. However, you have to provide for the financing of these trade deficits as they might develop. In other words, you have to give this safeguard; the payments union has to have this money behind it. As I say the money is not additional funds. 

It is theoretically conceivable, of course, that this payments union could operate without any settlement on the part of one country with another, but hardly conceivable, as a practical matter, because trade is not in balance. So they will have to look to us to supply the funds

to help iron out these trade deficits and keep them within this so-called swing margin. 

Mr. VORYS. What is the definition of "swing margin" "? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Will you explain that technically?

Mr. BISSELL. I will explain it if you wish, sir. It is the term that has been used in a great many payments agreements among these countries, and it is the margin within which one country can have a surplus or a deficit with the other country without the necessity for any settlement between them or any payment between them in gold or dollars or any hard money. That has been called swing margin_because it is supposed to provide for the seasonal swings in trade. For instance, Sweden has an export surplus all summer when the Baltic is open, and when the Baltic is closed in winter, it has no export surplus.

Mr. HOFFMAN. You will understand that one of the features of this is similar to that of a clearinghouse in a city for banks. In other words, as against the settlement of every transfer action separately between each one of the countries, in this case you only settle the net differences. That is, the currencies of all the countries come in here and are checked out. This saves an endless amount of work. 

Also we feel, and Mr. Bissell and experts in this field feel, that fundamentally there is no real difference between this plan and the present payments plan as far as the way the dollars are finally used is concerned; any dollars we put up are used eventually for goods needed to be bought in the dollar area. In the meantime the dollars serve to underwrite this payments union by providing funds to help take care of a part of these trade deficits as they develop. In certain cases it has been the opinion of the experts that we would take part of this money which we plan to withhold and supply it in the form of direct grants to those countries whose trade we know in advance will be out of balance due to the fact that they have taken bolder action in liberalizing their trade than some of their neighbors. 

Now I wish you would take over there and fill in the holes that I have left. I have attempted to explain in lay language, Mr. Chairman, a rather technical development. I think where I have missed, Mr. Bissell can pick up and correct or supplement. 

Chairman KEE. May I inject a question right there? Is it possible for you to give us an estimate of approximately the amount of money that will be required?

Mr. HOFFMAN. I will answer that myself: Last year, the payments plan required financial backing from us amounting to about $800,- 000,000. This plan, which is a better method, calls for around $600,- 

000,000. There is one thing to remember, that while the total purchases of these countries from each other will, of course, go far beyond this amount, the function it does have is to stimulate intra-European trade. We have had this same purpose, first with direct offshore purchases and second with the original payments plan. It takes out a great deal of the confusion. A notion has gotten around that we propose to underwrite all the currencies of Europe and that we propose to underwrite the credit of all the countries. This is not the case at all. The new Payments Union proposal is nothing but a logical and sensible plan for providing for stimulating intra-European trade in such a manner that, when we pull out, Europe will be back at a point

where there is convertibility of currencies on a perfectly normal basis.

Mr. BISSELL. I think it could, Mr. Vorys; yes. I think that that may very well develop. I think it could be part of it in this way. 

This year, in connection with the existing payments plan as Mr.

Then Belgium gives the equivalent amount as a grant in Belgian francs to countries like Greece, Norway, France, and England which want to make purchases in Belgium. That is very similar to counterpart funds, those grants that the Belgians make available that we call drawing rights, to the other European countries.
