TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

 The committee met, pursuant to call at 10: 45 a. m.

, in the Foreign 

(chairman), presiding.

We are resuming this morning our hearings upon the extension of the ECA program and we have with us Mr. John Kenney, Chief of the ECA Mission to the United Kingdom.

Mr. Kenney, we know, is very familiar with the problems we are facing in respect to the ECA and he can no doubt give us some very important information. We are very glad to have you with us this morning, Mr. Kenney. You may proceed with your statement. We will be glad to hear you.

STATEMENT OF W. JOHN KENNEY, CHIEF, ECA MISSION TO UNITED KINGDOM 

Mr. KENNEY. I would like to describe to the committee the events that have taken place in the United Kingdom during the past year. 

I will not attempt to go over the same material Mr. Finletter discussed with you last year. In the interest of time I have restricted myself primarily to the developments of last year which as we all know was both a dramatic and important year in the United Kingdom. I have also had put before each member of the committee some charts which I thought the committee might find interesting from the point of view of reference. They are in the main self-explanatory. So do not be alarmed since I do not intend to take up each one of them in any degree of detail.

The most dramatic event in the United Kingdom during year 1949 was the economic crisis of last summer and the resultant devaluation of the pound sterling from $4.03 to $2.80. In September the United 

Kingdom was required to devalue the pound sterling because her reserves had fallen to one-sixth of the purchasing powers of the reserves held before the war. Chart 1 depicts the change in Britain's dollar reserves that have taken place since 1946 and shows the drop from March 31, 1949, down to September 18, the date of devaluation.

She had lost gold and dollar reserves of over $500,000,000. In the lower part of that chart you will see the part which is depicted in 113

black which is the value of those reserves expressed in 1938 dollars, so that the loss of purchasing power that has taken place is even greater than the monetary loss.

From the point of view of Britain's external finances her situation was obviously critical, even though in other respects her economy gave continued evidence of recovery. The crisis has been described, and properly so, as a dollar crisis. In chart 2 are set forth the facts involved in the dollar crisis of last year. It shows the reduction of 

United States factory production and United States wholesale prices, which meant a loss in revenue from goods sold to the United States and a reduction in the amount of goods sold. You can also see that there was a reduction in United Kingdom exports to the United States. Section 7 of the chart shows the sharp decline in exports from the rest of the sterling area to the United States. 

None of the contributing factors and probably not the aggregate would, under normal circumstances, have been of sufficient magnitude to cause an economic crisis. In 1938 the United Kingdom lost reserves of $714,000,000 within a period of about 6 months without causing a severe disturbance in the financial world. However, because of the weakness in the external financial structure of the United Kingdom, the occurrence of these events last summer produced a worldwide lack of confidence in the fundamental value of the pound sterling and brought about a postponement of buying, delays in remitting dollars, and an extraordinary conversion of sterling into dollars. 

Devaluation was a drastic step, an act only justified by grim necessity.

By the end of 1949 devaluation was instrumental in reversing the trend of lost dollars, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer was able to announce that since devaluation the gold and dollar reserves had risen from the low figure of $1,340,000,000 to $1,688,000,000, and that, before Marshall aid, the dollar drain incurred during the third quarter of $539,000,000 had been reduced to a drain of only $31,000,000 during the fourth quarter.

Devaluation provides an incentive to dollar-earning exports, to dollar saving, and to indirect dollar earnings. Devaluation, however, is not without its risks, because it tends to encourage domestic inflation and consequent depreciation of monetary assets. Also, if costs and prices are permitted to rise-and one of the disadvantages of British goods in dollar markets has been too-high costs-the maladjustment will reassert itself and the trading advantage gained by devaluation will have been lost. An inflationary increase in costs could very quickly recreate the situation which required devaluation. 

Therefore, adequate steps were and are required of the British Government to prevent a recurrence of these conditions. The necessary corrective measures complementary to devaluation must be accomplished or else the British economy may proceed periodically from crisis to expedient, and then back to crisis. 

In October, after devaluation, the British Government, to restrict inflationary forces, directed a cut in expenditures of 280,000,000 pounds. In order to determine the adequacy of this and other corrective measures it is necessary to examine both the internal and external conditions of the United Kingdom.

A. INTERNAL ECONOMIC CONDITIONS 

1. Budget: The desire of the British Government to pursue a noninflationary fiscal policy is reflected in the budget for the fiscal years 1948-49 and 1949-50. The 1948-49 budget produced a surplus of £352,000,000, and it is now estimated that the 1949-50 budget will be in surplus in the neighborhood of £100,000,000. Chart 3 shows the make-up of the British budget, the sources of income and the breakdown of expenditures. The chart as you will see carries a notation of deficit of £2,000,000. The reason for discrepancy between that figure and the figure of £100,000,000 that I have given in my testimony is the fact that since my departure from England I have had a report that it is now estimated that the budget will have a surplus of something in the neighborhood of £100,000,000. 

2. Prices and wage levels: While wholesale and retail prices have risen above the prewar level, Britain has achieved a relative stability in the most essential items in the cost of living. Chart 4 indicates the trend of wholesale prices, retail prices and wage rates from 1939 down through the end of 1949. The upper portion in yellow is the period for the last 3 years of 1947 and 1949.

The voluntary policy of "restraint" in seeking wage increases, followed by the Trades Union Congress has resulted in wage increases of only slightly over 1 percent during 1949, even in the face of higher cost of living caused by devaluation, and a 5-percent increase in industrial productivity. This evidence of the willingness of British workers to exercise self-discipline for the common goal of economic recovery is a most heartening and encouraging feature and has played a prominent part in the struggle against inflation. 

3. Production: Remarkable recovery has been made both in industrial and agricultural production. Chart 5 shows the increases that have taken place as compared with the trend in the United States during the same period. It also shows the relative distribution of manpower in the two countries. I think it is very interesting to note the distribution of manpower. In the United States, 29 percent of the manpower is employed in industry whereas in the United Kingdom 43 percent is employed in industry. The United Kingdom is one of the most highly industrialized countries in the world. 

Industrial production has proceeded from the low point of 104 percent of prewar levels in 1946 to 133 percent in 1949. During the same period the industrial production of the United States went from 170 percent of prewar to 180 percent. In charts 6 and 7 are set forth the production records in the various industries, steel, electricity, chemicals, coal, cotton fabrics, rayon, and whisky, to enumerate a few. 

It is interesting to note that in all of those there has been a substantial increase in production except in the cases of coal and cotton fabrics. 

It is to be noted that coal production is now up almost to the 1938 level. 

Agricultural production, which is of extreme importance since Britain is and has been for a century a net importer of food, much of which comes from the dollar area, had an increase of 13 percent between the crop years 1946-47 and 1949-50. Compared to prewar, gross agricultural production is 15 percent higher. In chart 8 is shown the change in land use between the period before the war and

now, and the production of various agricultural items such as grains, potatoes, and livestock. The livestock figures are shown on chart 9. 

4. Productivity: In manufacturing there has been an increase in productivity of 20 percent per man since 1946-a creditable performance. Chart 10 depicts the improvement in productivity that has taken place since 1946 and in the subcharts B and C are shown the increase in productivity in certain selected industries such as coal, tin plate, pig iron, and others.

The labor force, aware that a high rate of productivity means full employment and leads to economic recovery, has delivered a production effort in much the same spirit as that prevailing during the war. 

The hours lost per worker since the war through industrial disputes in Britain has been one-ninth of the hours per worker lost in the 

United States. 

The work of our technical-assistance program, and the activities of the Anglo-American Council on Productivity have been helpful in increasing productivity. 

5. Husbanding of resources: Due to her straitened economic circumstances, Britain must utilize and conserve her resources to the maximum. The war brought about a reduction in houses, factories, railroads, machinery, et cetera, of 2 to 212-billion pounds the equivalent at the exchange rate in effect at that time of 8 to 10-billion dollars. Chart 11 shows the extent of this loss and how in the period from 1945 to 1950, the capital plant has been brought back almost to the 1938 level. This is still below the figures at which it should be, because, of course, between the period of 1938 and 1950 there has been an increase in population, so that the increment in plant is still inadequate to take care of that increase. 

About 20 percent of her total resources available in the present fiscal year is being devoted to capital formation. 

By greatly increasing her total production and by diverting an unusually large part of it into investment, Britain, with foreign assistance, has been making good these wartime losses and is now approaching the prewar level of capital. This program of capital formation is a real stride toward economic recovery. In chart 12 is set forth the percentage distribution of available resources, showing the amount in the years that has been devoted to personal consumption, for investment and for government, and also in the middle of that chart is shown, for the purposes of comparison, the same relative distribution in the United States. It is interesting to note that in the 

United States for the year 1949, the percentages of available resources devoted to investment was only 17 percent, whereas in 1947, 1948, and 1949, in the United Kingdom, the figures were respectively 19, 22, and 20 percent.

Britain has also limited personal consumption. Only 62 percent of the total resources available in the present fiscal year is currently being taken for consumption, compared to 72 percent in 1938, and 70 percent currently in the United States.

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, just what does he include in resources? 

Mr. KENNEY. The resources there are the gross national product which is the total amount that has been produced in the country, plus the excess of imports over exports. It is the total of the product of the country plus net imports.

Mr. JUDD. You are talking about goods when you speak of resources? 

Mr. KENNEY. Yes, goods and services, gross national product plus excess of imports over exports. 

To exercise this restraint on consumption, it has been felt necessary to continue certain segments of the rationing system, on some food items, soap, gasoline, domestic consumption of coal, timber for construction and the size of newspapers. Dollar expenditures which would otherwise be made for consumer goods are held down and these dollars utilized instead to procure goods more vital to sound economic recovery. Thus, Britain is still living with a tightened belt; although her situation is not of actual want, her standards of personal consumption are not high. In the lower part of chart 12 is shown a comparison of the consumption figures now as compared to what they were in prewar years. 

B. EXTERNAL ECONOMIC CONDITIONS 

1. Capital position: The war brought a striking deterioration in 

Britain's external capital position. Before the war the gold reserves of the United Kingdom in terms of present purchasing power were the equivalent of over $10,000,000,000, and her world-wide investments in terms of present commodity prices were equal to about three times that amount. Those assets have disappeared in the financing of the struggle against Hitler, and in their place is a net liability of approximately $5,000,000,000. This has been brought about through a substantial liquidation of many of the foreign assets of Britain, and particularly those in Canada and the United States, through the borrowing of large sums from the United States and Canada, and through large imports on credit during the war. Chart 13 shows how the 1938 reserves and capital of 18.5 billion dollars have gone down to a net liability of approximately $5,000,000,000. In 1938, the reserves and capital were made up of 4.2 billion dollars of reserves, from which must be deducted the sterling balances, owing to members of the sterling area and others, of 3.7 billion dollars, and net assets abroad of about $18,000,000,000. Since 1938 there has been a decrease in reserves of 2.5 billion dollars; there has been an increase of sterling balances by 5.3 billion dollars; new dollar debts of 5.5 billion dollars, and a decrease of net assets abroad of about $10,000,000,000, which results in a net liability of Britain's capital position of approximately $5,000,000,000. 

2. The sterling area, and sterling balances: The gold and dollar reserves of the United Kingdom are the reserves of the whole sterling area, an area with one-quarter of the population of the world and onequarter of the international trade of the world. The map on chart 

14 shows that portion of the world included in the so-called sterling area, and that portion in blue indicates that portion of the world in the so-called dollar area.

The sterling area is a complex and far-flung economy in which the pound sterling serves as the common currency for conducting transactions between its members. 

Thus, for example, Malaya, South Africa, and British West Africa earn dollars, but most of the other members of the sterling area lose dollars and the sterling area as a whole loses dollars. This system of arrangements within the sterling area, and the relationships that

exist, permit increased trade both within the area and between the area and other countries, notably Britain's partners in the OEEC countries.

From this far-flung economy vast resources were mobilized on our side for the prosecution of the war. For part of these vast expenditures Britain, herself, undertook the financial responsibility. 

She therefore now owes certain "sterling balances" which are part of her external monetary obligations. As of December 1945, the sterling balances were 3.7 billion pounds of which 2.5 billion pounds was owing to countries in the sterling area. This indebtedness has been reduced, to some extent, by periodic and limited releases for the purchase of essential imports by the creditor countries. The net amount of sterling so released up to August 1949 has been approximately £600,000,000. The release of these balances satisfies the need of the recipient countries for material goods-as for example, in the case of India, during a period of significant transition and in the case of Norway for rehabilitation of the merchant marine destroyed in the war. 

Mr. JUDD. IS Norway in the sterling area?

Mr. KENNEY. No. Norway is a country to which Britain owed sterling and they did have sterling balances. The balances are to members of the sterling area and to certain countries outside it. 

However, these releases have produced a drain upon the internal economy of the United Kingdom, and exert an inflationary pressure on it. In the first place they further emphasize the contrast between the abundance of sterling and the scarcity of dollars thereby affecting the dollar-sterling rate of exchange, and in the second place they create markets for goods for which there is no current return in goods or services the so-called unrequited exports. The quantity of “unrequited exports" must be diminished so that Britain can export more to the hard currency and particularly to the dollar countries. 

3. General balance of payments: During the operation of the ECA program, a large segment of the problem of the deficit with the world at large has been corrected, and the focus has been shifted to the dollar deficit. Chart 15 shows how the dollar deficit in 1938 of £70,000,000 increased to a deficit of £630,000,000 in 1947. On chart 18 we show how that deficit of £630,000,000 in 1947 has been reduced to a deficit estimated at £65,000,000 in 1949. Chart 17 depicts the balance of payments of the United Kingdom. It is interesting to note that 

Britain had an estimated trade deficit of £235,000,000 with the dollar area and a deficit on invisibles of £37,000,000 with the dollar area.

However, with respect to the so-called nondollar areas she had a favorable trade balance with £82,000,000, and a favorable situation with respect to net invisibles of £125,000,000. On her over-all balance she had net earnings on invisibles of £88,000,000, but had a deficit in her trade balance of £153,000,000.

In other words, Britain had a favorable situation both with respect to trade and net invisibles everywhere except with respect to the dollar area. 

Chairman KEE. At what period was that?

Mr. KENNEY. The chart shows, Mr. Chairman, the situation as it was in 1938 and then carries through and shows the situation in 1946, 1947, 1948, and 1949. The figures which I have just given you are preliminary estimates for the year 1949.

4. The dollar deficit: The magnitude of this deficit is the major current economic difficulty of Britain and it reflects the changed structure of the world economy, the disequilibrium of the economy of the United States with the rest of the world. 

During the period from April 1948 through June 1949, the gold and dollar payments of Britain totaled $4,500,000,000, while her gold and dollar earnings amounted to about $2,500,000,000. The $2,000,000,000 gap was bridged by abnormal financing, including $1,302,000,000 of 

ECA aid.

Chart 19 shows the source of dollar payments and the items of dollar expenditures and how this so-called dollar deficit arises. 

A deficit in merchandise trade is not a new problem to the United Kingdom, but the inability to balance that deficit with earned gold or dollars is of recent origin. The dollar deficit does not stem solely from the bilateral relationship between the United Kingdom and the United States, but is increased by the inability of the United Kingdom to secure payment in dollars from third areas, as she did before the war. Before the war the dollar gap was manageable because most other currencies were convertible into dollars and Britain was able to meet her dollar deficit on trade with the gold or dollars derived from her surplus on invisibles, for the most part earned in nondollar sources. 

With regard to chart 20, I would like to apologize for it. It is a complicated thing, but it does tend to show the change in pattern of payments that has taken place between the period before the war and today. It is, I believe, to a certain extent, illustrative of the complications of the situation and indicative of the changes that have taken place. The width of the various lines flowing between the different segments are supposed to reflect the quantity of those payments, so you can see the changes that have taken place in the period before the war and today.

Chairman KEE. The chart looks something like a smashed atom. 

Mr. KENNEY. Mr. Chairman, somebody asked me whether that chart was the original plan for the Pentagon Building. 

Mr. EATON. It does not appear sufficiently complicated. 

Mr. KENNEY. The dollar deficit is expected to lessen in 1950-51 when it is estimated that Britain will earn about three-quarters of the dollars she needs. The volume of United Kingdom exports to the 

United States is 114 percent of 1938, and for the rest of the sterling area is 176 percent of the 1934-38 level. A further substantial increase in dollar exports is expected in the next 2 years, primarily as the result of the double impetus of devaluation and the dollar export drive. There should also be an increase in dollars earned from services.

In chart 21, I have endeavored to show the annual reduction in the dollar deficit that has taken place in the United Kingdom since 1947.

In 1947 there was a deficit of $4,127,000,000. This was reduced in the first ECA period to an annual rate of $1,642,000,000. In early British illustrative figures for the year 1949-50 it was brought down, before United States or Canadian assistance, to $1,239,000,000 for 1950-51 it was then estimated that the gap would be in the neighborhood of $750,000,000, and in 1951-52 will be in the neighborhood of $480,000,- 000, which is in our opinion a manageable deficit. 

Mr. KENNEY. $480,000,000 is the estimated dollar gap for the period 1951-52.

Mr. VORYS. Are you going to explain what you mean by "manageable?"

Mr. KENNEY. Yes; I think I can explain that, Mr. Vorys. A $480,- 

000,000 gap in the last period of Marshall aid, in my opinion, is a figure which is not frightening or distressing. It is one which can be handled by increased dollar earnings and improved economic conditions in Great Britain in the following year. In other words, the fact that they will have an estimated dollar gap at that time in that amount would, in my opinion, be within reasonable limits. In normal trade and balances there will be years when they will have deficits and years when they will have surpluses. 

The increase in British exports to the United States is in our own self-interest because it is only with dollars earned that Britain will be permanently able to buy our goods. Without dollars there must be a cessation of British imports from the United States. Many American producers can already testify as to the markets lost because of the shortage of dollars. Marshall aid has to some extent alleviated this situation, but it cannot permanently do so because it is only an interim measure, a stop gap, to fill in until Britain can purchase with her own funds.

To restore her dollar balance, Britain has taken the corrective steps outlined above, many of them courageous and difficult acts. She has used Marshall aid carefully and to good effect. Substantial progress has been made, particularly since devaluation. However, it must be recognized that the British economy hangs in delicate balance. 

To relieve the precariousness of this balance the Government of Britain, a government duly elected by free people, 86 percent of whom voted in the elections of last Thursday, maintains many controls; controls over imports, exports, currencies, food, employment, and raw materials, to mention a few. The retention of many of these controls has been effective in combating inflation, but one senses at times the tendency to place too much reliance on controls. The resultant effect has been to contribute to the rigidities in Britain's internal economy.

Britain's internal controls, moreover, could not protect her from the impact of the rapidly changing forces in world trade which came into play last summer. Britain cannot insulate herself from contact with the outside world and the effect of the price movements of free economies. Last summer the complex economy of Britain broke down at the point of contact with those economies and she did not have the resilience or the reserves to withstand the impact of the changing forces in world trade.

An awareness of these facts should not cause one to overlook the important fact that Britain has an indispensable part to play in the economic recovery of the free nations of Europe and is our strongest. ally in the fight against communism. Any retarding of British recovery would have an adverse effect on European recovery. The 

Marshall aid program for the United Kingdom is designed to attain that recovery by 1952. The proposed figure for the fiscal year 195051 of $687,100,000 is more than 25 percent below the amount of aid for the current fiscal year. 

I also want to add that there is no question at all in the minds of the British people and in the minds of their government that Marshall aid ends in 1952. The British Government has prepared various

posters that it puts up in the plants that use raw materials obtained with Marshall aid. This one that I have here happens to relate to copper. It says: 

You work in copper.

In 1 year, about one-third of our copper imports have been paid for by Marshall aid. Marshall aid ends, 1952. As each month goes by, we must pay for more of what we need by our exports of manufactured goods.

The Government has done the same thing in other industries. Here is a chart put up in plants using aluminum. Here is one that was used in plants utilizing lead. It is an attempt to get the maximum amount of effort out of their workers and to impress upon them the importance of the fact that Marshall aid ends in 1952. 

That is the end of my statement, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Kenney, we thank you very much indeed.

Your statement was highly informative. It is very difficult however, for an ordinary mind to absorb that information all at once, but it certainly gives us something to think over. We appreciate your statement very much.

We will go to the questioning period under the 5-minute rule, and begin with Mr. Richards of South Carolina. 

Mr. Richards, have you any questions? 

Mr. RICHARDS. Mr. Kenney, those charts you showed, there, are they generally displayed in Great Britain in the newspapers, for example?

Mr. KENNEY. There has been a great deal of publicity about the 

Marshall aid in Great Britain. In fact, the amount of publicity is so great that the London Daily Worker commented on the fact that a man must be virtually deaf, dumb, and blind who is not aware of the contribution that has been made by Marshall aid. 

Now the great bulk of Marshall aid has gone into two types of things: raw materials of the type I have enumerated, here, and foods. 

By reason of Britain being as highly industrialized as it is, the two things most essential for her economy are the food for her workers and the raw materials for her industrial plant. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Is the program publicized by advertisement, posters, and things like that? 

Mr. KENNEY. Oh, yes; the things I showed you are posters. 

Mr. RICHARDS. And they are posted in the plants? 

Mr. KENNEY. Yes; and there are other types.

Mr. RICHARDS. Is any part of the ECA fund used this year to retire the national debt or balance the budget in Great Britain? They have a rather good budget picture there and they are to be congratulated on it, but I want to know whether any of the funds provided by the United States are still being used for that purpose. 

Mr. KENNEY. Of course, none of the dollars would, because when we are speaking of the budget, Mr. Chairman, we are speaking of the sterling account. 

Mr. RICHARDS. How about counterpart funds? 

Mr. KENNEY. I was going to get to that.

Until the end of the summer a certain portion of our counterpart funds were used for debt retirement. I would like to explain that briefly and tell why that was done: At the time any dollar material is provided to any user in Great Britain, the user is required to put up the sterling equivalent. Now because that currency has been taken out of the stream, any expenditure of that money would impose a new

inflationary force upon an economy which was already strained. You see, the British Government itself felt it was necessary, in October, to direct a reduction in expenditures of about £280,000,000. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Yes; but counterpart funds were not originally intended for that purpose, basically. 

Mr. KENNEY. One of the purposes for counterpart expressed in the act and in committees and on the floor of the House was that it was for supporting a sound fiscal policy. It seemed to the people in charge of policy at that time that you should not penalize a government that is operating not only with a balanced budget, but obtaining a surplus. They are fighting inflation. It would seem that we would be defeating our own purpose if we required the expenditure of these counterpart funds. However, since the end of last summer the counterpart funds have not been used; they have been held in an account in the Bank of England.

Mr. RICHARDS. How much was used in the last fiscal year for that purpose?

Mr. KENNEY. The total amount that has been used for debt retirement from the beginning of the ECA period, down through September of this year was a little under £200,000,000. Of that less than £57,000,000 was used this fiscal year. The present balance in the 

Bank of England is something in the neighborhood of £117,000,000. 

Mr. RICHARDS. You have given a good picture. I take my hat off to the British because they have punished themselves, they have regulated themselves, and they have character. 

You have told what they are attempting to do for Great Britain, and you have also told what they are attempting to do for the sterling area. 

However, you do not mention what they have done in the field of economic European unity.

Mr. Hoffman testified that after 1952, unless there is more unity in the economic field in Europe that we simply are never going to have a return of prewar prosperity. It seems to me that Great Britain is more concerned with the sterling area come-back, and with Britain's individual come-back. She must pay more attention to this European situation and I do not believe she is doing it to the extent she should. 

Mr. KENNEY. Let me explain that this way, Mr. Richards: There is no doubt but what Britain has an obligation to the sterling area. 

She is the banker for that area. It was from that area that large resources were mobilized for the prosecution of the war. It is probably the largest trading area in the world which is more closely analogous to that which we have in our present 48 States. However, because of that obligation she has to those countries-and I think we all must recognize the fact that she does have that obligation-complications are presented in the problem. Therefore, it makes it harder for her to proceed with the economic integration of Europe. And also 

I think we have to remember these two points: In the first place, the economic crisis of last summer had an extremely sobering effect upon the officials of that government. Also, they were aware of the fact that there would be an election this year. That produced a certain amount of caution on the part of people who I think by reputation always proceed cautiously. Therefore, I think there has been a slowness on their part, but I would not describe it, sir; as an unwillingness. 

Mr. RICHARDS. It is a complicated thing, but the point I want to make is if we are going to have prosperity in Europe, Great Britain

must be a part of it. The old empire system of Great Britain is gone and she might as well realize that. Much of her future is interwoven. with the future prosperity of Europe. She might as well put her name in the pot and fight for the same thing we are fighting for instead of fighting primarily for the British Commonwealth itself. 

Mr. KENNEY. I agree that her future is interwoven with that of 

Europe, and as I said earlier, I think those two obligations can be squared.

Let me say this in favor of what the United Kingdom has done: 

She was the first one to step up and remove the quantitative restrictions. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Do you refer to trade quotas? 

Mr. KENNEY. Yes, I refer to trade quotas.

Mr. RICHARDS. What is the position of Great Britain with regard to that? Mr. Hoffman is trying to get them to come across. 

Mr. KENNEY. In that move, I think it can be safely said Great 

Britain took the lead. 

Mr. RICHARDS. How about the unification of currencies in Europe?

Mr. KENNEY. The first plan for a currency payment union was one submitted by representatives of the British Treasury. Now our people in Mr. Harriman's office had certain questions about it. I put that in the category of a difficult problem that has to be worked out and not indicating an unwillingness on her part. 

Mr. RICHARDS. It must be worked out before 1952, must it not? 

Mr. KENNEY. That is quite correct.

Mr. RICHARDS. If it is not worked out by then it never will be worked out in our time? What do you think about that? 

Mr. KENNEY. I agree with you, sir. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Eaton, have you any questions?

Mr. EATON. Of course, this is all beyond me, but there is no doubt in the world that the United States has moved out now into the place of a world leader. That means a financial leadership and responsibility. That centers around the dollar.

I am wondering if it is possible, soon, to evolve some policy where the dollar will have to function, not simply as a give-away of the American taxpayer, but as a stabilizing, inspiring and developing influence throughout the world that will bring profit back to this country as a world financial center. In other words, it seems to me that wherever we have the dollar it creates a problem for us and does not seem to be doing such a tremendous lot of liberating the economic system of those with whom we deal. How are we going to make the dollar take its place in the world leadership of this country as the pound has done so long in the world leadership of England? 

Mr. KENNEY. Well, Mr. Eaton, that is one of the things that they are attempting to correct and improve in the work that they are doing in Paris on the development of a payments union, which will permit the improved transferability between currencies and eventually convertibility into dollars. At the present time there is a shortage of dollars in the world. That is our great difficulty. We must realize the fact that if foreign countries are going to buy our goods, which I hope they can continue to do, that they must earn the dollars to do it. 

Mr. EATON. They must have dollars, but how can they have it when it is impossible to convert dollars into their currencies, or their currencies into dollars?

Mr. KENNEY. If you get an improved balance of trade with goods flowing back and forth between countries, then countries are able to earn dollars with which to purchase-if you have a clearance union or payments union where currencies can be transferred between countries, you help to restore confidence in currencies. What you need to do, as I see it, is to restore confidence in currencies. There is not enough confidence yet in a good many currencies in Europe today, although it is much, much better than it was 2 years ago. The improvement of confidence in the currencies of the countries is quite remarkable. 

Mr. EATON. And that improved confidence will make it possible for them to be convertible into dollars? 

Mr. KENNEY. That is something that cannot take place overnight, but that would be our ultimate goal. Otherwise if we do not reach that result, what we have done is just to build barriers between the rest of the world and ourselves.

Mr. EATON. If we build barriers we would have to support them out of our taxpayers' money. 

Mr. KENNEY. Which I hope we will not have to continue doing beyond 1952. 

Mr. EATON. Thank you. That is all, Mr. Chairman.

If you were a farmer, Mr. Vorys, and you owed money which you finally paid off at the end of the tenth year with bushels of wheat, that would be an unrequited export in the same sense that we use the term here.

Mr. VORYS. That is right, an unrequited export from your farm.

Mr. KENNEY. That is perfectly correct. That is one of the difficulties in the resolution of the problem of the sterling balances, because it is an indebtedness and the British people, who are most fastidious about living up to their contractual obligations, are having a little difficulty in living up to them at the present time. 

Mr. VORYS. If you have a going concern like Britain, which is in difficulty, and they have a dollar shortage, that is the same thing that happens in our family at times and happens to a lot of people; they have a dollar shortage in that there are things they would like to buy with dollars, but they do not have the dollars. The normal way to handle a dollar shortage is not to pass the hat and ask for a present, but to say, "I would like to borrow some dollars."

I am wondering why, as far as Britain is concerned. Britain could not borrow $500,000,000 and next year $480,000,000 and then start paying it back with unrequited balances some time later.

2 tion. We must take into account the terrific damage that occurred to the economy of Great Britain during the war, and we must also take into account that the restoration of that economy is essential to stable conditions in the world as a whole.

Also, we must remember that Britain herself has. made great contributions toward the stability of other areas in the world. Up through August of 1949, the sterling equivalent of the amounts which she had given out for maintaining stability in India, Greece, and other parts of the world was almost equivalent to the amount of dollar aid that we had given. 

Now, of course, those two items are not necessarily equivalent, nor can they ever be equivalent, because in one case we are talking about sterling and in the other case we are talking about dollars. But I like to look at this as more of a communion of interests to restore world stability.

The industrial and agricultural recovery?

Mr. CARNAHAN. Is there any probability in the immediate future that free exchange of currencies will be a substantial source of dollars for any country, anywhere in the world?

Mr. KENNEY. The interchange of currencies, of course, is an integral part of world trade. One of the most important things about selling goods is how you get paid. Therefore, it is to be hoped that once you can provide that it will provide trade between countries and therefore improve the dollar situation insofar as Great Britain is concerned.

You see, Britain on her over-all balance of payments, as is shown in that chart 17, has only a very, very small over-all total deficit. 

However, she has a much larger deficit in dollars. 

Now, if she were able to balance off with dollars some of her favorable balances of payments with countries other than dollar countries against dollar deficits, she would not be in too bad shape. That is what she used to do before the war. She balanced off the surpluses that she had from invisibles, and those invisibles-by "invisibles," I mean her earnings in other countries in the form of shipping interests, insurance, and so forth-are largely earned from nondollar countries, but because of the fact that there was a relative parity between the currencies of the world she was able in the past to balance that surplus off as against her unfavorable balance of trade with the 

United States.

Mr. CARNAHAN. There are not very many countries in the world that have an excess of dollars. That seems to be the problem of most of them. So, outside of the dollar area, certainly the exchange of currencies is not very promising as a source of dollars. 

Mr. KENNEY. Your exchange of currencies between the other coun tries is a step toward financial stability and exchange stability from which we would hope at some time in the future to arrive at a point where there would be convertibility into dollars. I do not think that can be done this month or next month, or within the next 12 months.

Mr. JAVITS. This blocked sterling account, does, does it not, represent a dollar drain in the sense that unrequited exports could, at least in theory, be sold in a dollar area? Is that right?

Mr. KENNEY. There is the possibility that the satisfaction of those obligations does prevent Britain from earning dollars from goods that might be shipped to the United States. 

Mr. JAVITS. One of the situations we learned about while we were over there was that Britain pays out about $205,000,000 because she is the banker of the whole sterling area. 

Mr. KENNEY. The figure for the first 15 months of ECA was in the neighborhood of $300,000,000. That is for the first 15 months of ECA.

Mr. JAVITS. A good deal of that went to India, did it not? She is the biggest drawer on the blocked sterling balances? 

Mr. KENNEY. You are talking about two things there, Mr. Javits.

One is the drawing on the sterling balances, and the other was the dollar cost by reason of being banker for the sterling area. 

Mr. JAVITS. I have ended that dollar cost by reason of being banker of the sterling area. I am now asking you about India. India is the primary drawer on blocked sterling, as we do understand it. 

Mr. KENNEY. Of the £600,000,000 reductions, the largest individual portion of that I believe went to India and Pakistan. 

Mr. JAVITS. Do you believe that the United States, as a fundamental matter of policy, would be better off dealing with India in the sense of supporting the Indian economy with dollars directly, or do you believe it is better policy to do it through Great Britain, letting 

Britain act as the "honest broker" in the transaction?

Mr. KENNEY. My own feeling is that it is better to retain the relationship which has been built up over a long period of time. I would be a little hesitant to step in and disrupt and break down a pattern of banking, a pattern of trade, a pattern of relationships which have built up over a period of years. I just would not know what it would

do if we stepped in and injected ourselves into that. If we do it, I think we have to say: Are we ready and willing to undertake all of 

Britain's obligations with respect to all of the sterling area? It is a complex relationship and are we prepared to do that. We cannot just pick out one. They hang together.

Mr. JAVITS. We are spending about a fourth of the total ECA in order to enable Britain to be the banker for the sterling area. That is $300,000,000 over 15 months.

Mr. KENNEY. It is $300,000,000 over 15 months and out of a total of ECA aid of $1,302,000,000. The $300,000,000 represented the dollar drain by reason of that relationship. It is not exactly accurate to say that is the cost of Britain being banker for the sterling area. 

That is an oversimplification of the thing. It is a part of the British problem of trade relationships with all those areas. 

Mr. JAVITS. Have we a right to assume that in extending ECA we will be making a policy decision that Britain shall be permitted to use a large amount of the aid for enabling Britain to finance the sterling bloc with dollars; at least that far you will go? 

Mr. KENNEY. No part of the ECA aid strictly speaking goes for that purpose, actually, but I have given those figures to indicate the total dollar drain. What we are talking about is the total over-all balance of payments, and I think to give you a true and accurate picture of the dollar drain you have to have not only ECA dollars, but you have to have the so-called free dollars. That is why in that chart 19 you see a dollar gap of $2,030,000,000, of which $1,302,000,000 came from ECA.

Mr. JAVITS. I would like to conclude my questioning by making this statement: I have obtained from the ECA mission in Great Britain some very illuminating figures showing the ordinary income of the average man to compare in round figures with our own-for example, the average British worker gets $19.60 a week and the average American worker gets $56 a week. This is broken down in terms of his budget for the average family and in terms of the amount of his normal income to which is added what we call "Social income, health scheme, food subsidies" and so on. I have a letter from Mr. Abbot 

Low Moffat who is the acting chief of one of Mr. Kenney's divisions, taking off the tag "Restricted" which was on those figures. I would like to ask Mr. Kenney if it is agreeable to him that this information, which I think is fundamental to our whole thesis-showing that the British worker is very much worse off than anything we have any idea of here I want to find out from Mr. Kenney if it is agreeable to him for this to go into the record, and I will be glad to have him go over it to be sure that he agrees with his own division chief that the "Restricted" tag should be taken off.

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Without objection, we will include that in the record. (See p. 139.) 

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Mr. Lodge 

Mr. LODGE. Mr. Kenney, do you feel that an attempt is being made in 

England at this time, or has been made since ECA started, to provide incentives for equity investment in England? 

Mr. KENNEY. They issued the Treasury Regulation of this fall, I believe it was, which provided for a greater degree of convertibility into dollars of moneys invested in Great Britain after that period.

Are you referring to just external investments, or internal?

Mr. LODGE. Both. Do you think that the present economic system and the political trend that has been in vogue in Great Britain during the life of the ECA up to now has been an encouragement to the investment of equity capital within Britain? Is that a system of government under which equity capital investment is encouraged and prospers? 

Mr. KENNEY. In Great Britain, approximately 40 percent of the income is taken up in taxes. Now that has been necessary in order to balance their budget and carry on the various anti-inflationary controls that they put into effect. 

Mr. LODGE. Yet all of that does not go to inflationary measures, does it? 

Mr. KENNEY. No, it does not. A large segment of it does go for anti-inflationary purposes. Subsidy was what I had particularly in mind. Of course high taxation is always a deterrent to investment of equity capital.

Mr. LODGE. Much of that high taxation is due to the kind of political experimentation that is going on, is it not?

Mr. KENNEY. A large segment of your annual budget is used for that purpose.

Mr. LODGE. In other words, we can safely conclude that if they were not engaging in this experimentation, taxes would be lower and that therefore they would be increasing incentives for equity investment? 

Mr. KENNEY. I would say that that was correct. But whether or not that is a desirable thing to do is another matter. 

Mr. LODGE. I do not comment on that, but the thing I am coming to is that in your very interesting and provocative statement you say on page 5 that- By greatly increasing total production and by diverting an unusually large part of it into investment, Britain, with foreign assistance, has been making good these wartime losses and is now approaching the prewar level of capital. This program of capital formation is a real stride for economic recovery. 

In other words, you say something with which I completely agree, that capital investment and capital formation is a tremendously important factor in recovery. It seems to me that there we have a direct link without commenting on the other aspects of the question at all. 

We have a direct link between the program which the British Government has undertaken, nationalization and so on, with the problem of recovery which is a considerable burden upon the taxpayers of this country. Would you not say that we have there an inevitable contact and relationship?

Mr. KENNEY. Yes. 

Mr. LODGE. Therefore, when we address ourselves to that subject, we are not interfering with the domestic policies of Great Britain, but obviously since it effects our own internal policy we have a right to give it some consideration, is that not true? 

Mr. KENNEY. Oh, yes. However, let me say this with respect to our talking about the question of investment of equity capital: It is interesting to note that Great Britain which collects 40 percent out of its annual resources in taxes invest 20 percent of its annual resources in investment whereas we in the United States with a lower over-all tax burden invest a smaller percentage.

Mr. LODGE. I do not suggest that the equity investment market in the United States is at all satisfactory, and if you were to question me on that I would be glad to give you some answers. 

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). The time of the gentleman has expired. 

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Chairman, before we adjourn, if we are going to let the witness go, I had two questions which I wanted to ask him after the 

5-minute rule.

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Some of us have to go down to the floor, but we will have opportunity this afternoon to question the witness further. 

The committee is adjourned until 2:30 p. m. (Whereupon, at 12:15 p. m., the committee adjourned, subject to call of the Chair.)

WAGE EARNERS' INCOME AND EXPENDITURES IN THE UNITED KINGDOM 

It is very difficult to provide useful data on the income and outgo of the average British wage earner because of the lack of current budget studies. The 

Interim Index of Retail Prices is based on budget studies made in 1937-38 and carriers weights of the expenditure pattern of working-class families at that time. 

The index probably overweights expenditure on rent, fuel and household durable and underweights exepnditures on miscellaneous goods and services when present prices are applied to the old expenditure pattern. This pattern has undoubtedly changed importantly since these budgets were collected in 1937-38. The importance of this factor will vary in the future with the administration of price policy.

In a family unit of four, the average wage income of the principal earner before taxes and other deductions is about £7 ($19.60) per week. Many families have income producers other than the family head, and there is probably an important amount of multiple job holding by family heads, but no very satisfactory assumptions about total gross earnings of working-class families can be made on the basis of existing data. Family allowances (5s (70 cents) per week paid in respect of the second child in our family unit) are an element of cash income also although strictly speaking they originate as social or indirect income. 

Analysis of national aggregates of income gives a family gross cash income of about £10 per week, but they include elements of income other than wages (note 1 of table III). Rough calculations based on the number of incomes in the lowest bracket and the total national annual income in wage form indicate an average working-class family gross cash income of between £7 and £8 per week. (b) Social income

The table reproduced on the next page, prepared by the Mission's Research and Statistics Division, analyzes social or indirect incomes from the national outlay side. Inclusive of family allowances, which were referred to above, our family unit of four realizes a total social income of £2 16s ($7.85) per week. (c) Total money and social income We now have a total income of about £9 16s 0d ($25.44) of which approximately £7 10s ($21) is in cash form.

4. SUBSIDIES ENTERING COST OF LIVING 

At the present time in the United Kingdom, Government direct subsidies offset the cost of living only through those paid in respect of certain basic foods (whether directly as net losses involved to the Ministry of Food in the difference between the fixed selling prices and what it pays for commodities to domestic or foreign producers, or in free foods or reduced prices to children in school meals, or on the requisites of agricultural production-feeding stuffs and fertilizers, or to farmers for specified desired practices, etc.).

While the direct subsidy contained in purchase of the full rations and estimated consumption of other subsidized foods by a family unit of four is shown in table VIII to equal 10s. 42d. per week, the additional items of food subsidy give a total annual subsidy expenditure (£462m.) which is equivalent to 3s. 6d. per capita per week or 14s. per family unit.

Estimates have been made (R. G. D. Allen-London and Ambridge Economic 

Service, February 1949) that the abolition of food subsidies would raise the retail price index by about 12 percent. The overweighting of the food item (348) due to the relatively higher proportion of food expenditure in lower real and money incomes in the 1937-38 budgets has made food the logical target for price stabilization policy through price control and subsidies. 

(b) Housing 

While an annual housing subsidy of £66,000,000 is paid out of the Exchequer which enters indirectly into rents and therefore into the cost of living, the estimate of its effect on workers' rents is by no means straightforward. Not all workers live in local authorities' houses in respect of which subsidy is paid. 

Rent control has been of much more value in holding down the rent item in workers' budgets. It applies to all prewar housing not built by local authorities and landlords can only raise rents to cover local tax rate increases. The

in Tes he

REGRESA 

id largest amount of subsidy in rent has been the virtual one which has taken place at the expense of the landlords whose prices have risen significantly less than other prices in the economy since 1938. 

Table III above indicates a per capita housing subsidy expenditure of 6d. per week or 2s. for the family unit. The subsidy is included in table V, but probably ought not be treated as a direct subsidy since it has been paid in respect to building maintenance and depreciation as well as rentals. (c) Clothing and other important items in workers' budgets While no other direct subsidies are now paid by the United Kingdom Government, its policy of requiring the manufacture of "utility" lines of consumers' merchandise enters significantly into the cost of living. "Utility" clothing, textiles, and household furnishings must be produced as a specific percentage of total production to earn an allocation of raw materials for the manufacturer. 

They are price-controlled with low profit margins, and free of purchase tax. 

This policy has done much to make consumer necessities available to workers at higher quality and lower prices than would have been possible in a free market for limited supplies. 

6. OTHER SUBSIDIES AFFECTING COST OF LIVING 

The nature of other Government expenditures which affect workers' cost of living is a matter for a value judgment that we shall not attempt here. The social-security payments are contractual by legislation and are met to an important measure by employer and employee contributions, although the Exchequer contribution is still considerable. The bulk of the health service costs are met by the Exchequer. All relevant data to decide these questions will be found in tables III above and IX below. The latter will illustrate that "workers" more than pay for their own sicial-service benefits through direct and indirect taxes. Attention is called to the fact that these figures employ a £500 annual income basis and this is rather larger (£10 per week) than the typical wage earner's family cash income which we have placed between £7 and £8 per week.

f Mr. KENNEY. I would say that that has been relatively successful.

Mr. KENNEY. I will be glad to. 

(The information requested is as follows:) 

As in the case of the material inserted in reply to the question about the Middle East, the reply here must be couched in general terms. Since the total defense budget, although burdensome, is not unmanageable, it is difficult to say that any particular part of the whole stands in the way of recovery or the attainment of viability.

Britain's responsibilities in Trieste and Austria are relatively small compared to western Germany and, as in the case of western Germany, they have been diminishing.

The original United States-United Kingdom fusion agreement of 1946 did involve a direct dollar cost to the United Kingdom for certain German imports and the burden of this dollar cost was substantial. As amended in 1947, the 

British obligation was narrowed in essence to the provision of goods and services that could be obtained from the sterling area. The United Kingdom also contributed some sterling capital to western Germany. A contingent dollar liability remaining depended on the development of the trade position and an unanticipated development of the trade position did result in some gold settlements by the United Kingdom with western Germany. Recently, however, the trade position has returned to the expected direction. 

Outside western Germany, the United Kingdom did not have the obligation to contribute to the support of the occupied areas. United Kingdom security contingents in Austria. Trieste, and Japan were relatively small, and their maintenance in any case did not involve dollar costs.

If the scope of the question is extended to the consideration of United Kingdom responsibilities for maintenance of law and order, and of security in certain of its dependencies in the Far East, the burden of the obligation must be weighed against the fact that secure and peaceful conditions in the area would contribute substantially to the economy of the United Kingdom. In the case of Malaya, for example: Production of tin and rubber, both of which are very substantial dollar earners. could improve and Malaya make a net dollar contribution to the sterling area position as well as supply essential products directly to the United Kingdom and other participating countries without increasing their dollar expenditure.

Mr. JAVITS. Do you believe we should continue our present policy of direct bilateral arrangements with each of the ECA countries or that we ought to consider channeling the aid through the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, leaving it to that organization to make bilateral arrangements with the ECA countries? 

Mr. KENNEY. I think the procedure we have been following is much the sounder one. 

Mr. JAVITS. Will you tell us why?

Mr. KENNEY. One of the difficulties as I saw it in the way the program was initially worked out was that each country came in and presented its case for its needs before the OEEC. This had a tendency for each country to try to present the worst picture that it could. I think we got a much better result this past year when we were able to say that ECA aid is ending in 1952; there must be a reduction in the amount that is given, and we want to present the figure showing what you are going to do with what you are going to receive. They were not to come in and try to present the worst possible picture, because that procedure that they had in the first 2 years, I think, had a tendency at times to distort the picture.

Mr. JAVITS. You do not feel that the advantage we would get in building up the OEEC would recompense for that disadvantage? 

Mr. KENNEY. I do not. I certainly want to do everything possible to build up OEEC, because it has been a very effective, useful, and forceful organization.

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. KENNEY. I certainly think it is desirable that we know what our post-ERP policy is to be. Mr. JUDD. Mr. Kenney, on page 11 of your statement you speak about 

Britain's internal controls which could not protect her from the impact of the rapidly changing forces in world trade which came into play last summer. Were these rapidly changing forces foreseen or did they hit people unprepared? The reason I ask is because I recall that about last February Mr. Christopher Mayhew, the Under Secretary of Foreign Affairs or something of that sort, made some statement that they were out of the woods. He was very confident and almost cocky about the position of Britain and yet within 4 months they were so shaken that they had to take steps a few months later to devalue the pound sterling. If so world-shaking an event as that could not be foreseen as much as 3 or 4 months ahead of time, what assurance is there that any of this we are planning is any more than a hopeful guess? 

Mr. KENNEY. It is very difficult to evaluate. I think one of the most disconcerting things that happened last year is that this crisis hit Great Britain at a time when her own internal economy was on the way up. 

Her production was up. There was no unemployment. I think, if

I may say so, the mistake Mr. Mayhew made is that he was thinking in terms of the internal economy of Great Britain and had forgotten the fact that Britain has also a point of contact with the outside world. 

That was one of the most amazing things about the dollar crisis which did occur. It occurred with improving internal conditions, but at the point where she came in contact with the outside world, which was the dollar contact, and it produced a dollar deficit.

Mr. JUDD. In other words, he did not actually understand Britain's position himself? 

Mr. KENNEY. I would not say that Mr. Mayhew did not understand.

I do not think that that other part of the problem of Britain's economy was taken into account adequately in evaluating the situation. 

Mr. JUDD. It was not foreseen, was it? 

Mr. KENNEY. It did not begin to become apparent until the second quarter of last year.

Mr. JUDD. Did the ECA people, yourself and others, foresee it? 

Mr. KENNEY. The first time it began to become apparent to officials of ECA to the best of my knowledge was in the second quarter of 1949 when the figures on the dollar drain began to become apparent. 

You see the difficulty on these things is that the figures we get, which later made the crisis very apparent, were not available at that time. 

That is why I have put in chart 2 the various factors which are involved in it. It takes into account a number of different things: the reduction in United States factory production; the reduction in United States wholesale prices; the reduction in United Kingdom exports, and the rest of the sterling area's exports, to the United States; the obligation to pay certain dollars to other countries under their bilateral agreements. All of those things seemed to hit them at once. 

Mr. JUDD. That is true, but was it foreseen? I am trying to find out whether we have more than a hopeful guess in any of our predictions for the next year.

Mr. KENNEY. That it was not foreseeable in the first quarter of 1949, would be my estimate. I think we are in a little better position now than we were then because we have considerably more facts and we have been through this situation once so that now we are very much. aware of this particular problem. 

Mr. JUDD. You do not foresee in the next 12 months any rapidly changing forces of comparable magnitude?

not say there should be no unforeseeable complications, of course not, but you see no likely ones?

Mr. KENNEY. I put that in the category of a contingency which may or may not occur. We have to assume that it is not going to Occur.

Mr. JUDD. I think you have to assume that it is going to occur. 

Mr. KENNEY. We cannot assume that. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What are you doing against it? We are doing nothing out there to stop it.

Mr. KENNEY. That is correct. Now this probably could not be done but for the fact that Britain is the banker for the sterling area and that sterling is the currency for that area, so within that area sterling is freely accepted. 

Mr. LODGE. Would you go so far as to say that any tendency to break up the British Commonwealth of Nations would act to postpone and hamper European federation, European economic integration? Would you go so far as to say that the British Commonwealth system is a federating influence in Europe? To me that would be a

tremendously challenging and heartening thought. That is implied in this remark, it seems to me. 

Mr. KENNEY. That is correct, Mr. Lodge, and that is my thought.

Mr. LODGE. I think it is the most significant thing you have said in your whole statement. 

Mr. KENNEY. I am not speaking of the Commonwealth together in a political sense, but I think it would be a great mistake to break up the sterling area which is one of the largest trading areas existing in the world today. I think it can be a great force and factor in world recovery.

Mr. Lodge. I would say I agree with substantially all you have said. I will say that the relationship of the United Kingdom and the sterling area is not inconsistent with her relations with western Europe. I think we must recognize the fact that the recovery of

Mr. LODGE. Why was there that difference between 30 and 44 percent?
