TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED THURSDAY, MARCH 2, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

The committee met, pursuant to call, at 10:30 a. m., in the Foreign

Affairs Committee room, United States Capitol, Hon. Thomas S. 

Gordon presiding. 

Mr. GORDON. The committee will come to order.

Our chairman, Mr. Kee, has asked me to preside at this meeting this morning as he is attending a very important conference on the other side of the Capitol with a group of Senators. We have before us this morning Mr. David Zellerbach, chief of the ECA mission in 

Italy, who will testify on the extension of the ECA program. 

We will proceed under the 5-minute rule for questioning and we can proceed further in questioning after the 5-minute rule has expired. 

Mr. Zellerbach, you may proceed with your statement. 

STATEMENT OF J. DAVID ZELLERBACH, CHIEF, ECA MISSION TO ITALY 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I shall run over our situation in Italy very briefly-what we have been able to do what we have not been able to do-and then I shall be delighted to go into further detail as you like. 

The perspective is clearer now than when I had the pleasure of appearing before this committee last year. The indications of progress which were already apparent at that time have in most respects been born out-but progress in certain areas has been less than we had hoped for.

As we approach the midmark of the Marshall plan in Italy the conclusion is amply justified that the basic initial objectives of the program are being achieved. In general, Italy has continued to display good progress in industrial and agricultural production. Despite the serious drought which cut hydroelectric power output by about 17 percent, industrial production in 1949 was above the prewar average. Agricultural production just about reached the prewar average. 

Italy has achieved these levels while maintaining economic and financial stability-witness the strength displayed by the lira following the devaluation of the pound last September. Her budget position has steadily improved. She has gradually restored over-all consumption levels close to those prevailing in the prewar period. 

While the production picture is still spotty, and while consumption levels are still among the lowest in Europe, there can be no gainsaying the importance of this progress. 63307-50-pt. 1- -12 173

The major areas in which progress this past year has been less than I expected are in those of manpower and of dollar exports. 

Despite increased production, the economy has been able to do little better than absorb the natural increment to the working forces, leaving the substantial unemployment problem about as serious as it was a year ago. In other words, several hundred thousand new jobs have been provided, but several hundred thousand new hands have come along to fill them. Moreover, the expectation that increased emigration would drain off some of this pressure has likewise not been fulfilled. Although overseas emigration has increased substantially, the European market for Italian manpower has shrunk with the result that total emigration in 1949 was about the same as in the previous year.

As for dollar exports, 1949 saw a reversal of the strong upward trend. Dollar exports dropped to a relatively stable level, considerably below the peaks reached in November and December of 1948. When the final figures are in, exports to the dollar area in 1949 are expected to show a decline of about 50 percent from the 1948 levels. 

The problems of emigration and dollar exports, of course, cannot be solved by Italian action alone. On the other hand, much can be done to solve the manpower problem and to increase exports by adopting and implementing a sound and forward looking investment policy. 

Upon the basis of the financial stability which has been achieved, the Italian Government is now taking steps to expand the necessary credits and to provide policy guidance for accelerating the industrial and agricultural investment necessary to complete economic recovery. 

This was one of the matters at issue in the recent Cabinet reshuffle and the composition of the new Cabinet gives reason to expect that this policy will be pushed vigorously. The rate of achievement in this area will continue to be limited, as in the past, by the shortage of capital resources in Italy. The current improvement in this respect has not removed the serious problem which it presents. 

By the end of the current fiscal year, with the exception of continuing problems in unemployment and dollar exports, the basic objectives of the first phase of the recovery program in Italy will be well on the way toward achievement, and the prospects for maintaining this progress for the remaining 2 years of the Marshall plan are encouraging. Production will continue to rise, consumption levels will slowly improve, and this will be done without endangering financial and economic stability.

I have been greatly encouraged this last year by three developments that stem, at least in part, from the success of the Marshall plan in Italy thus far. The first is the Government's decision to move ahead with land reform. Our ECA mission has formally stated its cordial support of the program recently announced by the Prime Minister. 

Continued progress in this direction is vitally necessary from the viewpoint both of improving the lot of agricultural workers and of increasing production. We are doing more than approving it with words. We are actively assisting it by collaborating with the Italian 

Government in the planning of over 200 land-reclamation projects, financed from the ERP counterpart fund, which will make it possible for small farmers to make a living out of the improved land turned over to them.

The second source of encouragement is the decline in strength of the Communist Party. The most reliable estimates we can get indicate a drop of around 20 percent in the card-bearing membership of that party in the last 2 years, from 2,225,000 to between 1,500,000 and 

1,750,000. Since the last general election in April 1948, administrative elections have been held in 522 communes in Italy. The Communists and left-wing Socialists who are affiliated with them won only 91. 

The Christian Democrats won 304, of which 85 had formerly been controlled by the Communists and left-wing Socialists, and the other parties won the remaining 127.

The third reason for encouragement is the fact that the Communists have lost their exclusive domination over organized labor. 

Two years ago there was only one labor confederation, embracing just over 5,000,000 members. Since then two important segments have broken away and formed anti-Communist labor confederations. Just before I left Italy these two groups voted in favor of unification. The new non-Communist labor confederation will have a combined membership of nearly 2,000,000. The Communist controlled confederation is now down to under 3,000,000. 

Just a few days after my arrival in Italy in July 1948, the Communists called a general strike. Cities virtually died; all shops closed and iron shutters came down over the shop windows; public transport ceased; all factories closed; people left the streets and sidewalks for the shelter of their homes. Today, when the Communists call a general strike, the shops stay open, public transport operates with little if any interruption; most factories remain open; people throng the streets and sidewalks; and a casual visitor might not know that a general strike was on. This does not mean, however, that Communist strength is finally broken, especially in the industrial centers of the north.

In Italy the operation of the Marshall plan is visible through many public works and other improvements financed under the ERP counterpart fund which as you know, is created from the sale of Marshall plan materials sent free to Italy. These embrace agricultural developments, industrial installations, electric power developments, bridges, roads, aqueducts, public buildings, schools, workmen's houses, railroad stations or other railroad improvements, port developments, and the like. The people can see with their own eyes what the Marshall plan is doing for them and their children. Long after the Marshall plan has ended these improvements will stand as monuments to the wisdom and generosity of the American people.

With the fullest cooperation of the Italian Government, the Italian people are being informed in many ways that these projects which mean so much to them are financed from the Marshall plan counterpart fund. We do so through signs on the projects themselves, through regional maps, through radio programs, through documentary movies, through exhibits, through press stories, through sound and projection trucks-in fact, through every means we believe efficacious in going right to the man in the street and the man in the fields. 

We are continuing to get good cooperation from the Italian Government and people in our joint efforts to solve the difficult problems that face Italy. The people are working diligently to push forward with the reconstruction of their country. The Prime Minister and his

colleagues are fully aware of the vital role which ECA aid is playing in Italy's struggle for recovery, and have consistently expressed to me their most cordial recognition of this fact. What is more, they have backed up these sentiments with a readiness to seek joint solutions. 

This, while it does not eliminate difference of opinion, makes possible a constructve attack on these problems. 

The Italian Government has demonstrated a willingness-I could better say eagerness to cooperate toward economic integration in western Europe. The initial impact of such steps might be difficult for a country as poor as Italy to absorb. On the other hand, Italy, precisely because she is among the poorer nations of Europe, stands to benefit most in the long run from any such development. Most 

Italians in responsible places recognize this, and the policy of the Italian Government reflects this recognition. 

I am prepared to go on record as an American businessman with the statement that America's investment in Italy is paying off. It is paying off not only in economic terms, in the sense that it is achieving an economic recovery even more advanced than had been hoped for at the inception of this program. It is paying off also in terms of an increased political and social stability, so badly needed in the world of today.

I am prepared to high light the major aspects of Italian economic problems and progress with a few selected charts, after the close of these remarks. I believe, however, that the committee might be interested now in a few specific features of the general picture I have just given.

Industrial production: The general level of industrial production rose from 98 percent of the 1938 level in 1948 to 104 percent in 1949. 

This substantial progress was achieved despite serious limitations imposed by factors partially beyond the control of Italian business and Government. As a result of extremely unfavorable weather conditions the availability of hydroelectric power in Italy during 1949 was about 17 percent less than in 1948. In addition, the decline in exports which I have already mentioned dampened industrial production efforts particularly in the textile and mechanical industries, which are of paramount importance in terms of employment and which depend heavily on export markets. Major factors in the increase were to be found in construction, food processing, petroleum refining, staple fiber production, chemicals, and natural-gas production. For example, mining was up 18 percent over 1948, textiles 14 percent, chemicals 6 percent, petroleum refining around 40 percent, building materials 13 percent, and so forth. The only major sector which saw a decline was electric power, down 10 percent. In the vital sector of the mechanical industries, however, over-all progress continued to be slow. Although output increased from 80 to 90 percent compared to the 1938 level, this relates to a 1952 goal of 150 and represented a rate of activity no more than 60 percent of capacity.

Agricultural production: Agricultural production in 1949 also showed further substantial improvement, with the general level, according to Italian statistics, estimated at 89 percent of 1938, compared with 86 for the previous year and an ultimate objective of 105. Nearly all major crops were up substantially. Wheat production was around 

7,000,000 tons in 1949, which was only slightly below the 1936-39

average, and represented an increase of 13 percent over 1948. Corn, rice, and sugar beets were all at or above 1948 levels. The olive crop, rebounding from a bad year in 1948, was up more than 60 percent. Óf the major crops, only potatoes and hemp showed a significant decline from 1948 levels. This general increase in agricultural output was due not only to the increase of land under cultivation, but also to increases in agricultural input which raise per unit yields. During the first 10 months of 1949, 2,951 new tractors were registered as compared to 1,173 for a similar period in the previous year.

Use of nitrogenous fertilizers in 1948-49 exceeded the level of the previous crop year by 22 percent. Application of phosphoric oxide was up 44 percent. 

Moreover, the Italian Government and ECA have worked out a program to encourage the use of select seed. The success of this year's program for the use of 2,000 tons of American hybrid corn seed will undoubtedly result in increased future utilization. Agricultural production can be expected to continue rising as the lira-fund program of land reclamation and improvement brings more land under cultivation and as the land-distribution program brings presently unutilized holdings into productive use. The mission has given its support to the land-reform program recently announced by the Italian Government, and is working to coordinate its reclamation, irrigation, and other agricultural projects into this program in order to maximize the productivity of the land. 

Financial and monetary stability: Financial and monetary stabilization has been maintained now for almost 22 years. The sharp postwar inflation was stopped in September of 1947 when prices had gone up 60 times prewar. Since early 1948 prices and wages have remained substantially stable. The general level of wholesale prices is around 48 times prewar, compared to 52 in early 1948. This stabilization has been strengthened by improvement in the Government budget position, with revenues now covering about 85 percent of expenditures as compared to 52 percent in 1947-48 and 68 percent in 1948-49. The Government is living within its budget. Its credit has improved; Government bond prices have gone up and the Government is able to borrow at long term again. Two important measures on fiscal reform have been introduced into Parliament to improve the direct-tax structure and to effect allocation of tax sources between the national and local governments. In the meantime, the administration of the existing tax system is being gradually improved, partly through American equipment and technical assistance. Tax yields have been steadily increasing. In all, based on the consolidation of financial and monetary stability, it has become possible for the Government to move more rapidly in expanding its investment program. 

Credit policy has been relaxed through reduction in rediscount rates of the Bank of Italy and a dropping of reserve requirements of the banks. The new Government is committed to a major expansion in its investment program which will accelerate Italy's progress toward recovery. Confidence that this could be done without endangering the stability of the lira was engendered, not only by the above factors, but also by the firmness of the lira following the general devaluation of western European currencies last fall. The Government is. programing public and Government-encouraged expenditures for 1950-51 totaling 990 billion lire compared to 755 in the current year

as a part of its aggressive investment program for achievement of ECA objectives. 

Consumption: So far as consumption is concerned, latest official estimates indicate that over-all consumption in 1949-50, taking into account price adjustments made on the basis of the cost-of-living index, will amount to about 92 percent of the 1938 level. Consumption of foodstuffs in the current year will be about 4 or 5 percent above the level of last year, and will reach roughly 98 percent of the prewar level. The last rationing controls were removed during the past summer, when bread and pasta were freed from governmental distribution restrictions. Consumption of nonfood items is also gradually increasing, and the attainment of the long-term goals is in sight. 

Imports: In the last 2 years of the recovery program Italy foresees little change in the total value of Italian imports. In 1951-52, the program calls for total imports of $1,481,000,000 as compared with $1,475,000,000 in 1949-50. The shift in composition of the import program which is already taking place will, however, be considerably accentuated. The program foresees a continued upward trend in the importation of industrial fuels and raw materials as the Italian economy reaches higher levels of economic activity. In 

1950-51 and 1951-52 the increase in these imports will offset, in value terms, the tapering off of the machinery import program. The current year is the peak year for machinery and equipment imports, with these orders totaling around $300,000,000 in all currencies. From this peak, machinery imports drop off and industrial raw materials rise. It is estimated that imports of foodstuffs will remain virtually unchanged during the rest of the program at about $300,000,000 per annum in all currencies. This will support a continued modest increase in the Italian standard of living.

Anticipated dollar exports increase only from $120,000,000 in the current fiscal year to $142,000,000 in 1951-52 and exports to the United States are estimated at $73,000,000 of the latter total. A vigorous effort is now being made to increase the sales of Italian products in the United States through exhibits in leading United States cities, improved sales organization, and better merchandising methods. 

Special governmental organizations have been established during the current year to devote themselves entirely to the expansion of dollar exports. Italian exporters are being furnished with current information regarding the possibilities of dollar exports, with published reports on United States customs procedures and market areas, and with studies outlining dollar export possibilities and improved methods of selling in American markets. Plans have been completed for the opening of Italian business centers in New Orleans, New York, San Francisco, and Chicago. In addition, Italy will participate fully in the Chicago fair scheduled to be held in August of this year and in other fairs in San Francisco and New Orleans. It must be remembered, however, that there are many obstacles to the substantial increase of dollar exports, not the least of which is the fact that the major Italian export items to the United States are such things as cheese, olive oil, ceramics, and musical instruments. In general, the goods which Italy is now shipping to the United States are goods which are not urgently needed and the market for which cannot be easily expanded.

Of these total requirements, it is expected that imports in dollars will decline from about $560,000,000 in the current year to some $319,- 000,000 in 1951-52, again almost wholly as a result of declining needs for machinery imports. The dollar commodity imports for the last year of the program, so far as ECA financing is concerned, will be almost entirely composed of bread grains, petroleum, copper, and cotton. These commodities will continue to be the irreducible minimum of dollar import requirements in the period after 1952, and hence will set the magnitude of the problem of earning dollars to pay for such essential materials. It may be possible to reduce dollar imports of these items further after 1952, either by finding additional nondollar sources or by developing domestic resources. In general, however, it is clear that Italy will continue to have a large requirement for dollar imports and will have to make vigorous efforts to expand dollar earnings to pay for them.

Exports: Since this is one of the areas in which progress during the past year has been less than satisfactory, the difficulty is further accentuated. While total exports were up some 7 percent in 1949 compared to the previous year, exports to the United States dropped from about $90,000,000 to around $45,000,000 in 1949, a decline of 50 per- Although a large increase is foreseen in the total value of Italian exports by 1951-52, the bulk of these exports is expected to go to nondollar areas.

Emigration: The other major area in which results this year have been below expectations is emigration. Net emigration in 1949 was apparently just about at the 1948 level of 170,000. Overseas emigration rose from 95,000 to about 135,000, but continental movement declined from 75,000 to about 22,000-enough to offset the overseas improvement. A number of encouraging steps are now being taken. 

The Government has recently completed an internal reorganization which will serve to centralize responsibility for overseas emigration. 

It has also completed an over-all plan for the utilization of about $10,000,000 of its own free funds, together with technical assistance help from ECA, for the sponsoring of pilot projects in various South American countries. While these over-all plans are still in rather general terms, the Government is about to begin a specific project in Brazil on the basis of which future operations can be undertaken. 

It is evident that these activities cannot contribute very much to improving the actual flow of emigration in this current fiscal year, but it is hoped that sharp improvement will result in the last 2 years of the program.

Industrial modernization: One of the remaining major problems which will condition Italy's ability to stand on her own feet after 1952 relates to continued reduction in costs of production through modernization of her industrial plant and increased productivity. 

This involves both the provision of American machinery for modernization and expansion projects and the provision of American know-how through the technical-assistance program. With few exceptions, the most pressing need of Italian industry is improved efficiency of existing facilities rather than a general expansion of existing plant. The most important exception is electric-power production, which must be substantially expanded to support real industrial recovery. The mission has already approved major projects in this

category for about $56,000,000. The major modernization of existing capacity is being undertaken in the iron and steel sector, about $37,- 000,000 in projects so far approved, and the mechanical industries, $16,000,000 so far approved. Other project approvals have involved mining, petroleum refining, cellulose, and paper. In addition to these major projects, there have been over 1,100 approvals for cash purchases of machinery and equipment, mostly by small- and mediumsized concerns for total of some $30,000,000. In addition, some 290 medium- and small-loan applications for this equipment have been approved to a total of over $60,000,000. Machinery under the programs is going into a wide variety of enterprises in every segment of the economy. In addition, over half the funds being programed for technical assistance are for industrial-productivity surveys. 

Housing: One of the most encouraging developments in the Italian economy during 1949 was the revival of the building industry. About 

160,000 rooms were completed during the year, as compared to 120,000 in 1948 and 149,000 in 1938. This resulted in an increase of employment among building workers of about 150,000 and stimulated production in related industries. Figures on output of cement, bricks, and tiles, marble, hot-rolled steel were all up substantially above the levels of 1948. Most of the increase was due to the expansion of private housing activity. The progress was aided by Government programs known as Tupini and Fanfani housing programs, which provided for low-cost housing for workers. Despite the increase in private housing and the added impetus of these Government programs, the estimated requirement for rooms to restore the prewar person-per-room average is far above the present rate of buildings. 

The ECA and the Italian Government have, therefore, launched a supplemental housing program calling for 10,000.000.000 lire from the lira fund to encourage an even greater increase in activity. These funds will be used to establish a building loan revolving fund from which loans will be granted to finance low-cost housing construction. 

The actual projects will be undertaken by building cooperatives, or by building firms committed to sell the houses within a year at nonspeculative prices. While there will still be large unsatisfied needs, this will serve to accelerate an already remarkable rate of progress in this field, and to increase the corollary benefits in terms of employment and stimulation of related industries. 

Mr. GORDON. Thank you very much, Mr. Zellerbach, for your very informative statement.

I want to say that I had the pleasure of being in Italy in the fall of last year, and I have seen much improvement since my first visit there in 1947.

I am glad to see that finally a program on taxation has taken place. 

Could you describe that and tell us more about the program involved? 

I believe it would be of importance and of interest to all of us. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I would be glad to discuss that. The tax system in Italy is rather antiquated, as is the case in other European countries. In Italy it dates back to the formation of the present consolidated government in 1870.

We have an accumulation of tax laws, one on top of the other, which has resulted in a situation where if all of the taxes were enforced, it would take substantially over 100 percent of income. As a matter of fact, as everyone knows, it is impossible to enforce all the taxes.

The methods of collection are rather unusual. There is no requirement for the taxpayer to declare his tax. The tax is arrived at through negotiation. 

I can go into considerable detail as to the present situation, but what you want to know, I think, is what is being done about it. 

Mr. GORDON. That is right.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. So far under the technical assistance program we have authorized several experts from the tax department to come here to study our methods of tax administration, as well as our tax legislation. They have gone back to Italy to put into effect the results of these studies.

Legislation has been drafted and has already been introduced into the Parliament which will provide for a revision of the direct income tax system, which will put the obligation on the taxpayer to declare his tax, and which will tighten up the administration of the tax system.

It will make it possible for the taxpayer to be honest in his declarations by reducing rates to reasonable levels. Companion legislation will restrict the provinces and local communes in their taxes so they will not be in a position to utilize the declarations to assess taxes on the same sources which will offset the reductions the central government proposes to make. These changes are designed to make the direct tax system enforceable.

That is the plan that is under way, and it is hoped that that legislation will get through Parliament in the present session. 

Pending the passage of this legislation, tax administration even under the present laws has been tightened up, and tax collections have been increased materially over the past several years. This is a prepared paper on this subject in further detail. 

Italian taxation and tax reform: The Italian people as a whole are bearing a heavy tax load. In 1949, central and local government taxes, including social security taxes, absorbed approximately 29 percent of total national income. For a poor economy such as Italy, where annual per capita income is only $225, an average per capita tax bill of $65 is indeed heavy. By way of comparison, it may be noted that the ratio of taxes, Federal and local-including socialsecurity taxes-to national income in the United States is about 25 percent.

The Italian tax system today is a hodge-podge resulting from the cumulative piling of one tax law on top of another for decades. As one tax law proved less and less effective, the usual procedure was not to repeal or modify it, but to add a new one. The result is that full enforcement of all tax legislation on the books is now impossible in the absence of a complete reorganization and rationalization of the tax system. What has emerged is a revenue system based primarily upon indirect taxes. Such levies accounted for a total of 78 percent of the revenues of the central government in the last 6 months of 1949. 

Direct taxes, by which is meant all personal and business income taxes, estate duties, etc., provided only 20 percent of revenues during that same period.

The most important single levy included under the general heading of indirect taxes is the 3-percent IGE transaction tax which is paid every time anyone pays money for goods or services of any sort. Thus

when one makes payment whether for raw materials, semifinished products, rents, restaurant meals, or railway fares, he pays 3 percent to the National Treasury. It is a tax which directly affects costs of production, being particularly severe in nonintegrated industries where an article changes hands many times during the process of manufacture. The second major group of indirect taxes, those known as consumption taxes proper, have an incidence such as to distort the pattern of a rational allocation of scarce resources. Taxes levied on produce entering metropolitan areas, for instance, tend to prevent the proper movement of merchandise from one marketing area to another. Other taxes on Government monopoly products such as tobacco, salt, and matches are proportionately quite high. 

A tax system which places so much reliance upon indirect levies has the further effect of distributing the tax burden in such fashion that the lower-income groups are bearing a disproportionately large share. 

The ineffectiveness of the income tax is not the result of any mildness of statutory rates; those, as a matter of fact, are fantastically high and steeply progressive. The trouble lies in the manner in which the taxcollection system is set up and administered. 

At present the initiative in the payment of income taxes lies with the tax collector. A fiscal agent, who is a member of the military police, seeks out likely sources of revenue and makes his assessments on the basis of external criteria. In the case of personal income, this will be the observed general standard of living of the person assessed. 

One exception is the man paid a fixed salary; a withholding tax is deducted at the source. In the case of business enterprises, the assessor tries to estimate probable profits on the basis of such information as is available as to the size of the concern, its volume of output, the rate at which it has been operating, and the profit margin typical to that industry or business. Some corporations are taxed on the basis of bookkeeping accounts, which may or may not be kept with an eye to honesty in tax returns.

There then ensues a protracted period of bargaining between the taxpayer and tax collector. Actual collection of taxes is not done by the Government directly but by private firms to which the work has been awarded by contract. In his negotiation with this firm, the taxpayer tries to minimize his payments by concealing his income. Indeed, the rates are so high that an accurate statement in many cases would result in virtually complete absorption of the income. Enforcement of penalties for tax evasion is not very effective under these circumstances.

The ECA Mission, almost at the very outset of its arrival in Italy, pointed out to the Italian Government the necessity of correcting the above weaknesses in its tax system. The Italian Government indicated that it was cognizant of these weaknesses and in spite of the difficulties involved would exert all effort to carry out a comprehensive tax reform. It was pointed out that such reform would take time and could not be carried out overnight. A few steps on the road towards a better tax system have already been taken; more important measures are now being worked out. 

Among the measures already taken, most important are those designed to improve the administrative efficiency of the tax offices. 

Mechanical equipment is being provided; tax officers are being given training courses in improved methods of operation; some key officials

of the Ministry of Finance have been sent to the United States to study American methods under the ERP technical-assistance program. 

At the beginning of 1949, the IGE (transactions) tax was reduced from 4 to 3 percent in a move to lighten its burden and make its collection easier; the reduction was accomplished with no drop in the yield.

Legislation to overhaul the direct tax system is now being considered by financial committees of the Italian Parliament. The suggested legislation is intended to rationalize and improve the national income tax system. First of all, it would shift the initiative in collecting taxes from the Government to the tax payer by requiring him to file an annual return, as is done in the United States. This return would not be the starting point for bargaining but would be the basis on which the tax would be levied. Secondly, the rates and exemptions are adjusted to levels which make honesty in reporting and conscientiousness in enforcement feasible. The bill is expected to be enacted by parliament this spring.

Even so, a great deal will still remain to be done by way of tax reform. The penalties provided against noncompliance with the new income tax regulations are not heavy and may prove insufficient to secure compliance. Then again, even if national tax rates are reduced, the taxpayer will fear that the information contained in the national tax returns might be used as a basis for unreasonable demands by provincial and local tax collectors. Hence, additional legislation is now planned, looking toward a limitation on the powers of local governmental bodies to tax these same sources of income. 

In its contacts with the Italian Government, the ECA Mission will continue to press for adoption of the direct-tax reform measures which have been described above. When these first necessary steps have been taken, it is hoped that the Italian Government will work on other measures designed to improve further the efficiency and equitability of the existing tax system. Important among these are (1) an end of the system of farming out the actual process of tax collection to private agencies; (2) substantial reduction of indirect taxes which, by throwing up artificial financial barriers, tend to keep the flow of economic resources from moving into the most productive channels. This refers particularly to excessive consumption and turnover taxes. As the operation of the income tax improves and the yields increase, there should be sufficient room in the state budget to allow at least commensurate reductions in these less desirable forms of raising revenue for the state.

You might say it started with the First World War and then the period of fascism and the autarchic economic system which that involved, and then the Second World War and the period of occupation. During all this time there was a diversion of the small capital accumulation to what you might call noneconomic uses.

Then there are the losses resulting from the war and the destruction caused by the Germans in their retreat. 

There is a situation there where on top of an already weak position for building its economy, in that it lacks most important natural resources, there are these losses and diversion of the capital accumulations over a long period of time. 

So as of now, Italy is very, very short of capital which is necessary to build its industry and agriculture to support its very large population. Therefore, any reduction in the aid which we give Italy will have a serious effect on its ability to carry out the program.

Mr. GORDON. Mr. Carnahan, have you any questions?

Mr. CARNAHAN. Mr. Chairman and Mr. Zellerbach, may we have a more detailed statement regarding population trends in Italy. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. The population has been increasing in recent years at the rate of around 400,000 a year. If we go back through history we will notice that 1870 was the year of the formation of the Italian monarchy. At that time Italy had a population of about 

26,000,000 people. I can give it to you by decades if you would like to have it from then on. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. What is the trend? Is it leveling off?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Yes; it is leveling off. For instance, in 1871 it was 26,000,000. In 1900 it was 32,000,000; in 1920 it was 36,000,000, and as of now it is about 46,000,000. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. That is the total population? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is the total population.

Now the rate of increase is declining. For instance, the birth rate in Italy, today, averages, as a matter of fact, lower than in the United States for 1948. The rate for 1948 was 21.6 live births per thousand inhabitants. That was only 0.6 percent higher than France and lower than the United States figure, which was 24.4. 

If you go back to the 1919-39 average in Italy, it was 26.1. In the 

United States in 1936 it was 16.7.

Mr. CARNAHAN. Of course, with Italy, that is a country not capable of too much expansion, and an increased rate certainly is a problem? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I think the problem in Italy is not so much the birth rate, which seems to compare today rather favorably with birth rates in other major countries. It is primarily the fact that there are too many people living in too small a territory with too few assets in the way of natural resources. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Does the land-reform program offer very much?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Land reform should bring about an increase in production, as I pointed out. It will produce work for additional people. It is very hard to estimate just how many. 

Of course if you carry land reform to the point of introducing more efficient methods, you will reduce rather than increase the number of people on the land. Land reform will absorb some of the excess population, but I think the major reliance must be placed on development of industry and on emigration. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. The project you mentioned in Brazil, just what is that project?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. The Italian Government has been negotiating with several of the South American countries to provide emigration opportunities. They have people right now making surveys. It is proposed to establish a pilot settlement colony in Brazil, to try out methods of colonizing, before a more ambitious plan is undertaken. 

In that way I think mistakes that have been made in the past are likely to be avoided.

As you know, today the emigrant is no longer willing to go out with an ax and try to carve himself a home, as was done in the early days of the settlement of this country. When he goes out to emigrate he needs to have a place to go provided for him, and he needs capital assets, and he needs more than just an ax. He needs a home and tools with which to work.

A certain amount of preparation must be made before an emigrant can be persuaded to go out now and stay out. I do not mean one, but 

I mean in any substantial numbers. This requires very careful preparation in order to do an effective job. 

There is not much use in sending emigrants out to have them be dissatisfied and come back at the first opportunity. That has happened in Italy.

Mr. CARNAHAN. There is actually an experimental colony in Brazil? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Not yet. Preparations are getting under way to establish an experimental colony, which we hope will be done this year on a pilot basis. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Is there a vital need for dollars in the Italian economy?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Definitely. I have pointed out that as nearly as we can figure there will be a minimum requirement of about $300,-

000,000, which will be used to buy those materials and food supplies necessary to keep the economy going.

Mr. CARNAHAN. You mean those things must be bought from the dollar areas and cannot be had elsewhere?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Such things as cotton. There is a large textile industry in Italy, and today's price for cotton for that industry runs. around $100,000,000 a year.

There are no other places from which you can supply that requirement except in the United States. Some small amounts may be obtained in India, Brazil, and such places, but the major supply must come from the United States and must be paid for in dollars. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. I believe you said exports to the United States had dropped 50 percent within the last year? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is right. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Then the chance to earn dollars does not look too bright.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. There are opportunities to earn more dollars, beyond that, but that is going to require a considerable drive. I think the prospects for earning more dollars are encouraging. 

I think I ought to explain the drop of 50 percent from 1948 to 1949. In 1948 we were still in a seller's market. Therefore, Italy, along with other European countries, was able to sell many of its products for dollars, which it is not now able to sell in the United 

States market for competitive reasons.

I think there is another factor which has affected exports to the United States. That is as a result of the negotiations under the 

ITO. Certain reductions in tariffs are anticipated as a result of that, but they have not as yet been put into effect. 

We feel that certain buyers are holding off, waiting to get the advantage of these lower tariffs. I do not know what that amounts to, but it certainly has had some effect. 

As to the future earning of dollars, I would say the biggest dollar earner for Italy prewar, and we anticipate postwar, was and will be tourism. Tourism in Italy is getting back toward prewar levels, but it has not reached those levels yet. 

There was considerable destruction in hotel facilities, and until that is repaired-and incidentally we are assisting in that through the use of counterpart-the income from tourism will not be as great as it has been and will be. That should be a much larger dollar earner than it is now.

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Chairman, I have just one other question. 

Our European Study Mission report on Italy shows about 19,000,000 employed and 2,000,000 employables unemployed. We also show 1.7 on civil service rolls. Is that an actual picture of Italian employment and unemployment, or is there hidden unemployment in the sense of overstaffing both in private business and in Government; will you tell us about that? There is overemployment in industry, in agriculture, in Government service, and in the service industries. How much that amounts to is very hard for anyone to estimate. Mr. JAVITS. As a corollary of that, would the cessation of ECA aid bring that out in the open and present Italy with a great unemployment crisis?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I do not think it would have that result because the question of overemployment is pretty much out in the open now. 

However, where you have a situation such as you have in Italy with excess people who must be fed, it is a question whether, for social and political reasons, it is possible to force people off pay rolls and onto the dole, you might say. The result of the cessation of Marshall plan aid, which is dollar aid, would show itself up almost immediately in a reduction in standards of living, because of the impossibility of buying all of the food that is necessary to maintain the present minimum standards of living which exist in Italy, plus the impossibility of buying certain raw materials which are necessary to keep the industry going which is supporting a lot of people. 

I would say any stoppage of aid at this point to Italy would have very disastrous results, and very quickly.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. On the land question, as I pointed out, I think, last year, there is legislation already on the books which will permit the taking over of land by the Government for payment of its fair value, in the south of Italy. Certain projects are under way now in the south of Italy which will bring about the taking over of nonproductive lands, and which will provide methods for developing those lands and for turning them over to peasants on smaller farms. 

Now, the new legislation which has been under discussion for over a year has been kept under discussion perhaps for the same reason that a great amount of our legislation here is kept under discussion. 

It is a very controversial subject. There are many points of view within Italy as to how this job should be undertaken. Conditions are different in different areas in Italy. To draft a piece of legislation which will be workable in all areas and which will work to the benefit of the economy of the country and also bring about the social improvement desired is a very difficult job. 

Today Italy is about as democratic in its processes as we are. Even though the Christian Democratic Party has a majority in the Parliament, there are some differences of opinion within the Christian Democratic Party which have to be ironed out before the whole party will support legislation. That has delayed the passage of the Italian legislation and perhaps too long.

Included within this district will be some 110,000 acres of land which will be acquired from holders of agricultural land of over 300 hectares. 

That is about 750 acres.

That land will be developed and then divided into approximately 5,000 smaller farms which then will be sold on long terms to the peasants who will be settled on the separate farms. 

Within that area the Marshall plan out of counterpart funds is assisting in the financing of nine separate reclamation-irrigation districts. Most of the land in that particular area is not particularly productive. It is mostly pasture land and so forth. There is no use in taking that land and breaking it up into small holdings, putting peasants on it and letting them starve to death. 

In order to make the program a sound program you have to make part of the program the development of that land to make it productive so it is possible for the peasant to support himself on the farm which he acquires.

I think you will see the results of our efforts very shortly in a much more aggressive campaign on the part of the Italian Government to bring tourists into Italy. 

Of course, you know that when you go out to advertise your product, you want to be sure you can deliver it. In Italy the reconstruction problem up until very recently, you see, has really made it somewhat advisable to defer trying to bring a lot of people into Italy until it was possible to take care of them properly. Now the railroad system and the transportation system generally, the highways and communications, have been brought back pretty much to the prewar condition. 

There is still this question of the rehabilitation of hotels and the need to build additional hotels, so that Italy can take care of all of the people who ought to come there. However, you will see this campaign, I am sure, getting underway very soon. A tourist office has been opened in New York for over a year, now, and that activity I am sure will be expanded.

Mr. CHATHAM. I would only want to observe that money spent for a hotel may bring in more exchange than would a factory of some kind. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I quite agree with you. 

Mr. CHATHAM. Thank you. That is all. 

Mr. GORDON. Mr. Fulton, have you any questions?

Mr. FULTON. I wanted to ask about the separatist movement the "Unita," in northern Italy. Is it still strong to divide Italy into two parts, or has that pretty well gone by the board? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I do not think there is any movement of any importance to divide Italy into two parts. You know Italy is still a country of many parts. It is somewhat similar to the situation in this country. A man is an American but he is also a Southerner or a 

Californian or he is something else. There is that feeling very strongly in Italy. A man is a Florentine or a Roman or a Neapolitan. is Then there is this movement to set up more regional autonomy which very evident in Sicily and Sardinia. There is no separatist movement.

Mr. FULTON. There has been a movement sponsored by the Communists called Unita which was to cut the industrial cities off. I understand, as you say, that movement has died down and there is no particular relevancy at this time. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. No, it is not.

Mr. FULTON. We in America are going through a great building program, as you know, and in Italy they have many fine quarries and many idle people. A large group of unemployed exist there at this time.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is one raw material Italy has in abundance and, of course, they have the people necessary to work in that field.

In that connection we have many places where we could use good stone on plazas, fountains, and on bridge work. There seems to be no adequate place within the country from which we can get deliveries immediately. Would it be possible to ship these items from Italy in these ECA ships as ballast?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That I do not know. I doubt very much whether the steamship companies would carry it unless you paid their established rates for it. I will have our Italian salesman here in Washington come around and call on you immediately to go into this whole problem.

Mr. FULTON. We would like to speak with him very much. I have talked with many people in Pittsburgh and I think it would be a good source for getting dollars. In fact, we in Pittsburgh are very proud of the lending that Italy does of our very fine symphony guest conductor, De Sabata.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. When you hear the name of Mr. Boniver, who is the commercial attaché in the Italian Embassy here, you will know that is our salesman and I hope you will see him.

000,000 lira.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is the total amount that has been paid in.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. We have available now 195 billion lira, of which 

118 billion have been approved for withdrawal and 48 billion have been actually withdrawn."

I want to point out something in connection with these figures. 

That does not mean that more than that has not been spent, but there is a considerable amount of red tape that must be gone through to clear the various requests through the office which is similar to our General Accounting Office before the funds can actually be withdrawn. Therefore, a considerably larger sum than that has actually been spent.

I can point out one instance. Seventy billion lira have already been spent on the rehabilitation of the Italian railroads. The money has

gone. It has not yet been drawn out of the fund because the Italian 

Parliament has not yet put through the bill to appropriate the 70 billion out of the counterpart fund so it can be paid over to the treasury which has advanced the money to carry on this work. Therefore, a lot more than that has been spent. I can tell you what the funds have been allocated to. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I would appreciate that.

Mr. ZELLERBACH. The first years' lira fund, or the first 15 months, totals three hundred five billion lira. Of that, 70 billion have been allocated to agriculture and there are now some two hundred reclamation-irrigation projects approved. Most of them are getting under way. This is the start of that program. 

We expect before the end of the Marshall plan that between the counterpart fund and budget appropriations by the Italian Government that about 360 billion lira will be required to carry out this program.

Under the heading of public works we have 20 billion for general improvements. That is roads, aqueducts, public buildings, and so forth. We have 10 billion for reforestation and for vocational training which fits into the emigration program. That is, training of workers so they will become more desirable. That is part of the program.

We have 15 billion for low-cost housing and an additional 5 billion for miscellaneous projects. We have 7 billion allocated to the merchant marine. We have 80 billion total to railroads. We have 14 billion for the rehabilitation of the steel industry. Then we have 

6 billion for mechanizing the government bureaus so that they will be more efficient. There is 10 billion for loans to small industry, as a loan fund. There is 32 billion for a loan fund to assist industry generally, for long-term loans. There is 10 billion for loans to the industry particularly in the south of Italy. Other loans are for the south or anywhere else, but we have 10 billion earmarked particularly for southern developments. We have 10 billion for the revolving fund which I mentioned was for low-cost housing financing, and 8 billion is allocated to tourism. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. How is that allocated to tourism?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is for the rebuilding of damaged hotels, inns, and so forth and for the building of new ones. That is not grants; it is loans, except in the case of war damage, where it is grants. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you think that is enough to be allocated in that case? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is just the start. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You are personally in favor of using this counterpart fund for the various elements of tourism in order to build up dollar income?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. Very definitely. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. From your experience, what do you think would happen if we had a stronger guaranty provision written into our 

ECA bill? Do you think there would be any interest in American investment coming over into Italy and a desire by Italians to cooperate with American investment? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I will answer your last question first. I think there is no question about the desire of the Italian Government to

attract American investment. The legislation that they have on the books indicates that, as well as their attitude toward American investors.

The other question I will answer in this way: In the year and a half I have been in Italy I have had many representatives of many American companies talk to me about the possibilities of American investment in Italy. In almost every case the decision has been against American investment because of the risks involved, or rather the unusual risks involved. I do not refer to the normal business risks.

The guaranty provision, of course, is helpful. It has brought in some investment, but a very nominal amount. We have figures on that. Under the guaranty provision we have about $136,000. 

We have other projects which are under consideration and they are primarily for guaranties under the present law in the field of petroleum refining. The oil companies are used to taking risks of this kind. Outside of that, there are no major industries who have shown much interest in coming in under the present law. 

There has been interest shown in coming in, and I would think that if the ECA legislation had provisions somewhat similar to those proposed in Point IV legislation that is the risks such as war risks, expropriation and that sort of thing-I think more private investment would be attracted. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. There is some Point IV language modeled completely on the risk and guaranty provisions which had been presented in this committee and passed through the House last year. Do you think that would attract more American investment?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. It would attract more, but I do not know how much more. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. For every dollar of such money going into Italy, it would be that much less of the taxpayers' money that would have to go in. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. That is right.

Mr. RIBICOFF. And that brings along with it American know-how and American management that would also help in increasing the Italian production to which it was allocated. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I quite agree.

Mr. BURLESON. Referring again to this labor problem in Italy, Mr. Zellerbach, can we make a distinction between a large labor surplus and a large unemployment? In other words, there will always be, unless there is success in the shift of population, an excess of labor in `Italy? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I am afraid that is so.

Mr. BURLESON. Then we can distinguish a surplus of labor from unemployment. With that preface, what are the prospects after 1952 for 

Italy to be self-sustaining?

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I said last year that assuming the Marshall plan goes through as originally planned, and there are no general economic difficulties that develop let us say everything goes along normally, by 1952 Italy ought to be within reaching distance of becoming self-supporting at a very low standard of living.

Now, assuming these conditions, I also have to point out that Italy has not been able to support itself without outside financial aid since

the first World War, so that I think after 1952 Italy will require additional capital investments to keep its economy moving ahead, again because of the poverty of its natural resources which I have mentioned previously.

It seems to me, though, that that aid, under the circumstances, ought to be available either through private financing or through such agencies as the Export-Import Bank and the World Bank. I do not anticipate the need for extraordinary assistance such as is envisaged under the Marshall plan.

Mr. BURLESON. Perhaps the question as to what the prospects are politically and ideologically after 1952 is somewhat worn, but confining it to the present, today, if ECA was stopped what would be the prospect of Italy going communistic? 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. I think if ECA were stopped we would be playing right into Communist hands. It is my opinion that the trend toward communism was affected to a very large degree by, first, the promise of the Marshall plan, which gave the people of Italy hope that they could reconstruct their economy and have a real future. 

Of course, the American aid prior to the Marshall plan had an effect as well, the interim aid program. I am not claiming all credit for the Marshall plan; there are many other factors. 

The Communists have contended the Americans would not go through with this program and that the Americans would withdraw from Europe as we did after the First World War and that we could not be relied upon. That has been their propaganda line. Therefore, I think if we were to stop our assistance certainly we would be giving them a very strong assist in their propaganda against us. 

There is that side of it. 

On the other side, I think we all recognize that communism grows on poverty, and a man with an empty stomach, with no roof over his head and no hope of getting one, figures that he has not very much to lose if he tries something else. I would say that if we should stop our aid to Italy so that the standard of living were materially reduced below what it is today, because of inability to purchase necessary food and raw materials and so forth to keep the economy moving ahead, I should think that the risk would be very great of the Communists moving back and undoing all the good that we have been doing in the past year.

(The matter referred to is as follows:) ECA ACTIVITIES IN SARDINIA 

Sardinia, as a part of the Italian Republic, has, of course, benefited by all of the general activities of ECA. Imports of foods and raw materials have contributed to the recovery of economic stability and have provided work and sustenance for the people of Sardina. Moreover, the general achievement of a stable price level and cost-of-living index have benefited Sardinia as well as the rest of Italy.

The Marshall plan has helped Sardinia in a number of more specific ways as well. Perhaps one of the most important of these has been the contribution of the ERP lira counterpart fund to the battle against malaria on the island. 

With the aid of 3.4 billion lire from the ERP lira fund, the campaign to eliminate the anopheles mosquito and the scourge of malaria has been brought to a successful conclusion. This work was carried on under the direction of the Rockefeller Foundation. It could not have been completed without this ERP assistance. The successful conclusion of this struggle now makes possible the economic development of Sardinia in such a way not only as to contribute to raising the economic levels of Italy but also as to provide a potential outlet for Italian population pressure on the peninsula itself. 

Other activities financed on the island through the lira fund include repair of damaged housing, construction of new houses, building of aqueducts, construction of hospitals, improvement of railroad and highway communications, building of schools, and similar works. Of particular importance are five reclamation and irrigation projects in various parts of the island designed to bring additional land under cultivation and to increase the per unit yield of existing farms. In addition, financing has been provided which makes possible expansion of electrical installations and the undertaking of industrial projects, such as, for example, projects to utilize the island's deposits of low-grade coal. 

The following table indicates the amount of lire so far allocated for these purposes, and the attached map provides further detail.

STATUS OF THE LIRA FUND PROGRAM AS OF JANUARY 31, 1950 

1948-49 program Following is a brief summary of the present status of the 305.1 billion lire program to be financed out of the 1948-49 counterpart fund. 

A. Agricultural projects.-The 70,000,000,000 lire allotted to agricultural projects are to be spent on projects of two general categories: (a) Public works for land reclamation, 46.2 billions; (b) state expenditures, including subsidies, to encourage better private use of agricultural resources, 27.4 billions. ECA/Washington and OSR have given "general program" and "technical-economic project" approval to this entire program, leaving the more detailed study of specific projects to the mission. 

The mission does not authorize the Italian Government to proceed with a given specific project until it is satisfied with plans which the Government has formulated for carrying it into effect. This involves a great deal of personal inspection work by the Agricultural Division, plus consideration and revision of plans in joint consultation with representatives of the Italian Government. 

Individual projects completely cleared to date have been allotted 43.5 billion lire; public reclamation projects account for 23.3 billions of this total.

B. Public works projects.-The original program allotted 55,000,- 

000,000 of the lira fund to the general category known as public works. 

The following outline presents a picture of progress in individual sectors within this category. The expression "completely cleared" indicates that project approval at ECA levels has been obtained, and that the Italian Parliament has passed necessary authorizing legislation.

General works program: ECA has approved the use of 20,000,000,- 

000 lire to finance a limited program of expenditures voted by Parliament. Projects are not finally approved, however, until the mission reviews and approves the details submitted by the relevant Italian ministries. The total so approved to date amounts to 15,000,000,000 lire. 

Labor requalification courses: Fanfani Plan No. 2 calls for expend ing 5 billions to retrain unemployed workers at various centers throughout Italy. Completely cleared.

Reforestation: The Ministry of Labor will spend 5 billions to set up a series of reforestation camps. Completely cleared. 

Housing: The Government will contribute 15,000,000,000 lire from the lire fund toward the first year's cost of the Fanfani low-cost housing program. Completely cleared.

Special antimalarial program (ERLAAS): Completely cleared. 

The 1,200,000,000 lire previously advanced from the interim aid lira fund to finance this project are eventually to be repaid out of the ERP lira fund.

C. Industrial census.-The Italian Government has been notified that ECA approves the use of 773,000,000 lire to finance the cost of an official census of industry. 

D. Airport development.-827,000,000 lire are to be spent to develop and improve facilities at the Rome and Naples airports. Completely cleared.

E. Merchant marine projects.-The original program asked for an expenditure of 15,000,000 lire from the lira fund for the construction of merchant ships. ECA has approved the utilization of 7,500,000,000 lire for financing state subsidies during the first year of a 3-year building program which will ultimately cost 102,000,000 lire. Another 

500,000,000 lire will be made available for loans for the reconstruction of war-damaged vessels. 

The status of the other 7,000,000,000 lire available under this category for loans to the public or private merchant marine is still under discussion.

F. Tourism.-The Italian Parliament has enacted legislation pro viding that 8,000,000,000 lire be made available for loans and grants to repair existing hotels and build new accommodations. OSR and 

ECA/Washington have given "step 2 project approval" with the request that none of the funds be spent in the form of subsidies. 

The mission has approved the tourism program in principle, but is withholding final approval pending submission of projects which will give exact details regarding spending of the money. A survey of existing facilities and needs is now being conducted by an American hotel expert.

G. Railroads.-The joint mission-Italian Government consultation committee has recommended that 80,000,000,000 lire be allocated from the first year's counterpart fund for reconstruction and modernization of the Italian state railway system. This total comprises an earlier allotment of 70,000,000,000 lire which was released by the mission last May, plus an additional 10,000,000,000 to be channeled exclusively to improvements in southern Italy. The mission is now considering the details of the Italian Government's proposals on this supplementary 10,000,000,000 program.

The parliamentary position of these two allocations is still somewhat confused. Without prior clearance by the mission, Parliament had passed a supplementary bill to spend not 10 but 20 billions in the south, at the same time postponing action on the 70,000,000,000 program which had originally been scheduled for inclusion within the budget. Parliament must still reconcile these two propositions with the 80,000,000,000 total which the mission has stated is the maximum allocation possible out of the 1948-49 accumulation. 

H. Miscellaneous loan programs.-Steel: Final ECA approval has been granted to the plan for the setting up of a loan fund of 14.12 billion lire for loans to the steel industry. This sum would be lent to Finsider and Fiat to cover the local currency costs of developments already passed as dollar projects by ECA. Enabling legislation is now being considered by the Italian Parliament. 

Industrial and governmental equipment: A revolving fund of 

32,000,000,000 lire has been set up to make loans to private firms needing lire to finance the importation of industrial equipment. An additional 6,000,000,000 are to be loaned to Government agencies to buy office and professional equipment; these agencies are to repay the loans to the lira fund out of future appropriations allowances. 

Small businesses and agriculture: The mission and OSR approved a plan to allocate 10,000,000,000 lire to a fund for loans to smalland medium-sized business and agricultural enterprises. 

Southern industry: The Italian Government is preparing draft legislation to provide another 10,000,000,000 lire for loans to southern and insular industries.

Housing (revolving fund): The mission has approved, and sent to 

OSR and Washington for review, the proposal to set up a 10,000,- 000,000 lire revolving fund to finance private housing construction. 1949-50 program The exact size of the 1949-50 counterpart fund will depend upon (1) the final amount of ECA aid, (2) the percentage of aid classified as grants, and (3) the exchange rate at which notifications will be converted to lire when deposits are made to the fund. Based on the present aid figures, and assuming no further exchange rate adjustments, the fund will ultimately amount to about 220 billion lire. 

In its budget for 1949-50 the Italian Parliament provides for lira fund financing totaling 121 billion lire. Of this total, 60 billions were to go for public works, 57 for railroads, and 3.7 for post and telecommunications. 

A. Public works.-The Ministry of Public Works has formulated a program which calls for a total expenditure of 60 billion lire. 

OSR and ECA/Washington have given their "technical-economic" approval to this entire program, leaving it to the mission to screen out undesirable projects. The mission has notified the Italian Government of its final approval of projects totaling 37.9 billions. Suggestions for the use of the other 22.1 billions are being screened, and the Italian Government asked to supply replacements for those rejected by the mission.

B. Post and telecommunications.-The Ministry of Post and Telecommunications 3.715-billion-lire program has been completely cleared by ECA and the Italian Government.

C. Railroads.-Complete clearance has been given to 47.2 billions of the total allotted to railroads in the 1949-50 program. In screening the original Italian presentation, the mission rejected projects totaling 9.8 billion lire. Substitute proposals for spending this sum have been submitted by the Italian Government, approved by the mission, and sent to Washington for review.

Emigration: The expected increase in net emigration during the current year has not materialized. Difficulties in the receiving countries, and notably the inadequacy of capital availability in those countries, have replaced shipping shortages as a major limitation in 

Italian emigration.

Italy has greatly increased the flow of emigrants overseas, but the loss of European outlets has roughly offset this improvement. Net emigration figures for recent years follow:

Continental.. 

Overseas... 

Total.. 

Destination
