1949 74, 770 159,900 74, 860 6, 640 20,000 53, 780 95, 710 123,000 81, 410 213, 680 170, 570 143,000

It thus appears that net emigration in calendar year 1949 was probably very little, if any, above the 1948 figure. 

In Europe, France appears to be the only major continental outlet in the immediate future. Problems of housing, capital remittances, worker skills, and French unwillingness to accept large numbers from a single country constitute serious limitations. 

France has some 281 abandoned farms totaling 24,593 hectares which could be settled, if France were willing, with Italian farm families. 

In addition the Italian Government has made a study of the possibilities of creating small farm units in the Department of the Landes, recently damaged by forest fires. Switzerland continues to absorb a limited amount of Italian workers in her factories. 

Overseas emigration, particularly to Latin America, offers more substantial possibilities. The present outlook is uncertain and the basic problem of capital requirements is great. Italy is going forward with a program of overseas emigration in the current fiscal year, based primarily on the establishment of pilot projects and agricultural colonies in Latin America.

Italy is planning agricultural colonies in the following countries: 

Brazil, Venezuela, Uruguay, Peru, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and

Ecuador. The development of these colony projects will be accomplished in three steps: (1) Diplomatic agreement with immigration country to receive Italian farm families and to allocate areas of ground available for purchase, lease, or concession; (2) technical-assistance surveys of allocated areas, negotiations for acquisition of land, and engineering of pilot plant; and (3) development of colony by construction of roads and buildings, water supply, electricity, and equipping with necessary farm machinery, seeds, and beasts. 

Italy will request ERP technical-assistance funds for the implementation of step 2. Estimates given to the mission of dollar costs for surveys and equipping pilot centers amount to a little over a million

dollars. Step 3 will be financed by Italy with her own dollars to the extent of $10,000,000. 

Other possible areas include Africa, Australia, and Canada. Thus far the African colonial powers have given no encouragement to Italy for the possible settlement of Italians on their continent, though recent discussions within OEEC give hope that this attitude may change. 

Italy is doing her utmost on a diplomatic level to explore the possibilities of emigration to Australia and Canada. The basic difficulty is the reluctance to allow entrance to any but Anglo-Saxons. The possibility is not precluded, however, and negotiations can be expected to continue.

COMMUNIST INFLUENCE IN ITALY 

Communist influence in Italy has declined steadily since the initiation of the European recovery program, but there are still more party members here than in any other European countries aside from Russia and the Russian satellites. The influence of the Communist Party in politics and in the labor field has suffered severe set-backs since 1948, but the strength of the party at that time was such that even today it has managed to retain a power by no means negligible. 

Communist political influence: During the general elections held 

April 18, 1948, the Communist front polled 31 percent of the total vote. Since that date, local elections have been held all over Italy and the returns have shown a steady drop for the Communists. Complete figures are not yet available for the fourth quarter of 1949, but the results of local elections held through September 1949 are significant.

There are about 10,102 communes in Italy. Since April 1948 administrative elections have been held in 522 of these. The Christian 

Democrats won 304 of them; other parties in the Government coalition won 49; left-wing Socialists and Communists won 91; local lists (independents) won 72; right-wing parties won 6.

Of the 304 communes won by the Christian Democrats, 85 had formerly been controlled by the left-wing Socialists and Communists. 

The Communists won only 8 communes which had previously been controlled by the Christian Democrats.

Figures for some 20 local elections held during October, November, and December 1949, show that the left-wing Socialists and Communists won only 1 of them, indicating a continuance of the trend away from the extreme left.

Starting with the general elections in April 1948 and continuing in the local elections held since then, anti-Communist parties have united in an effort to beat the left-wing Socialists and Communist combine. 

Despite the encouraging results of local elections so far, however, there is a fear in informed quarters that the Socialist-Communist alliance is still strong enough to appreciably improve its present standing should economic conditions be allowed to deteriorate or the anti-Communist political front be broken.

Communist policy: Soon after the general elections held in April 

1948 the Ministry of the Interior was able to procure a copy of an order which was being circulated at secret Communist meetings held throughout Italy. The order said in effect, "Until the international situation permits us to raise our heads once more, we must concentrate our energies on reorganizing and strengthening our party 

---

Since the spring of 1948, the Communist Party has been engaged in purging a considerable number of its rank and file. All hangers-on and fellow-travelers have been weeded out. In so doing, the party intended to strengthen itself into a tightly knit organization composed of die-hards willing to follow party directives without question. 

Highest membership of the party has ever claimed is 2,300,000; a figure announced shortly prior to the general elections in April 1948. 

Today competent officials estimate that the party has somewhere between 1,500,000 and 1,800,000 members.

Most of the activities of the Communist Party during the past year and a half have been carried out behind the scenes. While quietly reorganizing itself, it has pursued a comparatively nonaggressive policy both in politics and in labor, particularly in the latter. 

During the past year, a definite Titoist or Nationalist movement has sprung up within the Communist Party. Center of the movement is Terní, a small town in almost the exact center of Italy, 50 miles northeast of Rome. High officials of the party are making frequent trips to Terni to give speeches and talk with the workers, in an evident attempt to smother the revolt in its incipiency. For the moment nothing momentous may be expected from the new movement, but its mere existence should serve at least to some extent as a brake on Russian political aggressiveness.

Prior to the general elections and before the initiation of the ERP in Italy, scarcely a week went by without violent disorders created by the Communist Party or Communist-front organizations. Such events rarely occurred during 1949. The party confined itself to calling minor strikes intermittently throughout the country. General strikes which were formerly called for at least 24 hours were confined to 1or 2-hour work stoppages.

In pursuing this policy of scattered strikes, the party was able to flex its muscles in the various provinces of Italy from time to time and thus obtain an indication of its strength. 

There are indications at the present time that the Communist Party is girding its loins for a labor offensive directed chiefly at the military-aid program. Strikes and agitation sponsored by the Communists during 1949 have evidently shown the party just where it is strong enough to attempt serious labor offensives. 

Communist labor leaders in all northern and some southern ports have publicly declared that the dock workers will refuse to unload supplies coming in under the MAP. Labor leaders in several factories in the industrial north have also publicly stated that the men will not work to manufacture arms. 

In addition, the Communist Party is active in agricultural sections of southern Italy, where its agents are inciting the landless peasants to occupy large estates. Continued postponement of the implementation of adequate land reform is causing many of the poorer peasants to look to the Communist Party for help. 

Communist labor influence: Most important Communist weapon in

Italy has always been, and continues to be, the absolute control it has over the CGIL-Italian Confederation of Labor. At the time of the elections in April 1948 the CGIL counted a membership of 5,000,000 workers. The organization had complete control over all organized labor in Italy.

Today that strangle hold has been broken. Two new labor groups have been formed.

Soon after the ERP started in Italy, the Christian Democrat labor leader, Giulio Pastore, broke away from the CGIL, taking more than a million workers with him. His action broke the paralyzing general strike which the Communists had called at the time of the attempted assassination of Togliatti.

In December 1948 Pastore formed the LCGIL-Free Italian Confederation of Labor-with an initial membership of about 1,000,000. 

It has since increased its strength to 1,300,000. 

In May 1949 the moderate Socialist and Republican labor leaders also left the CGIL and formed their own labor group, the FIL—Italian Federation of Labor. The FIL now numbers about 500,000. 

Membership of the Communist-dominated CGIL has now fallen to about 3,000,000, about half of its strength when the ERP came to Italy. 

The two non-Communist labor groups, LCGIL and FIL, are now discussing plans for unification. FIL, at its recent convention, voted by more than 90 percent for such unification; LCGIL had already adopted a similar resolution. Union is expected to be perfected in a month or two. The formation of a united anti-Communist labor group would undoubtedly further weaken the influence of the Communistdominated CGIL. 

The ECA Mission to Italy has been giving every encouragement to the non-Communist labor groups. Its labor division acts as liaison between labor groups in the United States and the non-Communist unions in Italy. Help, financial and otherwise, received by the Italian unions from the CIO and the A. F. of L., has greatly increased their prestige and contributed materially to the discomfiture of the Communist CGH.

An indication of the decrease in Communist influence in the labor field is shown by a comparison between the general strike called at the time of the attempted assassination of Togliatti in June 1948 and the general strike called December 1, 1949.

The first general strike completely paralyzed the nation's commerce, even before the wounded Togliatti had been laid on a hospital bed. Not only was all industrial activity and transportation halted, but all restaurants and stores were closed, farmers left their fields, and even beggars left the streets. 

By contrast, the general strike of December 1, 1949, was felt only in the north, where plants reported absenteeism running from 30 to 70 percent. Elsewhere in Italy the effect of the strike was negligible. Stores and restaurants remained open and transportation services were 98 percent of normal everywhere except in a few cities of the north, particularly Milan.

The comparison shows that the CGIL no longer has the blanket control it once had over the nation's economic life. It also shows, however, that the CGIL still wields a heavy influence in certain areas especially in the industrial north and is therefore still a force to be reckoned with.

Conclusion: There is no doubt that communism is on the wane in Italy. There is equally no doubt that this decline is due chiefly to the vigorous economic counterattack against communism launched 63307-50-pt. 1-14

under the ERP, or that relaxation of that counterattack at this time might permit the Communists to recoup their strength. The party organization is intact and more efficient than a year ago. It is lean and strong and waiting only for its opponents to drop their guard. 

But if the ECA's objectives are attained within Italy by mid-1952, and especially if the economic integration of Europe is well on its way by then, the Communist Party in Italy will have suffered a permanent set-back. 

AGARIAN REFORM 

During 1949 agrarian reform was discussed widely in both political and technical circles and the Government reiterated its intention of carrying out land redistribution as well as development through reclamation and irrigation. Tangible accomplishments in land development during 1949 are beginning to appear throughout Italy, thanks to ERP counterpart projects, but progress toward land redistribution has to be counted in terms of study, discussion, and the drafting of legislation. Concerning the related social-economic aspects of agrarian reform, improvements of the lot of workers and tenants and of their relationships to employers and owners, achievements must also be measured in terms of discussion and promises. 

Draft legislation regarding tenant contracts has been debated in Parliament throughout most of the year, agreement having been reached on a few points. Discussion and arbitration of landlordtenant relationships started nearly 2 years before the April 1948 elections. Other temporary measures undertaken to assuage agrarian unrest were the legalized seizure and occupation of idle or underused land (Gullo Law No. L. D. 279 of October 19, 1944, and Segni Law No. 

L. D. 89 of September 6, 1946). The area of such land occupied by landless peasants under these laws increased from about 10,000 hectares in 1944 to 166,000 hectares in 1949. Additional land was taken over during the fall of 1949 but the amount is not yet known. Bitter struggles between owners and occupants of this land occurred in Crotone (Calabria) during 1949 over a legal technicality and perhaps with communist prompting certain tenants did not pay the nominal rent and also made additional land seizures without following the legal processes established under the Segni law of 1946. On the heels of this trouble, which resulted in bloodshed and received widespread publicity, the Government began to move quickly by making public a land redistribution program for the Sila area of central Calabria which, in rapid succession, was submitted to the Senate and approved by the Senate Committee on Agriculture and is expected to be taken up by the Senate proper shortly. 

On the program for land redistribution, announced by the Premier on April 17, 1949, provided in article 4 of the constitution and promised by the Christian Democrat Party, no draft legislation has been submitted to Parliament. However, on January 3, Premier De Gasperi announced the outlines of the Government's latest plans for land redistribution to the Council of Ministers. These outlines imply a definite reorientation from the original concept of the application of a rigid principle of expropriation for the entire country in that the best-organized-and thus some of the richest-land, namely the irrigated Po Valley and practically all land reclaimed since 1930, is to be

exempted from expropriation, although the owners are to be obliged to undertake certain social improvements. Furthermore, no mention was made of an absolute upper limit for landed property. 

It appears that the Government wishes to give the land reform project high priority immediately following the cabinet reshuffle, so that at present technicians and political pressure groups are hard at work trying to secure a type of law that will conform to their various wishes. Some slight modifications may yet be made in the general outline, and, in any case, many of the larger and smaller details must still be worked out. 

Although remarkable progress was made during 1949 in land reclamation, the legal authority for expropriation of undeveloped land within established reclamation districts has not yet been used except for preliminary steps in a few districts (Law No. L. D. 1744 of Decem ber 31, 1947, amending the "Serpieri" law of 1933).

While the ECA special mission to Italy has considered the political aspects of agrarian reform a matter for the Italian Government to solve, the mission has stated publicly that the broad purposes of ERP cannot be achieved without broadening the base of land ownership. 

The mission realizes that redistribution and development of idle or underused land, both within and outside established land reclamation districts, is a necessity and that it will lead to the desired diversification of production in the areas affected. Also, there is a definite need for fair and orderly working arrangements between tenants and owners and between workers and managers. More precisely, the ECA mission subscribes to the principle of land reform in the broad sense. 

The mission believes that the limited lire counterpart funds may best and most effectively be used for basic developmental work in order to assure success to land distribution, leaving the purchase of land to be financed by the regular Government budget; it recognizes, however, that since the Government will have to compensate owners for expropriation and undertake land transformations outside those financed by ECA, extraordinary appropriations will have to be made in the Government budget.

The mission believes that the procedure proposed by the Government for land redistribution and development in central Calabria is a sound approach. In that instance about 45,000 hectares of land are to be expropriated from holdings of over 300 hectares. This land will be used to form about 5,000 small holdings. Land development and adequate technical assistance will accompany the redistribution. In that instance the region for land redistribution embraces nine landreclamation districts in which the mission has approved projects using ERP counterpart funds (Sibari (right part), lower Neto Valley, Sila, Rossano, Lipuda Fiumenica', Punta Castella-Capo Colonna, Alli- 

Punta Castella, Allip-Copannello, Middle Crati Valley (part)). In these districts the improvement work will go ahead, but within the framework of the redistribution program, with the Government providing money for compensation to owners whose land is expropriated and for other necessary assistance in the process of colonization. The mission will also agree to the use of counterpart funds within the region for these latter technical purposes, such as general land improvement on private farms, pest control, research, education, contri-

butions toward the purchase of draft animals, and machinery, and finally the formation of small holdings, in order to assist in every practical way the success of the program. 

The views of the mission supporting plans for land distribution have been unequivocally and publicly announced.

(The matter referred to is as follows:) [From the New York Times, October 10, 1949] ECA CHIEF KEEPS ITALIANS AMAZED-ZELLERBACH IS RESPECTED BY PEOPLE OF ALL TYPES (By John P. Leacacos, European correspondent) 

ROME, October 10.—Italians of all persuasions these days are watching the phenomenon of James David Zellerbach, the wispy, little, United States chief of the ECA mission in Italy, hardly able to believe what they see. For Zellerbach is showing Italy what American democracy means at first-hand. 

The method is simple but hard on the feet. Zellerbach gets around. He's had mud on his shoes for inspecting Calabrian irrigation ditches. He's had coal dust on his face from going down into Sardinian coal mines. He's been chilled to the bone climbing Mount Blanc to see for himself whether a tunnel from the Italian side is feasible.

On a road trip-and he has spent more time out of Rome than in it during his administration of a billion dollars' worth of Marshall-plan aid to Italy Zellerbach stops and talks to the local natives. He holds four or five meetings a day, listening to petitions and giving his views in return. 

SPEECHES WIN BRAVOS 

The brief Zellerbach speeches have a political artlessness that more than once have taken his audiences by storm. Down south in Italy he recently said the 

Marshall plan for Italy was just one means of paying back the debt the United States owed Italy for the Italian immigrants who helped build America. The ensuing bravos were terrific.

To Italians in the sticks who receive the very rare visits of Italian Cabinet ministers as if they were personages from another sphere, Zellerbach's homely Americanism comes as a joyful shock. He gives them a chance to beef to somebody who can report their grievances with authority to the powers that be in faraway Rome.

Those good American dollars he represents naturally elicit the greatest enthusiasm when Zellerbach rolls around in his customary three-car caravan plus staff. The staff invariably consists of his chic, 52-year-old wife, Hannah; his veteran press man, Andre Berding, and his sleek secretary, Ruth McCrystle, who has been with him for 20 years and treats Mr. Z. like a little brother. 

POPULAR ITALIAN BELIEF 

The popular Italian belief that Mr. Z. carries spare millions in his pocket was nowhere better illustrated than on a trip near Brindisi, at the heel of Italy. As he went through the piazza of a small town, a crowd surged around his car, blocking progress and thrust a petition at him. It was in English and textually read as follows: 

"Grand Sire Minister Zellerbach: Four thousand habitants of this laborios fraction, 'eminently agriculture.' Haste urgent need's of hydrogen-school house-road's repairing war damaged and of a telephone. They personally enquire me to reverse at you grande Sire a warm cordial and dispersed appeal in assurance that you may take in consideration what at them is necessary and give 'em the best you may hallow.-(Signed) The Citizen's of Pezze di Greco."

The Zellehbach passage through notoriously Red towns in this area, like Molo and the old city of Bari, on the same trip even brought street cheers from Communists, who apparently had no objection to accepting United States cash if they could get their hands on it. 

The natives have further profitable reasons to know Zellerbach. If some local conniver can be spotted shaking Mr. Z's hand, why his stock shoots up among his fellow citizens. And if he can get two words in with Zellerbach, he can brag for weeks about the inside track he has with the Americans. 

HAS CONJURING TRICK 

Mr. Z has a trick of his own for getting out of such situations. He takes out his Polaroid Land camera, snaps a picture, and in one minute flat strips off the developed film. This not only amazes the crowd no end but gets rid of the gold-brick salesmen.

Outside of the grind of having every minute from 9 a. m. to past midnight scheduled, the greatest threat of these trips is to Mr. Z's waistline, according to Mrs. Z. 

In a year he has gained 10 pounds from 3-hour Junches and dinners. 

It isn't only the fattening pasta one can never escape in Italy; it's the ice cream. 

This correspondent verified this fact on a recent trip with Z's. Ice cream was served-because Americans love it so-at 3 p. m. after lunch, at 8: 30 before dinner, at 10:30 after dinner, and at 12: 30 a. m. for a midnight snack. Personally Mr. Z would rather have a stick of licorice candy any time. He loves it. 

The pleasures and petty mishaps of his trips have not prevented Zellerbach from guiding the Marshall-plan program in Italy to the point where Italy now presents a picture of economic recovery which at least on the surface is one of the most encouraging in Europe. 

To achieve his goal of increasing production and fostering free enterprise Zellerbach does not hesitate to speak his mind to Italian Prime Minister Alcide De Gasperi and his government or to tell the big landowners and industrialists what they ought to do. 

HE COMMANDS RESPECT 

Zellerbach's experience as head of one of the largest paper companies in the world and a whirling dervish of civic and cultural enthusiasms back in his native San Francisco command respect even from cynical and lip-serving Italians. 

The American ECA chief has not been without criticism, however, on the grounds that he could air his views more forcefully and in public. Recently 

Zellerbach did make so bold as to hit against fancy long-range planning by Italians who should be concentrating on getting the most done in the quickest possible time before Marshall-plan aid ceases. 

But, add his critics, this Zellerbach complaint was more like a whisper than a roar. The point made was this: If the United States pours a billion dollars into 

Italy, it has the right to declare out loud whether it believes its money is truly promoting the common welfare, which the Marshall plan was created to assist, as a barrier against communism. 

There is no doubt that as an economic diplomat of the new school Mr. Zeller. bach has grown considerably in his knowledge of the tricks and pressures of Italian political and financial groups since he came here a year and 3 months ago. 

But he is still leery about sounding off, 'tis said, because his official political adviser, the State Department's Embassy here, believes that the United States must never, never hurt the feelings of a "friendly" government by telling the truth in public. 

[From the New York Times, October 17, 1949] ITALIAN REDS SHIFT ACTIVITIES TO ECA-UNITED STATES OFFICIAL WARMLY WELCOMED BY COMMUNIST MAYORS WHILE TOURING EMILIA REGION (By Arnaldo Cortesi) Special to the New York Times 

ROME, October 17.-A change in the Communist attitude of active hostility toward the Marshall plan was seen today in the friendly welcome received by 

James D. Zellerbach, chief of the Economic Cooperation Administration Mission to Italy, from Communist mayors in Emilia, during a 2-day tour of that region.

Emilia ranks with Tuscany and Liguria as a principal hotbed of Communist sentiment in Italy. Yet, the Communist mayors of all the leading cities greeted. 

Mr. Zellerbach personally, accepted invitation to lunch and dine with him and,. in some cases, even spoke in public acknowledging the powerful contribution of the ECA to Italian reconstruction. 

Political and diplomatic circles in Rome are wondering whether this indicatesa change of heart or a mere change of tactics on the part of the Communists.. 

Most authorities agree, however, that it is an important straw in the wind. 

The reception of Mr. Zellerbach in Emilia is generally regarded as part of the veiled peace overtures that the Communist leader, Palmiro Togliatti, recently has made to the Italian Government. Signor Togliatti's move did not get far because the Government took the view that peace with the Communists was impossible unless they gave clear proof that they had ceased to sabotage Italian reconstruction and social peace. 

Mr. Zellerbach started his tour of Emilia in Ravenna, where the Communist mayor lunched with him.

His next call was at the regional capital, Bologna, where both Mr. Zellerbach and the Communist mayor delivered speeches. The mayor said that Bologna "appreciates the necessary and desirable help that comes to us from a friendly people.' He explicitly acknowledged that the ECA had achieved concrete results and denied that the left wing parties wished to sabotage the Marshall plan or to impede Italian reconstruction. 

Mr. ZELLERBACH. As a matter of fact, I visited six provincial capitals on that trip, each of which has a Communist mayor. I went up there to open up an ERP exhibit in Bologna. It was opened up in the 

Palazzo Degli Podesta, I think, which is a very important palace on the main square in Bologna. This was made available to us without charge by the Communist mayor of Bologna. He accompanied me during the ceremonies of opening up the exhibit. He insisted on being photographed in the newsreels with me. He entertained me for dinner. He is one of the leading Communists of that section, or is supposed to be.

In the other five provincial capitals I received the same treatment from the Communist mayors. They all met me officially, they attended the official ceremonies, and it seems to me to be indicative of perhaps a shifting away by some of these people from the party line, certainly.

The same thing is true in Venice where they have a Communist mayor who comes and calls on me in Rome quite frequently to discuss his problems. In Venice there is the problem of keeping the palazzi from falling into the canals and so forth. I would not say they are unfriendly in the slightest.

STATEMENT OF ROBERT M. HANES, CHIEF OF THE ECA MISSION TO GERMANY 

Mr. HANES. I have a prepared statement here which I would like to speak from and then file the complete statement with the committee. 

Chairman KEE. Without objection, the prepared statement of Mr. 

Hanes will appear in the record at this point. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Hanes is as follows:) STATEMENT BY MR. ROBERT M. HANES, CHIEF OF THE ECA MISSION TO GERMANY 

Since the last time that an ECA mission chief from Germany appeared before Congress, profound changes have taken place within that country. Western 

Germany now has its own government, and almost complete fusion of the United States, British, and French zones has been accomplished. Military government has been replaced by a civilian body, the Allied High Commission. 

Under the new organizational set-up, the LCA mission chief performs a dual function. He not only represents the Economic Cooperation Administration, but also acts as the Director of the Office of Economic Affairs on the staff of the United States High Commissioner. The High Commissioner, on his part, also has ECA functions and is the ECA representative in Germany. During the year, GARIOA funds (Government and Relief in Occupied Areas) previously administered by the Department of the Army, were placed under ECA for administration and programing.

Under the occupation statute and the Allied High Commission the new German Government has assumed powers and responsibilities far beyond those held by the former German Economic Council. The German Federal Republic now has full rights and responsibilities for participation in the Marshall plan and its organizations. In October 1949, the Federal Republic of Germany became a full-fledged partner in the OEEC where it now represents, and talks for, itself rather than being represented by the Allies. In December 1949, a bilateral agreement was concluded between the Government of the United States and the German Federal Government. In January of this year that agreement was ratified by the German legislature. Germany now has its own delegation here in Washington which works in close relationship with ECA headquarters. An 

ERP mission was established within the German administration, and the vice chancelor was appointed as its head. Existing arrangements also include aid to the city of Berlin with whose particular problems I shall deal later. 

The tremendous upsurge in industrial production which marked the period from June to December 1948 slackened during the first half of 1949, but there were some further increases in production during the last 6 months of the year. 

German production has more than doubled since the beginning of the European recovery program. In May 1948 the production index stood at 47 percent of 

1936; in November 1949 it has reached a peak of 98 percent. This increase allowed Germany to make a start toward playing the important role it formerly held in the European economy, both as a producer and consumer, and as one of the principal participants in European trade. The rise in production has made it possible to meet many of the pent-up demands, particularly for consumer goods. During the past year prices in general have been stable, and in the last months there have even been some reductions. Rationing and price controls have been abolished for consumer goods, and today controls exist only over gasoline and a few agricultural and basic industrial items. The present levels of food consumption and agricultural production are considerably higher than a year ago. The average daily diet now reaches approximately 2,600 calories as against 2,900 before the war. Although quality has not reached the standards of prewar days, the diet affords a variety comparable to that period. This improvement in the food situation is, however, the result of food imports and unusually favorable weather. It does not stem from any substantial improvement in the methods of agricultural production and planning. 

In the financial field, the outstanding characteristic of the past year has been the trend from inflation to deflation. The currency reform of June 1948 had unleashed a buying splurge which in the latter part of that year threatened to become most serious. Establishment of a strict credit control policy and the slackening of abnormal consumer demands combined to halt the inflationary

trend and to stabilize the situation. In actual fact, definite deflationary pressures made themselves felt in the ensuing months. To combat this deflationary tendency, credit policies were liberalized and ECA counterpart funds were released for investment purposes. In the field of external finance, the German currency was devalued in autumn of 1949, following similar actions by other European countries, so that German exporters now have a better chance to compete in world markets.

The problem of the dollar gap remains the most critical in Germany today. 

Only one-tenth of German dollar imports are covered by exports to hard currency areas. The difference is financed by American aid, which is directly responsible for the recovery so far achieved. Still, serious difficulties in the economic field remain to be solved. 

I wish, at this point, to touch briefly on what we consider to be the four major economic problems facing western Germany today: 

1. Production 

Western Germany must raise both its agricultural and industrial production if it is to survive without external assistance. It can never raise more than approximately 65 percent of its own food requirements. In order to cut down on food imports, a determined effort is being made to increase indigenous production. Limiting factors in the agricultural picture are fixed prices, in particular for grains, which neither encourage the German production of otherwise dollar import foods nor discourage their excessive use. German agricultural methods are antiquated. Agricultural research and extension work have been grossly inadequate during the last 15 years. Through technical assistance programs efforts are being made to spread knowledge of modern techniques to the farmers. Lack of mechanization has resulted in high production costs, and has caused land utilization and reclamation programs to proceed very slowly. It is estimated that some 500,000 additional acres of land could be claimed for cultivation, if modern methods were pursued. Germany's backwardness in this regard can be illustrated by certain lands which extend across the Dutch border. 

On the Dutch side, the land has been brought into high production, while the German portion exists only as waste land. ECA counterpart funds are being made available for the reclamation of land and for investment in farm machinery.

Industrial production, although on a relatively higher level of efficiency than agricultural, is still inadequate and inefficient by American standards. Present 

German forecasts envisage a level of 107 percent of 1936 by the end of the ERP period. This, in our opinion, is far short of what can be accomplished. Industrial production can and should be raised to at least 120 percent of 1936. Limitations such as costly handiwork and lack of investment capital must be overcome. 

Western Germany's problem is to export the right goods to the right places, and to produce them at a cost which is competitive in world markets. This calls for a readjustment and reorientation of German industrial thinking, which heretofore has developed within the confines of protective markets, monopolies and cartels, and has not been fully exposed to the realities of a truly free, competitive market.

The German industrialist still thinks in terms of a small turn-over at a high profit, rather than of large production at low profit margins. In addition, German export trade is still hampered by the lack of adequate sales organizations, unfamiliarity with modern merchandizing methods, and, to some extent, by a still prevalent, although decreasing antagonism against German products abroad. 

2. Capital investment 

Critical to the problem of raising production is the shortage of investment capital. Where such capital is available, interest rates are high and the dangerous practice of using short-term credit for long-term investments has been adopted in far too many cases. A shortage of long-term capital is retarding the rebuilding of plants and the rehabilitation and modernization of equipment. 

In order to relieve, somewhat, this shortage, substantial amounts of ECA counterpart funds have been released. But counterpart funds alone cannot solve the problem. Only small amounts of investment funds are available from the capital markets. Neither private banks nor public budgets are in a position to make large credits available. The central bank, Bank deutscher Laender, seems to be the only immediate hope of relief but this is neither permanent nor satisfactory.

The capital shortage reflects itself in two of the most urgent problems in western Germany, namely, housing and unemployment. We find today the paradoxical situation of a country needing 5,000,000 homes while laying off men in the building trades. Counterpart funds are being used to stimulate the housing program, but much more needs to be done if explosive social and political consequences are to be avoided.

Unemployment has reached the level of 2,000,000 or approximately 10 percent of the labor force. The constant influx of refugees from the Soviet zone and the iron-curtain countries, about 20,000 per month, is a large contributing factor. 

While refugees constitute about 18 percent of the total western German population, they comprise 35 percent of the unemployed. They increase the pressure on housing and jobs, and they are considered outsiders and intruders by the local population. They bring resentment in their wake-a resentment which poses tremendous social as well as economic problems. 

Indeed, apart from its humanitarian aspects, this problem which is peculiar to postwar western Germany and does not arise in the case of any other ERP country, has far-reaching political implications. Only by a concerted effort to integrate these people into the economy and the body politic will it be possible to avoid unrest and the development of extremist political thinking in that group. While the problem is one which the German government must meet by its own efforts, I feel that it is deserving of special consideration in the allocation of American aid.

The lack of long-term capital for housing and industrial expansion, the tapering off of extraordinary purchasing power and a not fully developed export trade have played their part in aggravating the unemployment situation. Large numbers of jobless, mainly refugees, live in the agricultural districts where they are unwanted and where jobs are unavailable. 

In many cases their movement to areas where better opportunities for employment, and even scarce labor conditions, exist, is obstructed by lack of housing facilities in those areas.

Both the ECA mission and the German Government are vitally concerned with the unemployment situation. It is my personal view that western Germany cannot achieve either economic or social stability unless this problem is met head-on. 

An extensive housing program, financed in part by ECA counterpart funds, is one of the measures being taken to meet the immediate emergency. 

Over the long run, however, the very roots of the existing ills must be attacked. 

This will require great skill and foresight on the part of the Federal Government. 

Its action must be bold in obtaining the best use of all resources and must, at the same time, be cautious so as not to jeopardize monetary stability. 

Above all, production must be increased and productivity must be improved. 

In my opinion the existing monetary situation would permit a substantial expansion of credit for long-term investment, provided that adequate fiscal safeguards exist. The system of tax collections must be tightened and the tax structure so devised as to discourage luxury consumption and provide more funds for investment.

Credit facilities should be provided for projects which are of special benefit to the economy as a whole and which will create additional labor content, productive industries.

Finally a vigorous drive to increase exports, and in particular exports to the dollar area, must be initiated. 

3. Foreign trade and the balance of payments 

If western Germany is to reach its goals under the European recovery program, exports, and particularly dollar exports, must rise dramatically. The heretofore mentioned 10-1 ratio of dollar imports to dollar exports must be drastically reduced. At the present time, due to the far-reaching trade liberalization policies pursued by western Germany, her trade with other European countries is out of balance. The ECA mission is confident, however, that the near future will see other European nations buying more from Germany which should arrest the existing trend and, indeed, lead to the reestablishment of a German export surplus with western Europe.

It is to the dollar area, however, that Germany must look more closely and devote the greatest part of its efforts. Steps in this direction are being taken. 

A "dollar drive" has been launched. This drive includes the establishment in the 

United States of a market research organization, western German participation in international fairs and exhibits, and a current proposal to make available to exporters a certain percentage of the dollars they earn for imports of their choice

from the dollar area. Special attention is being given, both by the Federal 

Government and by the ECA mission, to tourism, an important dollar-earning trade.

The tremendous domestic demand within western Germany has made it easier in the past for the manufacturer to cater to home wants than to embark upon the uncertainties of foreign trade. It is necessary for the western German people to turn from this "line of least resistance" and face up to the problem of sustaining themselves when American aid ceases. To help the western German exporter, ECA is bringing into the country numerous experts in a variety of fields who under the technical assistance program will teach the German industrialist, trade-union representative, and farmer the most modern production techniques. 

In addition, the German people must be brought to appreciate the urgent necessity to forego immediate personal advantage in favor of expanding exports. 

To bring its trade into near balance, Germany must look to new sources for imports. Eastern Europe, South America, and other OEEC participating countries offer sources which can conserve western Germany's dollar supply. 

Most important for the survival of the country is the adoption of a freer trade system. The overcrowded western German area can no longer afford the protectionist devices which were developed to promote the self-sufficiency of the prewar Reich. This discredited policy must be replaced by one which will open new markets for western German exports and at the same time provide the foreign exchange needed to finance heavy imports in food and raw materials. 

To this end quantitative restrictions (especially for food imports) must be progressively removed, cartels and monopolies must be eliminated so as to abolish restrictions on industry and trade and to make it possible for small business to live and compete successfully, and incentives to exporters must be provided. I should like to say here that the Federal German Government has thus far acted boldly and promptly in the matter of trade liberalization. Indeed, it has outstripped every other ERP country, save Switzerland, in this regard. 

4. Berlin

The city of Berlin which is situated as an economic and political island surrounded by the Soviet zone presents very special problems. I am glad to report that during the past year ECA assistance was brought to this beleaguered city, and that under the terms of the new bilateral agreement between the Federal Republic and the United States, the German Federal Government has assumed the responsibility for financial aid to Berlin. This, I believe, will bring badly needed help to the former capital which due to its particular position has lagged far behind the economic recovery of western Germany because of the following reasons: 

1. Industrial production is only 25 percent of 1936; high unemployment, 25 percent of the labor force, is not only due to industrial stagnation, but because so great a proportion of Berlin's population was once directly or indirectly working for the government; 

2. The loss of approximately 80 percent of the industrial equipment because of bombing and removal by the Soviets prior to the arrival of the western powers in Berlin in 1945; 

3. High transportation costs due to restricted routes which increase shipping costs to western Germany; 

4. A relatively high wage rate which boosts production costs; 

5. The city's unstable financial condition. The budget deficit for the current fiscal year will be over $200,000,000; 

6. The enormous war damage to buildings of all kinds which must still be repaired; and 

7. The political uncertainties which make west German businessmen hesitate to trade with Berlin.

To combat these conditions, the ECA mission has suggested that the German Government and occupation procurement authorities stimulate orders in the Berlin area; that tax concessions be made to capital remaining in or going to 

Berlin, that the budget be balanced through aid from the Federal Republic, and that counterpart funds in appreciable quantities be directed toward the city. 

We are all highly conscious of the importance of the fate of Berlin for the future of Germany. Special measures have been necessary in the past and will probably continue to be necessary to insure its life and freedom. But we feel that the contributions which were required were well deserved by the Berlin people who have so resolutely withstood the economic and political pressures which have been brought to bear on them by the Soviets.

Germany has a very particular place in the Marshall plan. Never before has a victorious nation undertaken a positive program to rehabilitate a vanquished adversary. We have embarked on this unique venture because the experience of 5 years of occupation has demonstrated to us the tremendous impact which conditions in Germany have on western Europe as a whole. Germany is the crux of the European problem. In order to solve the German as well as the 

European problem, western Germany must be tied as closely as possible to western Europe and must not only be permitted but encouraged to buy and sell in the international markets.

We have spent many billions of dollars to eradicate Nazism from the world. 

It seems well worth while to spend a small fraction of that amount in western Germany to lay the foundation of an economic structure which can prevent the resurgence of any extremist ideologies which threaten the peace of the world. 

Mr. HANES. There have been profound changes in Germany_since the report was made to you last year by the gentleman whom I succeeded. Western Germany now has a government of its own. There has been complete fusion between the United States, United Kingdom, and French zones which were separate last year at this time, and the Allied High Commission has replaced the military government.

The ECA Mission Chief performs a dual function in Germany which is different, I believe, from any other country of the 17 or 18 countries, in that, as I said awhile ago he is not only Chief of Mission of the ECA, but is economic advisor to the High Commissioner, Mr. 

McCloy. Also, the High Commissioner has two functions. He is the representative of the ECA as well as being the High Commissioner. 

The German Federal Government now has full rights and responsibilities in the Marshall plan. It is now a fullfledged partner with the other nations in the OEEC, and has signed a bilateral agreement with the United States of America. It has its own delegation in Washington now working very closely with the ECA headquarters here. 

There has been a tremendous upsurge in industrial production in Germany since the Marshall plan began, there. 

In May 1948, the industrial index there was only 47 percent of 1936, whereas in November of last year it went to 98 percent and stands at 95 percent at the present time. This production has made it possible to meet the pent up demands especially for consumer goods in Germany and prices have been stable, rationing and price controls have been practically eliminated. Gasoline is rationed as are some forms of agricultural and industrial items. The present level of the food consumption in Germany is up to 2,600 calories per day per person as compared to about 2,900 calories before the war so they are being well fed and are well nourished. 

This improvement in food conditions though I regret to state is not because of better farming conditions or better methods of agriculture, but because of a very fine crop year the Germans had last year together with the imporations of food stuffs from this country. 

In the financial field, whereas after the currency reform, it looked as if they were going to have a wild inflation, by curbing credits and the like people very shortly got over their desire to spend their money so rapidly apparently. This has been brought into line and at the present time we have a deflationary trend. Present policies have been loosened. ECA counterpart funds have been put out. Six hundred million dollars has recently been de-blocked and is being put out in the German economy for all types of assistance.

Mr. VORYS. It is the equivalent in deutschemark, is it not? 

Mr. HAYES. It is deutschemarks. It is about $150,000,000. 

Mr. VORYS. In your written statement you said "For investment purposes," and just now you said "Assistance."

Mr. HANES. I can give you the list of uses if you would like to have it, sir.

Mr. VORYS. We can come to that later. 

Mr. HANES. We call this whole thing an investment program. It is for various uses, and I can give it to you broken down if you would like to have it.

The problem of the dollar gap still remains in that Germany's exports to this country are far below her imports, being about $50,- 000,000 of exports as compared with about $800,000,000 of imports.. 

So it leaves a wide dollar gap that Germany must some day meet..

We are hoping that with some of the work we are doing this year, part of this will be met. 

Four major problems we think are facing Germany today; one is, industrially and agriculturally, she must increase productivity. She never can produce all the food she consumes and never has. About 

65 percent of her needs are all that the most optimistic think she can produce. At the present time, she is only producing around 50 percent of her food needs. It is felt, though, with intensive farming, with more machinery and reclaiming a lot of wastelands that are now not being properly used that this production might be brought up to 65 percent of her needs.

Agricultural research and extension work have been grossly inadequate for the past 15 years, and we are trying to improve this by the technical assistance teams that are going from this country over there to advise with their farmers and by the teams that come over here representing German farmers to learn all sorts of better techniques in farming and dairying. 

It is estimated, as I said, that about 500,000 additional acres of land could be claimed for cultivation if modern methods were followed. 

Industrial production although at a relatively. higher level of efficiency than agriculture is still inefficient as compared to American methods. In the German program they expect to get to 107 percent of 

1936 in their industrial production by the end of March. We think that is grossly inadequate and they should go at least to 120 percent. 

That is necessary because the population of Germany is about 20 percent more than it was prewar, due to some 8,000,000 to 10,000,000refugees, expellees, and displaced persons who have come across the line into western Germany from the eastern section of Germany. 

She must produce more if she is going to be self-sufficient. 

More than that, we have to do a lot of work in reorienting the thinking of the German industrialist. He has been trained and accustomed to monopolize through cartels and protective markets and has not been exposed to the realities of a free, competitive market. The 

German industrialist still thinks in terms of small production and small turn-over with a high profit rather than large production with low profit.

German export trade is hampered by lack of adequate sales organizations, unfamiliarity with modern merchandising methods and to some extent the thing that still prevails is the antipathy many people

have toward buying German goods. You can well understand that. 

In France today there have been people who have been run over during their lifetime three times by the Germans. Belgium was overrun twice and Holland once. They still have a feeling that they do not want anything to do with the Germans at all. 

Then a second problem we face if Germany is to progress is capital investment. It is very difficult to get any capital for investment there at all. People do not have it. Private investment is practically nil. 

The savings banks and insurance companies have some, but the savings are very slow because people are not able to save. It looks as though we will have to turn to the Central Bank, which is patterned somewhat on our Federal Reserve bank, to furnish long-term capital. This is not satisfactory. It is not as we would wish it, but it is about the only source we have to turn to. As a drastic measure to meet very unusual times, that may be the expedient which will have to be adopted.

This capital shortage is especially acute. It is felt in the housing program which we are trying to get going as quickly as we can and for two reasons. In the first place, the Germans are woefully short of housing because of the tremendous loss through bombing, especially in the cities. Again we think a large housing program would do more toward helping the unemployment situation than anything else. Not only the people who actively worked in building the houses but the people who furnish the brick, cement, lumber, and all the things that go into a house.

We find quite an anomaly there in Germany where they need 5,- 000,000 homes and they are having to let people off in the building trades because they do not have funds to finance these things. 

We have tried to funnel counterpart funds into this field, and, as I say, we are going to try to get lot-term financing from the Central Bank and some of the other banks. 

Unemployment is a tremendous problem in Germany today and is getting worse. There are 2,000,000 unemployed and that is about 

10 percent of the working population. 

Of course, the whole refugee situation is another real problem with Germany. They are coming over the line at the rate of 20,000 a month from the eastern zones. Nothing apparently can be done about it because we have said to the Germans that they have to offer a place of refuge for people to come to. As I say about 20,000 a month are coming over the line and very few going the other way, which to my mind proves conclusively that the Germans are not intrigued at all by the Russian idea. If they were, I think you would see more of them going into the eastern zone. Although the refugees and infiltrees constitute only about 18 percent of the total German population they constitute about 35 percent of the unemployed. They are resented terribly there by the western Germans because the German Government has to take care of them and more than that they are competing for the jobs of the Germans who have been in western Germany all their lives. 

Mr. JUDD. Are they mostly Germans themselves?

Mr. HANES. Yes, most of them are. They are called the "ethnic" 

Germans. You will remember Hitler when he went into Poland, I believe he first went in saying he was to protect the minority group,

the Germans. These people say they do not want that to happen again. 

They have been put out. They are rejected. They come across the line with about 120 pounds of baggage, which is all they are allowed to bring. I have seen some of these fellows who are or were tremendously wealthy. I remember a family from Yugoslavia, two sons and a father who showed me a picture of plants they had. They made candies and sweet cakes in Czechoslavakia. They were put out with practically nothing. They have a $10,000,000 investment there, and almost overnight they had to leave and part with their whole invest- ment.

Mr. JUDD. How did they come, through the Russian zone of Germany or through Bavaria?

Mr. HANES. They came into Bavaria. 

Mr. JUDD. They cannot get through the Russian zone? 

Mr. HANES. It is more difficult. 

Apart from the humanitarian aspects this is a problem peculiar to Germany alone. None of the other countries have it. It has many implications and is of far-reaching political importance; only by concerted effort to integrate these people into the economy is it possible to avoid social uprising and social unrest in western Germany. 

Both the ECA mission and the German Government are vitally concerned with unemployment. In western Germany, as I have said before, the housing program is one of the ways they are trying to fight this unemployment and are trying to get as much long-term money as possible for that purpose. 

There are two things, production and productivity, which must be increased in Germany. The existing monetary situation we think and submit, would permit us an expansion of credit for long-term investment provided we adopted adequate fiscal safeguards. 

The system of tax collections must be tightened and the tax structure so made to provide for luxury consumption and provide more funds for investment.

Third, the question of foreign exchange and foreign balances is a problem with Germany. She has liberalized her trade and Germany today has more liberalized trade practices than any other country in Europe except Switzerland. About 60 percent of her imports have been on the free list, or the quantitative list. They expect to increase to 80 percent. As a matter of fact, they have said if the other countries will free all their trade, Germany will follow suit and do likewise.

In going as far as she has, she has gotten herself into a position where she has large debit balances in many of the countries. As a matter of fact, her position today is just about $100,000,000 in the red. 

She has unfavorable trade balances with other countries to that extent and a good part of this comes from the Netherlands. 

Her exports to this country are running around $50,000,000 a year, while the imports are running about $800,000,000, a larger than 10 to 1 ratio. As a matter of fact, the total exports for the calendar year 1949 was a little over $1,000,000,000, while imports were over $2,000,- 000,000, so she is earning 50 percent of her imports by exports. That is a situation she must improve. She cannot keep on that way. 

One of our men we have put on the staff is there to start a dollar drive. That is to increase trade with the Western Hemisphere and

with the dollar area, hoping Germany will earn more dollars with which she can buy more of our goods or close the dollar gap if she does not buy more. Also it is hoped there will be an increase in trade with our country to furnish the dollars she needs so badly. 

The Germans are also setting up a mission along this same line to advise the German manufacturers as to just what our market will consume that they can make and how they can best package it and sell it to our people.

In addition to earning more dollars, Germany must, in order to bring her foreign trade into balance, find new sources for her imports. 

She cannot keep buying in this dollar area unless she earns more dollars and the best we can hope for, we think, is that this dollar gap will still be at the end of the Marshall plan, about $300,000,000, if the same plan is carried on as it is today. Therefore, we believe that to the extent of this $300,000,000, Germany must find sources in the softarea countries for her imports. That is what we are encouraging her to do. As a matter of fact, we are forcing her to do so. In the trade agreement she is making, we are trying to force her to buy everything she can from the soft-currency areas, from France, from Holland, and all these other countries, to conserve her dollars as much as possible.

Then Berlin, of course, is a real problem in Germany. It is a problem to the Allies as well as to the Germans. 

With regard to the question of these expellees, these displaced persons and this tremendous group that comes across the line, we say to the Germans, "This is your problem, as is Berlin." As a matter of fact, we must consider it part of the Allies' problem, too, since we acquiesced in the Germans' letting all these people into Germany. 

Whether they like it or not, they have to keep a haven for political refugees or religious refugees or whatever they may be. 

Berlin, of course, we latched onto, and it is an island surrounded by the Soviets. It is a continual bone of contention, there. The Russians one week, as you read in the papers, will loosen up on the trading into Berlin, coming across the Russian zone. The next week they will cut it down to 4 or 5 trucks an hour, just to make themselves as ornery as they possibly can, hoping, I think, surely, that they will worry the Allies so badly that eventually we will get disgusted and pull out and turn Berlin over to them. The Allies cannot do that because Berlin is still looked to as the capital of a new Germany. 

I think the Allies would be wrong if they pulled out, but it means a tremendous outlay of money. Berlin has no chance of being selfsufficient. Berlin is running in the red all the time for many different reasons. In the first place, production is only 25 percent of 1936, whereas western Germany is now 95 percent. Unemployment is 25 percent. That is true partly because, Berlin having been the capital city just as Washington is here, formerly a great number of those people were employed in government, and the government not being there any longer, the employment is taken away.

Berlin lost about 80 percent of her productive capacity by bombing and through the stealing of the Russians. That is exactly what happened. They went in there and simply raided these industrial plants. 

In many cases they took the machinery from the plants, dumped it on the street, and broke it before they ever got it out of Berlin. Much

was badly packed and torn to pieces in shipping, and much of it today, I am told by people who have been in Moscow, is along the railroad tracks on either side for miles, lying out there rusting because they did not know what to do with it when they finally got it into Russia. However, it has completely prostrated Berlin's industry. 

The high transportation cost is another thing, the unstable financial condition of Berlin, due to the fact that she has an unbalanced budget, and the fear among those buying from Berlin that they will not get the material out are other factors contributing to Berlin's economic problems. They cannot get raw materials. The Germans have the same problem on the railroads, the canal, and the highways, so the businessmen in western Germany are really afraid to buy from Berlin because they do not know when they will get deliveries. 

We think Germany has a peculiar place in the Marshall plan. 

Never before in the history of the world, I believe, has a victorious nation undertaken a program to rehabilitate a vanquished adversary. 

We have embarked on this venture because the experience of 5 years of occupation has demonstrated to us the tremendous impact which conditions in Germany have on all western Europe. 

Western Germany must be tied in as closely as possible to western Europe and must not only be permitted but encouraged to buy and sell in the international markets.

We spent many millions of dollars to eradicate nazism from the world. It seems well worth while to spend a small fraction of this amount in western Germany to lay the foundations of an economic structure which can prevent the resurgence of any extremist ideologies which threaten the peace of the world.

That, in brief, is my report. I will be glad to answer any questions, sir, that I can.

I believe if western Germany can reequip herself, she can become self-supporting.

Mr. RICHARDS. We have provided some of it; have we not?

Mr. RICHARDS. You were talking about these people coming from the Russian zone and practically none going out of the western zone to the Russian zone.

Mr. HANES. I do not think there is any question, sir. It seems to me that if the nations of the Western World will give Germany half a chance to be integrated with the western countries, Germany will be with us.

She has no desire at all to go with Russia. There will be no difficulty if we give her half a chance to stay with the western group. 

Mr. RICHARDS. How many of these people are coming across every month?

Mr. HANES. Twenty thousand. They screen them very carefully at the checking points. You cannot control the whole border. A lot of them come in illegally. Germany cannot keep them out, because she does not have a sufficient police force. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Vorys. 

Mr. VORYS. I first want to join in Mr. Richards' statement that it is men like you who help us get religion on this. I have heard from many people who have come from Germany, unofficially and officially, and they have spoken highly of your work there. We have also heard of your work in North Carolina.

You have mentioned that they have almost eliminated rationing there. I have wondered why they can do that there and still have to have it in Britain to a much greater extent. 

Mr. HANES. Of course, Britain is rationing at home so she can ship as much as she can abroad to both the sterling area and the dollar area. 

As the banker for a good part of western Europe, she had many responsibilities and liabilities, really, that Germany does not have.

Mr. VORYS. But, with regard to food, Germany is more unself-sufficient than Britain.

Mr. HANES. I believe Britain has to import about two-thirds of her foodstuffs. I believe that is about the same as Germany. 

Mr. VORYS. You would not know why they could have less rationing in Germany than in Britain?

Mr. HANES. As I say, I think there are two diametrically opposite thoughts as to how to come out of this thing. We try to get Germany to take free enterprise and free business and have few restraints, make the thing as wide open as possible. Belgium has done the same thing. 

England has adopted a different method. They have this idea of socialistic government and many, many restraints. It is just a different philosophy that they have. They are trying to conserve everything they can, to use as little as they can at home, so they will have more to ship abroad to earn dollars and for foreign exchange. 

Mr. VORYS. Now the question that goes with that is, How Germany can afford to have the most liberal trade policies and yet apparently prosper from it. If Germany prospers from it, you would wonder why the rest of them do not.

T: 

Mr. HANES. We have, of course, pushed Germany into this because we feel that it is the only way western Europe is ever going to be able to succeed or to come back and be self-supporting again. We feel she must break down her trade barriers all over and that they should find some basis for exchanging their moneys so that when they do sell, one country to another, they can find some way of collecting. They must get currency convertibility as well as the elimination of trade barriers. 

Now, as I say, we have pressed Germany into going out further than the others, and she has taken on our advice that that is the way to really come back.

In the OEEC, there is some needling going on for the other countries to try to bring them up to the German position, and we hope Germany will go further. There are about 280,000,000 people in 

Europe as against the 150,000,000 in this country. If you ever get that into one market, you can start mass production, and they can produce on a much cheaper basis and make their products. More people would be able to buy them because they would be cheaper and they could get the cost of everything down. They now surround themselves with these trade barriers, each little country, and they can only produce what their little country consumes and very little more than that, because the trade barriers keep them out of the other countries. 

Mr. VORYS. Just in the period since I was in Germany in 1947, it would appear Germany has had the most remarkable recovery of any of the countries. Germany had been stepping more toward freedom in the way you have said. Is that because we have been in a position to get our ideas across more effectively there?

Mr. HANES. As long as we had military government and even now, we could tell the Germans in pretty positive terms that certain things ought to be done and they just about had to do it. 

Mr. VORYS. It looks as if we would be helping Europe if we used the same methods in other places so far as they will work. 

Mr. HANES. I agree with you. Perhaps we should have been tougher other places, but the ECA has adopted the policy, and probably rightly so, of not getting into the internal affairs of any country. 

Let them run their own affairs. The ECA had been criticized in England because it had been said we were financing the socialistic government there. However, it is not up to us to dictate what kind of government people must have as long as they elect the type they want through the process of a free election. 

Mr. VORYS. When the problems of these countries meddle in our internal affairs to the extent of imposing taxes and debts on us to support them, we feel we have a little bit to say over there. 

You mentioned $200,000,000 for Berlin. Does that mean that out of the five-hundred-odd million dollars of the deficit which we make up that $200,000,000 of it would go to support Berlin? 

Mr. HANES. I do not think I mentioned $200,000,000 in relation to Berlin. 

Mr. VORYS. In your prepared statement, you said:

The city's unstable financial condition. The budget deficit for the current fiscal year would be over $200,000,000.

Mr. HANES. You see, in the bilateral agreement which we signed in 

January the agreement with the German Federal Government was that

they would take over the handling of Berlin. It is up to the German 

Federal Government to care for it. 

Mr. VORYS. I wondered whether $200,000,000 out of the $500,000,- 

000, approximately, that we are supposed to put up for Germany would be going toward supporting Berlin.

Mr. HANES. It would not be that much. 

Mr. VORYS. It would not work out that way? 

Mr. HANES. It would not. We are hopeful Berlin is going to get a good part of the amount sent over to Germany, but it will not be that much.

Mr. VORYS. With yourself and Mr. McCloy there, a lot of us have great confidence in what is going to happen in Germany in spite of the enormous difficulties.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Chatham- 

Mr. CHATHAM. I have to be very careful in my questioning, because he is my local banker.

Mr. Kenny's chart 3 on the budget of the British Government shows 

72 percent of the British Government goes for defense and social expenditure. That is made up of defense, 20 percent; war pension, 5 percent; interest on national debt, 13 percent; education and health, 13 percent; national insurance, relief, family allowances, 7 percent; and food and housing, 14 percent, which makes 72 percent of their total budget.

Now, in the German budget, you have nothing for defense. 

Mr. HANES. That is right.

Mr. CHATHAM. How about war pensions? 

Mr. HANES. They are paying some; yes. They are Länder payments. Each state has their own pension system which they have to carry. 

Mr. CHATHAM. How about national debt?

Mr. HANES. No internal national debt. 

Mr. CHATHAM. Education and health? 

Mr. HANES. They have that. 

Mr. CHATHAM. Nothing like 34 percent. 

Mr. HANES. That is right. 

Mr. CHATHAM. That, to me, is the difference between the standard of living. If Britain was throwing this into food, and so forth, it would be different, but they are looking out for everybody. It is 72 percent here, and it is about 52 percent in this country.

Germany can control war capacity, I think she is the most important country over there.

Mr. HANES. It is certainly the crux of the whole thing, in my opinion. They will come back if they are allowed to do it.

Mr. HANES. Yes; the machinery going in is really very good. 

Mrs. BOLTON. And better than what we have in this country. 

Mr. HANES. I do not believe it is better, Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON. We have not been able to renew machinery at all, except to the extent of about 2 percent a year, under the Treasury order, which the Treasury could change if it wanted to and doesn't. 

The result is we are way under production in this country and are going to be way under production for a very long time unless something can be done to relieve the companies of this replacement burden. 

You say that sales are largely within Germany, or did I misunderstand you? 

Mr. HANES. The machinery sales; yes. 

Mrs. BOLTON. They do ship over here?

Mr. HANES. They export some. 

Mrs. BOLTON. They are exporting into our markets abroad, too. 

Mr. HANES. They are some; yes.

Mr. HANES. Of course, some special American machine tools and 

American machinery is imported into Germany, so they more or less offset themselves there. I think there is more coming into Germany than there is going out into the dollar area. 

Mrs. BOLTON. There is quite definitely more going in? 

Mr. HANES. Oh, yes. You have not seen a German automobile over here. You see American automobiles all over Germany.

Mrs. BOLTON. I was speaking more specifically of my machine-tool industry. 

Mr. HANES. Yes. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Would you say that the managed-currency situation had a definite effect upon the price of the machine tools that are sold here in this country that are made in Germany? Is that pricing done over there, or is it done in Washington, or where is it done? 

Mr. HANES. The pricing is done by them. They are perfectly free now to ship as they choose and, if they can get dollars, they can ship where they choose. However, they are still pretty well governed by the cartels. We are trying to break up these monopolies they have over there, break them down into small units and make them compete and get out and fight for a living like they could in this country. 

However, the prices are made by the companies themselves. 

Mr. CHATHAM. Will the gentlewoman yield? 

Mrs. BOLTON. Yes.

Mr. CHATHAM. The machine-tool industry takes a great deal of labor. I saw skilled workmen over there working for 50 cents an hour where I imagine it is $2 an hour in your place. That would make an enormous difference in price.

Mr. HANES. It is about a mark and a half an hour. That is about 

3712 cents. 

Mr. CHATHAM. That is for skilled people. The German workman is the most skilled person in the world. We cannot possibly compete with that. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Are they going to flood us with cooking utensils and so forth that are cheaply made?

Mr. HANES. I do not think they are, Mrs. Bolton. I think the estimates that have been made that all the things coming to America of a competitive nature will approximate one billion and a quarter dollars, are the most optimistic. Now $140,000,000 is not a lot. That is not enough to worry us at all. If we are going to have trade with western Europe, if we are going to sell them, we have to buy; there is no way out of it. There is no one-way street. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I think it is very interesting that in spite of the fact that a new management-labor group has been formed to fight reciprocal trades and fighting some of this, still the A. F. of L. is standing very valiantly for the imports into this country. 

Just recently, they made some renewed statement to the effect that that must happen. I think it is very helpful. 

Mr. HANES. I have been through a great many of the manufacturing plants. I do not feel there is any competition at all. We are so far advanced above them in our procedures, methods, and efficiency.

Mrs. BOLTON. Then it behooves us to keep up our plants and machinery so that we should have release from the Treasury on these machines or we will find ourselves in the hole. 

Mr. HANES. That is quite true.

Mrs. BOLTON. Does England send food into its displaced persons areas?

Mr. HANES. England does not. 

Mrs. BOLTON. She does not now?

Mr. HANES. No.

Mr. HANES. We have had most of these displaced persons from
