Chairman KEE. Mr. Ribicoff- 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I agree that the men running the ECA missions are very capable, but I would like to say this about Mr. Hanes. I think 

I had the advantage of observing Mr. Hanes under circumstances that very few of us have with other mission chiefs. Frankly, Mr. Chatham and myself made our European headquarters at his home. Although 

I understand that he is a host under the best traditions of southern hospitality, yet Mr. Hanes was so busy-and he had not seen his

brother-in-law for such a long time-that he had little time to spend with us outside of strict ECA business. I could see the neglect of family life because he was so busily engaged upon the Government work. I doubt whether anyone in private industry would have given as much of his time and energy to his own affairs as Mr. Hanes has given to the affairs of the ECA. Very few people realize what a public servant does for the common good, or for his Nation, as against his own personal interest.

There was one day that Mr. Hanes was seriously ill. Frankly, I think I would have stayed at home and doctored myself. He had an important engagement in another part of Germany. He got on a night train under very bad circumstances and went to do his work. 

He should have taken a vacation. He did not take a vacation. I for one want to pay personal tribute to a hard-working, loyal American who is doing this work because he feels it is necessary for this country's future. Mr. Hanes is one of the ablest and most sincere men 

I have ever known. I hope this Nation will find continued use for his talents.

Mr. Hanes, there is just one factor on which you might have left a wrong impression in the record by answering Mr. Vorys' question. 

I would like you to clear it up. Mr. Vorys said apparently the 

Germans have absorbed more of the American ideas than other nations. Now that may be true in the productive sense but I don't think you mean they have gained more from our democratic principles.

Mr. HANES. No. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. To inculcate democracy in Germany is a very, very slow process, I understand.

Mr. HANES. Yes. In competition and business, they are absorbing it much more rapidly. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Of course, one of the difficulties that I think you, as a businessman, appreciate that the very fact of this mass destruction in Germany will lead to Germany's eventual strength. In other words, where you did not have mass destruction, you have plants going along with antiquated equipment. Now, as I understand it, in Germany you are building up a new plant right from the ground up, which gives them new equipment, new plants, and better productive capacity and facilities than some of their neighbors. 

Mr. HANES. That is true. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. That is possibly causing some of the difficulty between the Belgians, French, Dutch, and Italians with the Germans. 

They feel they will be at a bad competitive disadvantage with Germany herself. Is that correct?

Mr. HANES. That is true, and I think much of the security talk we hear from some of our friends over there is really a fear of competition more than it is a feeling of fear for lack of security. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Everybody in Europe, including Germany, must have dollars.

Mr. HANES. Yes. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. There is only one market, basically, for which they aim and that is the United States. The question comes up whether each one of the European countries can, at the same time, use America

as her target to earn dollars. It is going to be a very difficult proposition for us to import that much even if we want to. 

Mr. HANES. That is right. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you or your assistants have the figures of the relative amount of German production that went to the east before the war?

Mr. HANES. The trade with the east before the war was normally about 15 percent of the total trade of Germany. Now it is a good deal less than that. I did not give you the figures before the war, but 

I can give you the exports and imports that I quoted a while ago. 

The exports were running just over $1,000,000,000 a year and imports over $2,000,000,000. Breaking that down, exports to the Western 

Hemisphere were $85,000,000; $917,000,000 to OEEC countries; to eastern Europe $62,000,000; to the nonparticipating sterling area $35,000,000; and to all other countries, $22,000,000. This is for the year 1949.

Mr. RIBICOFF. In other words, there was a great deal of normal trade with the east which has been disrupted because of the present more or less blockade between the east and the west-is that not true. 

Mr. HANES. Pardon me? 

Mr. RIBICOFF. A great deal of Germany's difficulty is due to the fact that she had a large trade with the east which was disrupted because of the so-called blockade.

Mr. HANES. That is right. In 1936, that trade to the east of Germany was about 15 percent of her total export trade and now it is down to 3 percent.

Mr. RIBICOFF. There is much talk that through subterfuge, at the present time, deals are being made between the Chinese Communist Government to reinstate the prewar trade between Germany and China, through brokers in east Germany who give the orders to west Germany and the merchandise finds its way to China. Of course, if that were the case, that would be contrary to United States policy at the present time.

Mr. HANES. I do not know how much of that is being done, Mr. 

Ribicoff, but just recently the Germans had a chance to bid on a very large order of steel railroad rails and we refused them the permission. Our understanding is that later the British were figuring on taking it, so it put us in a bad position with the Germans. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you mean the British were taking the rail business with China?

Mr. HANES. Yes. We have had to come back and say, if the British bid on it, we will have to let the Germans bid on it, too. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. In other words, we either have a common policy or we do not. 

Mr. HANES. That is true. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I mean a common policy with all of western Europe and the United States, or we do not, which causes all the difficulty. 

All of which leads to the fact that, without integration, certainly at the economic level and eventually in the political level, our entire policy is at cross purposes with itself.

Mr. HANES. That is right. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Judd.

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Hanes, I have not had a chance previously to know you personally, but I have known your brother and, from what I hear, you are just as good as he is, so that makes you all right. 

You spoke of having released a goodly amount of counterpart funds in order to overcome the deflationary pressure that was setting in. 

What percentage of the counterpart funds has been released and is in use?

Mr. HANES. I spoke of the release of DM600,000,000 that has recently been made. That is in deutschemarks. Then we have about 

DM400,000,000 additional in a program that has been passed that ought to be released immediately. We have another DM1,000,000,000 that ought to be released after that. The program is being set up for it now. It has not been passed. 

For the year 1949-50, there is about 2 billion deutschemarks in the counterpart funds. As I say, 600,000,000 have been released and about 400,000,000 are in the process of being released. The program is being set up for the other half being 1,000,000,000 deutschemarks; that is roughly $500,000,000.

Mr. JUDD. That is the total amount of counterpart that has been built up.

Is not the percentage released the highest of any of the countries we have been aiding?

Mr. HANES. That I cannot say, sir. I do not know what the release has been in other countries. It is not the highest receipt of counterpart funds. Great Britain always has more. 

Mr. JUDD. You have had a tough situation there in some respects; but when you get this third program through, you will have released, in trying to offset the deflation, all of your counterpart funds? 

Mr. HANES. Yes. Would you be interested in knowing how that is broken down, sir?

Mr. JUDD. That means all the counterpart funds that have been built up from the beginning of ECA to the present? 

Mr. HANES. No; that is just this year for that DM2,000,000,000. 

Mr. JUDD. Were all of last year's released, too?

Mr. HANES. Last year's have been released. I can give you that for the years. Would you like to have it for the years? 

Mr. JUDD. You say it was released for investment purposes. What kind of things has it been invested in? 

Mr. HANES. We call this an investment program. Of this 

DM2,000,000,000, DM250,000,000 goes into agriculture. For coal mines, DM280,000,000. We are trying to be very careful there to see that none of the inefficient mines get any of this. We are trying to get them to close their inefficient mines and use their counterpart funds on rehabilitating and using the mechanical equipment and the efficiency of the good mines so they can cut the price of coal. There was about 8 marks difference in the pricing of coal, the export and the domestic. They cut that to about 5 or 512. 

Public utilities, 400 millions: That is in generating plants and lines to go out to the rural areas to give more people the use of current and to rehabilitate some of the older plants. 

Transportation and communications: That is the railroad and the 

German post, 270,000,000; steel 80,000,000 only. That is to rehabilitate some steel plants. Large industry, 400,000,000 and in the very

small industries having 10 employees as a maximum, 60,000,000. 

Housing 220,000,000, and miscellaneous, trade, tourism, and so forth, about 40,000,000, making up the 2,000,000,000.

Mr. JUDD. You spoke of rehabilitating the steel industries. Has dismantling stopped?

Mr. HANES. It has been greatly reduced. There are some purely war-potential plants in Germany being dismantled. In some cases, only parts of the plant, where it has a war potential, are being destroyed and taken out, and the rest of the plant is left. This is so, for instance, if it is a power plant that serves the community or can be used for peacetime purposes.

Many of the plants can be used for peacetime purposes. 

We had a plant making magnesium and processing it. We destroyed some electric cells and some drying equipment. The balance of the plant could be used to make phosphates, fertilizers, and that is going to be equipped for that sort of purpose now. Where we can turn it into peacetime production, that is done, eliminating war potential altogether. Some of that demolition is still going on. 

Mr. JUDD. There are no further plants to be dismantled, however, upon which the work has not even started? 

Mr. HANES. There are a few over which there has been a lot of contention and work has not been started. Yes, that is true. In those cases, I think finally they will take part of the plant and leave the balance. Complete destruction, I think, is pretty well over. 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Ribicoff spoke about the question of perhaps exporting to the Far East. Has there been much agitation or is there now in the western zone, or do you know of any in the eastern zone, or offers being made by the Soviets, especially to unemployed Germans, engineers, technicians, and so forth, that there is a great future for them in the development of China and the undeveloped areas of east Asia under Communist leadership?

Mr. HANES. Do you mean by that, sir, that they are trying to entice the people to come in? 

Mr. JUDD. Yes. Mr. HANES. I don't think they have had any success with that at all. I don't think they are trying, except as propaganda, to say that all is milk and honey in the eastern orbit. They have 20,000 people coming to the western area each month telling them different stories about that. I don't think they fool the Germans on that. 

Traditionally, about 15 percent of the German export trade was with the eastern countries. It is now down to 3 to 5 percent. We are trying to get that increased. 

It is difficult because the Russians, really, and the satellite nations have very little they can ship into Germany. They need things so badly themselves. Foodstuffs are the things. Germany can furnish steel and machine tools of certain types. These are screened carefully to make sure it is not a war potential going to the east. 

If it is what would be normally used in the peacetime economy of these countries, and the quantity is not too large, which would seem to indicate they were going into war production or some subversive use, that is passed right on.

In return, we try to get foodstuffs, fats, sugars, things the Germans have to get from the dollars areas, we are trying to get them from the soft currency areas. 

Mr. JUDD. Thank you. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield, have you any questions?

Mr. MANSFIELD. Mr. Hanes, we are delighted to have you before this committee to get the precise picture of the situation as it is in western 

Germany at the present time.

Is it your contention that Germany is the economic key to the revival of western Europe?

Mr. HANES. I think Germany, with 50,000,000 people, is so essential that I don't think western Europe could ever be successful in supporting itself without German trade. I think that is absolutely true. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. Would you say there are possibilities that the old antipathy between the French and Germans is being broken down by 

Schumann and Adenauer?

Mr. HANES. Recently there was a trade agreement signed between the French and the Germans. Some $500,000,000 of trade was flowing each way. It was really a great victory, we think, for the Americans, because we were very much interested in getting this thing done. 

Mr. Conrad leads our trade and payments division over there. He had his men working day and night on these things. Many of the old inhibitions the Germans had and the difficulties the French had have been broken down. They are trading on a free sort of a basis. 

It is a very good trade agreement. It is the first trade agreement the 

Germans really negotiated by themselves.

Since that time they have negotiated with the British and the Dutch, and they are going to negotiate one with us now. But the Germans are doing that on their own. We are only observing, watching, and trying to assist.

Mr. MANSFIELD. That is very encouraging news not only for the 

Americans, but I would say for the Germans and the French as well. 

Now, at the present time, of course, Germany is in a weak position in western Europe, but it appears to me that this weakness has all the elements in it for eventually making Germany the strongest nation in western Europe. I base that on the possibility--and maybe it is more than a possibility that the Allied Powers in the west and the Russians in the east will begin vying for the Germans' favor, making concessions and in that respect each hoping it will have its own type of unified Germany.

I suppose when the Russians make their plans, they will want a unified Germany on the Russian model. But it seems to me that it is not too much to expect that under the right kind of conditions, the Russians will have a great deal more to offer to the Germans than we, in respect to, let us say, the transfer back to the Germans of some of the land which the Russians were responsible for expropriating from Germany and giving to Poland and to Czechoslovakia which, at the present time, are satellite states.

Those are factors, I think, that we have to consider, because while they are just possibilities at the present time, in view of Germany's bargaining position and in view of the Soviet's cards, it is quite possible that things might turn out there in a way that we would not like.

In that respect, or rather because of these circumstances, Germany may well become the strongest power in western Europe. 

Mr. HANES. I think that is a long way off, sir. There is no question about it being a real danger. However, it seems all the more reason we should work as hard as we can to integrate western Germany into western Europe and make her really a part of the western 

European economy.

Mr. MANSFIELD. I agree with you, Mr. Hanes. 

I have one more question: Is Germany being represented on the 

OEEC and on the Council of Europe?

Mr. HANES. She is on the OEEC; she is a full participant there now. She has her own people sitting in. In the Council of Europe, she is not in. The French and the British both object to her going on the other at the present time. We hope she will go on within a year, but she is not on just now. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. That is all, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. JAVITS. And a counterpart of that is to integrate into western 

Europe as a part of it?

Mr. HANES. She is anxious to do that.

Mr. HANES. I think up to this time they have been completely reliable. I think they want no part of the Russians and the Soviets, but if the pressure gets too great on them, I don't know whether they can withstand it. I mean if unemployment keeps rising, causing tremendous suffering. That is what always breeds radical ideas and notions.

Mr. HANES. On what, Mrs. Bolton? 

Mrs. BOLTON. The women who came over, whom we saw here. 

We took them to our homes. The first were newspaper women, magazine women, magazine publishers, members of their political councils, and so on. They comprised a very fine group. 

Mr. HANES. I do not know about that group specifically, but I have heard that these teams that have come over, many of them, have done tremendously fine work when they have gone back. Mrs. BOLTON. An impression has really been made?

Mr. HANES. I think unquestionably it has. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Were there not some unfortunate choices?

Mr. HANES. Well, we will get some bad ones. It is impossible to have it otherwise.

Mrs. BOLTON. I am very authoritatively informed that there are those who have come over to the United States and gone into teaching positions in this country who are just about as arrogant as any Hit- Îerite that was ever alive. They are simply unbearable and are teaching in our colleges. Two specific instances have been called to my attention. 

Also, I am wondering what was being done for young people. What has been the effect of the methods you are employing on children? 

What are the children going to be?

Mr. HANES. First, we are trying to do something about their education. I think that is most important. Unfortunately, apparently during the regime with the military governors-I say this without any criticism because I was not there and I imagine there was some good reason for it-although they had enough paper for newspapers, and it was necessary to inform the people what was happening, they did not have enough paper or did not use it to print schoolbooks. up until now, almost, the same books used by the Nazis, extolling the virtues of steel, iron, and blood and hard fighting and all that, are still being used. So

What the occupation authorities did was to take out what they had of that nature. They pasted a piece of paper over such passages. 

That only fired the childrens' imagination, and, of course, immediately they ripped it off and read them and it probably made more impression on them than it would have otherwise. 

Now we are printing schoolbooks expressing the free-enterprise way of doing things. It explains the Marshall plan, telling what the 

Marshall plan is doing for their countries in something of a subtle way, not being too outspoken about it. There have been about 1,000,- 

000 textbooks for use in German schools that have been distributed in the secondary schools. These books have proved so popular that we have authorized another 500,000.

We have another issue now of schoolbooks for smaller children from 7 to 10 years old. We are now publishing 2,000,000 books for children from 10 to 14 years of age, which will do the same thing, we hope, for them that has been done for the others. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What about the littlest people, the most impressionable people of all?

Mr. HANES. We haven't gotten there yet. There is a bracket from 

6 months to 6 years. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Who is influencing them during that period? Is it widows of SS troops and so on?

Mr. HANES. I expect they stay at home because I do not think they can afford kindergartens.

Mrs. BOLTON. I would just like to urge upon you the fact that there in that period from 6 months to 7 years is the most impressionable time of a child's life. It seems to me a very important thing what the influences upon them are.

With regard to the German women who have gone back, I am delighted to say here in the record that I was interested in the enthusiasm with which some of these women spoke of the work that had been done for them and with them by the wives of the officers who were there. They were told about women's clubs. They never knew there were any before. The Americans helped them form clubs on the regular American pattern, their first taste of participation in a democratic way of life.

I was wondering whether it was sufficient to come to your attention. 

Mr. HANES. I have heard of those; yes.

Another thing that is being encouraged and is now happening is in these farm meetings. They are asking women to come to those meetings and speak at those meetings, which is something never heard of before. They are taking a real part in these meetings. They express themselves.

Mrs. BOLTON. It seemed to me rather important that the young women be approached, because they do control the first years of the children. The ones I talked with when I was there in 1945 immediately following the war. They were very bitter and arrogant. It was truly terrible though understandable.

I remember asking the mayor of Berlin, a nice old fellow, what he was doing about the children when they went home at night. He turned white and said, "Please don't bring that up. It is something we haven't even thought of. It is too ghastly to consider."

I have been troubled about the situation as it has gone along, and certainly regret that 5 years have passed without a solution. 

Mr. HANES. It is a difficult thing. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. HANES. Thank you for the suggestion, Mrs. Bolton.

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Mr. Vorys. 

Mr. VORYS. Do you have any food subsidies there?

Mr. HANES. Yes. The difficult thing is the people do not know what is happening to them on this food-subsidy basis. It is handled by a bureau and some little clerk or bureaucrat handles the thing apparently just as he sees fit. No real public record is made. 

There are some things the Germans are buying cheaper outside and selling them higher inside. That profit goes into a fund which is supposed to pay for the supplies, the foods they buy at a higher price outside and subsidize inside. It covers only about 10 percent. 

We have said to them, "If you are going to subsidize food, it is none of our business, that is an internal matter, but you must put it in your budget, you must put it out in plain language so people understand what is happening to them."

Wheat, for instance, is imported at about $100 per ton into Germany, bought in this country. If Germany belonged to the wheat agreement, she could buy that same wheat at $80 a ton. They sell it to the 

Germans internally at $65 a ton. Subsidizing is at the rate of $35 a ton.

The politicians and Adenauer made a foolish statement when he first came in that there would be no increase in the price of bread.

In order to do that, he had to continue these subsidies. 

We said to him that had to be eliminated completely by June 30 this year, or they had to put it in their budget as part of the cost of running the budget. Corn, for instance, is imported at $75 a ton and sold internally at $50 a ton. It is so cheap at $50 that farmers will not raise root crops and fodder crops to feed their cattle because they can buy this corn more cheaply. They are using dollars where they should not. 

Another thing, the Germans are eating wheat bread almost altogether. A good percentage of them ought to be eating rye bread. As long as they subsidize wheat, wheat bread is cheaper and they are going to use it. That is another thing we said they have to eliminate. They have to go to France, for instance, to buy rye. They have to buy rye wherever they can.

We just cut 400,000 tons out of the German requirements for wheat. 

We told them they didn't need that much wheat in the first place. 

Mr. VORYS. How do they get the money to buy the wheat? Do you fellows give them the money?

Mr. HANES. It comes from the American taxpayers, indirectly. As well as we can figure, these subsidies run about $100,000,000. 

Mr. CHATHAM. But you have cut it out?

Mr. HANES. As of June they have to eliminate it or put it in their own budget and tax the people for it. 

Mr. VORYS. What you mean is there is $100,000,000 of our ECA money for which there is no counterpart because they do not charge anybody for it, is that right, and they do not tax for it?

Mr. HANES. No; they have to put up counterpart. When the wheat comes in, at the price it comes in, the German Government puts up

in Deutschemarks an equivalent amount of the dollar. Then as she sells the wheat to bakers or whoever buys it, they put up Deutschemarks to the German Government. The difference between the internal prices sold and the internal price they pay for it is a cost on the 

German economy.

Since we support the German economy, it affects the ECA program. 

Mr. CHATHAM. Will the gentleman yield?

Mr. VORYS. Yes. 

Mr. CHATHAM. The same thing is happening to a greater extent in 

Great Britain where they subsidize all food? 

Mr. VORYS. I never got around to Mr. Kenney yesterday on that to try to find out where it fits in. They say 14 percent of their sterling budget goes for subsidies for food and housing. I was trying to find out whether there was an honest accounting for it; that is, if it is in the price of the food or in the subsidy. However, I have not been able to find out. Do you know if they do it the same way in Britain? 

Mr. JAVITS. If the gentleman will yield, Mr. Kenney answered those questions. What he said was, it came in the spread between the wholesale and retail price. At that point, the subsidy was fed into the mill, so the retail price was low, whereas the wholesale price was high. 

Mr. VORYS. But here is the thing: Germany has an unbalanced budget and one of the things I would imagine unbalances it is issuing counterpart Deutschemarks for grain and not collecting the full amount either from taxes or otherwise. 

Mr. HANES. That is true. 

Mr. VORYS. You mentioned import experts working on this proposition of trying to devise ways and means for having Germany sell stuff here. Now, to what extent are those import experts working on stuff that is supplementary and not competitive here, or to what extent are they telling Germans how to make stuff to sell here in direct competition with products of ours?

Mr. HANES. They are trying to take things of large labor content which do not compete with our things. For instance, take cameras, which have been imported to this country for years from Germany. 

That has gone way, way down. A lot of the lenses used by Eastman are still bought in Germany. A lot of these field glasses, the Zeiss 

Works makes lenses. Pottery and glassware they have sold in this country for generations.

It is that type of thing that we are trying to encourage or shall try to encourage, which will enable them to get back in here. 

Mr. VORYS. You are treading on my toes when you get to pottery and glassware from Ohio.

Mr. HANES. It is a different type altogether from what we make. 

You take their Bavarian china, it is more on the pottery idea and is different from anything we make in this country. 

Mr. VORYS. Even in the line of pottery or glassware you attempt at least to guide them into lines which will not be competitive? 

Mr. HANES. Yes, if we can. 

Mr. VORYS. Did you say there is a $100,000,000 red balance?

Mr. HANES. As total. The Netherlands loan, though, is about $60,- 000,000. 63307-50-pt. 1-16

Mr. VORYS. Is there one particular big item that would account for that?

Mr. HANES. No. This thing jumped especially in December when 

Germany was buying a lot of consumer goods for the Christmas trade; tea and coffee and some textiles. But practically all of what they have bought was consumer goods. 

The difficulty Germany has with all of her foreign trade is she buys shelf goods, things brought in and sold at retail and consumed. Most things she builds are things that take a long while to build and collect for. For instance, she has a large deficit with Turkey at the present time. It does not concern us because she has two very large power projects that Germany is building for Turkey. 

In the meantime, she has built up a large debit balance with Turkey, but she will more than overcome that in the next 2 years when the Germans build these power plants, deliver them, and collect large pieces of money at a time. That is true of many of the exports. They are heavy things that take time to construct and build and you get large payments, but in the meantime they are building up deficits on the other side.

Mr. VORYS. It would appear to me that for Germany, as well as 

Italy, and perhaps some of the other countries, their most important export ought to be people, and I wondered if you have any plans for getting these refugees and expellees out of Germany. If they are a charge on Germany, that is reflected in the $552,000,000 on us, because it all comes back to Uncle Sam, and, as I understand it, properly so because we participated in the international arrangements that put these people out of where they were and into Germany. 

Mr. HANES. That is right. 

Mr. VORYS. Are there any plans under way for those people to migrate to Africa, South America, or some place where they could do as their ancestors did in this country, come to an open country and be the best type of pioneers?

Mr. HANES. It is being tried, but no country really wants people coming into it now. They are not looking for additional population. 

I think practically every country is the same. The South American countries agreed to take a few, but it is only a very, very small number as compared to the ones who ought to move. 

Mr. VORYS. There are places in Africa, I would think, and a few other places left in the world, such as South America, where conditions are rather rugged and there are not a lot of smart, intelligent people. 

Is anybody working on that?

Mr. HANES. I do not know that anybody is really extensively working on that; no. For instance, we are still at war with Germany, and we cannot bring Germans in here. 

Mr. VORYS. I do not want to bring them all over here. 

Mr. HANES. I think you will have to accept a certain number of them as part of our responsibility if we insist on other nations doing it. I think you are right. We probably should.

Mr. VORYS. I was thinking about whether or not there are areas in the world where there can be some pioneering done where they do not come in and knock some local fellow out of a job. 

Mr. CHATHAM. It would knock out a black man in Africa just the same as it would one of your pottery workers.

Mr. VORYS. If the African is not making shoes or farming as a 

European would farm, I do not think so. 

Chairman KEE. I have wondered if it would not be a good idea to bring in some of the refugees, for instance, Latvians and Lithuanians and other peoples from along the Baltic coast who are used to northern farming and locating them in Alaska in some of the fertile regions there.

Mr. VORYS. I have wondered about that one for years, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. There are vast quantities of land and timber in 

Alaska, and many areas with fertile soil. 

Mr. VORYS. They would know how to live there. 

Chairman KEE. They know how to live and farm in that sort of climate.

Mr. VORYS. I think the trouble has been, though, when we bring them into the United States and we say, "Now you are supposed to go to Alaska," they find out about the Great White Way or something and they leave their farms. That is what has been happening in 

Maryland and Virginia. They leave the farms, come in town, and get jobs that interfere with our own employment. 

Mr. RICHARDS. You said something about our being at war with 

Germany and they cannot come here. I believe we have a quota for them.

Mr. HANES. They must get a loyalty certificate before they can take out citizenship papers.

Mr. RICHARDS. I was under the impression that as long as we are at war with a nation, and we are technically at war with Germany, that the quotas would be suspended. I have found out they are not suspended. If that is the case, the quota could be increased insofar as the United States is concerned. Whether or not that would be a wise thing to do, I do not know. It might be.

Mr. VORYS. I do not think you solve anything by increasing the immigration into the United States to the extent that you destroy the balance here which has made us so prosperous. On the other hand, there is a geographer I know at home who says there are some underpopulated areas left in the world. I think the British are making certain studies of those, but they cannot be exploited on the old-fashioned colonial basis. What must happen is that you encourage these hardworking people from Italy, Germany, and I think from Britain—I think they are overpopulated there also-to get out and start the way their ancestors did in this country. 

Mr. RICHARDS. They could have something like a placement bureau in Germany and then consider taking part of these funds and helping to solve the problem by getting rid of some of the excess population. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. May I get into this cross-fire?

Mr. VORYS. This is anybody's game. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I had quite a few conversations in Italy on a similar subject. You find in the Belgium Congo, in Kenya, and in some of the 

French possessions underpopulated areas where you have great potential wealth similar to the position of the United States in the eighties when we were opening up the West. 

Now the Germans and the Italians make good colonizers, and their problem will never be solved until you solve their overpopulation problem.

Yet the Belgians and the English and the French, who do not have a similar population problem and have these underdeveloped areas, will not let these other people in and they are not sending their own people over there. I have always felt that possibly we could work out some arrangement where they would allow these excess populations of the Germans and the Italians to come into these underpopulated areas of the world where they could develop these areas for the benefit of the nations who own them now. One of the most intelligent men I spoke to in Italy felt you would never actually solve the problem of Germany and Italy, never, until you solve the problem of overpopulation. I think, Mr. Vorys, you have put your finger on a very, very important point right there.

Chairman KEE. Do you want this discussion among ourselves on the record? With no objection, it will remain in the record. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Mr. Hanes, I understood you to say that agriculturally the western zone is now producing about 50 percent of its needs. 

Mr. HANES. It is about 60 percent or 55 percent. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Now you feel that might be increased to 65 percent. 

Mr. HANES. Yes. That is a very optimistic figure.

Mr. RICHARDS. What is the commercial fertilizer situation in Germany now?

Mr. HANES. They could use much more fertilizer than they do. 

That is one of the ways we do suggest they increase their production, by using more fertilizer. They use animal fertilizer quite a lot now, but they do not use sufficient manufactured fertilizer. 

Mr. RICHARDS. We had testimony last year that there was a commercial fertilizer shortage in Germany. What is the situation now?

Mr. HANES. I do not think there is any shortage now. One or two of the manufacturers want to export some. 

Mr. RICHARDS. That is not the problem now

Mr. HANES. That is right. 

? Mr. RICHARDS. The trouble is that our zone is not naturally a bread basket?

Mr. HANES. It never has been. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Commercial fertilizer is not the total answer?

Mr. HANES. That is right. They have a lot of swamplands in Germany, particularly western Germany, which could be used if they had modern equipment to reclaim it. They have lots of meadowlands which could be farmed productively. 

Mr. VORYS. Will the gentleman yield on that? 

Mr. RICHARDS. Yes.

Mr. VORYS. When we were there in the fall of 1947, we were impressed by these so-called farms that included strips about as wide as this room, and we found that by inheritance a farmer would own one here, one 3 miles in one direction, and another 2 miles in another direction.

Mr. HANES. He would spend half his time going from one place to the other?

Mr. VORYS. That is right. The Germans told us that reform in their land tenure would do a great deal to increase their agricultural productivity. Is there anything being done on that?

Mr. HANES. We have tried, but it is difficult to get the job done. quickly. You see, under this old Napoleonic code, a man dies and

the land is split up among all his children. They die and it is split up again. Nobody will sell his land. They live in these little villages and go to these little strips of land all around. They are so small that they cannot use machinery on them. They do it all by hand. 

They drive an oxcart from one tract to another. You know the speed they have with oxcarts. Two things have been tried, first to break up the large estates into smaller farm plots, and the other thing is to consolidate a lot of these smaller plots and make larger plots out of them. However, to get four or five of these Germans to swap their land for another piece, it is difficult to get them to do it without a civil war. 

Mr. VORYS. I read last night in this week's Saturday Evening Post an article by a man named Hauser, on the Marshall plan. He made a good bit of fun about the fact that Mr. Hoffman and his associates were trying to get Europeans to mend their ways and pattern them after some of the things that had been successful here, and his article was to the effect that they are not going to do it and we might as well quit trying. And if Europe cannot survive unless they get to operating better, then that is a very sad recommendation. 

I wonder whether you read the article or what you think of that general thought.

Mr. HANES. It goes along very well with the experience our people have had in Germany in trying to get something done there to change this whole land situation.

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Hanes' statement today is to me most significant. 

You will note this remarkable recovery in the areas where we have been in the position to apply the most pressure, if you please, to have them do as many things as possible to free themselves from some ancient ideas that were strangling them. It seems to me that there is a little lesson in this.

Mr. RIBICOFF. Historically and philosophically, the Germans have been used to being told; whereas the French and the English are great individualists. Those are the great problems. Then you have a people who have been defeated. In Germany, I talked to many Americans at different levels, in the Army and elsewhere. They said that where the American position broke down and was the worst was where you took away controls and gave the German complete freedom. The

German did not know what to do with freedom because all his life he had been used to the proposition of living as someone else directed and he was lost when he did not have someone to tell him what to do. 

Chairman KEE. Are there any other questions? 

Mr. JAVITS. I think, Mr. Hanes, you have made a most excellent presentation. I mainly wanted to learn from you something about the fundamental policy in Germany. You have a statement here which says the Germans are heavily impressed with the idea of cartels. 

Mr. HANES. The German businessmen; yes, sir. 

Mr. JAVITS. At the same time you say that Germany is the crux of European production, in terms of the economy. How are the two statements consistent, unless it is a question of degree. In spite of the fact that they are cartel-minded and non-competitive-minded and operate that way, they still do it much less so than do the Belgians and the French and the British.

Mr. HANES. What I was speaking of there in one case was a small segment of the German population, the barons who run these cartels, as opposed to the smaller-business men and the laboring men who think as we do, that they ought to be broken up. 

Presently, we have a General Counsel of the High Commissioner who has brought a group of people over there from the SEC and other Government agencies and they are going to attack these cartels and actually break them up. 

Mr. JAVITS. The cartels still exist?

Mr. HANES. Yes. 

Mr. JAVITS. As a corollary to that will you tell us what you have found in the way of recurrence in important places in banking and industry of Nazi Party members or men who had high places under the Nazis, such as top men in these companies under the Nazis. 

Mr. HANES. I think most of the top Nazis have been liquidated or confined in prisons. These people had to be denazified before they were cleared to do anything at all. There is no question about it, if you lived in Germany and I have checked into this thing rather carefully during the Hitler regime, if you had a standing in business or politics or had a public job of any sort, there was a good deal of pressure to belong to the Nazi Party. As I say, many of these men yielded to this pressure. Otherwise they might be out of business or in a concentration camp. They went along in a mild sort of way and 

I do not doubt but what many of us would have been among that number had we lived in Germany, although we would not have been waving the flag and trying strenuously to put forth the National Socialist Party view. I have no doubt but what many people in high places were members of the Nazi Party.

Mr. JAVITS. In view of what the Nazi Party did, I do not think you would say, Mr. Hanes, that Americans, by and large, would just go along and chime in because they had to. I believe Americans, with all due deference, would have found ways for making their hostility and their opposition felt. After all, let us not be too bland about what these people did. They killed 10,000,000 Europeans and in conflict probably 10,000,000 others.

Mr. HANES. They did a horrible thing, there is no question about it. 

Mr. JAVITS. I just call to your attention that fact in connection with the statement that we might have done the same thing. 

Mr. CHATHAM. I think if you wanted to stay in business you had to join the party and contribute. I know some Germans who hated it, but they went along.

Mr. JAVITS. The danger is that the very same Germans, just as supine, may do the same thing tomorrow, using their power and prestige to forward it.

Mr. HANES. That is the difficulty. 

Chairman KEE. Is there anything further, gentlemen? If not, I want to associate myself with Mr. Richards as well as with other members, in their remarks in connection with the character of the men we have sent over to Europe as representatives of the United States Government in carrying forward this gigantic task we have assumed. 

During this hearing we have had before us the chiefs of missions sent by our Government to various countries and I can say that without exception they have all been men of very high character and qualifica-

tions. I have been very deeply impressed with their abilities and capabilities and with the manner in which they have performed and are performing the duties assigned to them in carrying forward this great work we are doing in Europe. I think Mr. Hanes is a very fine representative of the class of men we have sent over there. 

Mr. HANES. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. That is very kind. I appreciate being here. I appreciate your kindness, gentlemen, and your hospitality. Thank you very much.

Chairman KEE. I want to announce that tomorrow we will have as our first witness Gen. William J. Donovan of the American Committee on a United Europe. Tomorrow afternoon, if we meet, we will have Mr. Barry Bingham, Chief of the ECA Mission in

France and if we get through with him in time, we will follow with Mr. Boris Shiskin, Chief of the Labor Division of the Office of the 

Special Representative in Paris. 

We will meet again at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning. (Whereupon, at 4: 25 p. m., the committee adjourned, to reconvene at 10 a. m. Friday, March 3, 1950).

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED FRIDAY, MARCH 3, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

The committee met, pursuant to call, at 10:40 a. m., in the Foreign

(chairman) presiding.

We are continuing this morning our hearings upon H. R. 7378. 

We have before us Gen. William J. Donovan, Chairman of the 

American Committee on United Europe.

We are very glad indeed, General, to have you appear before the committee upon this weighty question we have now under consideration. If you have a written statement, you may read it or present it in any manner you wish.

STATEMENT OF GEN. WILLIAM J. DONOVAN, AMERICAN COMMITTEE ON UNITED EUROPE 

General DONOVAN. There has been handed to the members of your committee a green-covered pamphlet. This pamphlet contains statements made by 49 statesmen of Europe, many of them present or former prime ministers and foreign ministers. These statements are replies to a letter I sent on December 20, 1949, as chairman of the American Committee on United Europe, to each of 55 statesmen of Europe. I think it might help if I read parts of that letter, in which I ask certain questions that I think the members of the committee themselves might have asked. That letter is found at page 5 of the pamphlet. I should say that the purpose of the American committee itself is found at page 1 of the pamphlet. 

In that letter, as you see there, I say:

Since the Council of Europe met at Strasbourg, events having to do with the movements toward unity and integration in Europe have presented a confusing picture to Americans. In particular, the action of the Committee of Ministers on the proposals of the European Consultative Assembly, and reports that some members of the Council are reluctant to proceed along the lines suggested by the Assembly, have given rise in America to doubt and uncertainty about the future of the Council of Europe and of other methods of approach toward unity and integration. 

Then I say:

I have had occasion to note the reason for this uncertainty, because I watched the first session of the European Consultative Assembly in Strasbourg- 245

and I think I ought to say here that in the opinion of those of us in attendance there, there would have been no Strasbourg if there had been no ECA- I was impressed with the directness of its approach and particularly by its expressed aim-the creation of a European political authority with limited func tions but real powers.

On my last visit to Europe, I thought there had been little progress in this direction and I noted that individual members of the Assembly and also the press were inclined to fix responsibility upon the Committee of Ministers. 

The directors of the American Committee on United Europe have asked me to obtain your advice, and through your good offices the advice of other authoritative sources in Europe, about the situation I have described. 

Are there immediate prospects of the Council of Europe achieving tangible results in the direction of economic integration and political unity? 

If there are differences among the members of the Committee of Ministers which suggest that some are less prepared than others to make any rapid progress toward full European unity, what in your opinion can, or should, be done?

Then I pointed out as you will see in the letter, that we were going to enter into the debate on future Marshall plan appropriations, and that I asked particularly that the Secretary General of the European movement, which had been the active force in developing government action, I asked the Secretary General if he would personally go to these ministers, as many as possible, and by direct approach obtain a reply to the letter that I had written. 

On page 9, you will see the report that Mr. Retinger, who is a Pole, and who is Secretary General of the European movement, sent to me on February 10.

He said that "the activities of the European movement have been followed attentively by our friends beyond the Atlantic." He then named the most important meetings- The Hague in May of 1948, the Council or Congress of Europe; the International 

Council, Brussels, February 1949; the Economic Conference, Westminster, April 

1949; the European Conference of Culture, Lausanne, December 1949.

The swift action obtained from the government, mainly as a result of the movement's activities has been amply publicized in America. 

The creation of the Council of Europe, thanks to the initiative of the five Governments of Belgium, France, Great Britain, Luxemburg, and the Netherlands and the rapid adherence of the Governments of Denmark, Eire, Italy, Norway, and Sweden has been accomplished exactly 1 year after the meeting at the Hague. In less than 2 years the work toward European Union has passed from a completely private plan to the phase of official action. 

Further on, he said:

There are many who think that the Committee of Ministers has not shown the same willingness as the Assembly, that it has unduly protracted the study of experts, and has not taken any of its superior's initiative; some even think that the members of this committee have not, to the same degree, the will. to surmount the obstacles.

American public opinion puts before us today two very simple questions: what are, during the year 1950, the chances for real progress toward European unity, and how will the barriers which may oppose this march toward unity be surmounted?

He then describes how he went about this and I think from the human standpoint it may be important for you to see the seriousness. of the way he did it.

For 25 days, with my two main coworkers, George Rebattet and Dunstan Curtis, I have visited 12 countries, met with forty some men among the most distinguished members of European public life and I have not met with one refusal; all have agreed to answer my question and to make plain their hopeful

1 desire to see European unity achieved. Some seem of a very general nature, in some cases even very inaccurate to a noninformed observer. Upon consideration, one always finds in them a step forward in relation to the traditional position of the country in question, always a certainty, always a hope. Other statements are accurate, detailed; they sketch a solution to the problems inherent in the gradual realization of a permanent association among the European nations, because it has to be understood that it is not only a question of just any sort of alliance among the governments of Europe. 

If I may express my opinion, I would say that these statements taken as a whole are clear evidence to the fact that European unity is now the ultimate goal of European politics. 

If I may express my hope, I would wish to say that I hope that the men of

Europe give to the march toward unity the more lucid part of their time, the best of their intelligence, the strongest part of their will, and that they do not let themselves be dominated by small problems. 

Next, I would like to point out here what Mr. Spaak, who is President of the Consultative Assembly, had to say in his statement, because he epitomizes the vital force that exists, in that conference at Strasbourg. In the interests of saving time, I did some paraphrasing on this: In my letter, I said:

Since the Council of Europe met at Strasbourg, events having to do with the movements toward unity and integration in Europe have presented a confusing picture to Americans. In particular, the action of the Committee of 

Ministers on the proposals of the European Consultative Assembly, and reports that some members of the Council are reluctant to proceed along the lines suggested by the Assembly, have given rise in America to doubt and uncertainty about the future of the Council of Europe and of other methods of approach toward unity and integration. 

Are there immediate prospects of the Council of Europe achieving tangible results in the direction of economic integration and political unity? 

If there are differences among the members of the Committee of Ministers which suggest that some are less prepared than others to make rapid progress toward full European unity, what in your opinion can, or should, be done? 

Now I paraphrase the reply in the form of a letter to me from Mr. 

Spaak and which is included in this pamphlet at page 20: 

There is no doubt- 

Spaak saidthat the first session of the Consultative Assembly at Strasbourg was a successcertainly not a perfect success, but an important step in the right direction. 

The proofs of this success are, in my opinion: The European spirit shown by many of the delegates; the active realism which presided over the debates and the possibility of creating soon a political European organ of limited function but real power. 

For a first attempt- 

Spaak saysthis was truly not too bad, and we left Strasbourg confident and optimistic Recent months have not been so encouraging and particularly the position taken by the Committee of Ministers. But the permanent Committee elected by the 

Assembly has immediately reacted-and has reacted unanimously-without distinction of nationality or of party. 

The Assembly has thus defined at the same time its rights and its willingness to use them. It has done so in correct and energetic terms and I am convinced that its point of view will triumph.

Here is what Spaak outlines, and we have put that on as a separate page. That is on page 11. It is what he calls the program ahead: 

1. The integration of western Germany into the Council of Europe. 

2. The accomplishment of free convertibility of European currencies and a liberation of European trade.

3. The provision of a common minimum of legislation absolutely essential for the pursuit of the work. 

4. Practical steps which will permit a greater understanding between all the peoples of Europe. 

5. Appropriate means to transform the Council of Europe into a real political authority.

I have undertaken to put before you this evidence of western Europe's progress toward political union because, as you well know, western Europe is the most powerful political and economic ally that the United States could have. In two wars it has been our outer bastion.

Separately, each of these countries could not resist Russia, militarily and subversively. 

Political as well as economic union would give western Europe new strength and resources. It has today about 250,000,000 skilled and intelligent people; in combination with the United States, that means some 400,000,000 people.

Mr. Chairman, America has suffered a serious defeat to the Soviet 

Union in the conquest of China. Russia having taken over China has clearly indicated her intention to extend that conquest to Indochina, the Philippines, Siam, Malaya, Indonesia, and Burma. Russia is now the dominant power in Asia, and a further victory would make the Soviets dictators in Asia. To prevent this, we need the western bastion in order to secure our flank for anything we may wish to do in Asia. We must secure our flank in the west while we take the initiative in the east, which I think we ought to take. 

As I said to you privately, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me our difficulty is that we do not look at all these theaters of operations as a seamless garment. We do not seem to comprehend that what happens in one theater has its repercussions and effect in every other theater. 

The defeat of western Europe together with the loss of our positions in Asia could well mean the loss of the war to us without a shot having been fired. Therefore, I believe we have a stake in western Europe, one that we must not risk losing, because we must wage and win the war in which we already find ourselves. That war is nonetheless dangerous, though it is not a shooting war. In many ways it may be more dangerous because it is a subversive war. 

That is why I believe in the necessity of a united Europe and why I think that Congress should insist on unity for the security of the countries there concerned, as well as for our own. 

Chairman KEE. Does that conclude your statement, General? 

General DONOVAN. Yes, sir. 

Chairman KEE. We thank you very much for your statement so far as you have gone, but I fear you will not escape the task of going further.

General DONOVAN. Since I cannot escape, Mr. Chairman, I will have to stand fast.

Chairman KEE. We are going into the question period under the 

5-minute rule for the first round of questions. 

Mr. Gordon, have you any questions?

Mr. GORDON. I am glad to see the general before us today and giving us the latest information on the European developments. 

At this time, I will pass up my questions.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Vorys-

249: 

Mr. VORYS. General, in a way you are our most important witness. 

It was in this room that the opening in your pamphlet was drafted: 

It is further declared to be the policy of the people of the United States to encourage the unification of Europe. 

General DONOVAN. That is our motto. 

Mr. VORYS. Like the statement you quoted, ours too is short and general. A number of us think it might be well to make it more specific this year to indicate the thought of this committee, the Congress, and the people. 

General DONOVAN. Yes, sir. 

Mr. VORYS. Have you given any thought to any form of amendment to the ECA Act that would carry out our thought? I think the policy of the United States is more than to encourage the unification of Europe. I think Europe is a gone gosling without it, and everything else is rat-hole money without it. If that is so, we better say it. We better attach some conditions to our aid, one condition being the unification of Europe along the lines Mr. Spaak outlines in the Program 

Ahead. Have you given any thought to that? 

General DONOVAN. That would be a natural thing, Congressman, but I myself in dealing with it right at this point, where I have seen in operation the Consultative Assembly, and where I as well saw before my own eyes the effort made to establish a Socialist bloc in the Assembly defeated, and unity sought to be attained by a very simple device of having the members of that Assembly sit there, not as members of a political party or as particular nationalities, but as Europeans, by the simple device of having them sit alphabetically, have been more than favorably impressed. 

Now that very simple thing had a great effect upon the operation of that assembly, the alphabetical seating arrangement. Particularly with a fellow like Spaak at the head of it, instead of imposing "or else" conditions, I would rather see what they are going to do at Strasbourg before I would want to say to them "If you do not do this, we are going to withdraw our support," because I think, Mr. Vorys, you will agree that any such arrangement there is not going to be worth anything unless it comes out of the will, rather than by outside compulsion on the part of these people. If the people do not adopt it because they want to do it, I do not think it is worth anything to us. 

Mr. VORYS. On the other hand we have made the mistake twice in wars that we aked for no commitments while our help was needed. 

General DONOVAN. That is probably the case in wars because the way we get in, we get in under the gun and we have to shoot rather than to write. That seems to be the trouble. I think, too, the reason we did not get commitments in those wars is because in general we, as a people, thought that we were conferring a favor by going to help the Europeans, where to me, and I am sure to you, we saw it was in our own interest to do it. 

Mr. VORYS. At the same time you opened your statement by saying if there had been no Marshall plan there would be no Strasbourg. 

General DONOVAN. I agree. That is right. 

Mr. VORYS. I think it is quite clear from the testimony of other witnesses that if there were no Marshall plan to continue, that all attempts at unification might fail.

General DONOVAN. I agree.

Mr. VORYS. However, the Marshall plan has but 2 years to go.

Mr. VORYS. We need some sort of evidence of action in line with the principles laid down in the Marshall plan and agreed to, 2 years ago, and a lot more than we have had yet, before we will go ahead. Telling you what Congress is going to require-and the Congress requires something is to require it. Now, how do we state that? 

General DONOVAN. I think that is right. For example, with relation to the convertibility of funds and so on which was referred to in Mr. Hoffman's speech in November, and which was agreed to by the 

British particularly and the others, I think it was in December, those terms must be fulfilled. Now that is a little different, do you not think? It is one thing to impose the conditions. It is one thing to wait and see what one does and then if you are not satisfied say "All right, we are through."

My only suggestion is to let us look to see how this proposal, this program, what happens to this proposal in Strasbourg. Then to see what we will do. But I do not know that we can, in anticipation of that, tell them what they have to do or else we will not do anything. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield, have you any questions?

Mr. MANSFIELD. General Donovan, we are delighted to have you before the committee this morning. As far as the Union of Western 

Europe is concerned this committee is wholeheartedly behind your stand and your committee's stand on this particular matter. However, I would like to talk about another and perhaps a more practical aspect of the ECA program, having to do with a recent visit which you made to Hong Kong in behalf of an American company, registered with the Civil Aeronautics Board and having to do with some 71 planes which a British court recently awarded to the Communist government of China.

Now Britain, of course, is a recipient under the ECA program, and I suppose that with these planes in time will have to go parts. 

I would assume that on the basis of this transfer through court action that very likely these replacements would have to come through the 

British colony of Hong Kong. 

I wish you would give the committee the benefit of your observations on this particular matter because I think it is germane to the question we are discussing this morning. 

General DONOVAN. I do not want to launch into something that would be long; yet it is very difficult to condense a report of a fight that has been going on for 2 or 3 months. When I was asked to come into the case the following things had already happened. These seventy-some-odd planes that you referred to had already been abandoned by defecting employees. These defecting former employees tried to claim these planes when landed in Hong Kong on British territory. They had quit their occupation with these two companies and then sought to seize the planes. An injunction was obtained in the Hong Kong courts by the Chinese against their interference with these planes. Then it was that an American company, owning an air line out there, purchased these planes that would otherwise go into the hands of the Communists. They sought to purchase those planes for the enlargement and amplification of their own line. Accordingly they entered into a contract which ultimately resulted in

99 

The the transfer of title of these planes to the American company, a Delaware corporation. This was in December. When that occurred the 

CAC sent out its representatives to register the planes in American registration. That was accomplished. They then sought to take possession of the planes upon that registration. That was denied them. 

Before getting that injunction, the solicitors for the Chinese companies had gone to the Attorney General of the Colony of Hong Kong and had said to him "We do not see how the courts can give us any effective remedy. We think this ought to be done by executive action of the Foreign Office of the British Government." But the Attorney 

General said to them "No, what you ought to do is to go under the aegis of the court and get our order and then we will support you. 

They did that. That was before my firm was ever in the case. solicitors then went back to the Attorney General, who said. "This is sub judice now. You must await the court's decision." Then the 

American company sought to intervene in the case. It asked for a contempt proceeding against these defecting employees who were admitted to the airport, who in violation of the injunction had access to the hangars in which the planes were held which access was denied to the managers and employees of the American company. Our intervention was denied by the court. Because we saw these planes becoming a wasted asset we started an action to get them into the hands of a receiver. As a result of that proceeding the decision was made by the court that these men, these Communists, with no title to nor possession of the planes, with no recital of how they got that possession unlawfully and against the injunction issued by the judge who presided in this case, and that in addition, there had now been recognition of the Chinese Government, and under the terms of sovereign immunity, the judge had no authority to deal with it. 

That having happened, which put us back to what we said would happen, we then.called upon the British Government to deliver the planes to us or else we could assume no other conclusion but that they were more afraid of the Communists than they were of us and that is why these things were delivered. I should say to you, Mr. Mansfield, that I think that action was a very foolish action on the part of the British, and even more than foolish, tragic, because it naturally lowered the prestige or further lowered the prestige of America in that area, and also affected its own prestige because each day we were there, there would come the blast from the Peking radio saying to Britain, in effect this: "Well, all right, Mr. Britain, you transfer those planes to the Americans and we will take it out of your hide in the goods you have stored in Shanghai and Canton."

Now, the State Department is still attempting to get the British Government to turn those planes over to the American company. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. The State Department has been diligent in its efforts to protect the American company in this matter which has been decided by the Hong Kong courts.

General DONOVAN. Yes, it has. It has on each occasion, Mr. Mansfield. It has on each occasion when we have asked them, gone to either the Governor General in the colony at Hong Kong or to its representative in Washington, gone with us, but it still appears that the British do not think we are serious about it. The State Department has done everything suggested but it has not resulted in any action.

Committee of the Consultative Assembly-I was there in Decemberthat immediately the Economic Committee said, "Oh, no, we are not going to be kept out of this. They went to the respective governments, broke down the opposition, got their money, and had the meetings independently of the Council of Ministers.

British split their vote three ways before they were through.

General DONOVAN. Exactly.

The request is for 3.1 billion dollars during the next fiscal year. For example, 2.5 billion dollars might be sufficient if the program of integration were stepped up. 

I could not answer 

General DONOVAN. I could not answer that. that one way or the other. I have been out of the country up to 10 days ago and have been in another part of the world and could not answer your question.

Mr. MERROW. Certainly progress toward greater integration would make Europe much more self-sufficient. 

General DONOVAN. Certainly. The way we have to judge these people is not so much by the length of the step they take but by the direction in which they go. That is the important thing from our standpoint, and I can see where this committee or any other committee, if they saw that direction go left or whatever other way that was inconsistent with an integrated Europe, that aid could be stopped right at that moment. But as long as the direction is toward the target, I think you have to stick with them awhile. 

Mr. MERROW. May I ask you to expand on the statement you made toward the end of your testimony. You said that in your opinion we ought to take the initiative in Asia. I am wondering if you mean with respect to Indochina. What do you have in mind? 

General DONOVAN. I mean this: You know it is only a truism to say that the way you look at a thing determines the way you deal with it. If you look at the problem from the standpoint of Far East and southeast Asia as cubical theaters arising during the war because of service or other jealousies, you make a big mistake. But if you look at that area and conceive of it as one strategic entity, then the problem of dealing with it is easier, because all of these various parts fall into their position. Therefore it should be dealt with as a whole. One of

our great difficulties as a people is that we do one thing as an isolated thing without considering its relation to that which must be done, or that which has already been done. We have been setting up separate citadels, in other words, instead of a system.

Mr. MERROW. I agree fully with the general's statement. 

General DONOVAN. I am talking about it specifically there now with relation to Asia. You have to fit each thing into what you want to do there, whether it is Indochina or wherever you wish to speak of. 

Mr. MERROW. My point is, Will it not cost us money to keep the Bon 

Dai regime in power or make it successful?

General DONOVAN. You must measure all of these things by their ultimate result and the effect upon us. What do we want to do? Do we want to lose entirely all of southeast Asia? If we do, let's not increase a cent.

For what it is worth, my own view is, Mr. Congressman, that we are in a war, and I say let's win the war we are in. It will be a lot cheaper in the end than if we permit it to degenerate into a shooting war. Because the person who wins the subversive war, upon whichever side it may be, has the edge if it comes to a shooting war. 

It may prevent a shooting war altogether. Certainly you can fight this kind of a war much more cheaply than a shooting war. 

Now what is the problem of Indochina? I may speak rather emphatically because during World War II, I had to do with Indochina and Burma and Siam and China proper. I saw what it meant in the investment in funds to fight there. You see, in Indochina, the fight is a guerrilla fight. You go along the roads of Indochina and you can see what a disadvantage orthodox forces have, because the roads are built up high. You will see these troops, whether it is the Foreign 

Legion or whatever, moving along that road with heavy weapons. 

They are slaves to the road. These guerrilla forces, operating from the ditches or from woods, find them an easy target against the sky line.

To deal with the last you must set up counterguerrillas, and in all of those places, because they need it. To my mind Indonesia is the master key for us right now, because Indonesia is the place where we have had, at least for a year and a half, a consistent and definite policy. 

You have a young nation that wants help and advice. But they need schools for their police and for their guerrilla training. That is not going to be a matter of the movement of troops into there by Russia, it is going to be capitalizing on the fifth columns they have there. 

Look at Siam. Sixteen million people. Four million Chinese.

That does not mean all the Chinese are going to be with Russia, but it means a very good recruiting ground from which they can develop their fifth column. 

Mr. MERROW. Thank you.

1 did not seem to get to the Netherlands during a very important period and that delay or withdrawal of assistance may have had its part in forming a free republic of Indonesia.
