Under this law, he has the power to proceed summarily and effectively to carry out the provisions of the law laid down by Congress. That does not mean to evade or avoid the law, but to apply it. 

General DONOVAN. No; I have not taken it up with Mr. Hoffman. 

As I told you, I do not want to mix up my position here as a citizen with my job as a lawyer. 

Mr. VORYS. I appreciate your embarrassment.

General DONOVAN. However, at the same time I have already told you the terms I used to the Foreign Office, to our State Department, and to the Governor at Hong Kong. 

Now here I would be glad to have not associate counsel, but associate advisers, as evidenced by the look you fellows have taken at this thing, and to point out to the British for their own good, that they better do something to recover the prestige that both they and we have lost by their action in this particular. That is what I would like to see. 

Mr. VORYS. I feel quite sure that in view of the action the Secretary of State has taken there can be no conflict between his views and those of the ECA Administrator. 

Regarding your statement to the effect that we ought to let the peoples of the world know we are standing by them, I want to remind you there was drafted and placed into the Mutual Defense Act, a statement by the Congress that we are standing by the peoples of the Far East in their mutual efforts. 

General DONOVAN. I think you know better than I, because of your experience there, that that statute will not get very far with the boys in Siam or in Indonesia, so that we have to do something more than that to let them know.

Mr. VORYS. The fact that it has not been implemented in any way is not a matter that Congress can pass upon at this time. 

I have one other question: Which would be better, as far as the 

Marshall plan is concerned, to reduce the aid or to make a substantial part of it available only to a united Europe through, for instance, a European payments union?

General DONOVAN. If I were to suggest anything it would be only speculation and I think that question could be better answered from your standpoint by talking with the people who are there on the ground.

Mr. VORYS. My point is, you see, that one thing a free country has a right to do is to say we are going to make aid available to a united group rather than to individual members of the group. In that way we are not applying any coercion; we are merely making something available on terms that are satisfactory to us. 

General DONOVAN. But terms mean an awful lot to people who are in a hole. I think that if it would do good, I would not hesitate to say, "You fellows better come across here or we are going to cut this off," but I do not think it would do good; I think it would do harm. 

Therefore, I have to answer you that way. Now the particular way in which you frame this, to let them know how you feel about it, and

your uncertainty and displeasure, I think that is a perfectly proper thing to do. But I would give these fellows a chance, in the assembly, to see what they are going to be able to do, and then you always have the right anyway to act preemptorily if they do not do what you want them to. That is all, I think, Mr. Vorys.

Mr. VORYS. I do not know whether I have made myself clear. We are not threatening anybody with anything. Suppose the law were framed in this way: We are not threatening anybody with anything; we are simply making certain funds available solely to a united organization? 

General DONOVAN. But you are saying, "We have a delayed bomb, here, and I think you have such a bomb without talking about it and without using it as a weapon of intimidation." That is all that strikes me.

Now I want to make myself clear on this: I think that we, in the control of funds, ought to be absolutely relentless in cutting out aid or help or anything else to those people who are not on the level with us. I think that we ought to make that very clear, but I do not think it is a good thing, either directly or indirectly, to say, "You are going to have a united Europe or else we are going to cut out our help." 

You have to deal with the fact, what are you doing-let us look at each thing they are doing to see if it is aimed on the target that all of us want to see hit.

That is all, I think, Mr. Vorys, and I think in the long run it will be more effective.

Mr. VORYS. If you had the job of sitting here for 3 years and had enacted legislation in response to the promises and commitments from nations abroad, you might not feel as shocked at making further aid dependent upon performance of those promises and commitments. 

General DONOVAN. That would not shock me one bit, Congressman, but I am only thinking of what we can get done next week or next month.

The thing I am impressed with is to go around and see departments back here where there is not the sense of urgency or desire for getting this stuff done and getting it done together. 

Mr. VORYS. We are not talking about next week or next month, literally, we are talking about next year. There is sufficient money to carry ERP through until June, and so forth. What we are discussing is the third year, and possibly the fourth year of the Marshall plan, which has in it the requirement that from the start, all nations entered bilateral and multilateral agreements that continuity of assistance depends upon continuity of cooperation and that unification is part of that cooperation. 

General DONOVAN. As you were speaking there, Congressman, I was thinking, suppose I knew enough to be a correspondent of a British paper and I was sitting in this room, now. I think the kind of report, if I could write sufficiently vividly, that I would send back on what you said, to them it would be a lot more effective than anything you would write into a statute that no one would be reading. 

Mr. VORYS. Let me say one other thing: There was a member of

Parliament over here last year who told some of us "If you do not put 'or else' into your legislation when it comes to unification, you will be derelict in your duty to yourselves and to the future of Europe."

General DONOVAN. I would retain him over there, Congressman, to tell them that. 

Mr. VORYS. That is all. 

Mr. RICHARDS. I am sorry, I missed a portion of your statement. 

I will read it with great interest and care. I wanted to ask a question along the lines of Mr. Vorys' question: As Mr. Vorys said, we have been sitting here for 2 or 3 years and suggesting things. Only the other day we heard Mr. Hoffman say there was not the slightest chance of permanent economic recovery in Europe unless you have economic unification. 

General DONOVAN. Yes. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Now this program is supposed to end in 1952. Now, according to what Mr. Hoffman says, if we do not accomplish any more in that field than we have already accomplished, the chances are that this money of the taxpayers of America, that should be used to balance this budget, maybe, would be poured into a rat hole unless we have more economic unification there. 

Now we may just continue to suggest, or we may make our suggestions effective by being very firm about-in other words say certain things must be done before additional American funds can become available. 

General DONOVAN. I would not care how far we would go. What you are talking about, Mr. Congressman, I agree with. We have a right to do that. However, the whole question is not merely a matter of the words we use; it is a matter of our conduct. I think it is in our own interest, instead of saying, "Here is the rule we are going to put in. You are going to have unification, or else we are not going to give you funds."

Now, I just say that a rash thing would destroy the very thing you want to accomplish. 

Mr. RICHARDS. I understand, but suppose we said, "We are going to let you have so much funds. We will let you have $1,000,000,000 anyway, if you do not do this. But if you do follow our suggestions, we will let you have $2,000,000,000 or $3,000,000,000. 

General DONOVAN. I would say, first, with regard to the countries that are concerned now, if they have any wisdom at all or any intelligence system, they know what you gentlemen are saying here.

That is No. 1. No. 2 is a practical matter. It is a very interesting thing, in the study of the development of a new system of government, to go over and look at Strasbourg. If they see you gentlemen there taking a look, and if you make the same study that Mrs. Bolton made, they will know that you are there. Then if they are not acting in accordance with the way you think they should act, then you can deprive them of the funds.

I am only talking as a practical fellow on this, Congressman. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Yes. 

General DONOVAN. It is very possible they could say "All right" and then go through the motions, but there would be no lifeblood in it. 

Mr. RICHARDS. We would know by next year whether it was just shadow boxing. 

General DONOVAN. You know that without making a statement, and you can act. The only difference between what you are saying and

what I am saying is: Do not do the offensive thing, as long as you have the power, because, if you do the offensive thing, you are going to defeat what you want to accomplish. However, if they are not straight in what they are going to do, see whether they are straight or not and then act as you are justified in doing.

Mr. RICHARDS. We are appropriating a lot of money in this country for our farmers, for instance, and every dime of it is predicated on the idea that the farmer will do something to help himself; soil conservation and other things.

Mr. RICHARDS. If we cannot say that to a foreign government because of their keen sensibilities, I just do not get it. You say we will defeat our purpose. 

General DONOVAN. I say you will defeat your purpose if you say to them, "You unite or else." When you come to saying, "You unite or else," you are going further than holding over them a threat. You can say, "We want it shaped this way. We do not want a federation. 

We want something that would mean a government that is centralized." 

I just say it is nothing different from what we condemn Russia for doing. However, if we say, "If the way you handle convertibility of funds is not going to be conducive to building up economic integration-the very things Spaak is complaining of, himself; you are giving 

Spaak an instrument then to say, "What is going to happen? Some of these fellows will be over here and not like the way we are doing it and we are all through."

I just think, right at this moment, when every single thing that is done is exploited propagandawise by the Soviet Union, that we are doing the thing that hurts what we want to accomplish. 

Mr. RICHARDS. I am afraid these airplane people in the Pacific bought an international lawsuit, if you want the truth. 

General DONOVAN. You would be wrong about it if you said that. 

Mr. RICHARDS. I think the mistake of the United States with regard to the Pacific was that we were not more forceful in our position about the recognition of Communist China by Britain to start with. 

General DONOVAN. I go along with you in all of that. However, in all of the things that you say, if you feel that Britain is not doing right or France is not doing right, you can say, "We are through with you. We are not going to do this anymore." 

However, to stand up in the beginning and say, "Unless you unite, we are through with you," then you get something that is not worth the money you put into it. That is all I am saying. 

Chairman KEE. General, you say we would defeat our own purpose by doing that. I heartily agree with you that that is true. We are overlooking the purpose when we do that, because of the fact that our purpose is not just to give this money for no reason at all, but it is in preservation of our own national interest-our national security. 

General DONOVAN. That is what I am talking about. It is because

I think we have a stake that I am interested in this thing, Congressman. We need that outer bastion. An an American, I do not want to see it destroyed. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Thank you, General Donovan.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Lodge-

Mr. LODGE. General, I think you made a very good point there, because it occurs to me that, with some of these governments in Europe in such a state of delicate balance, we have to be extremely discreet as to how we operate and perhaps we have to recognize that the theory of open covenants, openly arrived at, has some very significant exceptions. 

With respect to the Hong Kong situation, I think Mr. Vorys has made a most vital contribution. I have it on excellent authority that the British asked us if we would help them to defend Hong Kong in the event that there was trouble, and that we gave them to understand that we would not.

Do you believe that that fact, if it is a fact, can be responsible in any way for the further fact that, while the State Department has made some representations, they have not yet raised this question of Hong Kong planes to the level of formal notes and have not hit the thing as hard as they could? In other words, do you suppose that they feel somewhat guilty about the recognition of Communist China by the British?

General DONOVAN. I am not enough of a psychiatrist to answer that one. I cannot tell what is in the minds of the gentlemen there. I can tell you this, as I have told you before, they have gone with us to the representatives of the British Government. They have supported what we have said.

Mr. LODGE. You are well satisfied with the support you have had from the State Department on this matter? 

General DONOVAN. I do not want to say I am not satisfied with the support. I think that the difficulty has been that the British are not quite sure that our people meant what they said. That is the difficulty. 

That is an entirely different thing. All I have urged is that they should be convinced that our Government meant what it said. 

Mr. LODGE. I was particularly glad, General, to have you stress the question of subversive warfare. That is a subject I have been harping on now for about 3 years. That is a twilight zone of action where the 

Communists have been particularly effective. You believe that we should be much more resourceful and imaginative in that entire field; do you not? 

General DONOVAN. What is needed, too, I think, is not alone the unification and coordination of orthodox methods of warfare, but also the coordination of those measures that we can use in waging and winning this kind of warfare. 

Mr. LODGE. I am delighted to hear you say that, General. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. I hope you did not mean what you said, about being dissatisfied with the efforts made by the State Department on this Hong 

Kong plane business. 

General DONOVAN. No; I said quite to the contrary. I said I was satisfied with what they did. They were meticulous in what they did. 

All I say, Congressman, is this: that I judge by the action of the 

British that they are not convinced in the State Department's sincerity, what it said, or they would not still be carrying on their stalling tactics. That is what I meant.

Mr. MANSFIELD. I think, for the record, it should be stated that the 

State Department has been very interested, and was interested in this

particular problem before you went to Hong Kong, and has exerted every possible effort to see that these planes did not fall into the hands of the Communist government, because they recognized just what a danger that implied.

I should also like to call to the committee's attention that another Marshall-plan country, Portugal, had been responsible for turning over some $2,000,000 worth of radar and other electrical equipment to the Communists from Macao, and on that particular occasion, also, we raised representations, but there was no court action whatsoever. 

This was unilateral action by the Portuguese Government. 

General DONOVAN. The Portuguese opened their warehouses at the insistence of the Communists and unloaded the contents of the warehouses into the barges furnished by the Communists, in spite of the protests we made in advance. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. That is all, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Ribicoff? 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I want to apologize for not being here to hear your testimony.

We have to realize that today we are constantly going from one dilemma to another in the whole foreign field. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Now, do you believe, actually, that we are going to be able to get out of Europe by .1952, the termination date of the 

Marshall plan?

General DONOVAN. I do not know anything about what we do with the Marshall plan, but we are not going to be out of Europe in 1952. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. In other words, we are not going to be out of Europe as long as we are the leaders of western civilization; is that correct? 

General DONOVAN. Yes. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. You mentioned that from a propaganda standpoint?

General DONOVAN. Yes. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Propaganda is important in two phases, from the 

European stage and also in informing the American people? 

General DONOVAN. That is right.

Mr. RIBICOFF. I think the American people are uninformed upon the realities in the world and the situations which face us today. 

General DONOVAN. That is right. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you think we would be better off as a nation by starting to tell the people of the United States that we are in Europe for a long time to stay, and when we get out of Europe it may be the beginning of our defeat, so let us recognize the realities of the world as it is on what faces us. 

General DONOVAN. I agree with you, Congressman, as a result of my own experience in trying simply as a corporal in civilian life—in talking to people and trying to explain out of our own knowledge what has happened. I think it is an essential thing for us to do. Your problems will be easier if they do understand. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. That is right.

Now we talk about integration. The Europeans know that our interests are inextricably tied up with their survival. They realize that. They do not want to go to Russia; they prefer staying with us. 

General DONOVAN. Yes; but you cannot make it quite as definite as that. There is a coming and going in this, and there is always uncer-

tainty. That uncertainty very often beclouds the knowledge they ought to have. I do not think they are any different than we are. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. No, because we are entering into these debates annually. We are taking it one year at a time, which may not be a smart policy, either-I mean, without having the long-range viewpoint. 

Let us say we want integration. We feel it is necessary. We know from our self-interest we are in Europe one way or the other. 

What methods will you propose for us to indicate our desire to have them integrate? We are making these sacrifices ourselves. We make them willingly, because they are mutually advantageous. How can we make Europe realize that they have to come along with us in this endeavor?

General DONOVAN. I think they can be made to understand, just as a result of this discussion on the part of you gentlemen, revealing your purpose and intention of integration. It ought to be the greatest impetus to have them get down to this as the first order of business. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. From the long-range viewpoint, can you see any long-range recovery of Europe unless we are in the picture, too? That is an integration of the free world, eventually? 

General DONOVAN. I think there are a good many steps to be taken before that happens. You could have an integration of Europe, which could work with the United States, that would be very effective. 

That is what I think is important, for us to accomplish. That would be a step to the ultimate of which you seek to accomplish, and it could be a very effective step. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Do you think it would help Europe to integrate faster if they realized that the United States recognizes the fact that eventually the United States must be part and parcel of an integrated world? 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Ribicoff, I beg your pardon for interrupting. 

Are you using "integration" and "unification" as synonymous terms? 

Mr. RIBICOFF. No; I am not. I am going from the narrow phase to the broader one, because I think it is important. I assume, when we speak of unification, it is just Europe by itself. However, eventually, if we want to make this world work, we will have to talk about the larger phase of it. I go along with the General that it will be a step at a time. I do not conceive this will be done tomorrow, the day after, or the year after next, but it certainly does not prevent our having an ultimate goal. When you look at western civilization, another 5, 10, or 15 years is a very short time. It is just a period in the span of civilization itself, but we certainly must have a goal and head toward a goal, if we ourselves hope to make it effective. 

I would like to get your viewpoint on that, General. 

General DONOVAN. It would seem to me that, like all of us, we have a mixture of motives. Certainly, if you are working on a united 

Europe, you work on a united Europe for the thing it can accomplish in itself.

For example, you and I would undoubtedly agree that we have to strengthen this bastion, on that flank, because the nearer Russia comes to us, the further we are away from her, and she would get nearer to us if we do not have this bastion. 

Also, some of us might be motivated by the fact that what we are doing is related by its accomplishment to what we may hope to see in the world order in a later day.

Mr. RIBICOFF. During my trip to Europe last year, I talked to the leading foreign statesmen, and with the exception of England, sensed that they also felt that, until the United States used its power-and it does not have to be on the surface, one way or another-that you will never have actual integration. 

It, therefore, becomes important how we are going to use it without destroying what we are trying to create. That is one of the dilemmas that face us as Congressmen, the welfare of Europe, ourselves, and the world.

General DONOVAN. It is important, in the meantime, to deal with the problem we all have, and see what will be done with that so that it will be of use in whichever way we go, whether we go into an integration with America, we who are in United Europe, or if we leave the United Europe integrated in and of itself, dealing with the United 

States by treaty or otherwise. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. The integrated or nonintegrated Europe for many, many years in the future, is going to have to have United States help. I think the time has come, and I think the administration, too, should start telling just that to the American people. I think this question of trying to kid ourselves that the terminal day is 1952, and then we are through, is one of the great illusions. I think we are doing our foreign policy and ourselves a lot of harm if we keep on telling the American people, "Boys, '52 washes this out of the picture."

General DONOVAN. We are not going to buy our way out of these things, anyway, Mr. Congressman. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. That is right. Dollars will not do it. 

Chairman KEE. Is that all, Mr. Ribicoff?

Mr. RIBICOFF. Yes. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Fulton? 

Mr. FULTON. You have had wide experience, in the Far East, I am sure.

General DONOVAN. Yes. 

Mr. FULTON. As page 3 of your statement, you have commented about the indications of further expansion tendencies in the Communist countries of the Far East. Will you comment upon the effect of that possible expansion, first, upon the cooperation or noncooperation of the British Government in Hong Kong with United States authorities or with United States people; and, secondly, the effect upon the expansive tendencies, the possible delivery of $100,000,000 worth of planes might have, permitting the Communist to expand further; and, lastly, have you had any personal experience, yourself, that might give the committee any ideas?

General DONOVAN. My own idea is that we should regard that area, as I have said here before, as a strategic unit; that we should set up a forward base under a Supreme Commander, who should have the discretionary authority to deal with military, political, economic, psychological measures in that area. If that were done, I am sure that leadership would be accepted in that part of the world by the British who are there, by the Dutch, and by the French. I think we ought to take the initiative. I am sure that the various countries concerned, who are working with their new governments, would be glad to accept it and would be glad to have the help that would be given. That is my opinion.

Mr. FULTON. Could you comment on the cooperation, or lack of it, of the British Government in that area? 

General DONOVAN. I think they would really want to do it. 

Mr. FULTON. Can you comment on the Hong Kong Government of the British, as to their cooperation either with us or with the Communists?

General DONOVAN. I think, of course, that the whole question of 

Hong Kong is sui generis, peculiar in itself. You have there a window looking to the outside in which, throughout a long history, British businessmen have been supreme. Now, when you have it in you, it may be pretty hard for you to believe that you cannot continue to do business at the same old stand. However, they should have learned that from their experience in Japan. At any rate, I think it is prompted mostly by the failure to realize that Russia is determined to take over. I think that is just a matter of time. The sensible fellows there would tell you so. 

Now, as I said here before, the action or failure to act on the part of the British to get these planes out of the hands of the Communists is connected with a statute in Hong Kong which recites that no one can act on behalf of any foreign power or any foreign potentate without the approval of the Governor of Hong Kong. Now, it is in the teeth of that statute that these Communists came in and seized these planes. 

I came back to that, Congressman, in saying that I felt the action had to come from the British Foreign Office in this, and not from the courts.

Mr. FULTON. Actually, it is a decision at this point upon a political level, based upon British Foreign Office policy, generally? 

General DONOVAN. That is exactly it. 

Mr. FULTON. So, if the decision is made, it will be flying in the teeth of what the American public thinks is the best course to be pursued to stop expansionism of communism any further in Asia? 

 At that point, I think I ought to say this, Mr. Congressman: You see, international lawyers say, "Well, recognition of a country does not mean you give it approval," but they forget that action is going to be interpreted by Siamese or Chinese coolies down the line, as well as by businessmen, not on any refinement of reasoning that a lawyer might indulge in, but by the simple fact that approval is given and that approval to them means approval. 

That is the difficult part of the situation. 

Mr. FULTON. What effect will this $100,000,000 worth of planes have upon the chances of the success of the Communist expansion further in southeast Asia; a small effect or a great strategic effect? 

General DONOVAN. I think it puts in their hands a chance to consolidate the area and it offers also great opportunity, if it comes to war, to have that means of transport. 

Mr. FULTON. It puts the Communist government in China in possession of an air force within a country that has no air force. 

General DONOVAN. And it allows them to drop their subversive agents in various parts of that country. 

Mr. FULTON. Do you have any comment on the chance of possibly expanding the Anzac Pact of 1944 between Australia and New Zealand as a defensive pact to include other countries or would you suggest

that we should encourage an organization of economic cooperation and development under the United Nations to be formed by these southeastern European countries, just as was done in OEEC in Europe, using the same pattern?

General DONOVAN. What I would try to do, first, is the immediate thing rather than the long range. The thing needed by most of the people there is a bowl of rice and a pair of pants. Then, put them in a position to resist infiltration and penetration and give them the confidence that a nation like us will be with them in that. 

Mr. FULTON. How would you effectively implement such a "bowl of rice and pair of pants" program, then? 

General DONOVAN. What I would do, I think, in those countries where we would set up a criteria of the kind of people we are going to support and the reason we are going to support them, in which there would be included those means by which we can assist them.

Now, you take, for example, Indonesia. There is a place where you could advance funds for capital expenditures, and know you would be repaid. You might work out something they could do for contiguous countries. You have to make a start; that is the point.

Take, for example, Burma, where I happen to know something about the situation; I went behind the lines in the early days of the war to arrange cooperation with the Kachens and the Karins, the Kachens being the rebellious tribe now. The kind of fighting they did with us, it was superb. We got an outfit of 12,000 guerrillas out of those countries. We urged on those countries 5 years ago, in return for what they had done for us, that we should set up agricultural schools as an evidence of our appreciation. You see the fight between the Karins and the Burmese Government there. There are chances for us to exercise our good offices as a nation out of the remembrance of those things, and you could avoid a great deal of trouble. Those are the practical things I am talking about. 

Mr. FULTON. You think, even in Burma, with a constructive policy that will help them to help themselves, there is a good possibility of success?

General DONOVAN. Certainly. 

Mr. FULTON. May I close in asking your comments on Indochina, then, where there is a colonial policy that we are supporting at a cost of about $1,000,000 a day through our French assistance under the ECA? 

General DONOVAN. I was in Indochina. Presently, you are confronted with a condition there, if you have Communist penetration into Indochina. Not only Indochina, but Siam, is in danger. That is our trouble today in Indochina. 

Mr. FULTON. That is all. Thank you very much for your fine statement. 

Chairman KEE. General, we certainly appreciate your coming here today. 

General DONOVAN. I am sorry to have inflicted so much upon you,

Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. I believe it quite possible that you were the one who suffered. 63307-50-pt. 2-3

General DONOVAN. No; it was educational for me. Thank you very much. 

Chairman KEE. I wish to thank you on behalf of the committee.

Gentlemen, the committee is in receipt of a letter from the Railway 

Labor Executives' Association dated March 1, 1950, over the signature of Mr. A. E. Lyon, which, without objection, will be included in the record at this point. The letter reads as follows: 

In January 1948, the Railway Labor Executives' Association adopted a statement in support of the Marshall plan. In that statement we said: "The Marshall plan represents the one major constructive proposal which has been offered to help place the war-devastated European economy on the road to recovery. It was conceived in a spirit of friendliness and goodwill to all our European neighbors as a means of placing at their disposal a small part of the technical resources and productive capacity of this great country. "Such a program will inevitably involve some sacrifices for the American workers and the country as a whole. But American labor has expressed its readiness to assume whatever responsibilities are deemed necessary to reaffirm its faith in the democratic processes and freedom to which it has so long dedicated its efforts. It can and will make its contribution now by supporting a program which will mean so much to the peoples of Europe in their struggle to perpetuate the heritage of democracy and independence which has been theirs." 

During the period which has elapsed since adoption of the European recovery program by the Congress and during its administration by the Economic Cooperation Administration, we have found no reasons for in any way changing the attitude we expressed. The program has involved some sacrifices from 

American workers and from our people as a whole but we feel that they have not been unrewarded sacrifices. Great gains for democracy and freedom have been made in all of the Marshall plan countries. 

We believe that it would be a serious error to fail to go forward with this program or to cripple it now with insufficient funds. The job is only half done. 

The cold war must go on and it must be won by the same kind of total effort and wise leadership that are necessary in hot wars. 

We respectfully ask that this expression, which is being sent to you as a result of formal action of the members of our association, be included in the record of the hearings held by your committee. 

Respectfully yours,

A. E. LYON, Executive Secretary.

STATEMENT OF BARRY BINGHAM, CHIEF, ECA SPECIAL MISSION TO FRANCE 

Mr. BINGHAM. I have a summary which I would like to read. The complete statement I will present to be included in the record. 

Chairman KEE. Without objection, the complete statement will appear in the record at this point. (The statement referred to above is as follows:) 

France is a vital area in peace or in war. That explains why the Soviets are making their strongest efforts to undermine the French recovery, with the help of a deluded minority of French Communists. It explains why they have gone all-out in France to discredit and to destroy the Marshall plan and the military assistance program.

The free world requires a strong, independent, democratic France. That is why the United States has spent over a billion and a half dollars through ECA in France since the end of the war. We are not there simply to repay the debt to Lafayette or to make a generous gesture toward our oldest ally among nations. We are there to help France get on her feet. We are there to help France stop the Communist wrecking crew. We are there to help the French maintain their fine tradition of freedom and individual liberty. Such a victory is not easily won. The battle must be fought every day on economic, political, and even military fronts, as in Indochina. But there were significant gains in this battle in 1949, and I want to report some of them to you today.

All of you remember the desperate situation that faced France in 1947. World 

War II had killed more than half a million French citizens, had destroyed 1 out of every 22 buildings, had demolished communications and disrupted the whole economy. France made a strong effort to come back under her own power. She liquidated $2,000,000,000 of her own foreign assets in addition to borrowings of nearly another $2,000,000,000 from the United States. But the job was too big. 

Mass unemployment threatened. Living standards seemed doomed to fall even below the levels of the German occupation days. In a word, democratic society in France was on the verge of collapse. 

American assistance came just in time, through interim aid and ECA. At first it was an emergency job of feeding people and giving them the strength to work. Soon there was enough improvement to take the edge off political and social tensions. Then the two main objectives of the program in France came out in clear view: The restoration of a sound internal economy and the achievement of self-support for France within the society of nations. 

GENERAL PICTURE 

The effectiveness of American aid to France can be measured in the achievements of the French people and the use to which they have put the dollars given and lent to them. Perhaps the best measure is the fact that, although American aid was sharply reduced in the current fiscal year, yet French production increased and the inflation was arrested. Direct aid in 1949-50 is $673,000,000, compared with $978,000,000 in the previous 12 months. An excellent indication of the extent to which France has been able, through our aid, to help herself is also shown in the probable reduction in indirect aid needed during the coming year as compared with that of 1948-49. Indirect aid, in the currencies of other European countries, was over $300,000,000 last year. It may be reduced by two-thirds, to as little as $100,000,000 this year. Thus there has been a reduction of about $500,000,000 in the total aid to France between 1948-49 and 1949-50. 

Progress seems certain to continue, although not at such a spectacular rate as during the past year. This progress depends, of course, on continued aid. France should be able to secure the vital dollar imports she requires if aid this year is reduced to $503,000,000.

Whereas, during the first year of ECA aid, France was forced to import many items which she can normally produce herself, the import program has shifted to commodities essential to basic economic demands and to those which will push 

French recovery yet further ahead. France no longer needs to import

those primary foodstuffs she was unable to produce in sufficient quantity in the immediate postwar years. French agricultural production is now able to supply all, or almost all, of the wheat, feed grains, fats, and oils she needs. 

Increased French coal production and the purchase of German coal have reduced French coal imports from the dollar area to negligible amounts of specialquality types of coal. American aid is no longer playing a role of relief to 

France; it is now contributing to the reconstruction and modernization of French industry. Instead of food, France is importing machinery to modernize her factories and equipment to step up production in agriculture and industry. In addition, France requires certain basic dollar commodities without which her industry could not function: raw cotton for the textile industry, nonferrous metals, and petroleum. These, with machinery and equipment, are essential to production and to the revitalization of the French industrial system. 

The bulk of these commodities come from the United States. Seventy-four percent of ECA funds is spent in the first instance in the United States; another 

12 percent, in other nations of this hemisphere. Only 14 percent goes to nations outside the Western Hemisphere. But this 14 percent enables the supplying countries, in turn, to buy in the United States. 

INFLATION ARRESTED 

The most spectacular effect of ECA assistance during the past 2 years has been the halt to the alarming inflationary spiral. Every year since the war, right. through 1948, prices were rising steeply each year, by 80 percent in 1 year, and never by less than 44 percent. The picture altered completely in 1949. In December 1949, wholesale prices were only 1 percent above the December 1948 level. 

The quantity and quality of goods continued to improve; the last vestiges of rationing disappeared.

This new stability brought with it new confidence in the French franc. This is reflected in its free currency market rate. In December 1948, when the Comunists called a crippling coal strike, the free market value of the franc reached its peak at 550 to the dollar. The official rate was then 315 to the dollar, a differential of 70 percent. Today the free market value is 390 francs to the dollar; the official value, 350. This difference of only 10 percent has been maintained for many months despite constant political difficulties which might have been expected to affect confidence and hence the value of the franc. This relative stability has been attained despite a number of other potentially inflationary pressures, such as the devaluation of the franc last September, a serious drought, a fierce and costly war in Indochina, and, of course, a sharp reduction in 

American assistance.

France's success in increasing the supply of goods on the market while at the same time controlling inflation could not have been achieved with dollars alone. 

Even while it faced the critical coal strike of 1948, the Queuille government was drawing up a program to combat inflation. They created tighter money conditions through more rigorous restrictions on bank credit. They increased tax collections and reduced Government expenditure. As a result, an increasing proportion of Government expenditures has been covered by Government revenue, thus reducing dependence on the franc counterpart of dollar aid and eliminating resort to the printing presses. They brought effective demand more into line with supply by halting the creation of new purchasing power. The French Government is concentrating on these efforts, and France will actually have in 1950 a surplus of current revenue over current expenditure equivalent to $1,240,000,000. 

This surplus will be used for the national program of reconstruction and investment, to meet such crying needs as building construction to rebuild houses and factories damaged or destroyed in the war. 

Taxes, which now amount to 30 percent of national product, have gone up each year since the end of the war. This is an impressive step forward toward the goal of an equitable and efficient fiscal system. In 1950 direct taxes will amount to 32 percent of tax revenues, as against 22 percent in 1949. France, with its many small enterprises and farms, will always find it difficult to collect the same proportion of tax revenues in income taxes as we do in the United States; hence the high proportion of indirect taxes (68 percent of tax revenue). But the fiscal system is steadily improving.

INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION 

I would like to come back to France's present financial stability and to stress the fact that it has been achieved without perpetuating internal controls and restrictions and without causing a deflation which would have seriously affected production and brought unemployment to a socially and politically undesirable level.

In 1949 industrial production rose very nearly to the 1929 figure, the highest peak in French history, and actually passed the 1938 figure by 23 percent. 

Immediately following the war, France's efforts to come back were seriously handicapped by lack of coal. Obsolete or damaged mine machinery, inadequate transportation, low output per man-hour due to poor diet, all affected French coal production and necessitated the importation of American coal. The lack of fuel and power affected the whole industrial picture. Today that picture looks very different. French coal production has passed the 1938 level and is nearing the 1929 peak. With that output and with the great increase in electrical power made possible by ECA assistance to the investment program, other heavy and light industries have been able in most cases to reach the 1938 production level and, in some, to surpass it. 

Energy remains a serious problem, however. France is today producing 

30,000,000,000 kilowatt-hours of electrical power annually, as compared to 18,000,- 000,000 kilowatt-hours in 1938. It is hoped that the present hydroelectric and thermal projects will produce 43,000,000,000 kilowatt-hours by 1952. Even at the present time, however, with the increased power now available, the French worker has only some 22 horsepower behind him, as compared to 7 horsepower per worker in the United States.

A steady flow of raw materials, the vast task of transportation reconstruction, the breaking of bottlenecks in power and steel, and the restoration of financial stability resulted in rapid progress from the desperately low level of production at the end of the war. But this high rate of increase in industrial production cannot be maintained, and the curve on the production chart is beginning to level off.

The actual rate of increase in production has, in fact, gone into a slight, if temporary, decline. This was to be expected as the French economy began to shift its resources from some of the uneconomic enterprises which sprang up during a period of acute shortages and severe inflation. But this very shift, this better utilization of resources, will soon make new increases in production possible. The introduction of real competition, of free movement of goods and services, and particularly a new era of competitive international trade, will impel producers to reduce costs and to improve production and marketing techniques. French businessmen and industrialists will have to adopt new and more vigorous attitudes. The old idea of a narrow and quickly saturated market must be abandoned. A growing market will be best assured if the French worker receives a greater share of the increased production. This increasing real purchasing power will call forth higher levels of production, and the worker will then be convinced that a democratic society offers far more for his own well-being than the false promises of communism.

AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION 

Agricultural production has been slower to come back, but 1949-50 will probably see it achieve nearly 96 percent of prewar output despite the serious drought of 1949. The drought most seriously affected secondary cereals and vegetables, and as a result, the cost of living rose again in the second half of 1949, after a marked decrease in the first half of the year. But despite the drought there was a record wheat crop, and the production of meat, milk, fats, and oil held up well. There is every prospect of an upswing in agricultural production in 1950-51.

LABOR 

A great help to the higher production levels reached in 1949 was the relative peace on the labor front. Only about 5,000,000 man-days were lost last year through strikes in comparison with near 23,000,000 such days lost in 1947. This plus marked improvement in the general economic picture has brought about a notable rise in output per man-hour since October 1948. By April of last year output had risen well above the 1938 level.

The firm action of the Government had broken Communist strength in the disastrous strikes of 1947 and 1948. Despite the present wave of strikes, related to the reestablishment of collective bargaining and the workers' demand for a cost-of-living bonus, it is less likely that the Communists can successfully call strikes of this magnitude again, thanks to the marked improvement in the economic situation. Nevertheless, the Communists will continue to take every opportunity to defeat France's recovery efforts as well as to sabotage French efforts to contribute to the defense of Europe. This is apparent in the present hysterical attempt of the Communist leaders to prevent the unloading of military assistance supplies and the shipping of war material to Indochina. It has been frequently demonstrated of late-in fact, ever since the 1947-48 strikes-that the Communists are increasingly unable to pull off politically motivated strikes. For this reason, the reestablishment of collective bargaining in France, which has been suspended for 10 years, is particularly significant. The freeing of wages in this way is a final step in the French Government's program to eliminate controls on the internal economy. Nevertheless, the sudden resumption of free wage negotiations may lead to serious labor difficulties, of which the present strike wave is symptomatic.

There is no doubt but that the French worker is far better clothed and better fed than he would have been without American assistance. The consumption levels of the prewar period are very nearly regained. But it should be recalled that the real wages of the French worker were low before the war. It is also certain that many inequities have grown up as a result of inflation and Government wage controls. Certainly, under renewed collective bargaining, the French worker will strive to improve his lot and to bring about a closer relationship between material rewards and efficient effort. 

My sincere hope is that French management and labor can mutually profit by collective bargaining to work out wage increases that will be directly related to increased productivity. The increase in real purchasing power will provide the market for increased production in a way which will lessen the danger of renewed inflation and at the same time insure a higher standard of living. 

TRADE 

I have already indicated how the increasing strength of the French economy has been reflected in an improved external position. A most encouraging development is the progressive closing of the gap in French foreign payments, mainly by increased exports. 

Nearly all of the improvement has taken place in trade with other OEEC countries. Less than 12 months ago France was running a deficit of the equivalent of $510,000,000 per year in its trade with the other participating countries. 

One of the striking accomplishments of 1949 was the conversion of this deficit into a temporary surplus of $105,000,000. 

The same favorable picture, unfortunately, does not exist in the dollar area. 

The dollar gap has been narrowed but only by shifting imports from the dollar area to other currency areas or by replacing them by increased domestic production. Export earnings from the dollar area in 1949 were actually slightly less than in 1948, averaging below $10,000,000 a month. Tourist receipts rose from $28,000,000 to only $50,000,000. 

These results are not satisfactory. France must more than double these current figures of dollar earnings from exports and tourist trade by 1952 to obtain even the minimum requirements of petroleum, cotton, copper, and a small amount of machinery. It is not pleasant to contemplate the fact that, even after 4 years of ERP aid, American exports to France may be limited to a narrow range of essential commodities. That is nevertheless a situation which may have to be faced. It can only be changed if, through an intensive mutual effort, French dollar earnings can be increased.

The French are keenly aware of this dollar gap, and they are making new efforts to close it. A franc-dollar committee has been formed to promote dollar exports, and its members are top leaders of French business. Market surveys on potential imports from France are being launched in the United States. Special inducements are being offered to French producers to sell their goods for dollars. 

INVESTMENT PROGRAM 

A more encouraging side of economic recovery in France is the important French investment program. Not only have shortages been gradually eliminated, price stability been reached, prewar consumption levels been approached, and

4 the need for American assistance reduced, but an extensive investment program has been carried out at the same time. France's economic problem was not solely the result of the war; for nearly a quarter of a century France has been living off her capital, her economic strength continuously diminishing. American assistance was intended to help France reverse this process, to provide an opportunity to augment productive capacity and to enable the French people, through their own efforts, to raise their standard of living. ECA aid has been used for this purpose. French investments are still low in comparison with those in the United States, but France is currently devoting nearly one-sixth of her national income to reconstruction and development projects, including depreciation and maintenance expenditure.

Fifty percent of this amount-the equivalent of approximately $2,000,000, came from public funds, of which over one-third was furnished by the counterpart of American aid.

Concentration on reconstruction and development-the key factors in the economy-is essential if France is to stand on her own feet in 1952. Fuel and energy, vital to increased industrial production, accounted for 23 percent of the investment program. Twenty-four percent of the program went into transportation and communications, to rebuild railroads, docks, and shipping which had been damaged or demolished by bombing. Twenty-two percent went to housing, to the reconstruction of bombed-out cities and villages, and yet France still has a great need for new housing. 

Even after 1952 France will have a herculean task of reconstruction and development ahead of her. But the continuance of ERP aid should enable her to devote enough resources to improving productive capacity so that France can carry the task herself in 1952. 

CONCLUSION 

The general picture is thus one of solid progress. lems that are serious and immediate. 

But France still faces prob One of the major problems is a continuing political, instability. France has been unable to constitute a strong central authority, and is thereby handicapped in dealing with the knotty problems of recovery. The constant need for political compromise has often deterred fully effective action. One aspect of this problem is the continuous Communist sniping at all Government efforts. Communist influence in France is weakening as economic conditions improve, but the orders from Moscow plainly call for a still more concentrated effort. French labor is tragically divided. A large group of French workers, basically patriotic but deluded, still follow the Communist-dominated labor federation, the CGT, despite its open subservience to Russia. 

Another major problem is Indochina. It must be remembered that France is not a nation at peace. French troops are fighting and dying every day in 

Indochina, in a conflict against Communist forces. The Indochina war puts a heavy financial drain on France, the franc equivalent of $475,000,000 in 1949. (Most of this sum is in francs, and only a small proportion represents direct dollar expenditures.) More than 143,000 French and native troops are carrying on the fight in Indochina.

Yet another problem is production. Despite all that has been accomplished, France needs more production at lower costs, to improve the standard of living of the French worker, and to earn money to pay for essential imports. ECA is helping French production in three ways: By financing new equipment, by paying for needed raw materials, and by furnishing technical assistance to develop modern methods of productivity.

What would happen in France if this ECA assistance were cut off now or too drastically reduced? The tremendous progress of the past 2 years would be arrested, and it would be impossible for France to achieve economic independence by 1952. The whole effort to modernize French industry and agriculture would be gravely threatened, if not completely halted. There would not be enough dollars to buy the minimum essential raw materials. France's cotton textile industry gets 70 percent of its raw cotton from dollar sources, for instance. Stop that flow, and the industry with the biggest labor force in France would be hit by mass unemployment. The investment program, which promises independence for France if it can be maintained, would have to be abandoned. The standard of living would take a downward skid. 

The worst time to abandon a job is when it is half done. We are at least that far in France, with a big investment behind us. We have an excellent chance of success if we stay the course.

There is another reason why this is a vital point in France's program of recovery. Complete economic health can only come to France through a real economic integration of western Europe. Almost every thinking Frenchman now admits the truth of this thesis, but some plead for a more moderate pace, for more time to adjust to the inevitable shocks. 

Yet now is the time when such a basic change could best be made in France. 

There is no use saying it will be easy. If France is to hold its own in an integrated western Europe, the whole outlook of French business and industry must alter drastically. The old protectionist philosophy must be exposed to the fresh, keen winds of competition. Markets will have to be developed and expanded, not just guarded by tight tradition. 

This bold new approach, so necessary to the future health of France, will cause some serious though temporary dislocations. I believe this difficult but necessary adjustment of the French economy could only be successfully carried out with ECA asistance there to act as a cushion. 

Yet integration is the future for France and western Europe. We have seen 

France through the earliest stages of recovery. Now we have reached the point where it is possible to create a permanently strong and stable France within a strong and stable western Europe. Surely this is no time to hesitate. The amount of American aid is being reduced each year in an orderly progression. 

What we are asking now is a sum sufficient to tackle the boldest, the most important, and the last part of our job in France. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much, Mr. Bingham. You have made a very fine statement indeed. 

We will now go into our questioning period under the 5-minute rule. 

Mr. BINGHAM. May I ask permission to run very briefly through some of these charts in this book. I think it may illustrate some of the points I have mentioned more clearly than I would be able to explain them otherwise.

Chart 1 illustrates 'the downward progression of dollar aid to France under ECA. As you will note, the first program year amounted to $978,000,000 for France. The second fiscal year in which we are now operating was brought down to $673,000,000. The estimate for 

1950-51, the requested figure, is $503,000,000, and for 1951-52, the estimate is $352,000,000. You can see how materially reduced that program has been each year. 

Chart No. 2 will give you a quick view of what commodities have been bought for France with ECA dollars. As you all know, the blue line indicates the procurement authorization for 1948-49, and the orange line shows the commodities that are being obtained in 1949-50. You will note that since the first program year, there has been a great reduction on food products and on coal. Those were items which were important in the program the first year, but which are now greatly reduced. The big items remaining are the historic imports from the United States and the dollar area into France. 

The principal one for both of those years as you will note is machinery, equipment, and vehicles. That represents the great French effort to modernize its industrial plant and its agricultural plant. The other items are for raw cotton, petroleum, and nonferous metals. Those are the continuing needs of the French economy which go on from year to year.

Chairman KEE. From what source do they secure the imports of machinery, raw cotton, and the other materials? 

Mr. BINGHAM. Mr. Chairman, almost all of the machinery and the raw cotton come from the United States.

The next chart indicates the source of all these dollar-products which have gone into France, but the proportion coming from the United States is even higher for the two items the Chairman mentioned, that is raw cotton and machinery. As you will note on chart 

No. 3, 74 percent of these dollars have been spent directly in the United 

States. Of the 12 percent spent in the other Western Hemisphere countries, a large proportion has been spent in Canada. 

Of the remaining dollars spent under ECA for the French needs, the money has gone to certain other countries and then has been used quickly to meet the dollar needs of those countries, so the dollars actually have flowed back to the United States in a rather rapid and steady stream.

Chart No. 4 illustrates rather dramatically, I think, the control of inflation which has been accomplished in France. As you will note, the wholesale price index rose giddily during the years following the war. It reached a steep rise in the year 1948 but at about the end of 1948, along in December when the Marshall plan really began to take hold in France, that rise leveled off very dramatically and, since then, it has only risen about 1 percent. The little table in the left-hand corner illustrates the same point in another way. It shows that during each postwar year, wholesale prices in France rose somewhere between 44 and 80 percent over the preceding year, but when we reach 

1949, suddenly that rise is reduced to only 1 percent.

This has been accomplished despite devaluation, despite a serious drought in 1949, and despite a good deal of political uncertainty in 

France in this past year.

Now just to add one more word about this table, the chart actually might show a slight further decline at the end for the month of February, for which we have just received figures. This figure actually went down about 1.5 percent.

Chart No. 5 is, again, a way to show what has happened in the fight against inflation in France. This is the black-market dollar rate. 

There was a time back in the end of 1948 just after the Communist-led coal strike, when the black-market rate for the dollar was actually 70 percent above the legal rate. That percentage has been brought together to the point where there is only a differential of about 10 percent and the transactions in the black market have been greatly reduced during that time.

Mr. VORYS. I wondered whether a 10-percent spread or some spread would be expected in almost any country between the formal and the informal rate. I wonder whether there is not some sort of spread that is about normal. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Any time, I think, when there is an exchange control, there would be some slight spread. This is roughly 10 percent. 

On some days, it is considerably below 10 percent, but it averages about that amount.

Chart No. 6 illustrates the increasing dependence of France on its own fiscal receipts to cover its expenditures. You will notice that in 

1938, tax revenues only covered 56 percent of France's total expenditures, as against 44 percent which came from borrowing and nonfiscal sources. You will also notice that, by 1950, the tax receipts have been brought up to cover 70 percent of the expenditures of the French Government. There is a much smaller reliance on borrowing, and the

reliance on the counterpart of the Marshall plan aid has been reduced in 1950 over 1949. 

Mr. VORYS. What does nonfiscal mean?

Mr. BINGHAM. Nonfiscal receipts include the profits of the state lottery, proceeds from the sale of capital and war assets, proceeds from the sale of reparations in kind, and income from public properties. 

Mr. VORYS. Why are those called nonfiscal?

Mr. BINGHAM. They are not actually drawn in tax receipts from the public in the way fiscal receipts are drawn. The lottery, for instance, represents a fairly sizable figure in French economy, but it is not a direct or indirect tax. It is a different form of receipt and, therefore, is segregated in a separate department. 

Mr. VORYS. It is an actual raising of francs and an actual application of them to Government expenditures. 

Mr. BINGHAM. It is, but it represents, to some extent, an extraordinary raising of francs. For instance, these war assets are not going to be long continuing. That is a rather special source of franc assets which the French now have and, therefore, it is not included in their regular tax receipts.

Chart No. 7 illustrates clearly the increased effort the French are making in 1950 in their budget. If you will notice on the left-hand side of the chart, direct taxes in 1950 are going to take care of 22 percent of all treasury receipts. In 1949, direct taxes only accounted for 

14 percent of the total treasury receipts. The proportion of indirect taxes is still high in France and far higher than ours. I think it is worth noting there that France is a country of small businesses, of small farm holdings, and, therefore, a country which will probably never be able to raise anything like the proportion of its taxes from income taxes that we do in the United States. 

The chart also indicates the extent of the tax program in France which goes far beyond what some people realize. It actually means that the French are raising from tax sources 30 percent of gross national product in 1950. Now, that compares to a figure for the United 

States of about 22 percent of our gross national product which we are raising in taxes. It indicates, I think, a quite heavy fiscal burden in France. I do not say that I consider it entirely a satisfactory tax program because I do not think it is quite equitable. I think it is too heavy on some classes of society and not quite heavy enough on some others, but it is a heavy fiscal burden, as you see. 

In 1950, the French will actually raise a surplus in their budget for their ordinary expenditures, a surplus that amounts to about 1.25 billion dollars. They will use that surplus for their large expenditures on reconstruction and investment. That is an area which requires tremendous effort on the part of the French. They are going to devote, as you see, 38 percent of their resources to reconstruction and investment in their budget this year. 

The counterpart of Marshall plan aid is also used in that portion of their program. It is used, in other words, for the reconstruction and investment portion of the French national program in 1950. 

Chart No. 8 indicates what has happened in industrial production. in France. You will notice that the general index shows industrial production got back to 23 percent above 1938, during the year 1949.

That figure is now running between 125 and 130 percent, using 1938 as 100. That is a very material increase as you can see. There has been a rather striking increase in the production of coal in France. 

It is up now to 67,000,000 tons a year, in 1949. That is almost up to the peak year of coal production, which is 1929, when they produced 

69,000,000 tons of coal.

On steel, they are up to 11,000,000 tons this year, by far the best year they have ever had on steel production except in 1929 when they produced 11,900,000 tons of steel. 

On electricity, there has been a very dramatic increase in the electric power output of France. In 1938, they were producing 18.5 billion kilowatt-hours of power in France. In 1949 they produced 28.4 billion kilowatt-hours, despite a serious drought which reduced that power output from what would have been about 30 billion kilowatthours in 1949. You can imagine what that is going to do for French industrial productivity, if they can increase the electric power output of the nation to that extent. The goal is to get it up to about 40 billion kilowatt-hours by 1952, and they are rapidly approaching that goal. 

On agriculture, shown on chart No. 9, the general index is up to about 96 percent of the prewar level. The picture here is somewhat mixed, largely because of the serious drought of 1949 which I mentioned previously. However, despite that drought, there was a very good harvest of wheat, above the 1935-39 level as you will notice. 

There are also a good production of milk and meat, during the early part of the year especially, but secondary cereals and vegetable production fell off rather sharply during 1949 because of the dry weather. 

Chart No. 10 is a quick one which merely indicates what has happened to productivity in France or output per man-hour to put it in another way.

As you will see, there was a sudden sharp increase in individual productivity in France back in late 1948, again the time when the Marshall plan really began to take hold in that country. Bottlenecks were broken in industrial production and productivity make a steady and sharp climb at that point. It is now up to about 3 percent above the 1938 level.

The next chart, No. 11, shows what has happened to working days lost by strikes in France. You will note that in 1946, very few working days were lost by strikes in France. At that time, the Communists were in the French Government. In May 1947, the Communists were kicked out of the French Government and the reaction shows very strongly on this chart. The Communists then began to perpetrate large, wide-scale strikes in France, which accounted for nearly 23,000,000 man-hours of work lost in 1947. That was cut down to about 12,000,000 man-hours lost in 1948, and down to less than 

5,000,000 man-hours lost in 1949.

Chart No. 12 gives you something about what has happened to the individual worker in France, which is a point of interest, of course, to all of us. It shows that the real wage position of the individual worker, taking an average for all workers in France at the bottom of the page, is now just about up to 1938 levels. Now, that takes into consideration not only his weekly wages but all social benefits, and it brings the average worker in France up to just about the level that he was enjoying in 1938. Chart No. 13 illustrates the export-import picture in France and will show that 1949 actually made an improvement over 1938. In other words, in 1949, the French were able to cover 67 percent of their import needs through exports. That compares to a figure of only 36 percent back in 1946.

Chart No. 14 shows, in another form, what has happened to French foreign trade. It indicates a reduction of the gap between their imports and their exports. You will see that this reduction is taking place at a rather high level of foreign trade, which is the way we would like to see it done, rather than at a low level which would mean that the French were giving up necessary imports because they could not cover them with exports. 

Chart No. 15 shows the balance of payment improvements that have occurred in 1948. In 1948, you will notice the balance of payment on net current account showed a deficit with all participating countries of $510,000,000. That was converted into an actual surplus of $105,- 

000,000 in 1949. With the entire sterling area, they had a deficit of $328,000,000 in 1948. That is now a small surplus of $38,000,000 in 

1949. With other participating countries, a deficit of $182,000,000 in 

1948 has been converted to a surplus of $67,000,000 in 1949. 

There are some special conditions which govern that situation in 1949 which may not continue through 1950, so we may not have quite as favorable a picture as that during this year, but it does represent a very strong effort on the part of the French to improve their position with other countries in 1949.

You will see on chart No. 16 the story of gross investment in plant and equipment in France. The French are making a very substantial investment in plant and equipment which is absolutely necessary for the economy of their country. That investment had been very low for a number of years before World War II, and they now have a backlog of investment which they need to take care of in these postwar years.

You will notice that, for instance, housing will take 22 percent of the investment program, or did take 22 percent of the investment program for 1949. That is not by any means going to cover all of 

France's housing needs, but it represents an investment of some $443,000,000 in francs in the housing needs of France. The other items are fuel and energy, manufacturing, transportation, and communications, and so forth. They represent the main areas in which 

France needs investment badly, and she is making a great effort to get the investment into the places where they will really increase her productive capacity and make her independent. 

Mr. VORYS. Of that circle in the middle, the gross investment, how much is the 38 percent shown on chart 7 of Government reconstruction and investment, and how much is private? 

Mr. BINGHAM. On gross investment about 50 percent is Government financed, and on net investment about 75 percent is Government financed, and about 25 percent private.

1 Chart No. 17 is the last chart on which I will comment, unless you have questions on the others. 

This illustrates the continuing political difficulties in France. As you will see, the coalition government, even though it brings three major parties together and some smaller groups, still only commands 54 percent of the vote in the French Parliament. It still leaves the 

Communists with 27 percent of that vote and the groups of the right with about 16 percent. Now, that means there is always a solid bloc of Communists and fellow travelers on the left, of DeGaullists and others on the other side, who are opposed to practically everything the Government does. That means, if the Government at any time loses any part of its own following in the Parliament it will be in danger of an immediate fall. It is a very touchy condition under which the Government has to operate. It means that they have always got to consider the smallest political considerations of any effort they make. Under such conditions it is often amazing to me that the 

French Government is able to carry through some of the program it does put through, such as the program of controlling inflation. 

That was not an easy program to carry through politically. It meant increased taxation. It meant putting on certain controls which are not popular politically, but they felt it necessary to do it and they were able to get away with it, even against this very large bloc of opposition.

Unless there are some questions about the other charts, I think I will omit them. I believe they are rather simple and easily understood.

You mentioned the operation in the coal mines and suggested that they needed more production and lower costs. Are the coal mines nationalized in France? 

Mr. BINGHAM. Yes; they are.

Mr. BATTLE. Are they able to control these Communist-inspired strikes by the militia, or how do they control them? 

Mr. BINGHAM. They had serious Communist-led strikes in 1947 and 

1948 in the coal fields when it was with great difficulty that the Government was able to control the situation. It cost the French Government a lot of money during those 2 years. 

Now, in 1949, there were some efforts to create strike conditions in the coal fields of France, but they did not succeed. In the coal strike of 1947 and 1948, they did use the militia and troops to help control the situation in the coal fields. 

Mr. BATTLE. Our problem here right now is not to get more production but to get some production. I would like to know how to do it without nationalizing our coal mines. 

What is going on insofar as our shipment of arms to France is concerned? I have noticed by the papers that we expect some difficulty. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Mr. Congressman, no arms shipments under the 

MAP program have yet reached France but there has been a great deal

They have made a strong effort to convince the French dock workers that, for patriotic reasons, they should not unload these shipments.
