Chairman KEE. Mr. Vorys- 

Mr. VORYS. You have given us a very fine statement, Mr. Bingham.

As I understand it, you have 11 percent of the current budget which is counterpart but all of that goes into reconstruction; is that correct? 

Mr. BINGHAM. It goes into reconstruction and investment; yes, sir. 

And what type of investment? It goes into all types of investment which add to the productive capacity of France. Now, it does not go into recurring expenses of the French Government. It goes into extraordinary expenditures of the French Government which they are using now to try to rebuild their economy. In other words, they are taking advantage of this opportunity to use Marshall plan counterpart, to do a job which will permanently benefit France rather than to use those same funds to make a temporary improvement in the standard of living, for instance, which could be done but which would leave them no better off by the time 1952 comes.

Mr. VORYS. May I say to you that that was the original idea that we hoped counterpart would be used for. I think the thing was invented in this room and it was hoped that the funds would be used a second time for permanent reconstruction and apparently that is being done in France.

Mr. BINGHAM. In France, that is definitely being done. 

Mr. VORYS. That would leave about 27 percent of the French budget for capital investment; is that right? That is, from the 38 percent as shown on chart 7, you took out the 11 percent of their budget which they are getting from the counterpart and it would mean they are actually applying over 27 percent of their whole budget to capital for investment. 

Mr. BINGHAM. That is correct.

Mr. VORYS. I wonder whether investing 27 percent in capital improvements is not like trying to run before you can walk? I would like to know whether that isn't really attempting to move too fast, and whether the budget and the effort should not be devoted a little more toward supporting them in the meantime and not so much in future investment which is capital investment, as I understand, and is supposed to be inflationary in its effect. Am I right or wrong about that?

Mr. BINGHAM. According to our estimates, gross domestic investment represents about 12 percent of gross national product in France. 

The French are convinced this is their opportunity to make that investment so they can make themselves independent after 1952. It seems to us, they are wise in pursuing that course. It does strain their resources to put that much into reconstruction and investment, but they have, as I said earlier, a great backlog of need in that area of their economy. They did not keep up their investment program to any great extent during the 1930's. There is a great need to go back and pick that up now as well as to help recover from the damage that was done by the war to the French economy. 

Mr. VORYS. Do you feel that their investment program is one that would fit in with an integration of Europe, or is it an autarchic investment program designed to make them independent, or is it both? 

Mr. BINGHAM. It is primarily designed for the domestic needs of 

France, but, as you realize, all of these things are weighed in the OEEC. All of these national problems are weighed there, and the 

French program, I think, certainly would not be inimical to an over-all recovery program for Europe.

Mr. VORYS. I find, in the statement that General Donovan gave us this morning, quotations from more French statesmen than any others. 

Would you say that the present French Government or the 54 percent, at least, are cooperative in that work, or are they dragging their feet? 

Can you make a statement on that? 

Mr. BINGHAM. Yes, sir, and I would like to very much.

I think the French are taking some real leadership in the field of integration. I would like to cite a few statements that have been made recently along that line. One of them is the statement which perhaps you saw here, quoting President Vincent Auriol in France. 

It is in the book General Donovan passed out among us this morning. 

Auriol ended up his statement by saying:

Upon the idea of unity and the efforts of Europeans to achieve it in cooperation and peace, hangs the prosperity and security of all the peoples of the world.

t That is a type of statement that is being made by a number of important figures in France today.

Another one I would like to quote briefly is by Andre Philip, former 

Minister of the National Economy in France. Philip said: 

The European union no longer is an ideal or a dream; it has become a vital necessity for us, an objective of political policy and it should be realized in the shortest possible time.

Mr. VORYS. Is Philip in the Government at present? 

Mr. BINGHAM. No, but he is an important political figure in France. 

I would like to quote also briefly from an official publication of the French Government which has recently been issued. It is a pamphlet called The Road to Peace, it is put out by the French Government to explain what the Marshall plan has done for France. It is being circulated through the schools of France, through the Chamber of Commerce, and other media. It is an excellent pamphlet, and I think it tells the story of how ECA has been able to help France in a comprehensive, clear, and fair way. I want to make a quotation from that as they touch on this question of unification. Here is one of them: 

That which a few years ago seemed a dream to most European countriesthe creation of a federation where each nation would be free and all will be united; where jealousies and bitterness will give way to the community of interests and solidarity of people, this is well within realization. To unite Europe and to construct a durable peace, France must depend and make a reality of this idea-one more easily attainable and thanks to American financial aid. 

I think it is worth noting that France is the only country in the world which has a specific provision in its constitution for turning over sovereignty to a greater power than a national power. That is actually provided in so many words in the French Constitution. In other words, the French sovereignty could be surrendered to a greater authority without even a vote of the French people. It could be done by a mere vote of the French Parliament. That is the only country, I believe, in which such a condition exists.

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Mr. Lodge 

Mr. LODGE. I should like to extend a personal word of warm welcome and say that I think you have given us an excellent statement. 

I should like first to ask you about this question which I think is extremely important in connection with ECA in general, and that is the demographic aspects of the French situation. Although the population is rising, there is still room in France. There is room in the 

French colonies. However, in Italy, the thing that weighs the heaviest on the Marshall plan is, as you know, the problem of overpopulation. 

Therefore, I have been giving my attention to that question for several years now, and I have been interested in seeing how we can work out a way whereby many of the people of Italy can be syphoned off into the colonies where there is a lack of people and where it seems to me that the reasons advanced for preventing their entry have been invalid. 

I wonder if you would care to talk a little bit about (a) the number of Italians moving into France either on a transient or permanent basis, (b) the number of Italians moving into French colonies, and (c) what is the prognosis with respect to that entire situation? 

Mr. BINGHAM. A certain number of Italian workers have moved into 

France since the end of the war. It was a fairly sizable figure during the first 2 or 3 years after the war. It is now somewhat reduced. 

There are active discussions going on between France and Italy on the subject of manpower. It is obvious that Italy has a great excess of manpower and that France certainly has no excess in that direction. 

However, it is worth noting, I think, that the French population for the first time in probably over 100 years is making steady gains. It is gaining about 1 percent each year since the end of the war. 

Mr. LODGE. Is that due to the special laws passed when Marshal 

Petain was the leader of France and which have not been repealed? 

Mr. BINGHAM. It is hard to say exactly what it is due to. The fact is that the birthrate is the highest it has been at any time in French history. That is due partly, I think, to the system of family allowances. 

Mr. LODGE. Was that inaugurated under Petain?

Mr. BINGHAM. Yes. It was started under the Petain government and considerably strengthened under de Gaulle. 

It makes an additional allowance for each child in a worker's family.

I do think also in the last 2 years, this high birth rate reflects a return of confidence in the future of the country. That return of confidence is such a notable element in French life now that I think this is one of many ways in which it is reflected. 

To go back to your principal question as to the possibilities for immigration to the French overseas territories, I think those possibilities are very decidedly hopeful. There is already a large flow of population into some of those areas. For instance, the city of Casablanca

in Morocco, I am told, had only about 300,000 people before World War II, and now it has about 900,000 people. There are boom towns in French West Africa and French Equatorial Africa which have increased even more than that in percentage. 

Mr. LODGE. How many of those are Italians? It is in Italy where the problem with regard to population is most serious. 

Mr. BINGHAM. I have no figures on the number of Italians that have gone in. 

Mr. LODGE. I would appreciate your obtaining those figures. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Certainly.

The Italians are very much family people. I am wondering whether you could throw any light on that particular part of the problem, and do you know of anything which could be done to ameliorate that particular situation?

Mr. BINGHAM. My understanding is that that definitely is not true, the idea that they cannot bring their families into France at the present time. There is a big housing problem in France which, of course, is one of the reasons immigration is somewhat slowed down.

Mr. LODGE. And the colonies?

In 1947 it is estimated that some 43,000 Italian workers emigrated to France and brought along with them 4,000 members of their families.

Mr. RICHARDS (presiding). Mr. Burleson- 

Mr. BURLESON. Mr. Bingham, I appreciate very much your enthusiasm and optimism, as well as do I appreciate what you have had to say. It is somewhat encouraging in the way you have presented your views and information.

On chart No. 12, with reference to weekly wages, the social benefits and so forth of the French worker are set out. Does that mean, Mr. 

Bingham, that they have reached a place of normalcy? What standard do you apply? Does it mean that they have reached a former standard of living that they enjoyed before World War II?

Mr. BINGHAM. We are using 1938 as the standard. I think I should say there that certainly from my viewpoint, the standard of living in 

France in 1938 was too low.

Mr. BURLESON. Well, is not the standard of living the real key to the many problems and not how much money they make, is that it? 

Mr. BINGHAM. This is in terms of real wages, you see. This is the purchasing power that the worker has from all that comes in to him by way of wages and family allowances and other social payments. 

Mr. BURLESON. It would not particularly mean the same standard of living they enjoyed in 1938.

Mr. BINGHAM. Yes, it would, because it is in terms of real wages and not in terms of the number of francs he receives. 

Mr. BURLESON. Does this mean that he can buy as much today as he could buy in 1938?

Mr. BINGHAM. Well, it varies considerably. A single worker is only getting 81 percent of the real wages he received in 1938 because he does not receive these family allowances, you see. He actually is getting a lower hourly wage rate than he got in 1938, but he was only working a 40-hour week then and he is working a a 44.5-hour week now, so his weekly wages are somewhat larger for that reason. However, the man who is doing materially better than he was in 1938 is the married man with a family. There has been a rather interesting evening-up in 

France among conditions in the workers. The lowest paid are doing relatively better than the higher-paid groups. The women workers have relatively improved their position as compared to the men workers. The workers of the country districts have relatively improved their position, compared to the Paris workers. There has been a general, over-all leveling of working conditions in France in that way.

14 Mr. BURLESON. That is a very encouraging picture to me. It indicates to me that this is vital and is the key to this thing we are trying to do ideologically in France, particularly, but also all over the world. 

France, however is a vital spot and that is encouraging. 

At the risk of asking a question, the answer to which I might not understand if you made it-getting back into this monetary situation, I am inclined to feel that very few people understand it. I refer you to chart 15, the sterling and dollar balance payments. 

Let me ask a hypothetical question referring also to chart 8. Now, in these advances that are made, electricity, steel, coal, artificial fibers, etc., all these countries must make these improvements industrially. 

We are talking about France, of course. They are having to spend dollars to do it. I do not mean entirely; they may be able to get some of the equipment, for instance, for a fiber plant or mill or whatever it may be; or refinery for petroleum production, or whatever they may use in a crude-steel mill, with franc expenditure. Much of such equipment must, however, come from the dollar areas. Some of it must come from the United States. Now, that being the case, it means a widening of the dollar gap because they are either spending ECA dollars or they are spending dollars they already have. Am I correct that far? 

Mr. BINGHAM. Yes.

Mr. BURLESON. We have been talking about this dollar gap for quite a while and probably will continue to do so. That seems to be of great concern all around the world. Up to that point, we have widened the dollar gap. Then, the products produced must sell in a dollar area to get back those dollars and sell more in order to close that dollar gap; is that correct? 

Mr. BINGHAM. They must sell more in the dollar area and increase their tourist receipts from the dollar area. 

Mr. BURLESON. He may sell a few lottery tickets over here. 

Mr. BINGHAM. He must sell something.

Mr. BURLESON. I am talking about those dollars they have put out and then must get back by export sales. That is as much as I can understand about this thing, but it is fundamental. How are they going to do that? I am thinking beyond 1952 when they are going to be self-sustaining. What are they selling and where are they selling it?

Mr. BINGHAM. I have a list of the principal French dollar-earning products which might be of interest to you. The French are selling a number of things in this country, most of which are noncompetitive with American products. There is a certain number of lines of French production which are historically attractive to the American market. 

They have not pushed those products, I think, nearly as hard as they might do. They are beginning to make a much greater effort in the dollar market than they had made previously. They have formed their franc-dollar committee, of which I spoke, to try to increase their sales to this country and they are now offering exceptional inducements to the producer who sells for dollars. They are going to allow the producer, for instance, who sells for dollars to retain 3 percent of his dollar earnings to use in any way he wants to use them. He will be able to buy whatever he wants to buy with that 3 percent of his dollar earnings. That, I believe, will be a decided inducement to the French producer to sell in the dollar area rather than sell in some other market which may be an easier one.

Now, there are three sources from which the French can obtain dollars in the future to cover their continued dollar needs. One, of course, is from exports to the dollar area. Another is receipts from tourism, dollar receipts, and a third would be receipts from dollar investments in France. Now, that third area is not at the moment a large one at all. The dollar investments in France since the end of the war have only amounted to about $23,000,000, but I hope that they will increase in the next few years.

They are now earning $110,000,000 a year by exports. They have $50,000,000 a year by tourism and they hope to get that up to $110,000,000. That may be a small matter to everyone except the Coca-Cola people, but that may be an example of some more of these trade barriers. Now, what do you think their attitude is going to be toward removing trade barriers in Europe and outside Europe?

1 2. Mr. BINGHAM. I think the French are convinced there must be a removal of artificial barriers for a liberal flow of trade among European countries. They fully realize there is no future for their own economy unless it can be a part of a larger European economy. 

France, as I have been saying, has gone ahead tremendously on production since the Marshall plan program got into operation, but they have to have somewhere to sell those products. 

I think they are fully conscious of the fact that they can only sell them in a larger European market. They have taken the lead in the removal of quantitative restrictions on imports, which is one of the artificial barriers to trade. 

As you know, there has now been an agreement whereby 50 percent of those restrictions have been removed. The French have already offered to go ahead with a removal of 60 percent in the near future and 75 percent of the quantitative restrictions to be removed by the end of this year. 

Mr. BURLESON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

many, and the field in which they have done it is the obvious one to begin with, which is the economic field. 

Mr. VORYS. In this country we say that two-thirds of all of our imports are on the free list, when anybody talks about tariff, and then one of these free traders says, "Yes, but that is the unimportant twothirds. What about this other third?" I had wondered about that 50 percent quantitative elimination of restrictions in Europe, whether it is the important 50 percent or whether the other half that is still restricted is the key to the thing. Is there an analogy that could be made between the two situations: our free list and the 50-percent free list over there?

Mr. BINGHAM. I think there is some analogy, Mr. Vorys. I suppose it is human that each country confronted with the necessity for taking off 50 percent of its quantitative restrictions, took off those quantitative restrictions which would cause the least howl from interests within their own nation. There are both agricultural and industrial interests in France which are very much frightened of free competition and obviously it is not politically popular to go into the areas represented by those industries. However, the French seem to me to be determined to go ahead with this liberalization, even though it is going to cause a great outcry from certain elements in French life. That is something that must be faced. It is something that is not going to be easy to get through with, because each man who feels that he may lose his job because of liberalization of trade, is going to be very unhappy about that, regardless of the fact that it may be for the future welfare of his country. And the French have got, I think, a hard job to do there but they seem determined to do it.

At the same time they are trying to develop off-the-beaten-path types of tourist attractions in France. al રા into that to a considerable extent when I was in France a year or so ago, and I was impressed at that time with the fact that while our people were working hard and were doing as good a job as they could with what they had, by and large the French were not paying too much attention to what we were saying about the purposes of the Marshall plan. Mr. BINGHAM. Let me answer the limited portion of the question first, as to cooperation with USIS. We have a large degree of cooperation with USIS operations in France and I think it is a successful operation. That exists both in Paris and in the regional offices which 

USIS operates. They have six regional offices in France where they are constantly giving out Marshall plan material, where they are arranging for speakers to appear, and where they are doing everything they can to help us get out the information we want to get to the French people. I think that cooperation is as good as it can be. 

Mr. LODGE. I was very much impressed with that cooperation. 

Mr. BINGHAM. I would like to say something about the information problem in France. It is an extremely interesting and delicate situation. The French have a very strong allergy to propaganda as you know, and they sometimes tend to confuse what we would call information with what they would call propaganda.

I think part of that is based on their experience during the occupation. At that time they were very heavily propagandized by both the Germans and by their own Vichy government. 

Mr. LODGE. But we should, in my opinion, make maximum use of their own vehicles of propaganda. That was one of the matters which we discussed. I think one of the good things which is being done in 

London is making maximum use of the British media. We should do the same thing in France in order to get away from the disadvantages of advertising the United States source. 

Mr. BINGHAM. There is not always a complete reliance on the part of the French in information they receive from their own Government. 

I think that is partly due to this effort the Vichy government made to propagandize France.

At the same time you will remember that the German master race had an idea for quite a while that they would be able to bring France into the happy German circle of nations. They actually thought they could convince the French to come voluntarily into this German master world. They propagandized the French very heavily in that direction. They were much disappointed in the results, but they left the 

French, I think, with a lasting distaste for certain methods of publicity. 

Now, those methods of publicity in America, where they deal with strictly information subjects, we think are perfectly all right. The 

French are somewhat suspicious of them. They are very suspicious if they come from an outside agency. They are even suspicious if they

come from the Government itself. That has interfered in the last few years with the effort of the French Government to give information to its own people. Not only information about the Marshall plan but information about everything. However, there has been a distinct improvement in the last few months in that field. Since the 

Bidault government came into office last November, I feel we are getting a much better degree of cooperation from the French on information. They have done a number of things which I would like to mention very briefly: For instance, they have put out three pamphlets recently. One of them was entitled "The Road to Peace," the one I mentioned a while ago, which is an excellent effort, I think. 

They are giving that very wide circulation. They are devoting five weekly radio shows on the national radio system there to Marshallplan material. They are putting out a number of films. They are distributing six documentary films which we have made and there are several more documentaries now being produced. That is also being done with the cooperation, as you see, of the French Government itself.

They are doing a number of other things in the information field which they did not undertake before, which I think are meeting with a very good reaction from the French people. It is very pleasing to me to see how it is working out. One of the things I particularly want to mention is the marking of counterpart projects. When I say "counterpart projects" I mean large dams, schools, hospitals, things of that kind, which are being built or rebuilt in France, with the use of Marshall-plan counterpart. The French Government has recently started a series of ceremonies at a number of these projects at which they put a marble or bronze tablet on the project which will stay there for all time as a testimonial of what we have done to help this French effort. I would like to read the wording of one of these typical tablets. This was a tablet erected recently on a dam in southern 

France, a very large project. Here is the way it reads: 

The Bimont Dam, whose waters will bring fertility and richness to 50 communities in the Rhone and Var Valleys has been built by the Bouches Du Rhone Department with the help of the Ministry of Agriculture and thanks to the generous aid of ERP furnished by the United States of America. 

A number of those ceremonies took place before I left. I participated in them and I will participate in a lot more after I go back. 

They are already scheduled.

Mr. LODGE. There was one particular problem which came to my attention while I was there and that is that there are three specific Communist publications, newspapers, I think, which were receiving at that time no rebuttal by the French, I mean specific rebuttal. Mr. BINGHAM. To mention the first one you took up, the Communist publication directed toward the farmer, that is a very serious thing,

when the Communists begin to make serious inroads into the French farm population which is essentially a Conservative population if ever there was one in the world. 

There was recently started a publication called La Terre Nouvelle directed toward the farmer which tells our side of the story.

Mr. BINGHAM. The Government does not participate directly in that effort.

We are doing another thing in the agricultural field while we are talking about that one. We have an agricultural exhibit which we have sent over a large portion of France. It is a touring exhibit on wheels.

Mr. LODGE. A mobile unit. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Several of them, in fact. They go into the farm communities and rural areas of France where people do not go to the movies, do not read a great many newspapers, and are rather out of touch with things. That touring exhibit has had great success. It started out up in Normandy on the anniversary of the landings there and has toured all through northern France. It is now headed south and will tour a large part of the southern and western areas of France during this year. It has had a signal success in attracting interest to our story of what is happening there.

You will find by the way a good many pictures and some figures and facts on this information effort in a blue-covered book which is there before you. This will give you some idea of the scope of the effort we are making.

We have a mobile exhibit for labor similar to the agricultural exhibit which I just mentioned, which is starting on the road this month. 

Now that is going into industrial areas where, of course, the Communists have also made a very strong effort to misrepresent everything the Marshall plan has done in France. This will be a factual presentation of what ECA has been able to do in that country in conjunction, of course, with the effort the French people have made themselves. 

That theme is always brought in. I hope that will be equally effective in counteracting some of the Communist propaganda.

Communist newspapers of Paris have lost about 30 percent of their circulation in the past year. 

Mr. LODGE. That is good.

Mr. BINGHAM. Also some of the former daily publications sponsored by the Communists in other parts of France have now become weekly publications. There is a distinct weakness in communism in 

France upon which I hope we can capitalize during 1950.

Mr. VORYS. I am much impressed with what you are doing and with what as you say the French are doing. I have not been over there for a while, but I hear a lot of returning travelers say that the French people still have no genuine appreciation of the Marshall plan. 

What would be your comment on that? Have you any way in which that could be answered both with your opinion and with any evidence you might submit? Do the French people seem to have a genuine appreciation of the Marshall plan and the ECA program? 

Mr. BINGHAM. The most recent poll taken in France by the Gallup people showed that 88 percent of the people of France knew about the Marshall plan. They were aware of its operations there. That is a figure that is comparable to the highest figures in any of the other 

Marshall-plan countries.

We have been collecting, of course, the references to ECA which have been appearing in the press in France to get some idea of how much coverage we are getting. That amounts to about 3,000 stories a week in the provincial press of France, that outside of Paris, about 3,000 stories a week. In Paris we get about 250 stories a week in the press about the Marshall plan. That is really quite an extraordinary coverage. Of course, everybody in France does not read a newspaper. 

There are many people in France who get their information from other sources. That is why we are trying to develop the media of radio, of posters, and of films. In all of those areas we are making very strong efforts to reach the people in France who might not ordinarily hear about our story.

Now I think there are some definite evidences that we are getting to these people. For instance, at our mission we have about 4,500 letters a week from French people writing us about our program. 

That is a far larger figure than any other mission receives. A very large proportion of those letters express gratitude for what the Marshall plan has done for France. Many of them ask for further information. They ask for some of our publications such as the pamphlet we have discussed here or some other. There is evidently a great awareness on the part of the French people of the existence of the Marshall plan and what it has done. 

In some instances the traveler who comes through France does not see that so obviously. I think one reason may be that in France it does not seem wise to do things like putting a great number of posters or a lot of flashy neon signs around indicating what ECA is doing for France. That is a technique that I think would backfire in that

country. They simply are not accustomed to American publicity techniques, so we try to do it there in a somewhat quieter, but I believe more effective way, and I believe we are beginning to reach the goal. 

There is another aspect of that program which I ought to mention just briefly. It is perhaps a negative one, but I think more and more people in France are becoming aware of what would have happened in their country had we not come in there with Marshall-plan aid. 

Now, the cotton textile industry, for instance, is a tremendous employer in France. They get 70 percent of their raw material from the dollar area, through Marshall-plan aid. If they did not get that raw material, they would simply be out of work. Those factories would be closing down and hundreds of thousands of French workers would be threatened with unemployment.

I think those workers are becoming increasingly aware of the fact that their jobs do depend on the Marshall plan, that we have been able to keep them at work. The Communists have constantly tried to impress on the French worker that ECA means unemployment. 

That is one of those big lies such as Hitler used to tell, and attempt to repeat so often that people would believe it. But it is so palpably untrue in terms of French economy that I believe more and more of the people of France are becoming aware of how big a lie that is.

Mr. VORYS. In your first statement I understood you to say the textile industry was the largest single group of workers. 

Mr. BINGHAM. The textile industry as a whole. I was speaking of the cotton group at this moment. 

Mr. VORYS. I notice the pamphlet which impressed me so much used the textile industry as an example. It should be very helpful in getting the story across. 

Mr. BINGHAM. There are nearly 1,000,000 people in France concerned with the textile industry and I think this will be particularly effective with them.

Chairman KEE. Has there been any great fluctuation in wage scales in France for labor? During inflationary periods? Any rise in the wage scale?

Mr. BINGHAM. The wages have been controlled in France ever since 

1940. They have just recently removed those controls, but in general the wage scale, plus social-security payments, has roughly kept up with the increase in the cost of living in France brought about by inflation. At times there have been large and rather sudden increases in money wage scales in France. At one time there was a 60-percent increase accorded by Government decree to the French workers to meet the very steep rise in the cost of living. But again I think it is worth noting that that rise in the cost of living in France is now leveling off satisfactorily. 

Chairman KEE. Is there anything further, Mr. Vorys? 

Mr. VORYS. I have nothing further, Mr. Chairman.

Since military operations naturally involve security factors, the question can be answered only in general terms. safe to say that the magnitude of shipments of arms from the United Kingdom to Egypt, Iraq, and Transjordan has not been such as to involve disruption of From information generally available, it is the rising pattern of British production. To the extent that such transfers have involved war surpluses, they have not constituted a burden on the current stream of production or exports. There is no discernible significant effect upon the dollar gap which should be attributed to such shipments. (See p. 133.)

The ECA defines dollar viability as the attainment of that situation in which a country can, by its own efforts, balance its dollar accounts at a satisfactory internal standard of living and with a rate of capital formation high enough to enable it to maintain its consumption and improve the competitive position of its exports in the world market. This is a complicated definition, and I should like to discuss each of its elements separately in an effort to make it clearer. 

The ECA has defined a satisfactory standard of living as the achievement and maintenance of the prewar per capita level of consumption in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Largely because of the increase in population and the destruction and lack of replacement of housing and consumers' durable goods during and since the war, the restoration of a prewar per capita living standard requires that a larger total volume of goods and services be devoted to consumption than was the case before the war. 

Once achieved, the maintenance of a satisfactory per capita standard of living depends in large part upon the attainment of a permanently satisfactory rate of productivity increase. sults mainly from an adequate level of capital investment, or capital formation, Such a satisfactory rate of productivity increase rein Europe. Both capital formation and the resulting increase in productivity will have to be large enough to provide consumers' goods and services for an increasing population and to keep pace with the improvement of productivity in other parts of the world, especially in those producing countries whose exports compete with western Europe's in world markets. So much for the internal aspect of the definition of dollar viability.

Turning now to the external aspect of dollar viability, the ECA considers that western Europe must earn through the sale of its goods and services enough dollars to enable it to buy the imports which it requires for maintaining its production, consumption, and investment at the necessary levels. This require-

ment is made more complicated by the fact that the key element is not the adequacy of total exports but the value of those exports which are sold for dollars or for currencies which can be converted into gold or dollars. Consequently, the external aspect of the definition of dollar viability must be qualified by the fact that all currencies are not now, and are not likely to be in the foreseeable future, freely convertible into dollars. In order to attain dollar viability, therefore western Europe must earn enough dollars or currencies convertible into dollars through the sale of its exports of goods and services to enable it to import from the dollar area at least those minimum quantities of dollar goods and services which are essential for the achievement of the internal aspects of the definition of dollar viability outlined above. 

The criteria by which ECA judges viability, therefore, have both an internal and an external aspect. It is possible for a country to balance its dollar accounts without achieving or maintaining either a satisfactory level of per capita consumption or a satisfactory rate of capital formation. It is also possible for a country to have satisfactory consumption and investment levels without being able to balance its dollar accounts. In neither case, however, could such countries be considered to have achieved dollar viability. Both aspect of the definition must be satisfied if the country is to be judged to have attained dollar viability. ?

 We are continuing our hearings today upon the ECA measure. We have with us Mr. Roscoe Drummond.

STATEMENT OF ROSCOE DRUMMOND, CHIEF, INFORMATION DIVI- SION, OFFICE OF SPECIAL REPRESENTATIVE, ECA, PARIS Mr. DRUMMOND. I am Director of Information for the ECA in 

Europe.

I have not prepared a formal statement, but I thought it would perhaps be agreeable to the committee if I describe the scope and character of our information program. 

Chairman KEE. That will be entirely satisfactory. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I assume it is not an offense to be brief, and I do not intend to go into more details than are reasonably necessary. I will make available to the committee a full and detailed presentation of what we are doing.

Chairman KEE. You will furnish that as a written statement for the use of the committee. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Yes. 

Chairman KEE. That will be kept available in the office of the committee.

Mr. DRUMMOND. I would like to begin by saying there are two principal instruments which the ECA overseas information program has and which are peculiar to the Marshall plan. One is the instrument of the bilateral treaties and the other is the instrument of counterpart funds. The bilateral treaties make it possible for us to obtain from the European governments a kind of full-size cooperation in telling the Marshall plan story that would not be otherwise possible. The counterpart funds make it possible to carry on an educational campaign of magnitude and energy, the major cost of which comes out of foreign currency. I think it is fair to say that at the present time four-fifths of our expenditures are in foreign currency and not more than one-fifth in dollars. 323

I think I can report to you carefully that the story of the Marshall plan is getting over to the European people, and I think there are numerous evidences of that fact. 

I would like to begin by saying that it would be unfair to claim for the information program primary credit for the favorable climate which exists among the great majority of European people toward the European recovery program. I think the favorable climate first stems from the evidence of recovery, from the program itself, and second, it stems from the determination of the people of Europe to get back on their feet. Thus the information program is really a part of the recovery effort and joins forces with the determination which is manifest among the European people to become independent of outside aid. 

I would like to emphasize that the information program is geared to serve the principal objectives of the European recovery program and is, therefore, focused on very concrete goals. One is to help overcome the psychological obstacles which might otherwise stand in the way of ERP's attaining its purposes. It is for this reason that, in addition to telling the direct story of American aid and American motives behind the Marshall plan we are using information to promote economic integration. That is perhaps the prime theme of 194950 in Europe, as part of our information program. We are using information to fight inflation, to teach better methods of production in both agriculture and industry, and by and large to hold up to the people of Europe a prospect and a vision of a secure Europe and a selfsupporting Europe and a Europe in which the United States is deeply interested.

I would like to explain certain problems with which we are faced. 

One is we are dealing with a continent that extends 5,000 miles. It is made up of 270,000,000 people speaking 14 different languages. That is one reason why it has to be an ambitious program to meet its objectives, and it is a program the cost of which can be paid mainly by the counterpart funds. You are probably aware that the people of 

Europe really receive an overdose of publicity and propaganda during the totalitarian regimes and during the French occupation. That has been a factor which had to be overcome by our demonstrating that in the Marshall plan's educational campaign in Europe we are dealing with fact and with a faithful report of what is going on. 

There have been many evidences of the returning confidence in Europe. There have been many evidences that the European people are rejecting police state concepts and are turning from Communist pressures at every opportunity that they have to choose. There has been not a single election since the beginning of the Marshall plan in which the people of Europe have not rejected communism. I think that rejection in large part rests upon the feeling of hope and faith that has come from European recovery and from an increasing awareness of what American assistance has meant to them. 

I would like to deal quite briefly with our principal tools of information. First I would like to say a word about the press in Europe: 

The press in Europe is the principal arm of communication. There are 2,000 daily newspapers in the Marshall plan countries, and they have a total circulation of 110,000,000 Europeans. At the present time these 2,000 daily newspapers are publishing a total of 4,000 Marshallplan news articles on an average every week. That is double the coverage of the Marshall plan that prevailed a year ago.

Chairman KEE. Are those articles supplied by your organization? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. They are supplied from three different sources, primarily. They are supplied in part by the ECA missions in each country; in part by our over-all information organization in Paris, and in equal part by the newspapers' own interest and own staff attention to what the Marshall plan is doing. 

Our best estimate is that approximately 7 out of every 8 newspapers of Europe are friendly to the Marshall plan. Since it is in the field of the press in which the Communist opposition to the Marshall plan is so greatly expressed, I would like to give you a brief report on the nature of the Communist opposition: At a distance it is understandable that what the Communists are up to may look sort of theoretical, but we are up against it in fact, and I would like to tell you a little about it. 

The official position of the Cominform was stated by General Zhdanov when he said, "The U. S. S. R. will put all effort in seeing that the Marshall plan is not realized." And as you know when the first 

Marshall plan organization committee was held in Paris, Mr. Molotov walked out of that conference and beckoned the satellite states to join him and stay away.

It is in France and Italy that you have the principal Communist opposition. As a case study I thought you might be interested in a few facts about the way the Communists go about their opposition in France and the means that they can use. 

There are Communist daily newspapers for every influential group in France. There are special papers for farmers, for intellectuals, for maritime workers, for miners, for young people, and for women. There are Communist papers in France printed in German and for the Alsace-Lorraine, for the Mediterranean coast, for mountain regions. 

There are large Communist daily newspapers, picture magazines, and political publications. There are 20 Communist daily newspapers in 

France alone with a total circulation of 1.7 million. There are 97 

Communist weeklies and 8 monthly Communist magazines. 

Mr. GORDON. May I ask a question there?

Mr. DRUMMOND. Yes. 

Mr. GORDON. Is that free distribution?

Mr. DRUMMOND. Those are sold. That is their paid circulation. 

Mr. PFEIFER. How does that compare with the general newspapers in France?

Mr. DRUMMOND. There are general newspapers of larger circulation, but in Paris, for example, L'Humanite is the principal French Communist daily newspaper, and it has a circulation of about 275,000. 

You may be interested in just a word about Communist finances in France. It has some bearing on what we ourselves invest in information. Perhaps it has or has not come to your attention that at the end of the war the French Communists seized 15 billion francs from the treasury of the Vichy government and that this was the nest egg which is financing Communist efforts to wreck recovery in France at the present time.

This nest egg, which is a sizable one, is supplemented by party membership dues, subscription income from publications, fund-raising drives, and contributions from members of the party who are elected to public office which run as high as 30 percent of their salaries. It is our estimate, which can be no more than an estimate, drawn from

French labor people who have reasonably close insight into Communist activity, that they are spending approximately $15,000,000 in France each year, which means that the Communist Party as a national political party would be spending $60,000,000 in the 4 years of the Marshall plan alone. 

Chairman KEE. Is that being used to defeat the purposes of the 

Marshall plan?

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is used at every opportunity to create opposition and help generate the kind of political strikes which have been going on in France in the past 10 days. The two principal targets of the Communists in France today are, (1) the military assistance program, and (2) the Marshall plan. When they are not attacking one they are attacking the other, or both simultaneously. 

Mr. EATON. What is their ground of attack on the Marshall plan? 

What is their chief ground?

Mr. DRUMMOND. Their chief allegations are (1) that the Marshall plan is doing nothing, and (2) that it is succeeding so well that it is turning France into a satellite of the United States. They do not necessarily have to be consistent. 

Mr. EATON. Do they have both of those statements in the same paper at the same time?

Mr. DRUMMOND. They try to avoid putting them in the same paper but they do not try to reconcile them very much. 

I worked out another expression of the extent of Communist opposition in France that you might be interested to note in passing. I have heard some say that this Communist menace in France is something dreamed up in order to scare us. I would like to just mention that if the Communists had the same strength in the United States that they have in France, as reflected by two facts: (1) The number of 

Communist Deputies in the French Parliament, and (2) the size of the Communist vote in the last national French election, the postwar election, then these conditions would prevail in America: There would be 23 Communist Senators in the United States Senate. There would be 124 Communist Members of the United States House of Representatives, and there would have been 14,000,000 Communist votes cast in the last presidential election.

That is something of the magnitude and nature of the kind of Communist opposition which we are combating in France, and I think as Mr. Shishkin will testify, combating very significantly and very successfully in the field of French labor. But it is not a small opposition and it ought to be recognized, I think, just for what it is worth. 

Now I am going to say a few things, if I may, about our concrete information tools. I told you in the field of press coverage we are obtaining about twice as much attention to the Marshall plan as a year ago and I think fairly substantial attention. 

In the field of radio we have received outstanding assistance from the participating governments, so that at the present time Marshall plan radio programs are going out over the national networks of all of the 18 participating countries and reaching, according to our best appraisal, approximately 40,000,000 out of a potential of 100,000,000 

European radio listeners.

In the field of radio we are utilizing the most successful techniques of American commercial radio. We are developing special radio programs of a dramatic content, of a music content, and of an entertain-

1 ment content, and in connection with these programs we include accounts of the recovery effort. We include expositions of how Europeans can make the Marshall plan more successful for them, and I think it is fair to say that one of the reasons why the Marshall plan radio programs are being accepted by the radio networks of Europe is that they are interesting, audience-appealing programs and are not such as would cause the listener to turn the dial when he listens to them. 

I would like to mention in passing that one of our radio programs called This is Europe, which has been used in the United States by the Mutual Broadcasting Co. and made available to them at their request, has been nominated by the Mutual Broadcasting Co. for the Peabody radio award. That is comparable in radio to a Pulitzer award, and the program has been nominated as the one best conceived to promote international good will.

I fear that some of my statements sound immodest, and I would like to say quickly with all the emphasis that I can, that without the qualified specialists in the field of films, radio, motion pictures, and exhibits, there is nothing a director of information can do. In addition, our concern for the coming year is to extend and deepen the understanding of the European people of what the American people are doing in their behalf and to create a state of mind in Europe which will be most receptive to European integration in order to secure and strengthen the recovery which has already been attained.

Mr. DRUMMOND. In my judgment, if gratitude is not to be taken for granted it cannot be created by propaganda. Gratitude is not something to build on. I believe understanding is something to build on. I believe European respect for what we are doing and why we are doing it is important. In the interests of trying to find out as nearly as possible the different states of mind in Europe about the Marshall plan, we have utilized the best available professional means of measuring public opinion in the different countries. I, for one, quite appreciate that public-opinion polls involve imponderables and do not present anything approaching precise information, but I am inclined to believe it is best to use professional methods rather than to attempt to poll 10 people on the street corner or to ask somebody in the Crillon bar in Paris what he thinks of the Marshall plan. 

European public-opinion polls here shown indicate these results: 

That more than four out of five Europeans show themselves aware of the Marshall plan, that from a quarter to a third of them have a detailed understanding of how the program works and can actually explain the operation of the counterpart fund, which I think is quite a measure of the understanding of the Marshall plan. 

I do not embarrass my friends in Washington by asking them to explain the counterpart fund.

PUBLIC OPINION RESEARCH 

The ultimate test of success or failure of an information program is its effect upon the thinking and behavior of the people to whom it is addressed. The measurement of these effects is a difficult problem but one for which scientific techniques of at least approximate accuracy have been developed in recent years. 

Systematic surveys have been used by ECA to test public opinion and the level of information about the recovery program. They provide the basis for the following careful conclusions: 

1. More than four out of five Europeans are aware of the Marshall plan. 

2. From a quarter to a third of them have some detailed understanding of the program and how it works. 

3. A majority in most countries unqualifiedly approves the program and only relatively minor percentages are unqualifiedly opposed. 

4. The total of those favorable to the program has steadily gone up during the past year and is still rising. 

The charts on the opposite page present these findings in greater detail. 

Considerations of good management and intelligent allocation of emphasis in the overseas information program would, in any case, have made it desirable to resort to the use of scientific field surveys. But because of existing European conditions in which we are attempting to give honest information a fair chance to compete with systematically propagated lies and slander, it has been absolutely mandatory to make use of such surveys as well as the most up-to-date techniques which have been developed in the United States in the varied fields of education, advertising, promotion, and marketing.

There has been some disillusionment with public-opinion surveys in the United States since the last Presidential election, especially among those who had been inclined to place complete trust not only in specific percentages but also in the

inferences and interpretations to which the figures seemed superficially to lead. 

ECA experience has been that surveys within a reasonable margin of errors provide vitally important clues about the weak and strong points of the information program as well as valuable assistance in locating trouble spots. The evaluation of these clues and the determination of action to be taken on the basis of them obviously requires the application of many kinds of information and the broadest possible judgment and experience. 

As a partial guide in selecting effective themes and determining the relative emphasis to be given various elements of the information program, surveys have been conducted in several key countries since mid 1949. 

In each country cross-sections of the adult population were taken, employing the interviewing and sampling methods accepted as standard by American polling organizations. Roughly 2,000 persons were interviewed in each country, representing the total population on the bases of geographical distribution, size of locality, age, sex, occupation, income, and social group. 

The polling has been conducted by private, independent research organizations in order to insure both technical competence and complete objectivity. 

The significance of the fact that about 90 percent of the people in the countries surveyed are aware of the Marshall plan, is difficult to evaluate, except on a comparative basis. Students of public opinion agree that such a level of general information is seldom attained in the field of public affairs. It compares broadly with the proportion of people in the United States who know about the United Nations and who, during the war, knew about the Treasury's war-bond campaigns.

The surveys did not stop with a measure of awareness but probed more deeply for the extent of detailed knowledge about the recovery program. 

On questions of fact, such as whether people who receive materials under the Marshall plan get them free or have to pay for them, an average of well above 60 percent of the populations gave the correct answers. On still more detailed questions about the nature of counterpart funds, an average of about 35 percent gave the correct answers.

In order to bring the information program into sharp focus on the most important problems, it has been useful to analyze by social groups the data collected. Such break-downs have made it possible to locate centers if misinformation, misunderstanding, and opposition. Generally speaking, it was found that the oldest people in all countries are among the less well informed, and women in all countries are somewhat less well informed than men. There is a great variation from country to country, however, and any generalization is subject to qualification. Norwegian women, for example, are nearly as well informed as Norwegian men, but Dutch women are markedly less well informed than Dutch men. Everywhere the least educated and the very poor are among the least informed.

Of the occupational groups, wage earners are somewhat less informed than the average.

OPPOSITION TO THE PLAN 

Outright opposition represents only 5 to 9 percent of the population in the surveyed countries with the exception of France. There, opposition to ERP remains about 16 percent, and, while composed largely of Communists, it also reflects the general dissatisfaction with governmental instability. However, current public-opinion polls indicate that considerable progress has been made in France during the past 8 months. The percentage of French people with a general knowledge of the Marshall plan has risen from 87 percent in June 1949 to 93 percent in February of this year. Even more significantly, 52 percent of the French people today wholeheartedly applaud the results of ECA aid; a figure fully supported by more than 4,000 letters received by the French mission every week.

An average of about 70 percent of the people in all countries expressed full approval of the Marshall plan. The remainder cannot be considered as opposed since there are from 10 to 20 percent who see both good and bad sides to the program, and another 10 percent who do not express an opinion. 

In general there is a small hard core of Communist opposition in each country which is reinforced very often by groups of retired old people. The latter seem to be more disgruntled than opposed, and their attitude toward the Marshall plan possibly reflects a negative point of view that would extend to many public issues. 

There is evidence that young people are more enthusiastic in support of the

Marshall plan than the old. Support for the plan is also particularly strong among the liberal professions and intellectual groups. 

It cannot be assumed, of course, that awareness or even general favor for the recovery program necessarily implies sufficient understanding of its objectives, and real appreciation of the steps that must be taken by individuals and governments in order to carry recovery forward. That a well-informed, hopeful, and cohesive population can do a better job of working its way to permanent recovery than a confused, ignorant, and despairing population, is self-evident. However, before information begins to make a measurable difference in the potential productivity of an area it must have penetrated to the point where individuals are clearly aware of the goals to be achieved, their self-interest in achieving them and the means by which they as individuals can contribute effectively to the common effort. There remains a great deal to be done by their individual leaders, private groups, and governments before these psychological conditions will prevail in Europe.

Mr. DRUMMOND. There is one other statistic which I think is important. In France, in 1945, the Communists polled 29 percent of the total popular vote in France. The Communists are implacably and totally opposed to the Marshall plan and, as you know, adherence to the Communist Party means adherence to its views. 

Our evidence from our poll in France shows that only 16 percent of the French people are unqualifiedly opposed to the Marshall plan as compared to the 29 percent who voted Communist in 1945. 

I think that represents not merely the impact of the information program, but the impact of the European recovery program on the thinking and the political loyalties of the French people. These are some of the evidences of the effect of the educational campaign that we are carrying out.
