STATEMENT OF BORIS SHISHKIN, CHIEF, LABOR DIVISION, OFFICE OF SPECIAL REPRESENTATIVE, ECA, PARIS 

Mr. SHISHKIN. I hope the committee will attach no significance to the fact that I will take a chair one notch to the left of Mr. Drummond. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Drummond is supplying us with a complete written statement for the use of the committee. 

Mr. SHISHKIN. Mr. Chairman, my name is Boris Shishkin. I am Director of the European Labor Division of the ECA, with head quarters in Paris, and am responsible for the operating phase of the European program in the labor field. 

I am very happy to have an opportunity to return once again to appear before this committee and give you a progress report since a year ago, and answer such questions as the committee might have. 

A number of the members of this committee have been in Europe and have visited the ECA offices during their survey of European conditions. I think it has been an extremely helpful and useful thing. 

I know that those who have been able to do so, from among the Members of Congress, have gained a much better understanding of the kind of problems with which we are dealing and the difficulty surrounding our task. 

In dealing with the labor program I want to make quite clear from the outset that, as this committee knows, we have a comprehensive, positive program, dealing with the problems of employment, the wage phases, the standards of living, housing, and so on. 

In addition to that, because of the attack against the Marshall plan and because of the penetration politically in western Europe which is relied upon by the Communists in trade unions, we also have a difficult responsibility of holding the hot sector of the cold war. 

With very limited resources, it has not been an easy task. 

Very briefly, Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say a few words about the way our work is organized and the problems we are dealing with, to give you a very brief report on the progress in our work and the

21 progress of recovery insofar as it affects the workers, and indicate a few areas of particular concern and interest as far as the immediate future is concerned.

The work of the ECA, in the labor phase of the program, is under the general responsibility of two labor advisers to Mr. Hoffman here, Mr. Bert M. Jewell and Mr. Clinton Golden, our top labor advisers with headquarters here in Washington. With their very limited staff, they have provided us with a very essential and important backing in our work in Europe by maintaining close contacts with the tradeunion field. These two have given us invaluable help in enabling us to operate as we have.

Chairman KEE. Will you please state at this point in the record the general character of your employment and the part you take in the effort?

Mr. SHISHKIN. As Director of the Labor Division, I have a small staff in Paris which has two major responsibilities, involving first all the major questions of economic policy with which the ECA is concerned; and secondly broad discussions of policy with the OEEC. As head of one of the major divisions of the ECA in Europe, it is my responsibility to advise the Ambassador on those questions and to review the program proposed. Too, the affirmative program we are doing is again divided into two parts. One has to do with the employment problems, the dislocations of manpower which do exist in Europe, the assurance that the purposes of the act in the employment field are carried out. 

This involves the formulation and development in European cooperation of a number of major programs that are completely new in the European field. The work to facilitate the movement of workers in Europe, the assistance in the settlement of displaced persons and refugees, also falls on our shoulders. The work in connection with such forms of aid and their direction to the source, as well as vitalizing the economic cooperation, mutual assistance, and self-help in the European countries to supplement the kinds of things we do, all fall within this category.

In addition to that, there is a major responsibility of building up direct relations with the European trade-unions. Our immediate responsibility in Paris is to deal with them at the international level. 

The ERP Trade-Union Advisory Committee, the newly formed In ternational Confederation of Trade-Unions, the international trade secretariats, are all working closely with us. They are supporting the 

Marshall plan. The ERP Trade-Unions Advisory Committee acting in an advisory capacity to the OEEC to insure European labor support and active participation in the formulation of the recovery program is also within the purview of our responsibility. 

In addition, the work that Mr. Drummond has described here includes a labor information program. It is headed in Paris by Harry 

Martin, who is the president of the American Newspaper Guild, and is an experienced newspaperman, having a staff of people in Labor Information.

Labor Information and the Labor Division work extremely close together and supplement each other. 63307-50-pt. 2- -7

We have, in 11 countries out of 16, labor officers in individual missions, and it is our responsibility to see that they are not operating in isolation, but that they are given guidance from our office. 

On the political aspect of the program, we are very keenly aware of the fact that the Communists are organizing their attack on unions, not in any individual area, not in any one country, but across international borders. It is for us to know where the attack is coming from and what form it will take in order to counter it by the kind of mutuality of information that we are developing. 

The picture, as it stands today, I think, is extremely encouraging. 

We have, broadly, this kind of a situation insofar as the ECA is concerned: We have made a tremendous degree of progress during the past 2 years in achieving the essentials of economic recovery. Those are economic stability, stopping of the inflation, and all the things that go with it, that give the psychological change to the mass of European workers, from the kind of despair in which they were plunged 2 years ago, in which there was lack of goods and inability to buy even the most bare essentials of life and inability to eat properly, people freezing in the winter, and things of that sort. They have been accompanied by this kind of thing, which has been disastrous: The rise in prices of the consumer goods and the familiar inflationary spiral meant that the wages paid to the workers were diminishing from week to week. That kind of thing has removed every incentive to work, to operate, to hope for the kind of reconstruction which ECA has made possible.

Today with ECA aid inflation has been checked. There is assurance and confidence. There is stability. The levels of living among the 

European workers by and large are still low. It is partly due to the fact that a very large proportion of the investment that has been made by the European countries has gone into the capital equipment and the tools and machinery making it necessary to build the foundation for future production.

With the cooperation of most of the trade-union movements-certainly the non-Communist trade-union movement-wage demands have been extremely moderate and, as a matter of fact, trade-unions have helped to withhold the demands for wage increases in order not to jeopardize the economic stability of these countries. 

We are now coming to the turning point in the program. The assurance must be given to the workers that sacrifices they have made to accomplish the recovery that is evident all around Europe is going to provide benefits for the workers as well. There has to be, even though it may be moderate, it may be gradual, it may be restricted, evidence that the wage earners of Europe are sharing in the benefits of the Marshall plan. The kind of wording that is included in the 

ECA legislation, and the kind of wording that we have given in talking to the workers as to what we mean and what we hope to achieve, now have to be backed up by policies and developments which reach the key points, the strategic areas in the economic program in order to make sure that the standard of living, where it is the worst, is improved, and that the major problems are settled in the most critical 

Take, for example, the question of housing. In a number of countries in western Europe a serious housing shortage exists. This is true,

Lot Lade oir eres cted nefe the tall nere read 

ritis

CO is tru despite the considerable amount of building activity made possible with our aid. You have heard Mr. Bingham's testimony about the use of counterpart for the reconstruction part of the program from the French budget, which has gone to a large extent for the construction of homes in the devastated areas of the north in the invasion path. 

For France as a whole, however, it has been an infinitesimal amount of aid as matched against the need. So we have the French economy facing a very serious problem for a country whose population exceeds over 40,000,000 today. From 1947 to 1949, 29,000 dwelling units were constructed, compared with 45,000 units in this year, and according to the present plans 75,000 units will be built in 1950. The need for the most immediate construction of housing in France is at least 10 times as great as the present construction rate to meet the most rugged minimum essential to enable workers not only to have the necessary shelter, but also to move to labor shortage areas. So pro- duction itself and recovery itself depends upon that provision of shelter on a minimum basis for the French workers. 

The important part of the report that I would like to make here on that score is that it has taken us a great deal of time to do such essential things as even to secure the necessary information for guidance as to what the conditions are. Statistical information, the reliable kind of information necessary for action, has not been readily forthcoming and it has taken us time to get that under way. 

So with the proposals already formulated when we have this information, with the work that has been done by the OEEC and the individual countries, most of the action is to be taken in this current year, the calendar year of 1950. 

Insofar as our part of the program is concerned, the workload and the load of the responsibility that we have in ECA will reach its peak probably in the last quarter of this year. We are building up to it, because of the nature of those programs involving manpower problems, involving migration, involving responsibilities which we have assumed, and on which we have really given in a sense a pledge of good faith in carrying them out. I think for this committee it is very important to realize in that sequence of a very narrow range of 4 years, in a pioneer effort in which international cooperation has not been begun, that we are now coming to a time when we have to initiate the major portion of our responsibility and use the remaining time to see that that responsibility is properly administered and discharged. 

In the field of productivity I think we are making a major departure and I want to say a word about that. Back in 1948 the United Kingdom created an Anglo-American Productivity Council. It was proposed by Mr. Hoffman and Sir Stafford Cripps at that time, and later implemented on a private basis with the creation of managementlabor committees both in the United States and the United Kingdom. 

This Council has undertaken a large and very important pioneer program to exchange information in order to improve productivity in Britain. Gaining from the experience of that, we have now ap proached a time in which a program is being launched on the continent on a large scale. 

I cannot overemphasize the importance of this program. No matter what is done in the way of achieving financial balance through fiscal policy, through monetary aid, budgetwise, the ultimate test of the

ability of the European countries to recover, to grow, lies in the kind of production that is accompanied by reductions in cost, reductions in prices, and fair distribution of benefits of productivity. So productivity lies at the root of long-term recovery of Europe and the ability of Europe to become self-sustaining. 

ECA's productivity program has been launched on this principle: 

That in each country there would be a productivity center upon which the country itself would rely. It would be their program and not ours. With that productivity center, in which government, management, and labor would be represented, in which the labor movement of that country contributes to the productivity drive and actively participates in assisting it, it would be possible to exchange technical assistance first among European countries. There are many skills and many forms of technology available in one country and not in another. The OEEC has tried to see to it that mutuality is provided in this.

The United States part of it is also to provide the know-how, the industrial information, the technical information, the contributions by unions as well, to make sure that modern technology is made available to the European experience. 

In connection with that, I just wanted to mention that a productivity center has already been established in Austria, that plans have been formulated in Belgium, in the Netherlands, in Denmark, that a program has been adopted in its major outline in Norway, and a great deal of work is already going on and a good deal of experience has already been gained in France for the exchange of technical information coming from France through the cooperation of the Bingham mission, and the planning commission of the French 

Government. 

I think it is a major program. It is extremely important, I think. 

I think it taxes us to a very minimum degree in cost for the dividends a program of this sort can pay. What we hope for is that after the machinery is established it will be possible to utilize not only government-aided assistance, but also private sources of assistance, private institutions, private firms if you will, private organizations and trade-unions here in the United States and elsewhere, in order to provide that assistance in exchange for the equalization of the standards of production and the standards of living everywhere. 

These are all positive things that we are doing. In one area there has been a particularly difficult and taxing problem which I also want to mention.

We now have not only Italy, which we had last year, where surplus population has been responsible for a large amount of unemployment and where it is a major problem and a major question of economic recovery, but also western Germany in which unemployment has grown, also largely because of the surplus of population. 

In western Germany today there are about 8,000,000 refugees from the east. In the document that I have presented here there is an appendix D, which states in detail the problem of the refugees in western Germany and Austria, including the displaced persons, the Volkedeutsche. It states the best available figures on the numerical distribution as well as an outline of the kind of program we are developing.

Here again we are concerned with the greatest utilization of those people in the reconstruction of Germany. It is largely a problem of their acceptance. They are in places where they cannot find jobs. 

They have to be moved in order to be integrated. 

There is a question of families and dependents, of clique, of women who are not needed in employment because in Germany the distribution of population has been knocked into a cocked hat by the war. 

I mean in their age groups over twenty, for example, there will be six women to one man. In that kind of a thing the demand for employment is not evenly distributed. Also there you have a situation where there is a need for outside migration. 

In Holland unemployment is on a smaller scale. In the Netherlands you will remember that as a result of the settlement in Indonesia there are now some 80,000 Dutch who were stationed in Indonesia, that are on their way to be returned and repatriated to their home country, and for a country the size of the Netherlands to absorb 80,000 people is a taxing problem. 

So the programs we are developing for industrial training, for improvement and coordination of employment services, have all been new in Europe but have all been helpful in dealing with problems of that sort and provide a basis for comprehensive resettlement programs.

The demand for additional workers is dwindling in Europe, itself. 

There is a greater need today than ever before to facilitate migration outside of Europe.

In Latin America, in Australia and some other overseas sections, as well as the overseas dependencies of the participating countries, there is a demand for European workers. 

We have been discussing with the International Labor Organization, as well as the OEEC, a comprehensive program of technical assistance to facilitate overseas migration. Here too I think a relatively small amount of help, compared to the size of the entire program, can be of tremendous benefit to western Europe. Migration is not forthcoming in many places because it is not known where people could properly go. What are the opportunities for employment? How would they fit and qualify in the jobs? The requirements are given. The ILO has experience and equipment in handling these problems.

We have been discussing with the OEEC a program in which we could provide assistance to the OEEC, which in turn would utilize the ILO as an international agency that will enable us to provide pilot projects in which officials could be trained in the receiving countries as well as in the countries of emigration, in order to be better able to direct the flow of migration of that kind. 

In most countries that I have mentioned, particularly, I think there is no question that where you have, particularly in the age group of the younger people, people coming into the labor market without any hope whatsoever of gaining employment, because there are no jobs and because all the jobs are taken, it becomes not only a very serious economic problem, but also an extremely explosive political problem.

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Chairman, would the witness mind an interruption right on that point?

Mr. SHISHKIN. Not at all.

Mr. JAVITS. Would you recommend that we provide anything in the ECA bill in the way of authority to enable the ECA organization to participate in this question of worker migration? 

Mr. SHISHKIN. I think, Mr. Chairman, that as the law now stands, the authority is adequate to cover the kind of a program that we have negotiated and contemplate. It seems to me that if Congress should wish to give particular attention, not to the ECA countries as such, but to other countries in which migration potential might develop, the study of forms of arrangements which can be made with those countries might be extremely useful and appropriate, but I am certainly not competent to discuss that aspect of it at this point. However, I feel that the congressional authority given us, both in the provisions of the Economic Cooperation Act dealing with migration and resettlement, as well as section 121 (a) which authorizes the President to establish cooperative programs with the United Nations and other international organizations, is sufficient. 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want merely to say this: We have a picture in Europe where we have now evidence of progress in the standard of living of the workers in the last 2 years which I think is truly remarkable. I think evidence has been seen by those who visited Europe. It is borne out by the basic facts. Yet we must be keenly aware of the fact that in many of the countries it is not and has not yet been possible to bring the standard of living that results, even though people do have enough to eat, even to the minimum of decency as we understand it. The recovery that has been accomplished so far has to be translated into the improvement of the wage standards, notably in countries where there has been a heavy lag such as France, and borne out by the forms of assistance programs which we have shown are possible and by the kind of cooperation that the European countries have given us. 

I have a series of charts we arranged which I thought might show the kind of progress that has been made in some ERP countries in achieving a balance between wages and retail prices and the type that is needed in some of the others. 

Chart 1 is wage-price trends in Denmark. This left wage bar shows the earnings of the workers and the red one the retail price. 

The earnings have exceeded the rise in retail prices. This shows in 

Denmark which has strongly relied on exports and relied on a heavy austerity program, that it was possible to increase, in the over-all, the earnings of the wage earners.

Chart 2 is Sweden's wage-price trends. I think the same thing is shown in Sweden, and in Norway, where also austerity has been very great, and even in Belgium where the controls and rationing have not been as firmly established. 

On the next chart you see in the United Kingdom there has been also a gain for the wage earners. This means that the rationing controls and distribution in England, which have been severely adhered to, have enabled the workers to improve their real earnings and achieve a somewhat better standard than they had before when they were coming out of very great depths of privation. 

In Ireland the picture is about the same, but the picture indicates considerable stability.

In the next country, Switzerland, which has been least affected by the war, the stability is reflective of the characteristics of the Swiss economy.

In the case of Italy, you have the indication here of the change in the real wages which has been made possible by the kind of defeat of inflation which I mentioned early in my statement. What happened in 1949 was the first time this kind of a picture could be achieved, because before 1949 the cost of living had been rising much faster than wages, and for the first time in 1949 you see that the wage increases have exceeded price rises. However, do not mistake the disparity between the two. This kind of a balance that has been achieved in Italy has been achieved at an extremely low level of earnings.

Mr. SHISHKIN. No; there were few consumer articles rationed in

Mr. JUDD. I was interested that the countries that did not have controls had the most drastic improvement in real wages. They improved more rapidly in the countries which did not have the rationing and controls.

Mr. SHISHKIN. I do not certainly advocate rationing and controls in themselves. I am merely describing the situation. 

It is true that some of the problems we are encountering in such countries as Italy, France, and Belgium today, Mr. Congressman, are due to the fact that you will find in those countries, side by side with people living in caves and mixing their pasta with mud water in order to be able to eat, the kind of luxury that I have not seen in this country yet.

I may say I mean one of the results is that in Italy you are still having today the Communists dominating the Italian trade-union movement. The non-Communists and those who want freedom are battling desperately and hopelessly sometimes, because people who understand fairness in its very simplest elementary terms do not see how the man who lives in vast luxury, that you do not see in England or Norway or Sweden or Denmark, right in front of their eyes, is justified, when they also see babies dying right before them across the street.

I think in that kind of thing if we bring stability to the point where equity is achieved you will get to the heart of the problem which we still have in Italy and France today of stemming the tide of communism because communism breeds in poverty. Communism breeds on the inability of the workers to gain food, to gain the necessary essentials of life, and unless those are provided I do not think we will be able to win.

Mr. JUDD. It does not happen unless some Communists are there saying to them "Your poverty is the result of capitalistic monopoly.

I think by and large the French are very much aware of the fact that ECA is anxious to see all possible benefits in terms of reduced prices and improved real wages of the wage earners that would not jeopardize the financial stability of France. 233

Mr. FULTON. Of course, many of us have been approached on this 

Morocco situation for United States businessmen. If you will let us hear what that might be from the terms of employment, perhaps of American nationals or business in Morocco, that would be helpful. (The information requested is as follows:)

As of January 1, 1949, the American consulate general reported that there were 267 American citizens resident in French Morocco. On the basis of reports submitted in 1948, it is estimated that at least 20 percent of this number are naturalized American citizens. Of this total, 181 were classified as heads of families and 86 were classified as dependents. Of the 181 heads of families, 14 were United States Government employees, 10 were representatives and employees of American commercial concerns and 61 were listed under the category of local merchants, manufacturers, importers, exporters, etc. It is understood that membership in the American Trade Association of Morocco (of which Mr. Robert E. Rodes is president) totaled 37 in early 1949.

The following general information regarding the situation in Morocco may be of interest. United States treaty rights in French Morocco are based on a treaty of 1836 between Morocco and the United States, the Madrid Convention of 1880, and the General Act of Algeciras of 1906. Under these international agreements, the United States enjoys certain rights in Morocco, including the right of extraterritorial jurisdiction, most-favored-nation treatment for United States commerce, and "economic liberty without any inequality." The right to freedom in matters of commerce is subject to an exception as regards the importation of a few specified products, including tobacco, opium, sulfur, powder saltpeter, etc., on which products the Sultan of Morocco is empowered to maintain a monopoly. The Sultan, under the terms of the treaties, further has extensive powers as regards the exportation of products from Morocco. Morocco is the only country in the world where the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction and maintains its own consular courts. Moreover, the United States is the only country that continues to exercise such rights in French Morocco. 

Because of our treaty rights in Morocco, and based on custom and usage, it has been customary for the Government of Morocco to obtain this Government's assent before considering local laws or decrees as being applicable to American ressortissants (American citizens and persons entitled to the protection of the 

United States Government).

In 1939, the French protectorate government, in line with similar measures taken in France at the outbreak of war, instituted, through various decrees, a system of exchange and import controls in French Morocco. These laws had the effect of subjecting foreign exchange to the control of the protectorate government and of requiring an import license for all imports save those from France and Algeria. At that time, this Government reserved its position with

1 1 1 respect to these controls and withheld its assent to their application to American ressortissants. In 1944, however, we assented to the application of exchange controls to American ressortissants but withheld our assent to Moroccan import controls. The withholding of our assent to import controls permitted Americans who established themselves in the import and export business in Morocco following the end of World War II to import more or less freely from the United States provided they did not ask the French protectorate for an official allocation of exchange to pay for such imports. The French alleged that uncontrolled imports were resulting in exchange transactions which they stated were exerting pressure on the value of the franc in money markets and were exercising a strong attraction for dollars to move out of the hands of the French exchange control system.

The French protectorate government, therefore, promulgated a decree on December 30, 1948, which had the effect of limiting imports without an official allocation of exchange to a list of nine items, and subjected imports of those nine items to the requirement of an import license. The import controls in question apply to persons of all nationalities in Morocco and to imports from all monetary zones with the exception of imports from the franc area (the Moroccan and French franc are freely interchangeable). The French protectorate authorities began immediately to apply this decree to American ressortissants without the assent of this Government and detained in the customs merchandise consigned to American importers.

The Government of France, specifically acting on behalf of the French zone of Morocco and other areas for which it has assumed international responsibility, agreed in signing its bilateral agreement with the United States pursuant to the Economic Cooperation Act, as required by Congress in subsection 115 (b) (2) to take: "Financial and monetary measures necessary to stabilize its currency, establish or maintain a valid rate of exchange, to balance its governmental budget as soon as practicable and generally restore or maintain confidence in its monetary system."

This Government recognized the temporary necessity for the import controls established by the Moroccan decree of December 30, 1948, since such controls were in conformance with France's commitments under the European recovery program. However, this Government also recognized that American businessmen in Morocco had certain legitimate grievances against French protectorate officials. These included certain discriminatory practices in the administration of import controls, the arbitrary valuation of imports for customs purposes, the detention of merchandise in the customs and the collection of certain consumption taxes to which this Government had not given its assent. The problem was, therefore, discussed with French officials early in 1949 and on the basis of proposals which partially met our requests (including the release of merchandise then held in the customs), temporary assent was given to the decree of December 30, 1948, on June 10, 1949, for a period of 3 months subject to further negotiations. Temporary assent was successively extended to December 31, 1949 during which time negotiations continued. On December 31, 1949, this Government gave its assent to the application of import controls to American ressortissants for an indefinite period on the basis of agreements which had been reached on that date regarding the application of the controls to Americans. 

The United States Government's note of December 31, 1949, to the resident general in French Morocco giving this Government's assent to the controls for an indefinite period stated: "These import regulations are regarded by my Government as arising from exceptional economic conditions now existing in Morocco and its assent to the application of these measures to American ressortissants is subject to withdrawal after 30 days notice to your Excellency."

In addition, such assent was given with full reservation of United States treaty rights including the jurisdiction of our consular courts. 

Throughout the negotiations which led to the giving of assent for an indefinite period, it was the consistent endeavor of the Department of State to obtain the best possible arrangements for American importers in Morocco and to protect American interests. The agreements reached with the French include the following provisions which were designed for the benefit of American importers: 

1. The addition of 11 items to the list of goods which may be imported more or less freely when no official allocation of foreign exchange is requested of the protectorate government. This brings to 20 the number of items which may be imported by Americans without an official allocation of exchange.

2. The establishment of a bidding procedure for all products susceptible of such a system and for which the protectorate government grants official allocations of foreign exchange. This provision is designed to permit Americans to participate in the controlled imports program of French Morocco on a competitive basis. 

3. The establishment of specific quotas for new importers on certain other goods included in the official imports program. 

4. The use of a uniform basis of valuation of imported goods for customs purposes, and under certain conditions, the issuance of import licenses for certain categories of maintenance goods. 

5. It was also agreed that the United States and the French protectorate government would maintain close liaison and consultation regarding the implementation of the measures agreed upon. The American consul at Rabat is carrying out this latter phase of the agreement and is in a position to observe closely the administration of the import controls with respect to Americans. 

The question of consumption taxes collected without the assent of this Government was not successfully resolved during the negotiations. The French contend that such financial and monetary measures, which are nondiscriminatory in character, must apply alike to persons of all nationalities and they challenge the necessity for United States assent to such measures before they are applicable to American ressortissants. These consumption taxes are not discriminatory in character since they are not directed at imports coming principally from the United States, and since they apply equally to products manufactured in Morocco. These taxes are collected on the goods concerned at the time of importation and are customarily passed along ultimately to the consumer in the selling price of the merchandise. The real issue in this problem is the question of the necessity for this Government's assent before such taxes are collected from American ressortissants. The Department of State proposes to continue its efforts to reach an equitable agreement with the French on this matter.

(The document referred to is as follows:) MEMORANDUM ON EUROPEAN PAYMENTS UNION (By Hon. Charles S. Dewey) PREAMBLE 

The first book of the Bible, chapter 11 of Genesis, offers an example of the importance of cooperation that might well serve today as a guide and warning to the members of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation. 

The Lord was opposed to the completion of the Tower of Babel, but He did not destroy the tower, but, by destroying the ability of the builders to cooperate, "babel" reigned and nothing was accomplished. "Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; * ** * and now nothing will be restrained for them, which they have imagined to do. * * let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech."

1 

FIRST STEPS TO BALANCE TRADE 

The recovery program outlined by the Organization for European Economic Cooperation in the autumn of 1947 was based upon four points: (1) A strong production effort by each of the participating countries. (2) The creation and maintenance of internal financial stability. (3) The development of economic cooperation between the participating countries. (4) A solution of the problem of the participating countries' deficit with 

American Continent.

For the purpose of this memorandum it is sufficient to say that good progress has been made in accomplishing item No. 1. The output of goods and services in 1949 exceeded that of 1947 by about 25 percent and a further increase of 10 percent is foreseen by 1952. Items Nos. 2 and 3 are closely associated; internal 1

financial stability among the countries of western Europe depends to a great extent upon the economic cooperation that exists between them and, without any doubt, the more use Europe can make of its own resources the less dependent it will be on American help and the closer it will be in 1952 to the solution of item 

No. 4 of the program. 

As has been stated, the national production of the participating countries has made a remarkable increase during the past 2 years-to such an extent in fact that certain commodities are in surplus in some countries that are vitally needed in others, the normal sale of such goods being obstructed by the lack of confidence of the seller in the stability and value of the currency of the buyer. 

As an example, Belgium has traditionally been an exporter of steel. Greece and Norway have imported it. Yet, Greece cannot sell enough olive oil, tobacco, and fruit to Belgium; and Norway cannot sell enough fish, lumber, and paper pulp to pay for the steel they wish to buy in Belgium; a certain part of the purchase price would have to be paid in Greek and Norwegian local currencies, which Belgium, doubting their value, would not accept. As a result full flow of what had been normal trade is interrupted and the recovery of Europe hindered, with the result of greater dependence on United States aid. 

THE INTRA-EUROPEAN PAYMENTS PLAN 

In September 1948 the first formal arrangement to employ ECA aid in assisting intra-European trade was devised, and called the intra-European payment plan. 

Its basic principle was simple. A part of the ECA-dollar aid to each creditor country (this is called conditional aid), which it needed to pay for necessary imports from the dollar area, was given only on condition that the recipient country extend grants in aid of the same amount in its own currency to other participating countries with which it has a trade surplus. 

In the parlance that has developed on this subject, such countries as Belgium which export more than they import are called creditor countries and the others that have an excess of imports debtor countries. Under the plan, the debtor country receives a drawing right, in the currency of each country with which it has a trade deficit (the amount of conditional aid and drawing rights were negotiated by the OEEC authorities).

Stated in terms of the example given above, Belgium receives ECA-dollar financing (as conditional aid) to pay for purchases in the United States on condition that it make a grant (drawing right) of Belgium francs to Greece with which Greece can complete its purchase-price requirement of steel in Belgium.

The intra-European payments plan has made a major contribution toward the freeing of European trade and the reestablishing of historic trade relationships. On its inception the member nations agreed to take steps to remove quantitative restrictions on at least 50 percent of their trade on private account with other participants. Further it has freed, to a considerable extent, the use of European resources, which will have the effect of reducing Europe's dependence on American-dollar assistance.

FAULTS DEVELOPED IN PAYMENT PLAN 

The main weakness of the payment plan is that it is based on ECA-dollar assistance as provided by conditional grants to creditor countries; further, it continues the practice of bilateral trade agreements. It has been continually urged by Mr. Hoffman that western Europe should strive to develop one market between the various participating countries similar to that which exists between the States of the United States. This goal can only be reached if bilateral trade agreements made between pairs of countries give place to multilateral agreements entered into between many. Due to the fact the plan is based upon bilateral agreements, a debtor country is restrained from shopping around to purchase its requirements in the cheapest market and further, the plan contains no penalties that would tend to induce a debtor country to bring its external trade into balance. The deciding feature, however, which requires consideration is that the plan offers no substitute for the assistance now being rendered by ECA which terminates in 1952.

1 

PROPOSED EUROPEAN PAYMENTS UNION 

The proposed European Payment Union, hereafter referred to as the "Union," contains all of the advantages found in the payment plan but corrects the faults inherent in bilateral trade agreements, and particularly prepares the participating nations to bring their intra-European payments into balance. The Union is in no manner a device by which the United States underwrites European currencies or protects overvalued currencies; in fact, the penalties provided by the Union for constant excessive imports by any participating country should tend to develop internal financial stability which is the prime requisite of currency convertibility. And right at this point it is well to remember that money and currency are standards of value in terms of which commodities are exchanged. If there is no accepted standard of value, convertibility cannot exist. 

The following paragraphs show in some detail how the Union works. It must be understood, however, that the experts of the OEEC are continuing their studies and changes and additions are to be expected, but in principle the Union plan has the support of the ECA and has been approved by the National Advisory Council.

The European Payments Union will be, in effect, a clearing house. Each country's deficits arising out of current trade transactions with some of its neighbors will be offset against its surpluses with others so that only a single net settlement on the books of the Union will be necessary. To make this settlement, the debtor country in question will have the right to draw upon the Union for any European currency it needs. Each debtor country will be given a limit to the total amount it may borrow in all currencies. A creditor country will provide its own currency to the Union as needed, up to a stated limit. Certain conditions, as will be described below, determine both settlement of debtor-countries balances, and the providing of local currency by a creditor country.

To refer briefly to the earlier example, Greece under the Union will be able to choose freely whether it will buy steel in Belgium, in Germany, or in Britain, for the reason that within its limit of credit with the Union, Greece may obtain any European currency desired, and hence shop around for the cheapest price. 

Instead of the ECA providing dollars to the various creditor countries as under conditional aid of the payments plan heretofore described, ECA will provide dollars directly to the Payments Union to reimburse creditor nations which lend their local currencies to the Union. The OEEC experts have not as yet reached final decision as to what amounts will be made available to settle trade deficits of debtor countries, nor what amount of ECA dollars may be required to satisfy requirements of creditor countries supplying their currencies to the Union. Certain tentative figures and rules under which creditor and debtor countries may receive gold or dollars, or be required to provide a percentage of gold or dollars to obtain credit from the Union, have however been arrived at and are explained herewith. 

It is estimated that about $600,000,000 of ECA dollars should be allocated from the total ECA appropriation in fiscal 1950-51 for the purposes of the Payments Union. This sum should be greatly decreased for fiscal 1951-52 and the institution should proceed on its own feet thereafter. 

The participating countries have agreed that, if the Union is formed, they will make it their aim to remove quantitative restrictions on at least 60 percent of their imports on private account from other member countries, and after June 30, 1950, they will attempt to increase liberalization to 75 percent and that in any event quotas existing after December 31, 1950, will have to be justified. 

Each country's account in the Union will be kept in terms of a new single European currency unit (the name ECU has been suggested). As the purpose of the organization is the balancing of intra-European trade payments, frequent consultation and recommendations should occur on nonrestrictive measures to balance payments and appropriate changes suggested in internal fiscal policies. 

The administration of settlements should be flexible and they and the Union be under the management of a supervisory board of highest competence making decisions by less than unanimity. 

---

The system of inducing both surplus and deficit countries to balance payments may work along something like the following lines: 

For countries incurring a deficit in intra-European trade 

This 

Intra-European debtors may receive assistance to cover their deficits. assistance will be similar to the drawing rights of the payments plan, and will be financed in part by ECA-dollar conditional aid to the countries from which the debtors buy. Such aid will be progressively reduced in the next 2 years and will, of course, not continue after ECA aid ends. 

Each country will receive a small revolving credit, or swing margin, in the Payments Union, to cover seasonal shifts in trade. For example, a country with important agricultural exports might receive enough credit to carry it until its crops are harvested and would grant credit to carry other countries until they can pay for the crops by sales of industrial goods. 

Beyond the swing margin the Payments Union will establish a medium-term credit quota for each country which may be determined as a fraction of each country's total trade with all other countries. Within this quota settlements for deficits would be partly made in gold and partly covered with credits from the Payments Union. In proportion as the country used its quota, the ratio of gold payments to credit would increase. For example, use of the first 25 percent of its quota might cost a country 20 percent in gold, while it would receive SO percent in credit. However, for the last 25 percent, the deficit country might be required to pay 80 percent in gold, while it would receive 20 percent in credit. 

For any deficit beyond the quota the country would pay 100 percent in gold. 

For countries incurring a surplus in intra-European trade Creditor countries would receive ECA-dollar conditional aid to cover small surpluses, in exchange for which they would grant equivalent "drawing rights" to deficit countries, through the Payments Union. Such conditional aid will decline over the next 2 years and will, of course, discontinue when ECA aid ends.

Beyond this conditional aid, a small surplus will be covered by the "swing margin," for which the surplus country will receive no settlement. Surpluses beyond this point would be financed on a quota system, similar but opposite to that of the deficit countries: For the first portion of the quota, the surplus country would receive a large gold payment and extend a small credit to the Payments Union; for the last portion of the quota, it would receive only a small gold payment and would extend a large credit. Beyond the quota it would have to finance its surplus entirely with credit. 

Through this payments system, it is hoped to give both creditor and debtor countries a real incentive to balance their payments. Since the introduction of automatic partial gold settlements in intra-European trade may impose severe strain on some countries, the ECA will set aside as mentioned above part of its appropriation to help make up any initial difference between gold paid into the Union by debtors and gold paid out of the Union to creditors. In addition, it may extend dollar loans to debtors on the condition that they take steps necessary to correct their deficits. As the positions gradually improve over the next 2 years, ECA aid will be reduced, and the Payments Union should be self-sustaining by 1952.

As an example under the plan, a "surplus country" may draw out 80 percent of its credit in gold and leave 20 percent to its credit account with the European Payments Union of the first one-quarter (25 percent) of its medium credit line. 

The second quarter (25 percent) will be paid "surplus country," 50 percent in gold and 50 percent to be left to its credit with European Payments Union. Anything in excess of the "surplus country" medium line will be accounted to it in full by credit on the books of the "Union."

Contrary to the operation for a "surplus country" which receives "gold" and a credit account with the European Payments Union, a debtor country pays out gold and has its "medium credit" line charged at the following rates: (a) The use of the first 25 percent of its line of credit costs the country 20 percent in gold and the line is reduced by 80 percent of the 25 percent. (b) The use of the second 25 percent of its line of credit costs the country 50 percent in gold, and the line is reduced by 50 percent of the 25 percent. (c) The rate of gold payment increases for each 25 percent, and the line is reduced by the remainder until entirely exhausted. Any settlement in excess of medium line of credit must be made 100 percent in gold.

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED WEDNESDAY, MARCH 8, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

The committee met, pursuant to call, at 11 a. m., in the Foreign 

(chairman) presiding.

This morning we find it necessary to break into our hearings upon the ECA bill proper, in order to receive some evidence in connection with our further aid to Korea. This proposition is also connected with the ECA, as aid to Korea is being administered and has been from the beginning, through the ECA. Therefore it is a matter connected with the European relief program, although the country being assisted is in the Far East. 

We have with us this morning, the Secretary of State, the Honorable Dean Acheson. We also have the Administrator of the ECA, Mr. Paul Hoffman. We will hear the Secretary of State first upon a continuation of our aid to Korea. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Secretary, we are always glad to have you appear before us. We will be glad to have you proceed in your own way.

STATEMENT OF HON. DEAN ACHESON, SECRETARY OF STATE 

Secretary ACHESON. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I am happy to have the opportunity to again come before your committee with Mr. Hoffman to discuss the question of economic assistance to the Republic of Korea. We are here today to consider a proposal for the continuation of the Korean economic recovery program into a second year. I believe all of you will appreciate from what Mr. Hoffman and I had to say on the occasion of our last meeting together that we regard this program as of great importance to the attainment of American objectives in the Far East. Since we have discussed this matter at some length only a short while ago, I shall try to be as brief as possible now. 

I believe the main questions we have to consider are: (1) The importance of the proposed continuation of the economic recovery program to the success of our over-all policy toward Korea; (2) the part which our Korean policy plays in the United States policy for the Far East; and (3) the probability of ultimate success of the effort of the Korean Republic to survive. 355

First, as to Korea: You will recall that the United States has taken the leadership among the nations to attain the realization of our fundamental declaration made at Cairo in 1943 with the United Kingdom and China (and later joined by the U. S. S. R.) "that in due course Korea should become free and independent." When our own efforts to persuade the U. S. S. R. to join in holding free elections to establish a united country were unsuccessful, we referred the matter to the United Nations. The General Assembly has used and is using its best efforts to bring about the accomplishment of this end, desired by all the Korean people. The success of its efforts has thus far been limited to assisting in the establishment of a free government, the Republic of Korea, in what was formerly the area of United States occupation.

Upon the establishment of the Republic, the United States undertook to assist it to survive and develop as a democratic representative government. To do this, the United States is providing the Republic with political support. Through our information and educational programs, we are seeking to help the Republic develop a sound educational system founded on principles of representative democracy. At the request of the Republic, we are maintaining there a military advisory group to assist in training Korean security forces and to insure the efficient employment of United States military assistance by those forces. Supplementing the prior transfer of military equipment under the Surplus Property Act, the Congress has authorized under the 

Mutual Defense Assistance Act the extension of military aid to Korea. 

And the Congress has recently authorized the Economic Cooperation Administration to undertake a program intended to bring the economy of the Republic as nearly as possible to a self-supporting basis. In doing so, the Congress authorized the expenditure in the fiscal year 1950 of the total sum of $120,000,000. 

By means of these and related measures, the United States hopes to achieve the objectives of strengthening the Republic of Korea to the point where it can (1) successfully withstand the threat of expanding Communist influence and control arising out of the existence in north Korea of an aggressive Soviet-dominated Communist regime; and (2) serve as a nucleus for the eventual peaceful unification of the entire country on a democratic basis. 

The testimony presented to your committee by Mr. Hoffman, Mr. 

Webb and other witnesses at the time of hearings on the bill authorizing the program for fiscal year 1950 indicated very plainly that the authority requested was to carry out the first year of a planned 3year program intended to help Korea make substantial progress toward a self-supporting economy. The program for which authority is now requested for fiscal year 1951 is the second year of this 3-year program. Since Mr. Hoffman will go into the economics of the program with you, I will not attempt to do so beyond saying that the Department of State has participated in the preparation of the program which he will outline and supports it fully. 

Second, as to the place of this proposal in our over-all far-eastern policy, I have said that the United States is taking the leadership

among the nations in helping the people of Korea attain the goal of a united independent nation, free from foreign domination. As a result of this initiative, the United States today is looked to not only by the people of Korea but by the peoples of the Far East and, in fact, by the people of democratic nations everywhere as the leader in the struggle for the survival of a Korean Republic, both for itself and as a possible nucleus for the eventual peaceful unification of that country. 

Broadly speaking, the United States foreign policy in the Far East is directed toward encouraging and assisting the efforts of the peoples of that area to improve their welfare and security, to stabilize and develop their economies, to strengthen free institutions, and to advance the cause of self-government free from outside domination. Korea is one place in which the United States can continue to take well-defined positive steps to help a free democratic country to survive in the face of efforts of communism to engulf it. Hundreds of millions of people of southern and southeastern Asia and the islands of the Pacific are now in a period where they must choose between the roads toward democracy or totalitarianism. As the President said in his message to the Congress on Korean aid in June of last year:

Korea has become a testing ground in which the validity and practical value of the ideals and principles of democracy which the Republic is putting into practice are being matched against the practices of communism which have been imposed upon the people of North Korea. The survival and progress of the 

Republic toward a self-supporting, stable economy will have an immense and far-reaching influence on the people of Asia. Such progress by the young Republic will encourage the people of southern and southeastern Asia and the islands of the Pacific to resist and reject the Communist propaganda with which they are besieged. Moreover, the Korean Republic, by demonstrating the success and tenacity of democracy in resisting communism, will stand as a beacon to the people of northern Asia in resisting the control of the Communist forces which have overrun them.

The people of Asia, as well as the people of Korea, have been able to see the way in which economic assistance from the United States has contributed already to the ability of the Korean people to move toward economic independence. The economic assistance program has increased agricultural production and the well-being of the large farming population of Korea. It has given food to the families of the industrial workers and, by increasing production, has brought about mounting employment. It has made possible a small surplus for export as a source of foreign exchange with which necessities may be imported. This progress, together with the rehabilitation of factories, mines, and fishing facilities important to the Korean economy, has helped to give them faith in their form of government, strength to resist the constant pressures of communism, and confidence in their future.

There is one further and fundamental question which must be considered: That is the probability of ultimate success of the effort of the 

Korean Republic to survive. In recent debates a number of Members of the Congress have indicated their feeling that the possibility of failure makes them doubt the wisdom of the United States giving a helping hand in this effort. It is my belief that American policy should be based on determination to succeed rather than on fear of

the possibility of failure. Despite the problems with which the Republic of Korea is beset both internally and externally, and despite its necessarily limited experience in self-government and paucity of technical and administrative know-how, conditions of stability and public order have continued to improve and the threat of Communist overthrow appears at least temporarily to have been contained. 

There is good reason to hope from progress made thus far that with our assistance, the Republic of Korea can survive and thrive. This cannot, of course, be guaranteed. However, it continues to be true that without our assistance there can be no such hope. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary, for your statement. 

Mr. Mansfield, have you any questions?

Mr. MANSFIELD. No questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Eaton- 

Mr. EATON. I wonder if the Secretary could tell us the main forms which the Communist domination of North Korea takes. Do the Russians give economic assistance in North Korea? 

Secretary ACHESON. I think not, Mr. Eaton. I think what has happened in North Korea is that a Communist government has been set up. There is a Communist police and military establishment set up. That country is in the physical control of the Communist authority, imposed by the Russians and used by the Russians for their own purposes.

Mr. EATON. Those authorities are composed of Koreans entirely, or are they Russians?

Secretary ACHESON. I think they are very probably Koreans who have been trained by the Russians. 

Mr. EATON. Do you think they have done a better job affiliating themselves with the people of northern Korea than we have in southern Korea?

Secretary ACHESON. No, sir; I think they have done a wholly different kind of a job. It is one thing to put some stooges in to organize police and military, and to require people by force to believe the way you want them to. We have not tried to make South Korea a satellite of the United States. We have tried to set it up as an independent country and give it independent help so it can survive as such. We want it to develop its own institutions in its own way. It will have to make its own mistakes and will have to correct its own mistakes. 

We are merely helping it to start off on this road. 

Mr. EATON. If we withdraw our assistance from Korea now that will be of immense assistance to the Russian program not only in 

Korea but through the Orient? 

Secretary ACHESON. Very great assistance, Dr. Eaton.

Mr. EATON. It does not appear to be a very profitable investment for the United States to assist Russia to take over. 

Secretary ACHESON. I should not recommend it. 

Mr. EATON. That is high authority. 

That is all, Mr. Chairman.

Chairman KEE. As a matter of fact, Mr. Secretary, the United 

States Government, in aiding the Koreans in setting up a free democratic government in South Korea, collaborated with the United Nations in that area, is that correct? 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes, sir. As a result of the discussions in

Moscow we tried to get agreement from the Russians so that we might all work together in helping the Koreans set up their own government. The Russians refused to cooperate in that and the matter was taken to the United Nations. The United Nations set up a commission on Korea which went to Korea, and in fact is still there. The 

Russians again refused to cooperate in any way so the Korean Government had to be set up in South Korea. We hope eventually that progress will be made toward uniting the country, but at the present moment that has not taken place and we see no imminent prospect that it will.

Chairman KEE. I believe the evidence we had before us showed the 

Russians would not even permit the commission to cross the line at the thirty-eighth parallel and enter the northern part of Korea. 

Secretary ACHESON. That is my recollection, Judge Kee; yes. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Zablocki, have you any questions?

Mr. ZABLOCKI. No questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Merrow- 

Mr. MERROW. Mr. Secretary, the problem of Korea seems to be but one phase of the whole problem in the Far East, one phase of the over-all problem. According to recent reports, the Department will send a mission to Southeast Asia.

I recognize that Southeast Asia is far from Korea, but is it not entirely possible that there will be a request made of the Congress for some aid, let us say, to Indochina? The reason I ask this question is because I want to connect it with the entire picture. I wonder when we can perhaps gets an estimate of what it is going to cost us for the next fiscal year in all of the Far East, of which Korea is only a part. 

Secretary ACHESON. I think it would probably be possible now to give some sort of an estimate. No estimate can fully appraise the possible directions of pressure by the Russians. If the committee wishes that, we can make the best estimate that we can at the present time.

Mr. MERROW. It would seem to me to be easier to get action by the 

Congress if we had some idea of what it is going to cost in all of Asia. 

This point may well arise: Korea is a part of the whole far eastern picture. We are asked to authorized and appropriate more money for 

Korea. Soon we will be asked to authorize and appropriate money for some other section. When is this going to end or how much do you estimate we will have to appropriate for the coming year? I think it would be very helpful if we could have this. 

Secretary ACHESON. We will try to do the best we can on that, Mr. Merrow.

(The information requested is as follows:) 

The present estimate of the total cost of all foreign assistance programs for fiscal 1951 including those now planned for the Far East is as set out in the table below. It is possible that when the results of the Bangkok conference, the report of Ambassador Jessup and of the Griffin mission have been received and fully assessed, recommendations will be made for additional assistance to other countries in the Far East. It will also be necessary, in making such recommendations, to appraise the use and effectiveness of funds already available for the area, another factor difficult to evaluate at present. For these reasons, it is not desirable to try to predict now what recommendations will be made. 

It can be emphasized, however, that the fact that conditions in this area are continually and rapidly evolving makes it important that there be flexibility in the use of funds made available for both military and economic assistance to the countries in the area.

STATEMENT ON TOTAL COST OF ALL FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS FOR FISCAL YEAR 1951 

The following table is based on the summary table (International Affairs and Finance) appearing on page M21 of the President's budget message, which gives the latest official recapitulation by the executive branch of the over-all financial picture of United States foreign assistance. 

In general, it can be said that, on an expenditure basis, all foreign aid programs now envisaged for fiscal 1951 will total about 4.5 billion dollars, as compared with 5.7 billion dollars estimated for the current fiscal year and 6.3 billion dollars actually expended in fiscal year 1949. 

It is expected that appropriations to be requested for fiscal 1951 will total about 4.8 billion dollars. Of this sum it is estimated that 513 million dollars will be to liquidate contracts previously authorized. The remaining 4.3 billion dollars would be new appropriations available for obligation. In addition there will be needed new contract authority of approximately 530 million dollars, making a total of new obligational authority for 1951 of about 4.8 billion dollars. 

The budget contains the best estimates by the executive branch of the total cost of foreign assistance programs for fiscal year 1951. In view of the present international situation, however, unforeseen developments might compel new approaches to the Congress beyond the programs now envisaged. 

Some allowance has, indeed, already been made in the President's budget for requirements to meet these unforeseen contingencies. It will be noted that the budget provides $3,100,000,000 for the European recovery program and other foreign aid. The administration's present request for $2,950,000,000 for the 

ECA thus does not exhaust the budgetary provision which was intended to cover not only ERP but also "any contingencies arising in the field of foreign affairs." 

The Department is now considering developments in various parts of the world and may determine that it would be in the United States interest in some situations to provide aid, which it is anticipated could be covered out of the residual sum. In addition, of the sums already appropriated under authority of the act of 1948 for economic assistance to China, there will remain unobligated at the end of fiscal 1950 approximately $100,000,000. Prior to expiration of existing 

China aid legislation on June 30, 1950, the executive branch will recommend possible disposition of such unexpended funds.

Mr. MERROW. Are there programs coming up for other countries in Asia such as Indonesia?

Secretary ACHESON. I do not say that at all. Insofar as Indonesia is concerned, we have just had discussions with the Finance Minister. 

He has had discussions with the Export-Import Bank. The Export- 

Import Bank has made available a very substantial credit to Indonesia and we have no thought of coming to the Congress and asking for appropriations in that field, outside the general Point IV program which is already before you and which you understand. Whether there would be something with regard to specific countries I just cannot answer this morning.

Mr. MERROW. Do you expect to have the answer when this mission. returns, Mr. Secretary?

Secretary ACHESON. We will have more information. The mission,. of course, will give us an advance idea of what could be done under Point IV. That involves no further appropriations beyond those you are now considering. It will look at various other questions, certain police and military matters which probably can be handled under the $75,000,000 which Congress has made available. 

Mr. MERROW. You spoke of confining it to Point IV, but is it possible that out of the recommendations of this mission that there will come other programs for aid in these various countries, other than 

Point IV? 

Secretary ACHESON. It is possible. I do not know of anything that will lead to that, but it is possible. You see, you just cannot deal with this situation in southeast Asia as though every eventuality were predictable. You just cannot do that. 

Mr. MERROW. I agree with that, Mr. Secretary. I am glad you have agreed to bring in an over-all estimate. I think, however, if the Congress has some idea of what it may expect in the way of requests for authorizations and appropriations for the various coun-tries in southeast Asia, that it will make it easier to handle Korean aid and make it easier for action in other countries. 

Secretary ACHESON. This is a program which we are in, and I think the real question before the Congress is whether it wants to carry it through or does not want to carry it through. There is such a thing as the frustration of the problem of the whole. If you begin to enlarge the question and say, "This one depends on another one and that one depends on another one and that one depends on another one," you finally get into a position of complete frustration. 

Mr. MERROW. I have a feeling that the problem of the whole may have a very frustrating effect on this one. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Pfeifer, do you have some questions?

Mr. PFEIFER. I would like to defer until I am through reading this. report.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Ribicoff- 

Mr. RIBICOFF. Mr. Secretary, I believe there is a great deal of cogency in Mr. Merrow's point. You certainly cannot take these problems piecemeal without realizing that the greatest problem is in southeast Asia. 

Would you care to answer a question on India? 

Secretary ACHESON. If I can. I will do my best. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I was in a conference this Saturday at Columbia

University with an Indian professor, discussing the situation of Nehru in the world today. The Indian Government wanted to purchase a great deal of United States surplus wheat for the purpose of breaking the Indian black market in wheat which was the most serious economic problem India faced. The apparent refusal of the 

United States to sell Nehru the wheat on reasonable terms caused a great deal of disillusionment to Nehru. I told him I had never heard of the incident. Do you know of what the gentleman spoke? 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes; I. know what he was talking about.

There was no refusal to sell Mr. Nehru wheat at all. The question was whether wheat from the United States could be sent to India,

almost on gift terms. There were legal, administrative, economic, and all sorts of problems in the way of it. That was thoroughly thrashed out when the Prime Minister was here with his staff. I cannot speak for him but my impression is that he thought the matter was given most careful attention and had no complaint about it. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I thought the argument made was a very good one as 

I understood it: Here the United States set up a policy for dealing with western Europe and the rest of the world, giving them wheat through the Marshall plan on very, very favorable terms. Suddenly we have a different method of doing business with India, when we are so seriously involved there and want India's good will, and Nehru could not see the double standard of doing business between the United States and the west and the United States and the Far East. 

It seemed to be a good argument and something we should give very serious attention to. It will take more than money in my opinion, to solve this far eastern problem. There should be some consistency along that line. We have so much wheat, it might be good statesmanship to let them have it on the same basis as western Europe. 

Secretary ACHESON. That whole question of wheat was discussed here at the time the Prime Minister was here. If that is a matter which the committee wishes to go into I think we could best go into it in executive session.

Mr. RIBICOFF. That is all. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Judd, have you any questions? 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Secretary, has Dr. Jessup gone to Korea? 

Secretary ACHESON. He has been to Korea. 

Mr. JUDD. Has he come back yet? 

Secretary ACHESON. No. He is expected fairly soon.

Mr. JUDD. The last time you were here we raised some questions on which you said you did not care to report until you had the full report of the Bangkok conference. Is the Department in a position to formulate any policies on the Far East on the information they have now, or must they wait until he comes home, too?

Secretary ACHESON. We are, of course, working on this on this every day.

It will be very helpful to get his personal impressions. 

Mr. JUDD. The element of time, it seems to me, is of vital importance. I recall that in 1947 we were called back into special session to take care, on an interim basis, of the immediate emergency needs in France, Italy, and Austria. I thought that was wise. But I just do not believe we have time for what appears to be such leisurely deliberation regarding the Far East. He goes out by boat and comes back by boat as if there were no urgency, when, as a matter of fact, the house is afire in Asia. 

I have been reading some of the Communist broadcasts monitored by CIA every day, and there is no question but what they have in mind very shortly-an all-out effort in Indochina. I am fearful that country may be gone before we decide what we are going to do. May 

I have your assurance that there are plans for a program in that area, or that the plans you have are further along than appears from the press to be the case? 

Secretary ACHESON. I think that is true. 

Mr. JUDD. I am glad to have that assurance.

I asked Mr. Harriman a question when he was before our committee. and he asked that it be referred to you. It also had to do with Indochina. I was trying to get some facts and figures as to how much of a drain on France's economy and how much of a deterrent to her recovery in Europe results from her military effort in Indochina. I asked him the question because it has been suggested in some quarters, not by me, that it might be better for France to let Indochina go and concentrate on her recovery in Europe, because her effort both economically and militarily in Indochina is beyond her strength-that is, the drain on her is allegedly jeopardizing her own recovering and her contribution to the security of Europe, and thereby forcing us ultimately to put more money in to accomplish recovery in Europe. 

He said that should be referred to you. Would it be your advice for France to let Indochina go to the Communists, rather than have the flower of her Army be shot down in Indochina and this terrific drain on her economy and military resources?

Secretary ACHESON. Of course, the French situation in Indochina is a very serious one. I do not believe there is any thought either in 

Paris or in the executive branch in Washington that it would be in any way desirable to have the French withdraw their troops from Indochina. I do not believe they are contemplating that and we certainly would not view that as a helpful step in any way. In fact, it would bring about a very serious situation. 

Mr. JUDD. Then her efforts in Indochina ought to be continued even though it does make more difficult her recovery in Europe?

Secretary ACHESON. All of the efforts of meeting this Communist penetration make recovery difficult for all of us-for us and the British and the French and Dutch and everyone but we just have to go ahead and do it. 

Mr. JUDD. You feel it is sufficiently important so that if necessary we should increase our contribution to France and Europe, in order to help them hold back the Communist tide in Asia? 

Secretary ACHESON. Well the whole question of cooperation between the French and ourselves in this problem is one which is under discussion and I would rather not testify about it now. 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Secretary, may I ask another question which I understand was also brought up in the Senate-whether you favor a continuation for another year of the unexpended balances for ECA type of aid in those parts of China that are still free. 

Secretary ACHESON. Yes; I was asked that question yesterday by

Secretary ACHESON. No; it would be available for economic only.

In places where we have not had such will, we have not found ways. to win. That is what has disturbed me regarding Formosa. Our investment there might be lost, as it might be lost in Korea too. But in the latter case we take the risk, in the former, we don't.

Secretary ACHESON. Mr. Hoffman has a program which the ECA has worked out applicable to Formosa. I do not think we should be asked to guarantee that that program or any part of it or any programs would be carried out. 

Mr. JUDD. I agree it should be kept flexible for all of them. The best way of saving Indochina is to keep the Chinese sufficiently encouraged to resist Communists so that the latter are so busy in China that they cannot give their full attention to Indochina and the rest of southeast Asia.

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Secretary, I would like to have you comment upon this conviction which I have which goes to the substance of your testimony. I am convinced we will not get anywhere in Asia until, either through a Pacific pact or through a far eastern recovery program, we combine those nations of Asia which remain free so that they may not only feel our strength, which is very distant from them, very far away, physically, but so that they may feel each other's strength. I ask, Mr. Secretary, whether you would care to comment-perhaps this is all so secret there is nothing you can tell us about it--but I am convinced, and I am passing over the idea of whether we will invite or they will initiate such an effort. I think that such an effort can be activated if the will is there; Secretary Marshall got it done, and I think this Secretary has the same capacity and the same capability. 

Can you get the nations of Asia together so that they feel their own strength as well as ours? I do not believe we are likely otherwise to be able to construct an effective policy. I would appreciate your comment.

Secretary ACHESON. We discussed this the last time I was up here, when Mr. Fulton asked some questions. I said not only is the policy stated in the act of Congress, which says we favor the getting together of these non-Communist nations in Asia, but the President has said that, and I have said it, and the very important factor is that it must be something which they do. 

There have been various moves under contemplation, various statements have been made by the President of the Philippines and others about it, and I think that what our attitude is is very clear. The problems in Asia are very considerable. I think they are being worked on by responsible statesmen in that area, and I have high hopes that they will come out with a successful solution. 

Mr. JAVITS. Are you satisfied we are doing everything we can to speed their effort?

Secretary ACHESON. I am sure of that; if we did more, we would hinder it.
