Chairman KEE. Mr. Lodge.

Mr. LODGE. Mr. Secretary, how much do you believe that the possible transfer of the 71 planes in Hong Kong would assist the Communist forces in China, and do you believe that we would have to ship more military aid into Korea as a consequence of any such transfer? 

Secretary ACHESON. On the latter part of your question, as to Korea, the answer is "No; I think not." I do not think that the planes in 

Hong Kong affect the Korean question. The planes in Hong Kong would be of substantial assistance to the Chinese Communists. We believe that they are registered American planes. We have been taking every action open to us to assert that title and that right. As you know, the court has dealt with that matter. We have taken the matter up again with the British Government and we are hopeful that our interests in those planes are going to be protected. We are doing all we can to protect American interests in those planes. 

Mr. LODGE. Hong Kong as we withdrew aid from Indonesia on the ground that what was happening there was not in the best interests of the ECA enterprise.

Secretary ACHESON. This is an avenue of approach that is open, but 

I think it would result in devastating failure. There is no aid going to Hong Kong. 

Mr. LODGE. On page 2, at the bottom, you say:

Hundreds of millions of people in southeastern Asia and the islands of the Pacific are now in a period where they must choose between the roads toward democracy or totalitarianism.

Secretary ACHESON. I don't think the word "free" is in the paragraph at all.

Mr. LODGE. In other words, we should not imply that this is a free choice. How then is it up to them to choose?

Secretary ACHESON. It is up to them to choose, and it has been chosen in every one of the countries. Where there has been a Communist uprising, it has been put down by the Government. They are taking vigorous action here to protect themselves. This has happened in Indonesia, Malaya, Indochina, India; it has happened in the Philippines and in all of these areas. 

There have been armed Communist uprising and resistance to the governments of those areas which they have fought against vigorously. 

Mr. LODGE. Do you think that in many instances there is no choice for these people?

Secretary ACHESON. I do not think there is a choice where any person with reasonable convictions would hesitate for a moment, but you have to take vigorous action to protect yourself. 63307-50-pt. 2- -9

Mr. LODGE. They are forced to choose one thing, which is the same thing as saying there is no choice. Therefore, the word "choice" has no meaning. If the word "choice" does not mean "free choice," I don't know what it means. Certainly the Hungarians had no choice. 

It seems to me that it is important to understand that a great deal of what they have to "choose" is forced upon them. I suggest that sentence is subject to some modification.

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, I note Dr. Pfeifer said that all these countries should be held until they fall, and I think our policy should be to hold "unless they fall."

Mr. Secretary, who decided not to do in Formosa what the committee was told last year ECA planned to do? Was it the State Department or the ECA? Who decided we should not do there all that we could unless it fell?

Mr. HOFFMAN. We said we would do anything that did not involve long-range investments. It is precisely the policy used in China. 

I do not think anything not done in China in connection with what we called our capital investment program in any way contributed to the result in China.

In other words, whenever there was a doubt as to whether something could be done to bolster the situation, we did it. We are doing the same thing in Formosa. The only programs we are holding up are programs that couldn't possibly contribute much inside of 

18 months, 24 months, or 3 years.

Mr. JUDD. But you suspended in Formosa the same kind of programs you are carrying on in Korea.

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes. We are not carrying on the same type of programs. 

Mr. JUDD. Capital investment, long-term, in Korea, but not in Formosa.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I think it was wise to hold up capital investment in Formosa until we had a better idea of what the whole far eastern policy might be.

Mr. JUDD. You have testified, and others have, that the situation in 

Korea has improved spectacularly with our help. I think you will have to agree that it has improved enormously in Formosa, too, even without such help; far beyond any possibilities predicted a year ago or even 3 months ago. The reason why we have been able to get improvement in Burma, Indochina, and Indonesia, particularly, is because the Chinese Government bought us a year of time by refusing to die according to the schedule periodically announced by the State Department. If China had not held on tenaciously and retarded the 

Communists, Indonesia might have gone under in the revolt in the fall of 1948.

Mr. HOFFMAN. We hope Congress will decide to make available this money not spent in the China program so that with changing conditions we can make the program. You have to play this one by ear. 

You cannot decide a year in advance.

What we have done in China quite beyond the fertilizer program, is to assist in advising and also assist in restoration and rehabilitation of certain of the facilities we have there. You know we kept J. G. 

White out there. We are ready to go ahead as soon as conditions warrant. I assure you that given the funds with which to work, our whole inclination is to go ahead where we feel we can and are justified in spending the American taxpayers' dollars.

Mr. JUDD. You had $100,000,000 and you spent $6,000,000 of it last year. I wondered whether you planned to increase the effort this year.

May I read two paragraphs from a letter which I got the day before yesterday, written the 25th of February, by an American now in

Formosa but who has been in China some 25 years and is one of the ablest and best balanced Americans I know. 

He said:

It appears that the State Department has written off Hainan Island even more thoroughly than it has Taiwan, for ECA has forbidden work in any program on Hainan although the latter is permittedthat is, ECAis permitted to continue work on Taiwan. I urge that this attitude be changed and have communicated my opinion to ECA, only to be told that the idea is hopeless.

Of late, in the press, Mr. Acheson has been quoted as being anxious that the 

Communists be barred from Indo-China. Next week a committee of inquiry will be dispatched thither to report on methods of promoting Mr. Acheson's idea. I submit that no method would be more effective than to pose the threat of an invasion of China from Hainan.

If Hainan is still uninvaded when this reaches you, it means that it will remain uninvaded until after the monsoon season. The fogs which aid the invaders during these winter months will be over. From March 15 on, at the latest, the weather will all be in favor of the defenders. 

The Chinese Air Force has demonstrated an unexpected striking power. The morale and preparation of the Army is good. Desputes among the higher command are apparently not as bitter as they are in the United States of America. 

The fortifications and the disposition of tank forces are excellent, in the opinion of United States military men who are familiar with them. At last, Nationalist 

China is united and appears to be fairly efficient. The civilian government is improving; it listens to and cooperates with ECA and JCRR. 

Meanwhile, Chinese on the mainland are disillusioned about the Communists. 

Famine stalks, guerrillas are increasingly active, students have begun to protest, unemployment in cities is serious. Now is the time to attack, before the Communists have time to "fix their fences" or the people become inured to their hardships.

A little economic aid to Hainan would give an important lift to the rising morale. Some rice and cloth to be paid out principally to the builders of roads across the island in several directions would both ease the poverty there, and would also create the means of maintaining order. Order is necessary not only as a basis of further improvement but also to counteract the Communist claim that they have a force of 20,000 in the interior. 

That is from a man on the ground. It is the same story as in Korea. 

A little help and some encouragement would do a lot. 

A Chinese once told me when I thought there was no hope, "Don't be too discouraged. You see, we only have one shirt, but we had only two to begin with, so this is not so bad." That was back in 1931 when 

I was about ready to write off China then. But here she is some 20 years later still unwilling to die. I think its survival is of the greatest importance to Korea and Indochina and all the things of which Mr. 

Javits spoke so convincingly. It has to be part of the total picture. 

Secretary ACHESON. I would be glad to talk with the committee on all this matter in executive session, but I am not going to have any public debate on military points.

Mr. JUDD. I was talking about economic aids. 

Secretary ACHESON. It is all related. 

Mr. JUDD. You quoted, Mr. Secretary, from the President's statement that Korea is a testing ground in the struggle between the ideals and principles of freedom and the practices of communism which have been imposed upon them, implying that the outcome depends upon what they do or do not do for the human beings there, the citizens.

I was distressed when I read a statement in the New York Times magazine section a couple of weeks ago by Raymond Fosdick. In my judgment, he is half wrong. He says this is not a war of armaments, but a war of ideas, it is a war to determine which of two systems is really dedicated to the public's welfare and which of the two is better able to produce concrete benefits. 

That just is not so. To the Reds this isn't a struggle that has anything to do with the peoples' welfare, except for propaganda purposes. 

He goes ahead, "You cannot stop ideas with bombs and battleships.' That is true. But it is also true that you cannot stop bombs and bullets with ideas. He says the only way to defeat a bad idea is with a better idea. That isn't so either. Bad ideas are winning throughout the world where they are supported with arms. Perhaps ultimately the better idea will win. I believe that. But we are just fooling ourselves when we say that the better idea by itself will win in any near future, if the poorer idea has behind it force, ruthlessness, and determination to win. I think we are completely deceiving ourselves and our people when we say "ours is the better idea and therefore will win." It won't unless we put the same vigorous support behind it. If we have a better idea and more vigor in supporting it, yes.

If the Communists are better organized, more determined and on the ground, they will win in the short run even if their idea is unspeakably vicious.

I am distressed to see such things going out to lull our people to sleep when, as you say, they need to be wakened to the desperate nature of the struggle in which we are engaged. That kind of talk just makes votes against ERP and ECA and aid to Korea by the score. 

It allows people to say, "Our system is better; it will do more for the people, so it will win." That is not so. I believe that communism will fail ultimately because it is immoral. If you stop it, it falls apart because it can't deliver on its fancy promises, but it will not fall apart in our time unless it is stopped and we cannot stop it with just ideas, in my judgment.

I am sorry to take the committee's time for that long statement, but I am fearful that not even ECA for Europe is going to get through the House, I will tell you frankly, if we lull people to sleep with that sort of wishful thinking.

I believe you have made today, Mr. Secretary, the most forceful statement that has yet been made by any official and I welcome and commend it. If we adopt a policy based on determination to win, rather than on calculating all the possible failures that might develop, all around the world, I think the odds are still overwhelmingly in our favor, in Asia as well as in Europe and I congratulate you, sir. 

Having criticized you on various occasions when I thought you were wrong, I am glad to commend you when you are so eminently right.

STATEMENT OF HON. PAUL G. HOFFMAN, ADMINISTRATOR, ECONOMIC COOPERATION ADMINISTRATION 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Mr. Chairman, and gentlemen, I have with me Dr. 

Edgar Johnson who is Director of the Korean Division of ECA in Washington, who will present the program which has been developed for the fiscal year 1951, and also Dr. Arthur Bunce, chief of the ECA mission to Korea, who has just arrived in Washington, and who can give an eye-witness account of what is now going on in Korea. 

I will restrict myself to giving a very brief statement on (1) the history of economic recovery activities in Korea, and (2) the conditions under which the recovery program has operated, and (3) other progress to date.

On September 9, 1945, the United States Army took over in South Korea, with full responsibility for setting up a civil government, also for military developments, as well as for relief and reconstruction. 

It is difficult to get precise figures, but occupation costs, including payment for troops, was something in excess of $500,000,000. 

The Army spent on relief and rehabilitation between September 9, 1945, and January 5, 1949, in excess of $300,000,000. 

During the last year of the occupation-that is 1948-allocation for relief and rehabilitation was $144,000,000. 

ECA took over the responsibility for the administration of a recovery program on January 5, 1949. From January 5, 1949, to June 

30, 1949, approximately $70,000,000 was expended from GARIOA funds. Twenty-eight million dollars of that was in cash turned over

to us by the Army and the balance consisted of goods on hand or in transit.

For the fiscal year 1950 we requested for the recovery program an appropriation of $120,000,000. Authorizing legislation for the recovery program has been passed by both the Senate and the House, but as yet appropriation bills have not been passed. However, we have received on a month-to-month basis $60,000,000 under appropriations made by Congress under first half of fiscal 1950, and under the authorizing legislation have been given the right to borrow $30,000,000 from the RFC. That is $90,000,000 in all we have had made available to us. There is still $30,000,000 to come to carry out the 1950 program. 

Next I would like to comment on the conditions under which the recovery program has had to be carried out: 

For a quick picture of Korea, I suggest you consider it as a counterpart of Germany. The country is divided, with Russia in control of 

North Korea, and the new republic of South Korea governing in South Korea. Approximately 11,000,000 people lived in North Korea and 

19,000,000 in South Korea, formerly. Since the Russians took over effective control of North Korea, approximately 2,000,000 people have fled from North to South Korea, giving South Korea the counterpart of the refugee problem faced in Germany.

It is just one more case where people flee from Moscow and not to it. 

The Korean Government is, of course, a new government. It has been faced with problems that would have staggered a thoroughly seasoned government. In carrying out its civil functions it has had to draw upon civil servants from a population who for almost half a century were never allowed to participate in government in any way whatsoever.

On the military front they have been confronted not only with protecting a northern border but fighting against guerrillas who infiltrated into the south from the north. 

On the economic front they have been confronted with the problem of supplying management for 90 percent of Korea's industries, because during the period of Japanese control no Koreans were allowed to hold supervisory positions.

Korea has also been confronted with the problem of trying to carry out a recovery program under conditions of uncertainty as to the amount of funds that would be made available, or as to when those funds would be available.

One favorable factor should be emphasized: The Army during its period of occupation did an excellent job. The ECA took over a going concern.

I would like to report on progress to date, under these conditions: 

Industrial production for the calendar year 1949 was 50 percent above 1948. The coal production was up 34 percent. Electric power generation up 35 percent. Exports from the country will be increased by 50 percent during 1950.

Under all the conditions, this progress merits the adjective "spectacular." It is attributable to the will and determination of the people of Korea to take full advantage of their new freedom. 

In 1950 there has been one problem which has constituted a real threat to the recovery effort, and that is inflation. It was not an unexpected threat because under present conditions Korea must carry

an army of 100,000 men and a police force of 50,000 men, which is, of course, an enormous drain on the resources of the country. 

During the past months, this inflation has been dealt with vigorously, but further measures are called for before it can be gotten under control.

Before I call on Dr. Johnson and Dr. Bunce, I would like to comment on something Mrs. Bolton said. I do think a very great responsibility rests upon members of the Foreign Affairs Committee to bring to the other members of Congress, if it is needed, an understanding of the type of struggle that is now going on in the world. I assure you that perhaps like you, I have lain awake nights to think of words, to quote Mr. Kipling, that would walk up and down the hearts of men, and persuade them that this struggle we are now in is a struggle that is of perhaps even greater importance than the struggle involved in World War II. I think that statement can be backed up by simply referring to what Russia has annexed in the way of territory as a result of this new kind of war which Russia is carrying on. They call it a "cold" war. The weapons are different. As I have stated heretofore, the weapons they have used in this war do not beget headlines, because they are using sabotage, they have used strikes, they have used propaganda. The weapons we have used, of course, in western Europe to fight them have, again, not been the kind of weapons which make headlines. We have used food to combat hunger and we have used materials in the way of cotton and other goods so they could go on with their manufacturing. We have supplied tools so that they could turn out better work, and as a result of that there has been a return of hope and confidence.

I fully agree with Dr. Judd that somehow or other we have got to make the American people and the American Congress understand that there would be no point in authorizing and appropriating funds for ECA, or for similar activities, which are activities designed to reach the minds and loyalties of men, unless there were also authorizations and appropriations for military funds, not because you can drive an idea into the mind of a man with a bullet, because you cannot, but you do need time. You do need time, so that those ideas can be presented and accepted by men. 

In my opinion the principal need of the moment is a military strength that is sufficient so there will be a discouragement to imperialistic Russia to attempt any shortcuts as a result of the use of military power.

I still contend, Doctor, that that is what they can do for us, that what we have got to do in activities such as ECA is to win the minds and loyalties of men with the time they buy for us. The evidence is too overwhelming that that can be done to ever admit the doubt of it, but here we are, as I say, in this struggle, that I think is going to determine the course of the civilized world for an untold period of time ahead, and this is a struggle that we must continue. 

I go back, and I think it cannot be repeated too often, the importance of this struggle is such that we have a perfect right to compare the cost of carrying it on, with the cost of carrying on World War II. 

I think the direct comparison is definitely in order, and World War 

II, according to Gordon Gray, will cost us $1,300,000,000,000 before we are through paying the last pension, and this struggle now going

on in Europe will not end with ECA, but this particular segment, which is a very important segment of that struggle, will end June 30, 1952, and the total cost will not exceed $15,000,000,000. That $15,000,- 

000,000 has financed American participation in a cold war, or in a struggle just as important as World War II. 

Mr. JUDD. Will the gentleman yield for just one observation? It will end if we don't continue ECA-and end in destruction of the kind of world we believe in.

Mr. HOFFMAN. As I say, if you can just find the words, Doctor, that will "walk upon the hearts of men" to get that across, then we should be able to get it across. 

I feel frustrated and futile because in spite of all we have been able to do you still hear people say, "Well, why should we give money to those Europeans?" And "Why should we give money to those 

Koreans?" "Why should we do this?"

That isn't the deal at all. This is a deal for the survival of western civilization. I think you have got to put it just that way, and I know you can put it much better, but you have to do it right here in this House and it has to be done in the Senate. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. I want to agree with what you said and I want to ask you a question I was going to ask Mr. Drummond because on the floor of the House last week a member got up and waved an article from a newspaper which stated that ECA was contemplating spending $250,000, I believe-a small sum-to bring home to the American people just what the European recovery program meant. 

I think you have to bring home to the American people as well as to the Europeans, that the ECA program is sound and that the money is well spent. I am just wondering if we should not have in the record an explanation as to why the ECA is going into this domestic program, the reasons behind it, so that we can explain an appropriation of that sort against the statements which are made in opposition to such a procedure?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Mr. Mansfield, I would like to say we have not departed in any way from our original concept, and that was, we do have a free press in this country, we do have fine news services, we have radio, and we have the magazines; all these avenues of communication are open to us. As far as we are concerned, all we propose to do is to try to make more readily available to the free press of America, and the free radio, information about what is going on, and also make it more readily available to Europe. But we are not departing from that because I happen to believe that that is a very sound regulation. If anybody catches us at any time putting out any blurb for ECA then we ought to be hauled before Congress and stopped. All we should do is to put out information, make it available to the press, and let the press tell the story. 

I don't think we have done as well as we should have done. I think we have not done that job which clearly is our job, as well as we could have done it, for expanding that activity, and nothing more. 

We do not intend to put out any money for programs. We do intend to make it very easy for the press to get the information. They are going to find that made easier for them, but I think that is as far as we should go.

Of course, we do not expect to please that particular part of the press that was quoted on the floor of the House. That cannot be done by any activity of this kind.

I feel very deeply about this. I think we have to rely upon the 

Congress itself to do this job with the Congress. 

Mr. RIBICOFF. I think this is even more important than what Dr. 

Bunce is going to say, if you will pardon my saying so. I think the press of America likes to center its news around personalities. 

The American people in many instances are away ahead of the average Congressman and average Senator in the United States. I say this very frankly and very bluntly.

Now, if you people think a Congressman is wrong or a Senator is wrong, there is no reason why you cannot come out publicly and say so, and I think the people of this country will rally in back of you, rather than the Senator or Congressman. I think some of the timidity shown by men of stature who corral people around them-some of your subordinates could not do it because their name does not mean anything to the people-but some of the men could go out and take the offensive and you would light the fire under the men in the United States Congress and the United States Senate and the people would back up the position of men such as yourself, Mr. Hoffman. 

I think one of the greatest responsibilities is that you must capitalize on the use of your name to get your ideas over to the people of America. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Mr. Ribicoff, I appreciate that observation. I do not happen to agree with it. My conscience is clear. I have made 150 speeches in the last year, and that is a lot of speeches and I don't know how I could have made many more and still carry on this job, but I think the first battle has got to be won here. I may be entirely wrong but I would not agree that it is wise for me personally to debate issues on a personal basis with anyone. This goes so far beyond individuals, it is so important, that I think we have to keep our discussion of this program at the very highest level. As far as I am concerned, I never expect to argue with a Congressman or a Senator, either one, at any time.

Dr. Johnson is here to present the 1951 program and Dr. Bunce is here to give you this account which I think you will find most interesting. 

Mr. MERROW. I have one question, Mr. Chairman.

I think you have made a very lucid statement and I am pleased to hear your appraisal of the battle for survival. 

Perhaps you will not want to answer this, but do you not think it will be necessary for us to extend economic and military aid to the non-Communist areas in Asia? That is, on as broad a concept as the 

ECA in Europe? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I think that is the kind of question you ought to ask the Secretary of State. I do not mind telling you that I have been involved in this cold war 2 years, now, and as far as I am concerned, I think Russian imperialism is what we are fighting. If

Russia wants to try and make communism work, as far as I am concerned, they can try and make it work, but I think the real fight is with Russian imperialism, with the Kremlin's desire to impose its will on the rest of the world, and its plan for world conquest.

I think that, with relatively few dollars, provided we do an intelligent job, because right is so much on our side, and the facts are so much on our side, and resources are so much on our side, we can and should stop them wherever there is an opportunity to do so. 

Mr. MERROW. You would not care to comment on how much in the 

Asiatic area and the reason I ask this is because there is going to be a very heated debate on the ECA authorization and appropriation in the House. The question of how much it is going to cost us in the 

Far East will come up. If we could somehow get a global concept so we would know what it will cost us in the West and at the same time get some idea of what it will cost us in the East, then I think it might win support for the program. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I just could not answer that, sir. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Pfeifer- 

Mr. PFEIFER. I have no questions, Mr. Chairman, except to make a statement that the entire country is well pleased in having a man of Mr. Hoffman's caliber at the head of the ECA program. 

I fully realize from his works that he is looking upon a sick world. of which we are a part. 

Dr. Judd in his discussion before was speaking about doing certain things for certain areas. Naturally he knows, being a doctor, that the treatment is individual and not collective. The country should be taken into consideration as a patient and as an individual. They are not all treated alike. That accounts for the fact that certain sections of the world are getting more than others. 

I realize that, the Secretary of State realized that, and I know Mr. 

Hoffman realized that. No one knows the amount of money it is going to cost, nor does the doctor know how much it will cost a patient and how long it will take to get well and what is necessary to be done in order to get well. It depends upon the recovery powers of the individual and the severity of the illness. 

Likewise in this situation we face today we are all behind Mr. Hoffman; and you can rest assured, Mr. Hoffman, the country is behind you, too, but we have to help you along.

Chairman KEE. Dr. Judd. 

Mr. JUDD. I have nothing to say other than to commend Mr. Hoffman again, not only for his inspiring leadership but his hard-headed realism in presenting the program. 

I might say that one of the things that has made many Congressmen cynical is the fact that, as Mr. Ribicoff says, the country was way ahead of the Congress. But the Congress was way ahead of the 

Department of State. 

Three years ago, almost to the day, I was trying to get the Secretary of State to realize that the loss of Asia would endanger the program he was urging for Greece and Europe. He said the situations were entirely different because, he said, "The Chinese Government is not in the position at the present time the Greek Government is in; it is not approaching collapse; it is not threatened by defeat by the Communists." And he added that he saw no reason why it ever should be. 

At that time we could not get our own Department officials to realize the nature of the Communist threat. Now we are belabored by officials who say the people and the Congress don't see it. Well, that is pretty hard to take. If the State Department did not see it when

there was time to prevent the mess, it is difficult to blame the people for not seeing it.

I think you will find in the record during the debate on ERP 2 years ago I was the only member of the House of Representatives who said on the floor of the House that this was a war of survival and aid to Europe could be judged only on the basis of its necessity for our own national security. At that time it was largely being presented by our own Government as a matter of helpfulness to these people in Europe with similar culture and civilization. It was regarded as charity and philanthropy, sort of an improved UNRRA. It was false to present it that way.

I would put it more strongly than you did. You said this might even be more dangerous than World War II. I think it is infinitely more dangerous because the enemy now is so much stronger and so much more clever and resourceful and better organized and wider spread. 

I think the last war was something of a back-alley squabble compared to this world-wide cold war. 

Look what we did as a people after Pearl Harbor. Why did we not do it before Pearl Harbor?

To use Dr. Pfeifer's illustration, one of the illustrations I tried to use on this very problem, which was not very effective, I guess, was that there was no use of a doctor saying to a patient, "Now, you have pneumonia. You are desperately ill. I will give you a million units of penicillin but if you do not get well with that million, I will not give you any more. 

That is crazy; there is no use in doing anything if we do not do enough to carry it through. I believed and believe that if we are prepared to do whatever is necessary to carry through, it will cost us less, rather than more.

As you have said, it is not going to cost us $17,000,000,000 but $15,- 000,000,000, if we carry through now with renewed determination or increased determination. We ought to be so much better educated regarding the nature of what we are dealing with, both the forces against us and the forces on our side, than we were when we started. 

The feeling that things are hopeless, which is prevalent in many parts of the world now, seems to me inexcusable. It was a shot in the dark when we started. Now we have demonstrated we can achieve success where we have the will. Well, I am saying all this now perhaps in rehearsal. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. I hope you have all the Congressmen there when you make the speech.

Mr. LODGE. That is right.

I might say that I have heard some responsible criticism to the effect that a lot of our businessmen are to some extent uninformed as to what ECA needs are, and therefore they are not in the best possible position to give you the cooperation that is desirable. I commend you for not wanting to do any special pleading on the matter, and simply give the information that is needed for you to carry on your work. It may be that these criticisms are without foundation. Certainly I would agree with Mr. Mansfield that the expenditure of $250,- 

000 to disseminate ECA information in this country is a minimal sum. it would seem to me, in an enterprise so vast and significant as this. 

I wonder whether you would care to comment as to whether you feel that the information transmitted to the American businessman whose cooperation is desired has been circulated in the right places and in sufficient flow and scope?

Mr. HOFFMAN. I feel in that particular phase of our activity a good job has been done. The information goes out through the Department of Commerce. You cannot help the businessman who will not help himself. Too many businessmen here in America have had the idea that we are a procurement agency placing orders for materials. 

We don't buy anything. They must go about their business in the normal way, go out and get the business. What we are doing is siphoning into the American economy, as a result of the contribution of the American taxpayer, several billion dollars. Now, who gets that money is just a matter of good old competition. 

What we have tried to do particularly is to see that information as to the kind of goods wanted by the European countries was made available to the smaller business enterprises. We have tried to publicize abroad the names of all suppliers, American suppliers, so that the purchaser abroad who is operating through normal private channels may examine this list of suppliers. But there is nothing we can do that can gurantee anybody any business. They have to go out and get it. That is something that has been a little hard to get across because they have looked upon us as an agency, a procurement agency, that was buying various kinds of goods, but we are not.

We finance programs; practically all of our business today is business resulting from the financing of recovery programs by ECA, and goes through ordinary private trade channels as the Congress directed it should. We do not dictate what they buy; we merely check prices to see that the prices paid are market prices, but we do not give out any purchase orders. 

Mr. LODGE. Thank you very much, Mr. Hoffman. I hope that your invaluable services will remain available not only until 1952 but even beyond. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Thank you very much, Mr. Lodge. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Carnahan, have you any questions?

Mr. CARNAHAN. Regardless of all the statements that have been made and the speeches that have been made, and all that has been done, it is my opinion that still the masses of the American people are not really aware of the fact that we are engaged in a struggle for survival.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I agree. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. I do not believe they realize we must win the cold war or we will have to start the shooting war, and if we loose the cold war we will certainly have to engage in a shooting war with perhaps not too much chance to win. If we can win the cold war, then we may not have any need for a shooting war. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Of course, I wholly subscribe to that. I just wish we could get it across. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Is there not an obligation to proclaim that fact perhaps a little more vigorously than we have in the past? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. If I had known how to do it I would have done it. I am not at all proud of the job we have done. I feel we are trying to expand it and we are trying to do a job. However, it is tough to compete with the spy stories and the H-bomb and the local murders and other things of that kind. I think the newsworthiness of a cold war is limited and it therefore creates a very great problem. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. If the democratic processes survive they will have to survive by their activities during the periods of peace and not in periods of actual shooting war. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. That is right.

Of course, there was a private survey which was made for our own information. We did want to find out what the status of public opinion was, to see how big the job was. We found that as far as can be determined, the support of the Marshall plan has in the last 2 or 3 months been increased as far as the public is concerned, and not decreased, but that there is still the same hard core of isolationism. 

The difficulty is, I think, that some false impression is given to public opinion. If you ask a man, "Do you favor economy?" he says, "Wonderful, yes.' 99 I have heard Congressmen express the idea that the public is economy-conscious and therefore they could not, of course, support foreign aid. That is utter nonsense. If you ask them if they are in favor of aid to the European economy, they say, "Yes." If you put that up to them they will respond. If they have an understanding that the cost of this program has been coming down, that this particular part of this cold war is terminating, I think, on schedule, then you get very substantial support from public opinion. 63307-50-pt. 2-10

Mr. JUDD. Will the gentleman yield for one short statement?

Mr. CARNAHAN. I yield. 

Mr. JUDD. I think, sir, if you will examine it, that the single biggest cause of lack of confidence in this program or questions regarding it is the disparity between our policy in Europe and that in Asia. That question comes up more often than any other. They say, "How can it make sense, and why is it so imperative to do this in Europe when we have an opposite policy or at least half-hearted policy in Asia?"

The ordinary person is convinced, regardless of what the experts say, that the loss of Asia will make it impossible for Europe to survive. Europe is a little peninsula projecting out of the great Eurasian mainland.

That the Government has not come up with a strong, vigorous organized policy for Asia as we have had for Europe in this program, I think, causes more doubt about its success and more opposition to it than any other single thing. If we get an over-all program, I think they will get behind it.

Just as Korea is a peninsula, so western Europe is made up of a couple of peninsulas, projecting out from the great Eurasian heartland.

Mr. HOFFMAN. As I say, I never argue with Congressmen but I would like to make this statement. As I say, I think if we can hold Europe-this does not argue against anything else; I am talking only about Europe-I think that flank must be held in order to see that we have a chance to hold on to it and that we have a chance to hold South America and that we have a chance some day to regain our position in Asia.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Merrow. 

Mr. MERROW. To the degree that success is attained in western 

Europe, to that degree it will cost us less to carry on, will it not? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes; but I would like to add this to it. The very strong reasons for trying to speed up the program which Europe adopted itself for a better organization of the continental economy, do not lie in the immediate savings that would be effected. The reasons lie much deeper than that. They go, I think, to the ultimate ability of the European Continent to provide the people of Europe with a standard of living sufficiently high so there could be no appeal from

any ism. In other words, I do not believe Europe can possibly realize on her great potentialities for prosperity and security unless there is a much better organization of the European economy than now prevails. That means much closer cooperation. There will be some immediate contribution, perhaps a year from now, but the great contribution would come later. 

Mr. MERROW. May I ask one thing more. Suppose the Congress decides to cut $500,000,000 from the estimate you have made; do you think that will increase, first, the cooperation in western Europe, and, secondly, how badly will it hurt the program? 

Mr. HOFFMAN. If we did not believe that $2,950,000,000 was the minimum amount to carry on the program, we would have used another figure. In other words, as nearly as we can estimate, that represents the lowest dollar upon which you can carry on an effective program.

My own opinion is that if the amount is cut in any substantial wayno man who lives can say whether $1,000,000 or $10,000,000 or $25,- 000,000 one way or another is the difference between success or failure; 

I am not making that statement-I think it might be extremely costly in its results, both in our efforts to close the dollar gap, which is the main problem, and, second, on the effort to encourage integration of the European economy. After all, in the Marshall plan, while we merely ask Europe to do what Europe promised to do, there are terrific difficulties facing every government as they get down to the practical matter of integrating these economies and unless there is support for them, financial support, you can understand why they would not dare undertake those risks. I mean the risks are real. When you start liberalizing trade, you take away protection from industries to a certain extent, you take away protection from a certain group here and there, and unless there is some backing available so those temporary effects can be offset, your government people would say, "We just cannot take the risk."

I think this year immediately ahead is a crucial year. 

Mr. MERROW. A cut this year, then, would do more damage than the cut last year?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Our estimate was cut last year from $4,000,000,000 down to $3,778,000,000. Really it was not a very substantial cut. We ourselves saved from the amount $150,000,000, so that we actually operated with something in the neighborhood of $300,000,000 less than the $4,000,000,000 that we asked for. 

Mr. JUDD. You cut $150,000,000 below that figure the Congress gave you?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes; that is right. It was almost $300,000,000 less than the total we figure, but we made it clear that when you are working in amounts of that kind you have got to make your estimates. 

What we had were much more favorable prices than contemplated and we had devaluation coming in there which helped solve certain problems, and a number of other factors came in. We only promised we would not spend any money that we didn't have to. Now it would appear there is some desire to penalize us for not spending it. 

Mr. MERROW. I think you should be commended for saving $150,- 

000.000. The idea that keeps recurring to my mind, however, is this. 

Perhaps with more cooperation-and I think you have done an excel-

lent job in setting forth the goals-integration could be stepped up, less money would be needed, and this would be a saving for the taxpayers.

Mr. HOFFMAN. I agree with you. We have made an arbitrary cut of 30 percent. We told them, "If you go ahead with this payments union, which is a part of our payments program, you can save, in our opinion, you can make better use of your resources and there will be a consequent saving." 

That has all been taken into account. 

I think the Congress forgets. You know about 6 months ago we were asked to save a billion dollars from last year, and now we come up with a figure of more than a billion dollars, considerably, and they say, "Can't you cut it another $500,000,000?"

Mr. MERROW. It is a very discouraging world we live in. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Zablocki. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I have no questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Hoffman, we thank you very much indeed for your excellent statement.

I have been very much interested in the discussion. I think it has done quite a great amount of good in bringing out clearly the necessity of the dissemination throughout this country of more information with respect to world conditions.

We have had trouble in getting across to the people of the United States ever since the initiation of this program the purposes for which it was started, and the end in view. I recall very clearly the statement made by Dr. Judd on the floor of the House when the question first came up. He remarked a while ago that he believed he was the only one who made this statement, but I remember clearly that I asserted on the floor that if there was any man in Congress who did not believe that this program, the success of the program, was vital and necessary to the security of our Nation, they should vote against the appropriation.

I believe that now, that it is for our own national security that we entered into the program. It is for our own national security that we want to carry it through to success. 

The difficulty, it seems to me, in getting the information across, is that we have tremendous competition. There is evidently a mass of misinformation competing with us and that misinformation is going out every day. The people evidently find great difficulty in differentiating between the true and the false, between real information and misinformation.

If we could only get across to the people all over the country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the fact that we are in a serious war, a war that we must win for our own national security, I believe we would have no trouble whatever in Congress. We would have the backing of the entire country from coast to coast. 

I hope we will be able to get that information across. 

Mr. JUDD. Is there any way you can get answers into the magazines, articles telling the other side of the story, in answer to what 

Hauser, for example, wrote in the Saturday Evening Post? 

You saw that article?

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes. 

Mr. JUDD. For one group who gets to hear you, there are a good many millions who read the Saturday Evening Post.

Mr. HOFFMAN. Yes. 

All we can do, and we propose to do it, is to make available to the 

Post full information in the hope that they will perhaps be willingand I think they will be-to publish other articles. We have that very much in mind, Doctor. 

Mr. JUDD. The thing that has done more damage in my district is a professor of German ancestry at the University of Minnesota, who was the most strenuous advocate of ERP when it first came up. He organized petitions and everything else to get ERP adopted. He was over in Germany this last summer and elsewhere in Europe. He came home and now is making speeches and getting resolutions coming into my desk saying it must be interrupted completely, it is a failure, is a danger, that it will weaken the United States and it will not achieve recovery in Europe.

It is hard to overcome testimony like that. He has been a respected professor for many years. He has been over there and he knows. He is regarded as an open-minded citizen. Everyone knows he was the 

No. I advocate of it in our area, and now is the No. 1 denouncer of it. 

It is not taken as an evidence, perhaps, of his instability, but as an evidence of the failure of the program. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. For that 1 man you have 500 who come back and tell the other story.

Mr. JUDD. But the Saturday Evening Post and others will print the story of the one who denounces it. 

Mr. HOFFMAN. The success of the program is not news, but if somebody wants to take a crack at it, that is news. 

Mr. JUDD. "Inept, incompetent, inefficient, undemocratic and corrupt"-that is news.

We will continue the testimony of Mr. Drummond.

FURTHER STATEMENT OF ROSCOE DRUMMOND, CHIEF, INFORMA- TION DIVISION, OFFICE OF SPECIAL REPRESENTATIVE, ECA 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Drummond, I am curious to know what are the most effective parts of the Communist propaganda in Europe today that you have to try to overcome. When we were over there with the 

Voice of America subcommittee 212 years or so ago, I remember there were three of four main arguments, that they had persuaded a surprisingly large number of the people in these countries to believe. 

One, of course, was that the Marshall plan was American imperialism, that we were trying to establish for Wall Street monopoly control for imperialistic reasons.

Another was that we were doing it to prevent an economic tailspin here. Karl Marx said there is always a depression after a war and therefore America must have a depression economically and this is an attempt to save ourselves. I was surprised at the number of people

1 in many countries who were not so much worried about what Russia might do to them as they were about whether America was going to have a big depression.

Then there was another one, that we were furnishing dollars, they were to furnish the military manpower. We were fighting to the last 

Frenchman, the old argument. I found in Scandinavia people who said, "We are caught between the two great giants and we are the people who will be crushed." They did not seem to realize that unless we resisted the communism giant, then it would roll over them and they would be enslaved. Offhand, those were some of the lines I recall that made a surprising amount of headway. I am curious to know what the general sentiment among the people of these countries is today with regard to these. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. My observation, Dr. Judd, would be that in the main the Communists are playing about the same music as they were when you were over there. They have changed it some. 

First they will argue that the people ought not to support the Marshall plan or work for it because it cannot succeed. Then they will argue that they ought to oppose it because it is succeeding so well that we are overdominating the European countries. 

In the main, they oftentimes play the neutrality angle, the idea, "Let the United States and Russia settle this and let us be about our business and stand on the side lines." 

Those themes are utilized over and over again in the Communist press and that is one of the reasons why the information job is never done. It is never completed. You have to return to the truth all the time in order to catch up with the lie and the misrepresentation. 

I cited the other day when I was here the fact that the percentage of opposition to the Marshall plan has gone down very considerably during the past year. 

Mr. JUDD. Twenty-nine percent, I think you said. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. From 29 percent to 16 percent. I think in the main that decrease in French opposition is a decrease wholly in the marginal ranks of the Communist supporters and is evidence that their repeated thesis is losing weight in the face of what is actually happening in Europe, in the face of both action and information at the same time and I agree they cannot be separate. 

Mr. JUDD. We were over there when the formation of the Cominform was announced. In the original declaration they had language which indicated their line was being changed from the old traditional theme about "workers of the world, unite," a movement across national boundaries above national loyalties and so forth, to the theme that the way to preserve Czechoslovakia, France, whatever the country might be, was to embrace communism. They apparently had discovered that nationalism was the strongest force they had to combat, and they were trying to jump on the nationalist bandwagon and say, "Become Communists to preserve your national identity" as against the old Trotsky line that the people of the proletariat must unite regardless of national ties.

What is your opinion of the way these two forces are moving, national versus the international theme? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. My observation is that the Russian actions have become so visibly contrary to the true interests of nationalism that the

Communist thesis of nationalism has lost a great deal of weight and impact in western Europe and that, of course, the development of the Tito-Stalin rift has had tremendous effects which have not yet come above the surface in the Communist Party throughout western Europe.

It is visible in the French Communist Party and you are getting a kind of intellectual Titoism which is going right down to the roots of the Communist parties in western Europe and I think it is because, while the Russians have tried to play the game of nationalism, their actual actions have been so against the national interests of the particular countries that that theme, however strongly propagandized, is not making headway.

Mr. JUDD. They are getting away with it more successfully in certain parts of the Far East. That is their main line out there. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Because their true purposes have not yet been exposed.

Mr. JUDD. They are saying, "We are the ones who will liberate you from your terrible oppression under the west and enable you to develop true Chinese nationalism or Burmese nationalism or some other nationalism."

I am glad to know that has happened in Europe. I was confident it would. I think it will happen in Asia if we keep them from continuing to win victories.

Mr. DRUMMOND. I would like to emphasize that while superficially and while to a certain extent it is accurate to say that the Tito-Stalin rift is ideological, it is an ideological rift that has a basic root in the economic situation and really it is an economic break because Russia wanted to utilize and adapt the Yougoslav economy to serve Russia and not to serve Yugoslavia. The fact that Yugoslavia has seen that the western countries under the impact of the Marshall plan, and that the grass is growing greener in western Europe, has been a big factor in accentuating and bringing to full fruit the independence of 

Tito. 

So I think in many real ways the European recovery program has helped to bring about the break between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union.

Mr. JUDD. The problem is in the areas where communism is still winning. It is the problem of holding it back until the people who haven't yet been devoured also see that this propaganda is wholly fraudulent and a hoax.

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is right. 

Mr. JUDD. They have the idea that once they get people under control, they have them and they can't do anything about it. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. One good example of that was the report which the Norwegian Trade Union representative made to the Norwegian people when they sent one group to the United States and one group to Russia. They made a most magnificent report of factual, careful consideration, comparing their experiences, and as a part of our information program, we have put that into 14 languages of Europe and we have circulated it to millions of trade-union people, in all the 

Marshall-plan countries.

Mr. JUDD. That seems to be the strongest kind of propaganda because it is out of the mouths of their own people.

Mr. DRUMMOND. It is Europeans talking to Europeans and that is the essential approach that we use at every opportunity. 

Mr. JUDD. This is a little beside the point, but I would like to just get your opinion: Obviously, the Soviet Union is more troubled about 

Titoism than anything else because that is the one real threat that has developed. Recently Tito recognized this Communist Ho regime out in Indochina and in return it has recognized Tito and established some sort of relations with him. 

Now, Ho's outfit is completely subservient to the Soviet Union. He could hardly have done that unless the Soviets wanted him to do it. 

Is there a possibility that the Soviets seeing that it is going to be difficult, if not impossible, to liquidate Tito just by denunciations and assassination or uprisings of any sort they aren't strong enough—are moving through this satellite to patch up the rift in some way or other without too much loss of face?

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is a very problematic question and it is hard to answer. I have thought about it. 

Mr. JUDD. It is hard to explain that action. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I have thought about it a great deal. I do know that in the last 4 or 5 days Tito has laid down exceedingly inacceptable conditions to Stalin in which he said, "You have dirtied the linen first, you have to apologize and you have to take the initiative. There will be no initiative from Yugoslavia. 

Those words are rather encouraging from our standpoint, and I should think that Tito has gone so far that the forces that are operating to keep the split "constructive" from our standpoint, are stronger, it seems to me, than the forces that are operating to bring it together. 

That is just a judgment for what it is worth. 

Mr. JUDD. I think it is true.

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think we always have to assume the worst. We cannot premise any policy, except on an assumption that they may throw their arms around each other tomorrow.

Mr. JUDD. That is right, and we have to be realistic and know that 

Vietnam Communists didn't do that without the Kremlin wanting them to do it for a purpose. Tito's action is encouraging because of the violence of it. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. You see, the concession he has made through recognition hasn't cost him much. That is a rather cheap little purchase. 

Mr. JUDD. I note in all the pictures in this very excellent book you have prepared that the emphasis all the time is put on "Marshall" and nowhere "U. S. A." Have you decided that is the best way to dramatize it? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. That wasn't really intentional. For example, all of our posters, all of our placards which are used by the Government making public works contain the words "U. S." and "E. R. P.," but we do use the Marshall plan a good deal because the name has become deeply associated with the most favorable viewpoints on the part of the 

European people.

Mr. JUDD. But they understand "Marshall" means the U. S. A. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I am sure they do and we do not minimize the use of "U. S. A." in all the markings. I appreciate your point and we are aware of it. 

Mr. JUDD. That is all. Thank you very much.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Zablocki, have you any questions?

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, I did want some information relative to an information program being sponsored by the OEEC. I understand the Trade Fair Committee of OEEC is planning an exhibition in Chicago in the early part of August. Perhaps Mr. 

Drummond could give us some information on that project. Undoubtedly the program is to enlighten the American people as to the past progress of ERP in Europe, and with the hope of instilling further interest and attitude toward the continuation of the Marshall plan.

Can you tell us if it is the intent of this committee to have the contemplated exhibition available to other cities in the United States? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I have discussed that with the OEEC in Paris. 

The purpose of the OEEC participation in the Chicago Trade Fair is twofold: One, it is to help sell European products to the United 

States; and two, there will be another part of the exhibit which will tell the story of progress in Europe under the European recovery program.

Now, that exhibit was designed for the particular purpose of being shown at the Chicago Trade Fair, and I believe that the final decision to participate in the fair is yet to be made. I think it is to be made shortly. I think there were some doubts on this side as to whether actually the fair was going to come off, at one stage I think that is not overstating it but on the assumption that the fair goes through and that the OEEC does participate, which looks likely, then it is my best judgment that the fair would not only be available, but desirable in other cities in this country. If anyone were interested in its use in a particular locality, and a request were to be made to the ECA here, it would be transmitted to me on the other side and I would be very glad to do everything possible to arrange it. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I would like to, at this time, transmit a request.

The city of Milwaukee is very interested in having the exhibit scheduled for Chicago to follow to the city of Milwaukee, which is going to have a fair, I understand, the week of December 9 to 17. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Would it be possible to have the representatives of the fair write to the ECA formally? That would really carry it to a definite decision. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Do I understand the request is to be forwarded to the ECA? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Here; yes. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. But I thought that the ECA is not sponsoring it.

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is right, but we are participating observers in all of the activities of the OEEC, so if the request for transfer were made to the ECA here, it would go to Paris and I would bring it up with the OEEC. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I understand you are leaving for Paris soon.

Mr. DRUMMOND. Yes. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Therefore it is necessary Milwaukee follow through on the request immediately.

May I ask you if there are any Marshall moneys expended in this promotional project? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Yes; a small percentage.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. To be spent within the United States? May I first clarify that: For the rental of the floor space, for example?

Mr. DRUMMOND. You are talking about the exhibit? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Yes. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. No; it is entirely financed by the OEEC. It is entirely financed by the participating governments.

Mr. JUDD. It doesn't require any dollars, does it? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. It requires some dollars for expenses. They have to spend several hundred thousand dollars to rent space. 

Mr. JUDD. How can they do it without our dollars?

Mr. DRUMMOND. They have a certain amount of free dollars. 

Mr. JUDD. They have just that many fewer dollars to buy flour. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I would like to state that I am not certain what the dollar content of the enterprise is, because that is not directly my business. But I would say there, Dr. Judd, that in order to earn 10 times as many dollars, you may have to spend a dollar in order to earn more.

Mr. JUDD. I don't think we should kid ourselves that it isn't ECA money because, if it is dollars, it is ECA money. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think broadly that is correct, but technically there are a fair amount of earned dollars in all these countries. 

Chairman KEE. I suppose they want to open up a market if they can for their goods?

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is correct. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. While we were in France, it was called to our attention that some very adverse publicity was given to the Marshall plan whenever some spoiled goods were delivered, and the particular people we interviewed said that the United States had not given enough publicity to the good the ERP program is doing for the recipient countries.

Now, is it within your category to do that kind of promotional information, or is OEEC negligent in that score. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. We are undertaking really an interconnected, collective information program. We work through the participating government with our information program. 

OEEC does a fair amount of information work, but if we were not over there generating a rather imaginative and vigorous information program, I wouldn't be surprised to see it rather timid and whisperish.

We would not hesitate to play a fairly active role in countering that kind of information. Actually I have been over there 6 months and I haven't seen a single point on that score. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In any particular country, or generally?

Mr. DRUMMOND. I am not concerned with all of the 18 Marshall plan countries and I haven't seen that as a very acute phase of our problem.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. How far have the Scandinavian countries progressed with films they intended to produce explaining and portraying to their people ECA aid?

Mr. DRUMMOND. At the present time we have films in all 14 languages shown in all the Marshall plan countries. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I believe, it was in Norway we were informed that a film was in the making. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Many of them are made by the participating governments. I cannot report precisely as to what the status of the Norwegian film is because I do not know. I will be very glad to find out

but actually we are getting government participation in the production of films in all the Marshall-plan countries now. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. This particular film was to be on a definite theme, showing how the Marshall plan had contained communism. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I don't know whether that film is completed. With the cooperation of the governments, we will have completed this year 59 documentary films and they will be shown in all the Marshall plan countries in all 14 languages. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Coming back to France, I wish to restate the only criticism we heard was, "You people don't tell us enough about what you are doing. We do not know what France is receiving, except when we receive anything bad, and then the Communists let us know." That was the only criticism they had. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I do not know that you were here the other morning when I was here. There has been a pretty full answer in the record on that subject, both from Mr. Bingham and myself. I think it is careful to say that despite a slow start, the French Government is really lending genuine cooperation in the field of information in France at the present time. We are getting motion pictures into the commercial theaters throughout France, we are getting special ERP radio programs on the standard wave national networks of France, and we are getting public ceremonies marking the opening of ERP projects in which members of the French Cabinet are participating and which are making very favorable and significant news. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Do you think the favorable news of recovery in

Europe could be had for use in our country so we would not have the anticipated trouble with passage of ECA in this Congress?

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think a very considerable and really objective presentation of the recovery that is going forward in Europe could be made available and could be used over here, and to quite an appreciable extent that is beginning to be done at the present time. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. We will have to awaken public sentiment on that score or we will certainly have a lot of trouble here. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think we have to make a careful and honest distinction between a faithful account of what is being done, and using it just to propagandize. I think a very faithful account can be made and is being made increasingly on this side, and that is one of the jobs which the ECA information programs in Washington needs to do. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. That is all, Mr. Chairman, Chairman KEE. Mr. Judd. 

Mr. JUDD. Has there been a study made of this work by other private firms like the March of Time? Have they made a film on ERP and sent it out commercially through our own movie houses in this country?

Mr. DRUMMOND. The March of Time has made two films for us. 

Mr. JUDD. I don't go often enough myself to see.

Mr. DRUMMOND. They have made two films and have been experimenting with them and have them near completion. I do not know when commercial distribution has been arranged but that is in prospect.

Mr. JUDD. I would think you ought to get hold of Eric Johnston and get it in every movie house in the country. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. We had an all-afternoon session with him last week working on this very thing.

Mr. JUDD. And if somebody like the March of Time does it, it carries more weight than if it is distributed by ECA. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. There is no question about it. 

Mr. JUDD. During the recent election campaign in the United Kingdom, the Conservatives charged that the Labor Government had not given proper recognition to or had not told the full story of United 

States aid to Britain. What is your comment on that?

Mr. DRUMMOND. I haven't detailed documentary evidence on it, but I have been much interested in it and it is my careful view, Dr. 

Judd, that we are getting the Marshall plan story told very well in Britain, that in the main both sides in the Government have substantially cooperated. Actually, I think the level of understanding and the width of understanding of the European recovery program you will find is as high if not higher in Britain than in many other countries, and I would say I am substantially gratified.

Mr. JUDD. Looking at this sheet you prepared telling of your broadcasts, you use the regular Voice of America facilities, do you not?

Mr. DRUMMOND. We use those facilities in addition on all these broadcasts. All these broadcasts go out over the standard wave national networks in participating countries. The Voice of America in the main gives news reports and some programs of their own, and while it is possible that there may be duplication of audience, I just say there is no danger of us being heard by too many people. 

Mr. JUDD. Do you have to buy the time on the local radio stations?

Mr. DRUMMOND. No. 

Mr. JUDD. There is one item here I was curious about. This symphony program. "Fifty minutes of music recorded by leading orchestras in Marshall plan countries." It goes out I guess once a week to each of the 17 countries? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is right. 

Mr. JUDD. What kind of music is that, classical music? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. Yes, and it is very well listened to in Europe, because they are orchestras with great reputations. It includes a 

10-minute interspersed commentary on European recovery and what

Europeans need to know in order to do the job better. 

Mr. JUDD. In the intermission you have Olin Downes, or his equivalent? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is just what we do. Incidentally, Dr. Judd, you will be interested to know that 500 radio stations in the United States have asked that the program be used over here, and it is going to be made available to them. 

Mr. JUDD. Send them this?

Mr. DRUMMOND. Surely. 

Mr. JUDD. Good. 

I have nothing further, Mr. Chairman. I want to congratulate 

Mr. Drummond for his patriotism in giving up his position of very great importance and influence in this country to do this even more important job, with less credit and more grief, in the ERP.

Mr. DRUMMOND. Thank you. 

Chairman KEE. I also want to congratulate you on having undertaken a difficult job in Europe and having carried it through very successfully. I only wish we had the same thing done in America. 

I think we need it here almost as much as they do over in Europe and

perhaps more. They have concrete evidence of what you are doing over there and perhaps know more about the purpose of it than we do. I think we should publicize it in this country, and especially publicize the purpose actuating us in carrying on the program, because our people do not seem to appreciate to a very large extent at least to the extent they ought to appreciate it, the real meaning of the whole program and what it means to us, and to our national security. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I appreciate what you say and I would like to say that if you have time and are so disposed, you will find it interesting to get a report from Mr. Mullen, who is the Director of Information in Washington, as to what his plans are and what the needs are and what can properly be done to more fully tell the record to the people of the United States in a way which would be satisfactory to everybody. I will just add that. 

Chairman KEE. I hope that won't come too late.

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Drummond, may I ask your opinion on an item that we talked about here when we had up the Voice of America bill 3 years ago? People always call it the Voice of America. I have wondered if it might not be better accepted and be more effective if we called it the Voice of Freedom or something like that. What has happened in America is not because it is America, but because America is free. The thing that should give them hope is not just to look at what has happened here; it is the belief that it could happen to them, if they too struggle to become free and develop a form of government and social system in some respects like our own, and work together to get security for this whole area in western Europe. People are sensitive, they do not like to be the recipients of aid and you can hammer that line too much. I have seen that sometimes efforts just to sell America can be discouraging because the contrast, the gap between what they are able to do in their immediate situation and what we appear to have with great comfort and affluence, is discouraging rather than encouraging. It seems to me that we might get greater cooperation in a common, mutual effort, if we called it the Voice of 

Freedom, or something like that.

Mr. DRUMMOND. I would like to respond to that, Dr. Judd, by saying not only do I think the idea is right but ultimately and as soon as possible we ought to find ways of making what you call the Voice of Freedom an expression of a collective free world information program, and I think that the pattern for what might be done has been tentatively laid by the bilateral treaties under the European recovery program, in which much of our information program is carried on, not by the United States, but by all the participating governments. I look forward to the time-and I shouldn't think it would be too long delayed when we would have an information arm of the Atlantic Community, so you would have the Voice of Freedom speaking for the United Atlantic Community. It could well become a part of the 

North Atlantic Treaty.

Mr. JUDD. I tried to get that done when we set up the Voice of 

America program and the supernationalists said it was against our interests, I thought that was the best way to serve our own long-term interests.

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think you will find new support for that, Dr. Judd. 

Mr. FULTON. Why could it not be the United Nations?

Mr. JUDD. Because the United Nations is not the Voice of Freedom. 

Mr. FULTON. I would like to hear from the other witness. Why could it not be a voice of the United Nations, under the United Nations? Is it possible to implement it not through just a particular community, but make it broader than that? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I would say that if you could get a united information program that would not have the hand of censorship laid on it by other countries in the United Nations it would be a good thing. In other words, I would be willing to test your own instant reaction, which

I understand very well, that we probably wouldn't be allowed to do it, but in principle a United Nations information program would be useful, although I must say that from the experience that we have had with both the delay and the opposition within the United Nations on the part of those countries which do not permit freedom, we would likely run into very great difficulties, and that because of those difficulties we actually had to have a North Atlantic Treaty. If the United 

Nations had been functioning properly-if I may be allowed to express an idea on policy outside of information-we wouldn't have had to have the North Atlantic Treaty. It is possible that the same line of experience would suggest that we ought to begin a Voice of Freedom information program where we would know we would have clear-cut, vigorous and united support for it. In principle I would not rule out the United Nations. 

Mr. FULTON. You and Dr. Judd were speaking of a forward point of action, looking at points you arrived at later, and I was then saying that if that is one step, could not the United Nations be another step? 

Mr. DRUMMOND. That is quite so.

Mr. JUDD. I would surely be opposed to having the Soviet dominated world be part of the responsible sponsors of a portrayal of what has not happened in their world but has happened in our world. We are in a war where there are no holds barred. We haven't too much to take credit for but I am not in favor of their appearing to be given the credit for what they have opposed. 

Mr. FULTON. Would you not be interested in the whole world getting the actual facts even though the facts might be favorable to the Soviet Union? 

Mr. JUDD. Surely, but I am not willing to let them get the credit or let it go out that what has happened under and in and as a result of the voluntary cooperation organization of free peoples, can be portrayed, interpreted, or accepted as having been developed in the Sovietdominated areas. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. So far Russia has refused to participate in 

UNESCO and if they would not participate in UNESCO I doubt if they would participate in this kind of a program. 

Mr. FULTON. If they would not participate it is through no fault of ours and if it is the United Nations doing it, I think it might, along with Dr. Judd's ideas, have a broader acceptance because it is on a broader level. 

Mr. DRUMMOND. I think I wouldn't be honest if I did not add further my own view that first there is the problem of whether Russia would participate. Then there is another problem which we haven't mentioned, which I have experienced quite definitely in Europe and that is the problem of getting any information program off the ground,

getting it going, getting the countries not only to agree with it in principle, but to participate with it and carry it forward. 

What is in the back of my mind is that the only way to do that in my experience thus far is to work with the nations that are not only theoretically willing but are acutely aware of the problem and eager to do the job. So we might find it very wise to begin with the Atlantic 

Community where we are already united behind a common program of defense, and in a slightly wider area, in a common program of economic recovery, and I think we need to emerge into a common program of information, and I like the idea of calling it The Voice of Freedom. I just add that out of my own experience for such value as it might be.
