Mr. DRUMMOND. Thank you, Judge Kee.

Chairman KEE. We wish you all the luck in the world. 

We have with us Dr. Johnson. Dr. Johnson is well known to all of us. He is Director of the Division of the Korea Program of the 

ECA. He has appeared before this committee on different occasions and we feel sure that he can give us the most reliable and up-to-date information with reference to the progress of the South Korean Republic.

Dr. Johnson, we are very glad to have you here and you can proceed in your own way.

STATEMENT OF EDGAR A. J. JOHNSON, DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF KOREA PROGRAM, ECA 

Dr. JOHNSON. There has been laid before the members of the committee two documents. One is the yellow book called Economic 

Guides. That contains the performance charts to which I will presently refer. It contains also on pages 16 and 17, this large spread which is the break-down of the Korean program for 1951. The top chart is the total program. The bottom chart is the break-down of the four largest sections.

The other document is this brown book called the Korean Aid Program. It has the detailed justification for the several projects that are contained in the entire program. I shall refer to some larger charts but practically all those charts are reproduced, or at least the substance thereof is contained in these two documents. 

I shall want to say something first of all as to why this sort of a program is necessary for the survival of the Republic of Korea. 

Secondly, I want to give you some idea of what must be done in order to insure economic viability of the South Korean Republic. In the third place I want to tell you what has been done and fourthly I want to tell you what we propose to do in 1951. . I do not think I need to reiterate the seriousness of this task after what the Secretary of State and the ECA Administrator said this morning, nor need I point out how difficult this joint Korean-American task is. It must be carried on in the face of persistent Communist interference. It must be carried on by a Korean Government which

is somewhat hampered by inexperience, and a Government which is confronted with baffling fiscal and technical problems. 

Governing a nation of 20,000,000 people is a large enough task under the best of circumstances. It is incredibly difficult when the normal commercial relations have been disturbed by tearing an economy the size of Korea out of its historical regional context, when the industrial plant and the transportation system have been undermaintained for a decade, when by reason of a fortuitous nationalization of industrial mining, banking, and commercial enterprises, all of these must temporarily be operated by the government, when the government must not only operate this cumbersome temporarily nationalized economy but must make acceptable plans for the transfer of these enterprises to private ownership, and concurrently, and finally, when all this must be done not under conditions of peace and quiet, but in the face of sporadic, well-organized, local disturbances designed to frustrate everything that is being done. 

In this culture of ours, we believe it is a very commendable doctrine of political science that homogeneous cultural groups should be encouraged by the family of nations to organize themselves into independent nations.

This concept of ethnic and cultural self-determination has deep historical roots and is accepted as being just and proper. 

But inasmuch as a particular culture group finds itself located in a certain amount of space on the earth's surface, it finds by historical accident it has certain resources with which to sustain its people. 

The upshot is that political independence may be only a pious hope unless the economy can be developed to preserve this political independence.

I submit, and this is merely my personal opinion, that it is rather easy for the Great Powers to assert that Korea ought to be free and independent. It is a much, much harder problem to work out the domestic and international economic arrangements that will make it possible for Korea to survive as an independent nation. 

There is little place for sentimental or emotional thinking in this kind of a problem. It is one that must be approached in a realistic, tough-minded way. All major elements of the total problem must be judiciously appraised. The technical difficulties must be faced frankly.

Above all, the whole task must be comprehended, and a program of action must be laid down which will accomplish the whole task, and that program of action must be followed consistently and relentlessly. 

What I am saying is precisely what Mr. Hoffman and Mr. Acheson said this morning, that if Korea is to survive as an independent nation and in terms of the realities of the cold war-I mean South Koreathen whatever the Korean Government does, whatever the United States as an assisting agency does, whatever ECA as an implementing agency does, must be squarely, persistently, intelligently, and faithfully pointed toward the single goal of making South Korea economically viable.

Now this does not mean that the plan has to be casehardened and inflexible, one that should be followed without change. The plan must of necessity be flexible, one that can and will be modified, both in terms of success and new difficulties. 63307-50-pt. 2- -11

But the goals and targets must be staked out and they must be reached, by one expedient or another. There can be no indecision if this job is going to be done. There can be no indecision here, no temporizing or vacillation. 

Those of us who have been concerned with the Korean problem honestly believe this job can be done. We do not pretend to be experts but we are not really amateurs.

Dr. Bunce, who is here to answer your questions, has been here on the job since 1946. He spent 6 years in Korea before that time. 

I have been in the midst of the Korean problem since 1946, in one capacity or another. Dr. Bunce's deputies and many members of his staff have been in Korea for 3 and 4 years. 

Now, that, Mr. Chairman, is the problem that we face. 

I turn now to the next item I want to lay before you: 

What must be done, what has been done and what can be done in 1951?

May I answer the first question in a very general way. What must be done? I do that so we can have constantly before us the central, all-important goal.

If South Korea is to continue as an independent nation-and I mean an independent nation after the ECA program is over, that is, an independent nation without foreign assistance she must be prepared to finance annual imports of about $75,000,000 by 1953. 

That is because she has no bituminous coal. That has to be imported. You cannot run rail locomotives without some bituminous coal. At least you cannot do it yet.

She has no rubber, and that must be imported, all of it. 

She can only produce about half or less than half of the lumber she needs because of the terrible denuding of her forests that has gone on for a long, long time.

She can produce only about a third of her raw cotton. She could produce more but that would mean you would encroach on the food supply because you would have to convert rice lands into cotton lands. 

This imported cotton is needed for minimum cloth requirements and when I speak of her cloth requirements, I am thinking of very modest cloth requirements of not more than 7 yards per capita as contrasted with between 35 and 50 yards in America.

She must import all of her petroleum products. There are no oil domes or oil shales in Korea, at least the geologists assure us there are none that have been discovered so far. 

She must import machine parts, fabricated steel, nonferrous metals, some of them, and essential chemicals.

Those are the major categories of absolutely necessary imports. 

Some are supplemental to domestic production. For example, she must import gypsum. She has cement shales and coals but you cannot produce cement without some gypsum. She must import some pitch. 

She has abundant quantities of anthracite coal but it is a tertiary coal, dust-like and must be bound together for most industrial uses into briquets and that calls for pitch.

Other imports are essential raw materials, as I said, that cannot be produced in Korea at all. Others are the critical items indispensable to the maintenance of modern industrial equipment. 

Now, to finance this $75,000,000 worth of imports by 1953, Korea must build up her exports as shown in this chart.

(The chart referred to is as follows:)

Dr. JOHNSON. Exports must rise by 1953 up to that total of $75,- 

000,000. We are on our way in 1950, right now. You can see we are already well on the way. But there is a long way to go. 

You will see, as I proceed, that the chief emphasis will have to be on rice exports. There is no purpose in trying to evade this problem. 

In the immediate foreseeable future, these are the only things, that are listed on this chart, that Korea has to export: Rice, minerals, marine products, some manufactured goods and a few miscellaneous items.

If more manufactured goods can be exported, or more marine products or more minerals, that is good. That will take the pressure off of rice. It simply changes the proportions. 

But there have been some careful estimates made both by the ECA mission and the military government which preceded it, and the Korean Government. These are the best projections that we can lay before you.

Our problem therefore comes down to this: How can the economy be operated to provide a tolerable standard of living for 20,000,000 people and at the same time build up net export surpluses by 1953 to a total of at least $75,000,000?

It will be obvious that great increases in agricultural, mining, and marine production are imperative. The task is to insure that they will be realized.

Now the biggest chunk there is rice. There are only two ways of increasing agricultural production: Either by increasing the amount of usable land, or increasing the acre yield of growing crops. In a country like Korea there are certain limits on the amount of new land that can be brought into use, and the major emphasis will therefore have to be placed upon increasing the yield per acre, but not to the neglect of increasing the amount of irrigated rice acreage. 

It is now contemplated and carefully estimated that if the projects which are now under construction are completed by 1953, that will bring into production enough land to produce under good weather conditions about 220,000 metric tons. That is almost half of the amount that will have to be exported in 1953. 

These projects must go on. You cannot stop in the middle. You have to have the iron; you must have the cement; you must have the form lumber. You must have the valves and gates and the rest of the materials that go into it.

We have here pictures to show you the number of projects that are now in process. There are 1,470 of them all together. Over 300 were completed this year, which will bring into use some 77,000 acres of irrigated land.

Now, the other problem, and the one which concerns us immediately, is the increase in the yield per acre up to the levels now attained in Japan. That means that commercial fertilizer must be supplied, not only at the present level but in increasing quantities. We have gotten the yields which I shall show presently as a result of the application of 77,000 metric tons in 1948, and 78,000 tons of contained nitrogen in 1949.

We are planning this year-and this is the program I laid before you last time-for 110,000 tons of contained nitrogenous fertilizer in 1950 but that is scaled. That is out there now and ready to be applied

1 on the land. In 1951 we build it up still higher to 130,000 tons of contained nitrogen but that is scaled in relation to the export goals which I have already explained. 

Now, you will notice that when I say that Korea has to build up exports to around $75,000,000 I did not include fertilizer. I did not include fertilizer as an import item. So it comes down to this: That unless some other solution is found to the fertilizer problem, you have an imbalance.

The annual cost right now for the fertilizer is in the amount of $40,000,000 and we can not visualize exports large enough to cover the import of the other indispensable imports plus that fertilizer. 

The upshot is that we must attack that in a different way. The fertilizer will have to be produced in Korea, out of Korean coal and out of Korean air. The import of fertilizer is the temporary commodity program. In the meantime, in the development of coal and power industry, that must go on, so that by 1953 we can taper off the import of fertilizer and Korea can produce her own nitrogenous fertilizer. 

Now the nub of this whole rice export plan, therefore, is fertilizer, first to be imported and then to be produced in Korea. 

May I have the first chart here?

Dr. JOHNSON. You will see when we look at this program in terms of financial categories, the overwhelming item is the fertilizer. 

That is the single import that the Korean economy cannot support and it is wasteful for her to contemplate importing fertilizer permanently when it can be produced by means of Korean coal. 

It will take 80,000 tons of contained nitrogen to produce enough rice to feed the 20,000,000 people. It is the production of a net export surplus over and above that food requirement that we must look forward to at the present time, and we are planning, as I have said before, the application, if this program is approved, of 50,000 metric tons in addition to the basic 80,000 tons, to generate the exports that are needed.

Whereas agricultural production can be increased by expanding the existing productive facilities, and by a sustained program of fertilizer application, the increase of marine production calls for the creation of new equipment, new fish-catching equipment. It will take a lot of it. I will explain the details all together later on, but most of the fishing at the present time is offshore fishing. The Sea of 

Japan, the Yellow Sea, the Straits of Tsushima are teeming with fish, and they are available not only for the nutrition of the Korean people but for increasing exports. 

The equipment must be made available. Trawlers of 20, 30, 50 tons; power ships. There must also be some equipment for the catching of sea animals, which is a relatively large undertaking. 

Mrs. BOLTON. May I interrupt you just a moment? You mentioned power ships. How about the gasoline to run them?

Dr. JOHNSON. The Diesel oil will have to be a continuing import. 

That has been contemplated.

Now, the mineral production has its own peculiar problems. Aside from scheelite, out of which tungsten is refined, Korea has no really first-class mineral deposits.

The Japanese in their frantic search for war potential, opened up many marginal mines. The lead, graphite, mica, is of fair quality. 

I think I would be extravagant if I went beyond that. The coal has anywhere from 17 to 45 percent ash. However, by historical accident, those are the resources Korea has. Those are the ones she will have to use. The technical problems are baffling. These low-value, low-grade minerals cannot be transported long distances. What is called for here as in so many other aspects of the Korean program, is a close integration with the Japanese industrial recovery program. 

The object of expanding mineral exports is the same as the object of expanding maríne products, namely, to take the pressure off the rice exports.

The export of manufactured goods is a most desirable goal but it is not something that will materially assist Korea to become viable by 1953. Modern consumers are hard to please. They want standardized, identical, mechanically perfect products. It will take many patient years before the Koreans are prepared to compete effectively on a large scale in consumers' goods markets.

May I summarize just this part of my argument? I have explained what Korea must do by 1953 to be able to survive without foreign assistance. It comes down to this:

She must be able to export goods to the value of $75,000,000 at least. She must be able to manufacture her nitrogeneous fertilizer because that is the biggest item that she cannot carry as part of her normal imports. She must be able to sustain domestic production so that 20,000,000 people will have a tolerable standard of living. There must be some visible proof that things are getting better. 

There can be only small increments of amelioration but they must be there.

Finally, she must be able to support, until the cold war is ended, a large army, a large police force, and a coast guard. It

Now, this latter obligation is not an inconsequential thing. means the production of many, many other commodities: Woolen clothing for uniforms, leather for shoes, truck and jeep tires for military vehicles, the logistic support for 150,000 members of the security forces now deemed to be the minimum necessary. 

The maintenance of domestic production is therefore of parallel importance with the generation of sufficient exports to solve the balance-of-payments problem.

That is the large task. That is where we must go by the 1953 goal.

Now, I turn to the third part of my argument, where are we now in this over-all program? I must at the outset tell you that I agree completely with the adjective that Mr. Hoffman used this morning. 

The accomplishment in the past year is nothing short of spectacular. 

That is due to the great efforts of the Korean people, they have more than met their goals of industrial production.

Dr. JOHNSON. May I have the bar chart on industrial production? 

This single chart shows the change from 1948 to 1949. These are percentage increases of production, in a long list of commodities. 

The buff columns are 100 percent in 1948.. The green are the aver ages over 100 percent in 1949.

That is a story, a story of great effort on the part of the Korean people to increase production all along the line. 

Mr. JUDD. What does it mean there where some have three lines? 

Dr. JOHNSON. The other line is 1947. 

Mr. JUDD. For some you don't give that 1947 figure. 

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes. The buff is 100 percent for 1948. The shorter line is fractions thereof for 1947, and the long green lines are the percentages for 1949.

We have this data to be presented in another way. Dr. Bunce's staff has compounded this into an index of industrial activity. You may say there is a certain artificiality in any compounded index. There is. 

Artificial weights have therefore been given: Mining, 14; utilities, 23; manufacturing, 48; fisheries, 15.

On the basis of that weighting, the red line is the trend line of industrial activity. You will see the very pronounced increase of 1949 over 1948. Dr. Bunce will tell you more vividly than I how the faint hearts said, "If you turn this over to the Korean Government, everything will go to pot." There were those of us who believed otherwise, that if you let people run their own business they will run it better than any outsider can, and the proof is there for you to see. 

There is the story then of industrial activity in 1949, the first year of an ECA assistance program. 

We are able to report to this committee that the forecasts we made last year about Korean exports have been met. 

May we have the export chart once again? 

Mr. FULTON. While you are on that point, may I ask a question?

The dire predictions of immediate catastrophe made in 1949 even by members on this committee have not come through in Korea; have they?

Dr. JOHNSON. Those dire predictions, Mr. Fulton, were made on the assumption that no funds would be made available, no ECA funds would be made available. Thank God, the Congress did make available $60,000,000 and there was, therefore, no hiatus. 

Mr. FULTON. I might say that the predictions were made by members on this committee that if they were not made available that it would be bad, and if they were made available it would be worse. 

They were made right on this committee in public by Mr. Jackson, of

Korean bill from going to the floor. 

So none of them came through; did they? None of these dire predictions, then, are true in Korea? 1949 has been higher, and 1950 looks as thought it will still be higher. 

Dr. JCHNSON. Yes, sir; that is true. I think it is not immodest to say that some of the credit should be given to the ECA for bringing in the right commodities in implementing this program and to the 

Congress for voting the money. 

Mr. FULTON. There have been two sets of dire predictions, one at the very beginning before ECA went in and another set of dire predictions when the bill was up this second previous time.

In your estimation, when this thing comes up a third time, there will be a steady increase, will there not, of Korean progress? 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is correct. That attests the fact that the Korean 

Government, with the assistance of ECA can use American money to purposeful ends. 

Mr. FULTON. Thank you.

Dr. JOHNSON. We are able to report the forecasts we made about exports have been fulfilled. It was a big assumption we made last year, I am frank to confess, that rice would be exported. It had to be. 

It was a very big decision for the Korean Government to make, and especially it was an unattractive decision for them to make to sell rice to the Japanese who had exploited the Koreans for 40 years. But the exports are now up to 27.4 million, as contrasted with nothing in 1946. 

These peaks in the chart for 1948 are a little bit deceptive. There were certain stock piles on hand that could be exported, surplus Japanese properties. There was also a very immense demand for edible seaweed which more than doubled the price. These are dollar values.

And so the physical outgo of goods is much larger than is reflected in these dollar yields. I should say the trend line in physical quantities is more favorable than is reflected in the dollar yields. 

In some programs of industrial reconstruction, we have gone, I think, twice as fast as we had any right to prophesy. 

You will remember, last June, when we laid this program before you, we proposed to build railroads into the Samchok area. I am sure the members of the committee will recall that the semicircle in the upper right of that map-and here is the blow-up of it-contains the richest mineral resources in Korea. The committee will remember that 

I pointed out that area was tied to Japan economically and not tied to Korea, and that it had to be tied back to Korea by railroads. Those are the green lines that you see here. 

That railroad from Chongju to Chochiwon, and this one from Chechon to Yongwol, and on to Hambaik were just ideas a year ago. I was out in Korea in March and the Koreans were just surveying those railroads. I came back in November. I rode out on finished tracks from

Yongju to Naesong and half way from Chechon to Yongwol. 

That is being done by Koreans who are doing this job because they know it is important, and you have thousands of Koreans with hand labor building the tunnels, breaking out the rock with sledges. 

These two pictures on the upper left show the sort of work that is going on. Those railroads will be built, and they will be built promptly, and they will unify the transportation system of Korea. 

It will make available the 200,000,000 tons of coal in the Samchok area. 

It will make possible the generation of more electricity. 

Now the Koreans have met the planned increase in coal production, a most difficult accomplishment. You may recall, last year, I explained the geological problems that are involved in mining coal in 

Korea, but here is the story.

The trend is upward. The recovery from 1946 to 1947 was by no means as difficult as the expansion which is going on at the present time.

We are about half way up to our goal. There must be produced about 2.5 million tons of coal by 1953.

With the help of loaned power facilities, with the help of some of our technicians, the power situation has been materially improved. 

Mrs. BOLTON. How can you loan power facilities?

Dr. JOHNSON. The Navy owns a large power ship. 

Mrs. BOLTON. So it does. I remember that you told us that last year.

Dr. JOHNSON. There is also an Army barge. This makes it more graphic because you see the contribution of the barges and the contribution of the steam plants. The committee will remember that hydro is limited in South Korea because the rainfall is concentrated in the monsoons and because there are no continuous-flow streams. Therefore, although we are attempting to complete a large hydro project which was begun by the Japanese, temporarily, the hydro with its seasonality gives you only a seasonal amount of power and the barges give a certain amount. The expansion has to come in thermalgenerating equipment. That is why we are concentrating in this program on the coal program so there will be more coal available. 

This, I think, is a dramatic story. This is the amount of electric power we bought from the Russians before they pulled the switch on the 14th of May 1948. The next bar is hydro. Now you see the seasonal peak in that, but it will smooth out to a pretty narrow band. 

At the bottom are the barges that came in as a temporary measure. 

But look at the peak in thermal that has been produced. That is the signal accomplishment.

The barges will have to come out sooner or later. We have them on an indefinite basis. They can be recalled at will. The problem then is to expand coal production and thermal generations as rapidly and as systematically as we can. 

Mr. JUDD. You said the rest was what you were buying from the 

Russians. That used to come from North Korea?

Dr. JOHNSON. Up until that time the Russian forces were ostensibly still in control. I do not recall. Dr. Bunce will know exactly when the puppet government was set up. 

Mr. JUDD. Who pulled the switch? 

Was it the Russians themselves, or the Russians through the puppet government? 

Dr. JOHNSON. I suspect the latter.

Mr. JUDD. There was no doubt but what it was the Russians that were behind it. 

Dr. JOHNSON. I have no doubt in my own heart.

Mr. JUDD. Because it would make it impossible for South Korea to become viable?

Dr. JOHNSON. The purpose was to destroy the economic program in 

South Korea. 

Mr. FULTON. Is that power supplied through the Army and Navy ships very high-cost power? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes; relatively. All Diesel oil power, when you have to bring the fuel that far, is relatively high cost. 

Mr. JUDD. Are the ships run by American personnel?

Dr. JOHNSON. I think we have now about 22 Americans. The way we are handling the ship now is by a contractor, selected by the Bureau of Federal Supply, on an open-bid basis to operate this ship. IM

I Now, at the same time I think there are about 80 Koreans employed. 

This is a large power ship. They are being trained in the operation of electrical equipment so that they can be transferred, after they have been trained by this staff on the power ship, to any of the steam plants. 

It is part and parcel of our training program, as well as our powergeneration program. 

Mr. FULTON. Could you give us comparisons on figures between

United States power per kilowatt-hour, and then what this is costing us on these Army and Navy ships?

Dr. JOHNSON. We will attempt to obtain that. (The information referred to is as follows:)

Average cost of power United States equals $0.007 per kilowatt-hour. 

Average cost of power barges equals $0.015 per kilowatt-hour.

Dr. JOHNSON. All these things have been accomplished and I think they are signal accomplishments. There has been a tremendous effort on the part of the Koreans. There has been judicious use of available supplies. There has been, if I may say this in the presence of Dr. 

Bunce, imaginative leadership on the part of the ECA mission to Korea. There has been excellent cooperation between Americans and Koreans. There has been an energetic effort at improvisation. 

There has been a firm attitude on the part of the Americans that the Koreans must put forward their best efforts. 

Take, for example, the power program. Dr. Bunce took the position that electricity generation had to be sustained. If the hydro would fall off, and if the thermal would run along on an even keel, the total would fall off. That meant you have to deactivate industry. His position was that it had to be sustained during the winter months. 

The result was a perfectly wonderful piece of cooperation between the Korean coal-mining section, to get out the coal, the Minister of Transportation to haul it up to Chechon, and then on the part of the Minister of Commerce to get it trucked over to the power plant. That power plant was built by the Japanese, up in the mountains. It is some 8 miles from a coal field and 32 miles from a railroad. It was stand-by equipment. As a matter of fact, the coal mines were expected to yield enough coal to run it. They have not. As a result, that power plant had to be operated at a rather low capacity. 

Now, the job was to operate it at a much higher capacity. Here is the thermal plant I am talking about, and it is a big plant. Here are some pictures of how the coal comes over the mountains in cable cars 8 miles away. Those are some of the technical problems we are up against.

The upshot was that the coal was trucked in; some 95 gondola cars of coal a day. 

Mr. FULTON. I see they need smoke control there. 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is not smoke; that is fly ash. That coal should not be burned that way. It should be beneficiated at the pit head so we would not have to transport noncombustible materials 8 miles on a cable. That is just exactly what we are doing. We are putting in beneficiating equipment so we will transport twice the amount of 

British thermal units over the cableway. 

Mr. FULTON. With regard to fly ash, there is a process that makes that very profitable. 63307-50-pt. 2-12

Dr. JOHNSON. That is being explored for the purpose of using it for cement and building purposes. 

Mr. JUDD. I hope it will be more successful than it is in Pittsburgh. 

Mr. FULTON. I want you to know that in Pittsburgh it is extremely successful, and Pittsburgh is now the cleanest city east of the Mississippi, including Minneapolis.

Dr. JOHNSON. The upshot was that this power plant was operated through the winter months at about four times the capacity at which it had been operated before. Presently, next summer, the railroad will be built in there and gondola cars can go right up to the steam plant. 

Chairman KEE. Do you have supplemental steam plants for your hydroelectric plants, to carry the load in time of drought?

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes. That is to say, when the hydro is running we stock-pile coal at the steam plants and cut down production there. 

Then when the hydro falls off, you eat into your stock pile, so that you use up much more coal than you are delivering to the plants during the dry months.

May I give another illustration. Take the export of rice. That was a very difficult decision for the Korean Government to make. It was loaded with political dynamite. To export rice, as I said before, was bad enough. To export it to the hated Japanese was seemingly impossible. It took perseverance on the part of the Americans to point out that this had to be done if you are going to implement a genuine recovery program. It took courage on the part of the Koreans.

Mr. FULTON. Regarding the exports to Japan, how much did that save us on the GARIOA program we are financing in Japan? 

Dr. JOHNSON. I do not know what the cost of delivering rice from the United States to Japan would be. The price paid by Japan was $142 a ton. Of course Korean rice, as everyone knows, is infinitely better than any other rice. 

Mr. FULTON. Except Minneapolis rice. 

Mr. JUDD. We produce eggs.

Mr. FULTON. Could you not set up for us just how much this is really costing the American taxpayers, net, because part of it is generating assistance to Japan. That logically could be cut from the cost of Korean aid.

Dr. JOHNSON. Not in that particular case, if I may disagree, Mr. 

Fulton. If certain fabricated commodities are manufactured in 

Japan, then, of course, the dollars do double duty because we spend our dollars in Japan and generate a volume of employment, and then the end products go to Korea.

If there is a lower dollar delivery cost of rice which comes from Korean production, the same would obtain. 

The best estimate I can make at the moment is this, that $240 a ton spent in nitrogen produces 10 tons of rice, so that is where you gain on this deal. 

Now, may I cite one other illustration of the effectiveness of cooperation. The ECA asked the Korean Government to make a national inventory of all supplies and equipment either in government or private warehouses that might be serviceable in the total recovery program, the inventory of things left by the Japanese and brought in by the Army, or elsewhere, things that they did not know about

and which would materially decrease the amount of things that would have to be requested.

It is, therefore, in terms of what Korea has, what could be improvised, and what can be financed with Korean imports that the 1951 program has been prepared. The program has been screened and rescreened in terms of needs, in terms of availabilities, in terms of prices.

Now, before I go on to the 1951 program, which I want to block out very quickly, may I explain what the year's program is designed to accomplish, which I am going to do in just a moment. May I just summarize in very, very sharp sentences what has been done to date. 

In the first place, Korea has become self-sufficient in food. We do not need to import any food into Korea. Korea is beyond that point. 

It is in an export position. Here is the chart. (The chart referred to is on p. 418.) 

Dr. JOHNSON. There is the story for 1946, 47, 48, and '49. There is a steady increase. It has been produced at a cost. I will not mislead you. It has been produced at the cost of fertilizer put in, just as I have said.

Korean exports have risen to 27.4 million. Coal production has gone up about half way to what must be done to carry out the whole program.

When the railroads that are now being built are finished, our power production will be about half way to what it should be. 

Industrial production, as Mr. Hoffman pointed out this morning, has increased 50 percent. May we have the car-loading chart? (The chart referred to is on p. 419.)

Dr. JOHNSON. This chart shows how a few good attempts at technical assistance can produce real results.

When the Koreans took over, you will see a valley there. You will see a valley right at the end of 1948. However, we had valleys before. As a matter of fact, that one is not as deep as the one we had in 1947. When we were the government, we had 133 Americans in the 

Department of Transportation. We have now eight technical assistants. It is the Koreans who are running the railroads and repairing the locomotives and repairing the rolling stock. They have moved more freight, kept more locomotives and railroad cars in operation than we did.

Mr. FULTON. While we are talking about moving freight, how about ships? What has been happening to those? 

Dr. JOHNSON. That problem has not been quite so favorable. Of the eight Baltic coasters that were loaned, one was sunk while we were the Government, so we cannot blame that on the Koreans, and one defected to North Korea, and that leaves six. They were not in good state of repair when we got them, and we had to use them as they were. They had to go back to Japan for repair. Three are back now. Three are back now, and three presently will be back. 

Here we have a new deal. Instead of American masters to run the ships, with oriental crews, a situation in which the crews had no particular love for the masters and the masters had no respect for the crews, what we have done now is to make an arrangement with the Pacific Far East lines, as a contractor, to train the Koreans. It is a training program that is being carried on now. 

The LST's that were purchased as Government surplus property are pretty well deteriorated. It is for that reason on the coal haul
