I have one or two other accomplishments in 1949. Three hundred and twenty-nine irrigation and reclamation projects have been completed, bringing 77,000 acres in. We have pictures here of these various projects.

New machinery will be presently put into the tungsten ore dressing mill, and that will approximately double the amount of tungsten exports. 

Mr. FULTON. Where are those exports going? Are any coming to the United States?

Dr. JOHNSON. All the tungsten concentrate exports come to the 

United States. They are stock-piled for strategic purposes. 

I said something about the use of responsible contractors. That is the program all along the line. We have dependable technical people to take care of engineering problems. That is true of the operation of the power ship; that is true of the engineering on the hydro dam that is being finished; that is true of the big Pusan marine repair base; it is true of the merchant marine training program, of the core-boring operation, and even in the technical training job, where the Illinois Institute of Technology will take over that job of training technicians in Korea.

I think this committee will appreciate that in view of what has happened in China I cannot afford to be extravagant in my statements, but I tell you in all sincerity, and with the objectivity of an economist, that the Korea program is really accomplishing its purpose. In many ways it is ahead of schedule. 

Mr. Eric Biddle, who had something to do with setting up the 

ECA mission to Korea, and who visited other ECA missions and who is not given to careless statements, told Mr. Hoffman in his staff meeting that in his opinion the United States was getting more for its money in Korea than anywhere else.

Now, the reasons are not hard to find. There are no generalities in this program. You can look down through this brown book, and we could explain precisely what these funds are to be used for. There are specific things for specific purposes. There is technical supervision by Americans that insures that the specific commodities are put to their intended use. Every effort is being used to put whatever equipment and facilities the Koreans possess into productive use. We have an ECA mission in Korea that knows its job, whose morale is amazingly high, and one that knows how to work with the Koreans- Mr. FULTON. If this is so successful in Korea, could this same pattern be used in other far-eastern countries? 

Dr. JOHNSON. I should think so. I know what can be done in 

Korea, but I am not adequately familiar with other southeast Asian countries to answer your question. 

Mr. FULTON. If you have Korea in a certain type of economy, and

Formosa possibly having a similar type of economy, of about the same relative size, would the same practices be practical in a place like Formosa, or is it just a peculiar thing that is for Korea alone? 

Dr. JOHNSON. I am not competent to answer that, Mr. Fulton, really.

I think I could say this, that there are certain conditioning cultural forces that have played upon Korea. They have, of course, a burning desire to maintain their independence. They lost their independ-

ence for 40 years. This is something valuable to them. Whether or not you have the same thing in the other countries, I cannot say. 

Chairman KEE. You probably have different political conditions in 

Formosa from what you have in Korea.

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes. I do want to add one last ingredient here in explanation of why the program has been successful. You have a 

Korean Government that knows that it must succeed because if it does not succeed it will fall victim to Communist expansion. That will to succeed is the key to the future of Korea; and it may be, Mr. Fulton, the key to the future of the Far East. 

Now, Mr. Chairman, I may be taking too much time, but I would like to have about another 5 minutes. 

Mr. FULTON. On the civil liberties and the newspapers that were suppressed and the members of the parliament that were ousted and arrested, could we have some comment on that? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Dr. Bunce is going to answer those questions. He is the man on the job, and he knows. Would you like to have those questions answered now? 

Chairman KEE. I think we had better wait.

Dr. JOHNSON. What is the program for 1950, the ones laid before you on pages 16 and 17 of the yellow book? We must arrange these programs when we chart them out, in financial categories, because that is the way we have to present this material a little bit later on when we come to the Appropriations Committee, and the whole machinery of accounting calls for it that way. But what I must do this afternoon to make this clear is to show that it is not just a matter of this quantity of fertilizer and this quantiy of lumber, and so on. 

The logic of it is what I am primarily concerned with this afternoon, because the 1951 program is really five interrelated programs. 

This is, first of all, a coal and power program, designed to produce enough energy to sustain and increase all forms of domestic production, and, secondly, possibly by 1953, the manufacture of 100,000 tons of contained nitrogen. 

The second part is an import-decreasing program, designed to reduce Korean imports of bituminous coal, fertilizer, cement, glass, salt, and other things, so as to get imports down so Korea can pay for them. 

Thirdly, it is an export-increasing program, designed to augment the production and therefore the export of rice, minerals, and marine products, and solving that phase of the problem. 

In the fourth place, it is a technical-assistance program calculated to supply Korea with urgently needed technicians, thereby filling the void created by the repatriation of the Japanese. 

Then, fifthly, it is a temporary commodity program designed to keep the economy going while the productive capacity of the Nation is being built up to a level which will permit Korea to function without foreign assistance.

I want to say just a few words about each of these five phases. First of all, the coal and the power program: To accomplish the recovery program, coal production must reach about 2.5 million tons. We are almost halfway, as I told you, to that schedule. 

The electricity generation must reach about 190,000 kilowatts. We are up to about 40 percent of that target.

The coal program is well under way, and if the funds that are requested for 1951 are made available, real progress will be made in the coming year. The basic geological verification has been made by experts loaned from the Geological Survey. A carefully planned core-boring program is beginning this month to find the richer seams where you can exploit with the same effort a larger amount of better coal.

The railroad will be finished next summer to Yongwol, making it possible to operate this big plant at full capacity. 

Mr. FULTON. Who is doing that coal boring, the Government, Korean Government, or private people? the Dr. JOHNSON. The contract for the immediate drilling job has been let by the Bureau of Federal Supply to an American concern. 

Mr. FULTON. What firm? 

Dr. JOHNSON. The firm is Longyear, I believe. 

Mr. FULTON. Was that open bidding?

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes; and the bidding is conducted by the Bureau of 

Federal Supply. We do not do this ourselves. 

Mr. FULTON. Do they try to get broad coverage to get those bidders in?

Dr. JOHNSON. They do. They advertise for bidders. On the 15,000kilowatt thermal plant, I think there were 27 bidders. 

The coal beneficiation equipment will be installed this summer, the first five coal ships will soon be built, so that until the railroad is built, coal can be moved from the Samchok mine where production is dependent upon rate of out-shipment. As soon as the core boring is finished, new entrees and shafts will be sunk to the richer veins. The coal program is going ahead full force. 

Mr. PFEIFER. Are you sure there is a large supply of coal there?

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes, sir. We had, first of all, the Japanese geological surveys. Not to be beguiled by that, the United States Geological 

Survey made an appraisal; and then, in specific coal fields, we had a team of five geologists provided by the Geological Survey. We have it on authority of Mr. Andrews, who headed that, that he will certify that the coal is there. 

Mr. MORGAN. Are these deep mines?

Dr. JOHNSON. No; the Korean coal is rather curious. It lay in seams originally. Then there was a violent upheaval of igneous rock, so that in the Machari mine, the coal has been wrapped up in lenses or in pockets, and it has been very, very difficult mining. You have to blast through what they call "horses" and then come into one of these lenses.

The object is to get below this most violent volcanic eruption where the seams are fairly continuous. They will be faulted, however, and that is the trouble at the present time. 

Mr. MORGAN. Is there any mechanical mining?

Dr. JOHNSON. No, sir; it is pick and shovel mining, once you blast through the "horses" and get into the lenses. Then there are simple tracks and wooden cars that are hand pushed. Inasmuch as the coalmining area is spread over a large territory, and you have to wind your railroads around the mountain peaks, you assemble a car from this opening and a car from that opening, and then you have a hauling problem. You sometimes have to haul, as in Machari, 7 or 8 miles before you get to the tipple, and therefore you have to have mine

locomotives, Diesels, operated to pull the cars. Then they go down inclines, and then they are made into cars again. 

Chairman KEE. Are they drift mines or shaft mines?

Dr. JOHNSON. They are the ones that slope in. It may be revealed, if there are deep seams, that shaft mines will be more efficient. The core boring will have to be done before that can be answered, though. 

Mr. FULTON. Without any inferences whatever, are the mine workers organized?

Dr. JOHNSON. Dr. Bunce can tell you more about that than I can. 

There are trade unions in Korea; yes, sir.

Now, about the power program: Here we are attacking in a double way. There are two steam plants, one in Pusan and one in 

Seoul. They were built by the Japanese to burn bituminous coal which came either from Japan or Manchuria. Our problem there is to convert those plants so they will use the largest amount of Korean coal, thereby minimizing the need for imported bituminous coal. Mr. 

Jones, who is a combustion engineer, has just returned. I talked to him yesterday. He assures me that in a matter of a couple months the big plant in Seoul can be converted so it will burn 60 percent 

Korean coal and only 40-percent imported bituminous. 

Mr. FULTON. From where are you importing your coal?

Dr. JOHNSON. From Japan. It is purchased now by the Korean 

Government out of their self-generated exchange, and they have imported the bulk of it from Japan, but some is now being imported from Formosa. 

Mr. MORGAN. Is all the coal in Japan bituminous coal?

Dr. JOHNSON. I do not know whether it is or not. The kind we import is bituminous coal.

Chairman KEE. How is this coal burned; do they burn it under forced draft?

Dr. JOHNSON. For power generation, it must be pulverized and then blown in. It has a large amount of fixed carbon, but it is very hard to ignite. Therefore on stokers it has to be mixed with bituminous.

Mr. FULTON. Could you give us for the record the coal that is being imported from Japan? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Do you mean the quantities?

Mr. FULTON. Not now, but later. Especially in relation to the fact that as far as I know the United States Navy has been buying coal for the armed services generally to be shipped from the United States to 

Japan. 

Dr. JOHNSON. We were paying $14 a ton laid down at Pusan and we were paying about $10,500,000 a year in the beginning. By virtue of this coal-economy program, the Korean Government is spending in the neighborhood of $7,000,000 a year. They are paying, I believe now only about $10, so I would estimate it is about 700,000 tons of coal that is being imported at the present time.

I can recite some of the other things that are going on, showing progress all along the line. 

The unfinished hydro project is being completed. The barge Electra will have new engines. Jacona will be in full operation again. We had some tough luck with the Jacona. A rat ran over the bus bar and shorted a generator and the generator speeded up and so that has to be repaired. One thing I cannot find out is whether it was a nice South

Korean rat that just unintentionally did this or whether it was a Communist rat that did it intentionally. 

There is new load-dispatching equipment being installed and then work will soon go forward on a new 15,000-kilowatt plant in Samchok area and a new 30,000-kilowatt plant in Seoul. That is the coal and power program. That is tied in with both the export-increasing and import-decreasing program. The import-decreasing program contemplates, as you see, the reduction of the import of bituminous coal by the conversion of burners to Korean coal. It contemplates the building of a nitrogenous fertilizer plant on which a sizable start will be made in fiscal year 1951. 

It contemplates the building of a flat glass factory to use Korean silica sand and thereby eliminate a $900,000 annual import. 

Mr. FULTON. Where are the imports of glass coming from now?

Dr. JOHNSON. They are coming from Hong Kong, most of them. 

Mr. FULTON. Where are the pig-iron imports coming from?

Dr. JOHNSON. The pig iron is coming from Japan. 

Mr. FULTON. Could I ask you this: If you put in a program of cutting imports drastically and increasing exports drastically in a particular area like Korea, where does that fit into our over-all policy for the Orient? You cannot do that every place.

Dr. JOHNSON. No. After all, a nation cannot buy more than it can pay for unless you are going to subsidize a nation forever. 

It has been argued, for example, it would be wiser to produce the fertilizer in Japan, but our question is, What will Korea use to pay for it? Consequently, it is only in these particular key areas that any change is contemplated.

Take salt, for example. Korea is only half self-sufficient in salt at the present time. You have to expand the salterns. There are no salt mines or salt wells. You have to evaporate sea water. The imported salt comes from the Red Sea. The freight costs more than the salt is worth. That is bad business. That is foolish, especially when the sun will do the work for you.

Mr. FULTON. We just had a conference to increase trade multilaterally among nations. It would seem to me a basic premise that if you keep reducing the trade to make each little geographic unit self-sufficient you will be defeating the main purpose. 

Dr. JOHNSON. Please understand this is not a narrow protectionist philosophy at all. It is only an appraisal of what the availabilities. are and how far you can increase certain exports and thereby put yourself in a condition to buy the absolutely necessary imports. Beyond that certainly there is no intention of industrializing Korea for the sake of nationalistic purposes or just for the sake of industrialization.

Mr. FULTON. How about inflation? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Dr. Bunce is going to tell about that. 

Chairman KEE. I think it would be better if we let the witness go ahead and complete his statement.

Dr. JOHNSON. Now, in the export-increasing program, I think I have already shown that rice exports must rise from 50 percent of the total as it is in 1950, to 65 percent in 1951, and it will have to continue at about that rate. The temporary fertilizer program and the

more basically remedial fertilizer-manufacturing project is the only thing that will solve the balance-of-payments problem. 

I have just one thing left. That is the commodity program which most people think is so important but which to us is the least important. 

The object of that is to merely keep the economy going until we can get it in shape to run itself and pay its own way. 

I often hear complaints about the fact that it is wrong to build up capital installations elsewhere. I contend that the weakest program is simply a commodity program. There is no bottom to that, because year in and year out you are not better off. The only bottom would be complete satiety, and that will never be reached. So the commodity program should be progressively tapered off as the productive facilities are increased, and that is persistently what this program is designed to accomplish. 

Chairman KEE. Does that complete your statement, Doctor?

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Pfeifer 

Mr. PFEIFER. I do not believe you meant that the Koreans could do a better job if left alone by themselves; that they would do a better job than we?

Dr. JOHNSON. No; I did not mean that. In the beginning we had to do everything. We had to run the railroads. Our whole policy in Korea has been one of turning over more and more responsibility to the Koreans, and it has paid dividends. That is what I meant. 

Mr. PFEIFER. In view of all we have been doing and intend to do to make them self-sufficient, tell me one thing. How can they get along after that, when we leave, if their exports are only in rice? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Their exports will be rice, minerals, marine products, and manufactured goods. Korea is one of the largest producers of graphite. They have talc, Kaolin, tungsten, ceramic clay, mica, molybdenum, and other minerals. 

Mr. PFEIFER. That is the only thing they could rely upon. Not manufactured goods? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Some manufactured goods, yes.

Mr. PFEIFER. What, for instance? 

Dr. JOHNSON. Well, there are straw bags that go to Japan which is not an inconsequential item. Ginseng, which has been processed, draws very high prices in Hong Kong. While we were the government we made our first sale in Hong Kong at $125 a pound. Just 

Ginseng ought to run $1,000,000 a year. Then as markets are discovered, manufactures of every kind. 

Mr. PFEIFER. Are we doing anything toward providing a better system of education?

Dr. JOHNSON. Not directly out of ECA moneys, except technical education. In technical education we are doing the following things: 

We have a technical training division. Once again, Dr. Bunce can explain this better than I, but it supervises and assists in vocational and technical education in the middle schools and in the colleges and universities. In the second place, it carries on extensive programs in agriculture. It is assisting the fishing industry. We propose furthermore to bring a limited number of Koreans to this country for instructional purposes. The most important thing we are doing is to set up

the technical training institute on a year-to-year program. It will be operated by a competent contractor, the Illinois Institute of Technology. The Korean teachers for that are now at Dunwoody Institute learning the techniques of real technical school education. That is the kind of a program we are carrying on. 

Mr. PFEIFER. Is any of this money of ECA going toward maintaining the police force in Korea?

Dr. JOHNSON. We are paying for the common use items until we are directed to the contrary. Unless we program them they will have to be diverted from the economy. I mean the policemen have to have shoes. The members of the army have to have uniforms. Our position has been that the only sensible thing to do is to program that. 

The cost will be in the neighborhood of approximately $500,000 for those items. As the Koreans export more goods, their Korean foreign exchange takes over some of the responsibilities. This coming year they will pay for the gasoline. We will pay for the Diesel oil, lubricants, and kerosene. They will pay for part of the cotton this year, cutting our figure from $13,000,000 to $7,500,000. Progressively we shift over to the Korean funding and that is why our whole program can come down from $144,000,000 to $120,000,000, to $100,000,000 to $85,000,000 and then, God willing, to zero. 

Mr. PFEIFER. You have great confidence in the people of Korea, insofar as maintaining a democratic way of life is concerned, after they have been helped?

Dr. JOHNSON. The democratic way of life will be different in 

Korea than it will in America, in the same way that Swedish democracy is different from American democracy or British democracy. 

Mr. PFEIFER. I mean insofar as the freedoms of the people are concerned.

Dr. JOHNSON. That, of course, is the indispensable thing, that there must be a continuation of democratic principles in Korea. 

Mr. PFEIFER. Insofar as you know at the present time, the same thing to do is to help them and the only thing to do is to help them? 

Dr. JOHNSON. I believe that sincerely. 

Mr. PFEIFER. That is all, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mrs. Bolton, have you any questions?

Mrs. BOLTON. I have no real questions, Dr. Johnson. I have been fascinated by your report to us because you have given it with a drive and a sincerity which is very helpful to us and you also have given us a sense of very great integrity with regard to the ECA in Korea. 

I think what you make very clear, without saying too much about it, is the quality of the people themselves, that they must have something which some of the other nations do not. I was very much interested in having one of the missionaries come to me on quite a different matter. It was a man whose wife was shot by the Communists. Not only was he going back himself taking his college daughter, but one daughter and her husband were over there and they would not leave for anything. So there is a confidence to be had in the whole picture that is very encouraging. I do want to thank you very much for your method of bringing it all to our attention so very clearly. 

Dr. JOHNSON. Thank you.

Chairman KEE. Dr. Morgan- 

Mr. MORGAN. Dr. Johnson, are there any Japanese at all left in southern Korea?

Dr. JOHNSON. There are none.

Mr. MORGAN. How about the ones who intermarried with Koreans during the 40 years' occupation?

Dr. JOHNSON. In the first place, I think there were very, very few. 

Are there still Japanese wives, Dr. Bunce?

Dr. BUNCE. I know of only one in Seoul and she has adapted herself to the Korean way of life. There was very little intermarriage. 

Mr. MORGAN. At the end of June 1950 we will have $476,000,000 in 

Korea. Does that include the Army funds before military withdrawal. 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is correct. 

Mr. MORGAN. That seems to be an awful lot of money. According to the break-down, the Army spent $212,000,000. 

Dr. JOHNSON. The Army spent $328,000,000, if I may disagree, because it breaks at January 1, 1949. 

Mr. MORGAN. What did the Army accomplish for $328,000,000?

Dr. JOHNSON. Well, they had to start from scratch. The coal recovery for 1946 and 1947 was done under the United States military government in Korea. The first beginnings of the power development. 

That whole program. They took care of the incoming refugees which number probably 4,000,000. Those were some of the problems. They of course had to bail out the economy before exports had developed at all. You will remember in 1946 there was not a dollar's worth of exports and consequently some $40,000,000 had to be spent for food in 1947 and about $32,000,000 in fiscal year 1948 and about $26,000,000 in fiscal year 1949. There was that job to be done. That takes a lot of money as did the fertilizer program. So the Army money went, shall I say, for food, fertilizer, and raw materials, and only to a limited amount for rehabilitation items. GARIOA funds were not available for reconstruction projects. 

Mr. MORGAN. Dr. Johnson, you said all the industries in Korea, with the exception of the fishing industry, had made magnificent recoveries. What held back the fishing industry?

Dr. JOHNSON. Two things. First, the loss of fishing boats. The military government vested all Japanese property, held in custody, in trust for the Korean people. That included all property located in Korea and all ambulatory property. The ambulatory property got away, most of it, and that included some of the best fishing boats. 

Mr. MORGAN. What has ECA been doing to help this recovery in the fishing industry?

Dr. JOHNSON. We have been importing lumber and other supplies for the fishing-boat program. We have been importing manila fiber for twines and nets, and many other supplies. The whole series of supplies for improving the fish-catching capacity. 

Mr. MORGAN. Is this program in effect now?

Dr. JOHNSON. It is. The recovery will be comparatively slow but 

I believe within a year you will see some rather definite effects of the program which has been instituted. 

Mr. MORGAN. I noticed in your 1950 budget that you have $310,000 for medical supplies and your estimated 1951 budget shows none. 

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes, sir. That is because in 1951 the Koreans will purchase their own medical supplies out of their foreign exchange. 

Mr. MORGAN. And same of the food?

Dr. JOHNSON. That is a manageable thing. We are going to pass over to them as fast as we can the responsibility for buying.

Mr. MORGAN. I also notice that the $34,391,200 for fertilizer in 1950 jumps to $42,000,000 in 1951.

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes, sir; because to produce the exports which will be necessary to solve the balance-of-payments problem, the yield per acre must increase and a greater application of fertilizer is the way to do it. So the application will rise from 110,000 tons of contained nitrogen in fiscal year 1950, to 130,000 tons of contained nitrogen in fiscal year 1951. 

Mr. MORGAN. That is all, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Do you have any further questions, Mrs. Bolton? 

Mrs. BOLTON. I have no further questions. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much, Dr. Johnson. You have given us a very informative statement and we appreciate your coming here. 

Dr. Bunce, will it be all right for you to come on tomorrow? 

Dr. BUNCE. I am at your service. 

Chairman KEE. I would like for more members of the committee to be present to hear your statement.

Mrs. BOLTON. It is a little difficult to miss the arguments on the floor.

Chairman KEE. The committee will stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 10 a. m. (Whereupon, at 4:30 p. m. the committee adjourned to reconvene at 10 a. m. Thursday, March 9, 1950.)

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED THURSDAY, MARCH 9, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

The committee met, pursuant to call, at 11 a. m.. in the Foreign 

(chairman) presiding.

We will resume our hearings upon the ECA program. 

We have with us this morning, Dr. Arthur Bunce, Chief of the ECA 

Korean Mission, who will testify with reference to the matter under consideration.

Dr. Bunce, we are very glad to have you here and you may proceed in your own way.

STATEMENT OF DR. ARTHUR BUNCE, CHIEF, ECA KOREAN MISSION 

Dr. BUNCE. Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege to me to appear before this committee on behalf of the Korean aid program and to answer any questions that may be raised.

There were several points that I thought I would like to bring up and discuss which were raised yesterday. I have not prepared a formal statement. My remarks are essentially off the cuff remarks. 

I hope you will excuse me for following that pattern.

The first thing I would like to say regarding the program that Dr. 

Johnson presented to you so ably yesterday is that this program is not purely an American program. This program as presented was developed by the Korean Government in cooperation with the ECA Mission. It is a joint program where the Office of Planning of the Korean 

Government worked with the specialists of the ECA Mission and developed an over-all program. We then forwarded that to Dr. Johnson and he reviewed it, and made certain changes because of certain conditions that they are aware of here that we do not know of in Korea. 

I want to emphasize this strongly, that the program is essentially a Korean program with the ECA Mission concurring and approving in that program.

The Secretary of State after his testimony was asked a question regarding the public order in South Korea and the action of guerrillas which had been reported recently in the New York Times. He referred that problem to me and I would like to speak frankly to this committee about the conditions of guerrilla activity. 429

Over a year ago there was far more guerrilla activity than there is today. Dr. Judd was in Korea 212 years ago. At that time you may remember Chejuedo was in a state of almost complete control by the guerrillas.

I imagine that almost 50 percent of the houses in Chejuedo were destroyed by the guerrillas. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Where is Chejuedo? 

Dr. BUNCE. It is an island south of Korea. 

Since the Koreans have taken over they have sent down their own Korean troops. The Minister of Defense, Mr. Shin, went to Chejuedo himself and they completely eliminated all the rebels on Chejuedo. 

It was a tremendous task. The island is full of mountains and full of caves, and that is one of the reasons that we had not been able to do the job. I think the Koreans are to be complimented on the way they tackled that job.

Chairman KEE. Are these people you call guerrillas followers of the communistic line?

Dr. BUNCE. They are communistic guerrillas and we know that many of them, and particularly their leaders, come into South Korea, either overland or are brought down by boat and landed in many of the little coastal areas. 

Chairman KEE. Do they come from the northern section?

Dr. BUNCE. They come from the north and move into South Korea. 

We know they are trained in sabotage and guerrilla activities. 

The second area I would like to mention is the Chirisan area right in here [indicating]. For 3 years we have been using the Korean forces to clear up that area. During this last year, that area has been almost completely cleaned of guerrillas and guerrilla activities. 

The remaining area of guerrilla activities lies on the east coast, here. 

In order to understand the difficulty of this task you should know a little bit about the topography of Korea. 

Korea has a mountainous range through the center with branches going toward the sea. The guerrillas flee into the mountains. 

The Korean people do not live on individual farms but live in tiny villages. You will have villages as small as 10 houses way up at the top of a little valley. There is no way that you can police those areas and protect those people. That is one reason why they have these self-protective associations. I think that the courage and fortitude and strength that the Koreans have shown in defeating the number of guerrillas they have in 1 year, in clearing up this problem, is amazing. 

In 1948 we had again, as you will remember, the Yosu rebellion. 

The Communists had infiltrated into the army. I think the colonel was converted to communism and they started a revolt. They took two towns. Yosu is a fairly large town. That was completely cleaned up and settled by the Korean Army. 

During this past year the Korean Army with the assistance of our military advisory group under General Roberts, has made remarkable strides.

I want to make it clear that in spite of this story in the New York Times, guerrilla activity in Korea today is infinitely less than it was a year ago, and less than it was 2 years ago. In other words, conditions are progressively getting more and more under control. 

I made a note on the remark made by Dr. Judd regarding French troops in Indochina and the drain on the French economy. I would

OF 

like to point out here that this action in Korea is being taken entirely and solely with Korean troops, under their own steam and under their own manpower and all we have is a very small group of military advisers. 

Mr. JUDD. Mr. Chairman, could I interrupt there?

Chairman KEE. Certainly. 

Mr. JUDD. Our military mission has not insisted that the Koreans enter into a truce with the Communist guerrillas, have they, give them cabinet seats, and things of that sort?

Dr. BUNCE. No. There are no Communists in the Korean Government.

Mr. JUDD. We have not advised a truce with the Korean Communists and a coalition government with them as we did in China, to our disaster?

Dr. BUNCE. No, sir. I might say that the Koreans themselves, one of their generals, issued an order which provided an amnesty for all the guerrillas who came in and would remain with them for a certain length of time and be reindoctrinated in democratic concepts and thoughts and be set free. The reason they did that is this: One of the 

Communist tactics in the wild, hilly country, such as you have in Korea is as follows: the Communists will come down and they will take one person from a family and carry him off up into the hills. Then they will tell the rest of the family, "Now, you play along with the Communists, or it is just going to be too bad," and many of the people who joined the Communists joined them under duress. 

That program of amnesty and retraining has released literally thousands and thousands of the people who were stooges of the Communists, and they are now very bitter against the Communists, and they are now strong supporters of the concept of democracy. 

Mr. JUDD. Is this also true, that when the Koreans started to clean out those who did not take advantage of the amnesty but who are hard and confirmed enemies, they were not hampered by too many sentimental humanitarian attitudes that have developed in our Christian civilization in the west, and which we are inclined to try to impose on or demand from those who do not as yet have those concepts as to the worth and importance of every single human being, and so forth. They are rather ruthless, are they not, and effectively so?

Dr. BUNCE. The difference is this: Where you have a guerrilla band that is armed and fighting, they are tried by a military court and sentence is carried out extremely rapidly. 

In the case of Communists that have infiltrated into civilian agencies and are not armed, and so forth, they are arrested and tried by the civil courts.

Mr. JUDD. When they catch these people out in the mountains they do not hesitate to execute them?

Dr. BUNCE. No. 

Mr. JUDD. That sometimes goes against our grain because it is not in accordance with our traditions, but they understand their people better than we do. I had to learn to grit my teeth sometimes in 

China when I saw things that seemed terrible to me, but they have been using those methods for hundreds of years and they understand each other. 

Dr. BUNCE. With the rapid sentencing of active armed Communists, they also have this program of retraining and amnesty which 63307-50-pt. 2- -13

has apparently been very successful. A very large number of the people in Chejuedo are people who were with the Communists and have been given amnesty and are now completely opposed to the Communists. The place is so peaceful that just a few weeks ago some people came over from Japan to go hunting, and went all over the island with no worry at all. That is the first time that has ever happened in 4 years.

The other problem that was brought up yesterday by Mr. Hoffman and referred to me was this problem of inflation in Korea, which, of course, could be a threat to the whole ECA reconstruction program. I would like to bring to the attention of this committee certain actions that we and the Korean Government have taken together in order to combat that danger.

First of all, we have appointed a joint committee which held its first meeting on January 24. You will be interested to see the caliber of person appointed by the Korean Government to that committee. 

The Korean members were the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Commerce and Industry, the Minister of Agriculture, the Director of the Office of Planning, and the governor of the Bank of Korea, and I appointed four representatives of the United States to work with those gentlemen. They have been working continually since that date, meeting almost every single day, and these are some of the things that they have achieved:

They have finalized the sale of 100,000 metric tons of rice to Japan at $142, net, to be delivered this month and in the following 3 months. 

That is one measure which will bring in 14.2 million dollars worth of foreign exchange. It is one of the steps toward attaining a balance of payments that we are insisting upon. 

Secondly, they took the last quarter of the fiscal year expenditures and they ct from those expenditures 9.6 billion "won."

Third, the President has given an order requesting the legal drafting committee to pass a bill which will bond all the people handling finances and establish a system of complete Government control over disbursements. 

Fourth, they agreed to raise the power rates to 15 "won" per kilowatt-hour. (In the old days the currency in Korea was the same as the 

Japanese. The new currency is called won instead of yen.) 

Mr. JUDD. What is the rate of exchange? 

Dr. BUNCE. The rate of exchange is 900 to 1, according to the last auction.

Mr. JUDD. As a means of comparison can you tell us what the rate of exchange was a year ago, roughly? 

Dr. BUNCE. A year ago the rate of exchange was 900 to 1, I think.

Actually they had a fixed rate and for a period of time they had dual rates of 450 and 900. I think the official rate was 900 to 1 for nongovernmental purposes. 

Mr. JUDD. And 450 to 1 for governmental purposes?

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. They attempted to maintain two rates because we demanded that ECA goods be paid for in the counterpart fund at what we call the official rate of exchange, so they designated the official rate as 450 but actually transactions occurred between individuals at a higher rate and we have insisted that the counterpart rate be raised.

The mechanism we used was to have an auction of foreign exchange and the auction rate was established at 900 to 1 and we have been raising the rate for counterpart deposits to 900 to 1. Right now we are obtaining 800 to 1 and next month we hope to have a new auction and ECA goods will be paid for at the new auction rate. We are trying to eliminate this dual exchange rate system which always implies hidden subsidies. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. Is 900 to 1 the highest exchange rate that has been in existence in the past year?

Dr. BUNCE. That is the highest official rate established. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. What about the others? 

Dr. BUNCE. If you take a greenback and sell it in the Korean market you can get as high as 3,000 to 1 for it.

Mr. MANSFIELD. Even today? 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

The fifth point they have agreed to is to raise the railroad rates of passenger services 125 percent. This was agreed to by the stabilization committee but the President thought it was too large an increase and he wanted to hold that increase in railroad rates only to 100 percent.

Sixth, the President and the Cabinet and the foreign exchange committee have all approved a new series of foreign exchange regulations and a new ordinance on foreign exchange. That is getting exactly at the problem you raised, Mr. Congressman.

Seventh, they have approved an ordinance to sell the vested property which was taken over from the Japanese by military government and then was turned over to the Korean Government. That ordinance has now been approved by the President and they are establishing the machinery to get much of this property into private hands where it can be used, we think, more efficiently and more effectively and also provide income to the Korean Government. 

The eighth point is that this committee is now considering a new budget for 1951 in which they have brought the regular income and regular expenditures into balance and have placed the burden of their extraordinary expenditures for rehabilitation and railroad development, building these plants, and the roads, essentially that are going to help Korea, on the counterpart fund. Those are positive measures that have already been taken since January 24. I believe it shows a record of willingness to tackle an extremely serious situation. 

There are two major factors that have caused the inflation. 

The first has been a very large expansion of bank credit; the bank credit has been expanded, for example, in order to purchase the rice necessary for the Government food program. As the rice is sold, much of this bank credit will be reduced and that itself will have a deflationary impact on the economy.

The second factor has been deficit financing by the Government, due very largely to the extraordinary expenses incurred because they had to build up an army of 100,000 and a police force of 50,000, together with the necessary installations, in order to be ready to defend 

South Korea and to fight the guerrillas.

The first year carried tremendous expenses, much beyond their income. These expenditures were financed by borrowing from the

Bank of Korea which, of course, meant that more paper money was printed by the Bank of Korea. 

I believe that the financial situation in Korea today is fundamentally sound, providing we continue the cooperation and the work that has already been started by this stabilization committee. 

There are one or two other points that I would like to bring out regarding the work in Korea. One of these things is that we have in 

Korea what is known as a United Mission. It is known as AMIK

the "American Mission in Korea." In AMIK we have these component parts: We have the embassy; we have the military advisory group; we have the joint administrative services; we have the United 

States Information Service, and, last but certainly not least, we have 

ECA. 

These groups are all working together for one purpose. 

I would like to say that the United States Information Service is doing a splendid job. It cooperates very, very closely with ECA in telling the story of American aid to Korea. 

The USIS has mobile units which go out into the remote villages in the hills. They do not depend on newspapers. They cannot depend on radio. The only way you can get the story across in Korea is to send small groups of people up the valleys and into the villages. They take a movie projector with them; they take some pamphlets with them. 

They have a Korean who tells the story in Korean and as soon as they arrive in a village they are mobbed. Everybody comes around. They have a meeting in one village and the people in 20 villages around will all come in, thousands of them. They will see the movies, they listen to the talk, and they take home the literature-they hit them three times at one meeting.

I wish Mr. Stewart were here to tell the story of what the USIS is doing in Korea, because I believe it is a very significant factor in making our work in Korea successful. 

On my staff I only have one officer on the ECA pay roll, Mr. Baldridge, who works with and uses USIS completely for telling the ECA story. In other words, we have eliminated overlapping and duplicating agencies of the Government.

I would like to give you a few examples of the work of USIS regard ing the ECA program: 

First of all, we told the Koreans that ECA aid was a gift to Korea. 

The Communists came back with a beautiful barrage of propaganda. 

They said, "These statements of the Americans just show how they are wolves in sheep's clothing. Mr. Farmer, don't you pay for your fertilizer? Mr. Cotton Manufacturer, don't you pay for your cotton?

Who gets the money? This is the forerunner of American imperialism. They are taking over the ownership of all the resources of 

Korea," and all that sort of thing.

That is difficult propaganda to combat because the farmer does pay for his fertilizer; the cotton mills do pay for the cotton. 

This is one thing that USIS did: In every single bag of fertilizer that goes out to the farmer there is a pamphlet which tells him that the money he is paying for this fertilizer goes into the counterpart fund of the Korean Government, that it is then used by the Korean Government for constructive expenses and development projects in 

Korea

This propaganda of the Communists was so strong that we made a counterpart film. It is a very clever device. It starts off with a picture of the farmer buying his fertilizer. There he is. He pulls out his paper money. He put a big mark on one of the 100 won bills he pays out. Then the film shows this marked bill going into the Bank of 

Korea and it shows a railroad construction project that is being developed in that farmer's area, and, strangely enough, that marked dollar bill comes back to the farmer's son for working on the railroad.

That is the story they tell in those simple films. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. May I interrupt there again? 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. Does the Information Service tell the Koreans that this aid which is a gift from the United States is a gift that comes out of the American taxpayer's pocket and nothing is returned to us in the form of payment? 

Dr. BUNCE. Absolutely. That is hammered home time and time again. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. There are no loans?

Dr. BUNCE. That is right. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. It is purely a grant-in-aid? 

Dr. BUNCE. That the Koreans understand. On every single joint project, on all the irrigation projects, thousands of them, and the railroad projects, we have big placards somewhat similar to this [indicating], and they are put up on wooden posts as permanent posters. This poster says:

This is a joint cooperative project between the United States ECA and the Korean Government, and the funds are a gift from the United States. 

Now these projects are very important and scattered widely all over Korea. For example, you have one picture here. It happened to be at the ceremony shown in this picture. I drove one of the gold spikes when they opened this railroad. It was the first time I ever drove a gold spike in my life. It wasn't really gold.

This arch depicted in the picture was erected by the Koreans. We had nothing whatsoever to do with it. The Ambassador and myself attended this ceremony. 

This is a very strange thing that was thought up by the Koreans [indicating]. That is a huge block of ice. After we got there, the 

Ambassador drove a spike, I drove a spike, the Prime Minister drove a spike, the Minister of Transportation drove a spike, and then the train came along.

Two of the ministers, the Ambassador, and myself stood back, pulled this block of ice, you see, and as the train came by we let the thing go and it smacked right on the nose of the engine. 

I could not understand what it was but the Koreans had heard that when you started something new and got together, first of all it was necessary to "break the ice."

Here is another poster [indicating]. This is a demonstration which was sent around the main cities, showing ECA aid supplies going into Korea. It covered everything from medical supplies, pitch, petroleum products, fertilizer, and the thousand and one things that we have been helping them to use in developing their economy. It was tre-

mendously well attended. Thousands and thousands a day come in and look over this whole program. 

Of course they have placards telling them, "This is a gift from ECA. The United States is attempting to cooperate with nations to establish a world of freedom." 

Chairman KEE. What percentage of the people are literate? 

Dr. BUNCE. The literacy in Korea depends upon two factors: One, whether you are talking about this script [indicating]-now, I am literate in Korea, in that I can read this script; but if you are talking about the Chinese script, then the literacy is much lower. Literacy, in terms of reading the native phonetic script, is very high. It was increased very greatly under military government, and now USIS has a book for teaching the Koreans this phonetic script and how to read. I should say that today 80 percent of the people of Korea can read the native script. 

Chairman KEE. You use that on your posters?

The Dr. BUNCE. Oh, yes. We appeal to the masses of the people. percentage who can read Chinese characters is very much smaller. 

Mr. JUDD. The newspapers are written in phonetic script? 

Dr. BUNCE. Part of it. They usually have two sections. We have a paper that goes out to all the farm villages. It is just a single sheet. 

It has a tremendously wide distribution. 

Chairman KEE. It is somewhat similar to the script used in the yen program in China and Formosa. 

Mr. JUDD. The Japanese have a phonetic script. But when they get down to the key word they usually have to write it in the Chinese character. But all the little words, the prepositions, the conjunctions, the adjectives, and the ordinary speech, that is in a script that everybody can read. Most people in Japan can read those key Chinese characters, too. :

The Japanese did a lot in improving literacy in Korea, did they not? 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. Under the military government for 4 years, and under the Korean Government in 18 months, we have doubled the school population from what it was under the Japanese and if you don't believe the schools are overcrowded you should go and see them.

Another point I would like to mention is that this work of USIS in bringing to these people not only what we are doing but the concepts of democracy in which we believe, is very effective. I have a staff of about 180 people. Many of them are scattered all over the country. 

They are up in the mines; they are up in the mills; they are up in the industrial areas; they do not sit in the Capital keeping a desk warm. 

The railroad men are out on the railroad. The people working in the factories are out there working with the factories. The strange thing is that when they travel through Korea, usually in a jeep because the roads are far too bad to use a car, when you go into a little village all the kids start running out and as soon as they see you are an American they have two words. They start waving and say, "Hello, O. K."

That is all over the country. There is tremendous good will from the masses of the people toward the American people. I think it is because USIS has brought to them what we believe in and what we are trying to do. 

Mr. JUDD. Is your USIS run wholly by the Voice of America program, or is it partly related to Mr. Drummond's work? Is he confined solely to Europe? Does your man cooperate with him?

Dr. BUNCE.

My man works with these other people to see that the 

ECA story is told. 

Mr. JUDD. Does he correlate his work with Drummond's work? In 

Europe, ECA has Mr. Drummond hammering away just on the ECA 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes, that ties right in with Mr. Mullen who heads the whole ECA information program. Mr. Drummond is handling the 

European end of it, as I understand it. 

Mr. JUDD. Baldridge is for Korea what Drummond is for Europe, is that correct?

Dr. BUNCE. That is correct. 

USIS program is run on a separate appropriation which Congress granted for this particular work. We also use the Voice of America, and we have on the Korean Broadcasting System, certain very desirable hours when the Voice of America is re-broadcast from Seoul, all over. 

The Voice of America is given in the Korean language. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Do they have the village loudspeakers?

Dr. BUNCE. We have at present a rather large number of radios which we obtained from Japan in which many parts were defective. 

We have established a group which is repairing all these radios and then they are distributed into the villages so that we can increase our radio coverage all the time. 

Mrs. BOLTON. You have it arranged so groups can listen to one set?

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

In addition to the USIS efforts, real progress has taken place in meeting the needs and desires of the masses of the people. In 4 years, tenancy in Korea has been reduced from 70 percent to about 35 percent. 

The remaining tenants pay only one-third of their crop. If you compare this to the past, when 70 percent of the people were tenants and when they paid as high as 60 percent of the crop in rent, you can see there has been an amazing social reform in agriculture. 

Under military government, we sold to 500,000 farmers the land which was taken over from the Japanese landlords when they left Korea. To my mind, the farmers of Korea are better off than they have been in any previous period.

Mr. CARNAHAN. What kind of a title do these farmers have to the land?

Dr. BUNCE. They have a complete title with a mortgage. Under the land distribution system initiated by the military government, they pay over a period of 15 years.

The Korean Government in order to complete the land reform has passed a bill which has been approved by the President and is now an Act and the machinery has been established to put it into force. Under the Korean bill, the length of the period of payment has been reduced and they are also reducing the period of payment which we established. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. And the title is from Korean Government to the individual?

Dr. BUNCE. That is right. 

I might say in regard to the Korean Government Land Reform Act, that the landlords are compensated for the loss of their land and they are given bonds in place of the land. The whole program is tied into the sale of vested properties, so that the landlord can take the bonds that he receives from the sale of his land and turn them in to the Government for the purchase of industrial and commercial property.

The land reform of the Korean Government when it is completed, I think, will meet the desires of these masses of peasant farmers who for years have lived almost as serfs. I think we have to recognize that in the Orient these measures have to be taken if you are going to meet the challenge of communism. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. May I interrupt there for a moment?

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

Mr. MANSFIELD. It seems to me you are on the right track there in giving these people something which they can call their own. Now, I am wondering what are the effects of contrast between individual ownership as you have mentioned it in South Korea, and collectivization in North Korea, as it is going on at the present time? 

What is the effect of that on the thinking of the people north of the thirty-eighth parallel?

Dr. BUNCE. Mr. Congressman, I can answer that very simply; after the land reform in North Korea, we had hundreds of thousands of farmers flee North Korea and come down to South Korea, because under the system established in North Korea, there was no individual land ownership. All land was owned by the state. It was allocated to farmers to operate. Then they were taxed by the state at an extremely high rate. 

Mrs. BOLTON. That is the regular Communist pattern.

Dr. BUNCE. These farmers, many of them who had fled, had been farm owners.

Their land was confiscated. 

One reason they fled in large numbers in 1947 was that the crop was not very good and the tax was assessed, not on the annual crop production but on a 5-year average, which happened to be rather high so that when it was applied in 1947, they had nothing to live on at all. 

That is one reason why we had this tremendous migration of farm families to South Korea.

Chairman KEE. Did not that influx from the north impose a serious problem on the southern republic?

Dr. BUNCE. It did. We had to take those people in. We had to establish refugee camps for them. We had to screen them to see whether they were Communist agents in the guise of refugees. 

Then we had to disperse them to avoid their concentrating in towns, to all the various counties, and move them into country areas where they would have a chance of making a living. It was certainly a very large problem. The other thing, in North Korea, regarding the land reform, which is very serious, was that any individual, if he ever said anything critical about the Communists or the Communist government, immediately lost his land. He had no right to it. In many areas where there had been opposition to the Communists, whole villages were uprooted and moved out and scattered into new areas. 

Much of the land was taken from the men who had been working it and who had owned it and given to laborers. It created a great deal of antagonism toward the northern regime. 

Mr. JUDD. Did the northern regime resist the movement of these people to the South? Did they have to smuggle across, or were the 

Communists glad to have them go to decrease the burden on themselves and increase the burden on the southern half?

Dr. BUNCE. It is very hard to say whether the north approved it or not. All I know is that they smuggled out and they came over high mountains.

Mr. JUDD. Obviously they were trying to escape.

Dr. BUNCE. That is right. 

There is one thing certain. I don't think they put anything in the way of older people coming down. They did not put anything in the way of Christian pastors and ministers. We had quite a number of them come down. The group that they retained in North Korea were the skilled laborers. They found it very difficult to get away. 

But the dissatisfied peasants wandered through the hills, swam across the rivers. With mountain ranges going up and down the thirtyeighth parallel, policing it so people cannot cross it is impossible to achieve. You cannot control it.

Mr. JUDD. Do you have any figures as to the productivity of the farmers in North Korea under the set-up the Communists developed as compared to the productivity in the south where the farmers own their own land now?

Dr. BUNCE. Dr. Judd, I am afraid we do not have accurate statistics on that.

Mr. JUDD. Of course, what you have said is the regular Communist pattern everywhere. They did the same thing in China. They sold it to the people as land reform. It was straight agricultural vandalism. 

They promised the farmers everything, and once they had them in hand, the victims could not do anything about it. The farmer would tell the visiting correspondent it was wonderful, because if he didn't say it was wonderful, he lost his right to even till the soil. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. Is the movement of population slowing down or are they still coming in from the north?

Dr. BUNCE. They are still coming in, Mr. Congressman, but the rate has declined.

Mr. CARNAHAN. The rate has declined? 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes, the rate of influx has declined. 

I might say, Dr. Judd, in reference to the agricultural production, in South Korea we have increased yields 23 percent in the past 4 years. 

As far as we know there is no indication that any such progress has been made in North Korea. I think the achievements in this field in 

South Korea are, again, using Mr. Hoffman's term, nothing short of amazing. I think this land reform has been one of the most stabilizing political influences in the whole of Korea.

Now, in regard to the question that was asked by Mr. Fulton regarding labor, I would like to say this:

With regard to labor there has not as yet been as much achieved as has been achieved for the farmer. I think this is probably due to two fundamental reasons:

Labor in industry in Korea is a very small part of the total economy. 

Korea is not an industrial nation. It is essentially an agricultural nation.

The second factor is that labor under the Japanese, and as we found out in the early days of military government, had been infiltrated with innumerable Communist cells, so that the first labor unions which were established were completely dominated by the Communists. 

Today there is in Korea a national labor union, which has just recently been accepted into the International Conference of Free Trade Unions, which, as you all remember, was organized and established in London a few months ago. In order to meet its obligations

under this international charter the National Union of Korea will have to make certain changes in its organization and in its actions. 

I might say that this month there has been called in Korea a national conference of all labor unions, at which time this whole problem will be reviewed by the leaders of the Korean labor movement. 

The progress, as I say, in this particular field, has been slow, and has been beset with very, very difficult conditions. 

I think that is about all I should say, and if you have any questions 

I would be very glad to answer them if I can.

Dr. BUNCE. I would have to check on that figure, Mr. Vorys. STATEMENT OF EDGAR A. J. JOHNSON, DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF KOREA PROGRAM, ECA 

Dr. JOHNSON. In 1951 from Japan there will be programmed $800,000 for cement, $591,000 in coal tar, pitch, and about $1,900,000 in iron and steel products. Some of the nonferrous metals will come from Japan and as much of the machinery as possible. In 1951 the imports from Japan are projected at $55,000,000. 

Dr. BUNCE. That includes free foreign exchanges as well as ECA purchases. 

Mr. VORYS. Is that $55,000,000 out of the $100,000,000?

Mr. JOHNSON. That is $55,000,000 out of $151,000,000, the total of the $100,000,000 we hope the Congress will authorize, plus $51,000,000 to be made available from Korean foreign exchange derived from exports.

Mr. VORYS. Does ECA function in Japan? 

Dr. JOHNSON. There is no ECA in Japan. 

Mr. VORYS. I understood under the GARIOA law that there was a provision which made the ECA sort of administration apply where applicable, or something like that. What is the connection between 

ECA and the economic recovery measures in Japan?

Dr. JOHNSON. We try to channel as many ECA dollars as we can through Japan so they will do double service. 

Mr. VORYS. The $14,000,000, I do not know whether that is the total or the increase for rice, the dollars obtained there will be occupation dollars from Japan?

Dr. JOHNSON. Export proceeds from Korean exports to Japan are computed in dollars. The Koreans will export rice and other commodities to Japan to build up their foreign exchange. The Korean 

Government will utilize both their self-generated exchange and our dollars for one collective recovery program.

Mr. VORYS. Where does the $14,200,000 mentioned for rice come from? Do they not originate from the American occupation and recovery costs in Japan?

Dr. BUNCE. Mr. Vorys, I would like to speak on this: We concluded sometime ago a trade agreement between Japan and Korea. That is now being reviewed. Korea is attempting to sell to Japan a large amount of products but we are buying from Japan a much larger amount of products. In other words, the net position is that dollars will be made available from Korea to Japan. And when I discussed this with General MacArthur, he told me that he had informed the congressional visitors who were there at that time, that to the extent that Japan is able to earn dollars from Korea, to that extent they had reduced their request for GARIOA appropriations. 

Mr. VORYS. I will ask the reporter to read my question. (Question read.)

Dr. BUNCE. I would say there will be no dollars paid for that rice but the rice will be paid for in terms of exports of machine products and cement and other materials shipped from Japan to Korea. The dollar figure is purely for bookkeeping purposes. Ordinarily this trade would be in yen and won, but we are using dollars because of the uncertainty of the exchange rates between the two currencies. 

Dr. JOHNSON. I am wondering if this is the point you are driving at: One dollar in fertilizer produces about $10 in rice. Some Korean rice is exported to Japan and therefore that makes available Japanese foreign exchange to finance the purchase of certain necessary commodities for Korea thereby reducing the total American bill. 

Mr. VORYS. Perhaps I can make myself clear. It seems to me we have to work out some sort of viable economy in the Far East, and since the American taxpayers are contributing heavily to the economy of Japan, and also the Philippines and also to one end of Korea, that an attempt to picture Korea as self-sustaining, if it means we are taking out of one pocket and putting it into the other is not very helpful here.

We run into the same thing in Europe where we find the German and the Austrian occupation and liberation forces are very sharp in trying to get dollars from each other and possibly wisely so, but it is important for us to get the total picture. I for one would very much like to know more intelligibly what the total picture is between the Japanese and the Korean economies. What is the total Korean budget, in dollars? 

Dr. BUNCE. Do you mean for the next fiscal year? The budget we presented for the next fiscal year for the Korean Government, the total ordinary budget estimate, was 89,000,000,000 won. 

Mr. VORYS. That is how many dollars? 

Dr. BUNCE. Roughly you can divide it by 1,000.

Mr. VORYS. It would be about $100,000,000. 

Dr. BUNCE. It would be $89,000,000. 

Mr. VORYS. So the support given the Korean economy exceeds their whole budget by approximately $11,000,000. 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

Mr. VORYS. You spoke of counterpart. You just have recovered. only half of the counterpart in the last year, by using this device of an official dollar.

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

Mr. VORYS. What happened to the other half? Where the ECA 

products were sold for won, were they sold at the official dollars? 

What happened to that other half?

Dr. BUNCE. The reason for this disparity between these two exchange rates goes back to the period of military government. When military government was first established, the official exchange rate between the won and the dollar was 15 to 1. Then they raised it to 

50 to 1 and later to 250 to 1. During the period of military government, in order to control inflation they followed a policy of selling GARIOA supplies and particularly food, which was a large item in those days, at low prices, in order to prevent wages from spiraling. 

When we came in and took over from the Army, we had a large amount of the Army pipe line supplies coming in. There had been established a practice of selling commodities at much less than they were worth on the open market in order to hold prices down and we had to take those prices from that low level and raise them up so that we get away from this business of using American goods to subsidize the Korean Government. We have taken very strong steps on that, Mr. Congressman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Mansfield, have you any questions?

Mr. MANSFIELD. I have no questions. 

Chairman KEE. Dr. Morgan- 

Mr. MORGAN. Doctor, this program is based on the premise that the 

38° parallel line will still be in existence? 

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. 

Mr. MORGAN. Is there any trade going on between North and South Korea?

Dr. BUNCE. A little smuggling. We did what we could to develop trade between North and South Korea, but there was one very unhappy experience which I can recall: A private trader in South 

Korea, made a deal with North Korea to ship up some cotton yarnand I think some sulfur and other products they desired in exchange for a shipload of fertilizer. He mortgaged one of his buildings in order to obtain the ship and sent the ship up there. They took all the goods off the ship and they loaded the fertilizer and then for some reason or other they arrested all the crew, they kept the ship, and later on most of the crew members got back down to South Korea. It was a very unhappy incident. I do not know whether this action of the North 

Koreans had anything to do with the action of the United Nations which 3 days before they confiscated the ship announced that the election in South Korea was held in a free atmosphere. Since that time there has been no official trade between the two areas. 

I would like to make another reference to Mr. Vorys' mention of trade: One thing we are emphasizing particularly in Korea is the expansion of trade through private channels and particularly between Japan and Korea; if Korea is to have a viable economy it is essential that a large amount of trade be carried on with Japan. We are taking that into account very definitely in our program and as you know President Rhee has made two visits to Japan, as the President of Korea. 

That I think is something which shows the trend of events. 

Mr. MORGAN. During the Japanese occupation practically 80 percent of the exports from Korea went to Japan?

Dr. BUNCE. Yes. Eighty percent of the exports of Korean products went to the Japanese Empire and about 90 percent of their imports came from the Japanese Empire. 

Mr. MORGAN. Is the ECA doing anything about forming new outlets of trade or are they still holding on to the previous outlets in 

Japan? 

Dr. BUNCE. We are developing trade with the East in many areas. 

For example, we have a very large volume of trade now with Hong Kong which is the center point for the whole of the Far East. Of course, tungsten, as was mentioned yesterday, is almost all coming to the United States.

Dr. BUNCE. It is true we will spend more dollars in Japan.

Dr. BUNCE. The thing that has happened in Korea during the last year-for two reasons, one because of the cut in the budget and second because of the delay in getting the appropriations is that the whole recovery program in Korea has been set back. We have not been able to go ahead, for example, with our proposed plan of core drillings, the development of the mines, laying the foundations and starting with the cement plants that we need if we are going to establish a balance of payments. That has been essentially the problem we have faced. Some of the cut, Dr. Judd, was taken up in the fact that lower prices prevailed. 

Mr. JUDD. Do you expect a further reduction in prices?

Dr. BUNCE. Further reductions in prices, Mr. Judd, were being considered very seriously by the Bureau of the Budget when it approved this $100,000,000 request.

Dr. JOHNSON. It could have been more spectacular; yes, sir.

Dr. BUNCE. NO; but I do believe that the program has been delayed.

Mr. MANSFIELD. Mr. Chairman, I would like to follow up one question Mr. Vorys tried to get some information on. I think it is very important we get this information showing the relationship of the

ECA appropriation to the budget. I have not got it clear in my own mind as to just what the relationship is, why we are putting in $100,000,000 into a country which has a budget appropriation of $89,000,000.

Dr. BUNCE. I would like to speak again to that: The original budget that was set up by the Korean Government was very much larger than 89,000,000,000 won, and because of the inflationary situation, we have been over that budget and have made very realistic estimates of the amount of income that would accrue and which could be spent in the ordinary budget. Now the 89,000,000,000 won is for the ordinary budget. There is in addition to that a separate budget which we hope to finance with the counterpart funds, and that counterpart budget will be approximately 100,000,000,000 won which will be entirely used for the building of the railroads, the construction of these new land reclamation and irrigation systems, in order to bring up the productivity of the country so that at the end of this period they will not be dependent on American aid. You have to take the two figures together to get the whole picture. 

There is a very good reason why it is that the Korean Government income has dropped and why it was as low as it was this year. When we went into Korea, as a liberating army, the Koreans welcomed us with open arms. They cheered and so on. They had flags flying. 

The Japanese all left Korea within about 3 months. The Japanese had been the people who had run the government; they had run the tax system. The whole government structure of Korea collapsed and military government was faced with this almost impossible, this gigantic task of trying to build up a functioning, effective government during its period of control. Now one of the things was the collapse of the whole tax structure. During the period of military government, the system of collecting taxes was never fully estab- Tished. It is only being really established effectively now, since the 

Korean Government has come into control and has faced these problems. That is one factor. The second factor is that when you get into inflationary situations where you have government expenditures and no income, so that they are financed by overdrafts on the Bank of Korea, you find that prices start to rise all the time; much of the income under the government of the Japanese did not come from taxes but it came from things like the tobacco monopoly, from the salt monoply, and from railroad fares; inevitably the tendency is for these prices to lag away behind the prices of other things that are going up. So government income always tends to lag. 

As I said, the stabilization committee raised railroad rates 125 percent and raised power rates to 15 won. Those steps are necessary to bring these charges for government enterprises up into line so that their income will provide more than enough to meet expenses. That is a difficult task and it is a task being faced by a new government that has only been in power about 18 months. They are facing it courageously.

I think we will find in another year the whole situation in the financial picture will be very much improved. 

Mr. JUDD. Do you supppose we could get them to help our government raise rents so they will be comparable to what food and everything else have risen to?

Dr. JOHNSON. I think, Mr. Chairman, there is a very serious confusion which has arisen here in the attempt to compare a national internal budget of Korea with the amount of dollars that are necessary to balance the balance-of-payments. 

It is quite unreasonable, it seems to me, to compare the internal costs of running a government in Korea where you can hire a soldier for let us say 10 cents a day and then reduce that into dollar terms.

The fact of the matter is that the budget is running in the neighborhood of 190,000,000,000 won. That is an internal matter to cover the costs of government administration in Korean prices, in terms of an entirely different culture.

The other problem we face is the question of financing the necessary imports in order to make this economy viable. The two things 

I submit are quite incomparable.

Mr. VORYS. I thought it was 89,000,000,000 won. 

Dr. BUNCE. That was the ordinary budget and then they have the extraordinary budget which covers the cost of utilizing the aid that we give them effectively.

Mr. JUDD. It comes out of the counterpart funds, they hope.

000,000,000 won or 190,000,000 dollars? 

Dr. JOHNSON. No, sir; 190,000,000,000 won. Those won are not transferable into dollars, sir.

Mr. VORYS. It is the name of their currency and it has a very floating and fluctuating value. In the past year we have said it is 450 and it has been on the free market at 900, regular rate.

Dr. BUNCE. We made a study, Mr. Vorys, of the impact of the 

Union of North and South Korea under democratic auspices. We made a very careful study to see how it would change the program. 

The main thing that would happen is that certain things that we now would have to import, we could obtain from North Korea, but certain things that North Korea needs would have to be obtained abroad. 

One of those things that we could obtain from North Korea probably would be some lumber. In terms of the over-all program, to establish viable economy in a United North and South Korea, we came to the conclusion it would cost just about the same amount in dollars, but with some very slight adjustments in the imports and exports that would be necessary, and we found at the end of the period we would establish probably a balance of trade for the whole of Korea, north and south, running in terms of about $80,000,000 worth of exports and $80,000,000 worth of imports. 63307-50-pt. 2- -14
