Dr. BUNCE. I would like to make it quite clear. I think the confusion arose as to whether you could establish a viable economy if Korea was united. I think you can, in both cases. I think we can in the case of South Korea alone establish a viable economy, and I think in the case of union between North and South Korea we can establish a viable economy and I think we can do it more easily. I would like to make it very, very clear. Now the $35,000,000 deficit which you referred to was the deficit at the end of the third year, and the year after that, as I remember the charts that were presented last year, it showed a very much smaller figure. We have here a chart giving the balance of payments as we see them [indicating]. 

This is 1950. These are the "in payments" and these are the "out payments." This is for goods which go into the Korean economy. 

This is the lack of balance we have at present. In other words, there is much more going in than is going out. The whole objective of the ECA program is to increase one and decrease the other so we get a balance. That is a viable economy in terms of international trade. 

In 1951 you will notice that our exports increase and our imports also increase. You will also notice these which are funded by the 

Koreans. These are paid for by the United States. You will notice that this bar is longer than this one. Therefore, the funding by the 

United States declines and we are throwing more and more responsibility onto the Koreans each year to purchase more and more of the goods they need.

In 1952 you find again exports increasing and the United States funding decreasing. There is the third year.

In 1953 it shows the lack of balance that we have left. 

In 1954 it is still smaller. It is a very small amount. 

It is our hope that as the situation becomes more stable, Mr. Congressman, that this amount here and this amount here, a smaller part of it might be taken up by the program of technological assistance which is now before Congress, and I hope part of it will be taken up by private capital investments.

The President told me before I left that he is very anxious to have an amount of American capital come into Korea with its technical know-how, to help rebuild and develop these things. It is my faith that if we can go ahead with this program, we can establish a viable

economy and any lack of balance here can be taken up by private investments in Korea. Now that is South Korea. If we include 

North Korea, we would find that it would be an easier job to achieve the task. I think that is the simplest way to put it. 

I certainly do not want to get the impression abroad that I believe we are facing a situation where Korea can never stand on its own feet. I do not believe that is true at all. 

Mr. VORYS. You are facing there the fact that some small portion of this planet cannot have a viable economy, it must trade with the rest of the world. It is similar in Europe. That law of economics is not repealed when we get to the international date line. It is true in the Orient. 

Dr. BUNCE. I am sorry you were not here yesterday when Dr.

Johnson presented the program because the whole program is designed to increase exports and to establish industries which will make it unnecessary for them to have that large volume of imports. One of the biggest things is the cost of fertilizer. In exports, one of the biggest things is to increase their exports of rice. 

Mr. VORYS. Expressed dollarwise, out of the first 2 years that I figured rapidly here, I figured 57.5 million dollars in plant improvement and equipment and the sort of thing which would not be recurring expenses. 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is right. 

Dr. BUNCE. That is right.

Mr. VORYS. Those three long red lines represent the investment stage, that would not be recurring? 

Dr. BUNCE. That is right.

Dr. JOHNSON. That is shown in these projections of exports. We are right here, now [indicating]. We have begun the rice-export program. That has been the difficult job. This is what can be materialized.

Mr. VORYS. Now I have two questions about the charts. I notice on page 9 of this economic guide, that brick chart, the flour chart, and the rubber-shoes chart show an ominous drop to be projected in to 1950. I wondered whether that meant that those productions were seasonal or whether there was some collapse taking place that would indicate this down trend at the end of each production chart, there. 

Dr. JOHNSON. With regard to the rubber-shoe chart, that was an intentional decrease in rubber-shoe production and a shift over to automobile-tire production.

Now the flour chart, as far as I know, is seasonal. 

Dr. BUNCE. Both the flour and brick production are seasonal. The clay for the brick is always dug locally from the surface-it is not deep-pit digging-and in cold weather it always drops down. 

Mr. VORYS. For those three it does not indicate anything except seasonal effects or a change-over in production. 

Dr. BUNCE. That is right.

In general, the production picture, Mr. Vorys, has been amazingly good. The estimate is that in this last year as compared to the previous calendar year, the industrial production has increased about 50 percent. In many things like cotton we have had well over 100 percent increase in production.

When I listened to Dr. Johnson yesterday, I thought it was an amazing job.

Mr. JUDD. Yesterday you gave us the things Korea would always have to import because she could not possibly have them. 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is right.

Mr. JUDD. She will always have to import this much on the chart. 

We are putting in this amount now, this is capital equipment and stuff to increase her productivity, so she can get up to here in her production of exportable commodities. She has to get beyond here, because that is what she is always going to have to import from some place.

Dr. JOHNSON. That is correct. These are her irreducible, annual, recurring imports. These show the wherewithall with which to finance those imports.

Chairman KEE. I believe, Dr. Johnson, you spoke about the expected construction of a glass plant. I intended to ask you yesterday if you have glass sand.

Dr. JOHNSON. There are abundant supplies of silica sand. 

Chairman KEE. That is fine. I was interested in the character of the coal that you called anthracite coal. Is that a hard coal very much like the anthracite we produce in this country, in Virginia and Pennsylvania?

Dr. JOHNSON. It is what the geologists call tertiary coal. I am not a geologist and I cannot go beyond that. It looks like a black dust. 

Chairman KEE. It is not bound together?

Dr. JOHNSON. Not at all. It is granular. It has, in a sense, been superheated by volcanic eruptions. It is difficult to use. It has a high fixed carbon content. It is very difficult to fire, however. That is why on stoker grates we must combine it with bituminous coal, which is much more volatile. 

Chairman KEE. You spoke of the way it was found in the mines. It is not compact. You do not have to break it up in the mines. 

Dr. JOHNSON. It is almost like sawdust. You swing a pick against it and it just falls down and can be shoveled up. 

Chairman KEE. Do you find it in bins, or something like pockets?

Dr. JOHNSON. Yes, sir; it is in lenses. It is like black, damp sugar. 

Chairman KEE. The only explosives you would have to use would be to get in to it? 

Dr. JOHNSON. That is right. You do not have to blast it to loosen it for shoveling. 

Chairman KEE. That is all. 

I was also interested in your description of what the Communists have done up in north Korea. It, in a way, answers a question that has been in my mind all my life. I have never understood that expression used in the Bible about "From him who hath not shall be taken even that which he hath." I think I understand it now much better than I ever did before. 

Are there any further questions? If not, Doctor, we appreciate very much your very interesting presentation. It seems to me that you are doing a wonderful job over in Korea and I certainly hope that we will be able to see at the end of it great success and I believe it will be successful under your direction. 

We will adjourn until 10 a. m. tomorrow, when we have Mr. Bissell before us. (Whereupon, at 12: 50 p. m., the committee adjourned, to reconvene at 10 a. m., Friday, March 10, 1950.)

As far as I know, while we have these budget estimate books-the presentation before the Appropriations Committee available here and they have been here for a week, and I have attempted to read mine, today, March 10, is the first that we have had any answer to those questions which will be the No. 1 questions on the floor. 

Chairman KEE. I think the matter has been covered pretty generally, Mr. Vorys. Mr. Hoffman and some of the other witnesses went into what the money would be spent for, in a general way. Of course they did not do it in detail. 

If there is no objection, the witness can go into that feature of the matter. 

Mr. BISSELL. As stated, the total authorization requested is for $2,950,000,000.

It is also correct, as Mr. Vorys has pointed out, that some $2,925,- 

000,000 is expected to be obligated during the fiscal year 1951, for socalled country aid programs.

In addition to that total for country aid programs we are requesting authorization for an additional $85,000,000 for certain special projects. 

Those fall into two categories. Some $40,000,000 of that sum is for international power projects, and $45,000,000 of it is for special projects in the overseas territories of the participating countries. 

The sum for country aid programs, together with the sum requested for special projects, gives a total for direct country aid of $3,010,000,- 000 which we believe should be obligated during the next fiscal year. 

There are two further items to be added to that to arrive at the total funds required for the period. The first is an item of $36,000,000 to finance certain shipments to Greece, which are items of a sort that are used both by the civilian economy and by the armed forces of Greece. 

These items in the past have been financed for the armed forces under the Greek-Turkish aid program. This item of $36,000,000 represents a proposed shift for the next fiscal year, to the ECA, of responsibility for what have hitherto been financed as military supplies. 

The final item that should be added is a total of 53.1 million dollars for other types of assistance and for administrative expenses. I can give the committee a further break-down of that item if they desire. 

This gives a total of funds required for the fiscal year of 3,099.1 million. It is estimated, however, that there will be a carry-over from the current year of 149.1 million dollars and making allowance for that carry-over from the current year indicates a need for $2,950,- 000,000 of new funds for the forthcoming fiscal year on the assumption that the appropriations for the current and the next fiscal years can be consolidated so that those funds may be carried over from the present year.

Chairman KEE. That carry-over in the appropriation is from the program for the fiscal year 1950? 

That represents our estimate of the extent to which it is going to be possible and is proving to be possible to make savings in the cost of the program for the current year below the cost originally covered by appropriation.

Mr. VORYS. That carry-over will have to be reauthorized or reappropriated, will it not, in our legislation? 

Mr. BISSELL. I believe the legislation before this committee, sir, provides for a consolidation of the two appropriations and would thereby make that carry-over possible. In that respect, similar action was taken at the end of fiscal year 1949, although we had no similar programed carry-over as it turned out. 

If I may refer to two tables in the budget estimate, to which Mr. 

Vorys has already referred, they give further information in reply to his general question.

The first of these is table 2, on page roman No. II-4 and is entitled, "Country Aid Program, 1949-50 and 1950-51." That table gives for each of the participating countries the amount of aid expected to be allotted to the country by the ECA in the current fiscal year and the amount believed to be necessary for the next fiscal year. 

The other table that I will refer to is one that has been submitted to the staff of the committee, entitled, "Estimated ECA-Financed Program by Commodity Groups for the Fiscal Year 1951," which gives, by countries, and in terms of some eight groups of commodities and of

charges for transportation, an estimate of the objects for which ECA program funds would be spent during the fiscal year 1951. 

Chairman KEE. What page? 

Mr. BISSELL. That is not originally a part of the budget estimates and I have submitted it separately to this committee. 

Mr. VORYS. That was furnished day before yesterday.

Chairman KEE. That is the statement of which Dr. Judd now has a copy. 

Mr. BISSELL. That is right.

Could I make one comment, sir, upon the last of these tables to which I have referred, namely, the estimated ECA-financed commodity program:

I think the committee should be advised that we regard this as a very rough advance estimate of the way in which ECA funds would be used. In very brief outline, the procedure of the ECA in determining the needs for current and future years, which I think has been discussed with this committee in preceding years, involves an estimate of the dollar deficit, the minimum and irreducible dollar deficit likely to be incurred by each of the participating countries. 

ECA aid is necessary and is granted in order to enable the countries to meet their dollar deficits. By their dollar deficits, I mean the excess of their necessary expenditures of dollars for essential imports and other essential purposes, over their estimated earnings of dollars from all sources.

In brief, then, the determination of the amount of aid by countries is on the basis of their dollar deficits.

In computing their dollar deficits and appraising the impact upon the several countries of a reduction in the amount of aid from year to year, it is necessary, of course, to examine with great care their proposed dollar expenditures and their estimated dollar earnings.

The major purpose of examining proposed dollar expenditures is to make sure that these are being held to the minimum consistent with progress toward recovery. In examining their estimated dollar earnings, the purpose, of course, is to satisfy ourselves, and, broadly, to satisfy this Government, that the countries have allowed for and that we are making allowance for the largest possible current earnings that under present circumstances it is at all realistic to believe they will achieve. In short, the purpose of both these examinations is to make sure the estimated aid required is the lowest figure that is consistent with the country's recovery. 

From this account of the process of estimating aid, it is probably quite clear that a part of the process of estimating, and therefore a proper part of our budget estimate each year, is a statement of the so-called import programs of the countries, with a special reference to their dollar imports; also an estimate covering their other necessary dollar expenditures, and an estimate of their dollar exports.

All of those estimates, of course, cover their total imports; likewise, their total dollar earnings. It is only as a very last stage in this process that we make any estimate of the imports likely to be financed specifically with ECA funds. In carrying out that last step in the analysis we will already have arrived at our estimate of the amount of aid needed for each country, our estimate of the total import program of that country, and also of the total dollar expenses for other

purposes. We will have arrived at our estimate of its non-ECA dollar resources; that is, the dollars it will acquire as its own dollar earnings.

In making this final estimate we then have, in effect, to guess at the particular kinds of purchases for which ECA dollar funds will be used as distinct from the other dollar resources of the several countries.

I say this both to explain why the last step in the operation is an estimate of what I have called the "ECA-financed import program," and also why I regard that ECA-financed program estimate as subject to a considerably wider degree of error than even the underlying figure, such as the total import program. 

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Chairman- Chairman KEE. Mr. Vorys. 

Mr. VORYS. Could I ask this at this point: As a matter of fact, what happened was that both ECA and the OEEC felt that the pattern of relative needs among the participating countries had been well established and the whole thing was figured on the basis of a 25-percent cut, and then you followed the pattern for division established in the past 2 years; is that not correct? 

Mr. BISSELL. That is substantially correct, sir.

If I may I would like to explain it a little more fully. The underlying logic of the program is exactly as I have described; it is an appraisal of dollar earnings and dollar expenditures and the resulting dollar deficit. In approaching that task in the fiscal year 1951 we felt, as you have said, that the division of aid among the countries in the first 2 years of the program had established a pattern that should be taken as the basis for our future work. Therefore, for this year, the process that I have described in general terms was carried out in two stages:

We first made an appraisal, not country by country, but for the whole group of participating countries as a group. That is to say, we made an appraisal of necessary imports, of dollar earnings, of the dollar deficit required to be covered, and thus have the total amount of aid needed.

It was on the basis of that over-all or aggregated judgment that we believed, as of last October, that the total amount of aid could be cut in the fiscal year 1951 some 25 percent below the amount required and provided for the current year. 

We, therefore, urged the European countries-and in this their organization agreed with us-in making up their programs for fiscal year 1951 for submission to us, to assume that there would be a cut in aid of 25 percent for all of the countries with the sole exception of Greece. In the case of Greece only a very slight cut below the level for the current year was believed wise. 

Our purpose in asking the countries to construct their own programs on that basis was to insure that they did not submit to us merely requests for aid based on their own conception of their needs without reference to the relationship of each country's needs to those of the continent as a whole.

What we preferred to secure from each country this year was not a brief in defense of a requested aid figure, but was rather an appraisal of the effect upon that country of the 25-percent cut in aid which our own research made us believe feasible.

ей Therefore the programs we received at about the end of the year already embodied the cut of 25 percent to which I have referred. 

We further studied these progrems, of course, after we received them. 

In this second stage of the process we examined not the over-all needs of Europe as a whole but we now examined them country by country to determine whether the 25-percent cut would be too great a cut for some countries, or whether possibly a greater cut would be possible in other cases.

As a result of that examination we felt that our country-aid programs could be cut somewhat further from a total of approximately $3,100,000,000 to the figure of $2,925,000,000 to which I have already referred.

Therefore, the country-aid programs for which funds are now requested, total a figure some 27 percent or 28 percent lower than the figure for the current year.

Mr. VORYS. I do not quite understand how you arrive at a balance of payments on current accounts and then have another settlement figure outside of that. I can see how capital operations would be perhaps something different, but I still do not understand the net settlements part.

5 Mr. BISSELL. The net settlements could be included in the current account balance, by a different definition, but our reason for excluding them is as follows:

In making our estimates of dollar imports, dollar payments for services, dollar exports and other dollar earnings, we have, throughout, included transactions which would actually be conducted in dollars. 

Thus, the dollar imports total includes, for instance, petroleum products from Venezuela, because they are actually paid for in dollars. 

It would not, however, include meat imported from the Argentine, because that is not paid for in dollars. In most cases, and in fact, throughout this table, I believe it is correct that it does not include purchases even from Switzerland, because they are not paid for in dollars. In the case of Switzerland, most of the participating countries have bilateral trade agreements which involve some offsetting of the elements of their trade. Therefore, after one has taken account of all the dollar transactions, it is still necessary to allow for payments that will be made between governments or between central banks, to cover a net trade deficit between one of the participating countries and an outside country.

For instance, most of the participating countries incur deficits on current account in their trade with Switzerland. Since we have not defined that as dollar trade, that is not taken into account in the total here for the dollar imports of these countries. It is necessary, therefore, to enter at some point in the calculation the dollars, or gold that will have to be paid by these countries to Switzerland month by month or quarter by quarter throughout the year, in the net settlement of their trading account with Switzerland. 

As you can see, by a different definition, we could have called Swiss trade also dollar trade, but we had to use a fairly narrow definition because it is the only manageable statistical way to put these figures together.

I have right at hand here, if you wish, the elements that go into this settlements item. 

Let me mention a few as examples to make clear what I have in mind.

The reasoning both of the European members of the organization in Paris and our own reasoning is that Greece has just finished, in the course of the last year, a civil war; that the civil war prevented any real start on recovery, and that Greece is therefore a good year and a half behind the other countries.

The logic of the arrangement is simply this: We could either give Belgium something in the way of $250,000,000 of conditional aid in return for which Belgium makes her own currency available as grants to her European neighbors, or, alternatively, if we did not do that, Belgium's neighbors would have to spend dollars in Belgium, and if they spend dollars in Belgium, whether they are ECA funds or their own earned dollars, the effect would be precisely the same. The dollars would reach 

Belgium and Belgium would earn in Europe more dollars than it needs to cover its purchases in the Western Hemisphere; Belgium would be able to build up her monetary reserves as she has for the last 3 years.

In this case there is, as I think the members of this committee are aware, not one dollar of so-called net aid going to Belgium. Every dollar of this sum of $256,900,000 will be matched by Belgian grants to other countries.

Mr. JUDD. Furthermore, if we did not make this grant to Belgium we would have to increase the grants to these other countries who are buying from Belgium.

Mr. BISSELL. Precisely, sir. 

Mr. JUDD. So we would not save any net dollars. 

Mr. BISSELL. That is exactly correct.

Mr. JUDD. Now, the other part of it: I see in the case of Norway, Portugal, and Sweden, you are proposing for this coming fiscal year to give them a larger amount of aid than their deficits amount to. I wish you would enlarge upon that. In other words, we have given the others less than their deficit but in the case of those three we are giving more than their deficit. 

Mr. BISSELL. That is correct.

I can best explain that by referring again to the general procedure we have used this year. In answer to a question from Mr. Vorys I stated we began with an over-all look at Europe's needs and thus arrived at our preliminary estimate of a 25-percent cut. We then received programs country by country and we studied them as I explained. When we studied them we came to the conclusion that the cut in country aid could be larger than our original guess of 25 percent and could indeed be 27 percent or 28 percent.

When we came to that conclusion we determined also to propose an allocation of aid by countries, which, with the exceptions I have just been discussing, would represent an across-the-board percentage cut, the same percentage cut for all countries, with the sole exception of Greece, which I have mentioned, and Belgium, for the reason that I have explained.

៦. 

Therefore, the column showing the proposed aid for each country shows figures arrived at in this fashion as an across-the-board cut. 

But then, in the examination of the implications of those cuts country by country, it appears as shown by the last column, that in certain cases this will cut aid slightly below the dollar deficit; in other cases it will not cut the amount of aid quite down to what we estimate will be the dollar deficit; and specifically we believe that this formula will extend slightly more aid to Sweden, Norway, and Portugal than would be required to cover their deficits, that it will furnish rather less to a number of other countries, notably to France, Germany, and Italy.

For the group of countries as a whole, we expect that there will be substantially no change in their reserves but inevitably if we adopt the principle of a flat across-the-board cut, it is going to mean that some countries receive a little less than could be justified and others a little more.

I would like to emphasize that the reason for the procedure is as Mr. Judd has, I think, in effect, explained: We have felt ourselves that to continue to administer this program entirely on the basis of need, would be to invite and to reward a lack of success; it would penalize and discourage success in accomplishing the very purposes that, of course, are those of the program. By making clear to each European country that it would not have the privilege of achieving recovery more slowly than its neighbors and thereby imposing an added burden on its neighbors, we supply a valuable and powerful incentive in the right direction.

Mr. JUDD. I agree with the policy. I just wanted to bring it out here on the record. The difficulty for these people who will not take the trouble to go into it is that two countries, Portugal and Sweden, which were neutral in the war and did not suffer devastation and occupation and a severe drain upon their economies, get an increase or at least more than their deficit amounts to, whereas some of the ones who suffered the most and have the hardest time recovering, do not get what their deficit amounts to.

We hope nobody will discover this in the tables, but I think your principle is entirely right. 

That brings me to my last question. 

Mr. BISSELL. Excuse me, sir. I wonder if I could just remind the committee of this point again, in addition to what you have said, and that is that this principle is not only one that in the ECA we strongly endorse and approve, but it is a principle officially adopted as such, and recommended to us, by the European organization. This is not something that has simply been imposed by us. We did suggest it, we strongly supported it, and we were very pleased indeed that the European organization, OEEC, recommended it. 

Mr. JUDD. Although you have adopted that principle and it shows up in the case of Belgium in figures here in the table, the fact is that 

Belgium is getting no aid from us in dollars? 

Mr. BISSELL. Not net aid, that is correct, sir.

Mr. JUDD. And she is being penalized to that extent, because she has probably done the most effective job of recovering? 

Mr. BISSELL. That is correct.

Mr. JUDD. But from here on there is no further penalty. Of course, you cannot penalize her below zero. 

Mr. BISSELL. No; that is entirely correct.

Mr. JUDD. You are not asking her to make a contribution. 

Mr. BISSELL. This aid Belgium receives next year will also be principally conditional aid. I think, however, there does remain some element of penalty on success. However, I think we have largely removed that from here on.

Mr. JUDD. You have cut approximately 27 percent or 28 percent this year. Are you going to be able to cut 50 percent of the remainder next year, do you think?

Mr. BISSELL. I think, sir, we will be able to cut, in round numbers, another billion dollars off the aid.

Mr. JUDD. And then for the final bill we have to knock off a whole $2,000,000,000 at one jump?

Mr. BISSELL. I think we would have to do that, sir. 

I would make these two observations on that prospect: 

First, I think that there may be two or possibly more than two, countries in Europe in a special position, in special difficulties, when this program is ended. I think that for reasons that are probably clear to the committee, I much prefer not to speculate on whether that will be the case or what countries will be involved because to do so again is to invite reliance on something that may not happen in the future. But I think that there probably will be some countries in difficulty, and I think it is very possible that the Congress will determine at that time that some very modest aid in other forms and administered in a different fashion may be necessary. 

The other observation I would make is of quite a different character and much more general. When this program ends there will be a considerable volume of purchases for which funds will have been obligated on the day the program ends. There will be cases where the goods have not yet been delivered. That is the pipe line. That pipe line will continue in the first year after the end of the ERP to furnish a considerable value of goods which will be received and will enter the economies of the European countries from previously obligated funds. 

I believe that pipe line will cushion the cutting off of the program. 

Therefore, leaving aside the first of these two comments of mine, it is our expectation we can cut approximately $1,000,000,000 from this figure for the fiscal year 1952, and barring any special situations with particular countries, no further ERP funds will be necessary or should be provided thereafter.

Mr. JUDD. I notice there is a reduction of $244,000,000 in the pipe line this year below what it was last year. 

Mr. BISSELL. That is a reduction, sir, that we believe will take place during the fiscal year 1951. During the current year the latest reports we can assemble indicate that the pipe line is, if anything, getting slightly larger-the volume of goods in the pipe line. We expect that during the fiscal year 1951 the volume of goods in the pipe line will shrink by approximately $250,000,000 and that during the fiscal year 1952 it should shrink by a considerably larger amount, perhaps as much as $300,000,000 or $400,000,000. 

Mr. JUDD. Does that merely reflect the reduced rate at which we will be sending commodities abroad?

Mr. BISSELL. We intended to have it refer to ECA funds, Mr. Vorys, and the way I would interpret the meaning of that statement is that if, for instance, in the course of the next year it appears that the need for aid for this group of countries as a whole is smaller than we had anticipated, or than the funds appropriated, we would again, as in the current year, try to make a saving, but we would do so, I would expect, in the form of a further across-the-board cut, bearing on all countries, rather than by reducing the aid of countries who have turned in a particularly good performance.

That is into the United Kingdom—

It used exchange controls to exclude the possibility that the American companies could take sterling or use it for purchases, whether or not they would agree to sell oil for sterling, outside of the sterling area in nondollar countries. 63307-50-pt. 2- -16

It made a bilateral agreement with Argentina which closed that nation as a market to the American companies. And it required these, when marketing in the sterling area, to buy specified quantities of their supplies from British or British-Dutch companies. I refer to, through the expansion of refineries on the Continent, is not a saving through a change in the source of supply; it is the saving that occurs by importing crude and refining it on the spot, with costs in their own currencies, as against importing these products, as the Europeans used to do so largely from the United States and the other Caribbean refineries before the war. 

Mr. BURLESON. You mean the end products.

That means of saving dollars permanently and economically-because this is not a discriminatory practice, this particular one I am referring to, and it is not a highcost practice that dollar saving is one which the European countries were most anxious to make on a large scale as soon as they could after the war.

It is perfectly fair to say we have facilitated that, and indeed I think it is a sound economic development in the light of the objectives of this program. But I think that even in the development with which we have had the most direct connection, we have facilitated and taken account of a line of development in the world petroleum industry that was well started before the ERP.

Suppose further that when the new refinery is in operation it operates on dollar crude oil-crude oil purchased from one of the American companies for dollars. There is still a large saving between the dollar cost of the crude oil for the European requirement and the dollar cost of the end products, gasoline, kerosene, lubricating oils, and the like that would have to be imported if the refinery did not exist and before it is in operation. That saving in dollars, even if there is no change in the source of supply and no resort to so-called sterling oil, the saving in dollars is still, I am sure, much larger than the carrying costs of the dollar investment in the refinery.

Now, again, if you would like a quantitative estimate of the order of magnitude of that saving, I think that Dr. Bransky could give you a better judgment than I could, but I am quite certain that this is one of the uses of dollars-that is, the investment of dollars in new refinery capacity—that is, on the whole, an economically healthy one and one that does not require discrimination and gives rise to a large saving in dollars over the years. I think it is for that reason that the European countries are inevitably placing a major emphasis on expanding their refinery capacity.

In making that remark I have assumed that these refineries are economic, in the sense that they have a suitable marketing area, that their location permits a low-cost operation. We, of course, have turned down a number of applications for the financing of refineries in Europe where we thought those conditions were not satisfied. 

Many of the small countries in Europe would like to build refineries so that they could enjoy this sort of dollar saving, but often in the very small countries such an operation would in the long run be uneconomic, it will be high cost, it will be a silly and wasteful use of resources in a nondiscriminatory trading world. In those cases we believe that it is improper that their dollars or ours should be invested in facilities that in a nondiscriminatory world could not stand on their own and could not perform an economic operation.

Mr. VoRYS. If there is a surplus in world production of petroleum products in 1952 or any other time, won't it have to be handled in one of two ways, either some sort of cartel or wheat-agreement arrangement, or on a dog-eat-dog competitive basis between the countries and the people who own the supplies which are in surplus? I think it is going to be, percentagewise, rather small. Therefore I think it may well turn out not to be so distrubing an element as it might appear in advance from this distance.

If we have a depression in this country we will have a vastly worse world surplus situation regardless of world refinery construction. 

If things go well and if we continue to have a dynamic and successful and smoothly functioning economy, our estimates of future consumption could well turn out to have been low. Therefore I will say that

The British companies overseas have a surplus right now of about 7,000,000 tons of refined products, or rather they expect in this calendar year to have a surplus of 7,000,000 tons,

We think the participating countries cannot go quite that fast in expanding their consumption. For one thing, they cannot manufacture the tractors, and so forth, fast enough. You can keep tabs on your refinery surplus, but crude oil you cannot do so much about.

Mr. BURLESON. Where is this increase in consumption of petroleum products coming from if it does not displace coal at the same time?

There are great possibilities there, and that is what the ERP countries plan to do. They plan to mechanize agriculture and increase the number of machines in factories, and so forth. There are great possibilities there. Coal has fallen behind. The coal mines are not as productive as they were before the war, and oil is taking a larger place. 212 times as many tractors in west European agriculture as before the war.

To my mind. the real danger is not that refinery capacity will out-run the market demand if these products are not rationed in Europe. Mr. BURLESON. Again emphasizing the point, will that be true without displacing the coal economies upon which Britain and France particularly are based?

Mr. BISSELL. Yes. Britain and France would still be importing coal from the United States if it were not for ERP. This is a highly uneconomic process because hauling coal across the Atlantic just about doubles the cost. While we can lay down coal tidewater cheaper than 

Europeans, our coal landed is anywhere from double the cost of European coal in the same locations, to a small amount above it.

Mr. VORYS. That is something I may know something about because

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Chairman, if we have concluded our investigation of the energy situation, I wondered if we could get on to this European payments plan, so as to get an explanation we can understand. 

Mr. BURLESON (presiding). Does Mrs. Bolton have any questions on this matter?

Mrs. BOLTON. You have covered the ground very well, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. BISSELL. I wonder if I'could make a very brief statement of two points of our policy which I think really have not come up very clearly at least. This discussion will be very brief. The first thing is this: 

We have not felt in the field of petroleum that we could urge on the British Government or others, policies or changes in their policies, if what we urged upon them would cost more dollars on balance for the British economy. We have thought as long as we are footing the bill that we have to give our first priority to cutting down the dollar drain.

That has meant and still means that in the field of petroleum policy and many others, this Government has to put up with policies that we do not like, and petroleum is one of the clearest areas where that is true.

I think this is a governmental position which all the agencies of the Government have pushed and pushed very hard: We take the position that if the British or any other government is pursuing policies, not in order to save dollars, but to gain commercial advantage, then we will certainly object to them if they are of a discriminatory nature. 

We could not, as I repeat, be urging them to pursue a course of action that would increase dollar costs.

Mr. BURLESON. I think this committee is aware of the fact that it must be the policy of this Government, ECA and otherwise, not to get in the position of dictating terms and conditions and procedures and policies to European nations but there must be some conditions defined, precedent to our assistance. 

Mr. BISSELL. It is not that we are perfectly satisfied with what the 

British are doing, but I mean there is a general policy. 

The other policy is this: I think, sir, as a matter of the analysis of the facts of the situation, that the important problem-and I think this has come out in much of our discussion-the important question is, how far should the British companies further expand their facilities? With reference to an earlier question of yours about the effect of the British taking over the Argentine market on the pushing of a surplus back into our own market, my own feeling, sir, is that as long as a surplus exists in the world, it does not matter very much whether that surplus appears in the Argentine and thus pushes American-company oil back here, or whether that surplus appears in South Africa, or where it appears. As long as there is the surplus, then there will be pressure on American companies, and the pressure perhaps to import more into this country, that you asked about earlier. 

So it would seem to us that the key to the situation is what is the proper rate of expansion of the facilities owned by these European countries.

On that matter, the principle we have endeavored to follow is this: 

We frown upon and we seek to prevent and to restrain any expansion of facilities, any construction of facilities, which would not be a good business risk in a nondiscriminating free-trading world. In other words, if a British company is building a refinery, that without any of the special advantages of selling in sterling instead of in dollars and without any kind of discrimination or protection by government in its favor, would be a good business risk, then we are happy to see them go ahead and build it. But if we think they are expanding their facilities to such a degree that the expansion would not be a good business risk unless they could assume continued discrimination in their favor, the right, for instance, to sell for sterling instead of for dollars, if that is the only situation in which the expansion is justified, we regard that, then, as an excessive expansion and an improper one, and one in which our dollars should not be used and one in which their own dollars should not be used, and we have so stated very clearly to the British and other governments. 

I do not say we have applied that principle perfectly, but that is the principle.

Mr. BURLESON. Mr. Chairman, we had just completed our discussion on petroleum and Mr. Vorys suggested we get into the Payments 

Union matter.

Chairman KEE. I believe we would like for you to give us in as simple language as possible for a technical man to give, an explanation of the proposal with reference to your Payments Union. 

Mr. BISSELL. I will try to do my best, but I know from experience this is not an easy subject to make clear. 

Mr. Hoffman has testified to this committee on this subject and he put into the record a statement that we had prepared on the matter, which I think has been available to members of the committee. I will repeat some of the reasoning of that paper if I may, and I hope, sir, that you or other members will enter in and interrupt me if I am saying things familiar to the members of the committee that do not need to be covered.

I feel that the easiest way to explain the proposed Payments Union is by reference to its history and especially the earlier payments plans. 

At the beginning of the ERP, European trade among the participating countries of Europe was being strangled by trade restrictions. 

That was not a new phenomenon, even after the war. It was a continuation of a state of affairs that began to develop in the 1930's, and developed increasingly in the prewar years. 

The origin or cause of these trade restrictions, I think, is generally accepted to be the shortage of dollars-more generally the shortage of foreign exchange-and the attempt of each country to conserve its own supplies of foreign exchange and especially to conserve its own supplies of dollars.

When I talk about a shortage of dollars, I think that term is very familiar. When I talk about a shortage of foreign exchange, I mean that for instance as of 2 years ago, France had a dollar deficit but it also had a deficit in its trade with the sterling area. It also was importing more coal from Germany than the value of the goods it was selling to Germany so it had a deficit in its trade from Germany. 

That is typical of a situation in which the country was not only earn-

ing less than it had to pay out in dollars, but found itself in the same position with many of the European currencies as well. 

The dollar shortage was a particularly serious cause of this state of affairs, because typically, any one country which incurred a trade deficit in its trade with another, had to pay for that deficit in gold, which meant, for all practical purposes, in dollars. Therefore, as of 

3 years ago, each European country was apt to regard a trade deficit with any other country as a drain generally upon its resources of foreign exchange, and potentially at least as a drain on its small gold and dollar reserve.

Given that situation, it was a natural reaction that the countries. should attempt to protect themselves by cutting down their imports, in all cases where they were importing more from another country than they were selling to it. Out of that effort there grew up the pattern of bilateral trading within Europe. 

There was and there still is in Europe, a whole structure of bilateral trade and payments agreements; that is, agreements between pairs of countries. As of several years ago, at least those agreements typically would list commodities that the two countries expected to trade with one another. These lists were drawn up to achieve as closely as possible a bilateral balance between the two countries, so that neither would have to settle a deficit by gold payments to the other. Usually, the payments agreement which accompanied the trade agreement specified the dates upon which surpluses and deficits would be settled. and the currencies in which they would be settled. 

Immediately after the war these bilateral agreements almost always provided for some extension of credit by each country to the other, or by the creditor country to the debtor country. But within a year or two, those credit margins were pretty well used up so that they no longer gave any flexibility to the trading under these bilateral trade agreements and, in addition, there was a large structure of short-term indebtedness between countries. 

Given that situation, it seemed to all of us at the beginning of the ERF that a most urgent task was to find ways of freeing trade in Europe or, at least, relaxing these very tight restrictions. 

The first, and administratively the easiest, method employed was simply to permit each European country to use some of its ECA aid to make dollar purchases in other participating countries. In that way, ECA aid could be used by any one participating country, either directly to finance its needed imports from the Western Hemisphere, or it could be used to finance needed imports from other European countries. If, for instance, France had a trade deficit in its trade with Belgium, it could use ECA aid to cover its deficit with Belgium or its deficit with the sterling area-that is, with England-or to buy imports from Germany as well as to buy imports from the United 

States. 

The dollars that were paid out by France in making these offshore purchases within Europe were not, of course, in any sense lost, because if France bought from Belgium or from Germany or from Britain, then the dollars were available to the selling country and could be used by the selling country to cover its own dollar deficit in trade with the United States and Canada. 

This was, I think, a natural device. It was, I believe, envisaged in the original legislation. Indeed there were provisions in the original

1 authorizing legislation of ECA that freed these ECA-financed purchases in Europe from certain of the statutory requirements and regulations imposed on purchases with ECA dollars anywhere except in Europe itself.

That system of offshore buying, however, had certain defects. It did operate, I think, in the early months of the ERP, somewhat to free European trade from restrictions, because it meant that a country which had been compelled to restrict imports now had a new source of funds with which to finance the excess of its imports from other European countries over its exports to them. 

Mr. CHIPERFIELD. Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question?

Chairman KEE. Certainly, Mr. Chiperfield. 

Mr. CHIPERFIELD. If you use ECA funds, say in France to pay off a deficit to Belgium, is that an offshore transaction?

Mr. BISSELL. It is. 

Mr. CHIPERFIELD. Thank you.

Mr. BISSELL. This system of offshore purchases was in Europe. 

However, it did have certain defects. The most serious of these defects was that it meant that a large volume of transactions between commercial buyer and seller was conducted actually in dollars. The seller would invoice in dollars and the buyer would have to make payment in dollars. As soon as it became established that certain transactions were to be in dollars, both governments and private sellers began to insist more and more widely on receiving payment in dollars. 

Our own policy in Germany at that time was to sell all so-called hard goods—that is, steel, coal, and other items in short supply-only for dollars. Certain other commodities-some of them nonferrous metals and many petroleum products-came to be sold even between the participating countries only for dollars. It was apparent, I think to all concerned, that if we continued this system in effect, the number of dollar transactions would spread more and more widely and the problem would begin to be aggravated rather than cured. 

It was at that time and in response to that need that there was evolved the intra-European payments plan, which actually went into effect on the 1st of October 1948; it was modified last July. It remains in effect until superseded or until the end of the current fiscal year.

The purpose of the intra-European payments plan was to accomplish exactly the same result that was already accomplished simply by letting France use ECA dollars to buy in Belgium; but to do it, I admit, in a somewhat more complicated way, but in a way which would avoid the disadvantages I have pointed out. As many members of this committee are well aware, the basic principle of the present payments plan is that the ECA provides a part of the aid that goes to any country which is expected to be a creditor in its trade with any other European country in the form of so-called conditional aid.

For instance, since Belgium is a creditor with most of its European neighbors, it happens that all of our aid this year and most of it last year to Belgium has been conditional aid. For every dollar of conditional aid from the United States to Belgium, Belgium makes a corresponding grant-in-aid to France or Germany or the Netherlands or the United Kingdom, in Belgian francs. 63307-50-pt. 2-17

By granting conditional aid, therefore, to each creditor country, by requiring each creditor country then in turn to extend aid in its own currency to the countries with which that creditor has a trade surplus, by that device, each debtor country is given, in addition to its ECA dollars to be spent here, some Belgian francs or some pounds-sterling or some German marks to finance a trade deficit with Belgium or with Britain or with Germany. The economic result is exactly the same; the mechanics are quite different.
