Mr. BISSELL. I might go on with what I have to say about the present payments plan. I will point out that it is the exact equivalent of what I earlier referred to as offshore purchases. For instance, suppose we had continued with the system of offshore purchases. We would then have to give a country like France or Britain not only the dollar aid to cover its own deficit in trade with the dollar area, but additional dollars to buy Belgian steel or Belgian textiles or German coal, or whatever it might be. Therefore, we would give more aid to the debtor countries than is here shown. 

On the other hand, if France were spending dollars on a large scale in Belgium, and if Britain were spending dollars in Belgium, clearly we would not have had to give any aid at all, as it has turned out, to the Belgians, because the dollars spent there by their European neighbors would have been more than enough to cover their needed dollar outlets. So if we had continued with the system of offshore purchases in Europe, more of the dollars would have gone in the first instance to the debtor countries. Fewer dollars would have gone in the first instance to the creditor countries. The debtor countries would have actually made purchases in the creditor countries with dollars, and that is the way in which the creditor countries would have earned the dollars to supplement their earnings in the Western Hemisphere and any aid they received.

So the picture would look differently. However, I want to emphasize that the economic results would have been just exactly the same.

I think increasingly we have felt, and I believe this has been the feeling in Europe as well, that the time has now come to try to progress beyond the payments plan, which I think has done a great deal to contribute to the revival of trade among the European countries but still has certain rather serious limitations. 

It is contributing to the revival of intra-European trade because it has provided a means of financing trade deficits incurred by each country, with any or all of its neighbors. It has had, I think, two basic defects. First of all, it has tended to perpetuate or has done nothing to break down the bilateralism of trade that I discussed earlier. It is still true that Belgium receives conditional aid, and then Belgium extends that aid in turn in specific amounts to France, to Britain, to the Netherlands, for instance. It is still true under the payments plan that France or Britain or the Netherlands receives a certain amount of dollars in aid tly from us. It receives a certain number of Belgian francs, a certain number of German marks, and a certain number of pounds sterling. 

Therefore, each of these European governments has, as it were, half a dozen different pockets with a different kind of money in each and a fixed amount of money in each. And the extent to which, therefore, a country that wants to buy steel can shop around, between Germany and France and Belgium and England, is very much limited. 

Now, that defect that is inherent in the bilateralism of these arrangements is reinforced by another of the mechanical sort. This payments plan has depended on forward estimates. Wherever those estimates have turned out to be wrong, a country will find that it is running out of, say, German marks, but it has a lot of sterling left. 

Well, that means that for a few months there is every incentive to try to buy in England to use up the sterling and restrict purchases in

Germany because they are short of marks, or whatever country's currency it may be. Clearly, that induces distortions. 

In the first year, by and large, I think the technicians guessed remarkably well, and this problem was not a serious one, but just about a month after they finished making their guesses for this year we had the devaluations of European currencies. They naturally completely altered trading relationships and trading patterns. The result has been that this year's guesses made in advance have turned out to be quite wide of the mark. 

For instance, I quoted France as an example of a debtor country and it was the largest debtor country in Europe in its trade with its other neighbors until last September, until some months before that, actually, but in the 6 or 8 months just passed, France has brought its trade within Europe completely within balance and indeed it now has, on a consolidated basis with all the rest of Europe, a small trading surplus.

Germany was running a large surplus as recently as early last summer in its trade with the rest of Europe and today Germany is by all odds the greatest debtor in Europe.

Britain, up to the devaluation in September, was running a heavy deficit in its trade with the Continent. Within a matter of weeks that was reversed and Britain has been in a surplus position ever since. 

Belgium I have quoted as the largest creditor on current account. 

I use the word "creditor" in this to mean a country currently earning more than it is paying out. It was the largest creditor until the devaluation. The Belgian franc was devalued much less than the others, and today Belgium is just about in balance with the rest of Europe. That means that for instance France holds large drawing rights on a lot of countries in Europe which it finds no use for and it would be most unfortunate if the French had an incentive to go out into the rest of Europe and deliberately build up their imports and buys goods just to use up these drawing rights. 

Similarly, in other trading relationships in Europe, what has happened is that the advance guesses have turned out to be wrong, mainly because of the devaluation. Consequently the bilateralism and the inflexibility of this payments plan are tending to distort trade in Europe instead of giving the maximum encouragement to competition, and the maximum opportunity to the buyer to shop around and buy wherever he wants at the cheapest price and from the best source of supply.

So, to sum up, the great defect in the present payments plan is that it remains bilateral in character and in consequence it has a great many inflexibilities in it, and it does not therefore give as great an encouragement to free competition in Europe as it should. 

The other defect is that although the payments plan-and before that, the system of offshore purchases-has, I think, operated to free European trade, and permits a large gross volume of trade within Europe, there is nothing in either of these earlier plans that tends to cure the disease. That is, there is nothing about them that provides any incentive to creditor countries or to debtor countries, to try to bring their trade into reasonable balance, or close to balance within Europe.

Therefore, what we have felt would be desirable is a different kind of payments arrangement in Europe, which would be completely mul-

1 tilateral in character, and which would begin to apply some pressurepreferably in an automatic manner-to the participating countries, to bring their trade more nearly into balance with one another. 

Now, the proposal for a new payments union is in a sense a modified payments plan, but very drastically different in its machinery and modified so as to accomplish the two results that I have just outlined. 

What is proposed is that there should be, as the name implies, a payments union which will in effect be a European clearinghouse. 

As with a commercial bank clearinghouse, each of the central banks in Europe will be a member of this central clearinghouse, and monthly or quarterly or however often settlement dates may be, each member central bank, like the Bank of France, and the Bank of England, will report the claims it holds, the checks, if you like, that it holds on other banks. Those will then be cleared in the clearinghouse exactly as they are in a clearinghouse among commercial banks in this country. 

As a result of that clearing operation there would be an offsetting of the debits owed by each central bank against the credits, the sums owed to that central bank. When the clearing operation is finished, then each central bank in Europe finds itself either in debt to the clearinghouse by the amount of its trade deficit with all the other participating countries during the preceding month, or else it finds that the clearinghouse owes it an amount of money which represents the payments surplus with the rest of Europe for the preceding month. 

That clearing operation itself, of course, is what is so important in making this a multilateral payments system instead of simply a bilateral payments system.

So the first feature of the proposed new machinery is a clearinghouse operating exactly as any commercial bank clearinghouse does. 

The second feature of the machinery concerns the way in which these debts of the national central banks to the clearinghouse, and of the clearinghouse to the central banks, are settled. What is now proposed is that they should be settled in part by the use of ECA funds; in part by credits advanced by the European countries themselves to one another, and in part by payments in gold. 

Before I go any further I would like to emphasize the purpose of this arrangement: Under the existing payments plan each country has drawing rights in the currencies of other countries which can be used by it to cover any trade deficit that it may incur with those other countries. Therefore, if the present payments plan works ideally, it is not necessary for a debtor country to make any gold or dollar payment whatever to settle any of the trade deficits that occur. Those trade deficits are covered by its drawing rights, and in that sense they are indirectly financed with ECA funds.

One of the specific purposes we have had in mind in the discussions leading to the proposal for a new payments union is that countries should, under certain circumstances, have to pay in part in gold or dollars, precisely so that they will have an incentive to bring their trade more nearly into balance. We propose that the settlements be partly in gold for that purpose.

Secondly, I have said that these settlements should be partly by credits extended by the European countries themselves. For instance, if England should continue to have a surplus in its trade with the Continent, that would show up each month in the clearing house as an 1

.

amount owed by the clearinghouse to the Bank of England after the clearing operation had been conducted, that is, after the debits and credits had been offset against one another. 

Now, what is proposed is that, with England or any other country that is in that manner regularly a creditor, owed money by the clearing house, although it will receive a part of that settlement from the clearing house in gold or dollars, the remaining part of that settlement will be covered by England's simply lending the money to the clearing house. In other words, England will receive a certain amount of gold or dollars and it will also receive an IO U from the clearing house, which it will hold for a long period of time, and which will be an obligation payable only in European currencies and not payable ultimately in gold or dollars.

Now, one of the purposes of that element in the procedure is to supply an incentive to the creditor countries in this system. We do not want to make it too easy for them to earn dollars in Europe. If it is too easy to earn dollars in Europe, these countries will not have the incentive and the pressure to earn dollars outside Europe. 

And, since earning dollars in Europe is merely earning them away from one or the other participating countries with which we are concerned, we obviously do not want to make that too attractive an opportunity.

Also, another reason for bringing this credit element into operations of the Payments Union is that we want to begin to build something now that will have the possibility of lasting beyond the ERP when there is no more ECA aid. And it is our view that by the time the ECA is out of the picture, this kind of a clearing house should be able to operate with the settlements made entirely in gold, plus credits among the European countries themselves, with no third elements corresponding to the conditional aid of the present payments plan.

To sum up, we have the elements of a clearing house. Each country's debits and credits with all the others are offset against one another every month. The clearing house operation leaves each national central bank either owing money to the clearing house if the country has been a debtor for the month in question, or owed money by the clearing house if the country has been a creditor for the month in question.

The settlement of these debts is to be partly in gold as I have said, and partly in credits extended by the creditor countries to the clearing house, and in turn by the clearing house to the debtor countries. 

Now, the third element that I mentioned earlier in these settlements is that they would still be partly covered by ECA funds by something corresponding in economic effect to conditional aid. The way that would operate is as follows: the clearing house itself would, we suppose, have certain dollar resources supplied to it by the ECA. The 

ECA funds supplied to the clearing house would be equivalent in economic effect to the conditional aid that the ECA today provides, for example, to Belgium. The clearing house would then use these dollars in the following fashion: to the extent of some part of the debts owed to the clearing house each month, the debtor would not have to pay the clearing house in gold and his indebtedness to the clearing house would be absorbed by the clearing house. The payment to the creditor, corresponding to that portion of the debtor's obligation,

E would be made by the clearing house out of funds supplied to it directly by the ECA. 

Let me try to sum up this rather complicated arrangement with an example. This example is still much simpler than the reality will turn out to be, I think, but I think it will make clear the way this works.

Supposing the clearing house had only two countries in it, country A and country B. Supposing after the clearing operation in a particular month, country A had been a creditor and country B a debtor to the extent of $10,000,000 each. Then country B would owe the clearing house $10,000,000 and the clearing house would owe country A $10,000,000. The proportions might work out this way: 

B would pay $2,000,000 of the $10,000,000 that it owed the clearing house in gold. For the rest of what it owed the clearing house, it would give the clearing house, in effect, its IOU. The clearing house might pay $5,000,000 of its debt to country A in dollars; $2,000,000 of it would be the dollars B had paid in and $3,000,000 would be paid for from the clearing house's dollar resources provided directly by us. 

Mr. VORYS. In that example you used gold and dollars interchangeably?

Mr. BISSELL. Yes. The balance of $5,000,000 owed by the clearing house to creditor A would simply be covered by the clearing house's IOU to the creditor. In that way, of the whole $10,000,000, $2,000,- 

000 of it will be covered by dollars paid in by B to the clearing house and handed by the clearing house to A; $5,000,000 of it will be B's 

IOU to the clearing house and the clearing house would in effect be endorsing it and giving it as an IOU to A. 

The remaining $3,000,000 of it will be covered by what would be similar in economic effect to the present "conditional aid” dollars put in by the ECA. B, the debtor, in other words, would have had his $10,000,000 trade deficit. He would have had to cover $2,000,000 of it with his own hard money, which is to give the incentive to him and $5,000,000 of it the creditor would have covered with a loan through the clearing house, and the other $3,000,000, in my example, would have been covered in effect as at present, by conditional aid, ECA dollars, which go into the clearing house and then to the creditor, and against which the clearing house can make a grant-in-aid to the debtor.

It is roughly in that fashion that the manner of making settlements between countries would be modified, so that the settlements would be made not just with conditional aid and the corresponding grants from creditors to debtors as at present, but partly in a similar way with funds made available by ECA to the Payments Union, partly with gold out of the debtor's own resources and partly with credit extended by the creditor.

I am sorry for making my explanation even that complicated, but it is hard to cover the whole principle without going into any of that. 

Chairman KEE. May I ask one question there: If the plan as pro posed in this act is put into operation, would that not relieve the necessity of the allocation to Belgium of this amount she used for conditional aid?

Mr. BISSELL. Exactly. A considerable part of Belgium's condi tional aid would not go as at present, direct to Belgium. It would go to the clearing house and would be earned from the clearing house

by Belgium. It is exactly for that reason that it is not proposed that any additional funds should be provided to finance the clearing house. 

The whole budget estimate presented by the ECA is based on, and is sufficient only to cover, the dollar deficits of the individual countries. 

But what we propose to do is to take at least $600,000,000 of the total appropriated to the program for next year, to withhold that from the country aid figures that are before you, to make that available, a part of it as conditional aid on the old pattern, but a part of it to the clearing house in the way that I have described. 

So a country which was as much of a creditor as Belgium has been or, for instance, as Sweden is at the present time, might receive some conditional aid from ECA, but a major part of what this year it received as conditional aid we would hope that next year it would earn as dollars from and throught the Payments Union. 

Mr. VORYS. Now, as I understood it in going over this memorandum that Mr. Dewey prepared, there is a further complication or refinement of the plan, in that it would be contemplated that the ratio of gold or dollars to credit would be very low for the first part of the settlement, or quota, and would increase as the quota was used up. To quote from his memorandum-I do not know whether these are exact figures or just an examplefor the last 25 percent, the deficit country might be required to pay 80 percent in gold while it would receive 20 percent in credit, and for any deficit beyond the quota which had been assigned, the country would pay 100 percent in gold. 

 That is merely illustrative. 

Chairman KEE. Have you read this? 

Mr. BISSELL. I have not read the one that Mr. Dewey prepared, I do not believe. I read one that was prepared by the staff of the watchdog committee.

Chairman KEE. We ordered that printed without endorsing it as being correct. I am a member of that committee.

Mr. VORYS. This is one which Mr. Dewey prepared. I asked him to prepare it after talking with him about it because I understood his talk about it better than I had any that I heard before. I have quoted part of it. It ends up with a statement of the gold and certain dollar assets of these countries, which are more than I had imagined. 

He got them from the International Monetary Fund.

He refers here to the fact that in the proposal involved there should be a governing board of some kind that would not have a veto by each member, so that things could function. Is that part of the plan? 

Mr. BISSELL. That is correct, sir. You have referred to one of the elaborations I did not touch upon; namely, the rising percentage of settlement required to be made in gold as the debtor's deficit becomes larger in relation to its trade. The Board of Managers and its function leads me to the other and final feature that is worthy of mention: 

I have described and have so far discussed an operation which would be almost entirely automatic in its nature. That is to say, there would be quotas determined in advance. They would relate to the total trade of each country. Each country would know, therefore, what schedule of settlements in gold it would be required to make under various circumstances, and in carrying out the entire operation that I have described so far, the clearing house would be performing a strictly automatic function.

Now, it is proposed that in addition to that, the Board of Managers should review the trade position from time to time of all the members, and that if any individual member was running into serious difficulty for instance, if one country was, as Germany is at present, incurring chronic and large trading deficits, and if that country, therefore, appeared likely to be faced in the near future with the necessity of settling perhaps three-quarters of these deficits in gold or dollars, the country might appeal to the Payments Union for special financial assistance to give it time to adopt remedial measures and improve its trade position. If the Board of Managers believed that such special further assistance should be extended to the country in question, it would so recommend, and that would be a recommendation to the ECA very similar to the recommendations that have been made in the past by the OEEC, concerning the allotment of aid directly to the countries.

I would like to say just a word more in explanation of that feature of the Payments Union proposal: One of the serious underlying problems, of course, in securing greater freedom of trade among the European countries and this problem has its counterpart in the world scale—is that these countries in part deliberately and in part accidentally, have not kept in step in their domestic, economic, and financial policies. 

What I mean can be illustrated this way: Today there is about 

10 percent unemployment in Belgium. There is more than that in 

Germany. There is at least that much in Italy. All three countries have been recently in a somewhat deflationary phase. As with other countries that have passed through an inflationary phase, somewhat as in our own country, they have passed over to the stage where they are very definitely buyer's markets. At the same time there is still strong inflationary pressure in Norway and in England and in Denmark.

If trade is made much freer as between, say, Norway and Belgium, if import restrictions are removed, what one would normally expect would be that Norway would promptly develop a large deficit in its trade with Belgium and Belgium would develop a surplus. Similarly, and generally, if trade is free between any two countries, or made free of quantitative restrictions between any two countries, and one is in a deflationary phase and the other in an inflationary phase, there will probably develop between those two countries a large imbalance in their trade which will create a very serious problem and which cannot indefinitely be financed by the country with the import surplus, with the trade deficit, out of its own reserves. 

The whole theory of the Payments Union proposal is, as I have said earlier, that by requiring partial settlement in gold it will reintroduce some automatic pressure upon the member countries to keep their domestic policies reasonably in line with one another. In other words, a major purpose is to put the pressure on the Belgians, let us say, to adopt reinflationary, or reflationary policies; to absorb some of their own unemployment; and to put pressure, if you wish, on the 

Norwegians to cut back somewhat their domestic investment program and try, therefore, to bring down the intensity of inflationary pressure. 

Now, it is recognized that such an automatic incentive will take time to operate. The changes in policies this incentive is designed to induce take time to put into effect and they take time to have effect.

Therefore, it is very likely that situations will occur in which, to continue my example, which is a purely theoretical one, it is perfectly conceivable that the Norwegians would decide that they should cut back their investment program to reduce inflationary pressure in Norway, and that it would take at least 6 months before the effect of such a government decision would begin to be felt. 

During that intervening period it might be desirable, and indeed almost necessary in the interests of trade liberalization within Europe, somehow to provide some accommodations to Norway to help it cover its trade deficit, pending the taking effect of measures of domestic policy that had already been adopted. It is to meet that kind of a situation that it is contemplated that countries should be able to seek special accommodation from the Payments Union. 

The reason for providing that there should be a Board of Managers to examine into such applications is in order to further the development within Europe of an international group of this kind that can begin by its deliberate investigation of conditions in particular countries and its deliberate recomendations to governments, can begin to exercise some deliberate pressure on them to keep in step with one another, and thus to supplement the pressure that we hope would be imposed rather automatically by the necessity of making some payments in gold.

Our belief, in short, is that by setting up such a board of managers, which could act by less than unanimity, and would be able to impose a sanction in that it could also make recommendations to us for the balance of the ERP period, that to create that kind of an institution would be a most important step toward a more permanent liberalizing of trade in Europe and perhaps a more permanent coordination of economic policies among the European countries which would hold together a freely trading European market after the end of ERP. 

Mr. VORYS. In the OEEC report, they discuss this a good bit. They mention,

The credit facilities of the system are not intended to be used to finance structural or exceptional deficits. 

They also say:

It will be an ECA responsibility to allocate ECA dollars in connection with such structural or exceptional deficits. 

Are those words, "structural and exceptional deficits" referring to the kind of instances you described that would be one outside the function of this plan?

Mr. BISSELL. For example, Norway has on order quite a lot of ships that are being built in Sweden and some in Britain. When those ships are delivered, they are, of course, a commodity import for Norway, but obviously they are colossally large commodity imports if the whole payment has to be made in a particular year. Now, it is perfectly foreseeable, therefore, that over the next year Norway is going to have a deficit with certain of its European neighbors, because it is going to have to make payment for newly completed vessels. To try to handle that kind of international payment through the mechanism of the payments union, would place a very grave strain on it and would probably break it down entirely, because Norway's quota will be related to Norway's normal trade with the other countries of Europe. Clearly, therefore, Norway is not going to have a right to

borrow from the credit union enough to finance the purchase of big capital assets like a number of ships from Sweden and from England. 

Therefore, the meaning of the paragraph you have just read is that where such an exceptional payments situation involving one country can be clearly identified in advance, if it were proper for the ECA to concern itself with that exceptional situation, the payment would be handled wholly or partly with conditional aid on the same basis as under the present payments plan.

In other words, if it is a known fact that Norway will have to make certain payments to Sweden and Britain next year in connection with the delivery of ships, presumably we would give some conditional aid directly to Britain and Sweden, and they in turn would give some grants-in-aid to Norway, some drawing rights to Norway, which could then be used by the Norwegians to finance these large nonrecurring exceptional payments. In that way, what the Norwegians will handle through the payments union will have to be only any trade deficit that arises in their normal trade, and not a foreseeable and exceptional trade deficit arising out of either nonrecurring transactions or, in some cases, arising out of a permanent economic relationship. Í should like to reemphasize that I am using Norway only for illustrative purposes. 

Mr. VORYS. To follow this example you have mentioned, I would think if Norway bought a ship or anything that big from Sweden, when we say Norway and Sweden, we mean someone in Norway, a private citizen or a ship company, would buy it from a Swedish company, because in either case you would not have an instance of state trading, would you?

Mr. BISSELL. Precisely. 

Mr. VORYS. If a company bought a ship from Sweden, they would say, "We are going to pay you so much down, and it will take us perhaps a year or two to pay the balance." Is that not the way they trade over there?

Mr. BISSELL. In fact, they have done that. I have oversimplified the example. They are not, in fact, making the full payment on these contracts upon delivery of the vessels. As far as I know, they finance them in various ways. In part, they borrowed dollars in New York privately to finance some of these purchases. In part, they have extended terms of payment.

As far as England is concerned, I think they have raised some of the capital in the London money market so they do not have an international payment. Nevertheless, when due allowance is made for extending financing, they may still have enough payments left so that it might put a rather serious strain on the Norwegian balance of payments with Sweden and England in the next 2 years. I deliberately exaggerated the example to make it clear, but, perhaps, I should amend what I said to say that neither the word "structural" nor "exceptional" are the best words to use. I should perhaps say, where there is a definitely predictable deficit between one country and another, instead of allowing that to be handled entirely through the ordinary operations of the clearinghouse and on a month-to-month basis as a sizable debit position for the Norwegian Central Bank, which would mean that the Norwegian Central Bank would soon have used up its credit facilities and would be making heavy gold payments; instead of allowing that to happen, the intent is to cover that kind of a situa-

tion by conditional aid in the way we have under the old payments plan. So, in my example, Norway would have its normal facilities through the payments union, and to supplement those it would have certain drawing rights, either general on the payments union, or on particular countries, to supplement its other resources and prevent an undue strain on the clearing mechanism and the payments-union mechanism.

Mr. VORYS. How did you arrive at the figure of $600,000,000? 

Mr. BISSELL. Mr. Vorys, that is still a very rough advance guess as to the amount of financing that might be required. Our feeling has been that conditional aid of the kind we have been extending under the old payments plan in connection with these exceptional situations that we have just been talking about, might require $150,000,000 next year. 

As for the automatic operations of the credit union, the provision of ECA aid in the form of dollars made available to the clearinghouse to be earned from the clearinghouse by countries that turn out to be creditors, we feel that that might absorb perhaps $300,000,000 more, and that some additional funds ought to be available for the kind of special accommodation extended upon the recommendation of the clearinghouse to particular countries, as I described a moment ago. 

But these are very rough figures and they are really based on some examination of the size of European trade deficits and surpluses in recent months.

Mr. BISSELL. I think we might very well, Mr. Judd. I think that is a point that is not finally settled. Mr. BISSELL. To this extent, I think we will. I think it will be a condition of entry into the payments union-and this is already proposed in Paris-that there be a further removal of quantitative restrictions on trade, and, let us say by the end of this year, perhaps 6 months after the payments union comes into existence, the remaining quantitative restrictions be made multilateral in character. In other words, country "X," if it maintained a quantitative restriction, instead of specifying the number of tons of steel that could be imported from each of two or three other countries in Europe would simply specify the total tonnage of steel that could be imported without specifying countries. So, I think that the character of existing bilateral arrangements would be drastically altered as a condition of membership but I think certain bilateral arrangements would undoubtedly remain.

Mr. JUDD. To the extent that it succeeds, it tends to make Europe a tighter and more integrated trading area. Will it also, while bringing down the barriers within Europe, tend to erect barriers between it and other trading areas and thereby, in some degree, defeat our Government's basic policy of fuller world trade.

Mr. BISSELL. I will say, sir, that if it did have that effect, it would be defeating other important objectives of United States policy. However, my answer is that I think very emphatically it should not do so, and there is no real reason why it should. 

My feeling is that by breaking down trade barriers within Europe and widening the area of competition, multilateralizing trade in Europe, we very much hope it will at the same time widen and intensify competition in Europe and that that will tend to push costs and prices down, rather than the reverse. 

Mr. JUDD. The greater the trading within the whole area the greater its prosperity, the more it needs raw materials from abroad and the more it is able to produce in industrial products, for example, to sell abroad to get the exchange to buy those materials. 

Mr. BISSELL. I think that is correct. I would utter only this caution. I think that the kind of cost reduction and improvement in efficiency of industries and productivity of labor that comes about by widening the market is a kind that comes about slowly. You do not suddenly convert three or four automobile industries into a single large, mass-production industry overnight by taking down trade barriers. I do not believe that within the next two years, the physical structure will be altered very much by any degree of trade liberalization, but I think the tendency is in that direction. I think the great hope is that if we can free competition to a greater degree in Europe, if we can make it harder for producers to restrict output and hold prices high, that that is going to be a very vital and almost wholly constructive force.

Mr. JUDD. When we say we want to rebuild Europe as a single trading area, we do not mean that that thereby will shut it off from the rest of the world. Our 48 States are one single trading area but the greater the prosperity and economic activity within this trading area, the greater impact it has upon the world at large and the greater attraction it has to the world. 

Mr. BISSELL. I think that is exactly correct, sir.

The argument is sometimes made that by liberalizing trade within Europe, we are defeating our purpose. The argument is that if a 

British manufacturer can sell in France or Italy or Germany or Scandinavia, he has less reason to look for markets in the United States. I think the only thing wrong with that argument is that it proves too much because, if that argument is true, the best way to put Europe on its feet is to stop all trade between European countries and when you turn that argument around, I think it turns out to be nonsense. 

I think it conceals a very important but a well-recognized truth. 

If there is continued excessive demand in Europe-in other words, if domestic financial policies permit too much of a seller's market, too heavy a demand for goods, too much of an inflationary pressure in Europe, and in the trading areas associated with Europe such as the sterling area-that, of course, is going to attract resources into uses in Europe when those resources ought to be going into exports to 

North America to earn Europe's way in the world. That, of course is what has been happening and it is still happening. For instance, in 

India and Pakistan-both countries, but especially India-there is

a highly inflationary situation that is sucking resources out of Britain and to some extent out of other parts of Europe. But it is that phenomenon, in my mind, that carries the danger and the proper way to see to it that European producers do not find too easy a market in the nondollar world and, therefore, are under no pressure to sell in the dollar area, the way to achieve that result is to see to it that the nondollar world is not a chronically inflationary world. So long as inflation is chronic in parts of the sterling area and parts of Europe, then European resources are going to be sucked into uses that are not the best uses either from our standpoint or from the European standpoint.

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Bissell, would the payments plan have anything to do with the unrequited exports, either the service or payment of the sterling debt of $9,000,000,000 or whatever it is? What would be the relationship there?

Mr. BISSELL. I do not believe it will have any particular relationship to that problem, Mr. Vorys. The two are interrelated in a number of ways. For instance, if the sterling area countries like Indian, Pakistan, and others which hold large balances in sterling take advantage of the Payments Union to spend that money on the Continent of Europe, then they will put Britain in a deficit position, even though the United Kingdom itself might be doing perfectly well and might be balancing its trade or running a surplus. That is a real danger, I think, for the British, and that, I think, is one of the problems they have been wrestling with in trying to determine how they could join the Payments Union themselves. Therefore, a partial answer to your question is that since the Payments Union would make sterling, as it were, freely convertible into other European currencies, the Payments Union migh make it possible for the holders of sterling to exercise that sterling as a claim not only upon British resources but also upon continental European resources. 

I feel, myself, that there are ways in which that danger can be guarded against. Obviously, I am afraid the Payments Union makes no contribution to the solution of the problem which the existence of these large sterling balances constitutes. That problem cannot be solved in these terms at all but can only be solved by some way of funding those balances or otherwise preventing their being spent at too rapid a rate. I do not think it in any way aggravates that problem. 

Mr. VORYS. You think there is a way it can be isolated or separated. 

Mr. BISSELL. Exactly. I think there is a way through which the 

European countries can be somewhat isolated from that potentially inflationary demand for goods.

Mr. VORYS. How much of this $1,396,000,000 of food and agriculture products could be obtained from the surplus stocks which we now own or hold? Do you have that there?

Mr. BISSELL. I think I have about the same figures. The total for food and agriculture for 1951?

Mr. VORYS. Yes. As I remember it, the amount that was to come from the United States and the amount of the program are fairly close together; is that right?

Mr. BISSELL. I was just looking at the table on page 245 which is the summary for the 17 countries of this total import program for 1950–51. 

Chairman KEE. Is that in the budget? 

Mr. VORYS. This is in the budget estimate at $1,626,000,000 for those products from the United States and the ECA-financed program, on this other sheet, Mr. Chairman, is $1,396,000,000, so it would look as though part of United States export is to be financed some other way than by ECA expenditures, but that the ECA expenditures for food and agriculture are larger than the amount that is to come from the 

United States. 

Mr. BISSELL. I think I can best answer your question by giving you more detail of what that $1,626,000,000 is made up of: the food item of 706.5 million dollars has, as its largest component, 528.9 million dollars worth of wheat. That wheat, of course, is a surplus commodity.

The next largest component in the foods are fats and oils. I would hate to make a guess at the proportion of that that might come out of surpluses because I am not entirely up to date on exactly which commodities are officially in a surplus status. 

Mr. BURLESON. I understand fats and oils are now in surplus. 

Mr. BISSELL. Generally speaking, they are. 

Chairman KEE. Is there any of it held by the Government, though?

Mr. BURLESON. I think so. 

Mr. BISSELL. On the other hand, I would guess almost none of this would be butter because the Europeans cannot afford to import butter from here. There would be other fats and oils they would be buying for the most part.

The other principal component I can identify in there is dairy products, 20.3 million dollars. I imagine a lot of that is cheese, dried milk, and so forth. Some of those would be surplus. 

Under feed and fertilizer, a total of 191.9 million dollars, 167.7 million dollars is coarse grains and I think they take less corn than other coarse grains.

Finally, coming down to "natural fibers," of a total of 558.3 million dollars for the United States, 525.1 million dollars is cotton. There is very little wool from here, and only a few other natural fibers. Last of all, in the "other agriculture products," 169.5 million dollars, some 

130.9 million dollars is tobacco.

Mr. VORYS. We have plenty of that on hand. 

Chairman KEE. That is incentive. We have been talking about incentive goods for 15 or 16 years. me. 

Mr. BISSELL. I would like to make this one point, if you will allow 

You are aware that these are advance estimates of the needs of these countries, and I think you are well aware of how very strongly we feel that any action which freezes the character of their import program could be exceedingly wasteful. 

For instance, in the current year, we have recently been carefully examining the estimates we made nearly a year ago for the current year, and the estimates that are in this budget estimate for the current fiscal year. They are still estimates because the year is only half

gone and our reporting lags a good deal behind that. However, it is extremely interesting to note the changes that have occurred. The biggest change is a saving through lower prices. The second largest change, however, is a sizable saving, because European crops last summer turned out to be quite a lot better than anyone expected. In fact, no one expected until as late as October how good those crops would be.

The biggest single improvement occurred in European grain crops because it was not as dry a summer as expected. We feared a serious loss of agricultural production through drought, but there was some late rain and it turned out to be the kind of summer that is desirable and especially so for wheat. Root crops did badly but wheat and other grains did well.

I think it would be disastrous if this action were taken which would freeze this program in any way so that it could not be adapted to changes in circumstances of that kind which are just inherently unpredictable within a certain margin.

I would also like to make one other point which I am sure you have heard from us many times, and it is essentially, if you like, a political point: You are aware that this program is constantly misrepresented by the Communists in Europe and elsewhere in the world as a dumping program, a means to get rid of American surpluses and nothing else. I think history clearly demonstrates that that is not the case, but that argument is nevertheless used. It also occurs. in another form in which I have heard it, a disquieting form in Europe literally. There are far too many Europeans for my tastes who believe we will have to continue the ERP after 1952, because they feel we have to get rid of our surpluses. I mean it feeds that kind of an argument if, legislatively, a large element in this program is explicitly a provision to dispose of United States surpluses. We have made administratively, I think, every effort to follow out the obvious intent of the legislation-namely, to purchase surplus commodities in the United States, to the extent to which they are needed by the European countries.

It seems to me that the ECA dollars that are then paid out in this country to buy wheat, fats and oils, and tobacco and similar commodities are just as effective economically even though there has not been an explicit provision in the legislation that made those commodities available in some other way and on some other basis. 

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Bissell, I am well aware of those arguments. They always weighed heavily with me in the past. I think, though, we have to consider political situations and the fiscal situation in the United States, as well as in Europe, and in my judgment, the time is here when there will be a choice between very large cuts in the entire program, or having a large part of the program geared to our surpluses. As far as the Communist argument is concerned, we may

give them an opportunity to say once more, "See, they are unloading some surpluses." That would be true. But insofar as we make this something that is immediately beneficial to our economy, we make it more possible to continue through the third and fourth year. 

That is not just my own view. It is one consideration which those on Capitol Hill who have the total problem to deal with are discussing. 

Mr. BISSELL. I wonder if there would be any use supplying the committee with an estimate we made recently of the extent to which in this past year ECA funds reduced the burden of the agricultural price-support program-I mean the financial burden on the United States Government. I think it is relevant to the point Mr. Vorys brought up.

Chairman KEE. I think it would be very helpful indeed. Also, I believe it would be useful if we could know just what percentage of the funds have come back to America in purchases. What percentage of the commodities have been sent over and what commodities were shipped elsewhere?

Mr. BISSELL. I think that is available in the report to the Public

GENERAL NOTE.-Data on gross debt outstanding were provided by the ECA special missions in the 

ERP countries in cooperation with the respective treasury departments. Only actual debt figures were included; estimates for the current fiscal year have been omitted. The fiscal year for which the debt is presented is shown in column 1. Gross debt outstanding represent debt of the general fund only; debt of governmental enterprises incurred in the name of and serviced directly by enterprises is excluded. Like wise, local government debt is excluded. For the countries, Denmark, Netherlands, and Norway, debt originating from German occupation is included because this debt, although noninterest bearing, is redeemed from surpluses of the Government. The percentage of total debt exclusive of debt owed to the central bank is shown in special footnotes. For Austria and Germany (Federal Republic and 11 Laender) debt owed to the central bank on account of the currency reform is likewise included; debt exclusive of the portion owed to the central bank expressed as percentage of national income is given in footnotes. Foreign debt excludes World War I debt but includes debt owed to international organizations, the latter figure being indicated in footnotes. The conversion of foreign debt into dollars has been performed at the latest official rates for domestic debt and for the portion of foreign debt which is not owed to the United States. For those countries for which a check with the data published by the Department of Commerce, clearing office for foreign transactions, proved that the countries did not revalue their debt after currency devaluation, the United States portion of foreign debt has been converted into dollars at the predevaluation exchange rate. 

Gross national product used for computing the percentages reflect current market prices.

TO AMEND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ACT OF 1948 AS AMENDED TUESDAY, MARCH 14, 1950 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D. O.

The committee met, pursuant to call, at 10:50 a. m., in the Foreign 

Affairs committee room, United States Capitol, Hon. John Kee (chair man) presiding.

We have with us this morning Mr. Henry Reuss, of the Americans for Democratic Action,

Mr. Reuss, if you have a statement you may proceed. 

STATEMENT OF HENRY S. REUSS, MILWAUKEE, WIS., REPRESENT- ING AMERICANS FOR DEMOCRATIC ACTION 

Mr. REUSS. My name is Henry S. Reuss. I am an attorney in Milwaukee, Wis., and I appear here today as the representative of Americans for Democratic Action. I have had some opportunity to observe the Marshall plan in action as deputy general counsel in the office of the special representative in Paris, until my return to this country at the end of 1949. In appearing before your committee, however, I speak only for the Americans for Democratic Action. 

Americans for Democratic Action thoroughly agrees with the testimony of Mr. Hoffman, Mr. Acheson, and others who have appeared before you that the Marshall plan must be continued for its third year. We believe that Congress' action in authorizing the plan, and the execution of the plan by the State Department and by ECA here and abroad, are among the really great achievements of our foreign policy. It is absolutely necessary that Marshall aid be continued according to schedule until 1952, both to keep faith with the people of western Europe, and to afford them a suitable environment for making the necessary changes if they are to erect the economic underpinning for a strong democracy.

I appear here today to make ADA's position on the sort of changes which it believes have to be made in Europe if the Marshall plan is to be, in former Secretary of State Marshall's phrase, "a cure rather than a mere palliative." We agree with Mr. Hoffman's diagnosis that the basic illness of Europe is low productivity. The so-called dollar gap and the low average level of western Europe's living standard-around one-fourth of ours-are in large measure due to western Europe's lagging rate of productivity growth. 521

The principal suggestion by this country to Europe as a "cure" for its low productivity has been the concept of "integration." Gratifying progress has been achieved already. The action of the Marshall-plan countries in reducing their import quotas by 50 percent, and their plans for further reduction of import quotas, a European payments union, and the elimination of double pricing, seem to us definite steps toward European unity. But it is disappointing that the European countries are currently dissipating their energies on two separate intergovernmental organs; the Organization for European Economic 

Cooperation, and the Council of Europe. The OEEC is an organization without much public support, but with a massive job to do. The 

Council of Europe is an organization with tremendous public support, largely because its Consulative Assembly deliberates in public, but without much to do. A merger of the two organizations would get rid of both weaknesses. A public statement that this country would favor such a merger would at least remove any doubts on where we stood. 

While we applaud integration as a method of helping to make Europe more productive, we recognize that merely knitting together a number of ragged economies will not be enough to get Europe off its unproductive dead center. To do this, western Europe, with our help and guidance, must take certain further steps. 

First, the Marshall-plan countries must get rid of the excesses of cartel restrictionism. ADA is not concerned with cartels as cartels. It is concerned, however, with the attitude of European governments which permits or encourages groups of businessmen to combine to keep out new capital investments, to restrict production, to allocate markets, or to prevent price decreases. These restrictions time and again make it impossible for those who want to be productive to get started. 

We have required every Marshall-plan country, as a condition of receiving aid, to sign a bilateral agreement prohibiting these restrictive business practices in international trade. This language is taken verbatim from the draft charter of the International Trade Organization. We recommend that each Marshall-plan country be required, as a condition of further Marshall-plan aid, to take similar steps with respect to restrictive practices in domestic trade-which is where most of the harm is caused today. 

Second, ADA believes that ECA could help increase productivity by the use of a device which it has already used with great success in another connection. In order to stimulate overseas development projects by the colonial powers, ECA has set aside a special fund of $20,000,000 available only for such projects. ECA could similarly withhold from its country-by-country allocation a fund for which countries could qualify by agreeing to channel ECA-financed machinery, equipment, and technical services to recipients in their countries perhaps at cut rates or on long-term low-interest loans in return for a commitment to be productive. Thus, a factory could get new tools or an efficiency engineering survey at reduced cost if it presented a modernization plan worked out by management-labor cooperation. 

Or a farmer could get a long-term loan for machinery or fertilizer by adopting sound farming methods. 

Such productivity plans would provide capital to those who have the will to be productive but lack the capital; it would provide the will to be productive to those who lack the will but have the capital. It would give the free trade-unions and the cooperatives of Europe, as

well as purely private and purely public enterprises, a long-delayed opportunity to participate directly in the Marshall plan. We do not believe that any amendment to the Economic Cooperation Act is necessary in order to channel some portion of Marshall aid as an incentive for increased productivity. We hope that ECA will endeavor to use part of any funds that are given it for this purpose. 

Third, ADA believes that the Marshall plan is missing an important bet in Europe today when it neglects full employment in Europe as an aim of our national policy. If Europe becomes competitive and productive, some businesses are going to go broke, and men are going to become technologically unemployed. For this reason alone, it is important that American policy toward the European worker stands for full employment. It is hard to square our importation of $500,- 

000,000 worth of Marshall-plan goods into Germany in the next fiscal year, for example, at a time when close to 2,000,000-15 percent of the working force are unemployed in Germany. We would like to see the goal of full employment added to the list of the Marshall plan's statutory purposes of high production, liberalized trade, economic stability, and European unification. Once we can tell the world that this is part of our Marshall-plan policy, we can then go to work and get rid of the inexcusable volume of unemployment in Germanyunemployment on which the totalitarian extreme right and extreme left both feed today. With our control over Marshall-plan dollar aid and Marshall-plan counterpart funds, and with our financial relationship to Germany as a member of the Allied High Commission, we can surely restore the flow of investment in western Germany today and make material inroads on unemployment. We cannot guarantee to wipe out unemployment everywhere in the Marshall-plan area. What we can do is to recognize it publicly as an evil and to do everything in our power to help countries deal with it courageously. 

Fourth, we must recognize even more than we have the psychlogical issue that is presented in Europe today by the cold war. Communism gets somewhere in those Marshall plan countries where standards of living are lowest, where jobs are unstable, where the ordinary workingman and peasant has lost hope that he can cross over to the other side of the street in his search for the better things of life. Communism is weakest in those countries which are achieving higher living standards, steady jobs, and hope for the individual that he may better his lot.

For us to work for better social conditions means, of course, that we are interfering with nature and with nations. But we have not hesitated to intervene in the domestic affairs of Europe where we believed that we had a vital interest at stake, as when we took sides in the 1948 Italian elections, or demanded that Marshall plan countries lower their import quotas, or backed Mr. Spaak for Director 

General of the OEEC. With a much slighter degree of intervention, we could have let the people of France know that we favor a return to collective bargaining and a more honest tax system; we could have been sympathetic to the cry of the Italian peasants for land reform; we could have been exceedingly unsympathetic with those Greek shipowners who salt down so many of their dollars in New York rather than turn them over to the Greek Treasury. Many Frenchmen or 

Italians, if asked today for the United States position on a return to collective bargaining or on land reform, would reply that we seemed

opposed to these things. With all our resources of Marshall aid and 

American diplomacy, surely we can dispel any notion that we are on the side of decay. By taking account of these human aspirations, we may surprise ourselves at the number of people who will repair to our standard. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much for your statement.

I noted that you recognized the unemployment situation in Germany. You know ECA has a condition unusual or peculiar to Germany, itself, because of the great infiltration of refugees from the Kussian zone who are crossing over into the western part of Germany. 

It is very difficult to take care of unemployment under conditions of that type.

Mr. REUSS. The refugees in the western zone of Germany have enormously complicated this unemployment problem. However, it is still a problem which must be met. We think that the present numbers of unemployed could be absorbed in Germany today by a more vigorous credit policy on the part of the German Republic, and that our American foreign policy would be advanced by making it clear to the German people and the people in the rest of Europe that that was a primary object of our policy and that we were using all of our resources of the counterpart, all our ability, both in the ECA mission and on the High Commission, to advise and consult with the German Republic, to wipe out to the largest extent possible, the unemployment that exists, recognizing, as you say, that it is a problem aggravated by the refugees.

Chairman KEE. It is very much aggravated. 

Mr. Gordon, have you any question?

Mr. GORDON. No questions. 

Chairman KEE. Have you any questions, Dr. Eaton? 

Mr. EATON. I have one question.

This very brilliant gentleman represents an organization called 

Americans for Democratic Action. Does that have affiliation with the political party of Democrats, or with what?

Mr. REUSS. No; the ADA is a nonpartisan organization that works for liberal political-economic ideals in whatever party it feels that that particular time and place is most suited for it. It includes, incidentally, among its members, great numbers of Republicans as well as Democrats.

Chairman KEE. Even Dr. Eaton would be welcome. 

Mr. REUSS. The invitation is herewith cordially extended. 

Mr. EATON. You approve of the ECA democratic action?

Mr. REUSS. Yes, sir; it seems to me our whole Marshall plan concept as carried out by ECA is a splendid example of democracy in action. 

Mr. EATON. That is a good endorsement from your organization.

Mr. REUSS. I have now left the ECA so I may speak with a little detachment on it. 

Chairman KEE. Is that all, Doctor? 

Mr. EATON. That is all.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Carnahan? 

Mr. CARNAHAN. At the bottom of the first page of your statement you speak of eliminating trade restrictions and you seem to indicate that restrictions in domestic trade are perhaps doing more harm than

restrictions in international trade. Just what domestic trade restrictions were you referring to?

Mr. REUSS. In talking about these trade restrictions, Mr. Carnahan, I am referring solely to restrictions by private producers and distributors. I am not talking about the governmental trade restrictions, the tariff walls, the import quotas, and the exchange controls, which are being so vigorously pursued now by ECA in its trade liberalization program. I am talking, in short, about the cartels, and the point made is that the international cartel today in Europe is more of a future threat than an actuality. The domestic cartel, however that is the group of producers or distributors within each of the participating countries which tends to control production and prices that is the force which is in our opinion impairing productivity to such a large extent. 

Mr. CARNAHAN. That is all. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Smith, have you any questions?

Mr. SMITH. Do I understand your position to be that any further aid we might give should be geared to conditions precedent? 

Mr. REUSS. Not quite that, sir. I think that the question of cartels and restrictions by private producers and distributors is very like the question of governmental trade barriers. On that point, Mr. 

Hoffman has recently testified before this committee, I believe that he thinks ECA can do more good if it is left flexible. That is today, if there are no ironclad conditions imposed, but if he, as ECA Administrator, is given discretion to do as much as he can. I think the same logic applies to this field of private restrictions on trade. In other words, I think it is important that Mr. Hoffman and the other 

ECA Administrators, take very determined steps to get the countries of Europe to pass legislation which prohibits these excesses of cartel activity. I do not think, however, that it would be useful to impose an ironclad condition, any more than it would be useful in the case of international trade barriers.

Mr. SMITH. For a long time on this committee we discussed the matter as to whether or not there should be conditions attached to the advancing of funds for the rehabilitation of Europe, and each time, when those suggestions are made, we are met with the answer that we ought not to interfere with the domestic economy of those countries. 

In other words, we ought to give them this money in the hope-perhaps a fond one-that they will work out their own salvation. 

Now, if I understand the temper of the American people today, they are becoming more and more convinced that the time has come for us to say we will help if you will do thus and so. 

Now we will help if you will immediately start a program to eliminate cartelism, as you have referred to it here.

As far as I am concerned, we have seen no evidence on the part of 

ECA Administrators that they are willing to do that sort of thing.

Mr. REUSS. Part of the purpose of this testimony, sir, is to express the view of our organization, that ECA Administrators should be more outspoken and aggressive on this question of cartels. I think, however, that the matter is best handled if it is left on a flexible basis. 

If the opinion of this committee is expressed, perhaps in the committee report, rather than an ironclad requirement of so much action by April 1, and so much action by May 1, simply because events frequently move too fast to fit into that kind of a calendar.

Mr. SMITH. We have been saying that very thing, Mr. Reuss, in our report, but today we have reached the point, have we not, in Europe, where nationalism is growing, where these countries' economies have been established and they are able to produce on a better basis and as a matter of fact have reached a point beyond the prewar economy, and yet we find they are striving more for self-containment and nationalism is apparently growing. 

Yet we apparently are not coming up with the answer as to how we can combat that situation, because that will not lead to the integration of the economics of that part of the world, nor political unity, as I see it.

Mr. REUSS. I feel, sir, as one who has been there in the past year, that Europe has made very sincere and definite strides forward in this field of integration, in trade liberalization. Lowering their import quotas by 15 percent seems to me a very massive step. What is suggested here, of course, is that more is needed of them and they ought to do more about their domestic cartel situation, too. 

Mr. SMITH. That is all, thank you.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Burleson- 

Mr. BURLESON. I have no questions, Mr. Chairman; thank you.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Javits- 

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Reuss, let me thank you for bringing your message here to the committee. It is of advantage to get the point of view of organizations which have no particular ax to grind although you say very clearly and we all know the ADA expresses what I know its officers and members like to consider as a liberal American point of view.

Now, I see you speak of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation and the Council of Europe, and recommend a merger. I would like to call your attention to the fact that there is strong sentiment in this committee for writing into the ECA act not only that Europe shall have economic integration as advocated by Mr. Hoffman but that Europe shall also have political integration. 

Many members of this committee look to a federation of Europe as a solution to Europe's problems. 

I ask you first how ADA feels about that, if you can quote themperhaps you cannot-and second whether you do not feel that the OEEC, being devoted primarily to economic cooperation, couldn't possibly replace the Council of Europe unless you did have a reorganization establishing the latter affirmatively as both an economic and political organism for cooperation. 

Mr. REUSS. If I may answer your second question first, sir, the intention of such a merger would be to merge the narrower into the broader and to have a strong Council of Europe, which included the economic functions of OEEC within its jurisdiction. Our thought there is that that would build up the Council of Europe by giving it a very potent agenda, and that it would replace one of the weaknesses of the OEEC, namely, the lack of a group which operates in debates and criticizes and suggests in public. 

ADA certainly shares the feeling of this committee as you have described it, that our national policy is best served by having in Europe the strongest kind of an organization for combined political and economic action.

Mr. JAVITS. I did not mean to describe that as the sentiment of the committee as a committee; I meant to describe it as a feeling prevalent among a great many members. We do not know yet what the committee thinks until we begin to write the bill. 

I am proposing myself to offer an amendment to this bill which will provide for the creation of a committee or a commission on post- European recovery program policy, very much analogous to the Harriman committee, which was a great factor in bringing about the ECA. 

My purpose in doing it is twofold: first to signalize the fact that we do propose ECA will end in 1952 and I do not believe silence or inaction will make that as crystal clear as it should be, and, second, that we do intend to continue, however, our participation in economic cooperation with western Europe in a way which we choose but that we are not unmindful of the need for studying the whole question and coming up with some answer, knowing that 1952 is not going to solve the problem but that we are determined to end this ECA program in 1952. 

Now, if you feel that ADA has any view on that, I would appreciate hearing it.

Mr. REUSS. My own view certainly is just as it is important that we continue the Marshall plan for its 4-year span, it is also important that we end the Marshall plan in the traditional Marshall plan sense, then. I think it is also highly important that we start thinking right now about these questions like the dollar gap, which will assuredly be still with us in 1952, the question of the general upbuilding in Europe of social conditions which are the basis of sound democracy. 

I feel sure that I speak also for ADA in endorsing the general principle of indicating to all the world that after 1952 there is going to be a different approach, an approach differing from the Marshall plan, and secondly, that it is a problem which does take some action and some thought now. 

Mr. JAVITS. I note what you say about German cartels. We have been informed by authoritative witnesses that that is imbedded in European thinking and that that is one of the great difficulties in the way of European recovery.

Do you feel by making it a condition precedent to ECA aid that we can help in rooting it out of European thinking? It is not so much countering bad people engaged in creating trusts as we conceive it in this country as it is there in dealing with a very firmly rooted idea in the minds of businessmen that that is the way to do business. 

Mr. REUSS. It is certainly true that to the European businessman the cartel is the normal way of life. It is also true that many of the free trade-unions of Europe, far from being trust busters, tend to feel that unrestrained competition might merely bring unemployment and bring a return of the dole and the bread line. 

It is also true that the Socialist parties of many of the countries of western Europe, far from being antimonopoly, tend to think that perhaps cartels are all right as a method of rationalizing industry. 

Mr. JAVITS. But you and ADA feel we must be antimonopoly in our ECA policy?

Mr. REUSS. I would add this thought about Europe, that despite that rather gloomy picture I painted of mass feeling in those countries, there is in almost every country in western Europe an identifi- 63307-50-pt. 2-19

able group of people who see the deadly effect on productivity of cartel thinking and cartel practices and are prepared to do something about it.

People like John Monet in France, people like Alben Johansson who is head of the cooperatives in Sweden, people in all these countries, if they can be identified and encouraged, are prepared to do something about cartels-perhaps not in the Sherman Act image but some legislation analogous to what the International Trade Organization draft charter does in the field of international cartels. 

I think it is important enough so that we should try to encourage those elements.

Mr. JAVITS. Most of these things you have suggested are administrative in character and you yourself have said they take no amendment to the law.

May I ask if ADA intends to lay these ideas before the ECA and the Secretary of State as its recommendations, as well as before us, because we do not administer-they do. 

Mr. REUSS. ADA does, I believe, intend to lay these positions before the administrative people as well as before the Congress. However, there are devices such as the statement of policy at the beginning of the statute. There are devices such as committee reports by which a committee of Congress, or Congress as a whole, may make its will felt on the Administration without in any way tying the Administration to an inflexible method of administration. 

Mr. JAVITS. May I say we will be helped if you submit the text of what you recommend we might write into the law. 

Mr. REUSS. We will be very glad to do that.

MEMORANDUM JAMES LOEB, Jr., Executive Secretary. 

MARCH 14, 1950.

To: James Loeb, Jr. 

From: Henry S. Reuss. 

Subject: Proposed amendments to Economic Cooperation Act (H. R. 7378). 

1. The goals brought out in my testimony this morning (March 14) before the 

House Foreign Affairs Committee may, in my opinion, best be incorporated in the Economic Cooperation Act, as amended, by amending section 102 (b) of the act so that it reads (portions added are italicized):

"PURPOSES OF TITLE 

"(b) It is the purpose of this title to effectuate the policy set forth in subsection (a) of this section by furnishing material and financial assistance to the participating countries in such a manner as to aid them, through their own individual and concerted efforts, to become independent of extraordinary outside economic assistance within the period of operations under this title. byetc. "(1) promoting industrial and agricultural production, increased productivity, freedom from restrictive business practices, and full employment, in the participating countries ;" 

2. The goal of "increased productivity" is not mentioned in the present act, although it is the main chance for helping to close the dollar gap and for raising western Europe's living standards. "Freedom from restrictive business practices" would give the Administrator a legislative basis for vigorous action to induce the participating countries to end the worst excesses of the domestic cartels. The words "full employment" are the avowed goal of each of the participating countries, as set forth in the Convention of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, signed at Paris, April 16, 1948, but have not hitherto been made an object of Marshal-plan policy. 

3. It is felt that stating these goals in generalized fashion will give the Administrator the necessary legislative mandate without depriving him of the flexibility needed to obtain the best results. 

4. From the viewpoint of the ERP nations themselves, it would be highly important to have these objectives written into the legislation authorizing the European recovery program. 

5. Any oher matters suggested in my testimony which might appeal to the committee, such as the suggestion for the merger of the Council of Europe and the OEEC, can, in my opinion, be better treated in a committee report than by inclusion in the legislation itself. 

Chairman KEE. Are there any further questions any member of this committee wishes to propound to this witness? 

If not, we thank you very much for your statement Mr. Reuss. 

We have today Miss Anna Lord Strauss, president, League of

Women Voters of the United States. 

Miss Strauss, you may proceed.

STATEMENT OF MISS ANNA LORD STRAUSS, PRESIDENT, LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF THE UNITED STATES Miss STRAUSS. I am the national president of the League of Women 

Voters.

The League of Women Voters of the United States is here today to support H. R. 7378 and urge continuation of the European recovery program. This is the third time that a representative of the league has appeared before this committee on the subject of European recovery. In 1948 the league spoke in favor of initiating a 4-year program. At that time there was urgent need for setting up machinery and for continuing the vital flow of goods to keep the European economy from collapse. In 1949 the league pointed to the first year's record of ERP as evidence that the program was off to a good start, and that it was being well administered. At that time, emphasis was on recovery—getting production up to prewar standards. Today the different problems that have come to the fore are a measure of the progress that has already been made. For not until these first hurdles were cleared could the program move on to the stage that it has now reached, where the need is for basic readjustments in the European economy to meet the changed conditions of the postwar world.

We think it important to look back at the situation 1 and 2 years ago in order to make a fair appraisal of the record of European recovery to date. In our opinion, the progress of the European countries has been substantial and gratifying, in raising production to well above prewar levels, in achieving greater financial stability, in improving their balance of payments positions, and in strengthening representative governments. The program at the halfway mark is well along the road toward achieving its goals. We consider the record sound justification for its continuation. The next 2 years will be more difficult than the first, both for the Europeans and for the United States. The toughest part of the job still remains to be done. 

The European nations must make painful adjustments to solve the trade problems that are now uppermost; they must integrate their individual economies if they are to be able to pay their own way once again in the world market. Integration will involve drastic lowering of trade barriers, coordination of national policies, and the development of new economic patterns which best meet the needs of the whole area. The European nations must also make basic changes in their industry and agriculture so that they will be more productive than they were before the war. 

In all of these tasks the United States can be of great help. The 

Economic Cooperation Administration proposes earmarking a good part of next year's appropriation to create a European Payments Union, a major step toward reestablishing multilateral trade in Europe. ERP funds can be used as an incentive for faster progress toward integration. Our technical assistance, already under way through ERP, can make an important contribution to increased productivity. Perhaps most important of all will be the role which the 

United States, as the world's leading creditor nation, plays in trade and investment; for unless the United States enables other nations to earn the means to pay their way, the European recovery program cannot succeed.

Because the problems ahead are in themselves more difficult and harder to understand than those of the past 2 years, we fear that there might be a dangerous letting down on the part of the American public in their support for ERP. Yet the coming 2 years are crucial, and continued United States support is essential if we are to realize returns on our initial investment. In the more than 720 communities where there are Leagues of Women Voters, we are working to help spread an understanding of these problems and the stake of the 

United States in their solution.

If I may, I should like to add my personal conviction, based on experience this summer in making a trip around the world with Town Meeting of the Air. From this vantage point, the wisdom of the 

United States in proposing and carrying out the European recovery program was strikingly clear. Its psychological value has been tremendous; it has brought the European nations hope and courage. It has shown them, as a practical possibility, the goal of once more standing on their own feet. It has brought them the needed help, for, with the best of effort, they cannot solve their problems entirely by their own endeavors. It has given them incentives to reach for higher standards. Most of all, the European recovery program has told the Europeans in unmistakable language that the United States

stands with them in the common task of building a sound economic basis for peace, our best insurance against another war. 

For these reasons, I am here today to testify in behalf of H. R. 7378.
