Mr. James Finucane, associate secretary, National Council for the 

Prevention of War. 

STATEMENT OF JAMES FINUCANE, ASSOCIATE SECRETARY, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION FOR THE PREVENTION OF WAR 

Mr. FINUCANE. You have had many witnesses before you, men whose intentions are beyond question and whose information and capabilities are extraordinary. But they have taken their broad directive from 

Congress, and to a large extent they have been reporting on how they have fulfilled your instructions. They have not questioned the general direction of the plan. That, in part, we would like to do. 

It is a pretty sure thing that the Marshall plan funds will be authorized in the requested or smaller amounts for the next 2 years. Our testimony then will bear not on the amount but on how to use what is provided toward ending the cold war with Russia and the stale war with Germany. It is our belief that doing these two things over the next 2 years would be the best way to maximize production in Europe and bring about a closer approach to peace. 

Ending the cold war is worth billions.

Ending the cold war-we will submit specific ways to do it in a minute will promote recovery by freeing investors from fear. This

I will permit and encourage the dropping of intra-European trade barriers, which are in part now "justified" by the drive for national self-sufficiency, in a war-threatened world. 

Ending the cold war will reduce defense taxes in the United States and Europe, releasing that much more of our and their national energies for raising productive capacities and the level of living. 

Ending the military drain on United States and European taxpayers will leave more money in the pockets of American buyers to spend on products from abroad and will reduce the cost of producing these commodities in Europe. Reducing these military taxes will lower 

United States prices also, bringing the United States commodities within range of European consumers for fewer dollars. 

Ending the cold war and making the ECA a straight, nonpolitical grant would reduce some of the current misinterpretations of the ECA in Europe, which views ECA as the purchase price for European participation in America's predicted hot war against Russia. 

How can this cold war be ended?

First, the United States must lift the commercial iron curtain it has dropped between western Europe and the East. The weight of this iron curtain, which is the American "blacklist," includes thousands of items forbidden to be exported. The New York Times of 

March 9, reported the addition of 600 more items to the blacklist. 

The Department of Commerce yesterday or the day before, reported that the existence of this blacklist stopped the exportation of $160,- 000,000 worth of potential war goods to eastern European countries and to Russia. That $160,000,000 just applies to the United States and does not begin to portray the amount covered by the effects of this blacklist on the Marshall plan countries. 

This blacklist is a purely military device to forbid strategic materials going to what is viewed as a potential enemy. The idea is it will prevent the industrial development of the eastern world. 

How well has it worked?

The Russians developed atomic energy 2 years earlier than anybody predicted they would.

Instead of preventing technical development in the banned countries, it has increased their self-sufficiency on the one hand, and on the other hand where self-sufficiency is not possible, it tends to force them to integrate their economies with the Russian economy. Viewed clearly from a military point of view, the blacklist tends to put the affected countries on a war-footing on the side of Russia. It detaches them from the west.

Economically, eastern Europe is an easily accessible source of supply for western Europe where the terms of trade are favorable to western Europe. Unrestricted trade with eastern Europe will give western 

Europe a supply and selling area, which would encourage the complete East-West area to develop trade equality with the United States, and end its imbalance of payments. 

If integration is desirable in the west, it is desirable toward the east, and for the same reason. The wider the area of trade, the greater the division of labor, the greater the efficiency of production, and the higher the level of living. 

To accomplish the freeing of east-west trade we would propose an amendment striking out a subsection, section 117 (d). I believe that is called the Mundt amendment.

This and a number of other things can be done through this act. 

But, rather than deal with them in generalities, it might be well to pick up the problems of a specific country, the key production country of Europe, Germany. Here we are now conducting the last pointless stages of a stale war against a Hitler who has been dead for 5 years. Germany will be a good example, because it is the economic powerhouse of Europe, until too recently kept an economic poorhouse. 

Germany would profit immediately from a revival of east-west trade. The eastern countries, now forced to be the economic satellites of Russia, would once more resume their close integration with Europe, of which Germany is normally the principal continental trader. 

The blacklist perpetuates a dependent Germany. 

Before the war German trade with the eastern and southeastern countries amounted to 15 percent of German exports and, roughly, 15 percent of German imports. In 1949 that trade had been throttled down to 4 percent of a much smaller total export-import trade. 

Before the war Germany received food and timber valued at $245,- 000,000 a year from the areas of its own country amputated by 

Potsdam. 

I think this committee ought to resent this map that is on the wall down here because it accedes, by the way it is drawn, to the permanent 

Polish occupation of a large area of Germany. One-fifth of Germany is buried in Poland there without even the recognition of a line being drawn around it.

Before the war Germany had a net gold balance of $45,000,000 a year with Russia.

This is now zero because of the blacklist. 

Some of these trade-cramping bans have even been extended to the eastern half of Germany itself. Western Germany, for example, is forbidden to ship steel to eastern Germany. Not counting this internal ban, the present backlist policy with regard to eastern countries, imposed by the United States, is estimated to cost Germany a total loss of $540,000,000 a year. 

This is a little bit more than we are proposing to give Germany under the Marshall plan this coming year. 

This might go a long way to explain the 2,000,000 unemployed in the western Federal Republic. 

Removing senseless and useless ceilings.

But the blacklist in the east and the failure of integration in the west are not the only things preventing Germany from playing its full and necessary part in European recovery.

Germany's industry, badly bombed and partially dismantled, still labors under arbitrary Allied restrictions. Although these restrictions are nominally for "security" purposes, many thoughtful observers believe them to be disguised competitive measures. For example, the "security" restrictions will not permit the Germans to build any ship bigger or faster than our outmoded Liberty ships. The news-papers report that we have 1,500 of these slow, stodgy craft tied up in our harbors because they are uneconomic to operate. Germany cannot sail competitively in ships 50 years behind the times. 

A dispatch in the New York Times of February 28, 1950, estimates the Germans could save $100,000,000 a year by using their own ships. 

Germany has a synthetic-petroleum industry which has been saved at the last minute from the dismantlers' blow torches. But under the existing prohibitions and limitations, it is not allowed to operate.

What good is it to save these plants and leave them there as monuments to our restrictionists folly? 

The philosophy in tearing down the plants in part was that when they would be moved to another country they would be put up and used for European recovery, but at the present time they are just keeping some where they are and are not tearing them down and are not using them.

Germany has a cramped ceiling on steel production. This means that owners of present capacity have a monopoly. No new or additional capacity can be created to challenge their dominance or lower their prices. Does it help European recovery to create this monopoly and freeze prices in a basic commodity? Currently the steel restriction is being enforced by dismantling at gun point, while starving 

German workers riot.

A lot of people in Congress assume the dismantling question has been settled by a rather generous concession on the part of the western 

Allies. Actually on December 6 the Department of Commerce adver tised here that it had 138 German plants in process of being dismantled and which it would offer for sale to buyers. This has aroused a lot of resentment in Germany against the Allied powers. I have here a clipping which quotes the bishop of Berlin, a recent protest made about this dismantling. With the chairman's permission I would like to put it in the record.

GERMAN BISHOP ASKS PRAYERS ON DISMANTLING OF PLANTS FRANKFURT, GERMANY, March 8 (NC).-Bishop Josef Machens of Hildesheim has appealed to the faithful to offer special prayers for the prevention of the dismantling of the huge industrial plants at Watenstedt-Salzgitter, which has been decreed by the Allied authorities despite widespread protests of the German population.

Nearly half of the population of that town, the bishop says, will be on the dole as a consequence of this measure, which unavoidably will lead to an increase of radical tendencies.

In that particular plant, in addition to tearing out the equipment they have also been tearing down the buildings and destroying the water supply. They are not only destroying a steel plant but they are making it impossible to reconstruct any peaceful industry there. 

The prohibitions and limitations strangle the machine-tool industry on which much of Europe has customarily relied for its productive equipment. Machine tools have long been a German specialty. The integration of Europe, which our Government is warmly sponsoring, implies a high degree of specialization and trading among countries. 

If specialization in machine tools is ended, and every country is encouraged to set up its own self-sufficient tool industry, you not only have uneconomic, high-cost duplication of facilities, but you also tend to defeat integration.

We have been informed by the people in the State Department and in the Department of the Army who are and have been handling this, that this could mean the ending of mass production of anything in 

Germany on the following grounds:

If they want to put out a new model of anything, for instance, a car, which they can market competitively, they have to retool. Under this prohibition or limitation on the tool industry they have to go to the Allied security officials and get permission to build a lathe or get permission to build some kind of cutting machine. Each item has to

be approved in advance and if there is a possibility that the item for which approval is sought could be used to manufacture wheels for an artillery carriage or something like that, they cannot make it. 

It was never intended that these prohibitions and limitations on industry be imposed permanently. In fact the occupation statute, which applies the prohibitions and limitations, is theoretically scheduled for review in May of this year. However, if the situation is not recognized for the costly one it is, and if inter-Allied officials are not given the proper nudge, this expensive anachronism might continue indefinitely. We suggest the following amendment to lift these restrictions: 

The addition of a paragraph, section 115 (b) (11), stipulating that participating countries remove any prohibition or limitation imposed jointly or singly on the industry of another participating country or area.

If the idea is to take restrictions off production in Europe, Germany is the first place to start. They have ceilings which prevent initiative and investment of new capital and they are hemmed in on the East by the black list.

STOPPING THE SAAR "GRAB" 

The illegal, de facto amputation of eastern Germany and the Saar from Germany could continue Germany's economic dependency on the United States indefinitely. They are normally among the most industrious and prosperous sections of Germany.

An amendment to express congressional opposition to these territorial changes could read like this:

The addition of a subsection, section 115 (h), which will state it as the understanding of Congress that any postwar territorial acquisition made by one of the participating countries at the expense of another shall not be considered permanent, unless or until it is agreed upon in a peace treaty. 

A precedent for this type of amendment was the understanding, inserted in the basic ECA Act of 1948, to help the German prisoners of war.

It resulted in speeding their release from western Allied captivity. 

If you will recall, it said approximately, "It is an understanding that all prisoners of war will be released by the end of 1948," and they were.

Because we and the other Potsdam powers agreed to the expulsion of all persons of German ancestry from eastern Europe into Germany, there is now a population density approaching 500 persons per square mile in Germany, as compared with a typical 13 per square mile in the United States. The expellees' presence goes a long way toward explaining the unemployment figure of 2,000,000. Unemployment is highest in Schleswig-Holstein and Bavaria, the states in which the expellees are concentrated.

To employ these people, an inflow of new American capital should be encouraged. You know at the present time it is not. 

Something should be done about making the investment guarantee clause of the ECA Act available for the development of German industry.

Emigration will help further. This can be encouraged by putting the expellees within the care and concern of the International Refugee

Organization, starting the wheels rolling through the following amendment to the Economic Cooperation Act: 

The insertion, in section 115 (e), of a clause instructing the ECA Administrator to encourage the modification of the International Refugee Organization constitution to bring the 12,000,000 expellees in Germany within the care and concern of that organization, from which they are now excluded.

The section alluded to there is one which directs the Administrator to cooperate with the IRO to arrange population transfers in Europe. 

This would broaden it to provide for this largest group of homeless persons. 

Providing spiritual Marshall aid.

Part of the failure to achieve the economic integration of Europe. is attributable to the failure of cultural and spiritual integration. 

Each country feels that it must be self-sufficient and not dependent on "strangers" in case of war. A vast exchange of students between participating countries would help overcome these fears, promote understanding and the will to get along. 

We are informed that the ECA Administrator feels now that there is no legislative bar to the use of counterpart funds for student exchange. We also understand that he favors it in principle. However, nothing has been done. A specific suggestion in this bill might help get things moving.

Mr. Foster, who is Mr. Hoffman's right-hand man, has issued a written statement saying he endorses the idea and he says nothing in the existing law would prevent the counterpart funds from being used for that purpose. A small amount, something like 2 percent, could provide a capital fund or endowment of several hundred million dollars which could be used for student loans and which would remain in Europe after the end of the Marshall plan as a permanent monument to our interest in their getting along together. The idea has also been approved by Clarence Pickett, of the American Friends Service Committee, and by the officials of the American Council on Education. 

We would propose:

The insertion, in section 115 (b) (6), of a clause specifically endorsing the use of counterpart funds for the international exchange and housing of students and other educational personnel. 

Germany should be reunited.

In asking you to devote the remaining ECA billions to terminating the cold war and the stale war, we are in reality dealing with two aspects of the same problem. It is the fear between Russia and the west which has led to the splitting of Germany and it is the quarreling over the halves of Germany that is largely responsible for keeping the cold war going.

Therefore, although it seems to be beyond the scope of any particular amendment to the ECA Act, we would like to suggest at this point that this committee, in its broader considerations of European policy, insist upon a reunification of Germany. 

The Germans in our zone held elections last year and set up the western republic. The Germans in the eastern zone are scheduled to hold elections October 15 of this year to ratify an eastern republic. 

Mr. John J. McCloy has made an excellent suggestion to prevent this from developing into an irremediable division, by holding Ger-

many-wide elections before the east-zone elections come this fall. We hope this committee will support his suggestion. 

We believe that improving the ECA Act as suggested in the foregoing amendments will help create a climate in which German recovery and east-west reconciliation will be more nearly achievable. 

It would create a climate in which we would stand an excellent chance of getting a dollar's worth of peace with every dollar's worth of recovery.

STATEMENT OF JOHN C. LYNN, REPRESENTING THE AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

Mr. LYNN. Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee, it is a pleasure for me to appear before this committee to express to you the views of the American Farm Bureau Federation regarding the European recovery program. The 1,409,000 farm families who are members have indicated clearly that the organization will continue to support programs designed to aid world recovery and to increase the prospects of lasting peace.

At the thirty-first annual convention of the American Farm Bureau Federation, held in December 1949, the following resolution was adopted:

The American Farm Bureau Federation has vigorously supported foreignaid programs designed to bring about world reconstruction and recovery. Our support of the foreign-aid program is founded on the principle that it must be a recovery program. We pledge our continued support of programs designed to attain these objectives.

The progress toward recovery made by western Europe under the Economic Cooperation Administration program is encouraging. We believe that the ECA program has reached a new phase which requires more emphasis on self-help projects in the participating countries and a development of closer cooperation between these countries. We believe that aid under this program should be limited to those countries willing to adopt programs designed to accomplish this end. Unless progress is made toward the elimination of trade barriers, convertibility of currencies, and a far-reaching increase of interchange of goods in western Europe, lasting recovery cannot be accomplished.

It must be recognized that European recovery is primarily a European matter. 

Money and materials from America can help can shorten the time required for real progress. The people of the United States are willing, and we believe are able, to make great contributions of goods, food, and technical assistance for this purpose. We seek only assurance that they are actually being used to promote prosperity and to increase the prospects of peace. 

Large amounts of local currency are accumulating in countries participating in foreign-aid programs in the form of counterpart funds. We urge that more study be given to the use of these counterpart funds on projects designed to contribute most to recovery so that these countries may continue their progress at the expiration of United States assistance. 

To the extent that our surpluses can contribute to recovery, they should be used. However, the United States should not use this program, or any program, to force surpluses on participating nations at the expense of other items which would contribute more to recovery. 

I might say, Mr. Chairman, that this statement I just read, the quote from the resolutions pertains to over-all aid programs and the remainder of this statement is confined to the aspects of the ECA. 

After 2 years of operation of the European recovery program, Congress and the American people are better able to judge its effectiveness. The program has been successful in the rehabilitation of the economy of western Europe from the low levels existing at the end of World War II. We believe that the communistic movement which was so prevalent in western Europe at the end of the war and in the immediate postwar years, has been checked. We believe the continuation of the ECA program in western Europe on a reduced scale, as has been recommended by the Administrator of the ECA, is essential to the continued development and recovery of western Europe. 

Farmers, as well as all other segments of our economy, have a great interest in the real recovery of Europe. For agriculture it constitutes the principal export market. Unless this program succeeds in attaining a sound, lasting recovery, the American farmers will suffer heavy losses in their export outlets at the termination of our dollar aid. 

We would like to take this opportunity to emphasize the following specific points: 

1. It is the stated policy of the United States, as expressed by Mr. 

Hoffman, Administrator of the ECA program, that free trade among the participating countries is essential to lasting recovery. We do not believe that the countries in western Europe have exerted their full effort toward the elimination of trade barriers and exchange controls. We recommend, therefore, that aid under this program be limited to those countries which earnestly attack and find a solution to these and other obstacles to increasing trade within western Europe. 

We believe that the proposed European payments union will be of great assistance in stimulating trade within western Europe. This agency should promote multilateral trade, which is very desirable if trade is to be promoted on a sound basis. We recommend that in the establishment of the European payments union, or clearinghouse, that the participating countries be required to deposit out of their free dollars, or gold assets, an amount equal to any contribution made by the United States. During the next 2 years the United States portion should be decreased and the European amounts increased so as to make the agency self-financing at the termination of ECA assistance. 

2. The most recent report of the Office of European Economic Cooperation Food and Agriculture Committee regarding future plans

! for agricultural production programs in ECA countries indicates increased efforts toward "self-sufficiency" as contrasted with "selfsupport." The report indicates that the objective is to reduce food and fiber imports from the dollar areas by $1,250,000,000 by 1952. 

We favor such increased production of agricultural commodities in western Europe, and throughout the world, as is consistent with the most efficient use of resources. However, we recommend that every effort be taken to insure that these programs be guided toward efficiency in agricultural production and that our assistance not be directed toward the encouragement of uneconomic production of crops that can be produced more efficiently in other parts of the world. 

We want to preserve the opportunity to develop sound trade programs with the farmers of these countries on the basis of the comparative advantage which each has in the production of many commodities. 

3. We feel that the countries participating in the ECA program have not made sufficient effort to stimulate exports into the dollar areas. There appears to be very little incentive for exporters to go to the expense and trouble to sell in the dollar areas. Since the dollars earned by private exporters are controlled by their respective governments, the individual has little or no control over the dollars earned. 

We recommend, therefore, that an effective plan be developed by the participating countries whereby an exporter who earns dollars may use a portion of these dollar earnings to stimulate further exports, establish foreign sales offices, and develop other promotion programs to increase trade with the dollar areas. 

4. We believe that the wise use of counterpart funds will play an important part in the recovery program. Further study by all parties concerned, and more guidance by ECA in directing the use of counterpart funds, is essential.

We believe that counterpart funds should be used primarily for the development of programs that will contribute substantially to lasting recovery. We recommend greater use of counterpart funds for the development of such programs as extension-type education for farmers, reclamation projects, development of tourist facilities, sales-promotion campaigns, and other projects designed to aid maximum recovery within the respective country, including the stimulation and expansion of trade on a sound and permanent basis. 

I would like to emphasize again the point made in our testimony last year "that the greatest underdeveloped 'crop' in Europe is her boys and girls." In the establishment of the extension-service programs in western Europe, we recommend that increased emphasis be given to youth programs similar to our 4-H Clubs and Future Farmer activities. În these young people is vested the future of western Europe, and if we can instill in them true democratic principles, we will have added greatly to the prospects of permanent peace. 

The people of the United States have made many sacrifices in order to assist countries throughout the world toward economic recovery. 

Our one great hope has been that by so doing, free democratic nations could contribute their share toward world recovery and peace. 

The American Farm Bureau Federation believes that the people of the United States are able and willing to continue their efforts toward the accomplishment of the objectives of the European recovery program. We seek only assurance that our goods, food, financial help,

and technical assistance are actually being used in ways which will best promote recovery and most significantly increase the prospectsfor world peace. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much. You have made quite an informative statement.

STATEMENT OF J. T. SANDERS, LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL, OF THE NATIONAL GRANGE 

Mr. SANDERS. Mr. Chairman, I have a statement here of which I have some typewritten copies. I will be glad to let you have such as I have here.

The primary interest of the National Grange in ECA, you would surmise, is that of the influence of ECA on farming and farm people, both in Europe and in the United States. The Grange is primarily interested in ECA as a means of promoting the general welfare and not primarily for promoting the interest of agriculture or any other group.

We trust that we have let the interest of the general betterment of mankind dominate in our judgments and actions concerning ECA, and we believe in general the interest of American farm organizations has been motivated by general welfare rather than the direct benefits of ECA on farm markets. Occasions have arisen in the past years with the American farm organizations where exports of grain with ECA funds could be made either from this country or Canada. If shipped from this country they would have helped to reduce threatening surpluses; but rigid commitments of Canada to Great Britain indicated the general welfare would be served best to let the wheat continue to be shipped from Canada; and the American farm organizations took a stand in favor of continued Canadian shipment. These facts are cited to indicate that the farm organizations are taking the long-time viewpoint of ECA influence.

The National Grange has passed resolutions each year warmly and wholeheartedly supporting ECA. We continue to give it support because, primarily, it appears to us to be the best means of helping humanity toward freedom and liberty, toward a more dependable and

satisfying material life, and secondarily, it appears to be the soundest, most economical means of saving our own democracy and living standards from the disaster of another world-wide military conflict with the evil forces of communistic aggressors. Our belief in ECA stems from the conviction that until Europe can produce enough wealth to sustain itself through production and trade, there will be trouble and threats of war. 

We said at the beginning that our primary interest is in the influence of ECA on our agriculture and on the farming of Europe. We believe our judgments on this phase of ECA can contribute most to the committee's problem of coming to a sound decision on ECA. We, therefore, do not intend to repeat to you detail figures which have already been given your committee on the surprisingly favorable accomplishment of ECA.

In general, we will say that we are well pleased with the accomplishments of ECA. After World War I, it took from 7 to 12 years for industrial production to completely recover its prewar productivity. Two years of ECA has accomplished as much as 5 or 6 years' efforts after World War I. Industrial production stands a fifth higher than it did prewar. The promising part of this is that this great increase since 1947 has taken place with very little increase in number of workers; that is, because of increased productivity per man. Almost the entire labor force of Europe is at work, working hard and interrupted with far less major strikes than have occurred here in the United States. In short, Europe is carrying out admirably its part of the bargain and is doing what the National Grange said in its first appearance should be a rigid conditional requirement, that the countries should put forth a maximum effort to help themselves. 

We do not want that statement to be misunderstood. We do not want to leave the impression that Europe is carrying out in every way possible the promoting of its own welfare and helping itself. 

The weakest portion of the ECA program is the failure of ECA countries to remove numerous kinds of barriers to a free flow of commerce between the several countries. 

It may, at first glance, appear strange for a farm organization to place greatest emphasis on rehabilitation of industry in Europe, notwithstanding the fact that agriculture was greatly ravished by the war. But that was our original stand on ECA-namely, that major emphasis should be placed on industrial rehabilitation and recovery. 

We still believe major emphasis should be placed on industrial and commercial recovery.

Our primary reason for asking for major aid to European industry is that industrial damage and mislocation is the primary cause of the economic woes of Europe and that when these difficulties are corrected, European agriculture because of its inherent recuperative powers will recover of itself along with industrial recovery. 

The damages of World War II to Europe were mainly that of agricultural devastation in eastern Europe and industrial devastation in western Europe. Fortunately, for the success of the European recovery program, agricultural recovery in eastern Europe and sound trade between the East and the West probably would normally tend to keep apace with recovery of western industries. If this has not been the case it is due to the obstruction of the iron curtain; and not due

to the lack of economic soundness of the general theory that major emphasis should be placed on revival of the industrial resources of eastern Europe. In other words, western industrial recovery is and will probably continue to be the limiting economic factor in a sound East-West commercial relation which is so necessary for the peace and prosperity of all Europe. It is believed that a sound recovery of this trade relation will greatly strengthen the forces of democracy and weaken the hold of communism in both eastern and western Europe. 

Before the war the western European cooperating areas had only 2.4 times as many people, yet produced 6.5 times as much industrial products, as did the so-called iron curtain eastern European countries-excluding European Russia. The Russian satellites in eastern Europe are predominantly agricultural producing areas. Over 

60 percent of all people in them are dependent on agriculture, compared with only 25 percent in the cooperating western European areas. 

Obviously, the agricultural part of the European production balance was to a considerable extent, and is still, east of the iron curtain; and the industrial part is west of it. Peace must be built in the long run around a sound return of this position of economic balance between theagriculture of eastern and the industrial resources of western Europe. 

Output of agriculture, so to speak, is stable by nature-tends to be stable in war or in peace, in prosperity or depression, from one year to the next. This is due to the fact that farmers operate with high fixed costs. In contrast, output in industry is highly sensitive to war or peace, to depression or prosperity, since its fixed costs usually run as low as 25 percent of its total costs. European industry is no exception. Add to this that industry is far more vulnerable to devastation of modern war than is agriculture. We believe European agriculture will rapidly recover following the lead of recovery of industry.

We want to emphasize that the steady powerful pressure of a fully recovered western European industrial capacity, under democratic regimes, and an inevitable recovery of eastern European agricultural production, will be an unremitting pressure against communism. No other force short of a shooting war can compare with the power of this tremendous East-West complementary economic relation for breaking down the iron curtain. It must be nurtured with the greatest of care. ECA is ideal as an agency for planned pressure for the maximum development of this desired commercial relationship. 

We would like to endorse the proposal of Mr. Hoffman to set aside a liberal amount of the proposed ECA funds to set up the proposed European Exchange Union. Since industrial production stands now around 20 percent above prewar and since this is an actual per capita production above prewar, problems of distribution now loom far greater than technical production problems. 

The introduction of greater flexibility in European payments is much needed and implies the introduction of some degree of greater flexibility in the use of ECA aid. If ECA wishes to change the present predetermined and frozen pattern of trade in Europe by introducing principles of competition and flexibility, it will need to be able to make its financing of European trade at least as flexible as the system it hopes to create. Once European trade is allowed free rein, ECA will no longer have a fixed pattern of balances requiring its financing

as the basis for a fixed pattern of distribution of its aid to European creditors. ECA will have to be able to shift its aid rapidly and to make it available in a form which can provide the basis for European credits some time before the final beneficiary of the dollar is known. 

We therefore consider ECA's proposal to set aside a certain portion of its aid in the form of free dollars to be a logical and necessary step toward the introduction of competition in Europe. As we understand the situation, the present requirements of ECA's law would make it extremely difficult if not impossible to shift dollar aid as rapidly as the pattern of trade in Europe would change once competition is introduced. Furthermore, the present type of aid could not be passed through any new central institution such as would be necessary to organize a move back to competitive principles in European trade. 

The problem of balanced distribution of this industrial output involves three distinct problems, it seems to us. One is the problem of a sound reestablishment of the East-West European trade discussed previously. A second problem, of course, deals with an ultimate balance of imports from and exports to the dollar area, principally the United States; and the third problem, of distribution, is that of inducing a far greater freedom of trade inside Europe between the ECA recipients. We would like to discuss briefly our views on these last two problems of distribution—especially the agricultural implications of them.

Figures indicate as might be expected, that grain, potato, and sugar production has more fully recovered in ECA countries than has production of livestock and livestock products. The National Grange believes that sound economics requires that greater emphasis be placed on recovery of production of livestock and livestock products than on further expansion of bread grains, potatoes, and sugar beets. Upgrading the diets of Europe, which is still sorely needed, will come in the main through expanded consumption of livestock products, fresh vegetables, and fruits. The lands of Europe that can best be employed in grass production are far greater than those best suited to breadgrain and root-crop production. European farmers cannot compete successfully on an expanded bread-grain area with the wheat farmers of the United States, Canada, Australia, and the Argentine. Therefore, sound economic considerations dictate that ECA should do its utmost to discourage further expansion of wheat, potato, and sugar production in ECA countries and encourage a more full use of the preeminently superior grazing and forage lands of Europe. Sound land utilization, improved diets, and permanently sound commercial relations of Europe, all impel us to use the resources of ECA to bring about this sounder balance of farming in Europe. 

To bring this about there must be a greater use of the fruit, oil, nut, and other subtropical lands bordering the Mediterranean Sea and a much expanded and less obstructed trade between these areas and colder ECA lands in northern Europe. Fortunately, the basic industries in these two parts of Europe are complementary in the main. 

ECA funds must be used to bring about maximum results in developing this greater freedom and greater amount of exchange between ECĂ countries. The proposed European Exchange Union heavily financed with dollar resources can be a far more persuasive means to bring this about than any other possible means. We strongly urge a full support of this request of the ECA Administrator.

With regard to the problem of the export-import gap with the dollar area, if we here look at this problem constructively we will realize that it is not a detrimental force but one that can clearly bring economic betterment to us as well as Europe. The ECA estimates that the needed increase of imports of European goods will probably amount to around a billion dollars, if we expand tourist travel to Europe and sound investment of American private capital in ECA countries. It seems. rather absurd that we would let a billion dollars of increased import be a detriment to us rather than a blessing. This is much less than 1 percent of our total national output. 

Some adjustment downward in our export of grain to ECA countries probably should occur. It is doubtful if exports of tobacco and cotton will or should be greatly reduced. If the Mediterranean areas develop their fruit, nut, and fresh vegetable production as they should, possibly exports of American fruit and specialty crops will need to be lower than prewar.

We believe that major sources for expanded imports from Europe must come largely from industrial products. Undoubtedly sound expansion in this respect will injure acutely some American industries. 

We probably should face such acute injury cases with specific assistance toward making their adjustment as harmless as possible both to the invested capital and the labor involved. 

In closing, we would like to express to you our high regard for the type of administration that has characterized the conduct of ECA in this splendid demonstration of the power of a militant democracy. We believe that the good that has been accomplished by this great demonstration of our faith in democracy cannot be estimated. 

In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to emphasize that we are a strong believer in the proposal Congressman Javits made with regard to a special commission to study the transitional problems of moving from ECA to a post-ECA type of program. We believe that it is very necessary that provisions of that kind be made immediately. 

Chairman KEE. It is understood, of course, that ECA assistance is going to definitely end in 1952, but some of the members of the committee and many of the Members of Congress have come to the conclusions that some aid must be continued after ECA ends. Where that aid is coming from and how it is to be given has not been determined. I believe Mr. Javits' proposal is that Congress appoint a commission to go into the matter and endeavor to find out and report just what aid will be needed and to what extent some aid, a similar amount or a larger amount, will be needed after 1952. 

Mr. SANDERS. Certainly it seems to us such a commission should study very carefully what should be the organized or united effort. of the peace-loving countries to develop a sounder economic and a more permanent relationship among themselves. We feel it is very crucial that such a study be started at the earliest possible moment. 

Chairman KEE. I take it we all would like to feel assured that there will be no more aid needed after 1952, but as matters now stand it would appear that some aid will have to come after 1952. It will not be ECA aid because ECA aid is going to end. That has practically been announced all over Europe.

STATEMENT OF ROBERT EMMET RODES, COMMANDER, MOROCCO POST, NO. 1, AMERICAN LEGION, NEW YORK, N. Y. 

Mr. RODES. I represent the American Trade Association of Morocco, of which I am president, and the Morocco Post of the American Legion, of which I am commander. These Americans went to Morocco with the idea of carrying out independent trade and development that would have been analogous to the development phases of the Point IV program except that no public funds or guaranties were asked. 

This seemed entirely logical because United States treaties with Morocco assure unrestricted two-way trade between the two countries. 

Last spring I told this committee that these Americans were being put out of business by an illegal campaign against them. Of the 37 

I then represented, 10 have closed up. The others are almost inactive. 

Administrative action which was promised on their behalf has not been taken. Moreover, a year's experience has proved that the regulations which destroyed their businessss are not obtaining any of the objectives claimed for them. 

Demaree Bess, in the Saturday Evening Post of last June 18, attributes conditions in Morocco to policies adopted by the ECA. He says that ECA "has suddenly thrown a monkey wrench" into the situation by transferring official recognition to French authority in Morocco and "is actively helping the French to consolidate their control.' وو 

Comment in the British New Statesman and Nation of November 19 

is similar. The writer states: 

In Casablanca I found that most of the Marshall-aid money allotted for the area is being diverted to French settlers and businessmen, while Moroccans receive what is left over. Moroccan trade is controlled entirely by France, though both American and British firms are struggling hard for a share in the market. The Americans are on firmer ground, since the United States never abandoned its treaty rights with the Sultan of Morocco, whereas Chamberlain surrendered Britain's shortly before the last war. 

He seems unaware that our Secretary of State was preparing to follow Chamberlain's lead.

It is not necessary for me to prove anti-American acts by the French protectorate authorities. Assistant Secretary of State Ernest Gross recapitulates them in a statement found on page 10975 of the Congressional Record for August 4, 1949, as follows:

FAILURE TO ALLOCATE TO AMERICANS A REASONABLE AMOUNT OF DOLLAR EXCHANGE 

The employment of delaying tactics in granting import licenses for goods which Americans needed for the maintenance of enterprises they were operating- I just got a letter this morning in which one of the boys over there told me he has been trying for 6 months to get spare parts for two busses he is running and cannot get them because of delaying tacticsthe assessment of customs duties on the basis of arbitrary valuations of imports: the assessment of consumption taxes * * and other matters such as the failure to install telephones, furnish adequate gasoline rations, etc.

He might have added illegal seizure of United States veterans' United States flags, preventing their appearance during a celebration of the anniversary of American landings in Morocco. 

Senator George and Senator Wiley took our problems up with the Secretary of State and other State Department officials. Their intervention led to a conference on March 24, 1949, in which Department officials promised to remedy the situation and to obtain reimbursement of moneys illegally collected by French officials, before considering further concessions in Morocco (exhibit A). The Department later explained that "heavy French pressure" made this action impossible. 

I realize that this committee's schedule will not permit detailed examination of all the abuses, so I would like to give one example. 

This is the matter of "consumption taxes." Morocco is committed by treaty to 122 percent customs duty. She illegally supplemented this by port taxes on weights of several products, for example, lubricants and tires, imported largely from the United States, while charging only legal duty on products imported principally from France, for example, jewelry and furs. The United States naturally protested and 

French diplomats agreed they were right. Our consulate told us we were "in no way required to pay these taxes." They were collected. anyway. Our Minister told me that he had arranged for their reimbursement. This was not effected. The Department of State told me that it would require reimbursement before even negotiating with Moroccan officials. This is clear in the file here labeled "B." However, final negotiations concluded by the Department of State not only did not recover these payments but provide for their continued collection. 

Here is a letter on other illegal taxes and duties permitted by the 

Secretary of State (exhibit C).

The principal treaty between us and Morocco, signed in 1836 (8 Stat. 

484) states:

Article XVII: 

and (United States merchants) may buy and sell all sorts of merchandise but such as are prohibited to the other Christian nations. 

Article XXIV: 

Whatever indulgence, in trade or otherwise, shall be granted to any of the Christian powers, the citizens of the United States shall be equally entitled to them.

I know that public statement has been made that those treaties are hard to interpret. Mr. Chairman, I do not think anyone reading that would think they are hard to interpret. 

In treaties of 1880 (22 Stat. 817) and 1906 (34 Stat. 2905) Morocco, with France's cosignature, reaffirmed the 1836 treaty in addition to granting us standard most-favored-nation status. The 1906 treaty

also assured the "open door" and fixed Moroccan customs rates and procedures.

Americans who established businesses in Morocco knew the foregoing and relied on it. In closest cooperation with the majority of French citizens and all Moorish business interests, we pressed for resumption of normal trade which had been suspended as a wartime measure to prevent trading with the enemy. Almost unrestricted. imports were resumed in Morocco in March of 1948. This free competition, with demand as the only criterion of what was imported, decreased dollar imports and lowered most prices. In other words, when you had competition you had 33to 40-percent decrease in prices and that meant that your dollar volume of imports was less. This was resented by interests who under wartime controls had derived assured profits from the protection of the licensing system, no matter how uneconomical their purchases were. Those were the cartels that were mentioned by witnesses in this chair a few minutes ago. During 

1948 independent Americans sold about one-third of Morocco's United 

States imports.

On December 30, 1948, the French Finance Director of Morocco announced a decree restricting all United States imports and embargoing most of those that Americans were selling. He explained publicly: 

I have always considered the competition of foreign merchants with French merchants very vexing. It is to remedy this that these imports have been suppressed.

The Governor General explained that this action was forced by Paris; that he realized it was against the unanimous wish of Morocco's elected assembly; that he had protested but had been overruled. The decree caused a storm of complaint from everyone except the official favorites who were to monopolize business again. 

Chairman KEE. That is the Governor General of Morocco. 

Mr. RODES. Yes, sir.

Chairman KEE. He is an officer appointed by the French Government?

Mr. RODES. He is appointed by the French Government as their representative to the Sultan. He is an administrative officer in the service of the Sultan. He is an honest soldier. Incidentally, he is the general who was offered command of all French forces under Montgomery under the initial post-hostilities Allied set-up and refused, stating among other reasons that Montgomery's job should have been given to an American. This is from a fairly accurate source. 

Since the restrictions set aside the treaty-guaranteed "open door" and gave a favored position to the French Union and even to Communist countries that have bilateral trade agreements with France, Americans formally protested them as treaty violations. The Department of State agreed with this position but said it was nonetheless sympathetic to the curbs and would consider them favorably after all American grievances in Morocco had been remedied. 

Meanwhile, treaty or no, the Department was unable to prevent Morocco from enforcing the embargo during the first 5 months of 1949. It was lifted on May 23. Then, although the previously stated conditions were not met, the Department gave its formal consent to the restrictions on June 10, 1949, for a temporary period during which

French treatment of Americans was to be observed and "negotiations" were to continue.

On September 27, 1949, the Department held a public hearing at which it was demonstrated that Moroccan officials had broken all their agreements and that the abuses against Americans were worse than ever; also, that the restrictions had increased Morocco's dollar deficit and that the only effect had been to channelize business through French concerns, the objectives stated by the Finance Minister. In spite of this the Department prolonged its temporary assent to the embargoes. 

This hearing was largely due to concern expressed by Members of the Senate that Department action in Morocco was unjust. Letters announcing it were sent to all who had expressed an interest (like the one to Senator Smith marked "Exhibit E"). These stated: 

United States consent * ** * will be given (or withheld) after taking into consideration the comment elicited by the meeting.

In spite of this the Chairman, Willard Thorp, when he opened the meeting, made it as clear as two paragraphs of pure Federalese can that acceptance of the decree in some form was a foregone conclusion. (See his memo marked "Exhibit F.")

The final decision was reached after a ruling that most of the issues raised includingthat Americans have been subject to discrimination in the administration of import controls- was "beyond the indicated scope of the meeting." (See excerpt from a letter to Senator Chavez, marked "Exhibit G.")

Action preceding this consent is indicative of the attitude of the State Department's economic personnel toward American businessmen. Negotiations were going on which would mean the survival or end of our entire postwar efforts and our French friends were warning us that we were being "sold out." The Department, however, beyond admitting that "heavy French pressure" would prevent it from obtaining the remedies it had promised, refused us all detailed information, stating that its negotiations always were confidential. This meant that its proposed action was being subjected to the practical analysis and comment of foreign businessmen while American businessman had no chance of rebuttal.

When Senator George was good enough to try to find out what was going on, Mr. Gross wrote him on June 1:

Efforts to reach agreement with the French on the more urgent problems are being actively pressed. It is not possible, however, to say when such an agreement will be reached.

The agreement which would wipe out our businesses was reached on 

June 4 and promulgated on June 10.

On June 11 the Department wrote me a letter, stating that negotiations were still under way and ending: 

Assent to the decree, if given, would be predicated on terms considered satisfactory by this Department and other interested agencies of the Government (exhibit CA).

Although the Department's reorganization should have placed decision in this matter under the Africa and Near East Division, it was retained by Mr. Willard Thorp. It was influenced principally by persons whose jobs depend on controlled economy. The most active

of these held the title, "Advisor for State trading." As representative of the only American organizations in Morocco, I was constantly in contact with the State Department, and with Mr. Thomas Wilson, Chief of the Areas Division of the Department of Commerce, who had visited Morocco and had advised against the State Department's action. Without my knowledge or Mr. Wilson's, an employee of the 

Department of Commerce was selected and sent to Morocco to "negotiate." His "negotiations" gave the French everything they wantedfar more than they expected. I met him only after his return and he informed me he had no instructions about treaty rights in Morocco. 

When the public hearing was called on September 27, Willard Thorp gave the 10 business representatives present copies of an eightpage agreement, told us to spend 15 minutes reading it and to give him our comments. The document had been in the Department's possession for 3 weeks.

On December 31, 1949, the Department gave its final assent, for an indefinite period, to the restrictions and embargoes. 

The reason given at times is that the restrictions have improved Morocco's dollar position and channelized its dollars into useful products. An alternate reason given is that if consent is withheld, I am quoting Mr. Willard Thorp—

There is no assurance that such regulations will not be enforced nonetheless, as was the case earlier this year. (From affidavit of Assistant Secretary Thorp dated October 4, 1949.)

In other words, his theory seemed to be, they are going to do what they please anyway in spite of the aid we are giving them and we might as well be graceful and let them do it rather than have them do it over our protest.

The second reason is certainly more valid. The first is untenable for four reasons: 

1. Morocco's United States trade deficit shrank under free competition and rose under the restrictions. Department of Commerce figures are: 1947. 1948. 1949. 

United States exports to Morocco 

United States imports from Morocco $36, 100, 000 $2,600,000 

28, 200, 000 6,700,000 

30, 600, 000 5,800,000 2. The regulations finally accepted permit soft-drink ingredients, radios, cigars and cigarettes, and so forth, but still exclude commercial refrigeration, cotton textiles, used clothing, and motor trucks and other primary necessities formerly sold by Americans. 

There is no doubt that when one looks at the two lists of products which were excluded and the products that may be imported, the only thing which governs is who makes the profit. 

3. The final arrangement also accepts many treaty violations having no connection with trade balances or exchange. These include: local 

French assessment of customs replacing that of the international commission required by treaties; recognition of an illegal transport monopoly; "consumption taxes" (that means Moroccans pay about 30

percent more for sugar than a Frenchman pays in Paris although the legal import duties are less); agreement that Americans must meet 

French cartel rules in order to receive ECA and other official exchange; and other terms precluded by treaties. 

4. The Department of State has tried but is powerless to prevent restrictions on exports of Moroccan products to the United States. 

Many products that would build up Moroccan dollar balance are arbitrarily forced into France and many even go to the iron-curtain nations.

These all indicate that our surrender was prompted by fear of "heavy French pressure," not by economic reasons.

This problem goes far beyond Morocco. The Secretary of State claims: 

"Assent by the Secretary of State is a matter of diplomatic as well as national concern. Consent may be granted upon the basis, inter alia, of what the President and the State Department believe will most facilitate accords with other countries as well as our own national well being. The factual foundation of the Secretary's action will frequently not be public or susceptible to judicial review." He is talking there of setting aside a treaty which several other Secretaries of State said they had no right to set aside. 

Safety of American property and endeavor abroad no longer depends on the terms of treaties which the Senate has approved. Ultimate disposal need not even be wholly consistent with our "national concern" or "national well-being" if, in the Secretary's opinion, these are outweighed by "diplomatic concern" or by plans which "will most facilitate accords with other nations." 

This attitude is all the more disturbing in view of the fact that Secretaries Knox and Lansing both had found that the treaty rights in question could not be set aside without Senate approval (exhibit H).

Neither the taties, the constitution, nor the Secretary's oath of office have altered since that time. 

Furthermore, our action in Morocco has been a set-back to the free economy to which the country is committed. It has extended exploitation, monopolies, and absentee ownership, often with United States funds. It has given a new lease on life to the cartels that came into power under Vichy and would have disappeared by now except for our aid. The attached letter to Representative Petersen shows how a 

French lead monopoly is being established with ECA funds while independent Americans are prevented from competing by an illegal export prohibition (exhibit I).

A French war veteran, a state councilor who got the highest popular vote in Morocco on a straight anti-Communist ticket, says: "We must get rid of these French restrictions." A respected French pioneer writes: "Abuses and blunders like these made the Thirteen American Colonies cast off the yoke of England." The French Chamber of Commerce in Casablanca insists that our Ambassador Culbertson promised "full economic liberty" in 1944. The president of the Moorish Chamber of Commerce says: "We should return to the open door."

In spite of all this, regimentation has increased, and those who are fighting it blame ECA for their defeat.

After a year of trying, I am convinced that we will get no help from either the Department of State or ECA and that the latter's money in

France will remain under the solid control of the people who have fought every move toward normal commerce in Morocco. I hope, however, that this committee will act to restore competition through the reestablishment of our treaties. 

Two amendments to the current ECA Act would do this without hampering the program: 

1. This is essentially a statement of policy. "Treaties between the 

United States and nations assisted hereunder or their dependencies will remain in full force unless renegotiated and ratified by the Senate." 

This will prevent the Secretary of State from succumbing to "pressure" to set treaties aside. 

2. "None of the local currencies required by section 115 (b) (6) of the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948, as amended, to be deposited in local currency accounts, shall be made available for expenditure by any recipient country so long as any dependent area of such a country fails to comply with any treaty between the United States and the said dependent area."

Chairman KEE. Those are the two suggested amendments you are offering the committee?

Mr. RODES. That is correct, sir. They will remedy the situation described by Mr. Thorp, that "there is no assurance that the regulations will not be enforced nonetheless, as was the case earlier this year. 

If you do this, Morocco will become a show place with private American capital and know-how taking a leading part. You will have development of a backward area, practical exchange rates, normal twoway trade. You will acquire strategic materials such as lead and manganese.

You will have a proving ground where our goods and products can be compared unequivocally with those of our future world competitors. 

Above all, you will have a reclaimed area of free economy that will be a shining example in Europe's quagmire of regimentation.

Chairman KEE. Have you there all that you want included in the record? 

Mr. RODES. Yes, sir. These are all supporting documents.

Chairman KEE. We will look them over and we certainly will have no objections to including those essential to your statement. 

Mr. RODES. You will find in many cases excerpts will do. In many cases I include the whole statement so you will see it is not out of context.

Chairman KEE. You have marked the excerpts there. 

Mr. RODES. Yes, sir. 

Chairman KEE. Have you any questions, Mr. Gordon?

Mr. GORDON. No questions. 

Chairman KEE. Have you any, Mr. Carnahan?

Mr. CARNAHAN. I have no questions. 

Chairman KEE. We thank you very much, Mr. Rodes, for your presence here. 

Mr. RODES. Thank you very much, sir.

NOTE-The above cable to the American Trade Association of Morocco was read over the telephone to Edward Martin, Acting Chief, Commercial Policy Division, Department of State, who stated that it coincided with his understanding of the action approved at the conference. 

The honorable the SECRETARY OF STATE,  

MARCH 25, 1949. 

MY DEAR MR. SECRETARY: In a conference yesterday with members of your staff concerned with the Moroccan situation I repeated that Americans in Morocco are unalterably opposed to any arrangement to accept the Moroccan Protectorate's decree of December 30, 1948, restricting imports. I suggested that the Resident General of Morocco be informed that, whatever the Department's original intentions had been, it could not act favorably because of the illegal and discriminatory acts against Americans that have come to light during your consideration of the matter; of the anti-American official statements made when the decree was promulgated; and of the illegal application of the decree to Americans, without your Department's consent. I asked that this be accompanied with a demand that all illegal or discriminatory acts against Americans cease; that officials consistently guilty of them or of public anti-American utterances be removed, and that custom duties and taxes paid in excess of legal rates be reimbursed.

After further discussion it was proposed that the Department instruct the chargé d'affaires at Tangier to inform General Juin that we would agree to consider, without commitment to accept, the decree in question on condition that Americans participate in official business fairly; that all discriminatory and illegal acts cease; that duties and taxes collected in excess of legal amounts be reimbursed; that final judgment would be after a trial period had proved that the conditions had been met, not on any promise or engagement of the protectorate. 

I repeated my views on acceptance but stated that if the trial period is for 1 year, if consistently anti-American personnel are removed, and if United States Foreign Service officers are final judges in all matters of equal treatment, this formula might be acceptable. 

Mr. Martin indicated that the trial period might be less than 1 year, and that consideration would be given to removal of anti-American officials. Mr. 

Vernon stated that the designation of our consular officials as sole judges would be asking for considerably more than we are allowed at the present time. I explained that all action on economic affairs in Morocco is based on our having accepted wartime exchange controls; since this was with the proviso that the acceptance could be withdrawn at any time, we may insist on any condition that pleases us in refraining to withdraw this acceptance.

As you will see from the above, the two positions are not nearly so divergent as they were during the first discussions with State Department personnel. The admission by all concerned that there is a definite anti-American policy in Morocco and that this policy has caused many illegal, discriminatory, and unfair acts against Americans is extremely gratifying. 

It is suggested that instead of linking acceptance of the decree with the insistence on adjustment of our complaints, the failure to make these adjustments be pointed out and that remedial action be required and observed over a long period. If this action proves satisfactory, the matter of acceptance of the decree then might be considered but Foreign Service field personnel would not be informed of this intent.

There are three reasons: One is that the proposal to consider after certain action has been taken might create misunderstanding with the French claiming a commitment to accept. Another reason is that the acquisition of rights which already are our due should not be linked with any other promise or concession on our part. If our diplomatic officers are unable to obtain these rights simply

because our treaties assure them and without other inducement, this inability should govern future decisions. This course, although only a slight modification of what your department proposes, would remove all urgency from the problem and give ample time for full objective consideration of the whole Moroccan policy as related to the many long-range considerations that are fundamentally involved.

I sincerely hope that your decision may be modified to the extent requested above, but if it cannot, I shall appreciate the opportunity of going over the matter again personally with Mr. Gross before final action is taken. 

I have cabled Casablanca and shall write you again suggesting points for consideration in requesting action by protectorate officials, and shall appreciate an opportunity of conferring with your personnel assigned to work out the details. 

Yours sincerely,

ROBERT E. RODES, President, American Trade Association of Morocco.

AMERICAN TRADE ASSOCIATION OF MOROCCO, 

Casablanca, September 27, 1984.

The UNITED STATES CONSUL GENERAL, Casablanca. 

DEAR SIR: When I was in Tangier, Mr. Plitt informed me that the chief of the diplomatic cabinet of the protectorate had accepted the principle that Americans could not be required to pay a usage tax (French taxe de consommation) in excess of that accepted by the State Department.

I stated in the course of the conversation that this and most other violations of our treaties were part of a definite anti-American policy practiced by the director of finance of the protectorate.

On returning to Casablanca, I am informed that, despite the decision of the chief of the diplomatic cabinet, the director of finance refuses to order reimbursement of the funds illegally collected. 

I revert to the statement and recommendation made to Mr. Plitt: That representations be made to the protectorate pointing out the many treaty violations and other illegal acts for which the present director of finance is responsible and requesting the replacement of this official by one who is more law abiding and more friendly to the United States and its nationals. 

The practice of combating each act after its commission is unsatisfactory. 

It has proved time consuming for both your staff and the members of this organization. It has had little effect in obtaining redress in the individual cases that arise and no effect of preventing the recurrence of similar cases. It is believed that this last flaunting of our rights, as admitted by the diplomatic cabinet, constitutes an excellent opportunity for an energetic attempt to eliminate the consistent source of most of our controversies. 

Yours very truly,

AMERICAN TRADE ASSOCIATION OF MOROCCO, ROBERT E. RODES, President. 

FEBRUARY 9, 1949. 

The UNITED STATES CONSUL GENERAL, Casablanca. 

DEAR SIR: A circular published by Morocco Post No. 1, American Legion, dated

January 14, 1949, and signed by me mentioned certain illegal anti-American practices by the French Protectorate of Morocco and recommended certain counteraction by the United States. This pamphlet was held up for 4 days by 

French censorship and a copy or copies were circulated among protectorate authorities.

One of the acts the circular complained of was "requiring Americans to pay custom charges that are as high as 500 percent in excess of legal rates." It also referred to the faking of Moroccan trade balance statistics and cited a case where "scrap tires costing $48 a ton were valued by customs 100,000 francs a ton." 

My next shipment of tires was appraised at 200,000 francs a ton, double the amount charged for identical tires in December 1948. The obvious reason for this 100 percent increase is reprisal for our having called the attention of the American public to the bitter anti-American campaign in Morocco. This is in keeping with the policy of baiting Americans that has been brought to your attention so frequently. 

In addition, I am ordered to pay a "consumption" tax that is 533 percent of the legal rate, an increase that your letter of July 15 assured me I was "in no way obliged to pay."

I have refused to pay these charges and am transmitting herewith customs declaration No. 402985 and all pertinent documents. You are requested to require that this shipment be cleared at legal rates and at the same time to make a general arrangement for reimbursement of all similar overcharges which have been paid by me under protest.

Yours very truly,

ROBERT E. RODES.

Mr. JAMES MOOSE, Africa Division, Department of State, 35 WEST SIXTY-FIFTH STREET,
