New State Building,  

DEAR MR. MOOSE: Further to our conversation about treaty abuses in Morocco.

Coffee, sugar, and tea.-The Department has admitted (Mr. Gross' letter of 

July 29 to Senator Saltonstall) that portions of these cargoes have been seized.

Since treaties fix duties at 12½ percent those seizures are patently illegal despite any amount of sympathy from proregimentation elements in our Government. 

Some of the amounts seized since June 15 have been returned. This, in itself, is a confession of the illegality of the confiscations. On the other hand, as you will see from the attached copy of a letter from the Essex Parcel Co. to the protectorate, exceptions are being made in some cases.

There is also attached a file of correspondence showing that Pierre Norel, an American veteran, not only is being required to turn over half of his sugar to the government, but to obtain a firm order, for the government, from a syndicate member, before his license is granted. This is rank discrimination and constitutes a new abuse begun since your department accepted the decree against 

American trade.

A prerequisite to further discussions of our rights in Morocco should be the ending of these abuses and the reimbursement of all seizures, since their inception in the fall of 1947.

Taxes and Customs.-It still seems logical that your Department should refuse further negotiation with the Protectorate of Morocco until all overcharges are returned. We have repeatedly been told that steps were being taken to obtain these reimbursements, since all of the overcharges are the result of unilateral action in violation of law and custom and usage of 40 years' standing. This action, begun in July 1947 was not possible as long as you kept a strong officer, of appropriate grade, in the consulate general. 

After a year of frustrating note writing and "representations" the consul general wrote me, on July 16, 1948: "Regarding the question of import duties, you undoubtedly now that this office, the Legation in Tangier, and the consulate in Rabat, have made the most energetic representations to the protectorate authorities. The whole matter is now before the Department of State." 

The most flagrant cases are "consumption taxes" that the consulate general advised us we were "in no way obliged to pay." The chief of the protectorate's diplomatic cabinet agreed with our Chargé d'Affaires that they were illegal. 

The finance director refused to be governed by his decision. Please refer to the Casablanca consulate's Note No. 35 of July 21, 1948, your answer, and the consulate's Note No. 40 of October 5, 1948. 

I note that Mr. Gross now writes about "discriminatory valuation." This, of course, should be eliminated and prior charges refunded. However, Moroccan duties are fixed by the General Act of Morocco, signed by the United States and France, at 12½ percent of the c. i. f. value. All charges above this amount are illegal and certainly should be reimbursed before further concessions are considered. This applies to overvaluation, discriminatory valuation, unilaterally established appraisal, rules, seizures in kind, and "consumption taxes." 68307-50-pt, 2- -21

While awaiting State Department action, I am asking that taxes claimed from Americans by the Minister of Finance be offset against charges protested by the consulate general.

Thanking you for the consideration you are giving this, I remain 

Yours sincerely,

ROBERT EMMET RODES. 

EXHIBIT D RECOMMENDED TERMS FOR NEGOTIATION RELATIVE TO CONCESSIONS REQUESTED BY FRENCH OFFICIALS IN MOROCCO 

1. As a prerequisite to all further negotiation: (a) The Moroccan Government will confirm that: (1) Treaties between the United States and Morocco remain in full force as they were ratified by the Senate and appropriate Moroccan authority; (2) Legitimate questions as to the interpretation of terms will be resolved by accepting the interpretation that prevailed in June 1939; (3) All deviations from the terms of the treaties as they are written and were understood in June 1939 are the result of written temporary voluntary concessions by the United States, or are illegal ; (4) The temporary concessions may be withdrawn at any time, and such withdrawal shall invalidate immediately all legislation or regulations based on the concessions; (5) The United States is the final judge as to the intent and interpretation of its voluntary concessions; (6) The United States cannot be expected to continue concessions that give additional power over its citizens to persons who have abused the power they already hold, who have been guilty of illegal acts against its citizens, or who have given proof of anti-American bias; (7) United States aid or credits will not be administered or distributed in a manner that will give persons competing with United States citizens a competitive advantage they would not enjoy had not the aid or credits been granted; (8) In general, concessions made to help France or the Allied cause during the war or postwar emergency will not be used to lessen American rights in Morocco or for other purposes not compatible with the spirit in which they were granted. 

(b) The Moroccan Government will: 

(1) Promulgate, rescind, or amend decrees and regulations so that those remaining in force will be consistent with paragraph (a) (3); (2) Take necessary steps to implement other subparagraphs of paragraph (a); (3) Refund taxes and customs duties collected from United States citizens pursuant to decrees or regulations inconsistent with (a) (3), and already protested by the Department of State; (4) Take appropriate measures for liquidating all legitimate claims of United States citizens for seizures and losses inconsistent with (a) (3). 

2. When the foregoing has been accomplished, negotiations will be resumed, along the following lines: (a) Minor changes in laws and regulations, not inconsistent with treaty terms, may be accepted after full hearings; (b) Such acceptance will reserve the United States citizens' right to court review, and will not be cited as defense by Moroccan authorities in suits challenging their legality; (c) Relinquishment, alteration, or waiver of treaty rights may be accomplished only by renegotiation of the treaty' in question, with advice and consent of the Senate.

A JOINT STATEMENT BY MOROCCO POST No. 1, AMERICAN LEGION, AND AMERICAN TRADE ASSOCIATION OF MOROCCO (By Robert E. Rodes, Hotel Willard, ) 

From 1836 until 1949, United States products could enter Morocco without restriction because of "open door" and most-favored-nation guaranties in treaties with Morocco ratified in 1836, 1880, and 1906. The last two were signed also

by France. In addition to assuring unrestricted commerce with Morocco they prohibited the latter from levying more than 12½ percent import duty, and limited taxes.

In July 1947, French officials began to disregard tax and custom provisions of treaties. Monopolies that came into power during the Vichy regime and others, established with more recent political support, have been strengthened and enriched, especially since ECA funds were placed at the disposal of the finance director.

In December 1948, the French finance director of Morocco passed a decree prohibiting most imports from the United States and drastically limiting those still permitted. He stated as one purpose the ending of competition by foreigners with Frenchmen. Americans in business in Morocco warned the Department of State of an apparent intention to make exceptions under the decree in pursuit of this purpose.

The governor general, the entire elected assembly of Morocco, the press and both French and Moorish chambers of commerce protested this decree as a backward step in their progress toward normalcy. 

The United States Department of State, at the insistence of American citizens, also protested it as a violation of our treaties although it expressed a sympathetic attitude toward the restrictions as a move to help Morocco conserve dollars. In spite of protests, the decree was enforced unilaterally and American goods were seized and held for 5 months. 

The Department agreed on March 24 that it would consider acceptance of the decree only after release of American goods, reimbursement of customs duties, and taxes collected in excess of treaty provisions, and the ending of all discrimination against Americans. It also would observe French performance during a trial period before considering acceptance of the decree, to assure the foregoing rather than to be guided by French promises.

On May 23 the illegally held merchandise was released. None of the other promised remedies were obtained. Nevertheless, the decree was accepted on 

June 10 for a period of 3 months. The Department's excuse for its defeat was "heavy French pressure."

Representatives of Americans in Morocco have given proof that illegal exceptions to the decree are being made as they predicted and are increasing drains on French dollars, also that discrimination against Americans continues. Several have already been forced out of business. Nevertheless, the acceptance by the 

State Department was extended until October 10, 1949. 

This means that independent Americans in Morocco have been prevented from engaging in their normal, treaty-guaranteed businesses for more than 9 months of 1949. Five months of this period was because of unilateral action by Moroccan authorities. The remainder has been with State Department acquiescence.

EXHIBIT F STATEMENT MADE BY MR. THORP AT MOROCCAN TRADE PROBLEMS MEETING, SEP- TEMBER 27, 1949, 4 P. M. ROOM 5106, NEW STATE BUILDING, WASHINGTON 25, D. C. 

This meeting has been called to discuss the outlines of a proposed modus vivendi for United States commercial operations in Morocco, during a period of French economic difficulties. It has not been called to discuss legal or policy issues associated with the Moroccan problem, such as the status of United States treaty rights in Morocco or the French protectorate or French law. It is proposed that the United States give its assent to Moroccan import regulations, substantially within the framework of the June 4 Rabat memorandum, as modified by United States-French discussions held in August and September. The form of the assent has in no way been finalized by either the United States or French Governments and this meeting has been called precisely for the purpose of receiving your comment and criticism of some of the proposals being considered by the Governments at the present time. 

In determining whether or not the United States shall give its assent to the draft understanding, a certain degree of compromise is obviously necessary because some of the important United States interests in the Moroccan problem are in conflict with each other. I think you are familiar with the dilemma. On the one hand, we are making substantial efforts to assist in the recovery program of France and other democratic nations of western Europe. This requires a harboring of resources and a screening of the use of foreign exchange for purposes most in harmony with European recovery. On the other hand, it is the duty of the American Government to protect and maintain important American interests in Morocco, to give American importers the protection to which they are appropriately entitled under the circumstances, and to afford to Americans an opportunity to participate equitably in the controlled-imports program.

EXHIBIT H EXCERPTS FROM AN ARTICLE BY EDWIN BORCHARD (HOTCHKISS PROFESSOR OF LAW, YALE LAW SCHOOL) ENTITLED "TREATIES AND EXECUTIVE AGREEMENTS—A REPLY" (54 YALE LAW JOURNAL, P. 616 AT P. FEJ (1944–45)) 

The United States enjoyed extraterritorial rights in Morocco under a treaty of 1836. France gradually took over the administration of the country and asked the United States to adhere to an agreement between France and Germany of 1910. The Department of State replied that— 

660 * * as the adherence of this Government to such an agreement would seem to imply the modification of certain of its existing treaty rights, the consent to such adherence on the part of the United States involves the conjoint action of the treaty-making powers of this Government; and our acceptance of the agreement in question could therefore be made only by and with the advice and consent of the Senate" (Foreign Relations, 1911, at p. 622).

EXCERPTS FROM HACKWORTH'S DIGEST OF INTERNATIONAL LAW, VOLUME I, CHAPTED II, PAGES 89-90 

On January 2, 1917, Secretary Lansing, in an informal note to the French Ambassador, reverted to the latter's notes of July 31, August 26, and October 3, 1916, regarding the recognition of the French protectorate in Morocco and said he had reached the conclusion that, owing to the pressure of business before the United States Senate, which would have to approve any treaty between the two countries on the subject, and in view of the desire of the French Government that the United States should take prompt action regarding the Moroccan situation, the best mode of procedure would be to consider separately the "question of the recognition of the protectorate and the question of our capitulatory and other rights in Morocco, as * * * [had] been done * * * by all the European powers in respect to their relations to Morocco." He stated that he was prepared to recognize in a formal note the French protectorate and to recommend concurrently that the item of salary for the American Minister in Morocco in the appropriation bill then pending in the Congress be changed to an item of salary for a "diplomat agent" in that country. He added that there would remain for later negotiation "the question of our capitulatory and other rights in Morocco, which could be taken up in due time."

On January 15, 1917, Secretary Lansing addressed a note to Ambassador Jus serand, stating that the Government of the United States formally recognized "the establishment of the French protectorate over the French zone of the Sheriffian Empire." In reply, the Ambassador in a note, of January 19, 1917, while expressing his appreciation of the recognition of the French protectorate in Morocco, pointed out that the protectorate established by France and Morocco under the terms of the treaty of March 1912 covered "the whole of that country"

and that every power, Spain included, had recognized that the French protectorate was "coextensive with the total area of Morocco." Subsequently, on October 

20, 1917, the Secretary of State addressed another note to the French Ambassador, informing him of the decision of the United States to recognize, and of its formal recognition of, the "protectorate of France over Morocco subject to the special rights and privileges of Spain in Morocco" and subject to his informal note to the Ambassador of January 2. Hon. J. HARDIN PETERSON, EXHIBIT I FEBRUARY 22, 1950. 

Chairman, House Public Lands Committee, New House Office Building, 

MY DEAR MR. PETERSON: A virtual monopoly is being established in France's lead supply. This is possible because potential competition from independent 

Americans was illegally stifled for 3 years, and because of ECA subsidies. Important United States interests, severe critics of United States aid to domestic mining, arranged and will profit from the subsidies. 

Treaties with Morocco, in full force, state: "(United States merchants) may buy and sell all sorts of merchandise but such as are prohibited to the other Christian nations" and "whatever indulgence, in trade or otherwise, shall be granted to any of the Christian powers, the citizens of the United States shall be equally entitled to them" (1). In spite of this, lead and manganese may be freely exported to France, not to the United States. 

Last June 23 I told the Appropriations Committee that independent Americans in Morocco, prospecting with their own funds, "resent the announcement that 800,000,000 francs of ECA counterpart funds have been given to a company of French politicians to enlarge their control of mineral resources in North Africa" and that "if we could export minerals, as guaranteed by our treaties, their development financing would be simple" (2): if I get Moroccan manganese, the United States gets it. If the French with their ECA backing beat me to it you may be sure that we are going to pay through the nose for it, if the United States gets it at all (3). I also testified: "I have a perfect right, under our treaties, to take lead mining machinery into Morocco, to export lead whenever I please and pay for my machinery with the proceeds. I am not allowed to do this" (4).

The attached Wall Street Journal clipping tells that Mines de Zellidja (a Paris company which already has received ECA counterpart funds for exploratory work) will receive $3,600,000 of ECA financing which will permit it to produce more than 70 percent of France's lead requirements. This Government financing was arranged by Newmont Mining Corp. who, together with its affiliate, St. 

Joseph Lead Co., owns 9 percent of the French concern.

Repayment will be with lead and zinc exports for our stock pile, which should receive them anyway under our arrangement to receive strategic materials paid for with counterpart funds.

An ironical sidelight on the foregoing is that in Senate floor debates on legislation which would have made the above situation impossible, independent Americans who will not put a plugged nickel into anything they can't control lock, stock, and barrel were accused of "acting as a front for French and Moroccan citizens" (5). Newmont and St. Joseph, whose Moroccan activities are 91 percent 

French owned, were listed among those described as "old line * * * American concerns doing business there (in Morocco) for a long while * * who are not complaining" (6).

Those of us who ask only the United States support to which we are entitled by the Constitution, could write our own tickets for five times 9 percent if we were not opposed by tradition and principle to being highjacked out of control of our enterprises. We resent it when our foreign competitors obtain monopolies through United States Government financing, arranged by giving a standing operation procedure to American intermediaries.

To climax it all, St. Joseph Lead who shares the standing operation procedure has circularized our legislators to the effect that public financial aid to domestic mining operations is against United States principles and economically unjustified.

A copy of a letter to the Department of State on this subject is attached. It has not been answered. 

Yours sincerely, (1) I Malloy, page 1212.

ROBERT EMMET RODES, President, American Trade Association of Morocco.

[From the Wall Street Journal, Washington Bureau] ECA TO ADVANCE FUNDS TO MOROCCAN FIRM FOR ZINC, LEAD DEVELOPMENT WASHINGTON.-The Economic Cooperation Administration announced the signing of a contract to aid the development of deposits of lead and zinc to meet French requirements for these scarce materials and to increase the United States Government's stock pile. 

Under the contract which was signed with Newmont Mining Corp. with headquarters in New York City, for the Moroccan firm, ECA will advance $3,600,000 in Marshall-plan funds to this corporation for the modernization and expansion of mines owned by the Societe des Mines de Zellidja, located at Boubeker, French Morocco. The American company is affiliated with and acting as an agent for the Zellidja firm. Newmont, in association with St. Joseph Lead Co., has a direct interest of 9 percent in the Moroccan firm. 

The ECA funds will be repaid over a period of 7 years in the form of supplies of lead and zinc for the United States stock pile. The money will be used to purchase equipment in the United States. 

After the development program is completed, it is expected the mine's annual production of 85,000 and 120,000 tons of lead and zinc concentrates, respectively, will supply more than 70 percent of France's future lead requirements and about half of her needs for zinc. This expansion will help France become self-sufficient in these two metals. The mine is now producing 20,000 tons of lead concentrates annually and its production of zinc, scheduled to start this year, is expected to reach 32,000 tons of concentrates next year.

STATEMENT OF L. DAN JONES, ATTORNEY, REPRESENTING THE INDEPENDENT PETROLEUM ASSOCIATION OF AMERICA 

Mr. JONES. Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee my name is L. Dan Jones. I am attorney for the Independent Petroleum Association of America, which is a national trade association whose members are engaged in various phases of the oil and gas industry in the United States, but our principal and primary interest is in the production of crude oil and natural gas.

Before I get into my prepared statement, I would like to make it clear that we do not appear here to comment on the ECA program in its over-all aspects, because we have not had the opportunity or occasion to follow the purposes of the over-all program or its results. We therefore could not offer any intelligent criticism or commendation as far as that goes, as to the over-all effects of the program. We have, however, endeavored to follow closely and to the best of our ability, the oil aspect of the program, and have endeavored to evaluate the effects and results of the ECA oil program. We think that after 2 years' experience we have before us certain facts that are extremely important which this committee and the Congress should have in mind in extending the program. 

Our purpose is to lay before you these few facts, which we think are salient and extremely important. 567

My comments, therefore, with respect to the extension of the ECA program will be confined to the petroleum phase of that program. 

At the outset, I wish to make one point clear. We are not here for the purpose of seeking for the domestic oil industry a greater share of the ECA oil program. We are here for the sole purpose of pointing out a situation which has developed in foreign oil areas, with the aid and contribution of the ECA, that is causing great injury to the oil industry here at home. Greater and more serious injury is threatened. 

Our association strongly feels that the oil program of the ECA has been detrimental to the domestic oil industry. I would like to introduce a resolution on this matter adopted by our association in October 

1949 if I may.

Chairman KEE. Without objection, the resolution will appear in the record at this point. 

(The resolution referred to is as follows:) RESOLUTION ON THE ECA PROGRAM 

Adopted at the annual meeting of the Independent Petroleum Association of 

America, at Fort Worth, Tex., October 3-4, 1949

The Independent Petroleum Association of America, heretofore has endorsed the basic objective of the ECA program for the economic recovery and political stability of war-torn areas. Developments to date show that the administration of the program as to oil already has gone beyond these basic objectives. Information as to the future plans makes it increasingly clear that the program threatens to make serious inroads upon the domestic petroleum industry. 

At the time the ECA program was first being considered by the Congress this association warned that the program might result in the use of public funds to the competitive advantage of a few private concerns. 

After a year's experience under the program this association asked the Congress to recognize that the program was having the effects which we had previously feared and was in effect subsidizing, with the American taxpayers' money, a few private concerns thereby permitting them to dump surplus foreign oil into the American market. The extent of this subsidization recently was evidenced by a refund of ECA funds by one company amounting to nearly $1,000,000 on a $4,000,000 transaction.

Information on future ECA plans indicates a huge expansion by the use of ECA funds of oil producing and refining facilities by both foreign interests and American companies. Such an expansion obviously would extend far beyond the essential oil needs of the nations concerned. The results would be subsidizing a large surplus of foreign oil that would seek a market in the United States, which is already adequately supplied by domestic oil. 

It is one thing to provide essential oil requirements for recovery in foreign areas. It is another and entirely different thing to establish by subsidy an unnecessarily expanded source of competition in the world oil market under the control of forms of government and types of enterprise inconsistent with our own: Now, therefore, be it

Resolved by the membership of the Independent Petroleum Association of 

America in annual meeting in Fort Worth, Tex., October 3-4, 1949, That we oppose the use of taxpayers' money for petroleum and petroleum facilities under the ECA's program beyond the minimum requirement contemplated in the basic objectives of that program; that we specifically oppose the use of public funds to the immediate and direct competitive advantage of a few large world-wide concerns, both American and foreign. 

Mr. JONES. When the ECA program was initiated in 1948 we expressed certain fears. We believe that the developments have demonstrated that our fears in this respect were justified. If our conclusions are correct as to the detrimental effects of the program on the oil industry within the United States, then they are matters of grave concern to this committee and the Congress because our national economy and national security are at stake.

Oil is one of the most essential commodities in terms of both our security and our national welfare. Two world wars have demonstrated its importance to our national security. In World War II more than half of all the supplies that were shipped overseas were oil products. The importance of oil to our domestic economy may be indicated by the fact that the value of oil and gas production is about equal to the combined value of all the coal, iron, copper, gold, silver, and all the other metals and nonmetals produced in this country. In 

20 States oil and gas are among the first 3 mineral resources. 

Oil is also a vitally important and very substantial factor in the ECA program. It is the largest single item in the dollar budget of the participating countries. Information made public by the ECA shows that for the first 21 months of operations of the program, the period ending December 31, 1949, the ECA had authorized for crude oil and petroleum products a total of $775,200,000. This, I believe, is more than 10 percent of total ECA authorizations for all commodities. 

Mr. EATON. Is that for American oil only?

Mr. JONES. No; that is for oil, no matter where it is purchased, and ECA information shows that more than two-thirds of that oil came from foreign areas and less than one-third from the United States.

Our principal objection to the ECA program as it has been administered is that it has operated to develop a condition in foreign areas that now threatens to destroy the ability of the domestic oil industry to meet its responsibility of providing this Nation with sufficient oil at all times. The ECA program has had the effect of abetting and encouraging the development of a world surplus of oil. It is generally recognized that today there is a world surplus. ECA and other 

Government officials recently have stated that this is the case. This surplus, at an alarming rate, is displacing the American industry and American labor. It is retiring an essential element of our economyvital in peacetime as well as in war. This condition has been brought about by various programs and policies of our Federal Government that have fostered and encouraged foreign development. It has been a process of several years duration. The results have become rapidly evident since World War II. The ECA is one of the current programs serving this end. Mr. JONES. The EČA has "subsidized" these seven companies. It has subsidized them with the American taxpayer's money. The result. has been that these seven companies now have a large surplus production capacity in the foreign areas which is exerting strong pressures, both politically and economically, in seeking a market outlet. 

It has already taken over a substantial part of the domestic oil industry's export market. Exports of United States oil, including all of the domestic industry's ECA share, have decreased sharply during 1948 and 1949. In addition, there has been a rapid and steady increase in imports into the United States of this foreign surplus. As this foreign oil invades the home market it displaces the domestic industry thereby hampering the domestic industry's activies and sapping its strength.

The extent of the "subsidy" that the ECA program has provided these seven companies is indicated by the share of the total ECA oil program which has been enjoyed by these companies and their subsidiaries. The other subsidies to which I have referred, I have quoted the word "subsidy," as you have noticed, since they are of the character of a subsidy.

In the case of Anglo-Iranian it looks to me like a direct subsidy. 

Chairman KEE. Would you characterize any purchase of oil from any company, say, from your independent companies, as a subsidy? 

Mr. JONES. I would not like to; no, sir. In the case of purchases from the domestic industry, though, Mr. Chairman, I believe there is a distinct difference. Any oil coming from the United States has market outlets, it has no trouble about getting dollars for its products. 

These companies operating in the Middle East and Venezuala must receive dollars for their oil because they are American companies and are operated on a dollar basis. The only way they can get dollars from the European market is for the United States to lay those dollars down over in the European countries so that the participating countries may purchase the oil with dollars.

Chairman KEE. I do not mean to push the question, Mr. Jones, at this point, but it does seem to me that if it is a subsidy in one instance, it is bound to be a subsidy in another. 

Mr. JONES. The ECA is providing dollars to the participating countries which are not available unless the United States taxpayers provide those dollars. Now, in the case of the domestic industry in its normal markets, the taxpayer is not involved. The domestic industry's participation in the ECA program, as I have pointed out, so far as exports go, is on a declining basis. In addition the production in these foreign areas would have no market outlets or would have very limited market outlets, in the absence of the ECA program. The ECĂ not only provides them dollars, but it provides them a market.

51 Chairman KEE. They would have to pay your companies dollars too, would they not?

Mr. JONES. If we participated in the program; yes, sir. 

Mr. VORYS. How would you suggest that this oil, purchased in September 1949, should have been purchased? Where should it have been bought, from whom, and who should have paid for it? 

Mr. JONES. The point I am trying to make is that a large portion of the entire ECA oil program is being funnelled into it is ending up in the hands of seven large concerns substantially interested in foreign production. A large portion of the entire ECA fund is ending up in these foreign areas and is stimulating the production and encouraging the production in these foreign areas. That production in turn, which has now become something on a surplus status, is threatening, we think, very dangerously, our home markets here in the United States, and that is our concern. 

Mr. BURLESON. May I make an observation at this point?

Chairman KEE. I would prefer postponing further examination of the witness until we get to the questioning period. You may make memoranda of what you wish to ask the witness and we will get to it much sooner than we will otherwise. 

Mr. JONES. On the basis that this month, September, is representative of the participation of these six countries in the ECA program to date, of the total of $775,000,000 authorization as of December 31, 1949, these companies would receive almost $700,000,000. 

A further measure of the extent of the subsidization of these companies may be determined from ECA Release No. 737, dated Washington, July 25, 1949, in which it was revealed that the Caltex Oil Co. made a refund of almost $1,000,000 on a single transaction involving an amount slightly more than $4,000,000. The release stated that this refund represented a price reduction on products shipped to the United Kingdom in 1948 and that the refund was voluntary. The refund was approximately 25 percent of the total amount. This would indicate that there was a serious overcharge initially. 

The above shows the extent of participation of these few companies in the ECA financing of purchases of crude oil and petroleum products. In addition, these companies have also enjoyed a high percent of the total ECA dollars provided for refinery expansions within the participating countries. The effects of the existing world surplus of oil upon the domestic industry already have been drastic. Serious injury has been suffered. 

This foreign surplus of oil has been an important factor in the following changes in the operation of the domestic petroleum industry: 

1. Oil production: Domestic production, according to Government statistics, averaged 5,380,000 barrels daily during the last half of 1949. 

This was a reduction of 10.3 percent as compared with the same period in 1948. 

2. Producing capacity: Domestic capacity under sound conservation practices averaged 6,380,000 barrels daily during the last half of 1949, according to authoritative estimates by industry experts. This represents an increase of 6.3 percent over 1948 productive capacity. 

3. "Shut-in" production: The difference between capacity and actual production shows that the domestic industry was "shut-in" by an amount averaging 1,000,000 barrels per day or 17 percent during the last 6 months of 1949. I might say that oil imports are what we are concerned with and it is the ECA contribution to imports that we are principally concerned with, and endeavoring to present to this committee. 

4. Oil imports: Imports of foreign oil during the last quarter of 

1949 averaged 766,000 barrels daily according to Government statistics. This compared with an average of 513,000 barrels daily during 

1948 and an average of about 150,000 barrels daily during the prewar period, 1935-39. The increase in 1949 over that of 1948 was most rapid.

I might say that we have just obtained the statistics for the month of January of this year, and the average during January was 885,000 barrels a day. You will see that is a still further very sharp increase over any other previous high mark. 

5. Oil exports: Exports of oil during the last quarter of 1949 averaged 289,000 barrels daily as compared with an average for the year 1948 of 369,000 barrels daily. The current rate is substantially below the prewar 1935-39 rate of 447,000 barrels daily and the 1947 rate of 

451,000 barrels daily.

You will note there again that oil exports from this country, including the ECA share that the domestic industry has enjoyed, have been on the decline and the domestic industry is actually caught in between a two-way vise, you might say, the export market which we are losing and at the same time the foreign production is invading rapidly and drastically the home market for oil. 

Mr. EATON. By "home market" you mean the market within the 

United States? 

Mr. JONES. Yes. 

6. Oil producers' income: On January 1, 1950, the United States

Department of Interior reported that the total income of domestic crude-oil producers in 1949 was $507,000,000 less than in 1948. 

Mr. JUDD. How much was it in 1948?

Mr. JONES. I do not have the specific figures in mind, Mr. Judd, but I know the total income is somewhere in the neighborhood of $5,000,000,000 from oil. 

Mr. JUDD. Down 10 percent; something like that?

Mr. JONES. Something like that; yes.

I have endeavored there in those six points to set out what we think are evidences of injury suffered by the domestic industry. I would like to briefly refer to certain agencies and bodies in addition to ourselves who have recognized that the domestic industry is being seriously injured.

First is the National Petroleum Council, which is the official industry advisory group to the Government. It is set up under the Department of the Interior. They recently submitted a report on this subject and one of the findings out of that report I would just like to read. 

The sharp increase of imports of crude oil and its products coupled with a continuing decline of exports of crude oil and its products has hurt the domestic oil industry.

There is also a similar advisory group set up for the coal industry, which is designated as the "National Bituminous Coal Advisory Council," which is also the official advisory group set up under the Department of the Interior. The coal industry has recently become alarmed over the invasion of the United States fuel markets by this foreign oil and they have a committee, this Council has a committee, that is now studying that problem and the committee recently submitted a report which shows that they are concerned. 

One thing they pointed out in their report is that in 1949, as compared to 1948, a study of a group of 26 utility plants in the New England States and the Middle Atlantic States shows how coal consumption in those large industrial plants has been displaced by imported residual fuel oil, which is industrial oil. It shows, comparing the month of September 1949 with September 1948, that the coal consumption in those plants went down from 973,000 to 442,000 tons; whereas oil consumption in those plants went up from 431,000 to over 

2,000,000 barrels, a fivefold increase.

Mr. VORYS. Did they mention whether ECA or John Lewis had the most to do with that?

Mr. JONES. I do not believe they charged ECA with all of that. 

In their report they made this observation, and I quote: 

Oil imports now make for an excess oil supply and still are on the increase. 

Their impact has been seriously felt within only a matter of a single year. 

They are speaking of the impact upon coal, there. 

Also, as I am sure this committee knows, the House Small Business Committtee has had a subcommittee studying the oil-import situation and on January 5, Congressman Keogh of New York, who is chairman of that subcommittee, issued a release in which he made this statement, which I would like to read into the record: 

The independent segment of the domestic industry cannot stand further invasion of domestic markets by imported oils since the import situation has now reached, if not passed, dangerous levels. 

Also, on January 26, Congressman Patman, who is chairman of the full House Small Business Committee, sent a report on the import problem to the President and in his letter to the President-the letter is dated January 26-he states as follows: 

It is my earnest recommendation that you take appropriate action under the provisions in the escape clauses in our respective trade agreements. This recommended action contemplates establishment by order or proclamation of restrictive quantity quotas on petroleum imports which will make sure imports supplement but do not supplant domestic production. 63307-50-pt. 2- -22

I mention that just to show the concern over this problem of imports is recognized by others than our own group. 

Decreased oil activity in the United States and reduced income from oil production affect American labor, Federal- and State-tax revenues, the prosperity of hundreds of communities in oil-producing areas, and the income and general welfare of the Nation. The experience of the industry proves conclusively that a loss in income means decreased drilling activity and a lessened ability to maintain producing capacity to meet national oil requirements. As this takes place, the 

Nation shifts its dependence for oil supplies from thousands of domestic producers to foreign oil controlled by a few large oil concerns operating on a world-wide basis. 

The dangers involved in our becoming dependent on foreign oil controlled by a few companies is evident from an incident recently reported in a daily oil publication. The item concerned a transaction between the Armed Services Petroleum Purchasing Agency and the California-Texas Oil Co. The company had a 5-year contract to supply the Navy special fuel oil at a price of $1 a barrel. When the Navy obtained an offer from another company at a lower price the Caltex Co. renegotiated its contract and agreed to furnish the oil at about 67 cents per barrel. If this is the treatment that these companies give the 

Government of the United States it is quite obvious that the individual consumer of the United States, if dependent upon foreign oil for a supply, would be entirely at the mercy of these few companies. This, it is our opinion, clearly demonstrates the inadvisability and unsoundness of our Government pursuing a policy that would lead the American consumer and our military to become dependent upon a foreign supply of oil controlled by a few companies rather than being dependent upon the domestic industry composed of thousands of individuals competing in the supply of the domestic market. 

In conclusion I wish to refer to section 112 of the Economic Cooperation Act, which provides as follows: (b) The procurement of petroleum and petroleum products under this title shall, to the maximum extent practicable, be made from petroleum sources outside the United States; and, in furnishing commodities under the provisions of this title, the Administrator shall take fully into account the present and anticipated world shortage of petroleum and its products and the consequent undesirability of expansion in petroleum-consuming equipment where the use of alternate fuels or other sources of power is practicable. 

The basis for this provision-a world shortage of petroleum-does not exist. The provision is entirely unrealistic. In our appearance before your committee last year we took the position that there was no shortage of petroleum and that, therefore, the provision should be eliminated. The fact that there is no world shortage of petroleum, but to the contrary a surplus, is more evident today than at that time. 

The provision, therefore, should be eliminated. 

That concludes my statement, Mr. Chairman.

Many oil companies participate in the ECA program.

Mr. JONES. Yes. Our main objection is not that it happens to be six companies or any particular company, but the result is that a large amount of the taxpayers' money is being used to stimulate production, unnecessarily, we think, in the Middle East and in other principal producing areas. It so happens that six companies are the principal beneficiaries of that. 

Mr. RICHARDS. Can those companies deliver oil in the ECA area at a cheaper price than they can buy it from independent producers of oil? 

Mr. JONES. Do you mean, Could ECA obtain it more cheaply from there? 

Mr. RICHARDS. Yes.

Mr. JONES. I think ECA purchases are all on a world-wide competitive basis. It is not the cost of production that governs the price they pay, but it is the competition that sets it, and therefore the competition that it meets over there in the participating countries is what sets the price.

Mr. RICHARDS. You do not mean to tell me that they cannot furnish 

France, for instance, oil from the Mediterranean area more cheaply than an independent in the United States could furnish it, do you? 

Mr. JONES. As I understand it, the ECA program has not endeavored to force the companies supplying the oil, say from the Middle East, to supply it more cheaply than the United States oil, but they determine what is competitive over there and they say the price must be this competitive price. Now, they can go lower, but I think the majority of the oil is sold on that competitive price that is set, and, of course, the American industry is a very important factor in setting the competitive price world-wide.

Mr. RICHARDS. I am just trying to get the information. I know very often big business concerns fix prices all over the world. However, here we are trying to bring about the recovery of Europe, and if they need oil, we are going to provide dollar exchange to get it. 

As you say, they could not sell it there unless they can get dollar exchange, and the only way to get dollar exchange is through these funds. 

Mr. JONES. Yes, sir.

Mr. RICHARDS. Well, if they have to have it, then I think we should get it at the most reasonable price, taking into consideration world conditions, whether you buy it from a big oil company or from an independent. That is my point. Certainly it seems to me there would be an advantage from the standpoint of finance to buy it from the 

Mediterranean area. 

Mr. JONES. The ECA law has a provision in it which sets a ceiling on prices and that provision, I think, roughly, is this: That no ECĂ price can be higher than the price of American oil, plus the transportation cost to deliver it in the participating country. That is the ceiling, you see.

Mr. RICHARDS. That is correct, but it does not set a floor. 

Mr. JONES. No, sir; it does not set a floor. It is a ceiling. That is the only provision of the law which is a directive to the ECA insofar as price of oil is concerned, as I understand it. 

Mr. RICHARDS. How much of this $700,000,000 worth of oil could the independent producers of America furnish at a comparable price? 

Mr. JONES. The domestic industry, of course, could not supply all that oil. At the outset I endeavored to point out that we are not here urging that we should even have a greater share than we have today in the ECA program. Although our export market is going down, it is not our purpose in appearing here before the committee that we ought to have a greater participation in the ECA program. 

Our concern is the ultimate effect that the creation of this excess world producing capacity is going to have on our own markets here. We fear it is going to move in here and take over the home market. It is the home market we are worried about and not the ECA market. 

Chairman KEE. Will you take the chair, Mr. Richards?

Mr. EATON. The gist of your statement is that the ECA in its oil policy has injured the interests of the American producers that you represent? 

Mr. JONES. Yes, sir; that is correct. 

Mr. EATON. How would you cure that disease?

Mr. JONES. That is, of course, a difficult one to answer. I tried to point out here what we think are important facts which are before us now after 2 years' experience with the ECA program-principally that the program has served to create this world production capacity in the foreign areas that is now threatening our home industry, here, which is essential to us in peacetime as well as in wartime. 

Just how you cure it, of course, is a difficult one and I certainly would not have any specific answer to offer the committee, but it is a difficut one and probably one that is solely for the Congress to answer. 

Mr. EATON. The gist of your objection, apparently, is that if this policy goes on, it will eventually make it possible for the American consumer to get oil cheaper than they are getting it now?

Mr. JONES. We fear it will have exactly the opposite effect, sir, if we become dependent upon a handful of companies for our source of supply in foreign areas, that the consumer in the end will be worse off than he is today. Today our consumer is protected by active competition from many companies within the United States. 

Mr. EATON. Your argument is that the foreign producers have an advantage over our producers and you want to have our producers have those same advantages? (No response.) 

Mr. EATON. That is like John Rockefeller when he got a rebate of a dollar a barrel on oil, a competitor came to him and said, "I object to these here rebates and draw-backs when I ain't in it.”

Mr. JONES. As I say, it is our thought that, if you want to call it this, our selfish interest in this case happens to parallel the national interest and particularly the national interest from a military-security point of view. If we become dependent upon a few companies who produce oil in foreign areas-say the Middle East, which is thousands of miles away by way of water transportation which can easily be cut off in time of emergency-we think that would be placing the consumer here in this country in an unfavorable position and it would be endangering our country from a national-security point of view. 

Mr. EATON. Then one of your contentions is that the policy of the 

ECA is to develop the foreign producers in such fashion that in a case of war, for instance, we would be under disadvantage in our home production?

Mr. JONES. I would not say it has been their policy to do what we have complained of, but their program has had that effect. I don't think they have done it deliberately with that in mind as their objective but it has had that effect.

STATEMENT OF HENRY HAZLITT, CONTRIBUTING EDITOR OF NEWSWEEK MAGAZINE Mr. HAZLITT. My name is Henry Hazlitt. I am contributing editor of Newsweek magazine and author of its business column. I am the author of Will Dollars Save the World?, an analysis of the Marshall plan_published in 1947, a condensed version of which appeared in the January 1948 issue of the Reader's Digest. I had the honor and privilege of appearing before this committee on January 27, 1948, to testify when the European recovery program was first being proposed. 

At that time there was a severe food shortage in Europe for which I, among others, recommended that special provision be made. This abnormal food shortage has now ceased to exist. At that time, also, a serious situation was brought about by the pegging of European exchange rates at highly fictitious valuations. These fictitious valuations, I then pointed out, increased Europe's trade deficit and socalled dollars shortage by stimulating European imports and discouraging or preventing European exports. The fictitious valuations have now been in great part corrected. 

But basically the situation has not greatly changed. I emphasized in my testimony in January 1948 that the decisive factor in European recovery in the following 4 years would not be the amount of American. governmental aid, but the economic and political policies adopted by the governments of Europe themselves. This has been true in the last 

2 years, and it will be true in the next two. Some European governments-we may especially mention Belgium and Italy-have made some reforms in the direction needed-that is, away from bilateralism and controlism and toward multilateral trade and free enterprise. 

But in general this progress has been very small. 

It is an economic and political scandal, for example, that practically every nation in Europe-and in fact nearly every nation in the world should still retain, more than 4 years after the end of the war, the totalitarian device of exchange control. This device was first introduced to the world by Soviet Russia and Hitler Germany. With exchange control usually goes the whole network of import prohibitions, licenses, quotas, bilateralism, drawing rights, multiple currencies, currency inconvertibility, allocations of raw materials, government planning, price fixing, profit fixing, and wage fixing that together constitute complete economic regimentation, kill incentives, and strangle recovery and production.

The sad fact is that our Government foreign-aid program has had exactly the opposite effect of the one its supporters hoped for. It has slowed down the pace of economic recovery instead of increasing it. It has set back economic freedom instead of promoting it.

I 

Let us imagine, for example, that the Marshall plan had never been devised or put into effect. Europeans would still have had a great need for American capital. They could have got it only by applying for private loans. And they could have got these only by restoring the confidence of American private investors. 

It is not difficult to specify the reforms Europeans would have had to make to inspire such confidence: 

1. They would have had to assure anybody who put money into 

Europe that he could get it out again. This means that they would have had to make their own currencies freely convertible into dollars. 

They could have done this simply by dismantling their wartime exchange control. 

2. They would have had to assure foreigners holding pounds, francs, or lire that these currencies would not depreciate. This means that they would have had to halt monetary inflation. To do this they would have had to return to balanced budgets. 

3. To return to balanced budgets European governments would have had to give up nationalization, which has meant huge deficits in the nationalized industries. They would have had to reduce to manageable dimensions food subsidies and overgrown relief and socialsecurity programs. 

4. They would have had to stop threatening still further nationalization, expropriation, and seizure. 

5. They would have had to relax or abandon controls over wages, prices, interest rates, and profits. 

6. They would have had to reduce excessive taxation. 

If Europe had been obliged to attract private capital, such reforms would already have gone much further than they have. They would have brought not only far more production, but the freer and more balanced trade, the currency convertibility, the multilateralism, and the integration for which our ECA officials have made futile exhortations. 

The reason for their futility is clear. As long as foreign governments can pick up easy money from our own Government they don't have to make these reforms. 

As a result European recovery has not only been slow and precarious, but the recovery that has taken place has been in the wrong direction. Production indexes have gone up; but the added production is not primarily for export, as it should be, but for home consumption. So foreign trade is still unbalanced; Europe's trade deficit continues, and its self-induced dollar shortage remains. 

The dilemma of the Marshall plan, the dilemma of every government-to-government "loan" or gift, is plain. If our Government imposes no conditions on its hand-out, the money is worse than wasted. 

If it does impose conditions, they provoke foreign resentment. 

Our ECA officials vacillate between the horns of this dilemma. 

First they say that they won't interfere in the internal affairs of these countries. Then, of course, the European governments getting our aid make in return practically none of the economic reforms so desperately needed. The British bureaucrats repay us by discriminating against American motion pictures and American oil companies. 

The French repay us by threatening the sale of Coca-Cola. Then our ECA officials talk of "getting tough." But when it comes to a show-down they dare not risk the international resentment that would 63307-50-pt. 2--23

follow their insistence on reforms that would be really effective. 

So we end by subsidizing foreign-government discrimination against our own industries.

Government "loan" and gift programs like the Marshall plan, to repeat, do not speed up world recovery; they slow it down. We are subsidizing and prolonging statism and socialism abroad, and imperiling our own free-enterprise system to do it. 

But I have not come before this distinguished committee to advocate immediate termination of the Marshall plan. I recognize that such testimony would in any case have been quite futile. I have made the preceding remarks chiefly because I wish to make clear my own conviction that, on purely economic grounds, it would do no harm to terminate ERP when the present appropriation expires on June 30. 

But economic grounds are not the only considerations we must take into account. Unfortunately, though there was not the slightest good reason for our doing so, we made an implied promise to continue our Marshall aid for at least 4 years. We would only bring on recriminations and charges of bad faith if we were to terminate it now. 

On the other hand, even the ECA now talks of terminating aid in 1952 and of cutting next year's appropriation by some 22 percent below that for the current year. But if ERP is to run for only 2 years more, the logical way to taper off would be to cut the appropriation by one-third now and by a second third for the following year. 

The appropriation for the current fiscal year was $3,778,000,000. This should be cut to, say, $2,520,000,000 for the 1951 fiscal year and to $1,260,000,000 for 1952.

To cut the appropriation by only 25 percent or less now would either imply at least a 3 years' continuance or require European governments to make a disproportionate adjustment at the end of the second year. It seems more reasonable to reduce Marshall aid by $1,260,000,000 in each of the next 3 years than to cut it by only $828,- 000,000 now and by, say, a similar amount in the following year, and by the remaining $2,122,000,000 in the third year.

I may say parenthetically at this point that the figures I have cited above may not correspond exactly with the figures before the committee. I am going on the assumption that the proposed authorization of $2,950,000,000 for ERP for the next fiscal year is to be compared with an appropriation of $3,778,000,000 for the current fiscal year. 

I have not had an opportunity to determine whether in all items these two figures are exactly comparable with each other. But I trust the foregoing figures will do for illustrative purposes. 

The point I am making is that if we seriously plan to terminate the ERP program even in 1952 we should begin to do it right now by equal, proportional cuts each year, instead of cutting too little now and leaving a disproportionately large cut to be made at the termination of the program. For if Congress adopts this latter course, then when 1952 comes around it is sure to be told that it is asking Europe to make too drastic an adjustment in a single year. Great pressure will then be put upon Congress to make still another so-called "transitional" appropriation.

If Congress decides to taper off Marshall aid in the simple, equal, proportionate way that I have just suggested, it should obviously act as soon as possible. I think it is also important that it should author-

ize now the appropriation both for 1951 and for 1952. The purpose of acting ahead of time in this way would be to give European governments plenty of advance notice concerning how much they could expect to receive from us. This would enable them to make their plans accordingly. And it would also forestall what would otherwise be constant propaganda for larger and continuing aid. 

The truth is that the amount set for ERP aid has always been an entirely arbitrary figure. There is no way in which a figure of socalled European needs or of a so-called excess here above our own needs can be objectively or scientifically determined. The amount fixed has been arbitrary from the beginning. To recognize this frankly would lead to enormous administrative simplification. Congress could simply direct that the reduced total sums it appropriated should be divided among the individual governments in the same ratio as in the current year. This would take from ECA officials a burden of decision that should never have been placed upon them. 

In fact, the whole ECA bureaucracy was unnecessary from the first. 

The elaborate ritual of "counterpart funds" and other such special earmarked accounts is meaningless as a real control. It merely serves to confuse both Europeans and ourselves. All Congress need do is to authorize the Secretary of the Treasury to pay checks at regular intervals to the Ambassadors of the recipient European governments. 

The ineffective but much-resented interferences of the ECA in the economic policies of these governments would halt. These governments would probably still have as strong an incentive to reform as present ECA pressure provides. It would be the definite knowledge that the aid was coming to an end. 

Such a plan would be far superior to the proposed new payments union for Europe. This union would be merely one more futile effort to do what the existing International Monetary Fund is already supposed and has failed-to do. It would actually apply "incentives in reverse" by giving the most to the countries that succeeded in getting themselves the biggest trade deficits.

I may say at this point that I think the payments union has other very serious objections to it upon which I might elaborate later if any of the members of the committee are interested. 

Simply to give checks to the European governments, without conditions, would be at least the simplest plan that we could adopt. It would be least likely to be misunderstood. On purely political grounds it is probably also the best plan open to us, because it would give no ground whatever for the criticism that we were trying to interfere in the "internal" affairs of the governments concerned. 

For purposes of identification I shall call this plan A. 

But this brings us back to our original dilemma, which is inherent in all government-to-government "loans" and grants. By not putting any conditions on our loans we avoid the charge of interference or domination; but we are unlikely to get the reforms in Europe necessary to make our aid effective. Certainly we are unlikely to get the reforms necessary to give our aid its maximum effectiveness. 

Congress may quite properly prefer to insist on economic and financial reforms in Europe in exchange for our aid. In that case the best plan would still be to abolish the ECA bureaucracy and turn our future aid program over to the Export-Import Bank.

I should perhaps say a word here as to the reasons why it is important to abolish the ECA bureaucracy that has been set up to administer our European aid program. The first reason is, of course, that of immediate economy. Obviously we should not have on the pay roll any officeholders that are not needed. If the distribution of ECA funds can be carried on without such officeholders, it ought to be. 

The second reason is that Congress should not leave to bureaucratic discretion the conditions and policies that it is Congress' own function and duty to prescribe. And this, I think, is the most important reason.

The present extremely wide range of administrative discretion for ECA officials has several disadvantages. For these officials then proceed to announce from time to time, in the name of Congress, policies which are not only dubious in themselves, but may not at all represent the policies that the majority of Congress would approve. 

Mr. Paul Hoffman, for example, has quite properly objected to the practice in Europe of what is called "double pricing" of coal and other commodities. But this is only a minor evil, affecting a comparative handful of commodities. The continuance of exchange control, on the other hand, is a major evil. It is almost the keystone of the European control system which prevents the restoration of freedom of trade and the balancing of such trade. It affects not one or two prices, but every import price and every export price whatever. 

Yet Mr. Hoffman seems to be relatively unconcerned about the continuance of exchange control, and assumes that continuance in all his own plans. This applies, for example, to his proposed "payments union," an institution of very dubious value. Everything that it proposes to do could be far better done by the simple abolition of exchange control. Again we are surprised to find ECA officials urging 

Italy toward the expropriation of land, or insisting that Germany impose more controls on its economy and move toward a controlled economy instead of toward a free one. I think all these policies dubious, and I think it still more doubtful that Congress would approve each of them if it were brought to a vote. 

But even when ECA officials insist on European policies of which Congress would approve, the mere fact that the power of such officials is merely discretionary, and known both by themselves and by European governments to be so, makes these powers ineffective. Mr. Hoffman may try to say, for example, that he is not going to give the British Government any more Marshall-aid funds as long as it discriminates against American oil; but the British officials may feel that Mr. Hoffman would not dare to take the personal responsibility for withholding such funds, and they may therefore ignore this request of his as they have others. Again, all ECA officials want to be persona grata with the foreign governments with which they are dealing; if they are stationed in any country they want to be liked there, and they are afraid to get tough and take the personal onus of withholding funds. 

Another disadvantage of this system of administrative discretion. is that it can so easily become discriminatory, or be thought discriminatory. Some foreign governments doubtless feel that they are being asked to make greater reforms or sacrifices to get American aid than are other foreign governments.

Finally, a weakness of the ECA bureaucracy is a weakness common to all bureaucracies. Many of the people who hold an office under

the ECA want to continue in that office. Many of the officials of the 

ECA, therefore, tend to become propagandists for the prolongation or perpetuation of the Marshall plan. Their testimony in favor of continuing this plan, and in favor of appropriations of a given magnitude, cannot always be regarded as wholly objective. 

I should perhaps say at this point that my recommendation that we eliminate unnecessary officeholders is not meant as a reflection upon either the competence or motives of any individual official. Many of the officials of ECA are men of unusual ability and are acting from the highest patriotic motives. I merely suggesting the elimination of the ECA for general organization and policy reasons. 

I wish to return now to what I should like to identify as plan B, which would be to abolish the ECA bureaucracy and turn our future European aid program over to the Export-Import Bank. I have no reason for preferring the Export-Import Bank bureaucracy to the ECA bureaucracy; but the Export-Import Bank already exists; it is capable of handling this program along with the work it already does; and to turn the program over to it would simply eliminate unnecessary duplication of organizations and officeholders. 

Under plan B the Export-Import Bank should be authorized to make loans guaranteed by European governments-not made to them but guaranteed by them-that conformed to half a dozen simple but mandatory_requirements of eligibility unequivocally laid down by 

Congress. For example: 

1. No loan should be made directly to any government, but only to some specific productive enterprise, private or governmental. Each loan must be fully guaranteed, however, by the government of the borrowing country. 

2. If the loan is to a going enterprise, private or governmental, that enterprise must be currently operating at a profit. 

3. If the loan is made to start any new enterprise, that enterprise must be private. Native investors must supply equity capital equal to not less than, say, a third of the total capital. 

4. The guaranteeing government must itself be operating on a balanced or overbalanced budget. 

5. The borrowing country's volume of money and bank credit must at least not be growing faster than its physical volume of production. 

6. The borrowing country must at all times maintain free convertibility of its currency, if not by going on a gold or dollar basis, then at least by permitting free exchange rates.

The general purpose of these conditions of eligibility would be simply to put pressure on European governments to begin to make, before the expiration of the Marshall plan, the reforms that they would have to make after its expiration if they hoped to attract 

American private investments.

It may be objected to plan B that few European governments would be willing to make the reforms necessary to qualify as the guarantors for such loans. But as long as governments do not make these reforms, our aid to them is misdirected and wasted anyway. 

Congress might provide that if at the end of 6 months, say, any governments had not availed themselves of the loanable funds allotted to them, these funds could be made available instead, in the

already established ratios, to governments that did conform with the eligibility requirements.

Plans A and B are, of course, alternatives. They could not be in effect simultaneously. But Congress could, if it wished, put plan A into effect for, say 6 months or a year to give European governments plenty of time to adopt the reforms necessary to make themselves eligible as guarantors for loans from the United States under plan B. 

For example: Congress might take the amount of appropriations suggested by the ECA for the full fiscal year 1951, cut it in half, and authorize the ECA to continue to distribute these funds until December 31 of this year. Its legislation might then provide that on January 

1 of 1951 the Export-Import Bank would take over, and be authorized not to distribute gifts, but to make loans under the conditions of eligibility Congress had laid down. This would give the European governments until the end of this year to make themselves eligible as guarantors for Export-Import Bank loans to projects in their countries.

At this point I cannot avoid commenting upon the extraordinary testimony of Mr. Hoffman before this committee on February 24, in which he actually declared that it would be "an immoral act" for Congress to extend Marshall aid to Europe in the form of repayable loans. He went on to say that 

It will take 50 years for Europe to come back to where she can buy and pay for what they need from us and service already existing loans. 

Now this is the exact reverse of what we were told when the Marshall plan was first proposed. Then we were told that the Marshall plan was not for "relief" but for "reconstruction" and "recovery."

The supporters of the Marshall plan at that time frequently compared Europe to a factory that had the building and the available manpower, but needed loans from us to enable it to put the machinery in repair, and pay the wages and buy the raw materials to get started. 

Now if this analogy had been a true one, then, just as the factory could easily have paid off the loans from the proceeds of the sales of what it manufactured, with a profit left over, so Europe could have paid off these Government loans if those loans had actually been sound. 

In fact, if this analogy had been a true one, what really would be immoral would be to have the owners of this factory borrow money to buy raw materials, turn these raw materials into finished goods, sell the finished goods at a profit, either at home or abroad, and then not repay the loan at all out of the proceeds, but continue to receive raw materials as gifts while they were paid in full for the finished product.

What Mr. Hoffman is saying now is, in effect, that our Marshall aid is in fact mere relief, a mere dole, that it is not sound from a business point of view, because Europe is not in fact currently producing the goods out of which it could and should repay the loans. 

He is saying, in effect, that Europe is on an American dole now, and he is implying that it will continue to be on an American dole for at least 50 years more. I can put no other interpretation than this on 

Mr. Hoffman's contention that Europe ought not to get sound repayable loans instead of continued hand-outs in the form of gifts. 

Finally, I should like to suggest what I shall call plan Č. I am putting this idea forward merely for consideration. There are a lot of

things to be said on both sides but I would like to submit it to this committee. This is not a third alternative; it could be combined with either A or B. Under plan C we would offer to forgive our entire loan of $3,750,000,000 to the British Government in lieu of further advances to that Government under ERP. As these advances do not promise to be more than about $1,250,000,000, in the next 2 years in any case, the British Government should be greatly tempted to avail itself of such a choice. It would be relieved of $3,750,000,000 in indebtedness, and it would improve its net position by some $2,250,- 000,000. From our standpoint, it would save us about $1,250,000,000 in further cash advances. And it would remove what will be otherwise a source of resentment and recrimination between Britain and America for many years. This is precisely the opposite of the original purpose of the loan. 

In conclusion, I wish to say this. Members of this committee could easily point out that there are inconsistencies not only between the various proposals I have just made, but between each of these proposals and certain general principles that I have put forward. I admit these inconsistencies; but they are inherent in the very nature of government-to-government "loans" and gifts. It has been said, for example, that to put conditions on our aid to Europe is both necessary and impossible. I agree with this paradox. Its existence is merely one of the reasons why some of us thought that the so-called European recovery program was ill-conceived in the first place. 

But we have the program, and we have the implied obligation to continue it. The problems that we face are these. How can we taper off this program in the way at once most economical for our own taxpayers and most likely to promote world recovery? How can we taper off the program in such a way that we really bring it to an end in 1952, without international recriminations and without making the shock of economic adjustment in 1953 too severe? 

It is toward the solution of these problems that I have ventured to place the foregoing proposals before your committee. That concludes my statement. 

Chairman KEE. Thank you very much Mr. Hazlitt. Your testimony is refreshing to this committee in at least one feature of it, and that is, it is different from all the other testimony we have heard in respect to the matter at issue and, in fact, is a contradiction of everything and of everybody we have had before us.

Mr. VORYS. Mr. Hazlitt, what you say is always stimulating and

We were told then that they would not have gone in in the past 2 years because they were afraid of Russia. A man who can lend someplace else is not going to lend in a possible battleground. Mr. HAZLITT. Congressman, you have raised many questions that I am tempted to answer. I would like to come back if I may to the first point you made and that was the question of prophecy. What you call my 1948 prophecy before this committee was not a prophecy but simply a conditional statement. What I said was: "Marshall plan or no Marshall plan, Europe will not recover as long as European governments retain the economic policies they have been following since the end of the war." Now they have improved their economic policies a little since then, and they have had a little recovery. What I am saying now is also not a prophecy but a conditional statement-that Europe will recover faster now if it has to attract private loans than if it gets more government hand-outs. Of course, such conditional statements can never be clearly proved or disproved by actual events, because there are always so many other factors and influences at work. 

However, I want to raise another point also with regard to the statement you make about production. The statistics of ÖEEC show that western Europe without Germany is producing about 35 percent more than in 1938. Now if that figure is correct it raises a very serious question. Why is it that with an increase of 35 percent in production, Europe today has a serious dollar shortage, so-called, and a serious trade deficit, certainly, and yet did not have a serious deficit in 1938, before it got its production up? This means that if the figures are correct Europe is producing the wrong things. In other words, it is doing exactly the opposite of what the plan was supposed to bring about, which was balanced trade. In other words, this increased production has not gone into straightening out the trade deficit but the trade deficit continues, and this is something that could not possibly have happened without a Marshall plan, because it is the money we give that makes the trade deficit possible. 

After all, trade always balances. It always has for the simple reason that people insist on getting paid for what they sell. And the only way Europe can have a trade deficit is by our Marshall plan aid-

that is to say by the money we give them. In other words, if we give the goods away then they can afford to take them. 

Now this is the situation that I think the Marshall plan has brought about. 

I would like to come back finally to your question, Congressman, that you asked me right at the end regarding what private investment would do because of the fear of Russia. Now there is no doubt that the fear of Russia is a very serious fear and there is no doubt that this is something outside of the control of the European governments. But 

I think that just as there has been some private investment, even with the policies that European governments are following, and even with the Russian threat, so there would be considerably more investment and I think very considerably more investment if these policies were changed-and I am simply talking about the internal and external economic policies. 

If you look at a nation like Norway, Norway has dollar bonds selling in this market and they are selling between 97 and 99. Now this indicates that in spite of the Russian threat—and the Russian threat is greater as against Norway, let us say, than it is as against England by a great deal-in spite of this threat American investors here seem to have a certain amount of confidence in Norwegian bonds. I think that if these countries remove the very serious penalties they are putting on our investments that there would be a considerable influx of private investment in spite of the Russian menace.

Mr. VORYS. Mr. HAZLITT. That must refer to the sterling balances held by India and Egypt and so on, plus the American loan. I do not know what the items are, of course, that he put in there, but those would be two very considerable items, and the two main items as I see it. You are talking about external debt.

Mr. VORYS. In this table the domestic debt of Britain is given as $64,960,000,000, and the foreign debt is $7,076,000,000, but I have a Department of Commerce statement that Britain owes us 7,552 million dollars, and I cannot figure that gross debt.
