Mr. HAZLITT. Of course, those figures refer to governmental debt. 

Now what I had suggested as a sort of transitional system would be loans by ERP to projects in those countries which would be, I would hope, dominantly private projects and they would only have government guaranties. As a protection to our own taxpayers that is, they would carry local government guaranties. But the soundness of each loan would depend upon the credit of the private project that is to say, whether or not the private project was a good one. 

I do not think you can take any definite figure and say whether you are "loaned up" at that figure or not. I do not think, for example, that the internal debts should be taken into consideration much when you are talking about external debts, because when you are talking about external debts the problem that you are talking about is the problem of the trade balance. The internal debt may of course affect the credit of the government but does not affect the trade balance problem, so I do not think the internal debts of these countries need be too seriously considered when you are talking about the trade problem.

Mr. VORYS. Now you mentioned Norway and it strikes me as a good answer to my question about fear of Russia.

Mr. HAZLITT. Yes. 

Mr. VORYS. Yet Norway seems to be a good risk for private investment.

I would be very happy if you could get us some figures that would help an ordinary Congressman to see whether this statement of Mr. 

Hoffman's is justified, that Europe is loaned up for 50 years. My own idea has been as expressed in the first bill, that 20 percent of it that year was loans and guaranties, pay-back money, out of the $5,000,000,000. I hoped that we could jump to 40 percent last year, 60 percent this year, 80 percent the next, and get Europe back on a basis of borrowing money for their needs and we would take our time about being paid back. I have been unable to get any figures this year to justify that position and these figures that are given me tend the other way, but do not give any indications on the private transactions at all. Could you get such figures that would be helpful to us?

Mr. HAZLITT. I could try. I have seen no over-all figures of Europe's external debt, either Government or private or segregated. 

Possibly the ECA has put together such figures, but I should doubt that they would in any way prove that Europe is loaned up. As to this whole question of lending up, I do not think you can take any particular figure and say it is an ultimate figure or an ultimate burden that cannot be exceeded. You will remember a lot of people said we could not stand an internal debt of more than $50,000,000,000 and now we have an internal debt of more than $250,000,000,000. What happens when countries have these big internal debts is that they repudiate them, not by failing to pay the debt but just by watering down their currency. This has been the way in which Europe paid off its First World War debts, generally speaking, by watering down the currency. You would have to calculate how much the currency

has been watered down to pay these debts and how much it was likely to be watered down in future, to know whether they were going to "pay off" the debt or not.

Mr. HAZLITT. It is because we are expected to make up their deficit that makes our own deficit larger, of course.

Chairman KEE. Mr. Smith.

Mr. SMITH. I think you have presented a very challenging statement. . Mrs. BOLTON. May I echo that, Mr. Hazlitt? 

- Mr. HAZLITT. Thank you. 

. Mr. SMITH. We have been listening pretty much to the same old story for a long time here with but very little on the dissent side and I am always apprehensive about ex parte hearings. 

I would like to ask you if, aside from the improvement in the productive processes in these countries that have been receiving our aid, there has been very much improvement in the dollar situation. Mr. HAZLITT. The dollar situation, of course, has improved somewhat, but here we come to a question in which a tremendous amount of confusion of thought exists. Even some of the English economists- 

Roy Harrod, for example-are beginning to say that the phrase "dollar shortage" is "one of the most absurd phrases ever coined." All of us around this table have a dollar shortage in one sense of the word, that we would like to consume more than we have the income to pay for. 

If someone gives us a present consisting of the thing we might otherwise buy, for instance à Cadillac, or what not, to that extent our dollar shortage is solved. But this whole dollar-shortage problem is an artificial problem brought about by exchange control itself. Now 

I do not want to go into the conditions which might conceivably have justified that in wartime, but the moment the war emergency passes there is no excuse for the continuation of exchange control, and exchange control prevents the recovery of private enterprise everywhere. A lot of people seem to think that exchange control involves nothing more than pegging the rates. But this is what is called a pegging operation and is a much milder operation than exchange control.

What exchange control does is this: If a British exporter sells, let us say, cars in this market, he earns dollars. Ordinarily, under a private-enterprise system, under a system of private property, under the system we think we exist under, he owns those dollars. But under exchange control, he does not own those dollars. He is compelled to turn them over to the British Government at an artificial or arbitrary rate fixed by that Government. Then the Government has those dollars. Then if this same exporter wants to import something for his own consumption, he has to go back to the exchange-control bureau which took over his dollars and try to get those dollars back-try to buy them back. And they say to him "No; 'we' haven't got enough dollars, 'we' have a dollar shortage, 'we' can't afford to give you this, 'we' are short," and so on. This collectivizes the whole idea of a nation's currency. It is just as if the United States were to declare tomorrow that all bank deposits had been seized because the Government feared a shortage of currency, but it would be given back to people at the same rates, if they could prove that they needed the goods that they wanted to buy. In other words, they could get their own money back if they could prove "necessity," and so on. 

This is what happens under an exchange-control system, and of course under such a system there is always a so-called shortage of dollars because the Government is deciding who is to get these dollars, and for what. But actually, if you did not have these European government controls there would be no dollar shortage whatever. Nobody

ever heard of a dollar shortage before the war. The phrase did not come into existence until Maynard Keynes started to use it. Now they have all got it. Every South American country has a dollar shortage, though they were not in the war at all. This dollar shortage is something that cannot be cured as long as you have exchange control. 

When a nation devalues-when England, for example, brings the rate of the pound closer to its real value, it tends to get, other things equal, less of a dollar shortage. But as the pound itself is not now a real currency, but only a sort of glorified ration coupon-you cannot use it to buy anything you want from wherever you want it-the pound falls in free markets even below the lower value the Government has officially put on it. 

This system creates the very problem it attempts to solve. Then 

European bureaucrats say "The American taxpayer has to make up for this dollar shortage that we have succeeded by our exchange controls in creating."

Mr. SMITH. It seems they are not only coming to us for the dollars, but we are now getting ourselves into the position through the rehabilitation of the economies of these countries where they are actually competing with American firms and the ECA and yet the State Department say: "We must have more imports. France must import more, Italy must import more, Britain must import more." 

Now that is in direct competition with our own people. And we are asked to pay it seems to me in two directions: one from the dollar standpoint and secondly again in actual competition with our own people in the domestic field. 

We are getting ourselves into an impossible situation because our people are beginning to complain, just as this oil man testified this morning about the oil industry in the United States. People out my way are complaining agriculturalwise. They are complaining about the cheese and the butter that is being imported. Well, we say Denmark has got to have dollars and some of these other dairy countries have got to have dollars. I am in a dilemma. I cannot rationalize my own thinking and come out anywhere on a reasonable basis. 

I just want to touch one more point and then I am through. 

Some reference was made this morning to this payment plan proposition. Now just what do you understand that to be? Do you have any comment to make?

Mr. HAZLITT. I think this is a very serious program that has not received anything like the scrutiny that it ought to have. This socalled payments union is in fact a proposal to have what you might call a Little International Monetary Fund. It proposes to do the same thing that the International Monetary Fund is already doing, but it proposes to limit this to the countries of Europe itself. Now I think the tendency of such a proposal, the tendency of such an institution, would be to make western Europe a sort of closed, soft-currency area, as against the rest of the world. It would encourage trade of the softcurrency countries with each other, rather than encourage them to sell more to the dollar areas. And I think that this is a very unfortunate proposal. I do not think that it is going to help to solve the problem at all; I think it is going to help to aggravate the problem of reaching multilateralism and freedom of trade. Its movement is in the opposite direction, it seems to me.

Mr. SMITH. That is all, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman KEE. Mr. Javits- 

Mr. JAVITS. I notice at the bottom of page 2 of your statement before you abandon the thesis that we should not have gone into the Marshall plan, you say the following:

The sad fact is that our Government foreign-aid program has had exactly the opposite effect of the one its supporters hope for. It has slowed down the pace of economic recovery instead of increasing it. It has set back economic freedom instead of promoting it.

Now I ask how you square that statement with the fact-and it is a fact that over-all production in the OEEC countries has risen, even including Germany which has been lagging behind the rest by about 20 percent over prewar; that export volume has increased from 60 percent of prewar in 1947 to 110 percent of prewar at the end of 1949, and that the Communist menace has been repelled—at least the active Communist menace has been repelled in France and probably in Italy-I do not see the reason for the dolorous statement in view of the obvious gains that the ECA has attained.

Mr. HAZLITT. This seems to me to be post-hoc-ergo-propter-hoc reasoning. What you seem to be saying is that everything that has happened for the good was because of the Marshall plan and everything to the contrary happened in spite of the Marshall plan. 

We have had recovery in production. The question is: Was that recovery in production because of the Marshall plan or in spite of the 

Marshall plan?

If you take a similar period after the First World War we did not have a Marshall plan but you will find we had substantial recovery in production in that same period.

This again brings us to the fact which I pointed out in my statement that the recovery which has taken place has been in the wrong direction. Why is it that in spite of a 35-percent increase in production, in industrial production, which would have been many times the size of the trade deficit in 1947, why is it that the trade deficit still continues? It means that they have been producing for the domestic market. It means they have not been making the production they should for the export market. There are two kinds of production they should have gone into-one the kind of production that reduces their needs for imports from us and second the kind of production that increases their exports. But European production has not taken that turn. 

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Hazlitt, I am not trying to debate the issue I just call attention to the sweeping assertion which seems to underlie your thinking on this program. Then you make a compromise and say to cut it down one-third at a time. 

Mr. HAZLITT. I would like to answer that, Mr. Javits. I have not retracted anything about my opinion of the Marshall plan. I have offered a compromise only because I know it is futile at this time to suggest the termination of the Marshall plan. In recommending a compromise, I say the compromise is better than going on the way it is proposed to go on. It is not that the compromise in itself is a very good thing.

Mr. JAVITS. In other words, you start on the premise and all your testimony is conditioned upon the premise that the Marshall plan was a mistake and that we should not have gone into it?

Mr. HAZLITT. That is right. 

Mr. JAVITS. Now you are trying to liquidate it the best way you can, is that right?

Mr. HAZLITT. That is correct. 

Mr. JAVITS. That is what I wanted to get very clear. 

Now as to the point you have made, I think it should be made clear of record-your testimony should not stand alone on that score, that the sources of raw materials for Europe, in the Far East and eastern Europe, and that the production of Europe itself, because of the war destruction, were very materially impaired if not dried up; that 

Europe had to look to the Western Hemisphere for raw materials, there was no other place to look; and that completely distorted the trade picture, both triangular trade and bilateral trade, and therefore the dollar shortage is not like our dollar shortage-my wife needs a fur coat and I haven't got the money-the dollar shortage exists because we are suffering from the distortion and the destruction which the war caused and which we tried to repair, at least in part through the ECA. I think it is only fair that the record show that. 

It is a fact that the sources of raw materials in the East Indies and in Malaya and the sources of timber and grain in eastern Europe were no longer available to western Europe. That cannot be argued away, that is a fact, and has had a determinative influence on the dollar gap. 

It is not just a question of bad regulation or exchange control. 

Mr. HAZLITT. It seems to me, Mr. Javits, that we cannot argue at the same time that Europe has had a tremendous industrial recovery and that it has not had an industrial recovery. If its production has actually increased 35 percent and if its trade gap remains, this must mean that this 35-percent increase in production is in the wrong things. 

It is not in the things that are balancing its trade. This is the point that I am making. In 1947, to cite a specific example, Britain's tradebalance deficit-including "invisible" items-was £630,000,000. In 

1949 Britain's national income had increased £1,275,000,000 over 1947. 

Now if that increase had gone into British export production or into reducing Britain's imports, either one, then you would have had a situation in which the trade deficit would have been more than wiped out by the increased production. But this has not happened, and it has not happened because under controls, production is diverted in these countries into the wrong lines, because the export trades are not given the incentives that they ought to have. 

Mr. JAVITS. Mr. Hazlitt, my time is up. I am not trying to whitewash the ECA countries but I would like to point out that you have just confirmed what I said because Europe could not have produced without the raw materials that came under the ECA, and as I said exactly that as being the basis for increased European production, the rationale for the Marshall plan is agreed to. You have a statement that they are producing now more than they did before but they are not producing the right things, I only point out that they are producing things they need to get exports because they are just climbing up the walls to get some dollars. But it seems to me the fundamental thing you agree to is that they could not have had this production unless they got the raw materials from somewhere and they got them through the Marshall plan. 

Mr. HAZLITT. That is right; and they got the raw materials before the Marshall plan also.

Mrs. BOLTON. In a different world.

TYPEWRITER MANUFACTURERS EXPORT ASSOCIATION STATEMENT 

We take this occasion to address your committee, which is now considering the extension of the European recovery program, for the purpose of bringing to your attention the irreparable damage that is being done to our industry and to other segments of American industry by the manner in which the ECA is carrying out that program. We do not believe that such damage is, or has been necessary, in order to achieve the objectives of the ERP program. 

This association is a so-called Webb-Pomerene group, formed for the purpose of promoting the export trade of its members. It has four members, Remington Rand, Inc.; Royal Typewriter Co., Inc.; L. C. Smith & Corona Typewriters, Inc.; and Underwood Corp.

During the 30 years prior to 1939 from 25 to 40 percent of the total American production of typewriters was exported, about half to ERP countries. In the last three prewar years, our exports to the ERP metropolitan areas, which took almost 50 percent of our total exports, amounted roughly to 116,000 machines per year. In 1947, prior to ECA, they amounted to 98,000; in 1948, to 56,000; and in 1949, to 32,000. By no means were all of these transactions financed by 

ECA; most were paid for with free dollars earned and allocated by the ERP countries for the purpose. ECA financed a portion-perhaps 10 to 15 percentof the 1947 and 1948 purchases by so-called reimbursement authorizations, but more recently requisitions for additional purchases have been almost entirely discouraged or refused.

This drastic reduction in typewriter exports is not attributable to a drop in the demand for American machines abroad. On the contrary, there is a large accumulated demand in ERP countries for American typewriters, and our foreign distributors have a substantial backlog of orders on hand which they are unable to fill. It results, rather, from the policy of the Economic Cooperation Administration that ECA dollars should not be used for the purchase of any goods or commodities that can be obtained from soft-currency countries. Since typewriters are being manufactured in Europe, ECA has taken the position that ECA dollars should not be used to finance the importation of typewriters from the United States. As a result, the ERP participating nations have allocated practically no funds for the purchase of American typewriters and have thus virtually excluded American machines from the European market.

At the same time, there has been a tremendous increase in typewriter production in Switzerland, Italy, Sweden, France, and the United Kingdom, as 610

compared with prewar levels. Some of this expansion was financed with ECA assistance. Taking advantage of the dollar shortage and ECA policy, European manufacturers have been quick to invade markets all over the world which the American industry had developed and held in the face of foreign competition for the last half century. Thus, soft-currency production has not been devoted to supplying only Europe's needs. 

It is our understanding that the administration of ECA has stated that ECA will not change its policy (not to use ECA dollars for goods which are obtainable within the ERP circle of countries) in the absence of a specific mandate from Congress to that effect. We now plead for such a mandate. 

Last year, appearing before the House and Senate Subcommittees on Appropriations, we urged an amendment to the ECA appropriation bill which would provide: "That none of such funds shall be made available to any country whose imports of necessary manufactured products have previously been obtained in substantial part from the United States, which does not permit a reasonable percentage of the imports of such products to come from the United States." 

At that time it was suggested that the matter could more appropriately be brought before the legislative committees, so we wish now to urge its consideration by the committee in the light of the facts here presented to you. 

There can be no underestimating the damage that has already been done to our export trade. Typewriter distribution abroad, as in this country, calls for efficient sales organizations backed up by service staffs competent to implement the service guaranties that accompany each machine. Over a period of 50 years and at great expense, the American typewriter industry has built up, trained, and maintained throughout the world distributing organizations which today represent an investment of millions of dollars. These distributors must, however, have something to distribute if they are to survive. Last year in our statement before the Appropriations Subcommittees we predicted that if the morbid condition of our exports were permitted to continue for any appreciable time we would lose "the men we have trained to sell and service American typewriters and in all likelihood they will have transferred their talents and allegiances to the service of foreign competitors."

Sad to relate, this prediction has commenced to come true. In some instances our distributors have abandoned their exclusive franchises with American exporters in order to undertake the distribution of machines of European manufacture. Other distributors have warned that they, too, will be forced to terminate their contracts unless they can receive some share of their normal imports to keep them going during the life of the European recovery program. 

The loss of these distribution channels and service agencies and the good will which they have built up for the American trade-marks over the years constitutes a death blow to the potential of our export trade. If a substantial portion of our foreign representatives find it impossible to exist on the starvation rations they have received over the past few years and become disaffected and go into the service of our competitors, the work of years will be undone. In such a case the restoration of free trading, in whatever form it eventually takes, will find us wholly incapable of taking advantage of the reopening of our traditional foreign markets, and faced with the time-consuming and costly task of trying to rebuild our distribution and service facilities and reconstitute our old markets in the face of far greater competition than we have ever had to meet before. It is doubtful, indeed, whether under these conditions the typewriter industry would ever be able to rebuild its export trade back to the traditional levels which are necessary in order to insure the full employment of its laboring force and the efficient utilization of its productive capacities. 

Because of the historically high ratio of export trade to total manufacture, perhaps the highest of any major United States industry, our case may be typical of relatively few American exporters, and probably ours is the most aggravated of all. That our situation is not unique can, however, be seen from the final declaration of the Thirty-sixth National Foreign Trade Convention, held last 

November, which stated: "The convention also reemphasizes the recommendation of the thirty-fifth convention that, pending the return to full competitive trading, American products be allowed to enter beneficiary countries in sufficient volume to permit the preservation of distribution channels, the maintenance of trade names, and the provision of sufficient spare parts and maintenance items to assure the continued satisfactory performance of American equipment." 

We heartily endorse the above statement. We cannot, and would not, condemn the increase in typewriter production on the Continent which the recovery

program has aided, but we do not believe that the basic philosophy of the Marshall plan anticipated that European industry should be stimulated by unnatural protection against the traditional competition of American manufacturers. We further believe that such extreme protection against American competition is, in the long run, as harmful for the protected industry as for its potential competitors in that it causes it to grow in an artificial climate, unprepared for the revival of free trade, which is, of course, the ultimate end to which the European recovery plan looks forward. It is probably not inappropriate to mention that the achievements of our industry have been made, since 1914, without benefit of any protection in the form of import duty. The United 

States has been a wide-open market, not until now seriously threatened by foreign typewriters.

We believe that the economic waste which will result in our industry if present policies remain unchanged should be abhorrent to a program which is dedicated to economic reconstruction. We believe that our request that Congress require 

ECA to allow us to keep open our traditional distribution channels so that we will not suffer the permanent loss of the export trade which constitutes such a significant proportion of our total business is consistent not only with the requirements of a sound domestic economy but also with the basic theory of European recovery which was to achieve some degree of equalization between the American and European economies by building the latter up to the high potential of the former and not to depress American industry to the low level to which its European counterpart had sunk. 

To that end, we urge the adoption of an amendment along the lines of our suggestion to the Appropriations Subcommittees last year, so that our trade channels may at least be kept open until the hoped-for day when free trading may once again be resumed in the markets of the world. 

Hon. JOHN KEE, JEWISH WAR VETERANS OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: We, the Jewish War Veterans of the United States of 

America, shall greatly appreciate the inclusion of this statement in the record of the hearings which your committee is holding on the Economic Cooperation 

Administration. 

At our anual encampment at Miami Beach, the following resolution was unanimously adopted:

Whereas the Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America has been a stanch supporter of the European recovery program and the Economic Cooperation Administration as the agency to carry out the European recovery program, and Whereas the results achieved by the Economic Coperation Administration Activities in the increased production, economic well-being and the consequent political stability of the participating countries, amply justify our continuing support of the Econome Cooperation Administration: Now, therefore, be it 

Resolved, That the Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America in convention assembled this 21st day of October 1949 support before the Congress, adequate appropriations to carry on the program of the Economic Cooperation Administration; and be it further 

Resolved, That our organization express its congratulations to the Honorable 

Paul G. Hoffman, Administrator of the Economic Cooperation Administration, for his leadership and effective work. 

That resolution was based upon my continuing observation and study of what the Economic Cooperation Administration has been doing since it was originally brought into existence. When your committee considered the original 

ECA bill, the Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America firmly believed that the ECA program would be successful in achieving its objectives and I was authorized to testify before your committee on behalf of the bill. 

Now that the ECA program is at the halfway mark, we feel that our confidence in the program and the confidence which your committee so tangibly demonstrated, has been fully justified by the achievement of ECA to date. 

Nevertheless, the full program originally contemplated, is only at the halfway point. Nothing in the record of ECA nor in the current world situation, justifies any slackening in the effort which our Government should continue to put forth through the ECA program. To make any serious cuts in the authoriza-

1 tions and appropriations requested by Administrator Hoffman, would, in our estimation, be a betrayal of the best interests of the United States and would shake the confidence of the whole world in our foreign policy. Only Russia and her satellites would benefit.

Those who think that cuts in ECA appropriations would spell a budget savings are doing wishful thinking. The weakening of western Europe which would inevitably follow the crippling of ECA, would simply burden us with the need for larger appropriations for the Department of Defense. Thus instead of a saving, we would have a loss. The strengthening of the economy of western Europe will be a continuing, profitable investment for us if we see the ECA program through to completion. 

All can agree that western Europe is one place where the progress of communism has not only been stopped but has been reversed. The despair, the unemployment, the fear, and the distress on which communism thrives, has been very considerably replaced by a degree of decency, dignity, and freedom of life which are the most effective bulwark against communism and the most potent weapons which democracies can use to fight communism. 

We respectfully urge, therefore, that Congress authorize and appropriate for ECA funds which the Administrator has requested for continuing the notable achievement which it has reported. 

Respectfully submitted.

REPORT ON EUROPEAN RECOVERY PROGRAM EARL BUNTING. 

As approved by the Board of Directors National Association of Manufacturers, October 26, 1949

As the European recovery program entered its second year and perhaps most crucial phase, the National Association of Manufacturers viewed it of the utmost importance to its own members and to American business in general to make a thorough appraisal of the programs made thus far and assess the prospects of achieving the ultimate purposes for which taxpayers of the United States have made such heavy sacrifices. 

Accordingly staff personnel and individual members have studied the recovery effort in many of the participating countries in Europe during the past sum- Their findings constitute a valuable guide to understanding the character and magnitude of the recovery problems still remaining and measures which appear to be necessary for their solution. mer. 

The NAM reaffirms its support for the European recovery program on the basis of the progress made thus far, and expresses its earnest hope that the European nations will achieve sufficient additional progress during the com-

ing year, in attacking their long-range problems, to enable the association to continue its support. 

The NAM expresses its desire to cooperate in the future, as it has in the past, with the Economic Cooperation Administration in its efforts to create a healthy, vigorous, competitive economy in western Europe.

The Economic Cooperation Act of 1948 declared its objectives to be "the restoration or maintenance in European countries of principles of individual liberty, free institutions, and genuine independence" resting "largely upon the establishment of sound economic conditions, stable international economic relationships and the achievement by the countries of Europe of a healthy economy independent of extraordinary outside assistance" calling for a plan of European recovery "based upon a strong production effort, the expansion of foreign trade, the creation and maintenance of internal financial stability, and the development of economic cooperation, including all possible steps to establish and maintain equitable rates of exchange and to bring about the progressive elimination of trade barriers."

Recipients put their signatures to agreements to adhere to the purposes of the program and to make adequate provision for attaining the objectives. 

The National Association of Manufacturers records its satisfaction with initial results achieved through ECA. With ECA aid, the peoples of western 

Europe have accelerated their recovery, normalized their production and transportation, and achieved a substantial degree of political stability in the western tradition.

Recognizing the importance of these accomplishments, the NAM notes nevertheless with concern and disappointment the growth of certain policies and trends in participating countries which threaten not only the success of the recovery program in those countries but the creation as well of permanent barriers to an expanding world trade.

In the light of these facts the NAM considers it necessary to condition its continued support of the recovery program and further congressional appropriations for this purpose upon the initiation of effective measures to carry out the original ECA principles and objectives. 

In embarking upon this program to aid the economic recovery of Europe, it was the intention of the Congress and the American people that European nations effect necessary internal and external adjustments in this period to enable them to become self-supporting partners in a world economic system based on liberal principles of trade and freely convertible currencies. 

It is apparent that the American public is viewing with increasing skepticism the fulfillment of those promises related to increased trade and stable international economic relationships as contrasted with reconstruction and restored production. There is particular concern as to whether further grants will prove warranted in the absence of a demonstrated determination to proceed immediately with measures necessary to the attainment of European economic cooperation and the expansion of international trade. 

In the knowledge that the interests of the ECA countries and the United States are closely interrelated; in the spirit of cooperation exemplified by the European recovery program as originally conceived; and in the hope that the recipients of aid will move rapidly and vigorously toward the fulfillment of the stated ERP purposes, the NAM commends to the consideration of all participating countries, including the United States, the following convictions: 

1. Future policies and operations of ECA and the participating countries should be based on the assumption that "extraordinary economic assistance" from the United States will be progressively reduced and finally terminated in 1952, or earlier to any recipient country which demonstrates an unwillingness or inability to cooperate in attaining original ECA objectives. 

2. Government, business and the people of all participating countries should recognize that the termination of this assistance requires major economic adjustments during the remainder of the recovery program if long-range solutions to their problems are to be found without a serious decline in their living standards. 

3. The participating countries may obtain substantial assistance in their further economic progress by establishing protection for foreign investment capital along lines stipulated in the NAM recommendations on the Bold New Plan-A 

Program for Underdeveloped Areas. 

4. ECA funds contributed by American taxpayers must not be regarded in the 

United States or abroad as subsidies for disposal of American surpluses whether industrial or agricultural in whatever degree, and efforts to direct the funds to such purposes should be firmly resisted.

5. As restored production shifts the emphasis to the importance of increasing and liberalizing trade, careful consideration should be accorded to the advisability of devoting ECA funds at least in part and at the proper time to purposes of currency stabilization loans rather than in the form of goods. 

6. European nations should take all necessary steps following revaluation of their currencies to maintain them in economically justifiable relationship to each other and to the dollar as indispensable to eventual complete convertibility and to the stimulation of trade within Europe itself and with all other countries. 

7. Bilateral trade must be recognized as being contrary to the stated objectives of ECA, and the economic policies of all participating countries should be directed henceforth toward the earliest possible restoration of multilateral trade as the only means by which proper economic health and adequate living standards can be achieved. 

8. Elimination of exchange controls and export and import licensing restrictions insofar as intra-European trade is concerned, and more rapid relaxation and elimination of such controls over trade between western Europe and other parts of the world must be recognized as prerequisites to the reestablishment of multilateral trade and he pursued with vigor and speed. 

9. Barriers which discourage tourist travel among countries also should be removed and additional measures taken to increase foreign exchange earnings from this source. 

10. European nations should recognize the necessity of reducing costs through increased productive efficiency and elimination of restrictive business practices in order to gain the benefits from full, fair, and free competition. They should place aggressive merchandising effort behind the sale of their products in all world markets in accordance with the principles of multilateralism rather than bilateralism. 

11. In many instances, budgets must be balanced at levels substantially below the present rate of expenditures, tax systems overhauled and tax collection practices made effective. 

12. The United States as the world's principal creditor nation must follow economic policies in keeping with this position and with the principles of competitive enterprise. This involves full recognition of the fact that exports of goods and services and return on foreign investment can only be paid for in kind. 

13. In the interest of greater efficiency and lower costs, further nationalization projects should be neither initiated nor continued during the period of "extraordinary economic assistance" from the United States, because NAM believes they will be detrimental to the European economy. 

The National Association of Manufacturers notes with the greatest of interest the initial relaxations of import restrictions and currency revaluation in Europe. These are important steps in the right direction. It urges the participants of ERP aid to hasten the removal of trade and travel barriers, the free convertibility of currencies, the elimination of quantitative trade restrictions, the abandonment of monopoly and cartel trade philosophy, and full adherence to the principles of expanded multilateral trade as the best hope for achieving "a healthy economy independent of extraordinary outside assistance." 

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT BY MAJ. HAMILTON LONG, 1702 NORTH LASALLE STREET, CHICAGO IN DEBATE BEFORE JUNIOR CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, CHICAGO, JANUARY 31, 1950, RE: "IS THE TRUMAN DOCTRINE-MARSHALL PLAN-ATLANTIC PACT PRO- GRAM SOUND?" SOME POINTS FOR THE NEGATIVE BY MAJOR LONG 

1. It's robbing the piggy-banks, the just heritage, of unborn generations of 

Americans, for whom we are trustees, by pouring endless billions of America's assets into the quicksand of Old World bankruptcy. 

2. It's sabotaging basic American principles and interests while pretending to safeguard them against evil communism and Kremlin despots. 

3. It's aping Hitler's slogan: "Save Europe from communism," in vain-because this can't be done with dollars or bombs and certainly not by our supporting bankrupt Socialist regimes whose socialism paves the way for complete, despotic socialism which is communism governmentally. 

4. It's causing our policy to overreach our power's limits, which is fatal. It ignores the horrible fact that the war made Russia all powerful in Eurasia-

able to seize Europe at will and to neutralize Britain and Japan with air weapons like the V-2; which we cannot remedy. 

5. It's building up Russia's war potential and gutting our own, robbing our national defense capacity, by building up Europe's armaments and industry for Russia's use in war; as in China. This is suicidal. 

6. It's paving the way for the planned scuttling of the priceless values of the 

American Revolution, of the New World dream, by fufilling the long-laid British plan to have America rejoin Britain politically. As planned by Churchill through 

Union Now, lately renamed Atlantic Union; including Britain's allies "the democ racies" to sweeten the pill. Union Now to United Nations to Union (?) Nix! 

The American reply! 

7. It's carrying out the wartime British plan to create a new empire-with 

America's billions. As proposed, in part, in Bevin's 1945 paper entitled: "Peoples, not pashas"-one source of the Point IV program-planning a vast colonial development in Africa and the Mid-East; which is their primary need for our billions, as Cripps admitted in 1947. Endless American billions to be poured into the 

British sinkhole for years to come, far beyond 1952. As planned when Roosevelt in wartime promised Churchill the initial postwar billions. When the fake 1946 loan, merely a gift, was put over. When in January 1947 Marshall and Bevin secretly agreed to put across the Marshall plan scheme, using aid-to-Europe as bait to get the American people to approve of more billions for Britain; on the false pretense that Britain would "integrate" with Europe economically; regarding which Britain is already welshing-as she welshed on various agreements since the war. Now that this false pretense has served her purpose, now that 

America is deeply enmeshed in her web under the Atlantic Pact Treaty, Britain is drawing away from Europe; demanding a separate, favored status about future 

American handouts of billions after 1952 when aid to Europe is supposed to end. 

All in typically British balance-of-power fashion; as Spaak, president of the 

Consultative Assembly of Europe, complained in a recent speech in Philadelphia. 

Just the way Britain double dealt with France in the thirties-helping Germany to rearm, partly against Russia of course. Devilishly clever but wickedly unscrupulous! 

8. It's heading America straight down the road to a Russo-American war, through our Atlantic pact military alliance with Britain and her allies in Europe; against Russia. This fulfills the long-laid British plan to use America's strength as a tool in their balance-of-power game in the Old World-now against Russia; in the old struggle between British imperialism and Russian imperialism, now blended with the world-rule aims of the Communist Kremlin despots. 

As planned by that peerless apostle of imperial impeccability, Churchill, in August 1941 when he had Roosevelt agree that British-American forces would police the postwar world; expecting the UN to be futile and to be used as a tool to this end. Bevin expressed approval in Parliament in November 1945; writing off the UN as completely useless. Churchill and Truman confirmed the deal publicly at Fulton, Mo., in March 1946. Yet in her usual double-dealing fashion, Britain now seeks to play off Russia and America against each other; using her West Europe and Commonwealth allies as part of her "bridge between 

East and West" as Pearson of Canada put it recently. Double dealing perfidious

Albion never changes; as other Continentals besides Spaak have begun to mutter aloud. Awake, America! 

9. It, in effect, makes America's strength the prop of British imperialism, they getting the profits and we the losses; which makes us the prize boob among nations and guilty of imperialism by proxy; indeed, of hooded imperialism, masquerading behind the false pretense of serving American principles, ideals, and interests which are being thus scuttled, desecrated. This guts the glorious New World dream of 1776, and America's true mission. America's bankruptcy in international affairs! 

10. The Kremlin is overjoyed with this British-American program for America; and fakes opposition thereto just to egg us on. The Communist chief tactic against America-"conquest through bankruptcy"-is thus working. Hence the 

1944 book of Earl Browder, then head American Kremlin agent, proposing a vast point IV program for America; quite like Truman's 1949 proposal-even alike in wording, strangely enough. The Kremlin's delight should be a warning for us, as trustees for posterity. 

11. For Americans to be on to the British and any other schemes to use 

America to their purposes is the minimum requirement of alert citizenship. 

It is not being anti anything but just soundly American.
